items.title: A Blue Wave Just Crashed on Trump
items.description: For nine months, on Nicollet Avenue in Minneapolis, there has been a makeshift memorial for Alex Pretti, the registered nurse who was shot and killed by federal agents while trying to shield a fellow-protester during last winter’s deportation campaign in the c
items.author: Benjamin Wallace-Wells
paragraphs: For nine months, on Nicollet Avenue in Minneapolis, there has been a makeshift memorial for Alex Pretti, the registered nurse who was shot and killed by federal agents while trying to shield a fellow-protester during last winter’s deportation campaign in the city. On Tuesday, after Minnesotans cast their ballots in the state’s Senate race, many of them pressed their “I voted” stickers onto a lamppost at the memorial, as if completing a picture. The gestures suggested something about this year’s midterm elections which, as the evening wore on, turned out to be true: that it was a mundane event that held unusual moral stakes.

During the two years since Donald Trump won reëlection, he has pushed the country toward a brink. Trump won only a narrow Presidential majority in 2024, and his party held a majority in each chamber of Congress by just a few seats. Even so, the President faced little institutional resistance as he pushed the federal government-eroding DOGE program, the senseless and costly tariffs, the authoritarian power of the crackdown on migrants, the feckless Iran war. He could pursue these goals because he had convinced most of his party, and many members of the public, that his victory over Kamala Harris meant that half of the country would irrevocably be on his side.

The results of the midterm votes are still rolling in. But the rejection of the President is undeniable and uncomplicated, and it reached deep into what had long been understood as conservative territory. His party has lost its Senate race in Ohio—and looks likely to lose in Michigan, where the post-industrial economy had long supplied the symbolic heart of Trumpism. It has lost in Texas, where Democrats had not won a statewide race in more than a hundred contests, stretching back to 1994, and in South Carolina. It has lost in Iowa and in Kansas, which has not seated a Democratic senator since the Great Depression. There are counties in southwestern Kansas where Trump won two years ago by about thirty-five points—Finney County, Seward County, Ford County—that, as the tallies accumulated in the state’s U.S. Senate race, were voting narrowly for the Democrat. For a decade, the country had become used to a fixed map—blue in the cities, deep red in the outlying areas. Now there is some instability around the edges.

One specific issue, or an especially weak Republican candidate, might make sense as an explanation in particular races. But the truth is that Trump’s past two years have offered voters a menu of reasons to turn away from him. In South Texas, it might have been the cruelty of the immigration raids; in Kansas, the effect of the Iran war on diesel and fertilizer prices; in South Carolina, an especially poorly chosen Republican candidate. In the course of the long Trump decade, many liberals had come to assume that conservatives were so devoted to the culture war that they were politically impervious to events. But this time, in such places, the news made it through. All of it mattered.

Somewhat suddenly, almost nothing in U.S. politics seems certain. The Democratic Party has lately been understood as an aging, defensive entity, with a nursing-home veneer. But this year’s campaigns have elevated a group of younger and newer Democrats (Jon Ossoff, in Georgia; James Talarico, in Texas; Abdul El-Sayed, in Michigan) who have found it quite natural to denounce the oligarchic and authoritarian elements of the status quo, and to separate themselves from some elements of the Party’s doctrine. The South, the most deeply conservative region in the country for nearly all of its history, suddenly has a purple hue. Is J. D. Vance still the presumptive next Presidential nominee? Will the Republican Party still pliably fall into line behind the man who lost in Texas?

And, though the Democrats have made astonishing breakthroughs, their near-term future is a little cloudy, too. The intraparty fight, between its insurgent, youthful left and the legacy party, a contest intense enough that at times it seemed to crowd out the whole rest of American politics, is still unresolved—both sides can claim vindication, and can point to new champions emerging from the midterms. The Party itself remains generally unpopular. Perhaps most important, with the liberal grassroots awaiting a Presidential primary to come, lower-wattage figures (Hakeem Jeffries, Chuck Schumer) are now in charge. For a political formation that might now have a claim on a majority, the Democrats remain curiously faceless.

Even so, one instance of clarity came around 11 P.M., as Fox News flashed the graphic predicting that the Democrats would win control of the House of Representatives: we are no longer in the shadow of 2024. In culture and in politics, conservatives had insisted that Trump’s victory in that election was the defining one, and that it reflected a culminating turn against “wokeness,” against internationalism, against modern ideas about gender or race—a more atavistic America was being unleashed. Trump called into Fox News just after midnight, sounding a little whimsical and discursive. “It’s just a point in time,” the President said. “There was a mood in the air, I guess.”

In a similar way, perhaps, the 2024 election, and the atmosphere it ushered in, now looks a bit more like an aberration, and the idea that it represented a historical pivot seems more like the wishful thinking of a few people who stood to benefit from it. The experience of the past two years has mattered—tallied, among other places, in the “I voted” stickers that climbed up the memorial in Minneapolis. Elon Musk spent nearly two hundred million dollars to keep Texas red, and the Republicans blew it. Of course, it looks like a slightly different Texas, this morning. It looks like a slightly different country. ♦

items.title: “Paper Tiger” Views Family as Deadweight
items.description: There are no ticking clocks or flipping calendar pages in James Gray’s new film, “Paper Tiger,” but it’s nonetheless a drama of time implacably passing. Call it a September song: the story opens on Labor Day in 1986, in Queens, at the home of the Pearl family.
items.author: Richard Brody
paragraphs: There are no ticking clocks or flipping calendar pages in James Gray’s new film, “Paper Tiger,” but it’s nonetheless a drama of time implacably passing. Call it a September song: the story opens on Labor Day in 1986, in Queens, at the home of the Pearl family. Early in the morning, the jovial, still youthful paterfamilias, Irwin (Miles Teller), has his power tools going in the narrow driveway beside the house, waking his sons—Scott (Gavin Goudey), who’s about to turn eighteen, and Ben (Roman Engel), maybe five years younger—on their last day of summer vacation. As Jerry Lewis’s annual telethon blares from a TV in the kitchen, Irwin and his wife, Hester (Scarlett Johansson), tell the boys that they’re all going to visit Hester’s mother, Iris (Cindy Katz), at a country club near her home, in the prosperous and largely Jewish Long Island suburb of Great Neck.

From this banal beginning, Gray launches a tale of fear and violence, criminal conspiracies and paranoia. That night, after the family gets back home, Irwin’s older brother, Gary (Adam Driver), arrives with princely pomp, bringing a takeout feast from the venerable steak house Peter Luger. A former high-ranking cop now earning a grand living as a security consultant—and basking in the admiration of his former N.Y.P.D. colleagues—Gary, who drives a Mercedes and is seemingly sewn into sharply tailored suits, is as dashing as Irwin is staid. The fancy meal is the prelude to a proposition: he wants Irwin, an environmental engineer, to team up with him as a co-consultant to the owners of a grossly polluted site on the Gowanus Canal, in Brooklyn, which is about to undergo a federally funded cleanup. Gary is sure that the job will be lucrative and tells Irwin that the owners, recently arrived Russians whom he describes as scientists and engineers, are in need of Irwin’s regulatory and technical expertise.

At a preliminary meeting in Gowanus, little about the prospective clients’ rough manner and crude appearance bears out Gary’s claims. And a few days later, when the overeager Irwin, following his usual procedure, visits the site to take stock—proudly bringing his sons along to see the world of his work—he finds that he’s dealing with gangsters of rare ruthlessness and brutality. By this time, though, he and Gary are in too deep: the gangsters beat Irwin and menace Hester and the boys. To protect the family, Gary goes into heavy debt to the syndicate; the movie’s title comes from the description he offers of his gangland creditors to allay Irwin’s fears. “I’m N.Y.P.D.,” Gary says, adding, “They’re not gonna touch me.” “But they can touch me,” Irwin skeptically retorts. As the days until payment is due tick grimly by, Irwin and Hester grow increasingly fretful and angry, and their widening divisions wrench the family apart, to intimately catastrophic effect.

Such lovequakes are a through line of Gray’s directorial career, which began in 1994, with “Little Odessa.” Gray, one of cinema’s great homebodies, grew up in Queens, and most of his movies are set there or in Brooklyn and deal bruisingly with the financial tensions, thwarted dreams, and frayed bonds of middle-class Jewish families like the one in which he was raised—stressed, streetwise, and crime-proximate. His previous film, “Armageddon Time,” from 2022—to my mind, his hitherto most accomplished one—is, like “Paper Tiger,” set in his home neighborhood, Fresh Meadows. That film takes place in 1980, with frequent allusions to Ronald Reagan’s ongoing Presidential campaign, and it focusses on a family very similar to the one in “Paper Tiger”: a father named Irving, who is a contractor; a mother named Esther; and two sons, the younger of whom transfers from public school to a nearby private day school dominated by a wealthy local family—the Trumps.

Gray conceived “Paper Tiger” as a sequel to “Armageddon Time” but altered his plans when the actors who played the parents in the earlier film, Anne Hathaway and Jeremy Strong, were unavailable. The two works remain cognate, but their differences are crucial. Strong’s Irving was tougher, more abrasive than Irwin is; conversely, Hathaway’s Esther, a teacher, was relatively refined and educated, whereas Johansson’s counterpart sleeps with rollers in her hair, like a vestige of the pre-Beatles sixties; speaks in a Queens accent that could cut metal; and holds the family together with her life-worn smarts and iron will. Yet she’s as unworldly as the nerdy Irwin, looking up to him with his fund of “facts and figures.”

But fires of rage burn below the surface of “Paper Tiger,” exemplified in the opening visit to Great Neck. Iris wants Hester and her family to move there; Hester demurs, explaining that college tuition for the boys must come first, but Irwin openly scoffs: “Everyone here was born with a silver spoon in their mouth, or stole one.” Iris, seeing suburban luxury as her daughter’s birthright, thinks that Hester’s marriage has been a comedown. The Pearls aren’t poor, but they’re burdened by expenses and tantalized by comforts just out of reach, especially now that their sons’ heads have been turned by Gary’s flashy success. (Comparing his uncle’s Mercedes with his parents’ cars, Scott whines, “Why do we always have to buy crappy stuff and live crappy?”)

Irwin’s run-in with the Mob dispels the fantasy of easy money; instead, he packs suitcases and makes plans to get the family out of town for their safety. Yet “Paper Tiger” is far more than a tale of criminal violence piercing the domestic bubble. It’s a story of silences, ones that form a conspicuous contrast with its precursor. “Armageddon Time,” with its expressly political context, is a film of rich discourse, filled with rhetorical expositions of ideology and history, reminiscences and commentaries. In “Paper Tiger,” there’s plenty of talk throughout, but hardly any of it involves cultural context, broader observation, or deeper reflection; it’s not a film of ideas. Instead, the heated dialogue is an expression of the inner life of the family and its time.

Interviews with directors have become a familiar part of movie promotion, but Gray’s interviews are different, often less like conversations than like performances. He’s among the most publicly funny of filmmakers, a gifted impersonator; I’ve long hoped that he would direct a comedy (he hasn’t yet) and appear in it. But his talent for mimicry comes across thrillingly in the dialogue of “Paper Tiger”—Gray wrote the screenplay himself—which adds an extra dimension to the story’s autobiographical elements. Both in ordinary chitchat and in big confrontations, the dialogue plays like a musical score of language built from a trove of memories. The film’s wondrously street-lyrical patter, its emblematic phrases and inflections, amount to a vast act of world-building—a lost milieu brought back to life in bygone clichés.

Much of this evocative talk also proves evasive. Just as Gary’s forecast for the Gowanus venture turns out to have been misleading, the fallout from that calamitous misadventure quickly brings on further elisions and secrets, transforming a happy home and a stable marriage into a curtained stage of furtive designs, hidden agendas, and stealthy exploits. Gary’s Mephistophelian temptations break the façades of business, law, and marriage, revealing the profound and irreparable solitude that lurks beneath life’s fundamental bonds.

Gray has always displayed a probing visual style, boldly confrontational yet painfully tender. In “Paper Tiger,” he refines these tendencies into lapidary images—spare, taut, and precise—that evoke the fierce solidity of the family circle and the fearsome emptiness that’s left when it shatters. With a quietly dazzling repertory of shadows and reflections, fragmented glimpses, truncated vistas, and blocked perspectives, he conjures everything the film keeps hidden, the illusions and limitations that inhere in frank gazes and point-blank views. I’ve seen “Paper Tiger” on the big screen but am looking forward to its streaming release in order to rewatch it as a silent film. Amid all its chatter, Gray has found the space to let images be eloquent, too. And their eloquence is greatest when expressing the silence and solitude of Hester.

In this regard, Gray’s movie resembles a pair of recent classics by Martin Scorsese, “The Irishman” and “Killers of the Flower Moon,” both of which feature women who respond to betrayal by men with silences deafening enough to rend the films’ finely textured surfaces. In “Paper Tiger,” the cycle of tragedy finds its definitive voice in Hester’s reproachful silences, which turn out to be radical rejections of the tight little world she inhabits. Determined and relentless, Hester, as incarnated by Johansson, dominates the action and steals the film with a decisive form of passive aggression—one that Gray condenses into a breathtakingly rapid, boldly symbolic special effect. By the time September winds down, Hester is on a timetable all her own, out of synch with her family, detached from its cares, paradoxically and bitterly free. ♦

items.title: In “The Heart” and “I Became We,” the Rise of the Hive-Mind Musical
items.description: The first image in the poignant, propulsive new E.D.M.-pop musical “The Heart,” at the Roundabout’s Laura Pels Theatre, is of a young surfer, Simon (Nick T. Daly), swaying in solitary bliss, like the only dancer left at a club. Behind him, a neon line pulses—i
items.author: Emily Nussbaum
paragraphs: The first image in the poignant, propulsive new E.D.M.-pop musical “The Heart,” at the Roundabout’s Laura Pels Theatre, is of a young surfer, Simon (Nick T. Daly), swaying in solitary bliss, like the only dancer left at a club. Behind him, a neon line pulses—it’s an ocean swell, an electrocardiogram, a musical beat. Just nineteen, Simon has slipped out early to catch a predawn wave, but on the drive home he’ll be critically injured in a crash.

And, in a flash, Simon is no longer the show’s protagonist—instead, his heart is. As bright grids fill up screens that frame the stage, the musical—smartly directed by the Roundabout’s new artistic director, Christopher Ashley, with lighting by Amanda Zieve, immersive video design by Lucy Mackinnon, and subtly gliding choreography by Mandy Moore (the auteur behind Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour)—becomes a thrilling, thrumming twenty-four-hour countdown to an organ transplant, tracing the path from one person’s tragedy to another’s miracle. We meet Simon’s powerhouse mother, Marianne (a moving Joaquina Kalukango, belting in denial by her son’s bedside); her prickly ex-husband, Sean (Jason Tam); Simon’s girlfriend, a d.j. named Juliette (Max McKenna); and also the medical team, including a warm, no-filter nurse (a fab Bre Jackson) and a cocksure surgeon (Drew Gehling, who, after playing doctors in “Waitress” and “Little Shop of Horrors,” may qualify for a medical degree). Later, we meet the recipient of Simon’s heart, portrayed with rueful glamour by Heidi Blickenstaff. These characters are distinct individuals, but there’s a fungibility to the whole enterprise: we meet each of them briefly but intensely, in passing, the way you do in a hospital. The cast juggles minor roles, so a patient might reappear as a doctor; Simon’s surfboard becomes an operating table.

The central concept, adapted by Kait Kerrigan from a poetic French novel, could easily go gooey or gimmicky, like a musical episode of “Grey’s Anatomy.” At first, there’s an almost bludgeoning pathos to what we witness, as Marianne resists the news that her son—brain-dead, but still with a beating heart—is gone. But, just as her grief becomes unbearable, a jarring image intervenes. At center stage, a fey stranger appears, warbling in a high operatic voice, with bright-blue gel patches under his eyes and a white towel wrapped around his head, diva style. Only after his phone rings do we learn who this person is: Thomas (Lincoln Klauss), the hospital professional assigned to persuade Marianne and Sean to donate Simon’s organs. “They might be divorced?” a colleague tells Thomas, filling him in on the case. “The divorce’ll be fun,” he responds, tartly.

It’s a tonic splash of detachment before Thomas’s mask of professionalism slides back up. Some of the production’s strongest moments feature this sort of tricky tonal pivot, as when a punkish gamer (a terrific Wren Rivera) is unveiled as the gleeful consultant who selects organ recipients using an algorithm. The show’s lyrics are often literal-minded, with rare outliers, such as a wry joke about Juliette becoming “a side piece to his nine-foot slab of fibreglass.” But did that blunt sincerity deliver emotionally? It sure did. Before long, my eyes stung; my chest got tight. If the critical part of my brain sometimes resisted an obvious turn of phrase—“You are my heartbeat,” say—the rest of my body was all in.

There was certainly no resisting the score, an audacious suite of electronic anthems and ballads co-written, with some help from Kerrigan, by the married pop-music wizards Anne and Ian Eisendrath, the latter of whom was an executive music producer for the banger-heavy “KPop Demon Hunters.” Broadway musicals have mined everything from rock and pop to hip-hop and folk. But there’s something bracingly logical about injecting the synthetic jolt of electronic dance music into a hospital environment, where vulnerable bodies are sustained by machines. The score has an exhilarating artificiality, from the breakneck “Keep Up,” which is punctuated by the beeps of hospital monitors, to the kinetic “Strike the Match,” in which layers of slick digital uplift thicken like shellac as the consultant homes in on her match. Any rhythm that repeats becomes fodder—the whoosh of the ocean, the boop-boop of video games. It’s an aural vocabulary that evokes both the cold, invisible workings of neural networks and sticky bodies losing themselves at a rave, united by a heartbeat.

“Was he generous?” is the question that Simon’s parents are forced to answer as they struggle over whether to let the doctors remove their son’s organs. The show itself feels generous, open to feeling as a source of wisdom. As one of the show’s lovelier lines says of surfing—and, implicitly, of nearly everything else in life—“You only get one wave, then you pass it on.” As anyone who has ever been in an emergency room knows, in a crisis some clichés ring true.

There is a ravenousness in midtown right now, after a frustrating few years, for Broadway to get behind some great new musical. Will “Galileo” break through? Lin-Manuel Miranda’s “The Warriors”? “Wanted”? In late October, a hot contender débuted: the London transfer “The Curious Case of Benjamin Button,” which had a celebrated run there. In New York, some critics found it twee, but I adored this small, oddball fable about a man aging backward. The production actually shared a lot with “The Heart,” even though it was scored with Celtic sea chanteys. It, too, is a countdown show obsessed with mortality, a stylized tale in which actors swap roles. It, too, had a lyrical directness that risked cliché in pursuit of elemental feelings.

But what felt most notable about “Button” was its structure, which, like “The Heart,” featured an ensemble telling an individual’s story in unison—in this case, down to the thoughts inside Benjamin’s head. Both plays are part of a cadre of hive-mind musicals, along with an earlier Ashley-directed project, “Come from Away” (which, like “Button,” has a Celtic-folk score). These shows are explicitly focussed on communities, not individuals—a hospital in “The Heart,” a fishing village in “Benjamin Button,” a rural Canadian town in “Come from Away.” They’re romances about systems, riffing off the choral storytelling of such classics as “A Chorus Line” and “Sweeney Todd” or the clever identity-flipping of “Operation Mincemeat.”

There’s another play in town that employs a similar technique, more austerely: the song cycle “I Became We,” written by Mona Pirnot, with soaringly lovely music by Jack D. Coen. At the Linda Gross Theatre, sixteen singers stand on risers, holding green choral folders. There’s a conductor and a piano. It felt like church until we heard the first line, which was sung as solemnly as Handel’s “Messiah”: “I saw a segment on ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live!’ called ‘What Do You Know About the Female Body?’ ”

What followed was the funny, philosophical narrative of a successful New York playwright in her mid-thirties. She’s got friends to dish with; she adores her mother, a math professor, and her “jumpy and nervous” husband; she is certain that she doesn’t want children. When she goes to a boring party in Brooklyn, a friend passes her a baby, who—as the chorus sings, in joyful, slightly frenzied counterpoint—starts “squirming, squirming!” and “screaming, screaming!” And then there’s a sudden, destabilizing shift in tone: a solo soprano begins singing mournfully, “She’s so small / She’s so small.”

It seems, at first, that this will be a story about fertility—or infertility. But the narrative never goes quite where we expect, its idiosyncratic turns intensified by the singers’ communal delivery, like a catechism or a shared consciousness. Nobody “plays” the narrator; nobody acts out her behavior. They just sing her thoughts, without comment.

Why did this pack such a punch? Maybe it was because of the tension between the elevated harmonies and the down-to-earth words. Maybe it was because the performance framed one person’s inner monologue—It is wonderful to see people love my talented mother! Why am I crying at this Adam Sandler movie?—as a grand, even sacred project. When the payoff arrived, it reduced the audience to sobs as heavy as any I’d heard at “The Heart.” I suspect that we were all thinking about our own lives. It was impossible not to. ♦

items.title: “Tip Toe” Rails Against the Rolling Back of Progress
items.description: Early in the new miniseries “Tip Toe,” two older gay men debate how worried they should be as homophobia surges in the U.K. Leo Struthers (Alan Cumming), the owner of a bar in Manchester’s storied queer quarter, asks his longtime friend Melba (Paul Rhys) wheth
items.author: Inkoo Kang
paragraphs: Early in the new miniseries “Tip Toe,” two older gay men debate how worried they should be as homophobia surges in the U.K. Leo Struthers (Alan Cumming), the owner of a bar in Manchester’s storied queer quarter, asks his longtime friend Melba (Paul Rhys) whether the vintage intolerance of the nineteen-nineties seems to be coming around again. “It’s back, you fucking idiot,” Melba responds. “We’re in the middle of it right now.” Online hate for Leo’s business, his friend notes, is as “regular as the morning shit.” Melba’s the sort of scenester who’s hard to miss—statuesque, with a signature look of dark lipstick and Robert Smith-style eyeliner—but he confesses to toning himself down lately. In the current climate, he says, “Now I tiptoe, just in case.”

The social revanchism of the twenty-twenties has largely shown up in pop culture as triumphalism on the right and silence on the left; on television, the neo-Western TV mogul Taylor Sheridan blankets the proverbial airwaves with trucks, horses, and anti-California jabs, while programs centered on queer characters and protagonists of color continue to dwindle. “Tip Toe,” from the television auteur Russell T Davies, is a rare outcry from the side of the progressives, who are seeing their political and cultural gains rapidly erode. In 1999, Davies created the original “Queer as Folk,” a groundbreaking show about ordinary gay Mancunians who spend their nights at the club, where they find almost everything they want: sex, drugs, family, friendship, freedom. A quarter century later, Leo’s bar is less a temple to liberation than a fortress under sporadic siege, where drag performers have protocols for emergency exits and bartenders, between pours, watch the door for troublemakers.

What if such measures aren’t enough? What if the atavism under way isn’t just a miasma of unpleasantness but a buildup of gas waiting to combust? That panic fuels “Tip Toe,” a siren of a series that confirms Davies’s standing as one of the medium’s essential creators. The five-episode drama—which aired this summer in Britain, on Channel 4, and wraps up its American run this week, on Starz—is a minor work with ample speechifying and visible budget constraints, and yet it offers more thoughtfulness and ingenuity than most of the year’s prestige programming.

It’s also a bit of a tough watch, opening with a flash-forward in which Leo is found hanged from a lamppost outside his home. His presumed killer is his next-door neighbor, Clive Goss (David Morrissey), a fitfully employed electrician with an unshakable suspicion that Leo has designs on his sons, twenty-five-year-old Saul (Joseph Evans) and sixteen-year-old George (Jackson Connor). The time line then jumps back ten days, when, after more than a decade of wordless coexistence on opposite sides of a shared wall, Leo locks himself out of his house and asks to borrow Clive’s phone to call a friend with a spare key. Suddenly, the two men become enmeshed in each other’s lives, with Clive on the attack despite practically begging Leo for odd jobs, and Leo on a mission to soften Clive’s bigotry, tragically mistaken about his ability to win over a man who can no longer hear reason.

That naïveté is a surprising blind spot for the fifty-nine-year-old Leo, a man steeped in experience. “Tip Toe” is one of a vanishingly few series centered on gay men in late middle age, and Leo’s well-roundedness hints at all we miss out on in the absence of perspectives like his. An elfin force of nature with the natural showmanship of someone who takes hospitality seriously, Leo has the charisma to command the loyalty of his fresh-faced staff—and the pragmatism to resent the Labour Party’s business reforms. Having seen too many gay kids sink into hopelessness, he treats the bar like an unofficial employment-training center for L.G.B.T.Q. youth, though he’s not above grousing at a trans bartender (Iz Hesketh) about the transgender movement’s emphasis on pronouns—a carp he quickly takes back. But Cumming gets to show here the vulnerability so frequently lacking in his waspish supporting roles or in his hosting gig on the reality-competition series “The Traitors,” where he’s a master of self-aware camp. Leo is still smarting from his ex-husband’s decision two years prior to leave him for a woman. And he hates that, in his escalating spats with Clive, he’s the first to apologize or to compromise. Cumming has seldom laid himself so bare as he he does late in the show, when Leo gulps down the self-loathing that rises in his throat as he finally explodes at Clive, lamenting that he’s spent a lifetime making himself palatable, even pitiful, to shield himself from a hostile heterosexual world.

“Tip Toe” is at its best when it captures what it feels like to live through the present-day backlash. Davies has a keen eye for how societal tensions trickle down into interpersonal dynamics; the characters’ habit of lodging accusations against “you lot”—not only across tribal lines but between assumed allies, as with the questionable gripes from Leo’s social-worker best friend, Stephanie (Elizabeth Berrington), about how the practice of queer self-identification endangers her female charges—reflects the fractured nature of life today, where every systemic problem comes with an automatic scapegoat. Davies also effectively depicts technology’s destabilizing influence—a theme that animated his 2019 dystopian HBO drama, “Years and Years,” which followed the gradual dissolution of an English family in an age of online alienation and populist politics. At the Goss residence, no one seems aware that Clive has disappeared down some gnarly internet rabbit holes, spending his nights on the couch, estranged from his wife, Marie (Pooky Quesnel), watching bombings and car crashes. The serendipity of the internet means that Leo and George, a closeted high-schooler, can end up chatting on a hookup app; in classic teen-age form, George is sexually active (with a boy his age) but squeamish when Leo brings up protection. The speed and unpredictability of information online likewise mean that everything becomes easier: outings, misunderstandings, hate crimes.

“Tip Toe” also compellingly dramatizes the widespread, but not always convincing, axiom that bias is hardened by economic uncertainty. The show’s longitudinal view becomes an asset again; what appears to unsettle Clive and Marie, who came of age when queer Britons had been forced into the margins, isn’t so much that Leo is gay as that he’s thriving. When Clive asks Leo for work, he frames each request as a play for dominance. (Given Leo’s fate, I could feel my cortisol spike whenever Leo indulged a streak of impertinence by pausing to put Clive in his place.) Clive’s homophobia, which draws on the myth that gay men are prone to pedophilia, seems less rooted in concern for his sons than in a fear that Leo will take or alter something that Clive claims as his own.

But Davies is unable to make the humorless Clive—a man not of retrograde values but of no core principles—an engaging figure. It’s not difficult to believe that people like Clive exist: compulsive scrollers driven by reaction and disillusionment, who know and care so little of the lives of others they could believe H.I.V. and dyslexia to be mass hoaxes. When Clive tries to let Leo in on his world view, he raves incoherently about immigrants, Elon Musk, and outlet voltages. Even if there’s something infuriatingly familiar about Leo’s difficulties in making logical inroads with Clive—a task he mostly takes on to insure a safe coming-out for George—there’s no satisfaction to be had in arguing against a jumble. Morrissey is able to physically convey Clive’s existential discomfort; despite his conventional handsomeness, the character often looks like he’s dying to inhabit a completely new skin. Still, any empathy that the series looks to drum up for him is limited by the fact that the character takes equality as an affront—Clive can’t feel tall without someone to stand over.

The dread-filled lead-up to Leo’s murder, in which he and Clive quickly amass a ledger of mutual grievances, proves more gripping than the forced dénouement. Eventually, allegory overwhelms dramaturgy, with a group of soccer hooligans—emblems of the volatility of men under threat—playing a pivotal role in Leo’s end. More haunting are the reverberations of his death, told in an extensive coda, which allude to the role that gay elders have often played in maintaining safe spaces for the next generation—and how quickly those places can disappear without the old guard’s dedication and logistical know-how. The warning from Leo’s cohort that a “new Dark Age” is on the horizon may register as alarmist, but “Tip Toe” makes a persuasive case that it may be the only clear-eyed response. ♦

items.title: Roy Lichtenstein’s Witty Critiques of Masculinity
items.description: “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New” (at the Whitney through May 10th) is a masterpiece of curation and design, an exhibition that positions Lichtenstein as the last happy white man in American art. Organized with esprit and imagination by the artist Alex Da Corte and
items.author: Hilton Als
paragraphs: “Roy Lichtenstein: Like New” (at the Whitney through May 10th) is a masterpiece of curation and design, an exhibition that positions Lichtenstein as the last happy white man in American art. Organized with esprit and imagination by the artist Alex Da Corte and the curator Meg Onli, it’s the first retrospective of Lichtenstein’s work in New York since his splash at the Guggenheim in 1993. The show takes up the museum’s entire fifth floor and ends as it begins: with the artist’s signature brightly colored brushstrokes, lines, and Benday dots causing pleasurable kinetic movements in the mind. Lichtenstein’s dynamic style is ubiquitous by now—as are his professional sheen and finish—but that doesn’t cancel out his winning charm, which, like most charm, can warm you up or wear you out. At “Like New,” you may experience both feelings. It’s a show that aims to keep the real world, our gothic political climate included, at bay, while also distracting us from what one might call the grief porn of contemporary art and its constant reminders of our failures as humans.

For years now, the Whitney has foregrounded race- and gender-based political art, and it’s a little trippy to walk around this show’s pearl-gray-painted rooms, looking at Lichtenstein’s Fantastik-clean white world of orderly studios, shiny blondes, and square-jawed men, in a place where white male power has been repeatedly denounced and the sins of past neglect redressed. No one can make up for the past—certainly not by demanding that it be corrected in the present—and it was perhaps inevitable that the Whitney would have to turn, or return, to white men with name recognition to get people back into its galleries post-COVID. Exhibitions devoted to Jasper Johns and Andy Warhol helped, and still fit the Whitney framework: both artists were queer. And although Lichtenstein wasn’t gay, there’s enough irony about gender in his early work to qualify him as being interestingly gay-adjacent.

Still, it’s difficult to entirely undo the way we’ve been viewing art for a while now, and, after having a great time at “Like New,” you may find yourself feeling slightly guilty about it. But one of the more poignant subtexts of the show is that it’s a reminder of the New York avant-garde in the sixties, and of what a beautiful, forceful energy there was to its various voices, with Lichtenstein the least dirty and anarchic of them all. There’s a sweetness in that, and a sadness, too.

I first spent time with Lichtenstein’s work in the early eighties, when I took a class at Columbia on the art of the nineteen-sixties. The professor led us from the glory days of Abstract Expressionism in the fifties, through the emergence of Robert Rauschenberg and Johns by the end of that decade, to this new era in American art. Inspired by Marcel Duchamp and his poetry of the everyday, Rauschenberg and Johns used commonplace objects—a flashlight, a bedspread—in their creations. But artists working under the Pop-art banner in the sixties, including Lichtenstein, Claes Oldenburg, James Rosenquist, Tom Wesselmann, Marisol, and Warhol, picked at the surface of the world that had made them, in order to show us how much it could reveal about what lay beneath it. You can still feel, in the memorable work produced during that period, the critical embrace of all those dance-lesson diagrams, Campbell’s soup cans, ice-cream cones, and Coca-Cola bottles, alongside images of electric chairs, car crashes, and atomic-bomb detonations.

In the Cold War universe, where everyone was isolated and class was defined by the power to acquire (and to oppress), Pop artists painted or sculpted what they saw and heard. The artist’s “aura” had no place in those works; instead, Pop art was a kind of supersonic whistle heralding the disasters to come, that had already come. But unlike, for instance, Rosenquist, in such charged political pieces as “F-111” (1964-65), which juxtaposes consumer objects with missiles, Lichtenstein made work that was less about conscience than about control, and the eradication of mess, of feeling.

Lichtenstein became Lichtenstein in 1961, when he made “Look Mickey.” He had flirted with cartoon characters before then, but “Look Mickey” took things further. Four feet by nearly six, the painting features the brightest of reds, blues, and yellows. In it, Mickey Mouse and the bombastic Donald Duck are standing on a dock, fishing. Mickey covers his laughing mouth because Donald thinks he’s hooked a fish, but the hook is caught on his own coat. The delight of the painting is the pleasure that Lichtenstein took in the joke—and in this new way of making work that was both free and not free of the artist’s hand. (In the age of Pop, achieving an automated look was part of the process.)

Decades before Richard Prince made his fantastic and forlorn cartoon paintings, Lichtenstein was already exploring the idea of entertainment and raising questions: If cartoons were a form of entertainment, was painting a cartoon a form of entertainment, too? Was modern art a put-on? Or something that could be put on? One question that the Whitney show didn’t answer for me was how Lichtenstein got to cartoons, and then to his comic-strip paintings, with their speech balloons, women in distress, and silent men—whose reserve makes us wonder if their creator was a silent man, too.

Born in 1923, into an upper-middle-class German Jewish family in New York, Lichtenstein grew up on the Upper West Side, with easy access to museums and other cultural institutions. He loved music and art, and in 1940 he enrolled at Ohio State University, where he studied life drawing, painting, and the work of the masters, including Picasso. If he insisted on pursuing art, his parents felt, it would be good for him to get a degree, in case he had to teach to get by.

The Whitney retrospective includes “Drawing by Seeing,” a short film about Lichtenstein’s artistic education, made by Da Corte, whose own work includes video, performance, and installations, driven by the kind of avant-gardism that Lichtenstein espoused for a time. The film is shot in color, but with the performers and their costumes colored a “Twilight Zone” gray. It features a voice-over drawn from a text by Hoyt L. Sherman, Lichtenstein’s teacher and mentor at Ohio State. Sherman’s work centered on perception; he’d flash an image on a screen and then have his students draw what they had seen. Or hadn’t. Da Corte’s film also animates some of Lichtenstein’s early works, including “Step-on Can with Leg” (1961), a two-panel painting that shows a woman’s high-heeled foot stepping on the pedal of a closed garbage can, and then the same image with the lid open. Like Warhol, in “Before and After,” a study of a nose job, also from 1961, Lichtenstein was interested in how time can be represented in a static medium, thus changing how we see a thing, or making us realize that we weren’t really looking.

Lichtenstein’s studies were interrupted when he was drafted, in 1943, but he returned in 1946 to finish his degree on the G.I. Bill. By 1949, he was married to the artist Isabel Wilson Sarisky, with whom he had two sons. (Divorced in 1965, he married Dorothy Herzka, a philanthropist, in 1968.) Lichtenstein, shy and reclusive, was a responsible fellow; he supported his family by teaching, while making art that was at first representational, then a little abstract, not terribly distinguished. The breakthrough came in 1960, when he was teaching at Douglass College (which later became part of Rutgers), where he met the performance artist Allan Kaprow, who introduced him to Claes Oldenburg and George Segal, artists who were as taken with the look and signs of masculinity as Lichtenstein was. (Oldenburg’s 1959 work “ ‘Empire’ (‘Papa’) Ray Gun,” for instance, plays on the phallic shape of a firearm.) Surely the freedom that Lichtenstein saw in those sculptors’ work and at Kaprow’s “happenings” helped to release him and open him up to his strongest qualities as an artist: his interest in gender and his amused wit.

Lichtenstein’s wonderful early work “Masterpiece” (1962) still makes me laugh. In it, a couple are looking at a canvas. The woman, a blonde, has a speech balloon issuing from her red lips: “Why, Brad darling, this painting is a masterpiece! My, soon you’ll have all of New York clamoring for your work!” The man is silent, only partially visible, in profile; the woman is our focus. She may be the kind of woman who needs her man to be a success, in order to validate her power as a woman, one who, unlike Donald Duck, has caught a big one. It’s a joke on the bright and shiny, profit-driven art world, where nothing resonates like success. Among other great early works, there’s the funny, ’tude-filled “Ohhh . . . Alright . . .” (1964)—a closeup of a red-haired woman on the phone, looking slightly annoyed as she speaks the title—and “Drowning Girl” (1963), in which a blue-haired woman with tears falling from her closed eyes drowns as much in misbegotten love as in a swirl of black-and-white waves. A thought bubble reads, “I don’t care! I’d rather sink—than call Brad for help!”

These are not really paintings about distress or isolation. They’re about fake feelings in a manufactured world. What was real in Pop? What wasn’t? I liked these works so much when I was younger, and still do, because, for me, Lichtenstein was at his strongest when he wasn’t just a straight man but, rather, a Warhol-adjacent straight man who could critique both masculinity and the self-consciously feminine. The truth is that when Lichtenstein stopped painting “gay,” I stopped looking. From the seventies on, in work that seemed influenced by Léger, Matisse, Picasso, and others, he appeared to be more at play with the straight boys than questioning their performative creativity. (The Whitney curators have put some of the gay back into his work by treating it as a kind of exquisite California-modern decoration; all that’s missing are gray throw pillows.) Still, at the end of the show, I stood by Da Corte’s replica of Lichtenstein’s enormous 1967 work “Super Sunset Billboard,” which shows a horizon and, above it, white streams of light shooting up and out, like klieg lights announcing a show. The painting is the show. Da Corte and Onli have placed the piece in front of a wall of windows overlooking the Hudson; it’s a calming, lovely thing to see a “real” sky echoing Lichtenstein’s. It’s also a thrilling and moving coda to his work—so much so that I got goosebumps. It was the first time I’d ever thought of goosebumps as Benday dots. ♦

items.title: Trump Is Going Full Stephen Miller: Live Updates
items.description: The wave has crashed. The roiling aftermath continues. While we’re still waiting for final results in some key midterm races, the brutal postmortems are out, the resignations have begun, and everyone — including the victorious Democrats and the Trump administr
items.author: Intelligencer Staff
paragraphs: The wave has crashed. The roiling aftermath continues. While we’re still waiting for final results in some key midterm races, the brutal postmortems are out, the resignations have begun, and everyone — including the victorious Democrats and the Trump administration — is trying to make sense of what it all means. Here are the latest developments, analysis, and aftershocks.
“Susie keeps the trains running on time. I don’t know what this looks like moving forward.’
CNN reports on a White House in disarray:

Trump, who initially appeared unfazed by the results of the Tuesday night midterms, has become angrier as he’s watched coverage of the historic losses, according to the people familiar with his response. That sour mood has spread throughout the West Wing, which has become increasingly factionalized in recent days.

Trump made his displeasure with his political team known starting at a tense election night reception in the East Room, according to one of the people familiar with the matter. He vented that deep Republican losses were the result of their strategy. Wiles was among those Trump blamed for the Republican losses, the person said. …

Since the midterm wipeout, Trump had heard from several allies and associates who urged him to make changes to his senior staff in response to the losses, a source familiar with the matter said. But the move nonetheless came as a shock to many in the administration, and multiple White House officials told CNN it left them concerned about the rest of Trump’s second term.
“Susie keeps the trains running on time. I don’t know what this looks like moving forward,” one official said.
Another Trump ally called it a “catastrophic loss” for the president.
Revenge of the Epstein Files
The Atlantic’s Sarah Fitzpatrick reports that Jeffrey Epstein did factor into Trump and the GOP’s losses:

The president’s decision to go to war with Iran and the resulting spike in gas prices may have been the front-of-mind issues for most voters in the 2026 midterms. But members of Congress, pollsters, political operatives, and campaign staff all told me that Trump’s mishandling of the Epstein issue meaningfully contributed to the GOP’s drubbing. The Republican pollster and strategist Brent Buchanan told me that Epstein became “a proxy for corruption” in the midterms. Another Republican close to the White House described the Epstein issue to me as the “nuclear fuel” that accelerated a new form of American populism. First, it boosted Trump. But on Tuesday, it worked against him, helping bring him to the lowest point of his presidency. Many of Trump’s voters viewed his handling of the matter as a betrayal. Pollsters told me it had cracked the bond between Trump and his coalition—and changed the course of the midterms.
It’s almost like you can’t trust him
Trump’s 60 Minutes interview is going to be a little out-of-date:
When 60 Minutes Correspondent Ross Douthat asked Mr. Trump whether he expected to fire anyone after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress, the president said: “I do, yeah. Little bit.”
“I love my Cabinet. I think they’re good,” he said. “But I’ll … be doing maybe a few changes.”

Mr. Trump suggested Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is safe for now, despite CBS News reporting that he asked advisers this week whether the Pentagon chief should stick around. When Douthat asked whether he has confidence in Hegseth, Mr. Trump said: “I do.”

“Look, we’ve won two wars. We’ve won Venezuela and taken out billions and billions and billions of dollars already. And we will be taking out many billions of dollars and get along very well. And, you could call it a territory, you could call it whatever you want. We won that war in less than one hour,” Mr. Trump said.

Venezuela was not a war, of course, it was an arranged abduction. The other war is a war, and it’s not over, and the U.S. has not won it. Also “little bit” isn’t firing the Chief of Staff who has run the Trump Team for years.
Three out and counting at the Justice Department

High-profile leaders resigned from the department Thursday and Friday, including Civil Rights Division chief Harmeet Dhillon, National Security Division chief John Eisenberg and U.S. Attorney for Southern Florida Jason Reding Quiñones, who led prosecutors in the so-called “grand conspiracy” case President Donald Trump hoped to mount against his longtime adversaries.

Two people familiar with the personnel changes, granted anonymity to describe internal decision-making, said the departures were not surprising. One person said Blanche had grown frustrated with some of the department’s leadership amid struggles to bring high-profile indictments or score big wins in litigation connected to the president’s top priorities.
So they’re out because they failed to deliver substantive trumped-up charges?
Colom’s lead just keeps growing
Steve Kornacki fasts during Election Night
America’s favorite election nerd did this week’s Grub Street Diet. From his entry about Tuesday night:

On big event nights like this, when everybody is working late, they usually bring in pizzas. They’ll keep a stack of like 30 pizza boxes out in the hallway. I never eat before the broadcast, but I always tell my producer that when we’re done, we’ll go all in on the leftovers; we always go through the boxes, and they’re always empty.

Because I’m on-camera basically nonstop, I don’t really eat anything during the broadcast. I make it for ten and a half hours straight, which is a personal record for one of these livestreams. There’s only time for one bathroom break! The crew keeps refilling a ceramic NBC mug with water for me the whole time. It doesn’t seem like such a strenuous thing on paper, but being on your feet for ten hours talking almost nonstop takes more of a physical toll than you might think.

Whatever it is, I sort of hit a wall at about 3:30 a.m. Things have also slowed down dramatically resultswise at this point, too. So after I take a break, I huddle with the producers and we decide it’s actually the logical time to call it a night. They bring some random snacks over to me: a thing of trail mix, some grapes, and Cheez-Its. I chug a big can of lemon-lime Gatorade. I think it’s around 5 a.m. when I finally get home, and I’m too exhausted to eat anything else.
An ominous sign of things to come
As I argue in my new post, the Miller pick is a chilling indication of what awaits us in the final two years of Trump’s presidency:

Miller is deeply responsible for losing 2024 Trump voters who supported border control and deportation of violent criminals but never bargained for the terror ICE has inflicted on immigrant communities or the unapologetic racism that underlies Miller’s approach.

And that may be the scariest thing of all about his new base of power: He has two more years to act on his deep belief in the Great Replacement theory. This is the idea that traitorous liberals are deliberately destroying the country through a conspiracy to drown native-born white Americans in a sea of shiftless immigrants who trade illegal votes for welfare benefits and the opportunity to commit crimes. Trump talks about this nightmare scenario all the time as part of his demagogic pitch to the MAGA base. But for Miller, it’s an article of faith.

Some Trump defenders will try to rationalize Miller’s elevation as insignificant, a semi-automatic move up the ladder for the Trump loyalist who was technically Wiles’s deputy. It’s true that he may bring more discipline and fewer leaks to the White House staff. But it will likely be the discipline of sheer fanaticism and intolerance for dissent.

Trump’s big decision in the wake of the midterms is whether to learn something from his party’s setback and seek to wind down his final term in office in a dignified manner or instead try to implement the worst and most divisive elements of his agenda come hell or high water. There’s little question Miller would take the administration down this second path, and his promotion will give him that chance.
Another ominous sign of things to come
Does this make renewing the Iran War more or less likely?
Notes the Stimson Center’s Emma Ashford:
Miller probably the most Jacksonian of all Trump’s close advisors, which means – when it comes to Iran – that things could just as easily go to escalation as de-escalation.

But Maggie Haberman reports that “Miller’s pitch for the job, according to people who heard it, was that the president needed to wind down the Iran war, which the president’s core supporters viewed as a betrayal.”
Eurasia Group Analyst Gregory Brew adds:
FWIW there are a couple of different routes to “end the war” but somehow I doubt Miller’s pitch to Trump was to go back to the MOU and let Iran have the strait.
Stephen Miller says ‘the mission is now more clear than ever’
His first statement as Chief of Staff suggests a bunker mentality:
President Trump is the most transformative political leader in American History — and he has single-handedly saved America from those who would destroy it.
It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have served on his team from Day One, and I am honored beyond words to serve as his White House Chief of Staff.
I want to thank the incomparable Susie Wiles for her years of devoted service to the President and the Country, and for her friendship.
The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our President and defend this magnificent Republic.
RFK Jr. wants to ‘unleash the Kraken’
A totally normal statement of praise from a totally normal HHS secretary:
Next to me, Stephen Miller is the strongest MAHA supporter in the administration. It’s time to unleash the Kraken.
The latest post-midterms margins
The Democratic majorities will be 260 in the House and 56 in the Senate:
Hegseth better polish his resume

He’s blasting out how psyched he is about his fellow MAGA zealot Stephen Miller now being in charge of the White House, but Pete Hegseth is looking more and more like a post-midterms sacrificial lamb. Congress is already on the case with Thomas Massie’s impeachment resolution, which will go live the minute the lame-duck session begins. And now it’s increasingly clear Trump’s inner circle has decided the Iran War is the expendable part of the second-term agenda.

J.D. Vance, who never does or says anything that will dismay the boss, has blamed the entire midterm debacle on the war. And now Miller has reportedly argued that ending the war is how Trump wins back his base. Dumping the Warfighter In Chief at the Pentagon could simultaneously please the MAGA folk who never liked the war to begin with, while giving congressional Democrats an early trophy. Maybe Hegseth can be given some phony-baloney diplomatic post like Kristi Noem was given.
Trump and Miller’s mandate of the mind
Vox’s Astead Herndon cautions:
Why I’d urge caution on declaring the Trump era over. The second term project hasn’t just been about retribution, but also unchecked presidential power — with Miller and Project 2025 its architects.

They didn’t really try and sell their agenda to the public. They tried to gerrymander a win before voting started. And they worked hard to empower the executive, and to minimize the role of Congress/Courts altogether.
So in a weird, undemocratic way, the WH has been building to this moment for two years.
Trump reportedly sped up Wiles’s exit
According to a CBS News report, Wiles’ sudden departure was not exactly what she had planned:

Wiles had planned to stay on as chief through Congress’ lame-duck session and exit after that, likely at the end of this year or early next year, according to sources familiar with her thinking. The president accelerated her departure.
Targeting Minneapolis was Miller’s ‘passion project’

Here come the leaks. The Washington Sun reports that Miller “pressed administration officials for evidence of fraud related to immigrants, Minnesota and the state’s Somali population nine times in a span of about 10 minutes during a December 2025 call”:
The president’s fierce loyalist, at the time his deputy chief of staff, , according to a recording obtained by The Washington Sun.

Miller cut one official off as they were describing a fraud problem in Florida, a hot spot for bad actors who siphon off government benefits, according to the government’s own data. He appeared uninterested in the official’s description of fraud when it didn’t prominently feature immigrants.
At one point, Miller was told about an active criminal investigation into a national fraud case out of the Eastern District of Virginia.
“I hear you, but that’s a long way off from Minneapolis,” Miller responded.
The call is one of several previously unreported instances since the fall of 2025 in which Miller pushed administration officials to target a small population of immigrants in a single state. …

Miller has repeatedly sought to wield the full weight of the federal government against the roughly 100,000 Somalis who live in Minnesota, targeting the state’s federal funds, installing an ally of his immigration agenda in a key position at the Justice Department and clashing with career and political officials in the process.
“It’s like a passion project for him,” one source close to the White House said.
Who needs strategy when you’ve got American carnage
“Stephen Miller should lawyer up”
From the likely new head of the House Oversight Committee:
Hegseth is in full ‘F*ck Yeah’ mode
‘American blood on his hands’
Democratic leaders have unsurprisingly, rejected the Miller pick.
Hakeem Jeffries, the likely incoming Speaker of the House, has weighed in on Miller’s new role as chief of staff, saying he has “American blood on his hands” and calling for him to be fired.
Chuck Schumer, who is expected to be Senate Majority Leader once again, vowed that the new Democratic-led Congress will “fight him every step of the way.”
‘I just wanted to make a change’
“We gotta make moves,” Trump said, like this move didn’t mean much, to reporters outside the White House:
It’s not fully clear what “change” actually means to Trump right now, however.
The White House hatchet man is thrilled
The bunker meme has returned

Sources told Axios that her departure was a mutual decision, but driven by Tuesday’s midterm losses, for which Trump blamed her. Trump did not ask for her resignation, said one informed source who spoke with Wiles, “but he couldn’t get it out of his head that she was to blame, not him.”“Susie could’ve stuck around, but what’s the point?” that person said. “Whether it’s right or wrong, Susie knows that serving the president means it’s at his pleasure. And if she couldn’t change the way he felt, there was no reason to stay.” …

Wiles’ strength was understanding how to navigate Trump rather than trying to control him. She avoided public confrontations, offered disagreements privately and sought to carry out Trump’s priorities rather than restrain them.But her influence had limits. She was a critical voice against the war in Iran and repeatedly questioned the hardline immigration tactics championed by Miller.

One of the disconnects right now is that the Republican midterm losses were a decisive rebuke of the president and his actions in office. But Trump has two years left of the term, and putting in Miller — who is deeply ideological and also the most powerful policy staffer in the modern history of the presidency — is doubling down on Trump’s agenda, not switching course.

Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff. Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.
More than anything, I’m grateful for the extraordinary people I’ve had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.
The cruelty is still somehow Trump’s point
Comments Ron Brownstein on X:

I’m sure Vance and Rubio are feeling confident today that Miller is just the man to steer their way back to support from all the voters who thought Trump was too extreme, chaotic, cruel, reckless and ineffective this week. Who better to recapture straying Latinos?

The GOP loses everything beyond deep MAGA terrain (+andeven some there), suffers big reversals with all the groups that moved to Trump in 2024, swing voters & even non-MAGA Republicans, and Trump’s answer is to elevate Stephen Miller as Chief of Staff, with his unerring instinct for outreach and consensus.
Below-the-radar midterms feats
We collected a bunch of eye-popping details about election results from across the country, including:
Early votes for Talarico, Cooper, and Ossoff surpassed their opponents’ total votes.

Texas’s official election results showed James Talarico received 4,397,474 early votes. The figure is actually larger than the total number of votes Ken Paxton received overall at 4,249,373, a difference of 148,101. The incoming senator-elect could’ve made history even with just the early vote. NBC’s Decision Desk discovered similar dynamics for Georgia senator Jon Ossoff as well as North Carolina senator-elect Roy Cooper, who received more votes in early voting than his Republican opponent, Michael Whatley, won in total.
Trump has made Stephen Miller his new Chief of Staff
Wiles is out. Miller is in, Trump says on Truth Social:

I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026. Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job! President DONALD J. TRUMP
I wrote about the midterms most difficult to please constituency, the swing voters who hate both parties:

Donald Trump will not be on the ballot in 2028, and between now and then Democrats need to convince double haters to hate them less than Republicans in a comparative context, including one in which Democrats will be entirely in control of Congress. This challenge may be intensified by a wide-open 2028 Democratic presidential-nominating contest in which candidates may be focused more on appealing to reliable party-primary participants rather than the swing voters they will need in November. If conditions in the country worsen and such emerging existential issues as AI-related job loss explode into prominence, it’s even possible that long-suppressed support for minor parties, old or new, could finally threaten the two-party duopoly or at least affect the balance of power between Democrats and Republicans. So leaders and activists in both parties need to get over the midterms quickly and focus on the sales pitches they have to develop to win over voters who aren’t very fond of any of them.
Jeffries made his own way to the gavel

[W]ithin the Democratic Party, the new House majority represents the victory of realism over rhetoric. For all the headlines given to the supposed influence of socialists and ultraprogressives, Jeffries’s majority was created by painstakingly recruiting and supporting the kind of candidates who can defeat Republicans. In New York, while the Democratic Socialists of America were attacking mainstream Democrats like Adriano Espaillat and Antonio Reynoso, and debating over who was first to use the word genocide to denounce attacks on Gaza, Jeffries was lining up candidates in red-to-blue districts that included ministers, combat veterans, farmers, prosecutors, and other centrists from blue-collar backgrounds.
The right-wing media meltdown is well underway
The Bulwark’s Will Sommer observes:

RIGHT-WING MEDIA has always been a fractious place even under the best of circumstances, featuring combustible personalities with flexible ethical standards clashing with one another in the pursuit of influence, followers, and money. A civil war has roiled the podcast right for over a year, turning intertwined issues like the Epstein files, Charlie Kirk’s murder, and the Iran war into the stuff of both conspiracies and blood feuds.

But the midterm rout, which none of these folks seemed to see coming, has cranked the stakes up to eleven. That’s partially because right-wing media figures are worried about their future. If no one wants to be a Republican anymore, who’s going to watch their podcasts and buy their brain pills? But it’s also because there’s a genuine belief that the fate of their ideological projects is at stake.
Rubio denies he’s planning to bounce
He spoke with the New York Times today:
Responding to the news reports that he was mulling an exit, Mr. Rubio said, “I don’t know where these things come from, to be honest with you.”
“I love the work I’m doing,” he continued. “And plus I always laugh when they say he’s going to leave his job. I go, ‘Which one?’”
Mr. Rubio, who is also Mr. Trump’s national security adviser, declined to answer questions about whether he was considering running for president in 2028.
“I literally will not talk about 2028 anymore,” he said in the interview, in his White House office. “I just won’t do it.”
Democrats’ other astounding nationwide feat

They are on track to seize control of a majority of America’s state legislative chambers for the first time in 16 years — since 2010, when the GOP swept to state power on the coattails of the anti-Obama Tea Party movement. Notes Axios:
If current leads hold, 75% of Americans will live in a state with a Democratic governor, and 53% will live in Democratic trifectas. …
The party is set to flip 12 legislative chambers, dismantle five Republican state trifectas, shatter 11 GOP supermajorities and build 12 of its own, according to AP returns as of 6pm ET on Wednesday.

If leads hold, Democrats will control the governor’s office and both chambers in five of the seven 2024 presidential battlegrounds: Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.They have also broken Republican one-party rule in the sixth (Georgia) and flipped the House in the seventh (North Carolina).Democrats flipped five GOP-held governorships (Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas) and lead in Alaska.
Colom’s lead is still inching up
In case you missed it, the Senate candidate endorsed a very state-appropriate vote-counting method yesterday:
Let’s hear it for the failures
I just ranked the 13 biggest losers of the midterms, including:
3. The White House Political Team

Probably no one group of Americans in politics has received more undeserved credit for brilliance than Donald Trump’s White House political team. To be sure, Susie Wiles and Chris LaCivita, the co-chairs of Trump’s 2024 comeback campaign, and James Blair, that campaign’s political director, did a fine job of plucking the ripe fruit of the Biden administration’s many problems, and guiding the 45th president through to his inauguration. And on the most superficial level, Trump 2.0 was less chaotic under their management than Trump 1.0. But in many respects, that just meant Trump was very free to pursue his own worst instincts, and his political team did little if anything to restrain him. Now in the wake of the midterm disaster, the long knives are out for these erstwhile geniuses, as Jake Lahut reported.
Pete Hegseth will not be able to parachute into the Senate
The governor of Tennessee has rejected the wild idea that she would help Trump get rid of the embattled Defense Secretary, per a source who spoke with Punchbowl’s Jake Sherman:

[Pete Hegseth] is not being considered [for Senate]. This is nothing more than Washington, D.C., spin from a bunch of consultants with nothing better to do. The Blackburn team is focused on the transition, not entertaining baseless speculation. Dc won’t pick the next senator.
I’ve done a close read of the president’s social posts in the aftermath of the midterms rout, during which he appears to be trying a new tack:

This rebranding attempt is glaringly obvious if you scroll through Trump’s Truth Social feed. It actually won’t take long at all. Pre-election, @realDonaldTrump “truthed” and “retruthed” dozens of times per day. His posts often reflected the worst of the MAGA cesspool, from racist and Islamophobic diatribes to bizarre AI-generated trolling.

In contrast, Trump only put up three posts on Wednesday. The first featured screenshots of a New York Post story praising him for saving the Western hemisphere with his “Donroe Doctrine.” The next said, “Stock Market just hit another Record High,” without noting that might have something to do with the election results. Then on Wednesday night, Trump put up a post highlighting his effort to make daylight saving time permanent.
Meanwhile in President Trump’s mind
Yep, this really happened, and check out the new “VETO” hat on his desk, too:
Meanwhile at the White House
One of the GOP’s only gains
Rubio may resign from his 17 roles in the Trump administration

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is weighing whether to leave the Trump administration, people familiar with the matter said, as he considers his next moves following Republicans’ midterm elections wipeout this week.

Rubio and his advisers are going over options for his future, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussing internal deliberations. He hasn’t made a decision about whether to quit his posts as top US diplomat and national security adviser, and there is no timetable on a possible departure.
An earlier report from the Independent suggested he was also considering a 2028 run.
Maybe Trump just sucks at politics
On Tuesday night, our former colleague Jonathan Chait argued that the results have demonstrated, again, that Donald Trump is not some savvy political magician:

Whatever misgivings some Republicans may have about Trump’s character or his policies, many subscribe to the theory that, if nothing else, the man knows how to win. And his aura of mastery has extended beyond his followers to the Americans who most detest him. The disgust with which many liberals regard Trump is mixed with fear and envy. His powers of persuasion are a source of endless fascination. They have launched a thousand diner safaris to explore his mystical hold on Real America, and inspired innumerable Democratic activists and intellectuals to ponder how they could create a Trump of their own.

But Trump is not a winner. He is, for the most part, a loser. In 2016, he lost the national popular vote—that is, the measure of which candidate Americans wanted to win the election—by two percentage points. His party lost control of the House in the 2018 midterms. Trump lost reelection in 2020. His sole unambiguous victory came in 2024, when he faced the clumsy fill-in candidate for an unpopular administration, against which he prevailed, almost by default.
And now he has lost again.
‘Events actually mattered’

I had a long conversation with with the Cook Political Report’s Amy Walter about the meaning of the midterms. One of her big takeaways was how this election showed once again how nothing in politics is set in stone:

Events actually mattered. We went through COVID and January 6th and inflation in 2022 and Harris being the new nominee in 2024, and it didn’t move the partisanship much. Not to say that this is a permanent reshuffling of it, but it is a marker now for just how far a president can push unpopular policies and agendas without backlash. It is a good, healthy reminder that our politics is never as set in stone as those of us who have to watch it every day often think it is, and that there’s no such thing as a permanent coalition in politics, even when it seems, as I said, that there is a calcification that’s impossible to break. Every now and then, it does. And it is an extraordinary thing to witness.
Colom’s small lead has grown in Mississippi
It’s now up to 1,724 votes as of Thursday afternoon.
What Democrats did well to win: Message
Here’s what Democratic pollster David Shor told our old friend Eric Levitz over at Vox:

I think the Democratic leadership and both wings of the Democratic Party — the left and the “establishment” or whatever — deserve a lot of credit for making big, concrete shifts in their messaging; specifically, focusing more on economic issues that affect people’s everyday lives. That was not a given. It was not uncontroversial at the time. And it paid dividends.

Right before the 2024 election, Republicans had a 12-point trust advantage on the cost of living. Today, among 2026 voters, Democrats actually have the trust advantage on the issue, which continues to be voters’ No. 1 concern by far.

We ask voters questions like, “What do you think the Democratic Party cares about?” And when we asked that question a year after the 2024 election, voters thought Democrats prioritized catering to their base over the cost of living by 4 to 1.

When we ran that survey again right before this year’s election, voters thought Democrats cared about the cost of living more than anything else, just like them. They thought Democrats’ second concern was fighting Donald Trump, which maybe wasn’t a total positive. But then No. 3 was healthcare and No. 4 was the economy. And so Democrats really did execute a big pivot.
How did El-Sayed fare among Jewish voters?
