items.title: 15 Eye-Popping Facts About Tuesday’s Midterms
items.description: While polling largely predicted Tuesday would be a good night for the Democratic Party, few were prepared for the sheer extent of the party’s successes in the 2026 midterms — victories that extended from the U.S. Capitol to statehouses across the nation. But b
items.author: Nia Prater; Chas Danner
paragraphs: While polling largely predicted Tuesday would be a good night for the Democratic Party, few were prepared for the sheer extent of the party’s successes in the 2026 midterms — victories that extended from the U.S. Capitol to statehouses across the nation. But beyond the marquee wins of a blue Texas and Congress returning to Democratic control, the night saw some other eye-catching developments. From an Iowa Democrat who won their race despite dropping out weeks earlier to the defeat of the Republican Party’s congressional campaign head, here are some notable details you might’ve missed about the results.
The congressman who ran the House GOP’s midterms strategy lost his seat

North Carolina was home to some of the Democratic Party’s most notable wins, including Democratic governor Roy Cooper flipping Republican senator Thom Tillis’s seat and winning several U.S. House races despite a statewide gerrymander designed to prevent those wins. Most notably, one of the seats lost in the blue tsunami belonged to Richard Hudson, a 13-year incumbent who was also the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, the party’s House campaign arm. Hudson, who was tasked with leading Republicans’ House campaign strategy, lost his 13th Congressional District seat to Richard Ojeda, a Democratic retired U.S. Army major.

Hudson’s loss is reminiscent of what happened to Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee chairman Sean Patrick Maloney in 2022 as the congressman lost his bid in New York’s 17th Congressional District to then–Republican state assemblymember Mike Lawler.
Cindy Hyde-Smith likely lined up her own demise

One of the most unexpected stories of the night is undoubtedly Scott Colom, the Democratic Mississippi district attorney who is on the brink of becoming the state’s first Black senator elected since Reconstruction. While the slim margin between him and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith is still being tallied (as of Friday afternoon, Colom currently leads by just under 2,000 votes), a Colom win would allow him to get a little revenge over the sitting senator.

In 2022, Colom’s nomination to be a federal judge on the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi was blocked by Hyde-Smith, who refused to return her blue slip, a Senate custom that allows senators to sign off on judicial nominations for their state. With Colom being only 43 years old, it’s likely he’d still be on the bench today had Hyde-Smith let his nomination through.
Marsha Blackburn nearly lost the Tennessee governors’ race

Republican senator Marsha Blackburn is poised to make history as Tennessee’s first female governor. But her victory nearly failed to come to pass as her Democratic opponent, Memphis councilwoman Jerri Green, came within striking distance. With 95 percent of the vote in, Blackburn received 45.5 percent of the vote to Green’s 43 percent, a figure likely too close for comfort.
A Democrat almost won Bill Cassidy’s Senate seat in Louisiana

The blue tsunami that saw Democrats flip Senate seats in Texas, Kansas, and Maine was close to sweeping Louisiana away from Republicans as well. Republican congresswoman Julia Letlow, who defeated incumbent Bill Cassidy following an endorsement by President Trump, just barely held on to become Louisiana’s next senator. With 95 percent of the vote tallied, Letlow stands at 50.9 percent to her opponent, Democratic farmer Jamie Davis, who received 49.1 percent, a nearly two-point difference.
Early votes for Talarico, Cooper, and Ossoff surpassed their opponents’ total votes.

Texas’s official election results showed James Talarico received 4,397,474 early votes. The figure is actually larger than the total number of votes Ken Paxton received overall at 4,249,373, a difference of 148,101. The incoming senator-elect could’ve made history even with just the early vote. NBC’s Decision Desk discovered similar dynamics for Georgia senator Jon Ossoff as well as North Carolina senator-elect Roy Cooper, who received more votes in early voting than his Republican opponent, Michael Whatley, won in total.
The Indiana GOP’s resistance to gerrymandering may have saved them from a blowout

Indiana Republicans found themselves out of President Trump’s good graces as the state legislators resisted a push from the White House to adopt an aggressive gerrymander aimed at making the state’s districts redder ahead of the midterm elections. But as one Indianapolis city councilor noted on social media, Democrats likely would’ve swept through the state had the gerrymander gone through:
One of the admirals Pete Hegseth purged won Nancy Mace’s House seat in South Carolina

Last summer, Vice-Admiral Nancy Lacore, then the chief of the Navy Reserve, was fired from her role by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth as part of his ongoing purge of U.S. military leadership and top officials. On Election Night, Lacore won her race to be the next congresswoman from South Carolina’s First Congressional District, flipping a seat previously held by outgoing Republican congresswoman Nancy Mace.
An Iowa Democrat won the race he dropped out of

On September 7, Eric Armstrong, a Democratic candidate for Iowa’s House District 20, announced that he would be stepping down from his campaign, citing “personal health issues that require my full attention and immediate care.”

By Election Day, Armstrong somehow found himself a winner, emerging victorious in a race he dropped out of and defeating Republican Keith Jones by about ten points, per the Des Moines Register. The surprise result was, no doubt, a signal of the strength of Democratic enthusiasm in Iowa, a wave that helped carry Josh Turek, whose seat Armstrong won, to the U.S. Senate.
In an interview with the New York Times following his unexpected win, Armstrong said he was “going to do my best to represent” his district even amid his continuing health issues.
The top Republican in the California Assembly almost lost his seat to a Democrat who spent nothing
A progressive is crushing a six-term House GOP incumbent by a 2-1 margin in central California

David Valadao, a moderate representing the heavily Latino 22nd Congressional District in California’s Central Valley, has served six terms in the House and is the sole remaining Republican in Congress who voted to impeach President Trump.

He’s only once before lost his seat, in the 2018 midterms, by 862 votes. (He then won the seat back in 2020.) This year, with 57 percent of the vote in, Democratic challenger Randy Villegas is beating Valadao by more than 33 percentage points.
Data centers were rejected in 40 out of 41 ballot measures

While data centers emerged as a top issue among voters relatively late in the election cycle, a clear message was sent on Tuesday as states across the country approved measures limiting the facilities. The Washington Post reports that voters in at least 38 different jurisdictions voted in favor of ballot measures that placed restrictions on data centers or even outright banned them from their communities.
According to a CNBC analysis, only one of 41 ballot measures across ten states centered on restricting data centers failed.
Democrats will now run the elections in 16 out of 17 swing states
Democrats made significant gains in secretary of State races Tuesday night, keeping the chief election-official roles in party hands ahead of the 2028 election cycle. Bolts magazine has a breakdown:

Out of the states that elected a secretary of state this fall, Democrats swept the swing states, and then some. They won all blue states, plus every state that Trump had won by up to 12 percentage points just two years ago.
They also secured the power to choose who runs elections in many other states — such as Texas, or Pennsylvania — where the secretary of state is appointed.

Out of all 17 states with the tightest 2024 presidential margins, the only one where the GOP is on track to control election administration moving forward is North Carolina — and that’s only because of a Republican power-grab in late 2024 to seize control from the Democratic governor.
75 percent of Americans will now be governed by Democrats
The vast majority of Americans will have a Democratic governor after the party flipped seats in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Nevada, and Iowa while holding onto power in states like Wisconsin and Michigan.
Two teen Democrats won state races

Two young Democrats were among Tuesday’s winners in their state races. Maricopa County, the fourth-most-populous county in the nation, just elected 19-year-old Sebastian Matta to become the next Superior Clerk for Maricopa County. Matta, a student at Arizona State University, defeated his opponent, Republican Jeff Dial, to win the seat.

In Massachusetts, Daniel Darris-O’Connor, also 19, defeated incumbent Republican state representative Marc Lombardo, who has held his seat since 2011. Darris-O’Connor was elected to his hometown’s select board last year, becoming its youngest member.
Joe Manchin went 0-6 in midterm endorsements

Joe Manchin, the former Democratic senator turned independent, has focused his post-congressional life on helping to support and elect independent political candidates largely through the Independent Leadership Council, which he founded with his daughter. Through the organization and in his personal capacity, Manchin expressed his support for a number of candidates across the political spectrum.

In the Senate, he said he supported former congressman Mike Rogers in Michigan and went on to endorse Maine Republican senator Susan Collins’s reelection bid, as well as Seth Bodnar’s Independent campaign in Montana. Then in the House, Manchin endorsed long-standing moderate Republican Brian Fitzpatrick’s reelection bid in Pennsylvania as well as Independents like Michael Bridgford in Iowa and the reelection campaign of California incumbent Kevin Kiley, who left the Republican Party earlier this year. But all six candidates would go on to lose their races.

items.title: Is Trump Trying to Save the Oval Office From Himself?
items.description: Since Tuesday’s catastrophic GOP midterms losses, Donald Trump has been soothing himself with his favorite hobby: turning Washington, D.C., into a gaudy shrine to himself. Soon, he may not even have that: Democrats are already talking about ways Congress might
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Since Tuesday’s catastrophic GOP midterms losses, Donald Trump has been soothing himself with his favorite hobby: turning Washington, D.C., into a gaudy shrine to himself. Soon, he may not even have that: Democrats are already talking about ways Congress might thwart his White House ballroom project, and on Thursday a judge blocked construction on Trump’s arch near Arlington National Cemetery as legal challenges make their way through the courts.

So it makes sense, on an emotional level, that Trump is trying to protect the Oval Office, as it’s the one renovation project he has near-total control over. But in the realm of logic, nothing about his proclamation designating the Oval Office and adjacent Cabinet room as national monuments makes a lick of sense.

The proclamation itself really has no legal force. As the AP noted, “Trump himself has reversed national monument designations made by his predecessors.” Trump said he would ask Congress to ratify the proclamation. But it’s unclear why Congress would rush to adopt the president’s wording when he’s repeatedly refused to obtain their authorization for his various D.C. construction projects.
Talking to reporters on Thursday afternoon, Trump said the goal of his first post-midterms executive action was to make these spaces “a landmark for the ages.”

“It won’t be able to be taken down, destroyed, touched, or anything else,” Trump said. “It’s a federal landmark. And when completed, and when we get the documentation fully done, legally binding, it’ll make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space.”

All the proclamation actually does is “proclaim the Oval Office as the Oval Office National Monument.” The document acknowledges that the entire White House is already “recognized as a National Historic Landmark,” but it says the Oval Office still “merits specific recognition” as a “discrete historic structure of national significance.”

You might assume Trump is trying to preserve all the gold junk he’s put up in the Oval Office, some of which he superglued with his own two hands. However, it specifically states that future president can redecorate as they please:

Nothing in this proclamation shall be construed to restrict the President’s authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument’s historic structure or architectural character.

The proclamation directs the Interior secretary to form a management plan that “prioritizes the preservation of the monument’s structural and significant architectural features,” and ensures that there’s a thorough review before any action that would “substantially alter or demolish” the rooms.
Basically, the goal is to make sure no one tears down the Oval Office. Trump gave reporters the example of a future president saying “Let’s make it square,” adding, per the Daily Beast:

I just thought it was very important that nobody be allowed to come in and take it down and try and do something with it, because every once in a while they’ll look and they’ll say, “Oh, maybe what we’ll do is we’ll put some glass that’s a little bit better or something.” And I’d say, “No, you’re not going to do anything.” We’re going to leave this as it is.

The only person you could imagine doing such a thing is Donald Trump himself. If the president really wants to preserve the Oval Office, he’d be better off putting a Post-it on his bathroom mirror that says, “Do not destroy more parts of the White House today.”

items.title: The Midterm Wave Was Hate-Powered
items.description: It’s a political truism that midterm elections are referenda on the party controlling the White House, and thus Donald Trump’s dreadful job-approval ratings are the simplest explanation for the huge Democratic gains posted on November 3. But in what that means
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: It’s a political truism that midterm elections are referenda on the party controlling the White House, and thus Donald Trump’s dreadful job-approval ratings are the simplest explanation for the huge Democratic gains posted on November 3. But in what that means for future elections, it’s important to understand that voters who reject a president’s party in the midterms won’t necessarily support the opposition party in future elections. In an era with a serious substratum of unhappiness with politics and government generally and a mistrust of any and all institutions, party affiliation can be a slippery thing. And thus many political observers have focused on voters who dislike both major political parties as important to the competition between them.

More often than not, these so-called double haters have been relatively friendly to Trump, perhaps because he has always posed as an anti-Establishment “disrupter” or simply because he’s a world-class hater himself. In 2016, one of the keys of his upset win over Hillary Clinton was that he carried the 18 percent of voters who had unfavorable views of both candidates by a robust 17 percent margin. It was significant in 2020 that the number of “double haters” dropped all the way to 3 percent of the electorate, though Trump still won them by 17 percent. In 2024, voters who didn’t like either Trump or Harris represented 8 percent of the electorate, and Trump won them by a smashing 20 percent. Double haters split evenly in the 2018 midterms, but Republicans won this 11 percent of the electorate by 17 percent in 2022.

So it’s definitely worth noting that in 2026, according to the latest exit-poll data, double haters bounced back up to 15 percent of the electorate and Democrats carried them by 28 percent (61 percent to 33 percent). Will these voters stick with Democrats in 2028? We obviously don’t know yet, but there’s no reason to assume they will. Presidential elections are typically comparative by nature instead of a referendum on the people running the country. Despite a Democratic skew in the 2026 electorate (those who previously voted in 2024 tilted to Kamala Harris by 5 percent, though some may be misremembering or misrepresenting their votes), the Democratic Party’s favorability rating was 47 percent positive and 52 percent negative. Only 16 percent of 2026 voters were “strongly favorable” toward the Democratic Party, while 35 percent were “strongly unfavorable.” Democrats rightly celebrating their wave election shouldn’t start singing “Happy Days Are Here Again” just yet. They may control Congress in 2027 but don’t command a reliable majority in public opinion or any positive mandate.

Donald Trump will not be on the ballot in 2028, and between now and then Democrats need to convince double haters to hate them less than Republicans in a comparative context, including one in which Democrats will be entirely in control of Congress. This challenge may be intensified by a wide-open 2028 Democratic presidential-nominating contest in which candidates may be focused more on appealing to reliable party-primary participants rather than the swing voters they will need in November. If conditions in the country worsen and such emerging existential issues as AI-related job loss explode into prominence, it’s even possible that long-suppressed support for minor parties, old or new, could finally threaten the two-party duopoly or at least affect the balance of power between Democrats and Republicans. So leaders and activists in both parties need to get over the midterms quickly and focus on the sales pitches they have to develop to win over voters who aren’t very fond of any of them.

items.title: The 13 Biggest Losers of the 2026 Midterms, Ranked
items.description: The 2026 midterms may have been a stunning string of victories for the Democratic Party, but it’s important that we also commemorate all the failures. Here’s a baker’s dozen, ranked in reverse order of loserhood:
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: The 2026 midterms may have been a stunning string of victories for the Democratic Party, but it’s important that we also commemorate all the failures. Here’s a baker’s dozen, ranked in reverse order of loserhood:
The Schumer-Jeffries Haters

White-hot progressive (or insurgent) rage at the two New Yorkers who head the minority caucuses in Congress was a regular feature of political life in the past two years of Democratic discontent. For years, Schumer has been widely mocked as an inept party messenger and strategist, and who can forget the excited progressives on New York’s primary night in June chanting “You’re Next!” when Hakeem Jeffries appeared on their television screens? Schumer’s getting pretty long in the tooth, and Jeffries may indeed be vulnerable to a primary challenge in his own district. But neither is going to be “purged” from a leadership post following this massive win. It’s probably already dawning on those hoping the democratic socialist “bloc” would form a powerful faction in the House that Jeffries’s majority will dwarf their numbers and also include a ton of new centrists representing districts Trump carried in 2024.

One very happy democratic socialist, though, is Nithya Raman, who is now projected to become the next mayor of America’s second-largest city, Los Angeles. But that means a very big 2026 loser is incumbent Democratic mayor Karen Bass, whose fortunes dropped rapidly when the outbreak of catastrophic wildfires in her city caught her on an overseas junket to Ghana. Raman was a Bass ally on the city council whose candidacy surprised, and then eventually removed, the mayor. More than likely, this is the end of a storied Bass career that flourished in the California legislature and in Congress before she came home to run her city.

At this point, Stevens still professes to be a Democrat despite talk of booting her out of the House Caucus during her final weeks in Congress. But her shocking last-minute endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers against the candidate who defeated her in Michigan’s August Senate primary, Abdul El-Sayed, turned out to be, among other things, a very bad bet. El-Sayed won by 7 percent, more than his lead in some preelection polls, and it’s possible Stevens’s effort to sabotage him actually increased his votes. In any event, her treacherous behavior and the erratic character it exposed have left her with a lot fewer friends and virtually no admirers.
Conservative Judicial Activists

A lot of people who otherwise aren’t big fans of Donald Trump have nonetheless supported him because of his success in stacking the federal judiciary–and most crucially the U.S. Supreme Court–with constitutional “originalists” and other products of the conservative legal movement. His power to do so (at least without lots of compromises with Democrats) ended with the destruction of the GOP’s Senate Majority. And the stubborn refusal of Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas to retire and give Republicans a chance to choose younger successors will now create a significant drought of SCOTUS appointments, particularly since the size of Democratic Senate gains makes it unlikely that Republicans will retake the chamber in 2028. Too bad Alito ruled out a 2026 retirement that might have created the brief opportunity to confirm a Trump appointment during the upcoming lame-duck session.
Republican Congressional Leaders

If Schumer and Jeffries are now secure, for a while, in their leadership posts, their GOP counterparts are toast. Perhaps in reality, Republicans can blame Trump almost entirely for the midterm debacle, but (a) John Thune and especially Mike Johnson did little to interfere with his agenda and his domination of GOP messaging and (b) culpability aside, you don’t get to continue as leaders if you lose that precious gavel and do so by such an enormous margin. It’s unclear to whom House and Senate Republicans will turn given their shared responsibility for toadying to Trump and pursuing a failed message. But in any event, they’re probably stuck with the current leaders during the very significant lame-duck session that will begin next week. That can’t be great for party morale.

The self-styled Secretary of War was already slated to be an impeachment target during the soon-to-convene lame-duck session thanks to a resolution from outgoing anti-Trump Republican Thomas Massie. More generally, Hegseth is by far the most convenient target for congressional Democrats, whose leaders will almost certainly try to create alternatives to a third impeachment of Trump himself. Aside from his regularly obnoxious conduct and his over-the-top Christian nationalist worldview, he’s very much the symbol of an unpopular Iran War that Democrats want to exploit if they cannot end it. And even if Hegseth cannot be convicted by the Senate, the heat could convince the president to sack him, as some reports indicate he is already thinking about doing.

One of the most shocking developments of the midterms was the U.S. Senate victory of Democrat Annie Andrews in the conservative bastion of South Carolina, flipping a seat Lindsey Graham and Strom Thurmond had held for 68 years. While the national Democratic wave and Trump’s constant interventions in South Carolina elections had something to do with this GOP catastrophe, some of the blame must be assigned to Lindsey’s little sister, appointed and then defeated senator Darline Graham. It was understandable that she received a courtesy appointment to serve out the final months of her brother’s term after his sudden death in July. But she then insisted on running for a full term despite limited political experience and no known views on major issues (especially the foreign-policy issues on which Lindsey was most focused). This definitely annoyed the horde of Palmetto State Republican pols who would have done anything to occupy a precious Senate seat, and some even openly slow-walked any support for Darline. In the end, she inherited both her brother’s baggage (he never fully earned the trust of South Carolina conservatives) and Trump’s, and added some of her own. In a terrible year for her party, she sank to the occasion.

This health-care billionaire came out of nowhere to push aside Trump’s designated candidate for governor of Georgia and then outspent Democratic candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms by an enormous margin, yet ultimately led his party to an ass-kicking unlike anything outside of Texas. Outgoing two-term Republican governor Brian Kemp probably remains the most popular politician in his state, but Jackson and his ticket mates squandered all that political capital, losing every single statewide office, not even coming close to threatening Senator Jon Ossoff, and astonishingly losing control of the statehouse in the bargain. It was by far the worst election year for the Georgia GOP since 1998, and defeated Republicans will long be haunted in their dreams by Jackson’s incredibly redundant autobiographical ads.

The hypereccentric and intensely reactionary trillionaire was doubly involved in the 2026 midterms. His wildly destructive DOGE regime tainted Trump’s second term indelibly, right off the bat. And then having feuded with and reconciled with the president, Musk made a vast and unprecedented personal investment in the GOP midterm campaign. He spent an estimated $474 million on GOP races and super-PACs — close to half of it in Texas alone, mostly in an effort to rescue Senate candidate Ken Paxton. His ROI was next to nothing, and indeed, he might have personally proved for all time that money cannot buy an election without a lot of help from smart politicians and, well, objective reality.

The giant money sink and scandal magnet named Ken Paxton may deserve his own spot on this list, but I dunno, the many losers among Texas Republicans are all worthy recipients of a raspberry. Governor Greg Abbott typified the arrogance and extremism of the Texas GOP during his 12 years in office. Unlike Paxton, he didn’t have to wage a wildly expensive primary fight this year. And for all of Gina Hinojosa’s many merits, she didn’t have James Talarico’s national buzz and incredible fundraising chops. Yet Abbott lost to her by over 700,000 votes and took the entire statewide Republican ticket, and his party’s control of the statehouse, down with him. Their humiliation was richly earned over a long, long time.
The White House Political Team

Probably no one group of Americans in politics has received more undeserved credit for brilliance than Donald Trump’s White House political team. To be sure, Susie Wiles and Chris LaCivita, the co-chairs of Trump’s 2024 comeback campaign, as well as James Blair, that campaign’s political director, did a fine job of plucking the ripe fruit of the Biden administration’s many problems and guiding the 45th president through to his inauguration. On the most superficial level, Trump 2.0 was less chaotic under their management than Trump 1.0. But in many respects, that just meant Trump was free to pursue his own worst instincts and his political team did little if anything to restrain him. Now, in the wake of the midterm disaster, the long knives are out for these erstwhile geniuses, as Jake Lahut reported.

In assessing J.D. Vance’s political chops in view of what just happened, it’s important to remember that he ran for office only once before catching a ride on Trump’s 2024 coattails and by most accounts underperformed in his own 2022 Ohio Senate campaign. As vice-president, he has tried to carry out the traditional attack-dog chores of a veep but has been consistently outclassed by his boss in the hard work of lying and smearing opponents, while showing himself to be an awkward communicator who is dangerously too online for real-world politics. Now, his political shortcomings have been graphically illustrated by the GOP’s poor performance in Vance’s home state; one moment that stands out was Vance’s aggressive defense of a nasty Vivek Ramaswamy ad that some Republicans condemned and virtually all regretted. With his Ohio base devastated, the big question now is whether the mantle of heir apparent to Trump as leader of the MAGA movement and presidential front-runner is still his and still worth its obvious downside. Unfortunately for him, Vance is still stuck in Trump’s shadow, chained to his unpopular agenda, and more or less powerless without his blessing. He can’t break with Trump but perhaps can’t really live down to his legend, either. He’s looking screwed.

This leads inevitably to the unquestioned author of the midterms, the president whose unpopularity afflicted every GOP candidate yet who insisted day after day that voters forget about the actual names on the ballot and instead think only of him. His brash 2024 promises about lowering living costs came back to bite him again and again, and instead of doing anything about it, he expressed fury at struggling Americans for their lack of gratitude toward his incredibly successful and benevolent rule. He loaded his Cabinet with personalities so clownish you expected them to show up in public with big floppy shoes and round red noses. He began a war of choice with Iran that made all his other problems immeasurably worse, and he appeared helpless to stop himself from waging it ineffectually. And his personal conduct and rhetoric steadily deteriorated to the point where even his legendary rallies were filled with empty seats and restless people. Ending the midterm campaign with a long speech touting the monuments to himself that he was building capped it all off perfectly.

Going forward, the question is whether Trump has lost interest in the non-ceremonial parts of his job and is equally incapable of fighting or working with the Democrats who now firmly control Congress. It’s going to be a long two years before his scheduled departure from office, and he’s looking more and more like poor, lost George W. Bush in the sad denouement of his own presidency. It may even be worse. Perhaps for the country, that sort of presidency is better than a return to furious relevance for Donald Trump, but for his party, it’s as bad as the Election Night returns so terrible that he couldn’t even pretend to have won.
- Trump Is Going Full Stephen Miller: Live Updates
- Stephen Miller’s Promotion Is a Chilling Sign for Final Trump Years
- 15 Eye-Popping Facts About Tuesday’s Midterms

items.title: To emerge from under an analogue rock, sometimes all it takes is tidying up your home screen
items.description: If someone asked me to list the reasons that my relationship has endured several decades and all the twists and turns that we have encountered en route, I would say love, a shared sense of humour, ice cream and margaritas. But he and I both know that what real
items.author: Andrew Tuck; Amelia Edwards
paragraphs: If someone asked me to list the reasons that my relationship has endured several decades and all the twists and turns that we have encountered en route, I would say love, a shared sense of humour, ice cream and margaritas. But he and I both know that what really binds us is that, without him, I would struggle to turn on the toaster. I am endlessly thwarted by technology. Left alone in the house for a week, I revert to living like an Elizabethan, dining on leftovers (the food-ordering apps are on his phone). I find myself wishing that we had a harpsichord to play a few tunes on when the TV media muddle defies my requests. My partner, however, loves technology. They have a thing going on. At dinner parties, I soon realise that we have been invited not because of my glittering wit but because our hosts need him to rewire their Sonos.

This week he had the temerity to travel to Los Angeles just as I was setting up my lovely new iPhone, a manoeuvre that most weaning babies would be able to complete unaided. Now I am a little haphazard in writing down the passwords for anything, including the app on my phone where I store the few that I have logged. He, on the other hand, has each one, including mine, and is usually very happy to remind me of the magic code in question. But this week I discovered that there is a limit to how many times you can phone your partner during important briefings. “What is it now, darling?” he said I thought a little testily during one such interruption. “Is it urgent or can I call you back?” I assured him that it was indeed urgent. I might have rashly used the word “critical”. He stepped out of the meeting. “What’s up?”
“I cannot find the password for Duolingo,” I explained, “and I am worried about losing my 2,800-day streak.”

Now some of these things, including how cosy I felt going to bed, were clearly down to him to sort, despite the time difference. He has insisted on us trying this hi-tech mattress cover that can heat or cool each side of the bed to different temperatures. Because even here we diverge: he likes it hot; I am a chillier kind of person. Yes, he has put the app that controls the device on my phone but, even if he tells you differently, he never gave me the password. So when I got under the duvet and it was warm enough to smoke a kipper, I had to call him yet again. By now he was looking through the phone book for an LA divorce lawyer.

There are other things that I have rolled with. I seem to have done something to my notifications and this week, while in London every day, I have been sent special offers galore by UAE delivery and taxi company Careem (I happen to know that there’s a flash sale on bananas and Nada Greek yoghurt today). Perhaps intuiting the sparseness of my provisions, even my UK train app asked whether I needed a burger delivered.

Last night, determined to take back control, I thought that I might cull some of the long-neglected apps that have transferred to my shiny new phone. But even if they were unused, I felt oddly sad about erasing their little tiles. There was the cute Gojek app that had once helped me navigate Jakarta’s traffic-knotted streets on motorcycle taxis. It would be sad to obliterate that. And the SPTH app that we had needed to enter Spain during the coronavirus pandemic. That’s a piece of history. They all stayed.

Then there were the credit-card apps. One wanted me to verify my account again and, as proof of identity, asked me to upload one of three things: a deed poll, a marriage certificate or a divorce certificate. They might as well have asked for the Dead Sea Scrolls and the original Magna Carta. I phoned the number on the card and explained that I might be able to get the divorce certificate but it wouldn’t be available until my other half got home from LA. Meanwhile, my photos – all 78,580 of them – transferred with ease. Perhaps that would be a good place to do some tidying up. I could delete duplicates and duffs. I managed to get the number down to 78,572 in less than an hour.

At this point I am feeling pretty smug. There are still a few things for him to sort when he finally gets home. But I can finally stop searching for “harpsichord” on Ebay and look forward to rejoining the 21st century this weekend. Hurrah.

items.title: Our ‘Design Directory’ 2026: The architects, studios and designers to know around the world
items.description: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the coun
items.author: Kate Lucey
paragraphs: As the stories in our Design Directory have demonstrated, the global design industry is thriving. Here we have compiled an international directory of the firms, studios and individuals at the top of their game, drawing on the crafts and vernaculars of the countries where they work to produce objects and buildings that enhance our lives.

Europe’s architectural and design landscape has a rich history, from ancient castles and cathedrals to modernist masterpieces. Contemporary designers are using this as a foundation for cutting-edge adaptive reuse and the establishment of circular economies, setting global industry standards.
The country’s contemporary designers build on a foundation of secessionist art and early modernist rigour.
This Vorarlberg-based studio’s practice draws on the region’s timber-building traditions and exacting craftsmanship.
+43 5574 44440, bernardobader.com
Innsbruck architect behind light-filled houses, schools and rooftop extensions, with a gift for breathing new life into existing buildings.
Höttinger Auffahrt 11, Innsbruck
+43 5122 38601, fuegenschuh.at
Architecture studio known for designing markets, civic buildings and public spaces. Most recently, it completed Vienna’s Naschmarkt, a hybrid timber market hall and public green space.
Schottenfeldgasse 62/2/22, Vienna
+43 1 890 8921, mostlikely.at
Tapping into a storied heritage of art nouveau and Flemish urbanism, modern Belgian design is a leader in minimalist creativity.
Landscape architect who designs with the climate and microclimates in mind, working with prevailing conditions to create welcoming, self-sustaining environments.
Place Eugène Flagey 7, Brussels
+32 2 219 75 21, bassmets.be

Square Eugène Plasky 92-94, Brussels
Architect and designer (and Molteni creative director) renowned for creating pared-back, material-rich homes and furniture.
+32 3 205 91 90, vincentvanduysen.com
Studio that fuses branding and identity work to create engaging, narrative-driven spaces.
Hessenstraatje 1G, Antwerp
+32 3 290 62 73, wewantmore.studio

Renowned for its thoughtful, community-minded approach to schools and civic infrastructure, including an extension to Prague’s Deutsche Schule.
Vaclavske namesti 828/23, Prague
Adept at marrying old and new, this studio has worked on heritage sites, transformed historic city gates and made gentle additions to civic spaces.
Hollarovo namesti 2275/2, Prague
Architecture studio that turns neglected urban spaces such as underpasses into sculptural skateparks and lively public areas.
+420 724 819 859, uustudio.cz
A new generation of designers is now standing on the shoulders of the country’s mid-century masters, ensuring that Denmark remains a leader in functional minimalism.
Cassandra Bradfield and Sofia Olsson’s studio for material-focused interiors and objects, spanning hospitality, retail and homes.
Sturlasgade 14, Copenhagen
Copenhagen studio that designs galleries, boutiques and furniture with crisp geometry and warm materials.
+45 22 25 65 47, atelier-axo.com
Designer making elegant utilitarian objects, from chairs and speakers to lamps and textiles.
+45 26 25 10 34, ceciliemanz.com
Danish-Italian duo fusing Nordic craft with Italian conceptual rigour, making furniture for the likes of Gubi, Koyori and Porro.
Vermundsgade 40B, Copenhagen
+45 51 90 01 17, gamfratesi.com
Founded in 1959, Henning Larsen is celebrated for light-filled civic buildings such as Reykjavik’s glittering Harpa concert hall.
Vesterbrogade 76, Copenhagen
Furniture designer winning awards for her sculptural contemporary updates to Denmark’s traditional design heritage.
+45 51 29 78 20, mariabruun.com
Danish practice with Japanese sensibilities creating pared-back furniture and restaurant, retail and hotel interiors.
Forbindelsesvej 12, Copenhagen
Nature-based studio of landscape architects and biologists creating biodiverse parks and urban spaces.
Njalsgade 17B, Pakhus 2, Copenhagen
Cross-disciplinary studio that specialises in world-building, combining architecture, scenography and furniture design.
The home of organic modernism, Finland has a contemporary scene that celebrates natural materials and human-centred design, while making room for new ideas and technological innovations too.
Helsinki practice that champions traditional construction materials and methods, such as the use of solid brick and natural ventilation.
Punavuorenkatu 1, Helsinki
Storied interiors firm that has completed more than 1,600 workplaces, schools and public spaces since its foundation in 1972.
Established by the late Yrjö Kukkapuro and run by his daughter, this Kauniainen-based museum continues to release colourful, playful archival designs.
+358 9 505 1080, studiokukkapuro.com
French design expands on centuries of haute-couture craftsmanship, pairing new technologies with exceptional handicrafts.
Design practice that plays with form and materiality to create sculptural, geometric architecture, interiors and furniture.
+33 1 71 20 31 01, corpus.studio
Dorothée Meilichzon’s studio weaves local history into cinematic hotels, bars, restaurants and lounges.

+49 69 82368081, sebastianherkner.com

+30 210 331 2860, objectsofcommoninterest.com

+39 02 0995 9003, studioklass.com
Creative agency responsible for the lived-in Simple Flair Apartments in Milan and New York that double as design showcases.
Milan studio that has a well-earned reputation for its warm, minimalist interiors and solid-wood furniture.
+39 02 3293 2044, studioutte.com

Yvonne Farrell and Shelley McNamara’s Pritzker Architecture Prize-winning practice reshapes communities for the better with its cultural, civic and housing projects.
12-14 College Green, Dublin
+353 1 671 3365, graftonarchitects.ie

30 Mountjoy Square, Dublin

Architecture studio working across interiors, identity and more.
+47 400 03 032, oslo.works

Architect, urbanist and graphic designer interested in housing and its intersections with sociology, economics and sustainability.

Alessi is expanding its celebrated kitchen range with this screw-themed moka pot, which takes inspiration from machinery in the company’s factory.

London-based designer Philippe Malouin worked with Italian brand Alessi to create this take on the stovetop moka pot. The piece draws inspiration from the threads of screws, with its spiral ridges and grooves referencing the twisting motion used to assemble the pot – making aesthetics part of the pot’s intuitive use. Its lower chamber is made from die-cast aluminium and its upper section features a heat-resistant thermoplastic-resin handle. Its colours are taken from the surfaces of machinery inside the Alessi factory. Adding to its appeal is the fact that it features a magnetic steel base that works on induction, gas and electric stoves.
Rediscover the joy of traditional film photography with this revamped camera design.

Kodak has provided an upgrade to the traditional plastic disposable camera with its new 35mm film model, the Snapic A1. It features a sharp three-element glass lens for crisp images, a two-zone focus (which allows you to switch quickly between close-up portraits and wide landscape shots) and a built-in flash. It also has a wide focal length that keeps scenes sharp: perfect for everything from travel and street photography to casual indoor shoots. The main appeal, though, is in its simplicity.
Free from distractions such as digital screens or phone apps, the Snapic A1’s pared-back design keeps its user in the moment and on the task.
Fiio CP13 Portable Cassette Player
Chinese brand Fiio plugs into the trend for retro audio players with this superior throwback.

Though China has long been disparaged as the home of cheaply made electronics, its new domestic makers are proving that the country has the manufacturing chops for quality audio. Analogue tapes are enjoying a resurgence in popularity (fans point to the allure of being able to “own” music) and Guangzhou-based Fiio’s CP13 Portable Cassette Player has found its way into New York’s Museum of Modern Art shop. It features old-school physical buttons, while its modern touches include USB-C charging and a 13-hour battery life.
The CP13’s 13 hours of continuous playback marks a significant improvement on the classic Sony Walkman.
Hay Outdoor Market Fire Pit
Light up your garden party or campsite with this versatile portable fireplace and cooker.

Designed in collaboration with Jasper Morrison, this fire pit brings to life the London-based product designer’s “super normal” ethos – an approach that aims to make everyday objects feel essential. Made by Danish brand Hay, its stainless-steel construction is portable, making it equally at home on a terrace or a trail. More than just an outdoor fireplace, it doubles as a cooker, thanks to its removable grill and charcoal basket.
There’s something about a fire pit that lights up our brains. Humans have evolved to associate flames with warmth, nourishment, safety and connection.
Looking for guides to visionary contemporary architects and era-defining design movements? Here’s our pick of five books to add to your shelf.
Published by oro Editions, Chairman is a new monograph documenting chair designs by London-based Yinka Ilori.
Oríkì: Material Affirmations in Three Acts from Apartamento Publishing is the debut work of Nigerian designer Nifemi Marcus-Bello, telling the story of a three-part sculptural series.

The Albanian Files: Freedom and Architecture, published by Lars Müller, chronicles two decades of urban change in the Balkan country. Tadao Ando has released Towards Light, which outlines his philosophies on life and architecture.
Riverside Modern explores the homes of Melbourne’s Studley Park, with photography by Jack Lovel.

The challenge for any specialist design publisher is to blend the academic with the entertaining. A good architectural book should translate complex information into inspiring, visually engaging content that also pushes readers to build better.
The Monocle Design Awards 2026: The best homeware and equipment

items.title: From historic emporiums to literary cafés: Our favourite bookshops in Barcelona
items.description: In a city where tourism is increasingly seen as a threat to local culture, Barcelona’s independent bookshops are thriving. Even as cinemas close and small music venues disappear, the city’s number of bookshops has climbed to 140, a 30 per cent increase since 2
items.author: Julia Webster Ayuso; Tabitha Sipp
paragraphs: In a city where tourism is increasingly seen as a threat to local culture, Barcelona’s independent bookshops are thriving. Even as cinemas close and small music venues disappear, the city’s number of bookshops has climbed to 140, a 30 per cent increase since 2008. According to the Catalan Guild of Booksellers, new openings have far surpassed closures in recent years, though some have struggled to keep their doors open.

In 2024, the threatened closure of the historic Llibreria Sant Jordi triggered weeks of public mobilisation. While it ultimately shut, it reopened a year later with a gastronomic offering. The episode underscored deeper anxieties over skyrocketing rents, the declining use of Catalan and the strain that a tourism-driven economy places on local life. And yet, while more retailers stock titles in English and other languages, Catalan-language publishing is growing too. Barcelona’s new wave of bookshops has become a valuable refuge for locals and foreigners alike.

Since launching as a small shop in Gràcia in 1962, Ona slowly built a reputation for its selection of Catalan literature. A few years ago, second-generation owner Montse Úbeda teamed up with entrepreneur Tatxo Benet to expand the business and, upon opening a 900 sq m space on Carrer Pau Claris in 2020, Ona became the world’s largest bookshop dedicated to Catalan-language books.

The boutique also stocks a selection of Catalan literature translated into 15 languages, from English to Mandarin. “We stock 1,500 references by authors who write in Catalan that have been translated into other languages,” says Ona’s director, Iolanda Batallé. “It’s painstaking work because we have to go publisher to publisher but we’re very proud of it.”

Ona has grown fivefold over the past six years, hosting book clubs, talks and live music in its café space, as well as a busy schedule of events in its vast children’s section. “Most bookshops have only about 30 per cent of books in Catalan because Spanish takes over,” says Batallé. “Shops like Ona are very important for the growth of the Catalan publishing industry.”
- Recommended novel: Ona director Iolanda Batallé is the author of I’ll Do Anything You Want, published in 2013
- Current bestsellers: Death in Spring and In Diamond Square by Mercè Rodoreda

When the longtime owner of Llibreria Sant Jordi, Josep Morales, passed away in 2024, the historic bookshop in Barcelona’s Gothic Quarter announced that it would be closing its doors. After an appeal urging book lovers to buy its remaining stock, hundreds of people turned up to purchase discounted books on art, photography, design and illustration. The event morphed into a spontaneous tribute to a local business which – with its listed 19th-century wooden shopfront – had been a fixture of the street since the early 1980s.

“The neighbours made it clear that they didn’t want yet another shop to close,” says Alba Biliotti, who now helps run the business under a new model. To the delight of locals, Llibreria Sant Jordi reopened its doors in December 2025 with most of its interiors unchanged. In the evenings after shoppers have left, the space transforms into a restaurant that hosts book clubs, literary discussions and dinners with authors. “Most people still come because it’s their local bookshop,” says Billiotti. “But now it has two different atmospheres. Some people come for dinner and walk out with a book, while others come to buy a book and end up staying for a drink.”
- On the menu: Piquillo peppers stuffed with cod brandade and caramelised foie with Kalamata olives and fig jam
- Current bestseller: The Little Frog’s Guide to Self-Care by Maybell Eequay

In 1980, four young women opened the doors of Laie on Barcelona’s Carrer de Pau Claris without much fanfare. “Back then it wasn’t customary to announce the opening of a bookshop; it wasn’t considered particularly newsworthy,” co-founder Conxita Guixà wrote for the shop’s 40th anniversary in 2020. “Perhaps three or four people came in during the first few hours.” Four decades later, Laie runs 35 outposts all over Spain, from Santiago de Compostela to Palma de Mallorca.

Fresh out of university, co-founders Conxita Guixà and Montse Moragas wanted to create a space dedicated to the humanities and critical thinking. It quickly became a meeting point for the city’s intellectuals, who would hide their favourite books in the wrong sections so that they could purchase them later. In the 1990s, a café and restaurant opened on the first floor. On any given day, you can still spot journalists, authors, playwrights and politicians conducting interviews or discussing book deals over a plate of ham croquetas or fish soup. “Gustavo Petro, the president of Colombia, walked in the other day and I had to act normal,” says literary director Damià Gallardo. “Laie has become a nerve centre of Barcelona’s culture; people have made it their own.”
- First book ever sold: An anthology by the Greek poet Giorgos Seferis
- Current bestseller: La Bola by Daniel Verdú, which was recently presented at the bookshop
- Recommended novel by Damià Gallardo: What I Loved by Siri Hustvedt

Huygens, a publisher dedicated to academic and educational titles, was planning to open its first bookshop in April 2020 when the coronavirus pandemic hit. When it finally opened months later, it was welcomed by locals who had rediscovered the pleasure of reading during Spain’s strict lockdowns. Founded by editor Mariana Sarrias and law professor Víctor M. Sánchez, Llibreria Byron – named after the British poet – opened with a café, quiet reading nooks and a space for events, designed with the ambition of giving neighbourhood residents a place to reconnect. “We decided to call it a bookshop but right from the start, we wanted it to be more than that: a place where culture is brought to life, not just sold in the form of books,” says Sarrias.

Byron has a large children’s and young-adult section, and a packed calendar of community events. Every Friday a group of neighbours from El Raval gathers for a philosophical coffee hour to debate a variety of questions from the dangers of consumerism to the role of uncertainty in daily life. These discussions often take place around a walnut-panelled fireplace that Sarrias found in an antiques shop and had restored before placing it at the heart of the shop. Though it’s powered by electricity, it still fulfils its intended purpose: to create a cosy, welcoming atmosphere for people to get lost in a book. In the evenings, Byron makes space for music too. The café’s grand piano is used for everything from jazz performances to renditions of Puccini’s Madama Butterfly.
- Recommended book: A Man Asleep by Georges Perec
- Poetry book-club pick: Hardly Creatures: Poems by Rob Colgate
- Bestselling Spanish-language book: Insular by Franco Chiaravalloti

Llibreria Finestres (Catalan for “windows”) opened in 2021 inside a modernist building by architect Enric Sagnier. Just a few steps from Passeig de Gràcia, the shop was designed by Quintana Partners and is furnished with carpets, sofas, well-lit reading nooks and a fireplace. The retailer describes itself as “a bookshop for reading”, where patrons are invited to curl up with a book inside or linger on the terrace with a glass of vermut.

A second location opened shortly after the first, dedicating its venue to comic books as well as publications on illustration and art. Thanks to its success, the business’s expansion has continued: another outpost arrived in the coastal town of Palamós last summer and in May, Finestres Palestina, an outlet devoted to Palestinian culture and literature, opened in the Gràcia neighbourhood. Designed by Valencia-based Palestinian architect Malek Murad Mateu, the latest addition features bright green sculptural bookshelves, hand-woven rugs and an indoor fountain inlaid with a mosaic map of Palestine.

Run by the Finestres Foundation, the bookshop is also behind several literary awards and writers’ residencies. Its impressively multilingual selection includes titles in English, French, Italian, German, Portuguese, Galician and Basque, alongside Spanish and Catalan.
- Phones off: The poor signal inside the shop serves as an unexpected advantage, stopping notifications and incoming calls from interrupting your browsing session
- A line from its foundational manifesto: “We know that there are a lot of bookshops in the city. We also noticed that there are even more readers than bookshops.”

After several bookshops in Catalonia closed following the 2008 financial crisis, journalist and writer Isabel Sucunza and historian Abel Cutillas teamed up in 2014 to open a space to showcase the work of new small publishing houses. Named after Catalan writer Pere Calders, who lived in the Sant Antoni neighbourhood in his later years, Llibreria Calders occupies a former button factory in a small alley. It has gathered a loyal following for prioritising local authors over bestsellers. “At the time there were very few independent bookshops in Barcelona,” says Sucunza. “There also wasn’t a single one named after an author.”

The space resembles a vast wine cellar, with dark bookcases set against bare stone walls. Customers seek it out for its well-stocked poetry section, as well as its selection of titles on theatre and dramatic theory. “Poetry wasn’t so central to the bookshop at first but as soon as we started hosting recitals, we noticed that there was a huge demand for it,” says Sucunza. Readers can continue to pay homage to one of Catalonia’s most famed writers at the nearby bar, Calders, which serves “dishes of exile” inspired by the author’s banishment to Mexico after the Spanish Civil War.
- Books recently presented at the bookshop: A new Catalan translation of Homer’s Odyssey by Pau Sabaté
- All-time favourite book: The Day of the Watusi by Francisco Casavella, a coming-of-age novel about Barcelona from the Spanish Transition to the eve of the 1992 Olympic Games
- Number of titles in stock: Between 10,000 and 12,000

A bookshop that specialises in art publications occupies a former shoe boutique on the corner of a 19th-century building in Sant Antoni. When the space became available in 2020, it caught the eye of Lucía Bonet and Luis Cerveró, who had long dreamt of opening a dedicated outpost of their publishing house, Terranova.

With the help of furniture design studio Owl, the pair restored the modernist listed building’s original features, including its tall ceilings and white wooden floorboards. The original bookshelves, which once stored shoe boxes, returned to their olive-green colour, while a custom-made central island that sits in the centre of the space was painted the same bright red as the Vico Magistretti Carimate chairs scattered throughout.

The shop features Terranova’s design-focused publications, alongside a broader selection of titles on art, fashion and design. Highlights include Servilletas, a book by photographer Felipe Hernández on napkins gathered from bars across Spain, and Sofia Coppola’s visual history of Chanel’s haute-couture designs.

Rather than sorting books by category, the duo has decided to arrange them randomly for customers to stumble upon as they browse. The shop hosts monthly exhibitions and houses a collection of rare books, which are available to view by appointment.
- Recent exhibitions: Madrid-based photographer Jesús Umbría Brito’s Familia Real, a series focusing on Spanish youth and counterculture
- Period covered by its rare-book collection: More than seven decades, from the 1950s to the present
- Year that publishing house Terranova was founded: 2014

With so many visitors regularly passing through the city, it’s perhaps not surprising that Barcelona is home to Europe’s biggest travel specialist bookshops. In 1979, Pep Bernadas founded Altaïr – named after one of the brightest stars in the night sky – in a small space in Barcelona’s El Raval neighbourhood, where he began to collect guidebooks. It quickly outgrew that first venue and, for the past 20 years, has occupied a vast space spanning three floors in the Eixample, where globetrotters can peruse an unparalleled selection of maps, travel guides and titles that cover every corner of the world. “The only country that we haven’t been able to get any books on is San Marino,” says Altaïr’s director, Helena Bernadas.

Books are organised by country in order of their proximity to Spain, from an extensive selection of publications on Barcelona all the way to a section on Oceania downstairs. Since 1992 the business has also housed a travel agency and an online magazine of the same name, both of which are centred on a “more anthropological than touristic” approach to travel. It is the bookshop, however, that plays the most important role in preparing for any trip. “We like to put together a curated reading list for our customers that includes guides but also fiction or poetry,” says Bernadas. “There are a million different ways to engage with Japanese culture, for example, so we try to find the titles that best reflect our customers’ specific interests.”
- Recommended book: The Innocent Anthropologist by Nigel Barley
- Number of maps in stock: 11,000
- Number of guidebooks in stock: 16,000

During his teenage years, Carles Armengol helped his parents’ business by serving tables at their restaurant in L’Hospitalet de Llobregat. When the establishment eventually closed in 2012 after 80 years in the family, Armengol began to write. His debut book, Collado: La maldición de una casa de comidas (Collado: The Curse of a Diner), was published in 2022 and explores his complicated feelings about the restaurant industry.

Today Armengol has brought his two passions – food and literature – into a single space. After he presented his novel at +Bernat, the bookshop’s owner, Montse Serrano, offered him the opportunity to open a café inside the shop. Today +Bernat describes itself as a place where “literature feeds you”. Walls lined with the latest releases surround tables where Armengol serves a simple lunch menu of classic Catalan dishes, such as fideu casserole or chickpea stew with calamari. He spends the rest of the day assembling sandwiches named after classics made with local produce, from Crime and Punishment (sobressada and Minorcan cheese, roast aubergine and honey) to Il Gattopardo (mortadella from Bologna with cashew pesto, scamorza and spinach). “A café and a bookshop are destined to work well together,” says Fernando Pelayo, who runs the bookshop while Armengol tends the bar. “They make each other stand out.”
- Recommended book: Beginning, Middle, End by Valeria Luiselli
- Bestselling sandwich: The Bikini (Barcelona’s iconic grilled ham-and-cheese sandwich). At +Bernat it is named Collado, after Armengol’s book
- Year that the bookshop first opened: 1978

items.title: Issue 61 - Kinfolk
items.description: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute
paragraphs: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute for Play, explains to us on page 154. Throughout the issue, we explore pathways to play, including expert advice on rediscovering your own play type as a busy adult and, failing that, five games devised and demonstrated by artist Carsten Höller for those who don’t know where to begin.

In a study of architects, psychologist Donald MacKinnon found that those considered most creative by their peers were often those who knew how to play; this is certainly true of John Outram, whose over-the-top masterpiece, Sphinx Hill, we visit on page 70. Painters play with color and line—a type of immersive flow state our fashion editorial explores on page 60. And musicians improvise and experiment, a process familiar to the band Balming Tiger (interviewed on page 78), whose alternative approach to K-pop subverts the genre’s perfectly synchronized image.
176 pages, offset-printed and perfect bound, full color on uncoated and coated paper. Printed in the United Kingdom.
