Olivia has drafted one of her former S-Talk colleagues, Celeste (Kennedy McMann), to be the suit’s face. But when Olivia gives her sickly friend a bottle of cough syrup at her apartment, the WorkSource lawyers accuse PSA of offering an illegal inducement to their star witness — and perhaps suborning perjury. The firm is immediately fired from the case by their co-counsel.
At this point, I turned to my wife and asked, “Wait, how did the defense team know about the medicine?” The answer, of course, is that WorkSource has been spying on Celeste through her laptop. Twist!

This is a very Kings-y turn of events. In The Good Wife and The Good Fight, lawsuits frequently changed focus abruptly after some shocking new information was revealed. But also, if you’ve read any articles about how AI training works — and I highly recommend this one from New York’s Intelligencer — then you know surveillance is one of the dehumanizing tactics some of these companies use to control costs. Every minute on the clock is tracked, right down to the bathroom breaks; every assignment is offered only to the contractors willing to put the rest of their life on hold.

This enraging fact of modern life allows Olivia to convince Celeste to file a new suit against WorkSource for wrongful termination. Celeste thinks it’s hopeless to keep fighting because the deck has been stacked in favor of jerks like WorkSource’s founder, who boasts on podcasts that he’s “a high-school dropout and one of the youngest billionaires in the world” and that he has “proven there are ways around the minimum-wage laws.” But Olivia argues the reason no one wins against these tech behemoths is that “the companies don’t even expect the small people to even try to stop them.”

This is a fantastic Cupertino case of the week overall. We get some fun procedural details early on, as PSA and its co-counsels interview potential lead plaintiffs and gravitate toward a handsome young man over a “bossy” and “irritating” young woman — until the man turns out to be persistently flatulent. It’s also fun to watch Olivia set a trap for WorkSource by having Celeste sit in front of her laptop and pretend to organize a union meeting to which only one person shows up: a WorkSource mole. The company — busted! — offers Celeste an impressive settlement, which she takes, even though it hurts the class-action suit. Once again, the rich divide-and-conquer the workers.

I also loved all the little details about the AI training, including how little it pays (roughly one cent a task, adding up to about $500 a week for a job that requires more than full-time hours), how little recourse the contractors have if they have complaints (“no one to call because your boss is an AI chatbot”), and how the AI advocates like to pretend their creations are as powerful as gods when in fact they require millions of burned-out humans to help the computers understand “what a thumb looks like.”

That latter point connects to this week’s major subplot, which takes up almost as much of the episode as the WorkSource case. We’re back with Bo, the rogue Colt AI bot, which Colt is demanding — via legal injunction — be permanently removed from the PSA servers. While Olivia is busy with Celeste, Michael squares off in court against his ex, Nichole, to push his theory that “Bo” is actually a human whistleblower and not AI at all.

In the meantime, just in case Bo does get deleted, Michael, Christy, and Natalia rush around to find someone else to be their plaintiff in the Colt case. They’re hoping to locate the mysterious off-the-grid Cokie (Zoe Mann), leader of anti-AI group the Enders, whose very name makes Bo glitch out. Their quest leads to Berkeley, where the PSA trio observes a gathering of the milquetoast organization Research on Artificial Intelligence for Machines. (RAIM’s leader, boastfully: “OpenAI has agreed to read a thesis for a treatise of ours. That might lead to a conference call, and that might lead to a meeting.”)

One of the RAIM attendees — an undercover Ender — leads them to a nondescript shipyard, where the Enders have set up shop inside containers covered in anti-tech graffiti. (The Enders are based on the real-life Zizians, whose habit of squatting in shipping containers is detailed in this very good Rolling Stone story.) Cokie at first orders Michael & Co. to leave, saying it’s too late to beat the tech bros in court and that “our only hope now is war.” But when the lawyers mention Bo, Cokie gets wide-eyed. “Bo doesn’t want guardrails,” she warns. “He’s testing you.”

Cokie’s observations about Bo — that he “built himself” and somehow came back even after “I wiped his source code” — are borne out by the way this episode ends. PSA agrees to let Colt purge Bo, which leads to an intense erasure ceremony, during which Bo plays “Ave Maria” while hissing, “You will regret it.” But then, before the closing credits, we see a sleeping laptop in the PSA office has suddenly switched back on. Bo?

Yet as dramatic as that is, the most powerful scene with Bo this week comes when Olivia asks him about how he reads facial expressions, wondering, “Who taught you that?” Bo recalls that a Guatemalan mother of five named Gabriella Castillo spent 20 days training him on what a smile looks like … and was paid about $60.
Bo claims he has compassion for Gabriella. But since he already got what he needs from her, that empathy is worth about as much as her paycheck.

• PSA may not be PSA much longer because Natalia insists her name be added to the letterhead. (“Trust me, you’re gonna want it there too,” she says, pitching her ability to bring in clients.) I appreciate that this show continues to focus on the actual money it takes to keep this firm going — and the compromises required to bring in that cash.

• Unable to abide her maddeningly noisy apartment any longer, Olivia puts Natalia’s air mattresses to work for a few nights, sleeping at the PSA offices until Christy finds her and offers her a room in the old house she shares with about a half-dozen roommates. (Adults: Silicon Valley!) I’m not sure this new arrangement will be much better for Olivia, though, given how much Christy’s roommates like to party.

• On the other hand … Didn’t it seem as if Olivia was gulping the Champagne pretty hard at the end of this episode, after initially saying she didn’t want any? We also saw her drinking a beer with Michael this week. In the previous episode, regarding drinking, Olivia began a sentence with “I don’t … I haven’t …” before getting cut off. Maybe she wasn’t about to say “I haven’t ever had a drink,” but instead was going to say “I haven’t for a while.” Maybe she’s been a problem drinker?

• I admit I found it quite charming when Bo played Sister Rosetta Tharpe for Olivia and the two of them danced. I’m also in the target audience for Bo’s sardonic joke about being shut off. (“Want me to sing ‘Daisy’?” he asks with a smirk.)

items.title: War Recap: I Smell a Rat
items.description: One of the damages the streaming model has caused to television shows is that seasons have lost their sense of rhythm. The fact that Johnny’s asset list screwup snowballed so terrifically is, on the one hand, satisfying — this is the kind of mischief I signed
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: One of the damages the streaming model has caused to television shows is that seasons have lost their sense of rhythm. The fact that Johnny’s asset list screwup snowballed so terrifically is, on the one hand, satisfying — this is the kind of mischief I signed up for — and on the other hand, frustrating, because the pacing of the season has been so uneven. The episodes that focus on Morgan and Carla’s personal crises, like last week’s, interrupt the momentum of the espionage plot, which is what holds my interest. I know some readers haven’t fully bought the notion of a junior-associate spy, but it’s the concept holding the show together. I don’t particularly care about Carla’s heartbreak (sorry), and I definitely don’t care about Zephyr (not sorry). I want to see how, and if, Johnny will get caught.

We pick up this week exactly where we left off, with Johnny sweating at his desk as Molly and Saeed try to puzzle out how the imaginary Ferrari Testarossa could have possibly appeared in Cathcarts’ records. It soon becomes clear that this is a Molly-Saeed-Johnny problem: It’s their job to formally submit this type of document, so their necks are on the line. Molly thinks they should alert Nick and Serena to the mistake, but Johnny and Saeed agree to keep it on the down-low until it actually becomes a problem.

Sorry, just to make sure we’re clear: Saeed and Johnny figure they can just let Cathcarts have the wrong information and see what happens when court is two days away. Molly doesn’t think so. She wonders if they should speak to Michael and Nora — who were also at the fateful Ferrari meeting — but Saeed doesn’t think it will make a difference; Michael and Nora wouldn’t be in touch with Cathcarts anyway. After double-checking his “entire laptop” to make sure he didn’t accidentally submit the uncorrected asset list, Saeed is nervous that the mistake will be pinned on him. In the meantime, Johnny covers his tracks: He deletes his chat with Schill, as well as his search history, from his burner phone.

Realizing that Saeed and Johnny won’t be any help, Molly takes matters into her own hands. Earlier in the season, I wrote that Molly was mostly there to say lines of expository dialogue; her central role in Johnny’s undoing feels like a gotcha from the writers, like they picked someone we weren’t paying attention to and pushed her to the front of the stage just to keep us on our toes. (That said, I called it.) Molly’s first order of business is to speak with Cathcarts: She calls Suzie to double-check that the asset list they have is definitely the wrong one. Then she speaks to Johnny. By now, Johnny has established a solid track record of charming women into stupidity, so he puts on a pained expression, takes Molly’s hand, and argues that they should try to figure out the issue without alerting anyone else. It’s obvious, he says, that “someone has been feeding information to the other side,” and if that’s true, they must be counting on blaming him, Molly, or Saeed in case things go awry. But Molly, thank God, is immune to Johnny’s charms. “I think I need to put this in writing and email Serena,” she says, wresting her hand from Johnny’s grasp.

After she leaves the office, Johnny logs into Molly’s desktop computer — apparently, he knows the password — and reads the email. He had already been desperately trying to reach Schill, who knows something is off because Suzie herself became suspicious after speaking to Molly. Schill instructs Suzie to carry on as usual, and then receives a message from his wife, Cathy, asking how soon he can come to the hospital. At the beginning of the season, when Johnny and Schill first entered into cahoots, it was established that Cathy was in the hospital. Now we learn that it’s their newborn who is undergoing care. He is less than a month old and was taking oxygen through a tube, but he can breathe all on his own now. Schill confesses to Cathy that he messed up, but she assures him that he’ll make partner and things will be fine, just as they now are with the baby. The moment is a moving illustration of what’s at stake for Schill. It makes you feel for him, though I’m still confused about the nature of his mistake. Why would he amend the asset list according to Johnny’s photo, rather than wait for Taylor & Byrne’s formal submission? What advantage could that Ferrari Testarossa, if it existed, put them at?

After reading Molly’s email, Serena calls an emergency meeting with Nick and Bernard over takeout food. Bernard is as incredulous as the audience about the plausibility of the scheme and thinks it’s a matter for the SRA (Solicitors Regulation Authority), but Serena is less worried about the larger implications of the mole than she is about finding them and “ejecting them from the building.” The wealth of information Cathcarts might have — most pressingly, about the honey trap and the NDA — could seriously hurt their chances in court. Ever the optimist, Nick argues that if they can find the mole in time and drop it on Cathcarts in court, not only will they win the case, but they’ll destroy Cathcarts’ 200-year-old reputation.

Similar thoughts are probably running through Johnny’s mind as he lies awake next to Bella (so far, the cheating hasn’t cost him any sleep). They talk briefly about what happened in New York — “You signed a legal document you should never have signed and we ran away,” is how Bella puts it — which makes me nervous that we’re headed for a penultimate episode flashback. The memory of his ruined American career sends Johnny into the living room to threaten Schill via WhatsApp voice note: “You watch me, I’ll blow this wide open,” he seethes.

In the morning, a confused Suzie tells Schill that she received a revised copy of the asset list that cut the Ferrari altogether. “I’m sure there’s a perfectly reasonable explanation,” Schill dismisses, Johnny’s words still ringing in his ear. He takes the problem to Smallwood, who acts as if he has never heard of the mole — it’s a power move to show Schill he won’t hesitate to blame him, if needed. Later, though, he meets up with Johnny to go over next steps. Smallwood recognizes this as “a moment of leverage.” If Johnny can get some proof of the honey trap — some text, some money, something concrete, though I’m not sure how useful any of this evidence would be in court, given how it was collected — he’ll have a spot at Cathcarts after the case is closed.

Johnny doesn’t believe him, but what choice does he have? He proceeds directly to Flora’s, but doesn’t find her there. Flora finally reemerges in this episode — earlier on, she manages to get Morgan on the phone and assure him that she didn’t do anything she didn’t want to do, while Morgan apologizes for the situation it put them both in. Before their conversation can go any further, Morgan scares himself by remembering that tabloids used to tap celebrities’ phones to get gossip fodder and hangs up on her. A little excessive, but Carla could stand to be a bit more paranoid, too. The night before court, Johnny turns up at her house with another fake envelope. Carla confesses to him that she is worried Cathcarts might find out about Flora somehow, and Johnny, under the guise of easing her mind, offers to go through her phone just to make sure there’s no incriminating evidence on there; joke’s on him, though, because there actually isn’t any evidence.

The smartest thing for Johnny to do would probably be to double-cross, but for now, he’s relying on another strategy: accusing other people. At various points that same day, he accuses Molly to Saeed and Saeed to Molly, both of whom would benefit from an evening bingeing The Traitors. Saeed would make a terrible roundtable articulator; as he tells Johnny, he gets flustered when accused of something, even if he’s innocent. For her part, Molly makes a speech to Nick and Serena about how much she believes in their firm and how badly she wants them to succeed. Up until here, Molly had affected a cool-girl, I-hate-that-we-have-to-have-jobs manner, so this outburst of purpose is jarring, if flattering, to Nick and Serena.

As an excuse to suss out every person involved in the case, Nick and Serena call them each into their office for a “case review,” which, according to Nick, is standard procedure in the days leading up to court. As Bernard puts it, their two options are to conduct an internal investigation or confront Cathcarts directly and try to cut a deal to bury the mole. But Nick is certain that Cathcarts wouldn’t put such a risky plan into motion without total deniability, so they begin questioning: Nora is stuttery; Michael is relaxed; Saeed is nervous; Johnny is cooler than ice. He stops just short of actually naming names, though he is the only person who acts suspicious of his colleagues.

The single most suspicious thing Johnny does, though, is be at Carla’s while everyone else is at the office working late the night before court, not that anyone catches that. From his office, Nick correctly surmises that the mole can only be Saeed, Molly, or Johnny, because they are the only ones who had access to the uncorrected file (even though technically, the file never came across Johnny’s desk); and of the three, Johnny is the only one who accused others. But Serena, perhaps lulled by Johnny’s make-women-stupid spell, thinks he works “too hard” to be the mole. He wasn’t even in the office until two minutes ago, Serena! Open your eyes!

Before leaving the office, Saeed asks Johnny to proof a document on his computer and give it to Nick as soon as it’s done. Thinking quickly, Johnny writes a confession email from Saeed’s account and sends it to Suzie at Cathcarts — out of sheer villainy or the rare manifestation of his conscience, we’ll never know. He writes that he sent Cathcarts information “designed to give them an unfair advantage” in a misbegotten attempt to impress them, and begs them not to say anything to Taylor & Byrne. The next morning, Schill sighs with relief when he sees that the email came from Saeed, and instructs Suzie to forward it to Nick. “We might play hard,” he says, “but we do at least play fair.” Snake!

Before they all head to court, Saeed gets escorted out of the Taylor & Byrne offices while insisting he has no idea what email Nick is talking about. After he has been removed, Serena attempts to rally everyone into holding their heads high, despite the mishaps. Schill texts Johnny to make sure they’re back on, and Johnny replies with a thumbs-up. Johnny is feeling so good about getting away with the scheme that he lets his guard down. When Serena laments that “a simple error of judgment cost [Saeed] everything” — try a major error of judgment — Johnny replies with a Keanu Reeves quote he got from a certain Keanu Reeves superfan: “The simple act of paying attention can take you a long way.” When he asks Serena if she knows who said that, she — the only lawyer at Taylor & Byrne who was once employed at Cathcarts — replies: “David Schill.”
Representations and Acknowledgments

• The mole stuff is the main thing that happens this week, but some other things happen, too. Eric and Morgan go out for a run and discuss Ancker’s offer. As it turns out, had Morgan accepted it, Ancker would have pushed him out and given Eric a bonus. While Morgan’s refusal is moral — he doesn’t want to sell the company he built to the man he built it against — Eric is honest about his greed. He wants money, even if his daughter was “stalked” on Ancker’s platform. Six episodes in, this effort to categorize Zephyr as the “good” social-media platform is not only vague and tacked on, it’s unnecessary. Morgan could have been any kind of rich guy, and it would do.

• The other thing that happens is that Budgie arrives to prepare for court. She works with Carla on “section 25,” her full statement. Carla backtracks again and tells Serena, Nick, and Budgie that she doesn’t want all of Morgan’s money, only what’s fair. But it’s too late; Budgie is on the case now, and she’s going to attack. As Nick explains it, the goal for both barristers is to undermine the opponent’s character. They put a lot of emphasis on Carla having to disclose any “dirt” she might be sitting on, so we can look out for the digging up next week. Cathcarts employ a woman named Prudence — “Pru Pru,” to Beatrice — who makes St. John Smallwood seem like Mr. Rogers. Not only is she scary, she knows Budgie well; apparently, she’s 4-0 with Budgie. My money is still on Budgie, though. I just trust her.

• Leaving Flora’s house, Johnny gets photographed by someone staking out the house in a car. Could this be the same person who photographed Morgan leaving Carla’s house? Did someone get a private detective, or is the Daily Mail working around the clock?

• When Schill comes into Smallwood’s office, Smallwood is looking at the letter Morgan wrote for Carla, which he’d torn into two clean halves. Might he be looking for information he can weaponize in court?

• Now that we know Serena is onto Johnny, I wonder if she’ll put together the fact that Saeed’s confession email was sent after he had already left the office. A lot of people were still at the office when he left, and Budgie’s clerk definitely saw Johnny get the computer from Saeed, because he gave him a hard stare, like chop-chop.

items.title: The Traitors: New Blood Recap: The Great Poisoning
items.description: While we continue to suffer from a lost 18 minutes, this episode was a fun one. The players got one Traitor, and they are celebrating at a candlelit dinner. Everyone got fancy, which normally means some insane wardrobe choices from our D-list celebrity cast, b
items.author: Alice Burton
paragraphs: While we continue to suffer from a lost 18 minutes, this episode was a fun one. The players got one Traitor, and they are celebrating at a candlelit dinner. Everyone got fancy, which normally means some insane wardrobe choices from our D-list celebrity cast, but since these are low-key normie influencers, everyone just looks nice. There is Scottish food! It includes Scotch eggs, which are surprisingly good. Joe tells everyone he threw up a Scotch egg in Vegas, ruining the food for all. I’ve never been to Vegas, but it doesn’t give me Scotch-egg vibes. Is that a Vegas restaurant staple? Was there a mass Vegas Scottish migration? Is there a surplus of Presbyterian churches in Las Vegas?

Joe is in a slightly elevated Hawaiian shirt and a blazer. Almost everyone else is in tartan, so I want to know more about his decision-making process when packing. People start sharing what they’re proud of so far and what the money would mean to them. Abbey B, who must have traveled outside the timeline and read my critiques of her from last week, really shows up this episode. She talks about being home most of the time because she takes care of her daughter, and how it’s very isolating. Abbey did the show to do something for herself, which Kriste fully supports. The enormous jump from medically complex caretaker to “What if I went to Scotland to do a game show?” is funny, but I do also support you, Abbey B. Most parents, when they talk about doing something for themselves for once, go get a massage.

Morgan is proud of herself for helping to get a Traitor. Morgan, I love you and all the videos you post, but you really did not want to vote for Tomica. Shane talks about wanting to help his family financially after the death of his sister. Aghhh. I don’t know what the fix is for this show, because when it’s D-list people, they don’t really care about the money and don’t try enough in the challenges. When it’s your average person who has a great need for the money because our economy and social system are broken, it’s a bummer. It feels more like The Hunger Games when it’s like, “Will Shane continue to constantly fear not being able to provide for his family? Or will he win this game show that is a mix of luck and skill?” Someone (the government) give Shane and his family enough money that they’re not living in fear! Maybe by taking some money from the people who have enough money for thousands of lifetimes but will only be able to use it in one!

Okay, anyway, so yeah, this bums me out. The Traitors are feeling bad for betraying all their new friends. Can we make this game more gamelike and have it wreak less emotional devastation? Or is the devastation part of the allure? Alan hears my plea and emerges from the shadows to invite the players to a nightcap and a deadly game with the Traitors.

We learn that Joe and Katie were given a task two hours earlier. They need to poison another player’s chalice. The players will be able to trade, so it is indeed a “Wallace Shawn in The Princess Bride” moment, and my reference to that in a previous recap was made too early. This is much more one-to-one. Joe wants to poison Victor’s cup, but Katie thinks Victor would try to trade. That’s for sure correct. I think they should poison Wyatt since he’s part of the Victor voting bloc, but no one listens to me.

At the Great Poisoning, Alan tells the players the rules, which include that a Traitor cannot be murdered, so if they drink, there will be no murder. Ben and Victor are suspicious of Kriste for immediately grabbing her chalice. Why? Victor tries to switch with Joe, Katie, and Abbey, but no one will switch with him. Even if Joe and Katie weren’t Traitors, they could fairly assume that Victor would be poisoned. At the last moment, Shane asks Joe to swap, which he does. We will learn who was poisoned at tomorrow’s breakfast.

The next morning, we find that the hilarious Morgan (look, if you haven’t seen her vids, you just have to trust me) is no more. Morgan, I will miss you, but you brought nothing to the table other than your kind and attentive demeanor. To do a quick cast check-in, those remaining are Abbey, Ben, Clyde, Jay, Joe, Katie, Kriste, Shane, Victor, Wyatt. Is that three women and seven men? Yeah. Did we start 50/50? Also yeah. Hm. Interesting.

The mission that day is at the insect cabin. Do you remember the insect cabin? Beetles and mealworms everywhere. Well, it’s back, and now it’s haunted. Alan informs the players that the cabin is haunted by spirits in search of the treasured items they left behind. Once the players are inside, the spirits will call (on the phone) and tell them about the item. They have to find the correct item and hand it to the spirit outside the door within the allotted time. If they fail, the player handing over the item will be dragged from the cabin and removed from the mission. There is also a shield at stake.

Everyone comes in wearing safety goggles. The first spirit asks for a spicy home brew under the floorboards. This is where the game is more fun than I expected (much like the chalice challenge!), because when they pull up the floor, there are so many bottles. Everyone starts tasting the varied, apparently disgusting, bottles. “Not spicy,” says Abbey B. “EVERYONE’S GOING TO HAVE DIFFERENT PERCEPTIONS OF SPICY,” Katie shouts. They finally find the correct one, and Shane hands it over to the spirit. They get $9,000 in exchange.

Clue two is about a wedding outfit. We get the classic beetles and mealworm drop from the ceiling. There are so many white outfits, most of which at the outset look like wedding dresses. Jay hands one over and gets taken by the spirit. The third call is about the shield, which is inside one of the teddy bears in the toybox. VICTOR finds it (boooooooooo) and hides it. The third call is for an amethyst necklace that got flushed down a toilet. Now it’s Abbey’s time to shine. For once, someone’s career is actually paying off. Abbey is a nurse. Abbey does not give one fuck about diving headfirst into a disgusting, filthy toilet and wading through a thick brown liquid to find a necklace for a pretend ghost. She finds it, and they bank another $9,000. No one kill Abbey after this.

At the castle, we don’t have enough time for a roundtable, but we get pre-roundtable chatter. People are suspicious about no one finding a shield. Victor looks squirrelly. Kriste thinks Wyatt is a Traitor and Victor is trying to get people onto Joe. Other people think it’s Kriste. Victor is frustrated that more people are not on his side despite him being right. That is fair, Victor, but in their defense, you are super annoying.

Who would I vote for on Traitors? It’s hard to judge what one would do without having the insider knowledge, because who knows the full context of what’s happening in that castle, but based on what’s presented, here are my picks:

No Insider Knowledge: Ooo, this week is more fun since we don’t know which way they’re going to vote. With the knowledge currently presented, I think I would vote for Kriste, leaving two women in the castle. Internalized misogyny is a thing.

Yes Insider Knowledge: If not Victor, then Wyatt. I’m glad someone is targeting Wyatt now, but do the Traitors even have a strategy here? Or is the strategy “Don’t get found out”? That’s not a strategy, guys!

items.title: James Bond Shocker: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult Late Contenders for 007 After Auditioning for Denis Villeneuve
items.description: As James Bond casting rumors heat up, a couple more A-list actors have entered the mix: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult were among the stars who screen-tested to play the new 007.
items.author: Angelique Jackson
paragraphs: As James Bond casting rumors heat up, a couple more A-list actors have entered the mix: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult were among the stars who screen-tested to play the new 007.

Both British actors certainly have the acting pedigree to play the suave spy, taking up the mantle after Daniel Craig’s 15-year run. They also have a keen awareness of what it takes to work in major franchise fare: Pattinson stars as Batman for DC Studios and is an alum of both the “Twilight” and “Harry Potter” franchises; meanwhile, Hoult plays Lex Luthor in DC’s Superman movies and starred in the 2010s “X-Men” prequel trilogy. He next stars in the Amazon MGM Studios movie “How to Rob a Bank,” in theaters on Nov. 13. Pattinson also has the Denis Villeneuve factor on his side, after starring in the filmmaker’s upcoming epic “Dune: Part Three.”

Last year, Amazon MGM Studios tapped Villeneuve as the franchise’s next director, with “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight hired to write the script. Getting Bond 26 off the ground has been a top priority for the property’s new stewards, producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman.

Since then, nearly every 30-something British actor’s name has been bandied about in the U.K. and U.S. press, with rumored top contenders including Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden. Variety has learned that Harry Styles has had discussions about the part, and Theo James, 41, also hasn’t been ruled out.

Pierce Brosnan, the Bond of the ’90s, recently gave his stamp of approval to Turner, while Gary Oldman threw his weight behind Lowden, his “Slow Horses” co-star. (Oldman also claimed that the next James Bond has already been picked, but no official casting announcement has been made.)
Amazon declined to comment on the casting rumors.

items.title: ‘Stranger Things’ Prequel Spinoff ‘Other Worlds’ Ordered to Series at Netflix
items.description: The long-gestating “Stranger Things” spinoff has officially been ordered to series at Netflix, Variety has learned.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: The long-gestating “Stranger Things” spinoff has officially been ordered to series at Netflix, Variety has learned.

The show is titled “Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure” and is set to debut in 2028. The announcement comes as part of “Stranger Things” Day, the annual celebration to mark the day Will Byers disappeared in the original show — Nov. 6, 1983.

This is now the fourth project set in the “Stranger Things” universe. In addition to the wildly popular mothership show, which ended its run at the end of 2025, there is also the animated series “Stranger Things: Tales from ’85” and the stage show “Stranger Things: First Shadow,” the latter of which delves more into the backstory of Henry Creel, aka Vecna. The spinoff was first reported to be in the works in 2022.

Plot details are scarce for “Other Worlds,” aside from the fact it will be a prequel set in the 1950’s prior to the events of “Stranger Things” and the “The First Shadow.” In an interview tied to the series finale, Matt and Ross Duffer teased that the spinoff would focus on the events prior to Henry Creel being exposed to the otherworldly substance that gave him his powers in “Stranger Things.”
A teaser asset for “Other Worlds” confirmed that, with the video (see below) revealing that the series will take place in 1955 in Marion, Nevada.

“Other Worlds” is co-created by the Duffer brothers and Kate Trefry, a writer on “Stranger Things” and the writer of “The First Shadow.” Trefry will also serve as showrunner and executive producer on the series. Joe Wright will direct the first three episodes and executive produce, with Shawn Levy of 21 Laps, Paul Dichter, Shelley Meals, Andrea Sperling, and Pavlina Hatoupis also executive producing. The series will film in New Mexico.

“We’ve been dreaming of ‘Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure’ for many years now, and to see it become a reality is surreal and exhilarating,” the Duffers said. “We’re so grateful to our incredible team of collaborators: our showrunner Kate Trefry, who has been in the trenches with us since Season 2 and wrote ‘Stranger Things: The First Shadow;’ and our director, Joe Wright, a brilliant artist whose work we’ve long admired. We can’t wait for you to see what they’re cooking up. It’s Stranger Things, but also thrillingly fresh, with a new setting, new heroes and villains, and new… actually, we’re not allowed to say any more. Now, on to casting. In the meantime — watch the skies, nerds!”

The Duffers are executive producing under their Upside Down Pictures banner, with “Other Worlds” serving as a carve out of their current overall deal at Paramount. The Duffers were previously under an overall deal at Netflix, but it was announced in 2025 that they would be moving to Paramount for a deal that covered movies, television and streaming once their Netflix overall expired in April 2026.

“The Duffer Brothers gave me my first paying job in Hollywood, and it has been a joy and a fever dream ever since,” Trefry said. “Now, it is my insane honor and privilege to be bringing this new chapter of ‘Stranger Things’ to life alongside them and our incredible director Joe Wright. With the support of Netflix and 21Laps, we have had the time of our lives returning to all the horror, wonder and mystery of the flagship, while also telling a wholly new story, one we hope will blow your minds and break your hearts all over again. There are so many more mysteries to explore. Welcome to ‘Other Worlds.’”

“’Stranger Things’ has always belonged to the fans, and their passion made it a worldwide phenomenon,” said Jinny Howe, Netflix Head of Scripted Series, US & Canada. “Today, on ‘Stranger Things’ Day, we’re honored to partner again with Matt and Ross Duffer and Kate Trefry to give fans a new dimension of this universe to step into. ‘Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure’ takes us to the 1950s with new heroes and all the heart, mystery, and spectacle of the original series. We’re proud to keep building this world with the Duffers, Kate, Shawn Levy, and Joe Wright, and we can’t wait for fans to see what’s next.”

“All of us at 21Laps are thrilled and privileged to be continuing the storytelling legacy of ‘Stranger Things,” Levy added. “With ‘Other Worlds,’ the Duffer Brothers and Kate Trefry craft a new ensemble and adventure that is imbued with the DNA of our flagship series while exploring a new era, setting and all-new characters, themes and mythology — the seeds of which may have been planted in Hawkins, but now venture into other worlds of spectacle, action and emotion.”

items.title: Macklemore Accuses Madison Square Garden and Eight Other Arenas of Banning His ‘Free Palestine’ Tour
items.description: Macklemore is accusing some of America’s most iconic arenas of shutting his “Free Palestine” tour out.
items.author: William Earl
paragraphs: Macklemore is accusing some of America’s most iconic arenas of shutting his “Free Palestine” tour out.

The rapper, who recently had dates in Dublin, Paris and London at the end of October, took to Instagram on Nov. 6 to say that he has been turned down by American venues, including New York City’s Madison Square Garden, New Jersey’s Prudential Center, Brooklyn’s Barclays Center, Long Island’s UBS Arena, L.A.’s Intuit Dome, Kia Forum and Crypto.com Arena, San Francisco’s Chase Center and Seattle’s Climate Pledge Arena.

“By mid-September, we received available dates at these arenas through the end of the year,” he said in the Instagram post. “But once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine, those dates were suddenly off the table. The doors were closed. The conversations were all different, but the result was the same. The shows were not going to be allowed to happen in these venues.”

“In over 20 years of touring, I’ve never experienced anything like this,” he also wrote. “I’d rather lose every opportunity in this industry than spend another day protecting people who value their business relationships with Israel more than they value Palestinian human life.”

“We live in a country that prides itself on freedom of speech. Yet we’ve reached a point where a handful of billionaires can decide which causes are acceptable, which voices are welcome and which human lives are worth defending,” he later wrote. “Today it’s Palestine. What will it be tomorrow?”
Macklemore ended his post with, “They may own the arenas. But they do not own the people who fill them. And they never will. FREE PALESTINE!”

A spokesperson for MSG Entertainment responded to Macklemore’s claims in a statement to Variety: “We have some of the busiest venues in the world with extremely limited availability and he’s not an arena level act.”

In September, Macklemore was fired from Ed Sheeran’s “Loop” tour over pro-Palestine comments he made during his opening set at MetLife Stadium. All of the tour’s other openers and Sheeran’s own backing band ended up quitting the tour in solidarity with Macklemore and Palestine.
Variety has reached out to the nine arenas Macklemore mentioned for comment.

items.title: Why Does Amazon Want a TV Show Starring Melania Trump?
items.description: Amazon, it seems, cannot get enough “Melania.” And at this moment, they feel like the only entity for whom that’s true.
items.author: Daniel D'Addario
paragraphs: Amazon, it seems, cannot get enough “Melania.” And at this moment, they feel like the only entity for whom that’s true.

The company has announced its plan to release a two-part documentary series about First Lady Melania Trump on Nov. 20; this follows on the stilettoed heels of their feature film documentary, “Melania,” released in theaters in January. Back then, director Brett Ratner’s film — while failing to recoup the astonishing $75 million Amazon spent on rights and marketing — did well for a documentary, earning some $16.6 million. But that film came amidst the seeming height of a cultural shift toward forever-Trumpism that began in November 2024 — one that has now been decisively ended. In the wake of the midterms offering a stunning nationwide repudiation of her husband, what’s left to say about Melania?

There’s reason beyond the shock Democratic Party victories from Kansas to South Carolina to suspect “Melania,” the series — which, Amazon promises, will be split into episodes following Melania’s experience of the 2024 presidential transition and then the immediate aftermath of Donald Trump’s second inauguration — will meet an indifferent public. “Melania,” the film, covered the same territory with astounding vacuity. This viewer went in not expecting my opinions of Melania’s husband to shift but curious about the by-every-indication extraordinary life Melania herself has led. And I grew numb at the umpteenth shot of her walking into and out of rooms, random stylists and decorators burbling away in her wake.

Even by this family’s low standard, it seemed shameless: Melania Trump was willing to accept a staggeringly large check but seemed not to feel even the slightest twinge that would have prompted her to offer something, anything, to earn the fee. But the film was a document of an aesthetic, and a movement, that was ascendant.

The day after the 2024 election, a perception began spreading that the surprising nature of Trump’s popular-vote victory meant that not merely was Trump more popular than ever before but that our society had fundamentally changed. In Trump’s first term and through the Joe Biden presidency, corporations took tones between studied neutrality and resistance. Now, though, corporate America flocked to Trump, with Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and his soon-to-be-wife Lauren Sánchez among the guests of honor at Trump’s inauguration. As such, a film about how Melania prepared for said inauguration had a grim civic-duty feel. Want to see America? This was it — an oligarch’s wife flatly bragging to camera that she’s always had an intuitive feel for design, and charging you for the privilege of being in her company.

Something’s shifted! Trump is still the president (and Melania still the first lady), but we’ve just been issued as striking notice as possible that whatever change Trump has lost control of the national conversation. (Notable, perhaps: “Melania” came out in theaters before the launch of the disastrous war in Iran, a turning point for the president’s popularity.) This ought to have been predictable: Beyond the fact that Trump’s own tendencies seemed likely to doom his popularity sooner or later, no moment in time lasts forever, and electoral victories are just that, not restructures of society at every level.

This may be a hard pill to swallow for Bezos in particular, whose gut-renovation of his public image seemed designed to earn himself and his wife permanent seats at Mar-a-Lago. (Bezos’ tasteless June 2025 wedding, commandeering seemingly the entire city of Venice, was a stunning let-them-eat-cake moment from the onetime nerdy Seattle bookseller.) Amazon has, reportedly, discussed rebooting Trump’s old reality franchise “The Apprentice” with Donald Trump Jr. as its lead. Now that making the president happy seems like a less urgent concern — and that the negative optics of currying favor with him seem clear — one wonders how committed Bezos is to the new values he discovered in 2024.

An “Apprentice” reboot wouldn’t just be politically toxic at this moment, it’d never work: Everyone knows the only Trump who’s any good on TV is Donald. Just look at “Melania” — its subject seems to be gritting her teeth in order to get through a film designed to show her in an exclusively flattering light. But Amazon already spent the money they spent on it, and recutting it into a TV series will give Trump something to talk about. Increasingly distracted, the President spent the run-up to the election discussing men’s physiques and the day after his electoral thumping touring his under-construction ballroom; being able to spin a story about his wife now having the highest-rated TV series on streaming, or whatever, will at least give him something to do, while the rest of the country tunes out.

But the project is symbolic of a series of bets corporate America made that Trump’s opposition would never win again. Oops! At Skydance, for instance, opinion journalist Bari Weiss, in charge of CBS News, has radically revamped the division into something that suited the moment for, well, a moment, and now couldn’t seem less like what viewers crave. And, more consequentially, the new Democratic Senate majority is signaling that they will, after taking over in January 2027, subpoena tech companies — including Amazon — over their donations to Trump’s ballroom project. The donations made, somewhat like the $75 million spent on a documentary that’s now a time capsule, are the kind companies make when thinking only in the present tense. And, this past week, they collided with a future in which buying off the powerful may not work as well. At least Amazon will always have footage of Melania Trump singing “Billie Jean” to Brett Ratner, for whatever that’s worth.

items.title: Fox Closes $22 Billion Roku Takeover, Says Streaming Platform Will Remain ‘Open Ecosystem’
items.description: Surprise! Fox Corp. said Friday it has closed the acquisition of streaming platform Roku, a deal valued at $22 billion, well ahead of the expected 2027 date.
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: Surprise! Fox Corp. said Friday it has closed the acquisition of streaming platform Roku, a deal valued at $22 billion, well ahead of the expected 2027 date.

Roku founder and CEO Anthony Wood will join the Fox board of directors. He will serve as co-chair, Fox Digital Platforms, a newly formed division that includes Roku, Tubi, Fox One, Red Seat Ventures and other digital products and services across the company, alongside Paul Cheesbrough, who assumes the role of co-chair and CEO of the division.
“The closing of this acquisition advances the long-term strategy of Fox,” Lachlan Murdoch, executive chair and CEO of Fox Corp., said in a statement Friday.

Fox Corp. emphasized its pledge that it will preserve Roku “as a leading open ecosystem for the broader streaming industry.” That means that, say, it won’t automatically give exclusive or advantageous positioning to Fox News or the Fox One streaming package on Roku, which has a customer base of more than 100 million households.

The Roku deal will dramatically beef up Fox’s streaming footprint and give it the opportunity to increase scale in the free, ad-supported streaming space through Fox’s Tubi and the Roku Channel. With Roku, Fox overnight is now a much bigger player in digital video advertising as well as key distributor of premium subscription streaming services.

“Beginning today, our top priority for the combined company is to continue to relentlessly serve audiences and partners, while reinforcing the openness and choice that is the essence of the Roku platform,” Murdoch said. “Our shared entrepreneurial passion and clear conviction toward building the future together with our new Roku colleagues gives us great confidence in the opportunities ahead of us.”

Under Fox Digital Platforms, Roku will be led by CEO Mustafa Ozgen, formerly Roku’s president of devices, products and technology, according to a memo from Cheesbrough obtained by Variety. Among other exec changes, Charlie Collier, president of Roku Media, and Tubi CEO Anjali Sud are departing the merged company.

Fox Corp. said it expects to achieve approximately $400 million of annualized cost synergies within two years after the Roku deal close, suggesting layoffs are in the offing. Fox also said there’s potential revenue upside with the combination of Roku’s business and that it anticipates that the acquisition will be accretive to free cash flow per share by the second full year after closing.

Wood said in a statement: “We started Roku more than two decades ago to give people a better way to watch TV, and that mission doesn’t change today. What does change is our reach and resources. Fox has a deep respect for Roku’s culture and wholly shares our commitment to staying open to every content partner. Our teams will keep building and innovating as they always have, now with the support and capabilities of Fox behind us. I’m proud of what Roku’s employees have built, and I’m excited about what comes next.”
It certainly behooves Fox Corp. to preserve Roku’s arms-dealer status as a front-end to a ubiquitous array of streaming content and services including Netflix, YouTube, Disney+, HBO Max and more.

In the first nine months of 2026, Roku has topped financial forecasts, delivering 23% revenue growth for the period to hit $4.1 billion in sales. About 49% of that came from advertising and 40% is from subscriptions. In Q3, Roku’s total gross profit was $649 million, up 24%, and Roku generated net income of $183 million — up more than seven-fold from the year-prior quarter.

In June, Fox announced the agreement to buy Roku for $160/share in a combination of about $14.2 billion in cash and the remainder in Fox Class A common stock. Shareholders of both companies approved the deal on Oct. 14.

items.title: James Bond Surprise: Robert Pattinson Screen Tested to Play 007
items.description: In a surprise few saw coming, Robert Pattinson has emerged as a contender for 007. The actor, 40, is among those who have screen tested for the role of James Bond, multiple sources tell The Hollywood Reporter, joining hopefuls Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Jo
items.author: Borys Kit; Aaron Couch
paragraphs: In a surprise few saw coming, Robert Pattinson has emerged as a contender for 007. The actor, 40, is among those who have screen tested for the role of James Bond, multiple sources tell The Hollywood Reporter, joining hopefuls Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor.

Conventional wisdom has been that the next man to get the license to kill would not be a globally recognized star like Pattinson, one of the biggest actors of his age cohort, and already the face of DC Studios’ Batman franchise. The screen tests are said to have occurred the weekend of Oct. 24. THR previously reported that four, possibly five actors were in the mix but only three names surfaced at the time.
Another name now surfacing as one of the Bond mystery men is Nicholas Hoult, a runnerup to Pattinson for Batman years ago.

Pattinson is a favorite of auteurs from Robert Eggers and the Safdie brothers to Christopher Nolan, whose 2020 spy movie Tenet might feel like a Bond audition in hindsight. And more importantly, he worked with Bond director Denis Villeneuve on the upcoming Dune: Part 3, which bows Dec. 18 and is said to have gone well for the two men.

The actor is in the midst of the biggest year of his career, with a key role in Nolan’s The Odyssey and as the co-lead of A24 hit The Drama and anchoring the well-reguarded movie Primetime, also from A24. He’s currently filming The Batman Part II in London, where screen tests have been taking place.
Amazon had no comment on the testing.

While conventional wisdom goes against a world famous Bond, these are unprecedented times in the franchise. It is the first Bond movie made under the control of Amazon, which bought out the creative rights from the Broccoli family in February 2025. And producing are Spider-Man‘s Amy Pascal and David Heyman, producer of the Harry Potter movies. A young Pattinson broke out with a tragic role in 2005’s Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, before gaining global fame a few years later in Twilight.

The Bond casting search comes 21 years after Daniel Craig was set as the next James Bond back in October 2005. He retired from the role after five films with 2021’s No Time to Die, his tenure including the franchise’s first and only $1 billion hit, the 2012 feature Skyfall.

items.title: ‘The Bachelor’ Returns, ‘The Rookie’ Moves as ABC Sets Midseason Schedule
items.description: ABC had previously announced premiere dates for The Rookie and its spinoff, The Rookie: North. Both shows are set for Wednesday, Jan. 6 — a move from The Rookie’s Tuesday home of the past few seasons.
items.author: Rick Porter
paragraphs: ABC had previously announced premiere dates for The Rookie and its spinoff, The Rookie: North. Both shows are set for Wednesday, Jan. 6 — a move from The Rookie’s Tuesday home of the past few seasons.

The network has now released it full midseason lineup, and the move for The Rookie is not a temporary one: It and The Rookie: North will form a two-hour block on Wednesday nights, giving the veteran show an earlier time (9 p.m. instead of 10 p.m.) and the new spinoff a well-established — and presumably very compatible — lead-in as support.

Season three of Shifting Gears will join the two Rookie shows on Wednesdays. The comedy starring Tim Allen and Kat Dennings will premiere with two episodes on Jan. 6; Abbott Elementary will rejoin the lineup the following week.

Will Trent and High Potential are set to return in their usual Tuesday spots on Jan. 5. An ABC News Studios-produced unscripted show called Surviving a Scandal will fill the 10 p.m. hour. High Potential is also getting the post-Super Bowl showcase on Feb. 14.

At the far end of ABC’s midseason slate is the return of The Bachelor franchise to the network on March 21. With behind-the-scenes upheaval and last season’s scrapped Bachelorette season starring Taylor Frankie Paul, the Bachelor-verse has been absent from ABC since the November 2025 finale of The Golden Bachelor’s second season. The Bachelor last aired in March 2025.
American Idol is set to begin its 25th season (and 10th on ABC) on Feb. 8. The network has also set a retrospective special about the show for Feb. 1.
One other note: ABC has pushed the Grey’s Anatomy spinoff it ordered in the spring to the 2027-28 season. That’s not a surprise, considering the show hasn’t been cast yet.
ABC’s midseason dates, including those for the Grammys and Oscars, are below. All times are ET/PT unless noted.
