items.title: Why Are These Huge Arc’teryx Boots Suddenly Going Viral?
items.description: Where were you during the Great Arc’teryx Jacket Phenomenon of 2022? If you’ve forgotten, the cult Canadian outdoors label went viral when young men on TikTok began filming themselves in the shower to demonstrate the hypnotic water-repelling ability of their G
items.author: Tyler Watamanuk
paragraphs: Where were you during the Great Arc’teryx Jacket Phenomenon of 2022? If you’ve forgotten, the cult Canadian outdoors label went viral when young men on TikTok began filming themselves in the shower to demonstrate the hypnotic water-repelling ability of their Gore-Tex jackets. The attention only seemed to further cement Arc’teryx’s techy outerwear as an inescapable part of the menswear landscape. Now, the Vancouver brand appears to have another crossover hit on its hands: a hulking beast of a winter boot.

The Postour is a two-in-one design that combines a weatherproof outer boot with a removable insulated slipper tucked inside. In what the brand calls “full-boot mode,” the high collar cinches shut with a utility cord, sealing you off from the elements. The idea is that you can spend the day stomping through snow and slush, then shed the outer shell and lounge around in the slippers. Though it almost looks like a chalk bag sprouted a foot, the silhouette still carries the sleek, hyperfunctional minimalism the brand is known and loved for. The oddness of the design seems to be part of the appeal.

Naturally, it’s equipped with all the technical bells and whistles you’d expect from Arc’teryx: a gnarly Vibram Arctic Grip outsole, weatherproof Gore-Tex shell, and the label’s proprietary Coreloft insulation. Perhaps most covetably, there’s also a giant skeletal bird logo—known to diehards as the “deadbird”—on the side. The same logo has helped make the brand’s beanies a favorite of everyone from Timothée Chalamet to Frank Ocean.

Much like Arc’teryx’s Gore-Tex jackets before it, the Postour has become unmissable on the men’s side of the fashion algorithm. It’s a viral object of desire for a certain type of menswear guy fluent in microtrends. (This is hardly the first time we’ve seen a polarizing boot take over the algorithm, after all.) The is-this-ugly-or-cool discourse only adds fuel to the fire—and the fact that the boots resemble a sought-after design from Yeezy Season 8 certainly doesn’t hurt. TikTok and Instagram are chock full with videos of dudes excitedly unboxing their boots, blasting them with hoses, and customizing them with colored wax. As a result of all this digital buzz, the $300 boot has been drifting in and out of stock on the official Arc’teryx website. At one point last week, it was fully sold out; as of press time, only a couple of sizes remain in stock (though REI currently has a full size run).

Of course, winter footwear has its own pantheon of heavy hitters, from L.L.Bean’s iconic Bean Boot to Sorel’s felt-lined stompers and Timberland’s “40 Below” Super Boot. Whether the Postour will earn a place alongside those classics remains to be seen. For now, Arc’teryx has made the rare winter boot that’s as hyped up online as it is useful in a snowstorm. Good luck getting your hands on a pair.

items.title: 22 Killer Watches I Saw at One of New York’s Most Exclusive Collector Hangs
items.description: This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.
items.author: Cam Wolf
paragraphs: This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

I knew the watch collector meetup I was going to was legit when its organizer sent this text to the group: “We’ve engaged an off-duty NYPD detective to work security for our dinner. So, now really no reason not to bring your best!”

Last Wednesday night, at a fancy steakhouse in Midtown Manhattan, I was reminded why I love these enthusiast-organized events. This one was relatively small in comparison to blowouts like Rolliefest, but the idea was the same: A dozen or so collectors brought along their most prized timepieces and plunked them down on the table unattended (besides the off-duty NYPD detective, of course). When I asked one attendee if I could take his Breguet—similar to one heading to auction this weekend with a $73,000 estimate—across the room to take a photograph, he reacted like I’d asked if I could breathe oxygen: Of course! What a silly question. Events like these genuinely reflect the best of the hobby: deeply passionate collectors who really just want to share their watches with like-minded obsessives.

Between bites of miniature beef wellingtons and medium-rare steak, the guests passed around and ogled the dozens of grails on display. There were new classics on the table—including Vacheron Constantin’s Ultra-Thin, a leading contender for watch of the year—alongside plenty of old ones, including every flavor of vintage Rolex, from GMT-Masters to Daytonas to Explorer IIs. I was standing with one collector as he examined a pretty vintage Rolex GMT-Master. He stopped and looked around. So-and-so must be here, he muttered aloud. How did he know? Because he recognized the shade of the patina on the dial.

This particular group started getting together a couple of years ago, after the collectors @HorologicallyMinded, @s_h_lemon, @null_islands, and @jmsfisk (everyone at the event asked to remain anonymous) met at another watch-related retreat. @HorologicallyMinded, or HM, says that collecting was at one point something he did in solitude. “People generally judge when they learn how much watches cost,” HM tells me. “You paid how much for that!?” But he and the other three founders began meeting up for monthly dinners before eventually taking turns to organize these larger events. “This group has been the most rewarding part of this hobby,” HM says. “It’s been so great to have a group of people that have a common interest, but it’s not work-related and no one judges.”

Although the group has grown, the core four are still instrumental in making sure the functions go off without a hitch, with just the right spread of watches on the tables. “It is very deliberate and the four of us generally coordinate on it,” HM says. “We specifically make sure there is something for everyone.” That means ensuring there are at least a handful of watches worth less than $10,000—this time, that included several Rolex Datejusts, a Vulcain Cricket, and a gold Breitling from the 1940s. “We knew we were having some relative newbies and different people have different budgets, and we want everyone to be comfortable.” On the other end of the spectrum, some grail-level pieces were special requests from other members of the group.

All the watches wound up getting plenty of TLC. “I love the fact that we’re a group that can, and did, totally geek out about a vintage Longines Legend Diver, while a Doré dial Patek is on the same table,” HM says.
Below are some of the very best pieces I saw that night.
A Patek Philippe ref. 3970, part of the house’s historic lineage of pieces that combine a perpetual calendar with a chronograph. The dial on this one is so tasty.
A skeletonized Breguet Ref. 3355PT00PA0—maybe the watch of the night for me—on a show-stopping platinum bracelet.

A few years ago, MB&F started making more approachable versions of its sci-fi-ready watches and allocating them through a lottery system. This is the M.A.D2, with an outer ring on the dial that spins around very quickly. It’s really fun.
The aforementioned Rolex GMT-Master is a ref. 16760, a model produced during the ’80s that’s nicknamed the “Sophia Loren” thanks to its curvaceous profile.
Omega has incredible stuff in its archives. This is a chronograph from the ’30s that’s controlled entirely through that single button at 2 o’clock.

A couple of real bangers here. The Vacheron on the left is known as the “Cioccolatone,” because it resembles a square of chocolate. At the center is the Patek Philippe ref. 3417, an antimagnetic watch with just about the prettiest typography you’ll ever see on a watch. Zohran Mamdani should adopt that cursive for signs in the city, because it can make just about anything look nice: Warning: Rats. Or maybe, No Dumping Here.
A cloisonné dial from—of all brands—IWC! I am such a sucker for a cloisonné, which refers to the intricate images carefully fashioned from wire and colorful baked enamel.

A beautiful example of one of the Seafarers that Heuer made for Abercrombie & Fitch from the ’50s through the ’70s, back when the latter was still a rugged outdoor outfitter. The shades of orange, yellow, and blue are dreamy.
A monochromatic take on the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar, which was produced in the ’80s and ’90s but looks incredibly modern.

Universal Genève finally relaunched last year after decades on the shelf, but it’s hard to beat the originals. This Polerouter comes on an extremely cool “wave” bracelet, which basically uses a repeating chevron pattern to make the slinky bit of metal appear to be in motion.

During World War II, a dozen watch manufacturers came together to make models following a strict set of specifications for the British Ministry of Defence. One of those brands was Longines, which produced this strapping piece.
You didn’t think we’d wrap this list up without a gorgeous yellow-gold Daytona, did you?
The ultimate fusion of sport and luxury watches. Heuer supplied this ’70s-era Carrera to Ferrari’s racing team, including legendary drivers like Jacky Ickx, Niki Lauda, and Clay Regazzoni.
This Patek is cool, but the bracelet is insane.

This isn’t your average Patek Philippe Nautilus. PP began producing this reference 3800 in 1981 as a smaller counterpart to the original. The few times I’ve gotten to try one on, I’m always struck by how perfect the proportions are. It’s nice and thin and looks just right on the wrist.
The United States Merchant Marines’ logo really punches up this Day-Date.
The ref. 6541 is the most beloved version of the Rolex Milgauss. It was produced in the ’50s and features a signature honeycomb dial. One sold for $2.5 million at auction in 2023.
Is there a better way to time your yacht race than with this Heuer Skipper? Probably not.

items.title: Martine Rose, Beloved Cult Designer, Is Balenciaga’s New Creative Director
items.description: Designer Martine Rose may not be a household name, but many fashion insiders are celebrating the news that she has been appointed Balenciaga’s next creative director. The Jamaican-British designer’s eponymous menswear line not only has a cult following, she’s
items.author: Kyle Munzenrieder
paragraphs: Designer Martine Rose may not be a household name, but many fashion insiders are celebrating the news that she has been appointed Balenciaga’s next creative director. The Jamaican-British designer’s eponymous menswear line not only has a cult following, she’s also no stranger to the French label founded by Cristóbal Balenciaga. She served as a menswear consultant during the earliest year of former creative director Demna’s tenure, helping to establish many of the familiar codes that defined that era.

“It is a true privilege to be appointed creative director of Balenciaga, a house with an extraordinary heritage and a fearless creative spirit,” said Rose in a statement. “Balenciaga has been shaped by remarkable creative talents before me. I am committed to honoring this legacy and look forward to creating the next chapter in this rich and beautiful story.”

“Balenciaga has always been a house of radical creativity, challenging conventions, and redefining the boundaries of fashion,” added Kering CEO Luca de Meo. “Martine Rose embodies this spirit with a fresh, fearless, and deeply contemporary vision.”

Rose will succeed Pierpaolo Piccioli, who exited the house yesterday after just 18 months. Although a talented and respected designer, Piccioli’s romantic Italian vision often clashed with the generation-defining streetwear look that Demna established at Balenciaga during his 10-year tenure. Reports suggest that de Meo envisions the brand as a connector between those on the fringes of culture and Gen Z buyers. Notably, menswear sales—which rose dramatically under Demna—had begun to wane. Rose may be a more natural fit to cater to the Demna clientele.

Rose, born in London’s working-class neighborhood of Croydon, graduated with a degree in fashion design from Middlesex University. She established her own brand in 2007, which for years existed under the radar. In 2011, she won the support of Fashion East, London’s nonprofit fashion incubator program. News of her behind-the-scenes role at Balenciaga helped to raise her profile among fashion insiders.

Since then, her line has enjoyed something of a cult status. A pair of neon heeled sneakers from a collaboration with Nike could be classified as fashion’s favorite It sneaker. Hailey Bieber has often been spotted in Rose’s outerwear (husband Justin is a fan too). Kendrick Lamar wore a Rose-designed jacket to perform at the 2025 NFL Super Bowl halftime show. Dua Lipa, Kim Kardashian, and Rihanna have all been spotted in her designs, while the stylists of several K-pop stars often dress their clients in her wares.
Cate Blanchett wore a translucent Martine Rose trench coat on the cover of W’s Volume 5, 2018 issue.

Rose finds inspiration in her Jamaican-British upbringing, ‘90s rave culture, and the everyday clothing of the streets, though always with an unexpected twist. She’s staged fashion shows in markets, her daughter’s primary school, and directly on the streets, and has long taken pride in her niche status in fashion. “I feel really proud of it all,” she told W in 2018 of he growing success. “But then I remember, I like being under the radar.”

Still, her frequent collaborations with brands like Nike, Napapijri, Clark’s, and Supreme have been commercial successes, and Rose’s name has been floated as a candidate for bigger jobs (reports suggest she was considered to take over as Louis Vuitton’s menswear creative director before the job went to Pharrell Williams). Still, the future of Rose’s own line has been thrown into question recently. In 2023, Tomorrow Ltd, a fashion incubator aiding up-and-coming designer brands, acquired a 60 percent stake in the Martine Rose label. The company has faced financial hardship in the past year (just this week, Coperni, another former Tomorrow Ltd brand, announced it was shutting down), and was sold to The Level Group earlier this year.

Rose’s new job will ensure her voice continues to be heard in fashion—this time, on a much bigger stage. She will take up the job immediately, though the timing of her first collection has not yet been announced.

items.title: The 2027 Met Gala Is Going Back to Basics
items.description: The Met Gala has a brand new theme and it’s all about basics. After the Costume Institute at the Metropolitan Museum of Art initially announced that the 2027 event would be held in honor of John Galliano, a deluge of opposition driven by Galliano’s past contro
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: The Met Gala has a brand new theme and it’s all about basics. After the Costume Institute at the Metropolitan Museum of Art initially announced that the 2027 event would be held in honor of John Galliano, a deluge of opposition driven by Galliano’s past controversies forced the designer to voluntarily step aside. As a result, the Met returned to the drawing board and on Thursday, November 5, announced a new (and decidedly less controversial) theme, sure to please museum donors and fashion fans alike. The 2027 Met Gala will honor the extraordinary within the ordinary and the beauty in the conventional. Here’s everything you need to know.
What is the theme of the 2027 Met Gala?
The Met Gala theme is “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday,” with a focus on commonplace garments and everyday materials transformed by designers.
Why did the 2027 Met Gala change themes?

Initially, the 2027 Met Gala theme was announced in August. The event was supposed to focus on former Givenchy, Dior, and Margiela creative director John Galliano and his influence on the fashion industry. Immediately, this choice caused a stir, given Galliano’s controversial past, including his previous racist and antisemitic public rants. Many spoke out against the Met’s decision to honor Galliano, considering his indiscretions, and donors to the museum threatened to withhold gifts as a result. The scandal reached such a boiling point that it caused Galliano to step away from the event. “After much reflection and discussion with all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time,” Galliano wrote in a now-deleted statement on Instagram. “I do not want the debate surrounding me to place The Met in a difficult position or to distract from the remarkable work of the Costume Institute. I also recognize and respect that an exhibition honoring my work would be painful for some.”

Andrew Bolton, the Costume Institute’s curator in charge, spoke for the first time about abandoning the original theme when the new exhibition was announced. “The cancellation of the Galliano show was disappointing for everyone involved,” he said. “I wanted an exhibition that I felt had something new to say, and that I felt was relevant to different conversations. I committed myself to this really quickly because it brings up ideas of value and consumption and resourcefulness and makes us question what we overlook and what we discard.”
What will be included in the 2027 exhibition?

Bolton has called “extraORDINARY” a kind of sequel to 2026’s “Costume Art” show, as both exhibitions focus on how clothes are worn. The “Costume Art” exhibition “placed the dressed body at the center of aesthetic experience,” Bolton explained. “I suppose it led me to think more about how we experience clothing in everyday life through habit and touch and movement and sensation.”

The 2027 iteration will feature 200 to 230 pieces, 30 to 40 percent of which will come from the museum’s collection. Fashion brands will donate or lend the rest. Visitors can expect to see items including a 1930s couture puffer coat by Charles James, pieces from Marc Jacobs’s controversial grunge collection for Perry Ellis, and the Calvin Klein jeans Brooke Shields wore in the famous 1980 ad. Matthieu Blazy’s trompe l’oeil leather jeans for Bottega Veneta will also be on display, a piece that perfectly encapsulates the exhibition.

The theme is two-pronged. One part will explore the elevation of archetypal garments, including tees and jeans. The second section will feature disposable materials like paper and aluminum, manipulated to create wearable art. There, one can expect pieces like the silverware-adorned dress from Maison Margiela's spring 2027 collection, as well as Hodakova’s spoon-laden pieces. “It will make us question: What do we overlook, what do we discard, what makes something worth keeping?” Bolton said. “I think that fashion is so often associated with the pursuit of the new and the ephemeral that I’m really interested in how possibilities can emerge through returning to familiar things. I think there’s something hopeful about discovering how much imagination the everyday can hold.”
When is the 2027 Met Gala?
The Met Gala will, as always, take place on the first Monday in May. In 2027, that falls on May 3. The accompanying exhibition will be open to the public from May 9 through January 9, 2028.
What is the 2027 Met Gala dress code?

Every year, the Met Gala theme corresponds to the Costume Institute exhibition, as well as a broader idea of what one can expect from the red carpet fashion. The dress code, though, offers more specific guidelines for attendees. As of now, we do not know the specifics of the Met Gala dress code, which will likely be announced closer to the actual event. Bolton has shared his hopes for guests to attend in their versions of jeans, T-shirts, and puffers. “I want visitors to leave looking differently at the clothes they arrived in,” he said. “With a greater sense of what is worth noticing, valuing, and caring for.”

And the Met Gala isn’t alone in its dress code this time. Bolton is encouraging visitors to the exhibit to dress accordingly, asking everyone to wear “their favorite t-shirt or their favorite pair of jeans or their favorite hoodie” to the show. “There’ll be a humanity to it,” he said.
Who are the co-chairs of the 2027 Met Gala?
The co-chairs have yet to be announced, but we do know that Meta and Moncler are sponsors of the event.

items.title: David Sims Looks Back at the Images That Defined a Generation
items.description: “I’ve always had a resistance to looking in my own archive,” says the photographer David Sims. “It’s a very dark and forgotten place. And seeing it en masse, it just became clear that this person”—i.e., himself—“was in a state of mild psychosis.” In fact, stud
items.author: Alex Needham
paragraphs: “I’ve always had a resistance to looking in my own archive,” says the photographer David Sims. “It’s a very dark and forgotten place. And seeing it en masse, it just became clear that this person”—i.e., himself—“was in a state of mild psychosis.” In fact, studying the torrent of photographs he has taken since the late ’80s felt so unnerving to the 59-year-old that he decided to give the exhibition it has yielded the title “The Hamster Becomes the Problem.” “If you’ve ever owned a hamster, you’ll know that they keep chewing on the cage bars and running on the wheel,” Sims says. “Eventually this delightful, cute, furry animal becomes a torment.”

Sims might have found looking at his old work tormenting, but few of the visitors to the Marta Ortega Pérez Foundation, in A Coruña, Spain, are likely to. “The Hamster Becomes the Problem” seems set to reveal to a wider public what insiders have always known: that Sims is one of the best fashion photographers of all time. “He doesn’t just define a style—he builds a character,” says Fabien Baron, the creative director who gave Sims an exclusive contract at Harper’s Bazaar when the photographer was just 26. “He’s learned the craft so well that he can do anything. In his use of light, he’s the most impressive photographer—and I’ve worked with them all.”

Many of Sims’s photographs convey a feeling that we know the person being depicted, or someone very much like them, perhaps from school or from the fuzzy depths of a long-ago late night. “He created characters and stories that were immediately identifiable to lots of people growing up in the 1990s and 2000s,” says Charlotte Cotton, the exhibition’s curator. “In 1997, he said to me, ‘I want to create the visuals of our time.’ And he’s done that.”

Given the consistently high quality of his work, it seems strange that Sims hasn’t had a full solo exhibition or monograph before. In 2000, he published Isolated Heroes, a book of extraordinary portraits of models taken backstage at a Raf Simons show, which commands huge prices on the resale market today; and in 2013, a touching exhibition named “Bowievirus,” in which a group of skinny male models embodied the Thin White Duke, was shown at the Institute of Contemporary Arts in London. But Sims has disseminated most of his work specifically through magazines. Before the Internet existed, that was how he could reach people in places that weren’t cultural hot spots like London or New York—people like his younger self.

Sims grew up in Sheffield, in the north of England, though his family’s roots are in Liverpool. His father sold contraceptive pills to pharmacies (“I always used to say that he was a drug dealer”), and his mother was a secretary. His extended family were musical—he remembers them singing together on Sundays in the pub—while Sims was an avid reader of music magazines about cult figures such as Iggy Pop, his hero. For the photographer, music is still essential on a shoot to conjure up the character and image in his mind; for years, he even employed his own DJ for that purpose. “There has to be a moment when the right song comes on,” he says.

Sims, who admits that he was “opinionated and frustrated” as a teenager, was hugely unpopular with his teachers. The head of his high school art department wrote to a college to which Sims was applying, warning them that Sims was the worst student he’d come across in 30 years. “When I tell that story, it’s like I’m taking pleasure in it,” Sims says. “But it was devastating.” Things clicked when he was offered a job in a photographic darkroom in his hometown. “I thought almost immediately, I’ve got this. I know what I’m doing. It was the first thing I’d been asked to do that fell into place, and I ran with it.”

Entirely self-taught, Sims learned photographic and developing techniques—“trying to produce the perfect negative”—and immersed himself in the medium’s history, studying masters such as Irving Penn, Richard Avedon, Robert Mapplethorpe, and the great war photographer Don McCullin. He moved to London, started working as an assistant to more experienced photographers, and quickly fell in with a fashionable crowd. “We were friendly with a few pop stars, so life was quite exciting,” Sims says. “I remember being ushered into clubs just because we were with Boy George.”

Yet, by the late ’80s, Sims was getting antsy. While he initially enjoyed the acid house scene, “that rave high suddenly felt way too chicken feed to me.” He thought that London’s excitement “had dipped a little bit—there was a resurgence of a more conventional middle-class influence in magazines. I thought, God, we’ve got to take back our ground here.” He found allies and collaborators in two like-minded stylists, Melanie Ward and Anna Cockburn, who had a similar iconoclastic urge to bring a new sense of realism to fashion imagery.

Baron remembers first seeing Sims’s early work when he was judging a photography competition in Monaco: “a bunch of pictures of guys and girls against a white background. Avedon-esque, but the spirit was more youth-based, punkish. There was an English flavor. They were in your face, but they had soul.” Magazines such as i-D and The Face started giving Sims work. “I had an Australian girlfriend, so I went to Australia for a month, which seemed an eternity at the time,” he says. “And when I came back, some pictures had come out and people were suddenly very interested.”

Sims was whisked to New York, where Baron and Harper’s Bazaar editor Liz Tilberis signed him, despite what Baron remembers as his grungy “yellow hair.” He started photographing supermodels and shooting major ad campaigns—“sucking on the corporate tit,” as Sims puts it today. “The thing that New York had that London didn’t was mounds of money. It was my first experience with that resource and what comes with it.”

It’s a mark of Sims’s independence that his work for big brands and big magazines was just as idiosyncratic as the pictures he’d made for himself. Pushed by Baron to photograph Linda Evangelista for Bazaar, Sims came back with a magnificently weird shot of her wolf-whistling. “He showed how you could maintain your integrity through these tiny little gestures,” says Cotton. More editorial and commercial work followed, with clients including Jil Sander and Helmut Lang—an image from a 1997 campaign for the latter brand, of a husky, topless young man wearing a cape, subverted both masculinity and fashion advertising conventions, and is now in the collection of the Victoria and Albert Museum, in London.

Nonetheless, Sims was burning out. “I’d driven my friendships too hard and exhausted them,” he says. When Jil Sander didn’t renew his contract, he decided to take a break, which lasted roughly three years—some of that period spent traveling with the barman of a pub in Devon, England, that Sims had visited while camping on a nearby beach. When he returned, fashion photography had moved from film to digital, and Sims was forced to follow suit. “I was horrified when it first happened,” he says. “I felt completely disoriented by it.” But he decided to experiment with the new medium, “to see the things that lay deep within it, and that’s when the psychedelic thing kicked in.”

As “The Hamster Becomes the Problem” will show, Sims’s 21st-century work often has a narcotic, dreamlike quality. Jagi is a 2019 image of someone standing at the top of what looks like the steps of a playground slide in a dramatically hued field, against a sky full of Turner-esque clouds. There will be an installation that focuses on his cousin Lee Armitage, a Liverpool-based painter with whom Sims has “a degree of fascination…we’ve led these sort of quantum parallel lives.” In one image, Armitage is topless, with closed eyes and an open mouth, which is colored bright pink, denoting some kind of ecstatic experience. Another room, Rave, contains hundreds of pictures and, Cotton says, is like “a fever dream.”

Sims’s work often digs into his memories of his childhood in the postindustrial north of England—barbed-wire fences, tower blocks, violently patterned wallpaper in council flats, people smoking dope while listening to Pink Floyd. He is still creating characters, but now he’s using his impeccable photographic techniques to venture deep into their inner spaces. “He’s not dialing it in, in any way,” Cotton says. “Helmut Newton, or any of those libidinously driven photographers, they go back to the same place every time they take a picture, like they’re pressing repeat. David doesn’t. It’s like you’re following a journey of a life.”

Sims says that his ultimate inspiration is his unconscious, and he hopes that his symbolism, though intensely personal, might nevertheless resonate with viewers. “I was looking at the archive and wondering, What the hell was I even thinking?” Sims says. “It’s a chimera—something you’ll never quite get to. You’re building a structure that will hold the illusion of your fantasy. Really, this show could have been called ‘Castles in the Air.’ ”
All images courtesy of David Sims.

items.title: Dior Enlists Rihanna and Robert Pattinson for a Hand-Drawn Holiday Fantasy
items.description: It is never too early to get into the holiday spirit. Everyone knows the Christmas season can be stressful, but the more you prepare ahead of time, the more you can enjoy all the magic. So while it may seem too early to start considering your gifts, in reality
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: It is never too early to get into the holiday spirit. Everyone knows the Christmas season can be stressful, but the more you prepare ahead of time, the more you can enjoy all the magic. So while it may seem too early to start considering your gifts, in reality, you’ll just be saving your future self a lot of stress. And luckily, the brands are, once again, ahead of schedule, already rolling out their holiday content for our benefit. Ferragamo, Dior, Chanel, and more have released their 2026 holiday campaigns, and the images are getting us in the yuletide mood. So while the leaves may just now be falling off the trees, soon they’ll be on the ground, covered in snow—and there’s no time like the present to dive into the 2026 holiday campaigns.

“It was a quiet night at the atelier at 30 Avenue Montaigne,” begins the animated short film, Christian Dior’s Night in Color. The seven-minute movie, directed by award-winning French filmmaker Sylvain Chomet and narrated by Robert Pattinson, tells a fictional story that weaves together key moments from the fashion house’s history.

Jonathan Anderson was inspired by the cinema’s transition from black-and-white to Technicolor for the Dior cruise 2027 collection. Christian Dior’s Night in Color once again explores that shift. The narrative follows Christian Dior as he rushes to make a dress for Marlene Dietrich and her Technicolor film.

The cast is filled with familiar voices: Louis Garrel as Dior, Josh O’Connor as a talking chair, LaKeith Stanfield as a director. Greta Lee pops up as a busy atelier bee, and Rihanna even makes an appearance as the star atop a Christmas tree. “Shine bright...like a Christmas tree,” she exclaims.

In the end, Dior is able to create a dress—the famed Junon style—and deliver it to Dietrich just in time. It’s a heartwarming story, filled with nostalgia, whimsy, and craft—all hallmarks of both Dior and the holiday season.

Louis Vuitton’s 2026 holiday campaign is an ode to those who travel for their winter festivities. The Oliver Hadlee Pearch images take place in a train station, the setting of magical reunions and exciting departures.

The campaign captures the last five minutes before a grand departure. Stories unfold on the platform and within the train cars. Friends reunite, children play, travelers rush around carrying their Louis Vuitton luggage. It’s a suspended moment that perfectly embodies Louis Vuitton’s Art of Travel.

Burberry is opening the doors to a gorgeous English country home for its 2026 holiday campaign, inviting Pierce Brosnan, Dwyane Wade, Gabrielle Union, and more friends of the brand to gather for an afternoon of winter fun.
“We wanted to celebrate 170 years of Burberry with a proper party,” said Daniel Lee, Burberry chief creative officer. “Family, friends, great gifts, and everyone dressed up.”

Set at Longleat House in Wiltshire—a historic, stately home built in the 16th century—the images capture a festive celebration of party games, gift exchanges, and, of course, a whole lot of Burberry check.

It’s time! The holiday season is officially upon us, which means Queen of Christmas Mariah Carey has taken the spotlight—and her rightful place on her holiday throne. Of course, preparations must be made, and the Gucci team is on it, making sure everything is ready for Carey to ring in all the merriment.

The iconic singer stars in Gucci’s holiday campaign video, directed by Harmony Korine and set to Carey’s hit song, “All I Want for Christmas Is You.” Accompanying images star friends of the house as they wait in anticipation of Carey’s arrival.

When Carey arrives at the party, she does so in Gucci’s new Butterfly special collection. Inspired by the insect, the collection embodies the iridescence of the butterfly, while paying homage to Carey’s signature motif and her 1997 album, Butterfly.

Chloé’s latest campaign is festive, but not in an obvious way. Shot by David Sims and starring friend of the house, Claudia Schiffer, the images capture a nocturnal spirit through a cinematic, after-dark atmosphere.
Schiffer’s enduring personal allure is reflected in the imagery, as her natural presence and distinctive character bring a singular perspective to the campaign.

Fashion, humor, personality, and New York energy collide in Marc Jacobs’s winter 2026 campaign, Let It Joy. Actor Meg Stalter stars in the campaign video, holed up in her hotel room during a snowstorm. When Mel Ottenberg invites Stalter over for a party, there’s only one issue: She doesn’t know his room number.

Chaos ensues as Stalter attempts to locate the party. Luckily, the comedienne does not give up and is able to follow the music. She eventually makes it to the holiday bash, ready to celebrate in her black Marc Jacobs shift dress alongside New York personalities and cultural figures like Knicks center Andre Drummond and model and actress Kai Schreiber.
Tory Burch presents a guide to the holidays, along with tips to celebrate the upcoming season the Tory way: with optimism, joy, and presents piled high.

Tory Burch’s holiday campaign comes with a list of rules to follow. Number two pertains to gifting (and receiving), suggesting we give generously and react dramatically. Number four urges us to embrace the festive spirit, while the last rule is a bit of a warning: Pace yourself; it’s a long holiday season ahead.

Alongside the tips, you’ll find more holiday inspiration in the form of images from Anthony Seklaoui. The shots are full of beaded sparkle, cozy knits, and community—the perfect recipe for a joyous season.

Michael B. Jordan, Yerin Ha, and Inde Navarrette star in the David Yurman 2026 holiday campaign. The three actors gather in snow-covered Washington Square Park for shots that capture the joy of togetherness and the magic of the holiday season in New York City.

Jordan and Ha face off in a spirited card game, while Navarrette searches for the perfect holiday gift. Of course, all three are bedecked in David Yurman designs, including 18-karat gold cable bracelets and pieces from the brand’s Starburst and Armory collections.

Fresh off her buzzy turn in You Can See Everything, Amanda Seyfried has returned to New York from Texas, just in time for the holiday season. The actor is Tiffany & Co.’s newest House ambassador and the star of its holiday campaign, “Love Is a Gift.”

As part of the campaign, Seyfried acts in a short film, “You & Me,” which tells the story of two different Christmas celebrations: one taking place in the present day, and one in 1992. Between these two moments passes a Bird on a Rock ornament, originally gifted decades ago and still a prized possession all these years later. It’s a story of tradition, holiday memories, and the connection between generations.

“I’m thrilled to join the Tiffany & Co. family as their newest House ambassador and to be part of a campaign that celebrates love, family, and the traditions we carry with us through generations,” Seyfried said in a statement. “‘You & Me’ captures beautifully how a meaningful gift can hold memories and become part of a family’s story. It was incredibly special to bring that idea to life with Tiffany this holiday season.”

The holidays are all about family, so it makes sense that Kim Kardashian enlisted her very famous sisters to star in the Skims Holiday campaign. Shot by frequent Kardashian collaborator Nadia Lee Cohen, the campaign takes inspiration from nostalgic holiday portraits, placing Kim, Kourtney, Kylie, Khloe, and Kendall in scenes you may recall from your own home videos.

The sisters are styled in pieces from the Skims holiday shop, wearing outfits with varying degrees of coziness. Khloe and Kourtney are covered head-to-toe in their respective patterned onesie and red long johns. Kylie and Kendall, meanwhile, show off more skin in bras boasting classic holiday prints. All the girls don retro glam—bouffants and old-school glasses. The result is a vintage scene with no clear time stamp. But it doesn’t matter, because Santa still clearly approves.

Gigi Hadid, Louisa Jacobson, and more gather in a grand townhouse to celebrate the holidays. The polished wood walls are covered in wreaths, the tree is bedecked with ornaments, and everyone is dressed in Miu Miu.

The wardrobe highlights contrasts between lifestyle archetypes and seasonal themes. Silk dresses are paired with upcycled knits and sportswear-inspired zip-front blousons. Cropped sweaters reveal button-down shirts, and utilitarian cotton canvas separates are layered over sequined bralettes.

But the models are not alone in this uptown space. They are joined by plush toy bears, rabbits, geese, and more. Treated like treasured guests, these additions provide whimsy to the scene, a composed portrait of bourgeois behavior subverted by humor and play.

Friendly furry creatures are not unique to the Miu Miu campaign this season—they pop up in the Prada world as well. This time, though, the woodland pals are hand-drawn by a team of artists led by cinematic animator John Pomeroy.

Sadie Sink gets down on the ground with a trio of mice to admire a patterned, calf-hair loafer. Maya Hawke faces off against a sly fox as she braves the elements of a frozen setting. There is a whimsy to these wintertime scenes, which emphasizes Prada’s humanity and a connection to craft that lies at the heart of the brand’s approach to creation.

Kris Jenner is the matriarch of the Ferragamo family in the brand’s 2026 holiday campaign, The Joy of Loving. “Ferragamo is all about family,” says creative director Maximilian Davis. “And when I design, I am always thinking about that, too: how a collection can be worn by different generations, but also how pieces you love will be held onto and passed down through them.”

The momager stars as the director of a fictional film, leading screen tests featuring the campaign’s various faces. There’s Paloma Elsesser and her brother, Sage; girl group The Womack Sisters; and Sofia Testino with her dog, Syko. Actress Joan Chen is joined by her daughter, Audrey Hui, while acting coach Nancy Banks poses with her son, actor Benny Buckley.

The campaign connects back to the roots of Ferragamo, and founder Salvatore Ferragamo’s original desire to build a better life for his family through his love of invention and creativity. “One of the founding values of Ferragamo has always been of beauty that develops from craftsmanship, humanity, and joy,” says Salvatore’s son, Leonardo Ferragamo. “This campaign is telling that story.”

Loro Piana invites you to a weekend at the cabin, where the elegantly falling snow outside matches the chic inhabitants’ wardrobes. Models are dressed in the brand’s holiday collection, an expression of style that plays out across textures, hand-finished prints, exclusive patterns, and elaborate stitches.
Loro Piana’s usually muted color palette is realized once again, this time in the form of dark greens and earthy browns. They are highlighted with pops of winter-white and marigold.

Warm jersey tops and trousers form the foundations of these après-ski looks. On top, classic Loro Piana outerwear like the Spagna jacket and Konny vest are crafted in wool and finely detailed with needlework; the wearer stays warm while also making an enviable sartorial impression.

Chanel is hitting the slopes for its 2026 Coco Neige collection. Bright-red knits and colorblocked puffers stand out against snow-capped mountains. The images have a retro flair, but the clothing is distinctly modern.
A snowball fight adds even more joy to this already playful campaign, while penguin and polar bear-shaped purses and earrings provide the perfect amount of whimsy.
Shearling caps keep ears warm, while winter whites are embraced with aplomb. It’s a reminder that dressing for warmth does not mean sacrificing style or charm.

Indulge in your sweet tooth with Dior’s 2026 holiday campaign, which sees the brand’s famous 30 Montaigne store reimagined as a sugar-dusted gingerbread house. Anya Taylor-Joy and Deva Cassel star in a joyous musical video. The house’s ambassadors prance around the store, snacking on Dior cookies, spritzing the brand’s famed fragrances, and trimming the icing-lined cookie Christmas tree.

items.title: Every Must-See Look from the 2026 CFDA Awards Red Carpet
items.description: On Monday, November 2, fashion heavy hitters and stylish stalwarts gathered at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City for the 2026 CFDA Awards. Now in its 45th year, the annual ceremony—often dubbed the Oscars of fashion—celebrates the brands,
items.author: Natalie Michie
paragraphs: On Monday, November 2, fashion heavy hitters and stylish stalwarts gathered at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City for the 2026 CFDA Awards. Now in its 45th year, the annual ceremony—often dubbed the Oscars of fashion—celebrates the brands, designers, and talent shaping the industry in America and abroad.

Hosted by Keke Palmer, the 2026 CFDA Awards promise to be as electric as ever. Tory Burch is this year’s Positive Change Award recipient for her philanthropic efforts through the Tory Burch Foundation as well as a nominee for American Womenswear Designer of the Year. Famed architect Peter Marino, who has designed flagships for brands like Chanel, Dior, and Louis Vuitton, is this year’s Fashion Icon honoree. Notably, Anthony Vaccarello is to be named International Designer of the Year, honoring his influential tenure at Saint Laurent. After a decade at the helm of the French brand and a final gold-dipped spring 2027 show in Paris, the designer officially left his role as creative director last month.

Along with a star-studded audience, select A-listers will also grace the stage to present. Lupita Nyong’o will announce the American Womenswear Designer of the Year, Matt Damon will present the American Menswear Designer of the Year, and Naomi Osaka will give out the American Accessory Designer of the Year. As has become tradition, before any awards are announced, the 2026 nominees and honorees will hit the red carpet with a handful of their friends and muses. For Vaccarello, that means likely appearances from his pals and house ambassadors Hailey Bieber, Zoë Kravitz, and Rosé. You can expect VIPs wearing custom looks from everyone from Khaite, Diotima, The Row, Luar, Colleen Allen, Michael Kors and more.
