items.title: Jennifer Lawrence Hopes You Won’t Hate Her New Project
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Angelina Chapin
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

Jennifer Lawrence has been here before. At this exact same sort of restaurant, the kind where celebrities discreetly mingle (this time, Gemma, the Italian trattoria attached to the Bowery Hotel), in a booth that gives her some privacy but not so much that her publicist and assistant can’t keep a watchful eye and ear from a table nearby. There’s always a stranger sitting across from her scribbling down notes on what she orders (a cappuccino and avocado toast with a soft-boiled egg) and what she’s wearing (an oversize bright-red sweater and a small beaded turquoise necklace). This is her cue to rehash talking points about her chemistry with a co-star or reverence for a director.

But when we meet for breakfast in early October, something about the familiar scene is different; she’s slightly outside her comfort zone. “I’m in this interesting transition,” she says. “For the last three years, I have been in this kind of delusional bubble where I can’t let doubt in. Now I’m experiencing doubt.” Lawrence, whose blonde hair is wavy from sleeping in loose braids last night, says any movie release comes with nerves, which she can normally soothe by bingeing the latest season of Real Housewives. This morning, though, she’s not here to talk about developing a Miss Piggy feature, working on a rom-com, or shooting a sci-fi thriller next spring. Instead, for the first time in her 20-year career, the 36-year-old is debuting a project you won’t find in theaters or on Netflix. And she’s still figuring out how to talk about it. “I have to pretend I’ve made the greatest thing on earth,” she says, her hands fiddling with the salt and pepper shakers. “Otherwise it gets too scary. It’s a form of forced manifestation.”

That thing arrives on October 27, when Lawrence will officially join the oversaturated world of celebrity brands by launching Mes, a “biodesigned haircare” company that is selling three products: a repair mask, a restyling serum, and a volumizing mist. She’s partnered with an MIT-trained scientist to develop new formulas they claim will change your hair in ways nothing else on the market can. That sounds great and all, but “what if nobody gets it?” she asks. “What if everybody hates it?”

Lawrence might seem like the type of actor who would roll her eyes at the celebrity–to–beauty brand pipeline. She has an Oscar and a production company and just shot a Martin Scorsese movie alongside Leonardo DiCaprio. Why spend time shilling a volume mist? Her answer doesn’t involve cracking jokes about girlbosses making #OOTD videos, the brand of self-deprecating humor she used as armor earlier in her career. Instead, she’s taking it very seriously, speaking about Mes as a natural extension of her art. “There is an undeniable energetic thing that happens when you’re creating things, whether it’s a movie or a product,” she says, twisting up her hair into a bun. “I got that same electric buzz I get from building a character. It’s like, Well, I have to follow this because it’s the same animal.” Lawrence has made peace with the humiliation inherent in being a creative person forced to talk about their work and doesn’t need to turn herself into the punch line. The baby-faced 22-year-old who laughed off tripping on the stairs at the Academy Awards is now more than a decade older and a mother of two. I watch her arrange her delicate features into a thoughtful expression while telling me how creatively satisfying it felt to develop a brand. I know she’s a good actor, one of the best, but I believed her.

Lawrence has always been a “hair girl.” “I feel like if my hair looks okay, then nobody’s gonna notice anything else about my face, clothes, or body,” she says. “I also can find myself using it to hide.” As a child, her thick curls would puff up in the Kentucky humidity, and she slept in braids to control the “floof.” In her teenage years, she ceded control to stylists, who did whatever they needed to get her camera-ready. “When you are a new and upcoming actress, you can’t be like, ‘Don’t put that on my hair,’’’ she says. “You sit in the chair and you say ‘Thank you’ and you shut your mouth.” Her strands would smoke and sizzle when the hair spray hit the straightening iron; her hair was dyed four different colors in one day for an X-Men screen test. After shooting the second Hunger Games film in 2013, her hair was so fried that she chopped it off into a pixie cut, a style she thought at the time “looked dope.”

Soon, Lawrence had bought every new product on the market in a desperate search for anything that would style her hair without hot tools. She even met with scientists about developing new products, but she struggled to find a like-minded collaborator. That is until 2023, when she watched a TED Talk by Jasmina Aganovic, a chemical biological engineer with a shiny brown bob and a beauty company who spoke about creating products that would fundamentally change the makeup of hair rather than just coating it in products — the industry’s current approach. Lawrence got goosebumps and emailed Aganovic to set up a meeting in the fall, just as the actors’ strike was ending. “It just seemed like a new way of going about things,” she said. “This is what I’ve been waiting for.”

Aganovic was initially less enthusiastic about the partnership. She had already founded a company, Arcaea, that uses DNA sequencing and skin microbiology to make, among other things, perfumes that reimagine extinct flowers or the smell of clouds. And while she wasn’t blind to the attention Lawrence could shine on her life’s work, she worried it could also be a distraction. “One of my biggest fears is having my work be misinterpreted,” she says. “Jen came across as credible and curious, but you never know how much she had actually looked into the company.” After a Zoom call, Lawrence set out to prove she wouldn’t be the kind of business partner with “25 assistants rescheduling something.” Within a few weeks, she flew to Aganovic’s Boston lab, showed up without an entourage, and smelled the smelliest bacteria in the fridge. Aganovic was impressed. “Jen literally said, ‘If you want to do this in five years, I’ll still be here,’” Aganovic remembers. “And I think that took the pressure off. I was like, Oh wow, she’s really serious.”

By fall 2024, Aganovic’s team of scientists was working on formulas that would make hair healthier while cutting down on styling time, damage, and shampooing. Lawrence had very specific ideas for the products, like a hair mask that would go on dry hair (and that could double as a “wet look”), a serum that got rid of her “floofs” without leaving residue, and a volumizing spray that wasn’t crunchy and improved her scalp. To execute her vision, Aganovic’s scientists had to become experts in lipids, proteins, and the scalp’s microbiome and experiment with different techniques, including developing a proprietary ingredient to promote a balanced, less oily scalp. “Hair masks are not usually applied to dry hair,” says Aganovic, “which is why it’s very expensive to produce them this way, without water.” (A 150-milliliter bottle costs $52.) Lawrence’s head became the guinea pig. She tried the products on her naturally curly hair, which she says makes her look like Isaac Newton. She tested the serum while doing promo for Die My Love and used the volumizing mist on the set of What Happens at Night, the Scorsese film she shot earlier this year. Her dedication was total, and she sent the serum back to the lab almost 150 times. At one point, she started to smell like fish after leaving on an unscented version of the mask for four days. “My husband was like, ‘If you don’t wash your hair, you have to get a hotel room,’” she said. Lawrence held firm.

When she wasn’t filming, she spent hours on weekly calls about the business and focused on developing the look of Mes’ logo and bottles. “I knew I couldn’t miss a Zoom and that I’d need to look over every single letter on the website,” she says. Sometimes it was hard to juggle everything. During one call, Lawrence tells me she was bouncing on a yoga ball at nine months pregnant when it occurred to her she was only in a bra. “I just turned my camera off and said, ‘I’m so sorry. I realized that I’m not wearing a shirt,’” she says, “And then everybody pretended like they hadn’t noticed.” But she wanted to stay in the weeds of the business. Lawrence took nose-training classes to help develop Mes’ scent; she sent product samples to everyone in her group chat and asked them for their feedback on fonts. She got so involved in the design that she had a colleague fly out to the New England beach town where she was vacationing so she could hold the 3-D-printed models in her hands. “I wanted them to be pretty,” she says of the bottles, which look like modernist mini-vases. “Bathroom products are always out, and it’s like, Why is this ugly?”

Lawrence trusts her eye, she assures me during our post-breakfast tour of the artist Robert Rauschenberg’s former Noho studio, a place she wanted to visit because it’s up for sale and could soon be turned into luxury condos. “I am good at telling when something’s going to be hot,” she says, now wearing a black baseball cap from her husband’s art business, American Pictures. After looking at a small exhibition of work by the mid-20th-century multimedia icon — “he’s kind of hot,” she says under her breath as she stands in front of a photo of Rauschenberg smoking — we sit in a room with sun pouring in through arched windows while Lawrence tells me about the vibe she’s trying to create. Mes, which is pronounced Mess (the latter was already trademarked), is meant to capture the kind of girl (gender neutral) who leaves the house with dewy skin and a rumpled-in-a-chic-way button-down shirt. “The moment something was fussy, it was like ‘no,’” she says. “Avoiding pretentious words and pretentious font is big. Our girl is not that. But she appreciates beauty.” Lawrence’s personal ethos is also looking good with minimal effort, despite the fact that she’s had a boob job and one day plans to get a face-lift. “I want to be a sexy mom,” she says. “At drop-off, I want to look like a woman that has her shit together even when I’ve just woken up and don’t have my shit together.”

But don’t expect to see GRWM videos in her bathroom before taking her toddler to school. She had resisted creating an Instagram account for her entire career — she did, however, make a Finsta to share memes with her friends — in hopes of keeping a few shreds of life private. But Lawrence knew Instagram was a necessity for any founder in 2026 and a few months ago met with a social-media expert, who explained that Lawrence’s strategy didn’t need to involve constantly pumping out content or filming her home life. Instead, since officially joining the platform in September, she’s only posted to the grid three times — “If anyone says anything negative, I will quit,” she deadpanned in her first video — and already has more than 8 million followers. She plans to do minimal promo for Mes, including product tutorials she might film in a “public or hotel bathroom” to keep her own sink offline.

It’s a tough time to jump on the celebrity-beauty-brand bandwagon. Fans tend to view these companies cynically, as cringe cash grabs rather than genuine passion projects. And the bar for success is high: The products have to be good on their own merits, and the celebrity selling them has to make sense. People want Kylie Jenner’s lips and Hailey Bieber’s skin, but on Reddit threads speculating about Mes, commenters are already questioning whether Lawrence’s hair is a standout feature. When I ask Lawrence if she feels pressure to have aspirational hair, she says, “That didn’t even occur to me,” with a look of panic. “Is that something people think about?” In her fortress of positivity, she hasn’t dwelled on the criticisms that could be coming her way and seems genuinely caught off guard when I bring them up. Is she concerned a highbrow beauty product is at odds with the every-woman persona fans love? “I think about how excited people will be to have something so sculptural and beautiful!” she says. “My little bubble is about to be popped.”

While beauty brands have turned rich celebrities like Rihanna and Selena Gomez into filthy rich business moguls, Lawrence scoffs at the idea that Mes was conceived as a source of financial stability amid Hollywood’s decline. “A smarter exit plan would be signing up for a big franchise,” she says. “Starting a new company to get rich feels like jumping off a cruise ship to land on a door.” And anyway, worrying about the bottom line is not her strong suit. When talking about the look and feel of Mes, she adopts the self-seriousness of any artist talking about their craft. But when it comes to the more technical sides of the business, Lawrence falls back on her familiar brand of self-mockery. “If you put a gun to my head and were like, ‘What are the numbers we would need to reach in order for Mes to be a success?’ I would have no clue,” she says. “Numbers don’t stick in here. I’m dumb but cute!” When I ask if the company has investors, she whispers “I don’t know” and redirects me to her co-founder. (Aganovic says her original company, Arcaea, which has raised $78 million, is funding Mes.)

But the shtick isn’t working so well this time — which is a good thing. It felt charmingly authentic when, in 2012, the Kentucky-born ingénue told David Letterman, “I hate myself. Don’t go see the movie. I’m a troll.” But Lawrence is in a much different phase of life. She’s a mother married to a prominent art dealer and serves as the face of Dior. In Hollywood, she calls the shots, green-lighting movies with her own production company and fielding requests from the most in-demand directors while slamming the industry’s pay gap. Even if she can’t balance a spreadsheet, it’s hard to believe she’s a buffoon in the boardroom. “It’s funny that she describes herself as the creative needing the business counterpart,” says Justine Ciarrocchi, who runs a production company with Lawrence and is her friend of almost 20 years. “I think she has an incredible business intuition, and she’s fearless when she is sure of something.” Molly Howard, the CEO of La Ligne — a brand whose coveted wide-legged pants are a staple of Lawrence’s “momboy” aesthetic — says her friend already has the most important quality in a successful founder: the willingness to pore over the most boring details of the business, from learning about EBITA to testing a bottle’s seal. “The ambition is that this becomes a Fenty Beauty of hair care,” Howard says. “I really think this could be a Rhode.” Lawrence actually has an even more audacious North Star in mind, one she’s too embarrassed to name. “If I told you, you would be like ‘Hahaha,’” she says. “It is so big and so huge that I’m aware Mes will never get there.” I beg her a few more times, but all she’ll say is that the aspirational brand is not beauty-related. “If I was Taylor Swift, the people on Twitter would figure it out.”

Towards the end of October, I visit Lawrence at her office in Tribeca, a Federal-style townhouse with exposed brick and barnwood panels. There’s incense burning on the long wooden coffee table, and as she curls up on a rust-colored couch, asking me at one point if I’m bothered by her bare feet, Lawrence claims to be feeling more calm than when we first met. “I’m back to being utterly and completely positive,” she says, wearing a sequined brown wool cardigan and a long black skirt. “I can always fall back on the product. It’s just kind of like, Well, these are obviously really good.” If she’s stressed about anything today, it’s a recent haircut that left her with uneven bangs, which she’s repeatedly tried to fix. “No matter what I do, it flicks out,” she says, pointing to a strand on the left side of her head. “And I went into a meeting today as a hair authority.” Come to think of it, maybe she is a little nervous, mostly about the idea that people won’t have enough patience to stick with the products. “If you make a texturizing spray, everybody knows what to expect,” she says. “These are brand-new products. So my fear is somebody will get a first impression without actually taking the time to figure out how it works with their hair.” She’s already dealt with a few emergencies, like the mask leaking during the ship test or the cap on the restyling serum squeaking. (“This isn’t luxury,” she remembers saying. “It sounds like I’m stepping on mice.”)

Earlier that day, the Mes landing page went live, featuring a video of Lawrence’s blonde waves bouncing as she dances in a red cardigan. She immediately texted her group chat asking for compliments, which includes Howard of La Ligne, Tracy Dubb of Isla Beauty, and two women she won’t name because they are “very private.” On October 27, the full website will roll out, and if all goes well, Mes bottles will start filling people’s bathroom cabinets.

In a material sense, whether Mes is a hit or not won’t have a big effect on Lawrence’s life. She’s already rich, and Paul Thomas Anderson probably wouldn’t blacklist an actor whose hair mask doesn’t sell. For Lawrence, the stakes are more personal. She has the antsy intensity of someone who’s desperate for people to join in their obsession rather than mock it, like a friend who’s become a javaphile and wants you to adopt a new coffee-brewing technique. “Tell me about your experience because the products take time,” she says, fixing me with an intense stare. “I can answer questions.” She’s itching to nerd out about the eccentricities of her creations, excited for people to log on to the website and see the microscopic images of how these products affect the scalp. As she’d told me during breakfast, “I’m nervous about someone putting on the restyling serum and being like, Oh my God, this went on really oily, without knowing that in 15 minutes, it’ll all dry.”

Toward the end of our talk, she catches her foot bouncing and says, “I think the nerves are in my body. I work really hard to keep my brain disciplined.” At some point, Lawrence knows someone from the Mes team will call and let her know if the sales numbers are good or bad. But the real risk is a bruised ego, the idea that people won’t like — or simply don’t care — about a product she’s devoted years of her life to perfecting. “I imagine it’s going to be like when a movie comes out, where there has to be this release of tension,” she says. “I’ll try and get Zen with it. But I’ll probably just have wine for breakfast.”

items.title: Mormon Wives Star Jen Affleck Has Filed for Divorce
items.description: The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Jen Affleck, 27, has reportedly filed for divorce from her husband, Zac Affleck, 30. On Wednesday, TMZ reported that Jen filed a petition for divorce on Tuesday in Utah as well as a proposed parenting plan. The couple shar
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Jen Affleck, 27, has reportedly filed for divorce from her husband, Zac Affleck, 30. On Wednesday, TMZ reported that Jen filed a petition for divorce on Tuesday in Utah as well as a proposed parenting plan. The couple shares three children, and Jen is currently pregnant with their fourth.
Shortly after news of the divorce filing broke, a source told People that Zac is “doing okay.” “He and Jen are staying focused on preparing for the baby and supporting their kids,” the source added.

In a statement to People on Thursday, Zac said that he will “always be Jen’s supporter.” “Hope she is happy in this next phase of life,” he told the outlet. “Just focusing on my kids and figuring out what’s next for me.”

Later on Thursday, Zac posted a five-minute TikTok detailing the split. He said that he found out about Jen filing for divorce from a “TMZ reporter” but that it was “something we’ve been talking about for a long time.”

“Jen came to me about a year ago after Dancing With the Stars and told me she was unhappy and wanted a divorce,” Zac said. “And I basically begged her to stay, told her [I would] work on things, fix things, become whoever she needed me to be, and ultimately just we couldn’t make it work.”

Zac said that his top priority was his children and that he fears that he “failed them.” “I’m worried that I’m going to cause them damage,” he said. “And I just hope that we can still give them a normal childhood. But as far as that goes, Jen and I are definitely on the same page of wanting to give them the best life we can, the best childhood we can and be teammates and work together and do that.” He also added that he would continue to “support” Jen and “be her biggest fan.”

Jen posted a TikTok of her own on Thursday, suggesting things were not so harmonious. It was an old video of her attempting to film her daily routine, with Zac offering his own commentary off-camera. “I hope you’re not making a TikTok looking like that,” he said, referring to Jen wearing a bathrobe. “Your boobs are literally like — your tits are sagging all over. You don’t want to post that, baby, I can tell you that right now.” The SLOMW star captioned the post “he was never my biggest supporter.”

The Afflecks — who may or may not be related to Ben — met in 2018 through a Mormon dating app. They got married in 2019 and had their first child, Nora, in 2021. They then had Lucas in 2023 and Penelope in 2025. In June, Jen announced she was pregnant again, calling it “Chapter Four” on Instagram. The couple’s oldest just turned 5, which means they narrowly missed having four under 4.

In July, Jen shared that she was suffering from prenatal depression, calling it “painful, confusing, and exhausting.” She later told People that she was “deathly ill” during her first trimester and that Zac had to step up. “There’s a lot that we’ve been navigating behind closed doors,” she said, “but I do have to say, I wouldn’t have survived the first trimester without him.”

Jen and Zac’s relationship struggles have been a central plot point on SLOMW over the years. Following the first season’s premiere, Jen said that the show found them “in a rocky place.” “Since filming, we’ve done therapy nonstop,” she told Vulture in September 2024. “If we continue in our relationship, there are changes that need to be made. If they’re not made, we might have to … look at other options.” The couple briefly separated after that first season but ultimately reconciled and announced their third pregnancy in February 2025.

The divorce comes at a particularly busy time for Jen. In addition to being pregnant, she’s helming the SLOMW spinoff The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County, which premieres next week. If you have questions about the end of Jen and Zac’s relationship, I assume many of them will get answered when the new series drops.
This post has been updated.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 6, 2026
items.description: Astrologically speaking, you’re likely to have a quiet day ahead. But that could change if Mercury and Saturn (in Scorpio and Aries, respectively) stir up stress and anxiety tonight. Especially if you’re up late, you might start spiraling, convincing yourself
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: Astrologically speaking, you’re likely to have a quiet day ahead. But that could change if Mercury and Saturn (in Scorpio and Aries, respectively) stir up stress and anxiety tonight. Especially if you’re up late, you might start spiraling, convincing yourself you’ve made bad choices or even that you’re a “bad person.” But you’re not likely to reach any useful conclusions thinking this way. If you’re trying to work through a dilemma, you’re better off sleeping on it. You’ll have more clarity and a more positive outlook in the morning.

Today, you might overreact to minor disagreements and small inconveniences. Even if you know, rationally, that none of these issues are significant in the long run, your emotions might run hot anyway. But if you try to suppress your “bad” feelings, you’ll inevitably fail. Whatever you try to bottle up today will end up coming out one way or another. So instead, make it your goal to find a healthy way to channel your energy today. It’ll serve as a powerful motivator if you can use it for good.

When your close relationships feel strained or contentious, you prefer to address the problem rather than avoid it. But today, the solution might be for everyone involved to take some space. With a bit of distance, you might realize that your issues aren’t nearly as serious as you feared. More than that, time apart will give you a chance to remember what you actually like about each other. Deep and difficult conversations can wait. For now, simply letting the issue rest might be all it takes to feel better.

Most of the time, you’re good at rolling with the punches. Even in the most stressful of circumstances, you can typically find something to work with. Today, though, you might not be as flexible as usual. If your routines are off, you’ll be more bothered by it than you normally would be; if your living space is untidy or uncomfortable, you’ll easily get distracted. So take some time to put the details of your day in order, to the extent that you can. It’ll make everything else flow more smoothly.

You make a point of considering your words carefully before you speak. You don’t want your ideas to come out wrong or to accidentally offend anyone. You’re not afraid of being controversial; you just want to be intentional about it! But today, give yourself permission to be spontaneous. If you take too much time to plan out what you want to say, the conversation might move on by the time you’re ready. So trust yourself, and if the moment comes to speak up, seize it.

You struggle not to wrestle with FOMO. Sometimes, you imagine that if you want to have interesting experiences and enjoy your life, you need to constantly chase the action whenever and wherever it’s happening. But today, try to slow down a bit. If you make a point of looking around with an open mind, you’ll realize that there’s plenty of excitement in your own community and your own life. You don’t need to go anywhere else to find what you want; you have everything you need already. You just need to notice it.

Sometimes, when you’re stressed out, you need to commit to doing less — bowing out of the obligations you don’t have to to fulfill, making fewer plans, and cutting down your to-do list. But if you try to do that today, you’ll only wind up feeling bored and dissatisfied. Don’t attempt to shrink your life down to a smaller, more manageable size at the moment. Instead, refocus your energy, and remember you’re capable of more than you give yourself credit for.

Taking the path of least resistance might seem, to you, like a form of laziness. Those who refuse to buck convention strike you as scared and tired, even boring. But today, you’d be wise to consider their perspective. Keeping things simple, straightforward, and “normal” right now might actually be the smartest move you can make. There’s no need to overcomplicate processes or to exhaust yourself simply so that you feel like you’ve done something different and “unique.” Do what comes naturally. You’ll get the best results that way.

This could be one of those days when everything feels a little off. You’ll struggle to shake the sense that you’re messing up, even if you can’t pinpoint how or even what you’re “messing up.” Right now, it’s likely that your problem stems from your own expectations: They’re too vague, and you keep shifting your own goalposts. Give yourself specific, tangible targets to work toward, and you’ll have a much better sense of what is and isn’t working. And once you’ve reached those goals, give yourself permission to celebrate.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

Usually, you’re not especially thin-skinned — but today, don’t be surprised if you’re more sensitive than usual. Comments that might not normally make an impression could move you deeply; your own feelings will be easily hurt. There’s nothing wrong with this, but try to be aware of it. It might be a good idea to avoid the more brash and callous people in your life. You’ll probably need some extra care, so spend time with the people most likely to give it to you.

Be thoughtful about who you spend time with today, because other people’s moods are likely to affect your own. Hanging around your most cynical friends could quickly make you feel jaded, too. And others’ anxieties could easily spike your own stress levels. Being influenced by your peers is normal — and just as likely to lead to positive shifts in your own mind-set! — but try to be discerning about who you’re taking your cues from.

You have a strong sense of self. You know who you are and what you believe in, and you’re more interested in staying true to yourself than being popular. But today, remember it’s okay to want to be liked. Sometimes it feels good to fit in. Even if you usually enjoy being the one to voice unpopular opinions or go against the grain, consider relaxing that stance for now. You don’t need to change who you are, but it’s worth considering how you can best relate to those around you. Focus today on building positive, supportive relationships.

Your own fear of making mistakes could hold you back today. If you’re so nervous about making a wrong move, you’ll end up convincing yourself you shouldn’t try anything new, just in case it’s a bad idea. But that’s no way to live — it’ll ensure that you never learn or grow. Today, take a breath and remember that errors are part of the process. Trust that if you do make a mistake, you can also make things right again.

items.title: Thomas Markle Was Arrested by the FBI
items.description: Thomas Markle, Meghan Markle’s father, was arrested by federal agents in Florida on a charge connected to child sexual-abuse material. In a press release, the FBI stated that Thomas was taken into custody and charged with one count of possession of child porno
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: Thomas Markle, Meghan Markle’s father, was arrested by federal agents in Florida on a charge connected to child sexual-abuse material. In a press release, the FBI stated that Thomas was taken into custody and charged with one count of possession of child pornography. He was arrested in Lakeland, Florida, where he had reportedly been staying at a rehabilitation facility following leg-amputation surgery last year.

Following a tip about a storage unit in Los Angeles, the FBI said they searched two storage units owned by Thomas in L.A. In the storage unit, officers say they found sexually explicit images of Thomas with prepubescent girls. First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli promised to “prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

Last month, Thomas Markle Jr. told the Sun that he had reported his father to local police and the FBI after discovering “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual-abuse images in Thomas Sr.’s Phillippines home. Thomas Sr. denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail, “I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

Meghan addressed the allegations against her father in a statement last month, saying she was “deeply distressed” by the news. She said that, in 2018, the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection shared a letter with her containing “troubling and disturbing allegations against my father” and told her they would be investigated. Meghan added she had distanced herself from her father in order to “protect” her children, who have never had any contact with him.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan said.

paragraphs: For more of the Cut’s favorite fashion, beauty, and home finds, sign up for the weekly Cut Shop Newsletter.

As a Gen-Zer myself, I’m well aware that my generation is known for a lot of things — impeccable taste being one of them. Sure, I might be biased, and I know that it’s hard to assume a whole generation can get behind certain trends and items. But if you read through this list, I can almost guarantee you’ll find the perfect gift for your Gen-Z bestie, co-worker, or sibling. And to be extra sure, I asked the other Gen-Zers on staff what they are hoping to get or gift this year.

From suede sneakers to trinkets and the sleekest kettle on the market, anybody with a Gen-Z mind-set will appreciate these products. (I know I do. Friends and family, consider this my holiday wish list.) And don’t forget Gen-Zers are very different from Gen Alphas (a.k.a. the teens). So even though we may love a trinket, we also love a matching cutlery set and an automatic wine opener. Duality!

And don’t let these items discourage you. You don’t have to belong to this group to wear or own these products. If this roundup is still not what you’re looking for, we’ve also got stocking stuffers and employee gift ideas that span the generational divide.

items.title: Exclusive: Harry Shum Jr. Wants The 'Glee' Reboot To Have This Mike Chang Twist
items.description: The Harry Shum Jr. Renaissance Is Nigh
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: The Harry Shum Jr. Renaissance Is Nigh
The actor opens up about being on Dancing with the Stars as Glee and Crazy Rich Asians return — from the set of Grey’s Anatomy.

Harry Shum Jr. has the best of both worlds — well, kind of. The actor is spending countless hours rehearsing for Dancing With the Stars, with his pro partner, Jenna Johnson, choreographing routines that get more intricate every week. But right now, just hours after landing a perfect score on Disney Night, he’s on the set of Grey’s Anatomy in full scrubs doing a whole lot of nothing in the ABC medical drama’s operating room. It’s safe to say he’s exhausted.

“We just shot a scene for three hours straight standing,” the 44-year-old actor tells Bustle from his car, taking a quick lunch break still in costume. “It’s crazy how we think dancing is tiring, which it is, but you’re moving a lot. I give it up to doctors and surgeons that stand for eight hours. I would rather be moving right now. And then when I’m dancing, I’d rather be standing.”

Shum Jr.’s hip-hop skills are well-documented on Glee, with his character Mike Chang carrying the New Directions on his back when it came to choreography. But on DWTS, he’s also proven himself a ballroom master, with him and Johnson becoming the first duo this season to earn two perfect scores in a row, positioning them as undeniable frontrunners. “I’m just flabbergasted,” he says.

Shum Jr. says the scores are even more “meaningful” because he and Johnson have focused more on creating dances they’re passionate about rather than strategizing how to win. “There was a switching point halfway through where I was trying to figure out what Dancing with the Stars is in terms of being on the back side, figuring dances out, whether it's creative,” he recalls. “Jen and I looked at each other like, ‘Let's just dance for ourselves and do what we want to do.’”

Whether or not he wins the Mirrorball, DWTS is just the beginning of the Shum Jr. renaissance. While he’s been in the ballroom, the return of Glee became official, and the long-awaited Crazy Rich Asians TV series was finally announced, giving him two easy ways to keep dominating our screens. Luckily, he’d jump at the chance to return to his roots in both franchises, especially Glee.

“That show did a lot,” he says. “It tapped into the zeitgeist, but also had this crazy anticipation before the pilot ever came out, then went on tour, had this cultural effect, and charted on Billboard, and also spotlighted things we never really address in terms of bullying and gay rights. I enjoyed being able to show the dynamics of an Asian family in a different way and having it still be entertaining.”

But for now, Shum Jr. is simply focused on spreading his love of dancing for as long as he lasts in the ballroom. “It's cool hearing how families are rooting for me and finding their entry point to dance,” he says. “Even guys who only watch sports are actually invested in this competition. That's awesome. I embrace the people trying to figure out what this all is, maybe being their own judge and holding their own paddle. That makes it fun.”
Below, Shum Jr. opens up about his most meaningful dance, his relationships with the Glee cast, where he sees Mike Chang on the revival, and his future on the Crazy Rich Asians series.
Which DWTS dance are you most proud of so far?

It always feels like I’m most proud of the last dance because it's the closest, but I have to say Dedication Night. I'm going to hold that forever as the most memorable thing, having three generations on that stage. I don't think my parents ever thought in their lifetime they would be on stage, especially on national television. And to dance with my wife [actor and dancer Shelby Rabara]... 20 years ago, we tried to audition for this dance commercial, and I didn't know how to partner and I messed it up for her.

During those times, anytime you try to get a job, it’s like paying rent. You need that job. And I lost it for her because I was stepping on her toes. I wasn’t doing the lifts right, and I froze. So for 20 years we didn't partner, and this was the first time we did on this show. Our relationship is great, but repairing that part of it was very meaningful.
You're currently filming Grey's Anatomy. How’s it been balancing the show and rehearsals? Are you dancing on the set when you're not filming?

A lot of that is happening. Jenna comes and tries to teach me some of the dance, but honestly, it's so hard to focus because I still have to perform well on the show and make sure I'm giving my all to the scenes. Today we have a long [operating room] scene, so there's absolutely no time for that. It’s a lot of work, I’m not going to lie, but I feel so privileged to be able to do both and to have the support of both productions and my team. It’s not just a one-man show.
Chris Colfer was telling me how amazing it was to be with your daughter watching you dance. How does it feel to have your Glee cast’s support all these years later?

It means the world. Especially in Hollywood, where you do a job and move on to something else and everyone lives different lives, to still be in contact and come out and support each other says a lot about the bond that we have. Honestly, no one knows what we experience fully other than us. It’s beautiful because everyone’s been so successful in doing the thing they've been wanting to do.
Has your daughter seen Glee?
She did watch the pilot and was blown away, so I don’t know when we're going to start that train.
Amber Riley and Heather Morris have been on the DWTS journey before. Did they tell you anything before you joined the season?

Amber said it’s a lot, and to remember who you are, and Heather said the same thing. I’ve never done anything like this before in my life, but a lot of people have opinions about what they want you to be for them. I love to take constructive criticism, and sometimes I look at things like, “Oh yeah, I need to do that a little more.” But in other ways, I took that advice.
How do you feel about Glee returning? Has Ryan Murphy given you any details about it?

I don’t know too many details about what he’s trying to do other than him writing the pilot. He’s really excited about it. When that show came out, the arts were being defunded, and the world was trying to figure out how to transition into a different era. We never really saw that type of humor in a musical. Everyone’s a lot more mature now. I’m still trying to figure out what it is, but I’m glad they’re getting everyone talking about it, and we’ll see if I’m involved.
In your head, where do you see Mike Chang today?

I feel like all of my characters play into the multiverse of what am I living. It’d be kind of funny if he just stopped dancing. I’m already playing a surgeon and dancing right now on another multiverse, I don't want to bleed too much into that. But there’d be something interesting if Mike stopped dancing and became a plumber or something, just to go against everything that his dad wanted him to do, and then seeing how he can find his rhythm back.
The Crazy Rich Asians TV show being announced the same week is also divine timing. Have you been in touch with the cast or showrunner Adele Lim since that was announced?

Adele’s my friend. We talk about wanting to work together on different projects. The character that I play is tied to another character [Gemma Chan’s Astrid], so we’ll see if they write that in, because there are so many storylines in the books. [Adele] wrote the first episode, so I don't know what it’s all looking like, but I still talk to her a lot, and I would love to reprise Charlie Wu. In the books, it’s such a fun storyline that I think a lot of fans want to see come to life.
Next week is Grammy Night. Can you give us a peek at what you have planned?
I can say that finally we get to dance to something where the style really fits into the song.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Exclusive: Maya Hawke & Lili Taylor Tease Easter Eggs In 'The Hunger Games' Prequel
items.description: Maya Hawke & Lili Taylor Bring Calm To Sunrise On The Reaping
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: Maya Hawke & Lili Taylor Bring Calm To Sunrise On The Reaping
The stars of the Hunger Games prequel open up about becoming Haymitch Abernathy’s mentors.

Maya Hawke and Lili Taylor entered the Hunger Games universe in very different ways. Taylor, 59, saw the films through the eyes of her teenage daughter, Maeve, before becoming a fan herself. “I almost felt a little bit like a kid,” she tells Bustle. Meanwhile, Hawke, 28, watched the Hunger Games movies “so many times” in high school that she can’t “even begin to remember” her first viewing.

However, she has a special memory with Suzanne Collins’ novels. “When I read the first book, I was on a family vacation,” she tells Bustle. “I was the most melancholy teenager, didn’t want to talk to anyone, wanted everyone to just leave me alone and let me read my book. And I was obsessed.”

More than a decade later, the two actors are joining Panem as the rebellious mentors of future District 12 victor Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), showing how The Hunger Games brings generations together. In the new prequel Sunrise on the Reaping, set 24 years before the original trilogy, Hawke assumes the role of brainy District 4 victor Wiress from Amanda Plummer, while Taylor steps into the late Lynn Cohen’s shoes as the nurturing Mags.

Like the film’s other blockbuster actors, fans who grew up with these characters praised both Hawke’s and Taylor’s casting. Naturally, that brings a certain level of pressure. “I’m glad that they’re excited,” Hawke says. “Maybe because of my experience on Stranger Things, you’re constantly like, ‘How much do I let this information influence me? How much do I take in?’ I’ve really made an effort not to take it in at all.”

As for Taylor, who has experiences in franchises like The Conjuring and The Maze Runner, she says the fans “fueled” her performance. “It felt like walking into a really warm room of people who want you to succeed,” she says. “Anyone could do well with that vibe.”
Below, Hawke and Taylor open up about channeling their characters’ trauma, their memories with the younger cast, and the Easter eggs they felt were important to include.
How did your characters resonate with you?

Hawke: Wiress resonated with me personally for a long time because of her behavior in her own games. I’m certainly a pacifist now and was a deeply moralistic child. The idea that someone had the strength of character to care more about protecting their morals than about prolonging their own life is just a beautiful thing to me.

Taylor: My kid plays soccer, and I love going to the games. I love supporting the girls. And it felt like on some level, Mags is there to support and help. When I talked to [director] Francis [Lawrence] and I brought up loving the girls playing soccer, that resonated with him for Mags.
Wiress is only a year out from her Hunger Games win, and it’s clear she’s still processing it. Tell me what it was like channeling that trauma into this performance.

Hawke: Having to send children down the same path that you had to walk down is a deeply painful and complicated process. I don’t relate to it at all, just because of the high stakes of that experience. But even though I wasn’t a child actor, when working with young actors, not even children, I often have some feeling of wanting to tell them the things that I was able to do that helped me protect my mind. I have all these younger siblings, and wanting to protect young people from pain and being unable to is such a human experience.
Lili, Mags is a helpful guide to the tributes. Similarly, did you give the young actors any advice when you were on set about tackling a movie this big and what was to come of it?

Taylor: The young actors are really mature and could probably teach some of the older actors some stuff. But if anything, I felt like I needed to let Joe [Zada] know that what he was going through was real, and that as an actor, there’s no way around it. You have to suffer it, and that’s the paradox. I understood what he was going through as a human being. It was really hard on him.
Maya, you’re mentoring these tributes in the film, but in reality, you’re not much older than them. How did that dynamic play out on set when working with these actors?

Hawke: What’s amazing is that, especially in actors, you never lose the kid in you. So the group of people hanging out in my scenes — Joe, Billy [Porter], Glenn [Close], Mckenna [Grace], Ben [Wang] — felt the same age. We were all so relaxed around each other, chatting and joking together.
Lili, did you have any favorite bonding moments with the cast when you all were filming?

Taylor: I actually went out with the kids a couple of times. I really love younger people. There are these Christmas fairs in Berlin. They’re a big deal all over the city, Mckenna’s obsessed with them, and they have rides and stuff. It was just so much fun being with them.
Is there anything you added to your performance that wasn’t scripted, or an Easter egg about your character that you wanted to make sure was in the movie?

Taylor: Mags came from a fishing village, and one of their things was that they could make things out of anything. So I wanted to make sure that she could make things if she had to in the moment, but I didn’t get a chance to show that.

Hawke: I really cared about Wiress having a mechanized watch, with her connection to Beetee. I wanted it to feel like something really unique and special that she had. And also, the “tick tock” is iconic. You got to pay tribute to the “tick tock.”
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Corn Porn, White Shirts, & 9 More Korean Perfumes You Should Know About
items.description: It’s no secret that K-beauty is everywhere. From salmon sperm to cushion foundations, Korean skin care and makeup have made their way into just about everyone’s routine. Fragrance wardrobes, though, have been slower on the uptake — at least, until recently.
items.author: Emma Stout
paragraphs: It’s no secret that K-beauty is everywhere. From salmon sperm to cushion foundations, Korean skin care and makeup have made their way into just about everyone’s routine. Fragrance wardrobes, though, have been slower on the uptake — at least, until recently.

According to Spate, interest in Korean perfume has jumped 147.3% year over year. In Seoul, perfume boutiques have become just as much of a destination for beauty lovers as Olive Young. And now, plenty of Korean fragrance houses are expanding stateside — meaning you no longer need a plane ticket to discover your next scent.

But what do Korean perfumes actually smell like? “Koreans often want people to lean in closer to smell them,” says Jun Lim, founder of BornToStandOut. “Nobody wants their perfume announcing their arrival on a crowded subway.”

That doesn't mean the category is all barely-there scents, though. “People love describing Korean fragrances as clean, subtle, delicate, and minimalist — which is funny, because anyone who’s spent a Saturday night in Seoul knows Korea is anything but quiet,” says Lim. “We’re a country of contradictions: deeply traditional yet obsessed with what’s next, extremely disciplined yet wonderfully chaotic.”

That push and pull is part of what makes Korean perfumery so interesting. As Elorea co-founder Su min Park explains, traditional Korean fragrance practices emphasized harmony between the body, mind, and surroundings — a philosophy that continues to influence how contemporary perfumers approach scent.

The results can be deliciously unexpected: toasted sesame, Korean rice wine, even buttered corn. With inspiration spanning everything from the kitchen to traditional Korean rituals, Korean perfumery is anything but one-note. Whether you're a minimalist who wants to smell like you (but better) or a gourmand lover with a sweet tooth, keep scrolling for 11 Korean fragrances worth checking out.

If you've always found floral perfumes a little cloying (or even old-ladyish), Elorea’s Prelude might change your mind. It's not the kind of rose fragrance that immediately gives you a headache. Instead, Korean wild rose and woody musks come together for a dry-down that's fresh and a little earthy. It stays close to the skin, making it inoffensive to wear every day — even to the office.

A perfume that smells like corn on the cob? Maybe it’s not the first thing that comes to mind when you think of smelling good enough to eat, but BornToStandOut is here to change that. “Imagine a steaming cob of corn absolutely drowning in melted butter,” says Lim. “Salty, sweet, sticky, almost obscenely delicious.” Basically, your Thanksgiving comfort food, bottled up.

Sandalwood perfumes have a reputation for smelling like luxury hotel lobbies (looking at you, Santal 33), but Nonfiction’s Santal Cream feels more like a chill afternoon at home. It’s still sophisticated, with cardamom and vetiver adding some spice and depth. But a hint of fig balances out the rest of the notes, making it feel creamier and cozier than other drier sandalwoods.

For anyone balling on a budget, Etleé should be on your radar. With prices ranging from $10 to $20, the fragrances are surprisingly well-rounded. Case in point: Sweet Lychee, which puts a fun twist on fruity floral scents. It opens with a tart burst of apple and lychee before settling into something warmer and more mellow, thanks to jasmine, vanilla, and sugared musks.

Craving the scent of freshly washed clothes? White Shirts by Loe is the next best thing to doing a load of laundry. Soapy and cottony with a hint of floral, it smells less like you just sprayed perfume and more like you hung your favorite T-shirt out to dry in the spring. And just like that tee, you’ll probably find yourself reaching for it on a regular basis — with a $45 price tag, why not?

Don’t let the boozy notes fool you: Elorea’s Cloud Daze is just as good for daytime as it is for a night out. Inspired by makgeolli, a Korean rice wine, it has that creaminess balanced by the freshness of lemon and juniper — which almost smell floral in this composition. In fact, everything blends so well that it’s hard to pick out one note. Instead, you get something that’s worthy of a signature scent: unique enough to get people to ask you what you’re wearing — plus, it lasts all day long.

K-pop stans, this one is for you. Tamburins’ Chamo is the reported favorite of Jennie — and for good reason. Imagine a cup of chamomile tea with a spoonful of honey stirred in: herbal but light, with just enough woodiness from the clary sage to balance out the sweetness. In other words, it’s perfect for a rainy day — or any day when you want something soft and skin-like.

On the opposite end of the spectrum, there are plenty of K-fragrances that offer a little more bite. Just take Pesade’s Oud Nights — a blend of leather, cumin, and saffron. It’s sultry (and quite unisex), but less heavy than your usual oud-and-leather perfumes thanks to the bright grapefruit opening.

Another perfume that wouldn’t feel out of place in a smoky cocktail bar? BTSO’s Drunk Lovers, which Lim describes as “a romantic evening where the lovers cannot keep their hands off each other.” Juicy red berries make that first impression — not overly sweet, but a little flirtatious as the cognac starts to settle in. Then, when the vanilla finally comes through, everything gets warmer and more intimate, like the moment you’ve stopped being nervous around each other and moved to the same side of the booth.

Looking for a morning pick-me-up instead of a nightcap? SW19’s 6am is a good place to start. It opens with crisp citrus, while basil adds a green, slightly peppery twist — like walking through a garden at sunrise. Even better, it settles into a woodier, musky scent that’s just as fitting after lunch.
11The Sophisticated Gourmand

If you want to dip your toes into gourmands without smelling like a sugar overload, try Dosigoh’s Sesame Shower. At first spritz, it smells like a black sesame cookie: toasted, nutty, and warm. But instead of getting sweeter, it gets fresher as it dries down. Vanilla and floral notes come to the forefront, giving it an almost soapy quality. Think dessert, minus the sticky fingers.

items.title: Exclusive: Jordyn Woods' Game Day Style Guide Has 6 Important Rules
items.description: Whether you’re a hardcore basketball fan who can give a play-by-play recap of the NY Knicks’ historic 2026 championship run, or a fashion girlie who can do a similarly in-depth analysis of unforgettable WAG ’fits, chances are you’ve heard of Jordyn Woods’ A+ a
items.author: Alyssa Lapid
paragraphs: Whether you’re a hardcore basketball fan who can give a play-by-play recap of the NY Knicks’ historic 2026 championship run, or a fashion girlie who can do a similarly in-depth analysis of unforgettable WAG ’fits, chances are you’ve heard of Jordyn Woods’ A+ accessory game. More specifically, you know about her “lucky bag” — the orange, ostrich-leather-inspired clutch from her brand, Woods by Jordyn Woods, that became the team’s unofficial good-luck charm.

But Woods’ chic game-day style goes far beyond one viral accessory. Throughout the season, she was a courtside fixture, marrying polished luxury tailoring with sporty pieces. Now, following an epic victory parade and a dreamy Malibu wedding to the Knicks’ Karl-Anthony Towns (KAT), she’s entering a brand-new era — and already giving fans inspo.

Between wrapping up her brand’s first NYC pop-up, launching new styles like a “Trophy Gold” edition of her famous clutch, and running a campaign with Love Island’s Aniya Harvey, the multi-hyphenate is busier than ever. She’s also making wellness a priority, staying hydrated, taking her vitamins, and moving her body. “Whether it’s Pilates class or cardio, fitness helps a lot,” Woods tells Bustle. She even teamed up with Walgreens for its “Don’t Get Benched by the Flu” initiative: “The flu shot was super helpful for me because I really can’t afford to get the flu right now.”

She’s even picked up a few wellness habits from her husband, including a love for infrared saunas. Her wardrobe strategy, however, is entirely her own. While she figures out her aesthetic for the next playoff run as a returning champ’s wife, the entrepreneur is sharing her foolproof guide to serving a game-day slay.
Keep It Cozy On The Sidelines

You may not be playing the sport, but comfort should still be a priority when getting dressed. Arena layouts typically require a lot of walking and climbing steep stairs, so you need an ensemble you can actually move in. “The perfect courtside outfit is really whatever you feel comfortable with,” Woods says, noting that you never know when your competitive spirit might take over. “I love something that you can jump around in if you need.”
Make A Statement With Your Outerwear

For Woods, a stylish coat is an instant confidence booster. “I always feel like a boss in a blazer and good tailoring,” she says. “I love outerwear — a good coat, a good trench — and accessories.” Plus, it handles a very practical problem: “It’s always so cold in there, and I’m always cold, so I love a good jacket.”
Shop Like A Fashion Insider

Team merch isn’t the only way to show up with a winning look. While some fans started bedazzling bags or even screen-printing matching tees (hello, Taylor Swift), Woods prefers a highly curated approach.

“I haven’t been shopping too crazy, but I did go to my first sample sale, the Alaïa sample sale. It’s a very New York thing. I got some really good ready-to-wear pieces,” she says. The style star modeled one of her finds recently, too. “The outfit I wore to Forbes’ [30/50 Summit], I actually got at the sample sale.”

Woods loves showing team spirit as much as the next fan, but she recommends pacing yourself when the season kicks off. An all-out fan look belongs in the postseason. “I don’t really go full orange and blue decked out until the playoffs,” she admits.

Instead, she’s treating the early months of the season as a trial run to fine-tune her game-day attire. “I would love to have a uniform and figure out my exact silhouette, but right now it’s just using an excuse to experiment and try different silhouettes.”
Bench Your Good-Luck Pieces

Every fan has their rituals — like wearing a jersey or carrying a literal lucky charm. But according to Woods, you don’t have to break out the superstitions just yet. She, herself, is keeping her trusty orange Tux Clutch Mini out of rotation for the time being.

“The bag can never be replaced, but it’s definitely retired for now,” she says. “For me, superstitions don’t really come until the playoffs. We’re very fresh in the season for me to put the pressure on 80-something games.”

Rather than forcing anything, she’s open to letting more lucky pieces develop naturally as the games go on. “I don’t really have fashion superstitions this early in the season. They are developed months down the line,” she shares. “For me, it’s just about getting to wear my clothes. If I have something I’m excited to wear, I have an excuse.”
Make Room For The Aesthetic Fans
Whether someone is a lifelong season-ticket holder or a bandwagon fan who jumped on board because the outfits were cute, Woods believes everyone deserves a seat at the table.

“I love it. The more the merrier,” she says. “I’m not here to tell someone they can’t be a fan of something, because all it takes is one game to become a fan. I don’t have ownership of the fandom. Any support is good support. People should be allowed to do whatever they want.”

At the end of the day, the arena is just another runway, and she’s here for the creativity. “New York is full of so many different characters, and there’s something fun and exciting every time,” Woods says. “There are always fun videos of people’s outfits, or even the phone accessories people would make.”
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Krysta Rodriguez Won’t Back Down
items.description: Krysta Rodriguez Won’t Back Down
items.author: Christina Amoroso
paragraphs: Krysta Rodriguez Won’t Back Down
In Broadway’s A Few Good Men, the theater vet plays a woman who knows how to make herself heard. In real life, she’s learning to do the same.

In the Broadway revival of Aaron Sorkin’s legal thriller A Few Good Men, Krysta Rodriguez plays Lt. Cmdr. Joanne Galloway — one of just two female roles in the play, which opened at the Vivian Beaumont Theater last week. She’s used to being one of the only women in the room.

“I often find myself in those positions, and you’re grateful to be in the room, but when push comes to shove, you don’t always have the allies who you might need,” says the actor, 42. “I’m very fortunate this group of men that I’m working with are all so lovely, and we’re having a great time. But as far as groups of people you want to look for when you need to feel like someone understands you, that’s not going to happen every once in a while — and so I definitely relate to Jo in that.”

The starry Lincoln Center Theater production, which runs through Jan. 10, features Bradley Whitford (who starred in the original in 1990 on Broadway) and Tom Blyth, who’s making his Broadway debut. Sorkin wrote much of the play on cocktail napkins while bartending at the Palace Theatre. And while its initial run wasn’t a hit — with critics or the box office — the 1992 movie, starring Tom Cruise, Jack Nicholson, and Demi Moore, was a smash that launched one of the most iconic lines in movie history: “You can’t handle the truth!”
“What’s been crazy is how many younger people know the line but never saw the movie,” Rodriguez says of the show’s new audience.

Rodriguez’s extensive TV and theater credits include Smash (both the NBC series and the Broadway musical) and Spring Awakening (the original production and the 2015 revival). She also recently wrapped up a turn as Roxie Hart in Chicago and moonlights as an interior designer, having fixed up dressing rooms for Broadway stars Jeremy Jordan, Megan Hilty, and Lily Rabe. For Jordan, she created a Jazz Age-inspired space for his run in The Great Gatsby.
So what does Rodriguez’s own dressing room look like?
“To be honest, I haven’t been able to focus on it yet. I always make this joke that the cobbler’s children have no shoes.”

Jo picked this career because there is a sense of meritocracy in it. Even with all the bullsh*t, she can still put together the right paperwork that will get the right thing done. So I relate to the desire to be in a system like that. I think I give off this appearance of being relaxed and cool, but I am the most anal, the biggest rule follower. I don’t know why I’m an actor, because I wish I lived in a meritocracy. I wish I lived in a world where A plus B equals C, and it just never does.

My life is so different day to day — I’m playing someone who’s skipping through the fields or I’m traveling to Budapest to shoot something or I’m working on my interior design business. What I wanted to tap into is the structure and the rigidity of somebody who went in through the academy, who woke up at six every morning, made their bed, did the routine, and made sure they didn’t step out of line or the whole house of cards would fall apart. For me, my whole life has been about stepping outside the line. If I stay too rigid, my life will fall apart. So I tried to find tiny things that would be a big deal for me, like making my bed every morning and making it really meticulously, or making sure I went to the gym every day — something that I noticed that I have committed to and I stay firm on.

Due to the rank Jo has, people have to listen to her. She gets to be less polite. Whereas in my life, I have to make sure I lead with a smile and am nonthreatening — kind of tiptoe around an opinion. And sometimes that can build up until the one time you do give an opinion, it actually backfires because you’ve presented yourself as so docile. I don’t think anyone believes I’m docile, but you do try to sand those edges so that you’re palatable. And when you do ask for what you need, it actually works against you. You could be nice for 400 days, and the one day you’re a little surly, that’s what they’re going to remember.

So what I’ve tried to learn in my life is that it’s actually helpful to be honest and clear from the beginning. And that’s what I need to learn from Jo — she’s clear, she is not presenting any sort of front. It’s actually impossible for her. And it has taken her far. She, through all of her chutzpah, makes everyone come in line with her.

What I love about Jo’s ambition is that it’s pure. She is there because she believes in justice. There is no altruistic motive in acting. When you’re young, you want to be a star. And then as you start to realize what that means and what you sacrifice for that — is it satisfying at all? So you start to recalibrate. And as I started to get older, some of the roles that were coming to me were less exciting, just as I became more interesting and complex. I wanted the parts to meet me there.

My mom likes to talk about balls and strikes, and sometimes ambition can mean waiting. It can mean making sure to do things that align with your values and what you want to spend your time doing. So my dream expanded. Like, the dream initially was to be on Broadway — OK, I got that. Like, the dream was to be a lead — OK, I got that. The dream was to be at the Tonys — I got that. Now the dream is like, can I enjoy my life? Can my career be positioned in a right-sized manner with the rest of my life? Can the ups and downs of it affect me in the same way as the ups and downs of the rest of my life? And will that keep me more curious, more relaxed, more free, and let me wait for the parts that really speak to me so that they are more worth my energy and my care? So I think my ambition has turned more caring.
On working with younger actors:

We have, like, 11 Broadway debuts in the show, and I’m lucky to be in it with a lot of young people who are just starting out. It’s so fascinating to see that ambition on display — “I want this and I want that.” It’s exciting, but you also want to hug them and be like, “This is gonna wear off.” So either use it now, or learn to make friends with it.

Tom is making his debut, but he went to Juilliard, so he’s not afraid of the stage. A lot of people who have only done film or TV take this opportunity because they really want to hone their chops in a new way, and I think this experience for Tom of just being able to show these chops now to people, or to get to pull them out of storage, is fun. Both he and Bradley are just so lovely to get along with, and it’s so nice because you never know what you’re going to get with a show where you don’t know a lot of people. I do so many musicals, so it’s almost impossible for me to do a show where I don’t know three-quarters of the cast. So for this to be a bunch of people who I’ve never met, and they’ve never met me, has expanded my life, but I think it’s been good for the show.

We don’t know anything about Joanne’s life outside of this show. Everybody’s got a backstory, and Jo has nothing. It’s literally a joke in the show — “Jo, you do whatever it is you do when you’re not here.” And while that’s a funny punchline, it is something that I think people are recognizing now, that maybe the female characters don’t get as much backstory. So I like to play around with this idea that Jo’s actually kind of fun at home. She’s a real good-time gal. Like, she can be married. She could have one-night stands. She could be going to the bar every night.

I like to make a playlist about what I think Jo might be doing at home. She’s got a little something rolling around underneath, and that’s what makes her rigidity so much more fun. I want Jo to be the most solid woman you’ve seen, and for women who come to see the show to be like, “That’s my bitch. I wanna be her.” So I have Beyoncé’s “Formation.” And anything that has some militaristic feel, like “I have got to wrangle people,” is on there. And some Lily Allen.
On memorable audience interactions:

What’s rare is to have a show where you have so many rules that could be followed — there are rule books after rule books about the uniforms and the bars and the salutes. What’s particularly moving is how many service members who have seen the show, and so many of them became service members or became JAG because of the movie. At some point I was at the stage door where this woman got my signature, and then she ran to the end of the line and went, “Uh, your skirt’s too long.” And I said, “Oh, we have a uniform consultant,” but he’s male, you know? And she said, “I’ve been JAG for 29 years, that skirt’s too long.” And this other woman who was next to her — and they weren’t together — says, “I’m Air Force. She’s right.” So I went to my costumer, and he raised the hem. So we have tried our best, but we want to make sure we reflect properly to the people who we're representing.

Every show is a little different, and I haven’t figured it out quite yet. Right now, I go home and go to sleep — I’m in my bed within 20 minutes of arriving at home. Anything else I need to do is happening while lying down, and it might be emails or planning for the next day or whatever. But my favorite way to unwind is grabbing food after the show with friends, people who have come to see it, and maybe having a nightcap. Right now, those things are not available to me as I learn how to train for this particular show, but I’m hopeful that those things will arrive. As the kids say, touch grass — and for me, touching grass is spending time with my friends.

Another fun thing is learning the spots around Lincoln Center. Vanguard Wine Bar is a spot that’s also in Midtown, so that feels comfortable — you’re like, OK, great, I know what I’m gonna get here. The Empire Hotel rooftop bar is really special. And I’ll go with my friends to Shun Lee, this really classic Chinese place around the corner, when we go to the opera and get dressed up. That’s like our ritual. We actually had a day during tech where Tom and Nick, who plays Sam, and I went to Shun Lee and had a defense team dinner, and it was so fun. We just had a blast and ordered as much kung pao chicken as you can possibly eat.

items.title: 28 Unique Fashion Gifts For Your Impossibly Stylish Friend
items.description: 20 Unique Fashion Gifts For Your Impossibly Stylish Friend
items.author: Jinnie Lee; Vivien Lee; Victoria Montalti
paragraphs: 20 Unique Fashion Gifts For Your Impossibly Stylish Friend
Marc By Sofia Book by Sofia Coppola

Fashion enthusiasts will adore this new book that documents designer Marc Jacobs' most iconic looks through director Sofia Coppola's eyes. Coming off the back of the A24 documentary this summer, this supplementary book was released, and we think it's the perfect gift (and coffee table book display).
Damson Madder Leopard Embroidered Apron

We love Damson Madder for its outerwear, matching sets, and winter accessories, but now the British brand has expanded into homeware. This looks like striped pillows, polka-dotted wine bags, leopard-print aprons, and more, allowing your space to be as whimsical as your wardrobe. Whether you cart up a hot water bottle sleeve or dog bed for your giftee, they'll appreciate the kitschy, joyful styles.
Drowsy Sleep Co Breakfast at Tiffany's Silk Sleep Mask

Whether they're a Breakfast at Tiffany's fanatic... or are just a fan of their beauty sleep, this sleep mask is a super luxe option for sleeping in style. The soft mulberry silk is gentle on hair and skin, and promises to deliver restful nights and slow mornings, just as Holly Golightly would like.
Quince Mongolian Cashmere Crewneck Sweater

Quince’s cashmere is a no-brainer because of its high quality and low cost. At just $50, you can stick to your budget, while delivering on timeless style. This crewneck in any colorway will no doubt be a welcome addition to anyone’s sweater drawer.
Ugg Tasman Western Slipper

Ugg boots are consistently at the top of holiday wishlists, and these new Western slides may just become 2026’s viral sell-out style. The embroidered shoes have a yeehaw feel and will have your giftee walking with a swagger, whether it's around the house or around town. (The stitched design is also available in a mini boot in women's and men's sizing!)
Collina Strada Gold Multi Constellation Studs

Your giftee probably doesn't want another necklace with their initials or bracelet with their birthstone. Instead, look out for unique styles that speak to their style and personality. For the maximalist, consider these designer gemstone earrings that will most definitely stand out from their everyday collection of hoops and studs.
Staud Lila Mini Satin Top-Handle Bag

The Lyst Index just released its Q3 report, and Prada found itself as the hottest brand and its Wish Silk Duchesse Pouch as the hottest product between July and September 2026. If you and your giftee have Prada taste, but not a Prada budget, there are some alternatives on the market to get the look, like this Staud satin bag.
Old Navy x Altuzarra Plaid Funnel Neck Overcoat

This collaboration between Old Navy and Joseph Altuzarra resonated with Refinery29 readers, so we're pretty sure your fashion-forward giftee will love it too. While many styles have sold out, you can still get your hands on this classic funnel-neck dress coat in sizes XS through 4X for under $100 while it's on sale.

Balaclavas have been huge for the last few winters, with the beanie-scarf hybrid being It-girl approved. More recently, purple has been rising as a trendy colorway. And this style in particular falls under $40. It's the perfect gifting trifecta for the on-trend giftee on your list.
Kate Spade Perfect Match Matchbook Key Fob

2026 was really the year of finding the best photo booths and collecting the best matchbooks. For the matchbook collector in your life, consider this luxe Kate Spade keychain which doubles as a key fob. The dangling matchstick charm is chef's kiss.

Think this is a flower vase? Wrong! It's a clutch! And it doesn't require watering! Cult Gaia's purses appropriately go viral because they're pieces of art that trick the eye. While any of the It-girl brand's designs would make for a jaw-dropping gift, we're all about this style's sale price.
TheAlchemistFinds Modular Magnetic Wall Organizer Storage System

Okay, I saw this wall organizer used as a "purse wall" on Instagram and I can't stop thinking about it! It's the most genius solution for holding all your purse essentials, like sunglasses, wallets, house keys, and lip combos, especially for the giftee who's constantly changing out their bag to match their outfit.
Guerlain Rouge G Satin Lipstick & Customizable Case

You may have seen these customizable lipstick cases in TikTok videos of people visiting Paris' Guerlain stores. But there's great news because you don't have to purchase an international flight to get one! Instead, go online and pick a shade, then personalize it with a case design, from fashion-forward animal prints and croc-effect leathers to colorful rhinestones.
Adidas x Asos Snake Print Oversized Track Jacket

Another fashion collab that has turned readers into shoppers is the Adidas Originals x Asos elevated streetwear capsule. This fifth collection features stylish tracksuits and sporty knits. And this snake-print windbreaker makes a bold statement, whether styled for hot girl walks or late-night raves.
Anthropologie Mini Bag AirPods Case

Okay, we're obsessed with these mini handbag keychains to hold our AirPods cases, because why shouldn't style extend to tech? Sure, your giftee doesn't need a croc-effect or woven bag for their headphones, but they'll surely get a smile on their face as soon as they receive one.
Petit Moments Bambi Faux Fur Scarf

Deer prints (more adorably called Bambi prints) have been trending this season, especially dotted across jeans, outerwear, sneakers, and accessories. We recommend gifting the print in winter accessories like scarves because despite the rise and fall of trends, your giftee can happily return to this sweet style winter after winter.
Coach Archive Tabby Puzzle

For the Coach connoisseur, this out-of-the-box gift celebrates the iconic Coach Tabby bag. The 500-piece puzzle features a 1970s catalog-inspired print that's giving old glamour. It's also the perfect fashion-lover activity on game nights and rainy days. (Plus, it doesn't come with a $300 to $700 price tag.)
Lululemon Daydrift High-Rise Wide-Leg Trouser

Give the gift of comfort and style with these editor-favorite Lululemon pants that look like a trouser but feel like a lounge pant. (How do they do it? The secret lies in the soft, stretchy fabric and drawstring waistband.) Available in several colorways and hem lengths, the perfect pant is one click away.
Owala FreeSip Patterned 24 oz Water Bottle

Owala's viral water bottles just keep getting more and more stylish. Beyond the many chic color combos available to peruse, the brand is also selling prints now, including florals and plaids, making them an extension of your outfit.
J.Crew Ostrich-Feather Brooch

We've seen flower brooches and feather brooches rise in popularity as a simple way to personalize any outfit, whether pinned onto a tank top like Carrie Bradshaw (or onto a blazer like SJP). Brooches always make for thoughtful gifts, but we're loving the texture and dimension of these styles. Plus, as seen from style influencers, they can also be hooked around heel straps and sneaker laces for a DIY shoe upgrade.
