items.title: Scorpio Season Is All About Death, Sex & Rebirth. Your Tarotscope Explains Why
items.description: Latines learning, remembering, healing, and finding joy in our diverse stories.
items.author: Tatianna Tarot
paragraphs: Latines learning, remembering, healing, and finding joy in our diverse stories.
Beautycon is a global platform that brings together beauty enthusiasts, brands, and industry leaders to explore the latest trends, innovations, and conversations shaping the future of beauty.

November opens with the dead, particularly our ancestors and beloved spirit guides. On November 1 and 2, Día de Muertos fills homes with marigolds, candles, and the favorite foods of those who came before us. At the same time, in Haiti and across its diaspora, Fèt Gede honors the Gede, the spirits of death in Haitian Vodou. They’re known for their dark humor, their unapologetic sexuality, and their power to heal. Neither tradition treats death as something to fear. Both treat it as part of life, a doorway, and a reason to celebrate.

This month, we are also deep in Scorpio season, ruled by the very things most people avoid talking about: death, desire, and transformation. Scorpio knows that nothing is reborn without first being let go, and that pleasure and power live in the places we’ve been taught to hide. The New Moon in Scorpio on November 9 plants the seed of who you’re becoming. Meanwhile, on November 13, Venus and Mercury both station direct, ending the review of your love life and your truth that began in October. What you learned in the dark is now ready to be lived.

Death, sex, and rebirth aren’t taboo. They’re sacred themes that help us embrace more life. Something in your life is ending. Something in you is craving more. And someone new is emerging from what you’re finally ready to release. You can’t fully live until you’re willing to let something die.
These tarotscopes will show you what’s ending, what you’re desiring, and who you’re becoming. Read for your sun, moon, and rising.

items.title: Everything We Know About Off Campus Season 2
items.description: To anyone with a smartphone and an outrageous screen-time average, it’s clear 2026 is the year we collectively obsessed over steamy hockey romance. If, like many of us here at Refinery29, you’ve smashed through the first season of Prime Video’s viral sensation
items.author: Ella Taverner; Kathleen Newman-Bremang
paragraphs: To anyone with a smartphone and an outrageous screen-time average, it’s clear 2026 is the year we collectively obsessed over steamy hockey romance. If, like many of us here at Refinery29, you’ve smashed through the first season of Prime Video’s viral sensation Off Campus, based on Elle Kennedy's beloved book series of the same name, and you're highly anticipated your next fix. We’ve got some good news to satisfy those cravings. Despite only launching on 13 May 2026, Prime Video has already confirmed a second season of the swoon-worthy drama set at Briar University and announced that it will officially return in April. Fans can now rest easy knowing they won’t have to wait long for more romance, drama, and campus antics.

The first season of Off Campus centres on a fake-dating plot between Hannah Wells (Ella Bright), a musician with big dreams, and ice hockey prodigy Garrett Graham (Belmont Cameli), featuring Josh Heuston (Heartbreak High) as magnetic musician, Justin Kohl. Capturing the hearts and minds of YA fans everywhere, here’s everything we know about Off Campus Season 2 so far — plot teasers, returning cast, and when you can expect it on your screens.

Before Season 1 of Off Campus aired, it was announced that Season 2 had already been greenlit by Prime Video, making eager fans suspect we might be back at Briar University sooner than we think. Speaking to Variety earlier this month, show creator Louisa Levy confirmed that "all eight scripts are written" for the show's second season. And now, Prime Video has confirmed that the show will officially return for Season 2 on April 28, 2027.

Much like Netflix’s Bridgerton, each season of Off Campus is set to follow the relationship arc of different characters. While the second book in Kennedy’s series, The Mistake, follows Logan and Grace, the showrunners have already proven they’re not afraid to deviate from the source material.

In May, Prime Video announced the new leading couple on Instagram, writing: "One couple made a deal. The next one is keeping the score. From Garrett & Hannah to Dean & Allie — the Off Campus love story continues in Season 2." And now we know that the new season will adapt the plot of Elle Kennedy’s third novel in the Off Campus series, The Score. In an announcement on Instagram, Kalyn and Hayes can be seen confirming the new season and dropping the release date news.
As for the rest of the main cast, Levy confirmed to Refinery29 that Josh Heuston would not be returning for Season 2, but that she would “never say never."
Other cast members set to return include Ella Bright, Belmont Cameli, Antonio Cipriano, Jalen Thomas Brooks, Charlie Evans and Khobe Clarke.
For Off Campus Season 2, India Fowler has been cast to play protagonist Grace Ivers, and Philipa Soo will play Scarlett.

While we don't have a trailer for Season 2 just yet, fans are anticipating that since filming seems to have wrapped and we've got a release date, a trailer drop is imminent. For now, a Season 1 rewatch will have to suffice.
Off Campus  is available to stream exclusively on Prime Video. While we wait for Season 2 to drop, all eight episodes from Season 1 are available now.

items.title: The New Moon In Scorpio Is Here — & This Is Your Opportunity To Reconnect With Yourself
items.description: The New Moon occurs on November 9th during the last weeks of Scorpio Season. This lunation will bring a mix of versatile vibes, some volatile and some favorable. We can pick and choose our own adventure and how we wish to navigate the New Moon, as long as we'r
items.author: Lisa Stardust
paragraphs: The New Moon occurs on November 9th during the last weeks of Scorpio Season. This lunation will bring a mix of versatile vibes, some volatile and some favorable. We can pick and choose our own adventure and how we wish to navigate the New Moon, as long as we're careful not to get pricked by the venomous stingers of the scorpion. To evade the drama, it's imperative that we stay in our lanes and do not honk our horns in traffic — basically, keep the commentary that doesn't involve us to a minimum and opt to take the high road, when in doubt of how to proceed.

Mars, Scorpio's traditional planetary ruler (modern ruler: Pluto), squares the New Moon. Mars in Leo aspecting the New Moon in Scorpio creates an intense external reaction to internal forces. We may feel as though other people are triggering us with their actions, stirring frustration in our auric field and prompting us to voice our annoyances and assert ourselves, even though we know the best move is to walk away from confrontation. The reason is that words can cut deep during this transit; we may not be able to take back or apologize for things that are said in the heat of the moment.

Getting carried away with our emotions is part of the vibe. IKYK that Scorpio is a sign that is penetrating and oozing with passion; when Mars comes into play with it, the exuberance intensifies, giving us the ability to accomplish our goals and set an aspirational path forward. Impulsivity runs high, so we tend to take shortcuts to achieve greatness and skip necessary steps. Working our way up the corporate ladder or starting a relationship slowly isn't a bad idea — to be real, it encourages us to know the criteria and scope of the job and provide companionship to someone we are familiar with. Wanting to rise to the top without understanding the requirements and prerequisites can lead to our downfall — so tread lightly. More importantly, do not rush the process. Savor the moment. Test the temperature of the water by dipping our toes in first, rather than jumping in.

Mercury retrograde in Scorpio and Venus retrograde in Libra are still moonwalking in the sky, creating erratic sentiments; this is a call to hone in, as the energy is unpredictable, meaning the unforeseen can come to fruition. A great way to harness this is to listen before speaking and think through the best response; also, don't commit before you know the details and expectations. That way, we know the rules of the game, and we can act accordingly. Of course, this won't be easy. But through discipline, we can control our behavior to ensure we conduct ourselves with dignity and treat others with respect.

The following day, Venus retrograde in Libra and Mars in Leo align, setting the stage for a grand journey that promises growth and development in matters of love. However, we'll do our due diligence to heal and transcend. Consider the New Moon as the catalyst for this venture. Forgiving others — especially ourselves — will be freeing because it lifts a burden from us. We no longer have to carry embarrassment, fear, resentment, and heartache. We are moving past it into a state of newness that replenishes our lives. The hurt we feel are in the natural rhythm and flow of mending themselves, offering hope and optimism for the future.

The asteroid Ceres, which is in Cancer, harmonizes with the New Moon. The mythology of Ceres is that of a mother whose daughter, Proserpina, was abducted by Pluto, unbeknownst to her. As the goddess of agriculture and fertility, Ceres stopped tending the Earth, which affected the harvest and caused famine when Proserpina went missing. She revolted against the Roman gods to get their attention and make them search for Proserpina. After finding Proserpina, Ceres struck a deal: she'd visit her daughter in the underworld for a few months and do her job to aid Earth the rest of the time, creating the cycle of seasons. We see Ceres as a testament to unconditional love and the depths we go to for those we care about. In this case, we are both Proserpina and Ceres. The New Moon is our opportunity to reconnect with ourselves or old friends, but only if we are ready to evolve. Let's get moving!

items.title: How to take notes that actually help you learn | Psyche Guides
items.description: is an associate professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience at Saint Louis University School of Medicine in Missouri, US. Her research focuses on the use of effective learning strategies and individual differences in learning. She is
items.author: Cynthia Nebel
paragraphs: is an associate professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience at Saint Louis University School of Medicine in Missouri, US. Her research focuses on the use of effective learning strategies and individual differences in learning. She is a member of The Learning Scientists and co-author of Ace That Test: A Student’s Guide to Learning Better (2023).

is an associate professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience at Saint Louis University School of Medicine in Missouri, US. Her research focuses on the use of effective learning strategies and individual differences in learning. She is a member of The Learning Scientists and co-author of Ace That Test: A Student’s Guide to Learning Better (2023).

Notetaking is a versatile skill. Perhaps you take notes during lectures in class, or as part of your job, or when you’re reading an insightful book, or when you have an important meeting. If you’re a notetaker, in any case, you want your notes to be as useful as they can be. And that starts with thinking about their function. Since taking notes is such a common activity, it’s easy to overlook the question of what notes are actually doing for us.

Many people assume that just by writing information down, they are doing something useful. But the cognitive processes involved in taking notes and the way you take them can make a big difference in terms of what you ultimately get out of them.

There are two broad goals of notetaking: recording and learning. The first is when you try to take down as much information as you can so that you don’t miss anything and can review it later. This might be necessary sometimes – for instance, if you are going to be tested on the information presented in a lecture, and you won’t have a recording, text, or slides to refer back to later. Similarly, if you are in charge of meeting minutes or want to do more research on what you’re hearing from your doctor, you may need to simply record as much information as possible.

But in many situations, the most effective and efficient way to take notes is to treat them as a tool for learning: that is, to use them to help you retain and understand the information by putting it down in your own words and organising your thoughts about it. This is the kind of notetaking that I’ll focus on in this Guide.

What do good notes look like, and how can you get better at notetaking? There is not one right answer to these questions, but knowing a bit about how and when notetaking is effective will help you to decide what kind of notes to take when, and what to do with them afterward. As a cognitive psychologist and director of learning services at a medical school, I have a lot of experience with the most effective strategies for notetaking and why they work. Below, I’ll explain how to use some of these strategies and the reasoning behind them.

Taking notes to learn is different from taking them to record. Sometimes you need to take down as much as possible. But if you hope to internalise the information, you’ll want to process it as you take notes.
Use paper if possible. Since it slows you down, you have to decide what the most important pieces of information are before putting them on paper, which supports learning.

Experiment with ways of processing. Organise the information in your own way – try making summaries, bulleted lists, drawings or charts – and note links between what you’re learning and other things you know.
Try a structured approach. In the Cornell notetaking system, you complement your main notes with a summary at the bottom and cues to practise recalling the information later.
Adopt a better review strategy. Don’t just reread or copy your notes – reorganise them in some way. Then test your memory and understanding and check your notes to see what you’re missing.
Use AI tools selectively. They can be helpful for creating detailed records, but don’t rely only on AI notes if you’re trying to learn.

You may have heard before that taking notes by hand, on paper, is better than typing them on a laptop. There is truth to this, but it is due to more than just the effect of handwriting. Writing on paper can be more effective because it is much slower than typing. It’s difficult to write down every word or detail, requiring you to decide what the most important pieces of information are before putting them on paper. When you do this, you’re engaging in a type of mental processing that leads to better learning. Taking notes on paper also allows you to easily jump back and forth between different concepts and to organise them visually (using a diagram, for example).

These things can be done electronically, but most people find that it’s clunkier. If you must use a device, my recommendation is to not simply copy what you hear or read verbatim, but rather to prioritise what seem to be the most important points, and to ensure you process the information by doing some of the things I’ll describe next.
Experiment with ways of processing

When you’re taking notes to learn, it’s essential to organise the information in your own way and to think about how it relates to other things you know (even examples from your own life). You could make bulleted lists, write summaries in your own words or write questions about the material. Maybe you also want to draw pictures or flow charts, or connect different parts of a lecture with arrows. All these activities involve somehow mentally processing the information, which leads to actual learning rather than just recording.

For example, some of my students will create a high-level outline of the main topics from a lecture; under each heading, they write a summary of the information in their own words once that part of the lecture ends. Other students try to anticipate how they might be quizzed on the material and write practice test questions in their notes.

Here’s an example from outside the classroom – let’s say I’m reading a book about a historical figure and want to better retain the information. How might I start? As I go from chapter to chapter, I could take notes in the margins, or in a separate notebook, about how each part of the book relates to contemporary events, other history that I know, or situations in my own life. I might find certain areas interesting or inspiring and write in my notes about why those things caught my attention. Again, these all involve mentally processing, or what we can call active (vs passive) reading.

Coming up with your own way of taking notes may seem like a big challenge. The good news is that there are existing notetaking strategies that can help you with this process. One of the strategies that is supported by research is the Cornell notetaking system, created by the Cornell University education professor Walter Pauk.

In this approach, you separate a page into three parts. On the main part of the page will be your ‘notes’. At the bottom of the page, you include a ‘summary’. In the lefthand margin, you label an area for ‘cues’. Here’s an example:
As you’re taking in the information (eg, in class or during a discussion), you use the ‘notes’ area to keep track of important points and ideas.

Afterward, you fill out the ‘cues’ section, which is primarily used to help guide your study later on, when you go back to review your notes. You might write down questions to help you think about the material that was covered, or prompts related to what is most important. These serve as retrieval cues to help you practise recalling the information later, which is a highly effective learning strategy. It could also be helpful to note in the cues section anything you don’t understand, to clarify what you might have to review further or follow up about. Sometimes, depending on the context, you might be able to fill out the cues section while you’re still taking down your main notes.

Last, you fill out the ‘summary’ section, writing down the big-picture ideas that came out of what you heard or read, in your own words. This allows you to take a step back and think through what all of this means and how it fits with other things you’ve been learning.

What’s great about this notetaking system is that it requires you to process the material in multiple ways. The system is also very adaptable. If, for example, you attend a lecture that’s very dense, you could take verbatim notes first and then take Cornell notes later, based on your initial round of notes. And if you need more space, you can reserve a whole page for the ‘cues’ section and subsequent pages where you put your notes, including a summary at the end.

While the Cornell approach is a reliable technique, there are other structured ways of taking notes that you might want to explore as well. For example, mind-mapping is a strategy in which you put the main idea in the centre of a page and organise related material around it using branching connections. With sketchnoting, you take advantage of the powerful interaction between verbal and visual material by creating notes that involve lots of pictures. And outlining can be an effective strategy because it requires you to consider what is most important and how various pieces of information support each topic. Each of these strategies is evidence-based and they work in different ways to support deeper processing.
Adopt a better review strategy

Once you have your notes, what should you do with them? Hopefully it’s clear by now that processing the information is key, so just rewriting the same notes is mostly a waste of time. When you do that, you don’t really have to think about the notes you’ve taken. However, if you reorganise your notes in some way – such as by summarising them, or creating diagrams, flow charts, or hierarchies – that is likely to be more useful, especially if you had to take verbatim notes at first. For example, after hearing about how the heart works, you could draw a picture with arrows showing the direction of blood flow, or you could create appropriate headings and subheadings to organise the main ideas and supporting facts.

Similarly, just rereading your notes doesn’t require a lot of mental effort. It feels like you’re learning, and you might get better at it over time. But if you’re trying to internalise and retain information for later (for example, if you want to be able to retrieve answers on a test), then the best way to prepare is to practise doing that. Instead of rereading, you could try using your ‘cues’ from the Cornell method to bring as much of the information to mind as you can. Then you can go back to your main ‘notes’ section to see what you missed.

If you’re using a different notetaking strategy, you could write quiz questions based on your notes that you can then answer from memory. Or, you could use your notes to make flashcards. Instead of just copying down the notes onto the cards, try using the front side of the card for questions that you could get someone to ask you, or for different ways of comparing and contrasting the information. For example, you could write: ‘Compare and contrast the upbringings of Alexander Hamilton and Aaron Burr.’ This will give you a processing benefit while you’re creating the cards, as well as the retrieval benefit when you use them later.

You could also do a ‘brain dump’, where you try to write down everything you can remember about a topic and then check your notes for accuracy and to fill in any gaps. All of these strategies involve more productive mental effort than rereading does, and they come with the advantage of helping you figure out what you do and don’t know.

If you’re recording a lecture or a conversation and you want a thorough transcription and summary that you can revisit later, AI tools can be useful for that. However, when you use AI to take notes rather than doing it yourself, you are bypassing the kinds of mental processing that will help you learn. Because of this, I don’t recommend relying on AI for notetaking if your goal is to retain the information. In situations where it’s important to have a detailed record and you use AI to create one, just make sure that you go back to those notes later and apply one or more of the review strategies above if you hope to remember the material later on.

Notetaking is not just one thing and you should adjust your approach depending on the situation. If the information is very dense and it’s not contained anywhere else, then trying to take down as much as you can makes sense – but you’ll still need to revisit and make sense of those notes later on. And when your aim is not to copy but to internalise what you’re hearing or reading, then the best way to take notes is to summarise, organise and make connections between the material and what you already know. Ultimately, the key is to think about what you’re learning, both as you’re taking it in and when you come back to it later. The best way of taking notes is the one that helps you do that.

items.title: How a revelation at home made me rethink delusion | Psyche Turning Points
items.description: The young woman sitting in front of me is sure she is dead. It – her dying – happened two weeks ago, she says. Now she simply doesn’t exist.
items.author: Ryan McKay
paragraphs: The young woman sitting in front of me is sure she is dead. It – her dying – happened two weeks ago, she says. Now she simply doesn’t exist.

I check the scrawl of referral notes, which don’t say anything about this. There isn’t much time; I’m supposed to administer her a battery of cognitive tests, dictate a brief report, and move on to my next patient. I want to reassure her, but her eyes dart about my office – small, over-lit and cluttered with stacked folders and a tangle of dusty cables.
‘Is this heaven?’ she asks.
It’s not clear how best to respond.

I’ve spent my professional life trying to make sense of cases like these: delusions. Part of the challenge is how to draw the line between who a person is and what has gone wrong with them. In the clinic this is often straightforward, and as a clinician or theorist trying to understand such cases there is at least a measure of certainty, and the possibility of detachment. But these questions are increasingly contested in cultural spaces – and sometimes they must be confronted not just at work, but at home.

Many of the most fascinating clinical examples of delusion concern personal identity and bodily integrity. Some patients look in the mirror and see a stranger; others believe their loved ones have been replaced by physically identical impostors. In one strange case, published in 2018, a man presented to an Australian emergency department convinced that his penis had been stolen and substituted with someone else’s.

Are delusions merely the dysfunctional products of a broken brain? Or might they in some cases be functional – purposive constructions that protect the self? Sigmund Freud famously described a delusion as a kind of psychic bandage, and many others have followed suit. Psychoanalytically inclined theorists have construed the conviction that you are dead as a paradoxical defence against death: if you are already dead, you have nothing to fear from dying. Others in the Freudian tradition have cast a young woman’s belief that her father has been replaced by an impostor as a way of denying that her sexual feelings for him – supposedly rooted in ‘penis envy’ – are incestuous.
Freud’s ideas are easy to pillory and caricature, and in lectures on the Freudian approach to psychopathology I have sometimes lightened the mood with an anecdote about my kids:
Two-year-old [noticing older brother’s penis in the bath]: ‘I want a willy.’
Seven-year-old: ‘Girls don’t have willies. Boys have willies, and girls have pyjamas.’

Yet the idea that delusions can serve a psychological purpose isn’t always far-fetched. And, of course, the idea that beliefs can serve emotional functions is not confined to clinical disorders. I’ve often wondered about the emotional underpinnings of my own convictions, particularly those concerning God and religion. Some psychologists have argued that atheism is driven by feelings of abandonment, perhaps from losing one’s father at a formative age. This theory doesn’t enjoy much contemporary support, but for a while I was quite taken with it: my dad had died suddenly as I was on the cusp of adulthood.
One prominent commentator has claimed that gender dysphoria is the clearest case of social contagion in history

That summer, I got a job on a gold mine, in the Australian outback. The work was hard, and I drank a lot. But for a while the new environment offered escape from the palpability of my dad’s absence. As the weeks passed, however, something began to give. While working a night shift, hurtling through the dark desert in a fuel truck, I felt him there with me in the cab. Afterwards I became fixated on the jarring discordance between the way we react to death and the comforting stories we tell about it. If it was true that my dad was in heaven, then why all the grief and grim faces? Why hadn’t my relatives arrived with beaming smiles to impart the good news about where he had gone? For a short while, the rawness of grief opened me to really believing, and I wanted to convince my family that his death was something wonderful, that we should feel joy. I was approaching an edge. But then I stepped back.

Thereafter, rigid analysis and brittle abstraction became both shields and weapons. I identified as a scientist and an atheist, and relished taking a scalpel to the Christian tradition I had been raised in. As a graduate student, I wrote a paper provocatively titled ‘Hallucinating God?’, arguing that religious belief is delusional. Part of the argument was that typical religious beliefs – virgin births, transubstantiation, bodily resurrection – often violate just as many established scientific principles as clinical delusions do. God, I was convinced, simply doesn’t exist.

However, the ‘bible’ of psychiatry – the American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) – specifies that religious beliefs are not delusional because they enjoy wide cultural acceptance. On this view, the impostor-penis patient was delusional not simply because his belief was false and harmful (he had cut and burned his penis), but because it lacked cultural scaffolding in Australia.

I was impatient with this perspective. After all, similar beliefs – also false, also harmful – have at times arisen in shared, collective contexts. Did that mean they weren’t delusions? So-called ‘penis panics’ have been reported in various countries. Such ‘collective delusions’ demonstrate that harmful ideas, sometimes untethered from biological reality, can gain a cultural foothold.

According to some commentators sceptical of the concept of gender identity, the recent rise in gender dysphoria is a Western ‘culture-bound syndrome’, part of a lineage of culturally mediated expressions of distress, from penis-theft scares in Asia and Africa to the collective delusions catalogued in Charles Mackay’s classic book Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds (1841). Indeed, one prominent commentator has claimed on social media that gender dysphoria is the clearest case of social contagion in history.
Given the hard-nosed mindset I had spent decades cultivating, I could understand the pull of claims like these.

A summer’s night, and I’m reading to my younger child, who is now seven, in the soft glow of a rabbit-shaped lamp. One of the characters in the story describes something as ‘queer’, and I’m immediately asked to explain this word. I say it means strange or unusual, but after a moment I add that it also has another meaning: that some people use it to describe themselves, people who might be gay or not comfortable with their gender.
‘I don’t know, love, that’s for you to decide.’
‘I’m not comfortable with my gender.’
This has been clear for years by this point. I no longer tell the willies-and-pyjamas story in class.
‘It’s not your fault, Dad. I might have selected the wrong gender in Baby Heaven.’

I learn that Baby Heaven is an endless playground of fun where you play until you’re born. You arrive on a flying bus after God creates you, and while you wait to be born you choose your gender, eye colour and skin colour. God chooses other things, like which country you’re born in or which parents you’re born to.
I can’t help seeing the rise in trans identification not as a wave of delusion but, in part, as a wave of visibility
I switch off the lamp, and we study the sticker constellations on the ceiling: a makeshift Southern Cross, an improvised Saucepan.
‘I’m glad I got you and Mum as parents.’
Memory is fallible, but this moment still feels vivid and glimmering. A bulwark against what might lie ahead.
As a parent, scenes from the boarding school I attended increasingly return to me, like scraps of a language you once spoke emerging unbidden on return to that country.

No one in the boarding house would have dreamed of admitting to being gay, but signs of homosexuality were scrupulously monitored. Mornings could be tough, especially in the earlier years. An older boy would burst in and tear your blankets off, and you were ushered straight into a communal shower. The only respite was a quick visit to the urinal on the way to try and kill off the erection you had inevitably woken with. Taking it into the shower with you was unthinkable.

Although pornographic magazines were traded fairly openly (care was taken to avoid housemasters, who would confiscate them), there was an extremely strong taboo against masturbation. Presumably we were only reading these magazines for the articles. This taboo called for extreme caution. One unfortunate boy who was caught in the act became a social pariah. While I wish I could say that I’d stuck up for him, or even that I’d empathised, my attitude towards him was more a mix of anthropological curiosity and contempt.

It’s clear to me now that the strikingly low prevalence of homosexuality and masturbation in the boarding house reflected taboo rather than true absence. One of my closest friends there later came out as gay; I had absolutely no inkling before he phoned to tell me. He had somehow survived years of pressure to keep this invisible. While trans and gender-questioning youth still face a hostile climate, bullied today at twice the rate of their peers, I can’t help seeing the rise in trans identification not as a wave of delusion but, in part, as a wave of visibility – less a contagion of identity than of permission to be seen.
‘Dad, were you happy when you realised I was trans?’
A year or two has passed. We’re in the changing room of our local community swimming pool. It’s not really a conversation I want to have in such a public place.
‘Let’s just finish getting dressed, and we’ll talk about it in the car.’
Back in the car, I sit in the driver’s seat. My son climbs in behind me, and when the door shuts, I start to talk. I choose my words carefully.

I don’t say that the experience of being his parent has forced a sometimes-uncomfortable realignment of my own beliefs and identity, that it has surfaced some of my own prejudices and many of my fears.

I don’t admit that, for a while, I’d been irritated by phrases like ‘assigned at birth’, or that I’d resented the growing pressure to state pronouns in email signatures and social media bios, that I’d considered this performative. That it took having a deeply personal stake to consider what such practices might mean to people like him.
Rather than ceding authority for who he is to God or biological happenstance, he claims it for himself

I don’t talk about how I’ve been distressed by the viciousness of the rhetoric I’ve seen online, but humbled by the kindness and unhesitating acceptance of people in our own community. I don’t say that I recognise now that people’s beliefs and identities are not my intellectual playthings, not just specimens on my board. That they can be vessels of anguish and fragile, questing hope. I don’t tell my son that I’m awed by his courage to be himself.

I do try to explain that, as a parent, you want your child to be who they are, without having to pretend, to wear a mask. But at the same time, you worry about them having a difficult path through life.
I talk for a minute or two, and when I stop, there’s a silence.
‘So, does that make sense?’
I’m worried I’ve upset him.
Another silence. I turn around, and he looks up.
He hasn’t been listening at all. Must have tuned me out almost immediately.
A mix of emotions. Annoyance, obviously – I’d spoken with care, and thought I’d acquitted myself well.
But mostly I’m relieved. For the time being at least, this subject is not the be all and end all.

What I find quietly inspiring about my son’s musings on Baby Heaven is also what frightens me: rather than ceding authority for who he is to God or biological happenstance, he claims it for himself. His cosmology is a metaphor for self-authorship, but also for accountability. It opens the door to pride, if others acknowledge what is authored, but also to shame or even erasure, if they do not.

A book from my own childhood that my kids have enjoyed is an Australian classic: The Bunyip of Berkeley’s Creek (1973) by Jenny Wagner. The titular bunyip wanders about, asking others (a platypus, a wallaby, an emu) what bunyips look like.
‘Horrible,’ they say, with ‘horrible feathers’ and ‘horrible fur’.
When a scientist tells the bunyip that bunyips ‘don’t look like anything’ because they ‘simply don’t exist’, his reaction is mournful but understated: ‘What a pity.’
A common gender-critical refrain is that ‘There is no such thing as a transgender child.’
Perhaps, for such commentators, this denial is a swish of the lab coat, an abstract intellectual dismissal. But to a trans child, it may land as something closer to annihilation.

items.title: That feeling of values crumbling has a name: civic grief | Psyche Ideas
items.description: If reading or watching the news feels less like staying informed and more like a daily horror or heartbreak, you’re not alone. Many of us are carrying a kind of civic homesickness. It’s what happens when the truths we presumed were universal start to crumble.
items.author: Rebecca Lewandowski
paragraphs: If reading or watching the news feels less like staying informed and more like a daily horror or heartbreak, you’re not alone. Many of us are carrying a kind of civic homesickness. It’s what happens when the truths we presumed were universal start to crumble. Sometimes, differences of worldview so profound have emerged that even dinner conversations feel like foreign policy negotiations.

How do we give shape to this disquiet? We might call it fatigue, burnout, or ‘just needing a break from the world’, but often it’s grief – mourning for a faith we once had in fellow citizens to recognise a certain decency or sense of fairness. It isn’t partisan; it’s human, and it has a name. Civic grief doesn’t care which side of the table you sit on. It can visit anyone who has seen their values of citizenship and belonging abandoned or even opposed by their neighbours or friends or country.

If this sounds familiar, take heart. The ache itself is proof of care, a sign that some part of you still believes we can do better. Around the world, survey after survey shows people losing faith in institutions, leaders, and even each other. Freedom House’s 2026 report found that global freedom declined for the 20th consecutive year in 2025, with political rights and civil liberties deteriorating in 54 countries and improving in only 35. Those numbers have lived counterparts: military coups, efforts to weaken constitutional safeguards, violence against peaceful protesters, attacks on courts and journalists, and families increasingly unable to discuss public life without treating one another as hostile witnesses. The grief, in other words, is not floating above reality. It is responding to it. In naming civic grief for what it is, we can find a more honest place to begin, and perhaps a way to see what is still in common even across bitter divides. First, civic grief needs to be understood more clearly.

The first stage is denial, a most civilised coping mechanism. It wears a suit, reads editorials, and insists that things are not as bad as they look. We might remind ourselves that democratic government has survived worse: wars, recessions, demagogues, corruption. We use history like a sedative, and call the system ‘resilient’, confident the pendulum will swing back. We vote and try to convince ourselves that the institutions are working as they should. Denial has its uses, but slowly we begin to absorb the scope of the crisis in small, unavoidable doses.

The trouble comes when denial hardens into complacency. In places where the erosion of our civic life is subtle, it is easy to believe that real breakdowns aren’t a crisis. If we decide events are a ‘temporary disturbance’, nothing fundamental has to change. Scaled up, it turns into a false, reassuring voice saying ‘institutions are basically fine’ long after the evidence disagrees.
The cycle of scandals, polarisation and moral fatigue accumulates until they register as the new reality

When denial cracks, anger usually walks in, puts its feet on the table, and opens a social media account. Biologically, it is the nervous system in fight or flight. The amygdala turns up the volume on threat, stress hormones spike, and attention narrows to villains and blame. It can fix on corrupt officials, apathetic neighbours, ‘elites’ or ‘the media’. In one country, it centres on police violence or election fraud; in another, on inequality or culture wars. It often shows up as indignation at bias, apathy or the endless loop of shouting heads who look like they are debating but are mostly performing disbelief, showing they still care enough to be furious. Algorithms love this, which is why anger is the grief stage most compatible with modern technology. We mistake outrage for engagement, and forget that noise and signal are not the same. Yet anger has a purpose. It is the immune response of conscience. The task is to keep it from turning autoimmune, and to let it fuel stewardship instead of scorched earth.

The next stage of civic grief is bargaining. It sets in once the adrenaline cools. This is the ‘if-then’ logic of the optimist feeling despair. If we educate the next generation better, if more people vote, if we just talk across the aisle, things will get better. Bargaining is democracy’s prayer: let us return to normalcy, and we promise to behave better this time. It is noble but delusional, for it assumes the old ‘normal’ can be restored. Still, bargaining reveals something precious: the refusal to give up. Even naive hope has moral worth. Bargaining may not save democracy, but it prevents cynicism from claiming the soul entirely.

The fourth stage of civic grief is depression, the weight of disillusionment. The cycle of scandals, polarisation and moral fatigue accumulates until they register as the new reality. This is the stage of numbness: when people withdraw from the public sphere not out of apathy, but out of emotional self-preservation. The ballot box feels like theatre. Debate feels like déjà vu. Facts feel negotiable. Philosophically, this is a dangerous moment, when the demos, the people, cease to believe their will matters. This is a kind of soft despotism from long ago: not tyranny of chains, but of indifference. Depression acknowledges that idealism has limits. Here is when people often ask, what if the system is functioning exactly as designed? What if the system is no longer democratic?

Accepting the stages of our civic grief is important and does not mean surrender. It means we can move on to seeing more clearly. It is where citizens begin to understand that democracy was never an inheritance, but an ongoing responsibility and an act of stewardship and creation. Acceptance is where we stop waiting for ‘the adults in the room’ to fix things and recognise that we are the adults. The work of democracy, it turns out, is not glamorous: it’s reading city budgets, attending community meetings, and listening to people who annoy us. It also requires humility. The idea that one political side or ideology can ‘save’ democracy misunderstands it. Democracy, by nature, is a tense structure built to hold disagreement without collapse. The goal was never unanimity, but coexistence. Democracy was never meant to eliminate conflict. It was meant to civilise it, to keep disagreement from becoming dehumanisation, and to turn competing claims into conditions where dignity, security, opportunity, collective wellbeing and belonging remain possible.

Coming through to the other side of civic grief means no more nostalgia for the previous order. Instead, it brings us to reinvention and action. This kind of hope insists that, even when institutions falter, individuals must act to represent democracy and can still support democratic values of curiosity, empathy, courage, restraint. Hope becomes real when it stops being a feeling and becomes a discipline. It means choosing one part of the common life and tending it close to the ground: a school, a library, a neighbourhood association, a local campaign, a food pantry, a veterans’ organisation, an environmental group. Democracy is rebuilt there, through habits that may outlast us: transparency where suspicion could take root, listening where contempt would be easier, and enough restraint to remember that opponents are still people, not symbols arranged for our convenience.

Emotions are not irrational storms; they are intelligence about what we value. Civic grief says that fairness, dignity and shared obligation were precious enough that their loss hurts. In the body, it feels like heaviness or fatigue. In the mind, it becomes questions: who are we if what we were told to trust keeps failing us? What does it mean to be a ‘good citizen’ when the rules feel soft for some and razor sharp for others? How do you keep caring about an ‘us’ that no longer feels shared?

It can be unsettling to realise that the person who seems to live on the other side of every issue may be grieving a different story about what was lost, but they still felt something crack where they thought ‘we’ lived. Calling this civic grief does not erase our differences; it gives us a shared language for the ache and a first step toward something more useful than fighting or shutting down.

items.title: Why astrophysics needs to abandon the ‘Big Questions’ | Aeon Essays
items.description: In the story of cosmic history, one of the most important supporting characters is dust. As clouds of interstellar gas cooled and condensed in the early Universe, dust grains absorbed and re-emitted radiation, eventually forming stars. Later, dust provided the
items.author: Dylan Jow
paragraphs: In the story of cosmic history, one of the most important supporting characters is dust. As clouds of interstellar gas cooled and condensed in the early Universe, dust grains absorbed and re-emitted radiation, eventually forming stars. Later, dust provided the raw material from which planets could form and grow. Dust grains may even have been the surfaces on which the first complex organic molecules formed. Yet, if you ask most cosmologists, they’ll tell you that dust is a sheer nuisance.

In astrophysics, ‘nuisance’ is a quasi-technical term. Astrophysicists call any phenomenon that gets in the way of the thing they actually want to study a ‘nuisance’. Dust grains emit polarised light that can mimic subtle signals from the afterglow of the Big Bang (the cosmic microwave background) that cosmologists have spent decades and billions of dollars trying to detect. A cosmologist studies dust not to uncover its role in shaping the cosmos, but to subtract it – the term ‘sweeping under the rug’ couldn’t be more apt.

This dichotomy between ‘signal’ and ‘nuisance’ is found across many sub-fields in astronomy. Astronomers who study a phenomenon called ‘weak lensing’ use the subtle distortions of light caused by gravity to map invisible dark matter. For them, the ordinary matter that makes up everything we can see is a nuisance. Pulsar timing astronomers use rapidly spinning neutron stars called pulsars as extraordinarily precise clocks to detect the passage of gravitational waves through the galaxy. For them, the nuisance is ionised interstellar gas, which scatters and disperses the light from pulsars.

Yet one astronomer’s nuisance is another’s treasure. Just as a laser beam reveals the intricate swirls of smoke in a dark room, pulsars illuminate the fine structure of the interstellar medium, the unlit space between galaxies. If you want to study the interstellar medium and its role in shaping our galaxy’s evolution, the light-scattering gas is an invaluable resource.

Whether a phenomenon is a nuisance or something worth studying in its own right clearly depends on the investigator and their interests. But in a discipline as collaborative as astronomy, shared priorities must be developed. Gone are the days of Galileo and other lone scientists in the tower, pointing telescopes built by their own hands wherever curiosity dictates. Modern astronomy is a highly specialised discipline, marked by large collaborations. The tools of the trade – telescopes – are designed, built and maintained by hundreds of scientists and engineers across many institutions. But you can’t just stroll in and ask to use one. Investigators must fiercely compete for time with these advanced instruments. To guide how that access is allocated, the research community has developed a set of shared priorities. Some questions are elevated to the status of ‘Big Questions’ to which all others inevitably become subordinate.

But are these Big Questions necessarily the right ones? Who decides where to draw the boundaries between signal and nuisance, or big and small? Fields of enquiry are defined by the questions they seek to answer. If we want to understand modern astrophysics, it is not enough to understand the scientific and mathematical content of its theories. We also need to understand the human forces that shape the questions themselves and cause some questions to be prioritised, and other questions to be viewed as irrelevant or merely means to those bigger ends.

To identify the Big Questions that dominate the field, you need look no further than the flagship projects set to shape the discipline for decades. These include the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, the James Webb Space Telescope, the Vera C Rubin Observatory, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, and the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna. Each of these projects will cost several billion dollars over its lifetime.

When we look at the stated science goals of these projects, consistent themes emerge. For example, the Square Kilometre Array Observatory at Jodrell Bank in the UK is a massive radio array that will define the field of radio astronomy for the foreseeable future. Its website contains a list of science goals. On that list, the early Universe, gravitational waves, dark energy and cosmology are all listed before stars, the interstellar medium and the origins of life. The official page for the much-covered James Webb Space Telescope similarly lists the early Universe – the ‘cosmic dawn’ – before more prosaic matters such as stars, planets and dust. Such priorities are often reflected in media coverage of these projects, which further shape perceptions among young researchers, politicians, funders and the general public about which questions matter most.

The boundaries between the big and small questions often fall along the lines between ‘fundamental’ physics and ‘messy’ astrophysics. This is reflected in the language of many cosmologists who study dark matter, for example. For decades, the study of dark matter has focused on the largest physical scales – giant clusters of galaxies – where the gravitational effects of dark matter can be directly inferred. On small scales, within and around galaxies, dark matter’s effects become entangled with the complex dynamics of interstellar gas. To use the terminology that is widely adopted by cosmologists: the physics of dark matter on small scales is obscured by the astrophysics of interstellar gas. Implicit in this framing is the idea that astrophysics is messy and complicated, and, ultimately, subordinate to clean, fundamental physics.
When the fundamental is elevated above everything else, it’s easy to see why an impressionable young mind might be captivated

Young researchers encounter this supposed predominance of physics over astrophysics long before they set foot in a laboratory. Growing up, I loved space, as many children do. My parents bought me an amateur telescope, and I spent many nights in the backyard becoming familiar with the winter night sky (the summer sky was more elusive because it appeared after my bedtime). But, by the time I entered graduate school, I had largely forgotten about my early childhood passion for the heavens. Like many of my peers at the time, I wanted to study theoretical particle physics.

Particle physics enjoys a kind of mythical status in popular culture as the apex of the natural sciences. After all, the purported goal of particle physicists is not just a theory of particles, but a theory of everything. Of course, such a theory would be a theory of ‘everything’ only in the limited sense that it would describe how all matter behaves on a fundamental (microscopic) level – never mind the fact that such a description would be functionally useless to describe even basic chemical reactions due to the mathematical complexity. But when the fundamental is elevated above everything else, it’s easy to see why an impressionable young mind might be captivated.

In the end, I did not study theoretical particle physics as a graduate student. The competition was intense – almost all of my classmates were vying for the few positions available. So, I rekindled my love of astronomy and decided to study astrophysics. But the truth is, at the time, I viewed astrophysics as something of a consolation prize.

This hierarchy, which ranks fundamental physics above all else, is a historical contingency. Over the course of the second half of the 20th century, astronomy transformed from a distinct discipline into a sub-discipline of physics. Historically, astronomy was a science of mapping, cataloguing and observation. But the successes of mid-century nuclear physics, the rise of physical cosmology and the discovery of dark matter and dark energy began a process that fused the two disciplines.

The discovery of general relativity, which describes gravity as a warping of the fabric of space and time, provided a new framework that enabled the quantitative study of the dynamics of the Universe as a whole. Cosmology, which had previously been the domain of philosophers, became the domain of physicists. In the closing decades of the 20th century, this framework enabled the dual discovery of dark matter and dark energy – both mysterious substances unaccounted for by the standard model of particle physics. Crucially, these gaps in the standard model would have gone completely undetected without the observations of astronomers.

The heavens, then, transformed from an object of study in its own right to a new laboratory for testing fundamental physics. This shift is preserved in our vocabulary: the term ‘astronomy’ was demoted in favour of the more prestigious term ‘astrophysics’.
I saw astronomy as a means to an end, a stepping stone on the path to a theory of everything

The rise of astrophysics was, in part, fuelled by the geopolitics of the Cold War, which saw an unprecedented surge in funding for physics, in addition to a rise in the cultural prestige of physics in the public imagination. Governments invested large sums of money in physics mega-projects, cementing a culture of large collaborations dedicated to the study of fundamental, high-energy physics. This was the era of the particle accelerator, in which subatomic particles are accelerated to extremely high energies to test theories of physics that manifest only at those energy scales. But then the Cold War ended, and the cash flow stopped. In 1993, the US Congress cancelled the Superconducting Super Collider project in Texas, after billions had already been spent.

Suddenly, a generation of particle physicists found themselves without the experimental tools to test their theories on Earth. Astronomy, however, provided an attractive alternative. The Universe revealed itself to be the ultimate, free particle accelerator: full of violent events, such as supernovae, colliding black holes and the Big Bang, reaching energy scales that no terrestrial collider ever could. If only the complications of real astrophysical environments could be modelled and accounted for, then the heavens would be the perfect new laboratory for physics.

It was precisely this logic that sold me on astrophysics as a new graduate student. At the time, I saw astronomy as a means to an end, a stepping stone on the path to a theory of everything. I was interested in the messy complications of astronomy only insofar as understanding them would enable us to disregard them.

Today, this ‘physicisation’ of astronomy has left a deep imprint on the cultural norms of the discipline. Modern astrophysics is characterised by massive, hyper-centralised international collaborations, and an often tacit belief that ‘fundamental’ physics sits at the top of the scientific pyramid, while the questions of real ‘astrophysics’ are mere nuisances.

This ideological elevation of the fundamental over the particular is evident in the architecture of modern big-data astronomy. The past few decades have been characterised by experiments yielding massive volumes of data. Yet, these pipelines are not neutral data-gathering machines; indeed, their very design reflects and reinforces the institutional bias towards astrophysics as a barrier to fundamental truth. The logic is that, with enough data, the rich and diverse astrophysical phenomena that manifest in particular cosmic environments can be statistically modelled and averaged away, leaving only what is fundamental.
AI models inherit untested assumptions about the physical processes they aim to illuminate

Consider, for example, the phenomenon of weak gravitational lensing, where astronomers measure how gravity distorts the shapes of distant galaxies. They can use this to build a map of the dark matter in the Universe, which is otherwise invisible. However, weak gravitational lensing is equally sensitive to the gravitational effects of all matter in the Universe – the dark matter and the ‘ordinary’ matter. The physical interactions that govern ordinary matter complicate inferences of the underlying dark matter distribution. Data analysis pipelines for modern weak lensing surveys flatten the complex physics of astrophysical environments to a set of ‘nuisance parameters’, which, with enough data, can be averaged away. Rich astrophysical phenomena are, from the very outset and in the survey design itself, framed as statistical obstacles to fundamental truths.

This paradigm is further reinforced by the turn towards artificial intelligence (AI). A natural symbiosis exists between the petabytes of data generated by modern observatories and the massive datasets needed to train deep learning architectures. Driven by the hype, if a project promises to use AI, it helps attract funding and allocation of computational resources, even when its capacity for genuine discovery remains unclear.

Foundation AI models are heralded as the best way to digest datasets too massive for detailed human analysis, promising to automatically infer complex astrophysics from raw images of the sky. But there is a fundamental disconnect between the statistical patterns these technologies learn and the underlying physical mechanisms that generate the observations. Whereas you might train an AI to learn what a cat looks like with a set of images of known cats and non-cats, there is no set of galaxy images where all the relevant astrophysics is known. Instead, models need to be trained with synthetic data drawn from astrophysical simulations. However, computational limitations force these simulations to rely on simplified approximations of the very physics in question. As a result, AI models inherit untested assumptions about the physical processes they aim to illuminate.

This is not a problem if your goal is simply to account for complex astrophysics in massive data sets to infer the underlying fundamental physics. These models are, after all, exceptional at identifying and correcting for subtle correlations in the data. But if your goal is to understand the complex physics of the astrophysical phenomena themselves, the benefit is less obvious.

Thus, modern astrophysics appears to be oriented towards a paradigm of modelling massive data sets to uncover fundamental constants. This paradigm is mutually reinforced by the questions that are institutionally prioritised and the tools used to answer them. However, this loop of reinforcement can create an illusion of field-wide consensus around what the most important questions are, which obscures the daily realities of many working astronomers.

This is nowhere more visible than in the discourse surrounding the ‘Hubble tension’ – the fact that different methods of measuring the Universe’s expansion rate (the Hubble constant) yield contradictory results. Across white papers and popular science articles, the Hubble tension is touted as a profound crisis in physics. If the discrepancy is real (as opposed to a statistical fluke), then it could be an important hint about the nature of dark energy, which drives the expansion.

And yet, in the trenches of astrophysics research, attitudes are markedly different. At nearly every talk I have attended on the Hubble tension, the reaction from working astrophysicists is surprisingly muted. If this discrepancy is the great white whale of modern cosmology, why do so many researchers respond with a shrug?

The reality is that most scientists are passionate and obsessive creatures, devoting many years of their lives to extremely niche topics that others might struggle to care about. Such people naturally find their work intrinsically interesting, not just as a step towards some bigger question. Of course, scientists have complex motivations that are shaped by their institutional environments and that shape the long-term trajectory of their careers. But, on a day-to-day basis, many astronomers really do just care a lot about dust, or gas dynamics, or cosmic magnetic fields.

For myself, the further away I got from physics proper, the more I rediscovered my love of astronomy for its own sake. Whether or not astronomy unearths new fundamental laws of physics, it has much to tell us about our place in the Universe and what it means to be human. Since Copernicus, astronomy has gradually demoted humanity’s position in the cosmos, from occupying the literal centre of everything, to merely occupying an unremarkable planet, orbiting an unremarkable star, in an unremarkable galaxy in a potentially infinite Universe. At the same time, as the bounds of the known Universe expand, we have increasingly understood the rarity and fragility of life in the cosmos. Astronomy, therefore, plays a critical role in the story of the human species. While I remain hopeful that astronomy can lead us to new fundamental physics, that hope is no longer the driving force of my interest in the heavens. I suspect this is the case for many of my fellow astronomers.

Despite this, investigators are required to play a rhetorical game, justifying their deeply specific research within the context of the predetermined Big Questions. When you apply for academic jobs, the advice is: Always, always, always link your work to the Big Questions. Since hiring or grant committees typically comprise faculty with a diverse range of expertise, an applicant cannot rely on the committee sharing an intrinsic interest in their niche topic. Justifying your science in relation to the Big Questions is more likely to lead to a successful application, even if individually none of the members of the committee are particularly passionate about those questions.

Scientific journals reinforce this rhetorical game. The most prestigious journals demand that their articles represent significant advancements in the field. In other words, they require that the research they publish make progress on the pre-defined Big Questions. Investigators are incentivised to frame their papers in this context. I have personally written papers that motivate the work as a step towards resolving the Hubble tension. While technically true, this framing misrepresents the reasons I embarked upon that research and the real reasons I find it interesting.
If you could uncover the nature of dark energy, or discover alien life, which would you choose?

This is not to suggest that having shared priorities across a research community is somehow wrong – indeed, it is inevitable. But it is important to recognise that these priorities are historically contingent and, to some degree, arbitrary. When investigators play the rhetorical game of justifying their research, the game ends when they link their work to a fundamental question in physics. But why stop there? Why is the search for dark energy or dark matter inherently more justified than the lifecycle of interstellar dust? The ‘fundamental’ questions are no more or less intrinsically justified than the nuisances that get in their way. Rather, we choose which questions are ends in themselves and which require further justification.

Many commentators have made a great deal of the crisis that faces high-energy physics today. Terrestrial collider experiments have failed to reveal any signs of the new physics they were built to find, and we may well be reaching the limit of what astrophysics can tell us about fundamental physics. Even if the Hubble tension is confirmed, we may never settle on the correct physical theory of dark energy. Even as we better characterise the gravitational behaviour of dark matter, its particle nature may remain a mystery forever. The Big Questions are beginning to lose their lustre, and some are beginning to ask whether the billions of dollars spent on mega-projects are diminishing in their returns. But if this is a crisis for high-energy physics, there is no crisis for astronomy. Astronomers will continue to investigate all the weird and wonderful things the Universe has to offer.

If you’re an astronomer reading this – or anyone who would like to play along – I invite you to consider the following hypothetical. If, tomorrow, you could uncover the nature of dark energy, or discover alien life, which would you choose? Both would guarantee a Nobel, but which one actually feels like the bigger, more meaningful discovery? Although I can speak only for myself, I suspect many astronomers – even bona fide astrophysicists – would choose the latter.

Astronomy has a unique place among the natural sciences. Its immediate practical benefits are limited – especially the further away from Earth you go. It’s hard to imagine a detailed understanding of galaxy evolution directly leading to some technological benefit in any foreseeable timeline. Yet astronomy excites the public imagination like no other science. It’s not because astronomy has the potential to uncover new physics at high energy scales. It’s because we, as a species, have always looked up to try to understand our place in the Universe.

Peering through my backyard telescope as a child, I had no concept of fundamental physics. But looking at the fuzzy haze of the Orion Nebula and realising that I was watching the birth of stars – well, there are no words to describe the sense of wonder I felt. If astronomy must justify itself according to some Big Questions, let them be these: where did we come from, and what is our place in the cosmos?

Ultimately, the priorities of a field are not immutable facts but a choice. Shifting priorities need not be seen as a crisis, but as an opportunity to ask ourselves why we study what we study in the first place – an opportunity to make different choices that better align with those reasons. Astronomers, then, have an opportunity to reorient the priorities of the field away from a reductionist view of physics, and to reclaim the value of the nuisance.

items.title: The more we rely on tech, the more we deskill our bodies | Aeon Essays
