items.author: Sarah Hendrickx
paragraphs: How would it be if you woke up one morning around 4 am, consumed by an idea that felt like the Best Idea You Ever Had. You spend the next two hours fervently researching said idea, watching videos, reading in-depth articles, compiling a spreadsheet comparing costs, techniques and options, then buying a whole load of books and equipment, and signing up to courses to teach you how to bring this fantastic, life-changing idea to fruition. You book a viewing for the new house in a new country that you are going to buy after investigating climate, housing options and work opportunities. You book the flights for that trip, to a Pacific island, where you will learn to scuba dive and set up a business as a dive instructor having fully understood the tourism industry and its legal implications. You sign up for that master’s programme in hypnotherapy/mushroom-growing/road-building after comparing the cost and quality of all colleges offering these courses. Your research is deep, your conclusions well justified. These are all good choices.

Buzzing on your own brilliance at finding the answer to all of your problems, your true calling in life and, basically, frigging nirvana, you are desperate to wake your beloved, who is lying beside you, blissfully unaware that their world is about to be rocked. You think about waking them because you can’t contain all this excitement alone and need to share it, but it’s only 6 am and you know from experience that this wouldn’t end well. So you sit, fidgeting, watching the clock until 6:30 am. Surely, that’s late enough? Perhaps if you bring them coffee, they won’t be so mad. Yet how could they be mad, when what you’re about to reveal to them will make them say: ‘Why didn’t you wake me up sooner, you genius?’

But as you sit impatiently waiting for an acceptable hour to rouse your beloved and blow their mind, your whole self shifts sideways, like someone just turned the TV over to another channel or a changeling took over your mind. You suddenly realise that your previously designated Best Idea Ever is full of holes and is actually a Terrible Idea. You are puzzled that you didn’t see this sooner. What were you thinking? You can’t move house because your kids are in school here, you have a full-time job and bills to pay, and you don’t have the attention span to read your horoscope, let alone do a master’s. And you can’t even swim.

What idiot thought that any of this was a good idea? Oh… it was me. OK… time to cancel it all and hope that you didn’t lose too much money and that it will all be back in the bank account before ‘they’ wake up.
And hope that you don’t do the same thing again tonight.
Welcome to the world of AuDHD.

You will likely have come across the term AuDHD used as a shortcut to describe those given the dual diagnosis of autism and attention-deficit and hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). It is a relatively new label and for good reason – until recently, no one individual was clinically permitted to be given both diagnoses and therefore there was no one to whom the term ‘AuDHD’ could officially apply.

In 1994, a mere 32 years ago, the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th edition (DSM-IV), included Asperger Syndrome for the first time. In 2013, the diagnosis was removed from the 5th edition (DSM-5) and subsumed under the broader category of ‘autism spectrum disorder’. Asperger Syndrome had identified individuals who met the social and behavioural aspects of the diagnostic criteria for autism but who did not have intellectual disability or the language-development differences then associated with an autism diagnosis. As a result, an autistic person reading this magazine today would have been unlikely to receive an autism diagnosis in the past: there was simply no diagnostic category that fit their profile. That helps to explain the huge rise in adult diagnoses in recent decades.
Autism and ADHD were long considered mutually exclusive

Alongside this, diagnosis of ADHD in adults has been a similarly recent arrival. Having been considered a predominantly childhood condition for most of its history, the idea that children can continue to experience ADHD features into adulthood was not seriously considered until the early 2000s. Earlier versions of the DSM required that symptoms had to have been present prior to the age of seven years, and focused almost entirely on childhood behaviours to form the diagnosis. In 2013, with the publication of the DSM-5, the onset age of ADHD symptoms was raised to 12 years, and fewer symptoms were required for adults to meet the diagnostic threshold – which took into account development changes and challenges within adult settings, such as work – thus opening up ADHD diagnosis to adults.

This means that a person without intellectual disability and with relatively typical language development has been eligible for an autism diagnosis for only 32 years. And the ADHD criteria have been explicitly adapted to better recognise the disorder in adults only since 2013. That history is one part of the AuDHD issue.

The second part is that autism and ADHD were long considered mutually exclusive. It was thought that their apparently contradictory traits of rigidity and impulsivity effectively cancelled each other out. This meant that a person – either child or adult – could not be officially diagnosed with both conditions until 13 years ago, when the DSM-5 removed this exclusion and allowed both diagnoses to be given to the same person – opening the way for what is now widely called AuDHD.

At first glance, existing diagnostic criteria for each condition may look like contradictions of each other. While a stereotypical autistic person may present as socially awkward, precise and cautious in language and behaviour, requiring predictability, sameness and calm, our ADHDer looks like the complete opposite. ADHD diagnostic criteria typically present as someone socially driven, scattered and impulsive in language and behaviour, seeking novelty, variety and stimulation. How can it be that both of these seemingly opposing traits can exist in one person, and what is it like for that person when they do?

Given the relatively recent formal recognition of this comorbid profile, research into its impact is unsurprisingly scarce and, aside from a small handful of papers, has been focused on children and adolescents. The earliest research into this overlap I could find was published in 1999; those investigators concluded that autistic features were common in those with ADHD, and that a dual diagnosis should be considered in some cases, even though this was not clinically permitted at the time. This overlap has been one of the most frequently studied aspects of AuDHD.

A 2023 systematic review identified 9,050 articles and ultimately included 23 studies; across these, estimates of the prevalence of ADHD symptoms in autistic young people without intellectual disability ranged from 2.6 per cent to 95.5 per cent. Another paper suggested that 50 to 70 per cent of autistic people present with comorbid ADHD. If you are reading this article with a diagnosis of autism or ADHD, you may want to think about whether you may be both, because it’s looking increasingly likely that you are.

Of course, there have always been differing opinions and concerns about the pathologising nature of diagnosis in neurodiversity. Where does one neurodivergent condition end and another begin? Can we really separate these aspects of ourselves into neat clinical categories – often deemed necessary to permit access to a particular support service, therapy, fund or setting to meet the often-disabling needs of being neurodivergent in a neurotypical world? The reality is that no one knows the answers, so here we are with our rigid clinical diagnostic criteria, which – as we can see from the alterations in the DSM-5 – are changing as understanding grows. Forgive me for working within these uncomfortable neat boxes, but they are all we have right now; and, for at least some people, they can be a helpful way of understanding the contradictions of living with AuDHD.
My former life had failed to meet my autistic need for routine but had satisfied my ADHD need for novelty

The example at the top of the article is one from my own life and it has resonated with many of the 69 AuDHD adults and parents of AuDHD children whose stories and words I had the privilege to gather for my new book, The Complete Guide to AuDHD (2026).

My own AuDHD story is a typical one. I was diagnosed as autistic in my 40s after having written five books on autism and neurodiversity and achieving an MA in autism – I knew my stuff, and myself, or at least I thought I did. Yet I had led a chaotic life of multiple jobs, house moves and plans and schemes of one kind or another – I am known for it by those who know me; they take bets on how long I will stay in one place/job/course/project – which upsets me, but which is hard, logically, to take umbrage at.

I had never considered that I would meet the criteria for ADHD diagnosis because I was too logical, too organised and too set in my ways. I am the Queen of the Spreadsheet, the Mistress of the Plan. After bringing up two kids, I worked as a trainer and speaker for 15 years, travelling the country and overseas on a crazy schedule of driving, hotels and public speaking. Not surprisingly, I crashed horribly into years of panic attacks, agoraphobia and severe physical and mental burnout. Eventually, I gave it all up and began working locally and remotely, removing 90 per cent of the stress and unpredictability of my former life. At first, it was wonderful, I remembered what it was like to wake up without a brick of dread and anxiety on my chest. I slept in the same bed every night and knew what each day would bring. Perfect. Until… a few weeks into this blissful new existence I recall a feeling that I verbalised at the time as ‘I feel like I’m dead.’ I felt flat, blank, nothing, emotionless. Over a period of reflection, I realised that I had never actually sat still my whole life. While my former parenting and working lives had failed to meet my autistic need for routine and predictability, they had entirely satisfied – what I now understood to be – my ADHD need for constant dopamine in the form of novelty, variety and excitement.

Those who have the same experience of a second diagnosis of either autism or ADHD share the same feeling I did – it’s the final piece of the puzzle. The first diagnosis made sense of a lot, but it didn’t explain it all. There were questions and gaps: ‘I’m too social to be autistic.’ ‘I need too much order to be ADHD.’
This sense of two selves, of the push and pull of opposing wants and needs, is the core of the experience

Since the dual diagnosis of the two conditions is fairly recent, it is still unusual for both diagnoses to occur at the same time, with most adults currently having received one diagnosis first and the second at some point later, as did I. And although autism and ADHD were deemed contradictory for much of their joint history, both sets of diagnostic criteria need to be met for each diagnosis to be given: there is no allowance made for ADHD characteristics masking those of autism, for example – which they often do – during the diagnostic assessment.

Which diagnosis comes first varies from person to person, with either autism or ADHD often appearing as the primary profile. Perhaps ADHD appears more ‘visible’ for a child challenged by sitting still at school, or autism for an adult struggling with the social and flexibility requirements of a job – with the other lurking behind ready to throw a spanner in the works or offer a helping hand. Given that the second diagnosis was simply not an option for so long, the thought of it was generally never given the time of day, although a number of AuDHD people I have assessed often say they’d felt that the first diagnosis had answered some of the questions they’d had throughout their lives about why they were different, but not all. For others, it was a complete surprise. As one person I interviewed for my book explained:
My ADHD assessor said: ‘Many of these symptoms could be explained by the autism,’ to which I replied: ‘What autism?’

For many, this ‘primary’ profile is not fixed. Female hormones are known to affect the severity of ADHD. The time of day and associated stress and fatigue play a role. And the impact depends on the activity contemplated – does it require speed and creativity, or accuracy and focus?

The idea of the autistic and ADHD selves as separate entities is hardly definitive, and experts differ here. Some research finds autism and ADHD symptoms to be largely segregated along existing diagnostic boundaries; others that they have overlapping features; while others suggest that the co-occurrence of autism and ADHD may represent a distinct combined phenotype. Regardless of the thoughts of academics, this sense of two selves, of conflict and contradiction and the push and pull of opposing wants and needs, is one that formed the core and essence of the experience of the participants in my own research.

An article by Siân Boyle in The Guardian in 2024 described this contradiction in the AuDHD label as one of ‘oxymoronic nature, perpetual internal war and rollercoaster of needs’, which nicely sums things up.

The realisation that there is a name and an explanation for the persistent inconsistency that accompanies the AuDHD lived experience can be liberating – it’s a relief to know that you are not actually crazy, because that’s the way it can feel. In the words of my research participants, it is:
Having to keep two different beasts fed and cared for, after having spent most of my life being told by others that neither beast existed.

A lightbulb moment when I realised that my hectic brain being pulled in two different directions at all times throughout my whole life actually had a reason and it wasn’t that I was stupid or incapable as I always believed before.

Despite this sense of contradiction, the two conditions do share some characteristics. Both are highly heritable and run through families. As far back as 2009, a team led by the child and adolescent psychiatrist Aisling Mulligan at Trinity College Dublin found that autistic traits in children with ADHD ran in families, along with the ADHD itself. More recent research shows that mothers with ADHD are six times more likely to have a child with ADHD – and 2.5 times as likely to have an autistic child. Other studies suggest a shared genetic base between autism and ADHD, explaining the high prevalence of both conditions in the same families. Twin studies provide further evidence of this genetic overlap.

People with either autism or ADHD may find it challenging to read subtle social nuances and engage in reciprocal conversation, making it harder to sustain friendships and relationships. Both often have intense passions and interests, although these tend to last longer in autism than in ADHD. And while sensory features are not mentioned in the diagnostic criteria for ADHD, both groups may have atypical sensory profiles. As a very broad generalisation, autistic people find sensory experiences overwhelming, leading them to avoid some sensations and seek out comfort. On the other hand, ADHD people may seek sensory input and stimulation to feel grounded and focused. Although it is early days for research and the number of papers looking at AuDHD are small and focused almost entirely on children and adolescents, the general consensus is that the combination of autism and ADHD makes things worse socially, adaptively, behaviourally and mentally. I could not find any research-based evidence that sought or found examples of the dual diagnosis making life better. It seems that, in academic studies, questions relating to the advantages and joys of AuDHD were not asked, and that the focus was entirely on problems, challenges and deficit, as is often, disappointingly, the case.
Every day needs to be filled with entertainment and stability, learning and fun

The inconsistency brought by these apparently opposing sets of features does cause considerable frustration for the typical AuDHDer, who lives switching – often rapidly – between seeking both order and disruption, sameness and variety, impulsivity and risk-aversion, social motivation and solitude, single focus and multi-focus. When needs and wants shift so quickly and vary so wildly, decision-making and balance can feel impossible, leading to a far more chaotic life than would be expected from someone with an autism diagnosis. As one of the research participants said:
For my child, it’s like living with Bert and Ernie from Sesame Street in his head at one time. Bert wants quiet but Ernie needs noise… The internal tension is real.

Yet the participants in my own research reported the joys of AuDHD as well. For me, the combination of the detail and diligence of autism and the creativity and impulsivity of ADHD have likely led to my deeply interesting and varied life, because I couldn’t have tolerated it any other way. Every day needs to be filled with entertainment and stability, learning and fun. Others in my research agree:

The absolute chaos and rhizome-like thinking enables me to be very creative in all aspects of my life and see things in a way that others don’t. The ability to feel and see so much; a complete all-encompassing joy over very small tiny things and details that most other people miss, sometimes it feels like I can almost see or feel an extra dimension compared to those around me, and it brings me so much joy.

For me, it feels like a life of two halves, like living as a pair of twins who argue a lot but now and again will sit on the couch together and watch a movie. We know we have to have a schedule, eat the same foods and get things done. We know we have to physically move – a lot – keep switching tasks, and force ourselves to stop when we’re just done. We know we find it hard to begin, hard to keep going and hard to stop, and we’re continually developing ways to work with all of that at any given time in all given circumstances.

And although Autism has to step in to keep ADHD in check, and force it to sit down and do the dull, important things for a few minutes – rather than spending all day watching videos about giant tortoises on the Galápagos Islands – ADHD also needs to break through the rigidity of Autism’s need for productivity, tell it to lighten up – and come watch some of these great videos on giant tortoises on the Galápagos Islands. And then, once ADHD has piqued Autism’s interest with today’s Best Idea Ever, Autism can become a world authority on tortoises, research the climate, food, cheapest flights and best hotel on the islands, and build a spreadsheet to get this trip on the road. What a team!
We only have to hope that Autism knows where the passport is.

items.title: Damien Jalet: “I’m Not Just Making Steps. I’m Trying to Create Worlds”
items.description: This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man:
items.author: Barry Pierce
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man:

What, exactly, is a body for? Ask a doctor and they may tell you that, on paper at least, it houses the organs that work together to keep us alive. For Damien Jalet, the body means much more than this, and is the vessel by which to explore and interrogate the mysteries of life. Jalet, who just turned 50, is more aware of his body today than ever. As we chat on one of his rare days off, he is feeling good about his half-century milestone. “I arrive at 50 with an incredible amount of experiences, of dreams being realised. I feel like it’s a great vantage point,” he tells me from his hotel room in Guadalajara, Mexico.

Jalet is in rehearsals for a restaging of Omphalos, a work that first premiered in Mexico City in 2018. On a darkened stage, a huge satellite dish rotates into view. Across its curved surface, dancers weave their bodies glacially, until – suddenly – pausing in unison. The bodies appear less like those of a corps de ballet than a strange collective organism controlled by a single force. Following choreography on a flat stage can be challenging enough, but on a curved surface, pitched and rotating? It’s precisely these limitations that excite Jalet.

“Something that I’m always trying to remind you in the work I do is that you are made of the world that surrounds you,” he tells me. There is a sense, when talking to Jalet, especially about the body, that he has spent many years building a personal philosophy around it. Words like “porous” and “organicity” come up again and again. “I often think of the body as being a root – we absorb. We are a moving root, we are wanderers,” he says.

Much of Jalet’s central philosophy, and his spiritualism, stems from his interest in animism. Rooted in the traditions of many Indigenous cultures, animism is the doctrine that the natural world is imbued with spirit or agency, and that humans exist in relationship with the animals, landscapes and forces that surround them. He describes the ritualistic volcanic dances of Indonesia, and how the Tenggerese people gather on Mount Bromo to appease the spirits. He believes that this relationship with dance, and a wider relationship with our bodies, has been lost in Western culture, partly due to the influence of religion and its dogma around the body as something to distrust. “I have a very intimate conviction that we would not be in the situation we are now if we had kept a more animist point of view, or more of a spiritual connection with nature,” Jalet, who studied anthropology and ethnomusicology, says.

Jalet is quick to acknowledge that some could misinterpret his beliefs as New Age. “I’m not hugging trees and giving them offerings,” he laughs. “I’m a very contemporary person. I’m not just there to say, ‘Oh, let’s go back to our roots, let’s leave everything we know.’” There are other more modern concerns flooding Jalet’s day-to-day thoughts, too. The rapidly expanding field of artificial intelligence could be seen as the greatest existential threat to dance since Achilles tendinitis, he says. “In the world of AI, where the body disappears, where there’s no more feelings, everything just becomes information. I think it’s incredibly important to go back to the body before we lose nature for good.”

Initially thinking he’d become a theatre director, Jalet studied at INSAS, Brussels’ National Institute of the Performing Arts. The 1990s in Brussels were, according to him, a time when disciplines collided and contrasted. Choreographers were branching out into theatre, visual art, music and design. Jalet, meanwhile, was finding himself in the city’s gay clubs. “I love the physical collective energy of gay clubs. They are such a space of freedom. They connected me to my body.”

The collective energy Jalet describes is not so far removed from the principles that would come to define his choreographic practice. In it, the human form is porous, responsive and shaped by the bodies it interacts with. Perhaps that is why, years later, Madonna would make Jalet a close collaborator and the lead interpreter of her music through dance. But before there was Madonna, there was Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui.

“We met in 2000, in a ballroom, where we were teaching contemporary [dance].” The occasion was Bal Moderne, a Belgian festival where choreographers teach short dances to the public. By this point, Jalet had abandoned his ambitions to become a theatre director. After a stint in New York, he joined Les Ballets C. de la B., a renowned Belgian dance theatre company. Meanwhile, Cherkaoui was making a name for himself as a young choreographer to watch. Their friendship was immediate. “I felt that we already had so much in common: same age, same double nationality, same feeling of being a bit uncomfortable with the way of things.”

Quickly, they became more than just choreographer and dancer, but close collaborators and artistic partners. Their first major work together, D’Avant, came in 2002. Mention the work to Jalet now and he lets out a little giggle. Meaning “from before”, D’Avant saw Jalet and Cherkaoui, alongside Luc Dunberry and Juan Kruz Díaz de Garaio Esnaola, work as both choreographers and dancers. It was a physically demanding piece, a slapstick epic in which its creators embodied medieval serfs, football hooligans, cross-dressing brides and contorting body illusionists. At one point, they play football with Jalet’s head while singing along to 12th-century polyphonic music. “It was probably the most challenging piece as a performer,” Jalet recalls. “Because not only were we dancing and acting, we were also singing maybe 16 songs that were incredibly technical and that were all about finding harmony.”

A few years ago, Jalet posted a clip from D’Avant on his Instagram. It went massively viral and currently sits at around half a million likes. The reaction totally blindsided him. “The recording looks like it’s from 1973 or something. But it became this phenomenon, this work from literally 20 years ago.” Of the 80-minute show, that short clip is really all that exists of D’Avant now. It’s a problem you run into a lot when looking back over the careers of choreographers: a painter produces a canvas, a filmmaker releases a film, but a choreographer, by contrast, makes something that can only be experienced to its fullest in the moment. Dance is an ephemeral art form – something Jalet thinks about a lot. “Nobody talks about the level of energy that goes into a dance show,” he tells me. “If you feel sick and you have to perform... I can tell you, there is nothing worse. This is why I think of dancers as spiritual people, because they’re doing it for the art, for the act of it. You’re putting all of your life into something that only exists in the moment you do it.”

In 2016, Jalet was contacted by Luca Guadagnino after the director had fallen out with his original choreographer on a forthcoming remake of Suspiria. “It allowed some of my work to survive, to be shared and experienced first-hand,” Jalet says of his first foray into cinema.

On a night out on the Rue de Charonne in Paris in autumn 2015, Jalet was standing near a young man who, moments later, pulled out a gun and started shooting. He ran for his life. Jalet had found himself at the epicentre of the coordinated terrorist attacks that ended in the deaths of 130 people. He describes it as an incredibly traumatic event, saying that his career and work can be divided into two: before and after the night of Friday November 13th. His pieces Thr(o)ugh (2016) and Skid (2017) are direct responses to that night.

Skid, which has become one of his most enduring works, was performed on a flat surface tilted at 34 degrees towards an orchestra pit below. Throughout, the dancers perch precariously on the acutely angled surface. At other times, they appear at the top and slide down into the abyss below. “It’s a piece about vanishing, about being there and disappearing the next second. It’s been an acceleration of things since 2015,” he says. “That was such a near death experience it kind of brought me even closer to my intuition. All the choices I’m making now are still related to this.”

The work Jalet has produced over the last ten years could fill the CVs of several choreographers across entire career spans. There have been major stage works including Vessel (2016), Brise-lames (2020) and Chiroptera (2023), alongside collaborations with Paul Thomas Anderson and Thom Yorke on Anima (2019), Palme d’Or winner Jacques Audiard on Emilia Pérez (2024), and Madonna, for her Madame X tour and a musical short film for her 2026 album Confessions II.

But to talk to Damien Jalet in 2026 means bringing up “Storm”, his viral video for the Swedish rapper Yung Lean. Working with the acclaimed director Romain Gavras, Jalet’s clip for the song is, at the time of writing, nominated for a VMA for Music Video of the Year, a category in which he is competing against himself, with his video for Confessions II in the running too. In “Storm”, Yung Lean stands motionless at the centre of a group of identically dressed schoolboys, who swarm around him in tightly choreographed formations, their movements becoming increasingly frenetic and febrile as the sequence builds. It is unmistakably Jalet, turning simple choreography into something closer to a ritual.

When Gavras described his initial concept to Jalet, all he could see were the myriad ways it could go wrong. “He sent me some references to dances done by groups that obviously spent the whole year rehearsing to get to that level of synchronicity,” he divulges. In the economy of the modern music video, Jalet knew he would have mere days to pull off Gavras’s vision. “I was sent hundreds of videos of people dancing in front of the Christmas tree, because we had planned it over Christmas,” he laughs. From there, he had two days to create the dance and another two to rehearse it. Upon its release, Jalet’s work on “Storm” was instantly hailed as a career landmark. “I had no idea that it was going to be so crazy,” Jalet admits. “I didn’t see it coming.”

Jalet is at a point, now, where everyone wants a piece of him. “I only [collaborate] with people who I’m really truly fascinated with, that I love what they do,” he says, defiantly. Consequently, he has spent the last few months turning down the kind of offers that could easily make him enough money to retire tomorrow. “I say no to so many things because I need to feel a deep connection.”

Jalet cannot help but be amused by this new surge of interest. “I think people have suddenly seen the power of choreography. I’ve never seen the word ‘choreography’ written as much as when ‘Storm’ came out. It felt like, ‘Oh, finally, we have a bit of respect.’ I don’t want to look like the Joan of Arc of dance, but I have experienced how much dance is reduced by the commercial world, how it is tamed.” He wants filmmakers to move beyond using choreography as a lazy way of injecting energy into a scene, and for their contributions to be properly recognised. “Emilia Pérez got 13 Oscar nominations and I was completely expelled from the campaign because I could not get them any awards as a choreographer,” he says.

He recalls the very beginning of our nearly two-hour chat. “What do I have a body for? Is it just to consume? Is it just to be productive? Or is it a tool to sense, to understand more the balance of the world and how we are connected?” At the peak of his powers, Jalet seems ready to share his philosophy more widely. “I’m not just making steps,” he says. “I’m trying to convey ideas, to create worlds.”

Photography JORDAN HEMINGWAY. Styling ELLIE GRACE CUMMING. Hair TASOS CONSTANTINOU at Streeters. Make-up CHARLIE MURRAY using ELEMIS and YSL BEAUTY. Set design SAMUEL OVERS at New School Represents. Photographic assistants MADISON BLAIR, JAMIE SINCLAIR and CHESTER LEWIS. Styling assistants CHARLIE EDWARDS and SAM THAPA. Set design assistants HENRY HAWKSWORTH and FELIX VILLERS. Production ROWAN MACKINTOSH KING. Studio director TARA COMPTON. Studio assistant CAEL DEVERS. Studio intern ALEX BEARDSWORTH. Post-production PURPLE MARTIN
This story is taken from the Winter Spring 27 issue of AnOther Man, which is on sale from 5 November 2026

items.title: Parker Posey and Steve Buscemi on Wild Horse Nine
items.description: Two luminaries of US indie cinema sit down to discuss their roles in Martin McDonagh’s dark comedy caper, democracy in peril and weeping openly at mass on a south Pacific island
items.author: Miriam Balanescu
paragraphs: Two luminaries of US indie cinema sit down to discuss their roles in Martin McDonagh’s dark comedy caper, democracy in peril and weeping openly at mass on a south Pacific island

At the centre of the gunslinging black comedy Wild Horse Nine is an old married couple according to director Martin McDonagh: CIA operatives Lee (Sam Rockwell) and Chris (John Malkovich). Trying to tear them apart is Lee’s actual wife, Marge (a needling Parker Posey), and the pair’s control-freak boss, bureau chief MJ (Steve Buscemi). On the cusp of the 1973 Chilean coup, the two agents take a trip to Easter Island – where old-timer Chris has requested that he live out his final days, if Venice doesn’t work out.

It’s a happy coincidence, then, that the film screened in competition at Venice Film Festival, where Buscemi and McDonagh also first discussed a potential collaboration in 2022. “I had met him a couple of times, but I got to know him when he was here with Banshees [of Inisherin],” says Buscemi, when I speak with him and Posey before the premiere in the resplendent gothic Hotel Danieli. “When I read that in the script I was like, ‘Do you know this film is going to come to Venice?’”

Aside from its central bromance, Wild Horse Nine is primarily about reckoning with guilt. With the spiritual backdrop of Easter Island’s ancient moai, Chris, a lapsed Catholic, is forced to reflect on a career of bloodshed, presidential assassinations and American meddling with foreign democracies, not least the currently unfolding crisis in Chile. There are flavours of McDonagh’s previous films: the masculine brooding of In Bruges and Banshees, and the propulsive shoot-outs of Seven Psychopaths.

A Catholic upbringing is one thing that unites McDonagh, Buscemi and Posey. “I went to Catholic school first, second and third grade, but it marked me for life,” claims Buscemi, explaining that the theme wasn’t what drew him to the role. “It’s always the relationships, how they’re drawn, how people relate to each other, what’s going on underneath.”

“I did get to go to mass on the final Sunday at Easter Island,” Posey interjects, describing the service as a combination of indigenous and Catholic traditions. “Venus was in the sky. [It’s a] really bright star at that time of the year [...] The way they were singing brought me to tears because it was so from the gut, and I just started crying. Did you want to hear how it sounded? People are going to start running. Now I’m embarrassed to do it, but I’m going to do it” – at which point Posey cries out an indescribable sound. “If [only] I could go back to my child self who wanted an adventurous life and then go like, ‘Oh my God, I actually got to see something like this.’”

Most of McDonagh’s characters have a reason to want Chris dead. Acting out most of their scenes on the other end of the phone line (shot in real time), Buscemi and Posey vie for Lee’s attention. Playing Lee’s unfaithful wife reminded Posey of her shoot on Ari Aster’s Beau is Afraid, where she was also holding the phone receiver. As in theatre waiting backstage, her job was to “fill in all the colours, get as much information as [one] can to slide in there and hit the right notes.” Her and Rockwell acted as sparring partners: “Couples become one kind of entity of humour [...] It was a lot [of] smoking and screaming.”

“[McDonagh is] Americana, but he’s also Irish,” she continues, recalling how McDonagh would push her to “twist the knife”. “Irish people are, like, really tough. I feel there’s this toughness that [Martin] likes to write.” But beneath all the characters is an unexpected, undeniable softness. As Buscemi observes, “You can’t be hurt by someone that you don’t love.”

Meanwhile, Buscemi was reuniting with his villainous co-star from Con Air for the first time in nearly 30 years. “In this movie, [Malkovich] won’t even give me the time of day,” he chuckles. “He has such disdain for me, but in Con Air, one of my favourite moments is [when I] take off my Hannibal Lecter mask and John says to me, as his character talking to mine, ‘I love your work.’” He jokes wishfully: “No, that’s John saying that to Steve. So this relationship was quite different.”

Both Rockwell and Malkovich have been tipped as major contenders in the Oscars race. Malkovich as Chris is a revelation, cold-blooded and nihilistic on the outside but warm, fuzzy and hopeful within. “I thought this character was so different [...] from a lot of the stuff that he’s done and yet it’s so him,” says Buscemi. “You go, ‘Wow, this is the performance we’ve been waiting for’ from him, even though he’s done so many amazing things.”

McDonagh’s film is timely, arriving in the wake of Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro’s abduction by the US. On the Trump administration, Buscemi says, “I don’t even want to get into it because it’s just so frustrating […] And to see that this stuff has happened before, and it can happen, and it’s happening now. And if we don’t learn from it, it will keep happening. And democracy is fragile. And we shouldn’t take anything for granted.”
Finally, I ask, what’s the meaning behind Wild Horse Nine’s title? “I can't help you there,” says Buscemi earnestly. “I’m still trying to figure out what Reservoir Dogs means.”
Wild Horse Nine is out now in UK cinemas

items.title: Death and Entrances
items.description: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
items.author: Susannah Frankel
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
Among the earliest and most famous depictions of a female nude is the Venus of Willendorf.

There are many Venuses, a broad – and obviously retrospective – nomenclature for figurines originating from the Upper Palaeolithic period, dating back 10,000 to 40,000 years. The Venus of Willendorf is carved in oolitic limestone. Standing a mere 11.1 centimetres tall, she is reputedly 30,000 years old. She has swollen breasts and a protuberant belly, both suggestive of pregnancy. Many thousands of words have been written about her. Is she, in fact, pregnant? Is she an ancient fertility doll, designed to be held in the hand of prospective or birthing mothers? Is she not pregnant at all but a symbol of beauty as it was perceived at that time? Also conjecture: the perspective of this Venus and more than a few of her Venus sisters, the fact that she has no facial features, or indeed feet, has led some to surmise that her creator was female – she is a self-portrait. Of course, nothing is proven. The issues this little Venus’s provenance raises, though, seem pertinent now for Harley Weir, whose exploration of the female form – and just the female – including her own, has led to some of the most striking and evocative imagery of the past decade.

In the history of art, depictions of pregnant women are few and far between. They are predominantly seen through the eyes of male artists. Their bodies are either hidden – through the medieval and Renaissance periods it was the fashion for women to wear voluminous clothing – or idealised. The Madonna is the most prevalent of all pregnant females in art history – the mother of all art historical clichés? – and her baby’s conception was immaculate. In myriad portrayals, myriad Annunciations, that purity is signified by the presence of a white dove. Of that same era, for many years critics speculated that the female figure in Jan van Eyck’s The Arnolfini Portrait (1434) was pregnant. Emblems of fertility – a carving of Saint Margaret of Antioch on a chair by the bed, ripe oranges, a symbol of prosperity but also fecundity, on the windowsill – are present in the painting’s background. The fullness of her famous green dress has since been attributed to the extravagance of its fabrication, however. Three-dimensional laser scans of Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa (1503–17) captured some 20 years ago now are not so easily dismissed. A fine gauze veil – or guarnello – seen over her dress, until that point hidden by aged varnish on the painting’s surface, is typical of those worn by soon-to-be or new mothers of that time. Representation of pregnant nudes in classical painting, meanwhile, are likely negative. Titian’s masterpiece Diana and Callisto (1556–59), which hangs in the National Gallery in London, is the best known. Nymph Callisto’s shaming, the revelation of her naked, pregnant body and subsequent fall from chastity, is subject to the goddess Diana’s fierce disapproval. Raped by Jupiter, Callisto was later transformed into a bear by that god’s wife, Juno. Or so the story goes.

A few centuries on, and modern artists from Gustav Klimt to Pablo Picasso and Lucian Freud painted (and sculpted) pregnant women, but always – inevitably – from a distance. Klimt’s Hope paintings, dated 1903 and 1907–08, of his favourite model Herma were executed against her better judgment, and the earlier rendition, portraying her naked surrounded by mythical monsters, caused a scandal. Picasso’s 1950 sculpture La Femme Enceinte was inspired by his partner at the time, Françoise Gilot, who had recently given birth to their second child, Paloma; he used ceramic bowls and pitchers to create the figure’s rounded breasts and stomach. Freud’s portraits of pregnant women, some carrying his own children, were forensic in their attention to detail: the subject as specimen.

It wasn’t until the last century that female artists’ representations of pregnancy began to enter the gallery setting. Paula Modersohn-Becker’s nude self-portrait of an imaginary pregnancy in 1906, Alice Neel’s paintings of pregnant women, clothed and nude, in the Sixties and Seventies and Chantal Joffe’s pregnant self-portraits are impassioned in their bid for reclamation, showing not only pregnancy’s beauty and power but also its complexity. For the first time, there is a sense of women’s alienation from their own bodies antepartum, for their feelings of intense love alongside, and never unreasonably, fear.

Harley Weir is no stranger to the self-portrait. Her 2022 Beauty Papers monograph, dedicated to “all the dolls in the world”, is an unflinchingly visceral – at times grotesque – representation of the tropes of femininity and the preconceptions those raise. Four years on, and ten weeks pregnant, Weir began to regularly take pictures of herself naked or near-naked in the relative privacy of her bedroom. At 32 weeks a further, more studied series was taken, including portraits of Weir, now helped by John Kelleher, her husband and the father of the baby, and of a body double wearing a pregnancy belly and Harley Weir mask. With styling by her friend and longtime collaborator Georgia Pendlebury, these images serve as Weir’s visual response to her physical and emotional transition at a time that may be as challenging as it is joyful. And intimate, but: “The real private self isn’t this though,” she says. “It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait.”
SUSANNAH FRANKEL Do you know the Venus of Willendorf? She’s got no feet. People think a woman may have made her.

HARLEY WEIR Because she’s looking down at her body? I’ve been documenting my pregnancy from week ten and there are a lot of looking-down pictures and also looking up in the mirror. When you’re pregnant there are so many blind spots. My husband helped take many of the pictures for that reason. The series is called Death and Entrances because, from what I’ve read, it’s like an ego death. You’re giving birth but you’re also dying, you change. I felt, physically in this story, as if I was wearing a disguise.

That’s something I think connects back to the Venus of Willendorf, this idea of a woman looking down at a body that is powerful, but also unfamiliar. During pregnancy, your body becomes the most visible thing about you, but at the same time it can feel like it no longer belongs. Here, I don’t have my usual breasts, I don’t have my usual stomach. I felt almost free from the shame of being nude because the bump isn’t me or us.

SF The physical state of pregnancy is extreme. We are taught from an early age to control our bodies and our body image. When you’re pregnant, you surrender that control. Perhaps your body is preparing you for becoming a mother, because once that happens your life is not your own in the same way.

HW Yes, it feels like that. It feels good. I’ve always been self-conscious about my breasts because they were so small. Now they are engorged and full of stretchmarks, but I don’t care who sees them. They’ve become functional objects. And there’s a safety in that. I feel much more at ease. I love being this blob that will bring purpose to someone new and it in turn gives my body purpose, a reason for its irregular shapes that before felt like deformities.
SF Is there any fear involved?

HW There was a lot more at the beginning. But I’m still at the stage where you don’t really know what’s about to hit. I’m in the phase where I feel this is the baby, it’s this bump. But no, the baby is going to come out and rock my world.
SF Have you looked at the way pregnant women are represented in art?
HW I haven’t seen much pregnant art – especially from the past. There’s the Virgin Mary, but we rarely see her pregnant. She didn’t even have sex. The virgin and the mother.
SF There’s that – the Christian ideal – but also some quite violent portrayals.

HW I have to say I can’t think of one classical painting where you see a pregnant woman. Klimt maybe. My mother talks a lot about how, even when she was younger, you had to cover the bump up, you couldn’t show it freely. I feel now we’re having a renaissance for mothers. The mother is more celebrated. I didn’t feel secure enough to be having a kid until now. And I’m getting on. I’ll be 38 when it comes out.
SF People called me a geriatric mother. I was 37.
HW But they’ve changed it now.

HW I would have been, but they stopped using that term recently, which is great. I do think this is an amazing moment for mothers. On Instagram there are so many inspirational women sharing their motherhood stories. Once you get pregnant your algorithm knows and they’re everywhere. So many cool mothers online, which I feel is something you wouldn’t have seen in the early Noughties. Mothers were dismissed or hidden. There was the fear of overpopulation and that having children was bad for the environment,

I used to hear that a lot. Now in the west fewer people are having babies, pregnancy is a positive thing again. It goes in cycles, I suppose. I’ve just finished reading Born [The Untold History of Humanity by Lucy Inglis]. It’s fascinating how attitudes shift. During the Roman Empire, people would kill unwanted babies, by “exposure” – especially girls.
SF In China and Japan they are now rolling out financial incentives to persuade people to have babies.
HW Exactly. First China wasn’t allowing more than one baby. Now there aren’t enough. For now, it feels like we’re in a baby-positive cycle.
SF The death part of the equation is the old you saying goodbye to your old life.

HW And saying hello to the mystery of what is about to begin. I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed.

SF You’ve photographed yourself before. How much of that process is about showing yourself to the world and how much is it about introspection, working out what, in this case, your pregnancy means for you?
“I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed” – Harley Weir

HW My life is already very bump-forward. Wherever I go, it’s the focal point of conversation. It’s hard not to be obsessed by the pregnancy. At one point people argued that because the baby takes so much nutrition, the mother’s brain shrinks by 20 per cent. Now they are calling it rewiring. I’m rewiring. And my way of coping with things is photography – it’s like therapy. It’s a way for me to work out those ideas and also to detach from them. I was thinking how I’m kissing goodbye to this flat-chested girl and becoming a woman. The pregnancy at this stage is visual, the changes are reflected in the mirror. Every Wednesday I read my update that tells me how big the baby is.
SF How big is your baby now?
HW Honeydew melon. You know, it’s so silly. Apparently, there’s a dog one too.

SF How interested are you in the relationship between us as voyeurs and you as the subject? I looked at Beauty Papers. That’s overtly sexual, about fetishising women. This is almost more like you fetishising your own pregnant body.

HW I do think there’s something in the fact that I’m still a sexual being. In old tropes you become a mother and your sexiness was stripped from you. Almost as some kind gesture of respect that we never asked for. That’s what is interesting about fashion. It’s been a way to explore the female – that’s what I do. There are also many personal secrets tucked away inside the images, where they often look overly sexual – rarely my first thought, if thought about at all. There’s an undercurrent of personal meaning. Some images in the story are overlaid with pictures from my dad’s favourite beach. That’s seaweed. Mother earthing. My dad has Benson’s disease, so he’s not able to communicate any more. But I still want to include him in my life in ways that I can. It’s sad when I think of how good he would have been as a grandfather.
SF This story is so intensely autobiographical. Do you think all of your work is?

HW It is. I graduated from art school in 2010. I loved emotive art and started as a painter, which seemed to be the most primitive and uninteresting trade at the time. There was a bit of a backlash against people like Tracey Emin – who wore their heart on their sleeve. People whose work was too autobiographical, too self-involved. I loved her diary works and felt a kinship to them but my era was having a conceptual moment that I didn’t fit in with. I will always be an artist first but fashion allowed me to continue to use emotive language more freely and the impulse has never left me. There’s a picture of me with a pushchair on fire. I wanted to express the fear of being a bad mother. That’s my neighbour’s shed. It’s like a doll’s house. The dream gone wrong.
SF Very few artists have represented fear in pregnancy. Probably because they are mostly men, so maybe it’s not their place to look at that.
HW Yes, that was nice. They left it for us.
SF But being pregnant can be really frightening at times.

HW Part of the story I wanted to show was my thoughts of, oh God, am I going to be a bad mother? Am I going to drop the baby? Am I not going to love the baby? Am I going to have postpartum depression? What’s amazing is that there is so much information about those things now and people talk about it all the time.
SF That anxiety goes on for ever, I think. Did working with a body double in a mask feel strange to you?

HW So strange. Every time I look in the mirror now, I see the mask. It’s terrifying. When you ordinarily look in the mirror you see what you want to see. You think you look good or you think you look terrible. It doesn’t matter what you actually look like. I asked Chaïm, who made the mask, to get all the bits and bobs in there. Go hard on the skin blemishes. I knew they were there but when you actually see them looking back at you, it’s quite grotesque. My face like a piece of meat, you really see it that way. When I show the photos to people, they can’t understand that it’s not me in those pictures.
SF Did you do it for purely practical reasons?

HW Not only. There is something very laborious about taking a self-portrait, the tripod, the focusing etc, but I also wanted to divide myself – the divided self. She was supposed to be the idealised version of me, unstretched and glossy. It’s a shame we didn’t have more time with Anna, who wore the suffocating mask along with the fake bump and wig. There was so much more fun to be had.
SF The image with the snake is referencing Avedon’s Nastassja Kinski and the Serpent [1981]?
HW Yes. I thought that was funny. It’s my “pregnancy picture”.
SF You know the thematic of this issue of the magazine is cliché?

HW So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask.
That’s a real snake crushing me in the picture. I put make-up on in that one too, to cover the pigmentation on my face, to be the idealised pregnant woman for her pregnancy shoot.
SF And there’s an apple in another image. Eve’s apple.

HW Yes. Purity lost. And for taking the apple we must suffer in childbirth. But I actually feel purer than ever. There’s something in the body becoming so functional, it’s before shame. The instinctiveness and the nakedness of breastfeeding, for example, feels like that moment before the apple when there was no shame attached to the naked body. There’s one really disturbing breastfeeding image, the masked me breastfeeding me, the idea of a mother still needing a mother. There’s also me breastfeeding from John. Which takes the breast even further away from the sexual, because he doesn’t have one. It’s about becoming dependent on each other in a new way as a family and recognising that we all need to be nurtured.

SF You are photographing something that is transient, and by photographing it you’re fixing it in time. I suppose that is what photography is more generally, but it feels somehow more pronounced in this context.

HW The permanence is scary sometimes. I only thought about showing my child these images today. I thought maybe the baby never sees these. It’s very different because it’s still inside me. Baby out, different.
SF Do you think about that often, with explicit imagery?
HW I think about it all the time, but I try to be free. I don’t always get it right and people correct me. I like that conversation though.
SF Do people ever talk about your nudes, or look at your nudes, in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable?

HW It’s hard to put yourself out there and be judged. The real private self isn’t this though. It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait. Looking back, I realised I was trying to seem approachable, not too attractive or too sexy. But I’m obviously aware of the camera and that annoys me. I wanted to catch myself in a real state, but because I’m the one taking the photograph, that’s almost impossible. Some pictures are ugly because I felt I should include them, so I wouldn’t seem vain, which is probably the vainest thing you can do. In one I’m standing nicely, in another I’m slumped and badly postured. Sometimes I feel I can be quite vulgar. That’s part of me, letting people see a little too much. Not necessarily deliberately.

“So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask” – Harley Weir
SF And you don’t lie awake at night thinking about that.

HW Sometimes. You don’t want to read the comments too much. I don’t put much on Instagram for that reason. I would say that I have some boundaries, but the idea of vulgarity is something I subconsciously play with a lot. Or at least it seems my tolerance is higher than most. There is me covered in milk with my legs up. It reeked, because it came from France in a heatwave with Leana the make-up artist. I was trying to photograph what the baby would see coming to get the milk. Unfortunately, I didn’t get a linea nigra, the dark line that can appear when pregnant, apparently as an arrow to direct a new born to the breast.
SF There’s also the cliché of the earth mother, and that huge power, but equal to that is vulnerability.

HW Since I’ve become obviously pregnant, when I’m not with John, I don’t like walking around at nighttime. I want to be with my husband. I know most people are not thinking bad thoughts, but I feel vulnerable. There’s something of the mother earth in the photo of me feeding the fawn. This instinct to nurture, but also suggestive of how exposed motherhood can make you feel. I read that, in England, they used to use puppies to keep the milk supply going if your baby was away from you, fawns or pigs in other countries. And if your milk wasn’t working, they would bring round a donkey or a goat for the baby to suckle from.
SF Some of your self-portrait imagery displays a complete lack of vanity.

HW Art and fashion both rank quite high in the thoughts of the self. Oddly with fashion, being the voyeur that I am, possibly the less self-absorbing of the two. It’s so much about the other. It’s rare to see the photographer. We’re like ghosts haunting the image but we are never really there. I often photograph some of the most attractive people in the world and then sit with retouching comments to make them look even more attractive. So it’s hard to think, damn I look hot here, because in my mind, by comparison, I look like a gremlin. Me looking vain as hell to the public is probably me thinking I look real and unfiltered. It’s hard to be objective when it’s me in front of the lens but I like to think I show both sides. Perfection isn’t interesting.

Styling: Georgia Pendlebury. Hair: Alex Brownsell at Streeters using KEUNE and BLEACH LONDON. Make-up: Leana Ardeleanu at Artlist using MAKE UP FOR EVER. Mask: Chaïm Vischel. Manicure: Lauren Michelle Pires using Le Vernis in Garconne and La Crème Main by CHANEL BEAUTY. Set design: Phoebe Shakespeare. Casting: Gabrielle Lawrence for People-File at MiniTitle. Model: Anna Ramfel. Talent: John Kelleher. Studio manager: Melissa Arras. Lighting director: Jordan Lee. Photographic assistants: Chiara Croserio and JJay Johnson.
