items.title: The Overwrought Insistence of “La Bola Negra”
items.description: It starts with a bang—a fiery explosion, a cloud of smoke, a horrific bloodbath. The year is 1937, deep into the Spanish Civil War, and a group of villagers have gathered to cheer on the right-wing Nationalists against the left-wing Republicans and to welcome
items.author: Justin Chang
paragraphs: It starts with a bang—a fiery explosion, a cloud of smoke, a horrific bloodbath. The year is 1937, deep into the Spanish Civil War, and a group of villagers have gathered to cheer on the right-wing Nationalists against the left-wing Republicans and to welcome the intervention of Benito Mussolini’s troops. The consequences of their Fascist alignment land with a fuck-around-and-find-out swiftness that would be funny if it weren’t so hellish: just as a band starts to play, Italian planes drop a friendly-fire payload, killing many and sending survivors fleeing in terror. Among them is a wide-eyed young trumpet player who makes a detour through a ruined church, where a large, toppled statue of St. Sebastian blocks his path—a sad sight, but also a happy accident. Grabbing onto the thick arrows protruding from the statue’s chest, he clambers over the wreckage and makes his way to safety.

So begins “La Bola Negra,” an extravagantly overwrought epic from the Spanish directors and screenwriters Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, with the first of a few clever, if tortured, winks. The trumpeter (played by the singer Guitarricadelafuente, in his screen-acting début) is himself named Sebastián, though when he beholds that fallen statue he sees only a means of escape, not a famously martyred namesake or a marble-muscled icon of homoerotic desire. The filmmakers see all, though, and not always to their advantage; they approach their characters with an omniscient loftiness, a big-picture grandiosity that too often crowds the smaller sculptural details out of the frame. “La Bola Negra,” which runs close to three hours and unfolds acrossnearly a century, wants to be a sweeping historical epic of gay longing—a film about what it means to be a man who desires other men in times of war and peace, and who must either resist or surrender to the fascism of the closet. Upon the ruins of St. Sebastian, Ambrossi and Calvo mean to erect a cinematic monument for the ages; instead, they have produced a film that insists, arrogantly and aggressively, on its own monumentality.

Sebastián’s mother is killed in the attack, a presumably devastating shock that is waved almost impatiently aside. He survives, barely, by joining the Nationalist Army: “I’m one of you,” he promises, and his words hover unsettlingly in the air. There’s a delicacy to Sebastián, a hushed fearfulness, that sets him apart from his new comrades. At a seaside military base, he looks on, with furtive lust, as the other men walk, play, bathe, swim, piss, and practice formations in the nude—a sequence to remind some, fondly, of “Sebastiane” (1976), Derek Jarman and Paul Humfress’s feverishly horny reimagining of the saint’s life and martyrdom. The soldiers here are fine-looking men in service of an ugly cause, and one thing that “La Bola Negra” gets right, and trusts us to grasp on our own, is that beauty draws no moral distinctions. Sebastián’s attention can be readily magnetized by his fellow-Fascists one moment and by a prisoner of war the next, which is exactly what happens. When Rafael Rodríguez Rapún (Miguel Bernardeau), a Republican freedom fighter with piercing eyes and a lower abdominal wound, is wheeled into the infirmary, Sebastián is assigned to watch over him and extract information. Yet Rafael, willing and even eager to die for his antifascist principles, returns Sebastián’s gaze without flinching, and with a sense of rebuke that is complicated by unspoken yet unmistakable flickers of desire.

Sebastián and Rafael are not the only characters of note. Ambrossi and Calvo go by the two-in-one moniker Los Javis, and so it shouldn’t surprise us that they approach their narrative in a similar spirit of multitasking compression. The movie consists of three stories, set in three different time frames, and unfurls them simultaneously, in a hyper-controlled frenzy of crosscutting. Sebastián’s tale, adapted from the play “La Piedra Oscura,” by Alberto Conejero (who is credited as Ambrossi and Calvo’s co-writer), is the most substantial of the three, and the other two stories coil around it tightly, like tensile vines. Not long after meeting Sebastián, we are whisked off to Granada, in 1932, where Carlos (Milo Quifes), a reserved, elegantly dressed young man, applies for membership at an exclusive casino. But the casino committee rejects his bid, owing, we later learn, to cruel yet accurate rumors of his homosexuality: “Bola negra, bola negra, bola negra” goes the refrain, as one damning black ball after another rolls down the pike. Carlos’s rich, image-conscious father orders him to return to the casino the next day and refute the suspicions. His mother, a more quietly supportive soul, encourages him to move to Madrid, where he can live more freely.

We get a bracing taste of that liberation in the third strand: it’s 2017, and Alberto (Carlos González), a Madrid-based historian, need only look to Grindr to satisfy an urge (“Sex now,” he types, before he’s uttered a word). Quite the contrast with Carlos, who must stalk some potential trade through the streets at night, and with Sebastián, whose throat goes dry at the mere sight of Rafael’s bare chest. You could argue that Ambrossi and Calvo are old-school romantics at heart, alive to the teasing thrill of the forbidden, and accordingly skeptical of the modern age and its all too convenient spoils. Alberto himself seems nostalgic for the tensions of a crueller bygone era, if the thesis that he’s writing—it involves queer dissident musicians from the nineteen-twenties—is any indication.

A knottier research project awaits him. Alberto learns that his grandfather—whom his mother, Teresa (Lola Dueñas), was bitterly estranged from and never introduced her son to—has recently died and left him a curious inheritance, a mystery that needs untangling. The answers, the viewer can probably guess, will bring the 1932 and 1937 chapters into unifying focus, and although González makes Alberto an engaging enough sleuth, he can’t transcend the passive, puzzle-solving function that the character has been assigned. In the words of Alberto’s concerned boyfriend (Julio Torres), revealing more about the film’s shortcomings than he perhaps intends, “Isn’t it funny that the only story you don’t care about is your own?”

Before “La Bola Negra” won the Best Director award at this year’s Cannes Film Festival (an honor it shared, hilariously, with Paweł Pawlikowski’s exquisitely minimalist “Fatherland”), Ambrossi and Calvo were known for many things. They were a Spanish-entertainment power couple for more than a decade before ending their relationship late last year. Their past collaborations include several TV series—including the popular “Veneno,” a portrait of the transgender sex worker and entertainer Cristina Ortiz Rodríguez—and a feature film from 2017, “La Llamada,” adapted from their own stage musical. They are also card-carrying cinephiles, as their recent interviews have taken pains to flaunt: “La Bola Negra,” they’ve said, carries the artistic DNA of wartime-youth classics such as Andrei Tarkovsky’s “Ivan’s Childhood” (1963) and Elem Klimov’s “Come and See” (1987), and also Claire Denis’s masterwork of soldier-sublimated eroticism, “Beau Travail” (2000). My own mind drifted toward other great films, including Hou Hsiao-hsien’s “Three Times” (2006), a century-spanning trilogy that at once preserves and subverts the boundaries of linear time, and Terence Davies’s “Benediction” (2022), a wrenching biographical portrait of a war veteran and poet who regards his own same-sex desires with profound ambivalence.

But the queer art-house touchstone I’ve heard referenced most often in connection with “La Bola Negra” is Stephen Daldry’s “The Hours” (2002), a mutually unflattering comparison if ever there was one. In both films, everything comes in threes, the incessant crosscutting is accorded a flashy metaphysical weight, and time itself is manipulated, distorted, and rearranged to the point of meaninglessness. The complexities of human longing across the ages are not explored so much as solved, in the manner of a mathematical proof. But what, exactly, is being proved here? The universality of suffering? The magic of editing? Perhaps it’s simply that the most self-consciously expansive films are so often the most reductive, the most diagrammatic—and, incidentally, the most inclined to take refuge in a great artist’s shadow. “The Hours” framed itself as a morbidly repressed valentine to Virginia Woolf, and “La Bola Negra,” with uncloseted exuberance, hitches itself to the mantle of another queer literary giant, Federico García Lorca. Although Lorca isn’t granted his own narrative, his life and legacy—the passion of his left-wing activism, the subversiveness of his art, and the open secret of his homosexuality—make up the tissue that connects all three of the film’s stories.

History has no need for spoiler warnings, but anyone hoping for an untainted experience of the film—a description that applies to no one who’s read this far—might want to skip over the facts that follow. The first is that Rafael Rodríguez Rapún, the P.O.W. who catches Sebastián’s eye, was a real person: a football player, an actor, and a close friend and eventual lover of Lorca’s. The second is that, in 1936, not long before Lorca was murdered by Nationalist forces, he began writing a play called “La Bola Negra,” the bare bones of which—he got only four pages in—inspire another part of the film. No wonder, then, that the tale of Carlos’s blackballing seems to float in a more poetically diffuse register than the other two, at least until the closing stretch, when it takes a hard detour into uncharted realms of snowily lyrical bombast. The wispiness of the written source can go only so far in justifying the fan-fiction tedium of the onscreen result. By this point, Ambrossi and Calvo aren’t so much paying tribute to Lorca as trying to outdo him.

All three stories, whatever their theatrical provenance or cinematic intent, are marred by the same odd insubstantiality; it’s as if the directors, brandishing a rigid narrative and thematic blueprint, were unable to marshal character, dialogue, and action in service of their overarching designs. The 1937 chapter, intended to serve as the film’s spine, suffers most noticeably as a consequence. It isn’t just that Guitarricadelafuente, called on to embody a blur of moral and sexual confusion, settles for looking straight-up perplexed. Even a seasoned performer might have had trouble pulling off the scene in which Sebastián, unable to bear the troops’ violent attack on Rafael, retreats into a corner with his musical instrument and quite literally trumpets his agony to the skies. That’s “La Bola Negra,” more or less (and mostly less): rote trauma divorced from psychology, flailing gestures divorced from meaning. The sole performer who survives this chapter is Miguel Bernardeau, intensely charismatic as the physically frail but spiritually fortified Rafael. Here, in the film’s most memorably composed image, is a man hovering between life and death, his wounded body bathed in an almost celestial light—another allusion to St. Sebastian, and one that signals a tragedy to come.

The other indelible moments in “La Bola Negra” are isolated affairs—focussed, pointedly, on three women on the narrative periphery, whose roles are amplified by strategic, diva-like concentrations of star power. As a cabaret musician who entertains the troops, Penélope Cruz is a wickedly brassy marvel—vamping up a storm one minute, grumbling about her menstrual cycle the next, and eventually coaxing even Sebastián out of his mopey shell. Glenn Close, as a Lorca scholar with an earnest backstory of L.G.B.T.Q.+ allyship, arrives bearing the script’s best intentions and its dreariest dialogue, and yet she rises, by dint of her ineffable Closeness, above the dross of the writing. And then there is, most powerfully of all, Lola Dueñas, known for her work with the director Pedro Almodóvar (who is credited as an associate producer in “La Bola Negra”). As a most un-saintlike Mother Teresa, Dueñas gives voice to a seething, inconsolable fury, an assertion of pure, ferocious will, that exposes the preciousness of Ambrossi and Calvo’s poetic and structural conceits. This film is no monument; it’s a bust. ♦

items.title: Russia Haunts Emmanuel Carrère’s New Book
items.description: In the fall of 2022, the French writer Emmanuel Carrère visited Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia, for the first time. Carrère, who has been called “France’s greatest writer of nonfiction,” was sixty-four at the time; though he was of mixed Russian and Georgian
items.author: Madeleine Wulfahrt
paragraphs: In the fall of 2022, the French writer Emmanuel Carrère visited Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia, for the first time. Carrère, who has been called “France’s greatest writer of nonfiction,” was sixty-four at the time; though he was of mixed Russian and Georgian descent—when he visited, his cousin Salomé Zourabichvili, was then serving her fourth year as the country’s President—he had never before set foot in his ancestral homeland.

Why did Carrère wait so long to visit? He asks himself this very question toward the end of his latest book, “Kolkhoz,” a conflicted family history that won the 2025 Prix Médicis. His mother, whose father was the son of a prominent Georgian intellectual and whose own mother was the daughter of a Russian aristocrat, never went at all—she had a fraught relationship with the success of Zourabichvili, whom she treated with “condescending affection.” One would be forgiven for assuming that, as a friend of his joked, Carrère had waited to visit the country until a member of his family was running it. But Carrère’s explanation, characteristically self-effacing, is as shamefully self-interested as it is startlingly frank. “I am my mother’s son, I felt Russian like her, not in the least Georgian,” he writes, “but it’s become so awful to be Russian today that I’m searching for other roots.”

In the course of the past decade or so, there has been a flurry of memoirs and autofictional novels by émigré writers and their descendants, grappling with the challenging inheritance of Russia’s twentieth and twenty-first centuries—the suffering, and the guilt. On the more poised side is Maria Stepanova’s “In Memory of Memory”; on the more beguilingly chaotic is Keith Gessen’s “A Terrible Country.” “Kolkhoz”—along with Evan Gershkovich’s prison memoir, “This Cursed Beautiful Land,” also out this fall—is the most prominent such book to have been published since the beginning of Russia’s war on Ukraine. It is also the most virtuosically, infuriatingly honest.

Carrère, who broke out with his 2000 work of literary true crime “The Adversary,” is one of the most confounding figures in French letters. Written from the surreal intersection of narcissism, self-absolution, and investigative journalism, his books purport to be “about” subjects of general interest—yoga, the iconoclastic Russian writer Eduard Limonov, a perplexing murder spree on the Swiss border—but are, without fail, about himself. More often than not, they are also about his marriages and the extramarital affairs that end them. But, somehow, Carrère never entirely alienates his readers. There’s something refreshing about his frank insistence on his shortcomings, and the way that he manages to neither glorify nor vilify them.

The shortcomings in question are notably pronounced in Carrère’s 2007 memoir, “My Life as a Russian Novel,” which investigates two mysterious disappearances: that of his Georgian maternal grandfather, who vanished after seemingly collaborating with the Nazis in Occupied France, and that of András Toma, a long-lost Hungarian prisoner of war who was discovered in a remote Russian psychiatric hospital at the turn of the millennium. It also brazenly exposes the private life of a Parisian named Sophie, the object of Carrère’s erotic obsession, whose outrage and fascination with him mirrors the reader’s. At one point in the book, Carrère has Sophie declare, “Emmanuel doesn’t vote because he’s afraid he’ll vote for the right.” (Carrère rarely discusses politics, but if he had a conservative bent it would hardly be surprising, given his vocal praise of the works of Michel Houellebecq and Louis-Ferdinand Céline, two of French literature’s biggest provocateurs.)

Carrère can be particularly inflammatory on the subject of Russia. During his research trips to the country in the late nineties and early two-thousands, he befriended, as he put it, “colourful characters who were not necessarily reputable” and devoted years to writing a biography of Limonov, a fervent Russian nationalist opposed to Ukraine’s independence. In other words, no one should look to him for an objective account of Russia’s recent history.

Crucially, an objective account isn’t what he’s produced at all. After all, this is the writer who opened “The Adversary” with the line “On the Saturday morning of January 9, 1993, while Jean-Claude Romand was killing his wife and children, I was with mine in a parent-teacher meeting.” In a Profile for this magazine, Ian Parker described Carrère’s books as enacting “the experience of someone being brought out of himself—diverted from disappointment or dickishness—by the unearthing of a story worth telling and by the desire to be admired for telling it.” For all Carrère’s insensitivity—at one point he refers to sanctions falling on Moscow “like the missiles on Kyiv”—the sense of urgency with which he feels he must tell his family’s story redeems him. It’s not that he thinks doing so will necessarily explain what’s happening in Russia today, or even that it will explain how he feels about the situation, but, rather, that the telling itself is enough.

The birth of “Kolkhoz” coincided with the death of Carrère’s beloved mother, Hélène Carrère d’Encausse, and is concerned almost exclusively with her side of his family. Hélène was born into a world of Russian nobles in exile who transposed their aristocratic geography onto the suburbs of Paris (Meudon, where Hélène grew up, became Miedonsk) and whose Russophone children only began learning French at school. Her Georgian father—from whom she inherited the undeniably foreign surname Zourabichvili, a cause of merciless schoolyard teasing—eventually assimilated completely into his wife’s circle of White Russians. When Hélène married Louis Carrère d’Encausse, a French insurance man, she shed the Georgian designation altogether.

Until adulthood, the only Russia Hélène had ever known was the one these Russians had dreamed up in and around the French capital. Motivated by a desire to preserve this rarefied world, and to learn more about the country that her parents had fled, Hélène enrolled at Sciences Po and became an expert on the region. Later on, she was named the Académie Française’s “perpetual secretary.” In this capacity, she oversaw the latest edition of the French dictionary, and occupied a grand, Académie-provided apartment on the bank of the Seine. By her death at the age of ninety-four, she had become supremely, officially, French. President Emmanuel Macron spoke at her funeral.

It’s ironic that Hélène’s path into the French élite was via her parents’ homeland. Carrère deftly captures his mother’s inner conflict, flipping between contradictory descriptions of her persona: she is at once “proud of her aristocratic and cosmopolitan ancestry” and “French by choice . . . patriotic to the point of chauvinism.” She viewed the rise of Vladimir Putin as a promising development for Russia’s transition toward democracy. Her obstinate sympathy for him not only went against French public opinion; it was also a blow to her cousin Zourabichvili, whose decision to run for Georgia’s President was motivated by Russia’s illegal occupation of the country’s northern territories. The day before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Hélène argued on a TV broadcast that Putin was “a brutal but rational man who looked out for his own interests . . . Of course he would never, ever, do such a crazy thing.”

What prompted Carrère to write “Kolkhoz” was less Russia’s invasion itself than the fact that Hélène was so wrong about it. After Putin’s attack, the French media was as unrestrained in its criticism of Hélène as she had been in her permissiveness toward him. She attempted, soon afterward, to pass her error off as a form of prescience. “If I was wrong, who could have seen clearly?” Carrère relays her saying to others.

In January, 2023, she was profiled by the journalist Raphaëlle Rérolle in Le Monde. The headline read, “The Great Russia Expert ‘Shrouded in Fog.’ ” “Her love of Russia is real, deep-seated,” Carrère writes, paraphrasing the article, “but unfortunately it’s morphed into an indulgence for Putin, so that for twenty years she hasn’t stopped speaking on behalf of the Kremlin at the Élysée, repeating to Chirac, Sarkozy, Hollande, Macron and their successive foreign ministers that Russia is a great country which cannot be judged by our standards, and that Putin is a man of peace.” Hélène was stung by the characterization. Rérolle’s article and the media pile on that followed, Carrère writes, “affected her to such an extent that I heard her say she no longer wanted to live in a world where the supposedly honourable press had reached such depths of ignominy.” His tone crackles with frustration at his mother’s defensiveness. “I’ve reread these articles,” he writes, “they’re harsh, but you can’t really say they’re ignoble, and my mother must have been very unaccustomed to criticism to complain that she was the victim of a media lynching.”

At the time of Hélène’s death, in the summer of 2023, Carrère was grappling with the war in his own, very different way. He was at work on a book about the Black Sea port city of Kherson, and had been travelling back and forth from the front line, collecting accounts of the occupation. “Of all the historical events I’ve witnessed,” he writes, “none has riveted my attention as much as the war in Ukraine.” Around the same time, he became compelled by the fact that, as Russia’s hold on Kherson weakened, in October of 2022, they had exhumed the bones of Prince Grigory Aleksandrovich Potemkin—the Russian Empire’s chief colonizer of the south. The metaphor must have seemed too good to be true: Putin’s Army, despite hemorrhaging men, was preoccupied by preserving the skeleton of the Russian imperial idea. The retreating soldiers took the bones east, into occupied territory, horrified by the thought of them remaining under Ukrainian soil.

What lies beneath the Russian earth—roots, remains, ruined imperial cities—pervades “Kolkhoz,” especially in its portrait of Carrère’s mother. The first time that she visits Soviet Russia as a young woman, during a layover on the way to a research trip in Uzbekistan, Hélène spends her precious few hours riding the Moscow metro, “the deepest and most beautiful in the world, with its mosaics, frescoes, colonnades, chandeliers and mouldings.” Everything touches her: she is even “rocked” by the mundane metro announcement, “Dveri zakryvayutsya. Nie zabyvaete svoi veschi” (“The doors are closing. Do not forget your things”), simply because it is in Russian, the intimate language of her childhood, suddenly writ large. At an underground kiosk, she buys “a map and some postcards,” and naïvely tells the salesclerk behind the counter that she speaks Russian because she’s descended from exiled aristocracy. (The salesclerk, predictably, is less than impressed.)

“She prided herself on understanding the Russians,” Carrère writes, “probing their hearts and souls, vibrating in unison with them”—one imagines a young Hélène literally vibrating in unison with a million strangers in the rattling Soviet cars of the Moscow metro. Despite his pained awareness of his mother’s imperialist delusions, he finds a grain of truth in her conviction that she is in touch with the Russian spirit. If Russia has a collective unconscious, Carrère seems to suggest it might resemble his mother—a proposition in which, against his own better judgment, he clearly finds both pride and comfort.

Like the Russian state, Hélène appears to have buried many disturbing facts as deep down as possible, not least of which is her father’s alleged collaboration with the Nazi regime. It’s chilling to see Hélène’s allegiance to Russian oligarchy prefigured by her youthful affection for the right-wing figures of postwar France. Describing former Nazi collaborators’ visits to the grave of the fascist journalist Robert Brasillach, Carrère sheepishly admits that he’s “far from thrilled to say that my mother, at the age of twenty, consorted with this society of pariahs.”

What emerges from Carrère’s excavation of his mother’s past is a strikingly nuanced portrait of a brilliant, problematic scholar. Moreover, he excels in extrapolating her life onto more than a century of Russian history. In his hands, she becomes a kind of Russian Zelig—a character who appears, conveniently, at every major moment in history throughout her life. She is omnipresent in the immediate aftermath of the Soviet collapse, staying often at the Hotel Ukraina, Moscow’s famous Stalinist skyscraper, and attending events such as “a cocktail party at the French Embassy to celebrate Franco-Soviet scientific exchanges.” Even when she herself is absent, there is always a relative at hand, as in the case of the October Revolution: a great-uncle walks from Petrograd to Finland to escape the Bolsheviks, a family friend is torn to pieces by his serfs.

These historical anecdotes have a scope that brings to mind the great Russian epics. “My Life as a Russian Novel” would have suited the book as a title had Carrère not already used it. In the nineteenth century, Russian literature was instrumental in the formation of the Russkaia dusha, or “Russian soul”—the national myth that Russians are uniquely adept at emotional intensity, spiritual awareness, and suffering. As the twentieth century dispersed Russia’s literati, some left this nostalgic concept behind, while others trailed its shadow with them into exile, burying themselves in the great Russian novels that had formed its foundation. In “Kolkhoz,” it seems to be something of a fixation for Carrère: the émigré dream that Russianness just might be able to exist as a primarily literary mode.

When it comes to this dream, Carrère is caught between competing impulses. On the one hand, Russian literature acts as a means of framing both his reporting and his personal life. On the other, he makes sure to examine it through a post-colonial lens. He and his mother, he notes, are each compelled by the work of Dostoyevsky, entranced by his descent into the darkest, most complex facets of human nature. Hélène’s devotion to the author, “the almost religious conviction that there is nothing better,” is a point of humorous preoccupation throughout “Kolkhoz.” When Carrère discovers a love of Leo Tolstoy’s “War and Peace” in adulthood, he knows his mother will not approve. A friend remarks, sarcastically, “My goodness, what a transgression!”

For Hélène, Dostoyevsky is a symbol of Russian greatness that transcends politics. But, as Carrère acknowledges, in the wake of the Ukraine invasion the author has become an embodiment of Russian nationalism. In the Ukrainian novelist Oksana Zabuzhko’s commanding 2022 essay for the Times Literary Supplement, “Reading Russian Literature after the Bucha massacre,” she convincingly argues that Dostoyevsky was not only a fervent anti-Ukrainian but also a Russian nationalist who constructed an ideology that posed a dangerous question: Can any amount of violence be absolved by surrender to the Russian Orthodox Church? Yes, the ending of “Crime and Punishment” insists: even Rodion Raskolnikov, an infamous perpetrator of senseless violence, can have his Christian awakening in a penal colony in Siberia. “It barely needs pointing out,” Zabuzhko writes, “that Putin’s offensive on February 24 owed much to Dostoevskyism.”

Carrère’s strongest critique of the novelist occurs via proxy. While gathering material in southern Ukraine, Carrère travels with a group of Ukrainian soldiers, one of whom, a brooding young man named Serhiy, reminds him of a character from a Dostoyevsky novel. In an excruciating scene, Carrère, emboldened by more than a few rounds of vodka, decides to begin speaking Russian to his companions, who have made a point of speaking only Ukrainian. None of the soldiers respond, but the next day Carrère’s “Dostoyevskian” figure offers to recount, through a translator, the story of his life. It turns out that Serhiy had been taken prisoner in occupied Donetsk, and subjected to a mock execution. Once he’d finally been freed, he asked his captor why she did what she did. “Because I’m interested in knowing what a man feels when he thinks he’s going to die,” she said. Serhiy replies, without missing a beat, “Read Dostoevsky.” Serhiy, like Zabuzhko, locates his captor’s impulse to torture him in the very pages written by the Russian novelist.

Carrère notes, in passing, that his mother’s “favourite adjective” was “haunted.” “Kolkhoz” is haunted not only by the spectre of his mother but by the question of whether it’s possible to write affectionately, if critically, about Russia today—a question that is at the center of much memoiristic writing about Russia, both by the descendants of those who have left the country, such as Carrère or Evan Gershkovich, and by those who remain.

In the final analysis, perhaps Carrère’s obsession with Russia is not so far removed from his compulsion to write about himself. Writing what he knows, Carrère is consistently, paradoxically insightful on what he doesn’t know. In starting from himself—his childhood, then his mother, then her mother, and so on—he has uncovered something meaningful about the psychology of the Russian Empire that made his grandparents, and those who have followed. More than that, he has masterly evoked an empire just as powerful and just as slippery: the idea of Russia. ♦

items.title: Trump Tests Out Gentler, Bipartisan Rebrand on Truth Social
items.description: When you think about Donald Trump, what words come to mind? “Understanding”? “Gentle”? “Tall?”
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: When you think about Donald Trump, what words come to mind? “Understanding”? “Gentle”? “Tall?”
Probably not. But the president is trying to change that.

Early on Election Night, a White House official told multiple outlets that the mood in Trump World was “defiant.” But Trump himself sent a very different message later in the evening, once it became clear that they had absolutely nothing to be defiant about. In calls to multiple outlets the president was shockingly conciliatory. He told Politico “I don’t want to blame anybody” when given an opportunity to scapegoat some GOP candidates. He also noted, “I have a lot of friends in the Democrats. It’s an interesting phenomenon. We’ll work with the Democrats and we’ll make things work out well for the country.”

Trump has had some trouble sticking to this new persona. (He called Texas governor Greg Abbott a “RINO” minutes after the Politico call.) But overall, the president’s demeanor has been wildly different since Tuesday night.

This rebranding attempt is glaringly obvious if you scroll through Trump’s Truth Social feed. It actually won’t take long at all. Pre-election, @realDonaldTrump “truthed” and “retruthed” dozens of times per day. His posts often reflected the worst of the MAGA cesspool, from racist and Islamophobic diatribes to bizarre AI-generated trolling.

In contrast, Trump only put up three posts on Wednesday. The first featured screenshots of a New York Post story praising him for saving the Western hemisphere with his “Donroe Doctrine.” The next said, “Stock Market just hit another Record High,” without noting that might have something to do with the election results. Then on Wednesday night, Trump put up a post highlighting his effort to make daylight saving time permanent:

Absolutely no one was thinking about daylight saving time on Wednesday, particularly because the latest clock change already happened over the weekend. But it seems Trump was looking for a way to show his commitment to bipartisanship, and his support for the Sunrise Protection Act was all he could come up with. He even tried to play up his reasonableness, saying he “didn’t want to make a big deal out of this” before the election because it might hurt certain senators at the polls (which is absurd).

Thursday’s posts weren’t much different. Trump started by reposting a message suggesting he bravely chose to make tough political calls, knowing he’d suffer political consequences but be proven right by history:

Next, Trump reposted this White House video showing him reopening the Reflecting Pool. The original went up on Monday night, but at that point Trump’s Truth Social account was feverishly publishing last-minute candidate endorsements. Now Trump wants to make sure everyone has seen this gauzy video of him musing about how he’s rehabilitated a D.C. “work of art” over music that sounds like the soundtrack to a baby-food commercial:

So, is the softer side of Trump really here to stay? It makes sense for him to rebrand as asweet old guy who just wants to putter around D.C., cleaning up landmarks and maybe cutting some deals with his many friends in the “Democrat” party. But there are already signs that Trump may have a hard time keeping up the facade. In his latest Truth Social post, he couldn’t resist lashing out at the “Fake Dan Sullivan” and the “other ‘slug’ that the Dems put on the Ballot” in Alaska.” People have been predicting the Trump pivot for a decade now, but it seems petty insults and nasty policies are just who he is.

items.title: J.D. Vance Is Just Going to Pretend He Didn’t Sell His Soul for Trump
items.description: Once upon a time, James David Vance not only understood what Donald Trump was all about but was willing to say it out loud. “Mr. Trump is unfit for our nation’s highest office,” he wrote in an New York Times op-ed in April 2016, a couple months before the rele
items.author: Bess Levin
paragraphs: Once upon a time, James David Vance not only understood what Donald Trump was all about but was willing to say it out loud. “Mr. Trump is unfit for our nation’s highest office,” he wrote in an New York Times op-ed in April 2016, a couple months before the release of his memoir Hillbilly Elegy. “I’m going to vote third party because I can’t stomach Trump,” he said on NPR that August. “I’m a ‘Never Trump’ guy. I never liked him,” he told Charlie Rose two months later. “Trump makes people I care about afraid. Immigrants, Muslims, etc. Because of this I find him reprehensible,” he wrote on social media on the eve of the election, around the same time he suggested he believed Trump had committed sexual assault. “Trump is a moral disaster,” he told a friend in the summer of 2017. In case none of that was blunt enough, made his feelings pretty clear when he described the guy as “America’s Hitler.” He also liked a post — the ultimate 21st-century endorsement! — featuring a photo of Trump and O.J. Simpson with the caption, “Here is an old picture of one of USA’s most hated, villainous, douchey celebs. Also in picture: OJ Simpson.”

Yet fast-forward a few years and Vance started singing a very different tune, one that went something like “I will sell my spine, every last bit of dignity, and anything that’s not nailed down to the floor to be vice-president.” Of course, no one aspires to be just vice-president — they see it as a stepping stone to the ultimate job in politics. And in Vance’s mind, he obviously believed hitching his wagon to a guy he once likened to a genocidal maniac was worth it so long as he could ride that thing all the way to the Oval Office.

But sad trombone for J.D.! Because after the events of Tuesday, wherein voters repudiated Donald Trump and the GOP in a historic flogging that pundits have run out of words to describe, his chances of becoming president in 2028 appear to be rapidly dwindling. Luckily, though, he’s got a plan. And the plan, it seems, is to disavow and distance himself from unpopular things his boss has done in office, starting with the war in Iran. In a 600-plus-word tweet published Wednesday morning, Vance told followers “The reason we lost is the war.”
According to some reports, the White House was aware of in advance, and fine with Vance’s post. According to another, he went somewhat rogue.

Complicating things is the fact that Trump told reporters he thought Vance’s post was “good,” though, to be fair, it’s also entirely possible he neither read it nor has been told what it said. (He does, after all, have an aide whose entire job is to keep him in a bubble of delusion.) And there’s the fact that he said he would not have done anything different re: the war. Furthermore, there seemed to be hints of tension when Trump mused to reporters that maybe the VP “won’t run” for president.

Should Vance continue to try to distance himself from Trump’s wildly unpopular policies, it seems more than a little likely that the president will completely turn on him, which has long been his m.o. (Whether or not he goes full Pence on his second VP remains to be seen.) But even if Vance doesn’t have to worry about the wrath of his boss, the question remains whether or not his weaselly attempts to separate himself from the administration in the eyes of 2028 will work. And the answer, according to some people, is absolutely not. “It’s possible for him to modestly differentiate himself,” a Vance ally with ties to the White House told Politico. “But there’s no way he can totally separate. He’s still Trump’s vice president. This is still a Trump administration war. They’re still both unpopular. He’s not as unpopular as Trump but he’s unpopular.” Or, as one House Republican put it, “I think he’s done.”

items.title: Annie Andrews Flips South Carolina In Senate Race Against Lindsey Graham's Sister
items.description: Few people outside South Carolina knew who Annie Andrews was just six months ago. But in the 2026 midterms, she has made history as the first Democrat to win a statewide Senate election in the deeply red state since 1998, according to CNN.
items.author: Eve Batey
paragraphs: Few people outside South Carolina knew who Annie Andrews was just six months ago. But in the 2026 midterms, she has made history as the first Democrat to win a statewide Senate election in the deeply red state since 1998, according to CNN.

Andrews was poised to take on longtime senator Lindsey Graham when she won the Democratic primary in June. When Graham died unexpectedly in July, it threw “us for a loop,” Andrews told Vanity Fair's Aidan McLaughlin. Andrews pivoted to campaign against Darline Graham, the late senator's sister, who was appointed by Governor Henry McMaster to fill his seat through January 2027.

With the blessing of President Donald Trump, Darline Graham opted to run for a full term, facing off against Andrews three weeks ago in a tense debate, during which the Democrat physician faced off against the political neophyte. “Why would we hand Darline Graham a full term in the US Senate? She is unserious and unqualified,” Andrews—who previously ran against Republican Nancy Mace in the 2022 race for South Carolina’s First Congressional District—said.

“In order for a Democrat to win in South Carolina, you need three things,” Charleston political operative Tyler Jones told Vanity Fair in July. “You need a popular Democrat, you need an unpopular Republican, and you need a favorable national environment." With Trump's support eroding across the US, Andrews has at least one of those—and if the most recent polling numbers are accurate, Andrews' popularity has just continued to grow.

Now, she must make good on her promise to “go to Washington and solve problems.” If Lindsey Graham had remained “a John McCain–style center-right Republican,” Andrews told McLaughlin, “I probably wouldn’t have gotten in this race.”

items.title: Hasan Piker’s Lawyer Says Suing Scott Jennings Is Just the Beginning
items.description: The clash between left-wing political commentator Hasan Piker and his media detractors is moving from the chatroom to the courtroom. One week after Piker filed a $72.5 million defamation suit against conservative commentator and CNN personality Scott Jennings,
items.author: Abigail Sylvor Greenberg
paragraphs: The clash between left-wing political commentator Hasan Piker and his media detractors is moving from the chatroom to the courtroom. One week after Piker filed a $72.5 million defamation suit against conservative commentator and CNN personality Scott Jennings, his attorney, defamation lawyer Daniel Watkins, tells Vanity Fair Piker is “just getting started.”
“There are other people and other entities that will likely receive outreach from my law firm in the coming days,” says Watkins. “They know they have a reckoning coming.”

The Jennings lawsuit, which accuses the former Republican strategist of falsely telling listeners of his Salem Media podcast that Piker advocated for lynchings, comes at the end of a busy, and tumultuous election cycle for Piker, who—after years of online politicking—became a popular surrogate for far-left insurgents, and a popular boogeyman for virtually everyone else. It’s an apparent payback for the mainstream media, whose obsession with villainizing Piker has meant guilt-by-association for everyone Piker champions (and has far outpaced Piker’s actual name-recognition and influence).

On the podcast, which aired on August 11, Jennings shared a spliced montage of the Twitch streamer appearing to make racist and incendiary remarks, some of them about lynching. It’s packaged as an attempt to dissuade Michigan voters from voting for Senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed, Piker’s “best pal and campaign partner,” Jennings said.

I watched the October 2024 stream from which the most inflammatory snippets in Jennings’s sizzle reel were spliced together. On the stream, Piker is live-reacting to a YouTube video from the popular channel Jubilee, in which a Black conservative debates a Black liberal.

At one point, an incredulous Piker pauses the video and very clearly mocks the Black conservative by saying, “Can we go back to a better time when lynchings were happening?” At another point, after a commenter asks why he’s “always doing too much with black people” Piker responds sarcastically, “Yes dude, it’s because I’m racist, that’s why. It’s because I’m fucking racist dude.” Both of these clips are included in the Jennings segment without context.

At the end of August Watkins sent a retraction demand and spoke to Christopher Henderson, Salem Media’s chief legal officer. Absent a reply, they proceeded with a lawsuit. (At the time of publication Henderson and Jennings have not responded to a request for comment.)

Piker’s suit against Jennings is seeking $27.5 million in compensatory damages, and $45 million in punitive damages. Piker says he left it to the lawyers to crunch the numbers. “I don't know what I'm worth, if we're being real,” Piker told Vanity Fair in an interview this week.

“I have been very deliberately anti-litigation for a very long time,” Piker said, “but something shifted that’s been bubbling up where…people like Scott Jennings, and there are others as well,” he claims, “started trafficking in outright lies, defamation, and slander.”

“It is particularly pernicious to misattribute a quote to someone,” Watkins said. He explained that for Piker, “who has built a career at a platform based on advocating for marginalized people and taking stances that are not necessarily popular,” such misattributions are “disgusting and vile and dangerous.”

For Piker, the turn to legal action is partly a pro-truth crusade against “pundits who’ve gotten far too comfortable thinking that they can just get away with making ridiculous claims about people.” He pointed out what he claims is a pattern where outlets circulate clips that omit key words, fundamentally transforming the sentiments of their subjects. “I’ve observed this with the likes of James Talarico, for example. He’ll say something and then they’ll cut it right before you can associate with the full context of the statement,” Piker said.

He also admitted that it’s personal. “First and foremost, [the lawsuit is] for me.” He cited what he alleges is “reputational harm,” “emotional harm,” and “financial damages,” sharing that the lynching comment had spurred someone to “stalk a public event [he] was at.”
“When is the last time you experienced eight consistent months of [mainstream media] having one primary villain?” Piker asked. “It’s not fun at all. It sucks.”

Discussing the Michigan race where the controversy with Jennings began, Piker noted El-Sayed’s primary opponent Haley Stevens’s surprising Sunday endorsement of Republican nominee Mike Rogers. Explaining her party defection, Stevens made specific reference to Piker, criticizing El-Sayed for associating with him.
Piker believes Stevens’s statements will backfire in El-Sayed’s favor as the votes are tallied in Michigan.
“Okay, a Twitch streamer is the reason why you’re endorsing ICE raids in every city?” Piker said, referencing Rogers’s platform. “That’s ridiculous.”

Piker maintains, as he has since July, that his political interventions do more good than harm—for everyone except him. In the case of his surrogacy for El-Sayed, he said, “The only person who got attacked in the process was me. I was the one who had his reputation destroyed in the process.”

As for Piker’s own relationship with El-Sayed, he admits it’s not quite as buddy-buddy as Jennings suggested. Piker stumped for the Michigander in the primaries before receding somewhat. “My relationship with him has always been one of…a transactional nature,” he said.

Piker will spend election night streaming live from his home in LA and checking in periodically with candidates. When the midterms are over, he seems prepared to continue delivering comeuppance to those he feels have unfairly represented him during this election cycle.
So who else can expect to get hit with a lawsuit?

Piker didn’t say, exactly, but he did note that Ronna McDaniel, the former chair of the RNC, who, on C-Span last week, repeated the claim that Piker supports reinstating lynchings. He also pointed to Sen. Ted Cruz, who re-shared the clip from Jennings on X. Last week, Piker responded to the X post with a link to the news of his lawsuit against Jennings and wrote, “hey ted you seen this ?” (Cruz and McDaniel did not respond to a request for comment.)
When asked if Piker’s post on X was a clue as to a future lawsuit against Cruz, Watkins answered: “Buckle up.”

Piker did not disclose other specifics regarding future litigation, saying only this: “if you felt as though you could outright fabricate quotes and make up totally ridiculous claims about me, you should probably work on your retractions immediately.”

items.title: Future Assembles His Avengers With Drake, Travis Scott, and Loe Shimmy on 'Ya Hit'
items.description: The distorted, bass-heavy production that opens the latest Future single “Ya Hit” could soundtrack the beginning of a grand battle sequence in a film. Fittingly, the rapper brings out his best fighters for the record, which features appearances from Drake, Tra
items.author: Larisha Paul
paragraphs: The distorted, bass-heavy production that opens the latest Future single “Ya Hit” could soundtrack the beginning of a grand battle sequence in a film. Fittingly, the rapper brings out his best fighters for the record, which features appearances from Drake, Travis Scott, and Loe Shimmy.

Future announced “Ya Hit” earlier this week, but never mentioned Drake and Scott were among his collaborators. In the caption of his Instagram post, he refers to the whole team as the Avengers. Shimmy leads the chorus, while Drake punctuates his lyrics with ad-libs from Sexyy Red.

“Caught a ho lackin’, went took back the G-Wag’, ya hit/Told a lil’ ho, “Go and find you a new daddy,” ya hit/Been up for a week ’bout to drop me a new bag, ya hit/Try to play with the zombie, you know you get hit, ya hit,” Future raps on his verse.

The single marks the first release from Future since the arrival of his 10th solo studio album The Real Me in August. “Future can’t avoid being symptomatic of a mainstream rap industry that feels artistically exhausted, too uninspired to imagine new vistas beyond the old “bitches”/drugs/wealth dichotomy, and desperate for crossover gimmicks to spark waning audience interest,” Rolling Stone wrote in a review of the record.

Collaboration seems to be Future’s way of hitting reset. It has worked in the past, with the joint album Pluto x Baby Pluto with Lil Uzi Vert and the drama-starting double-header We Don’t Trust You and We Still Don’t Trust You with Metro Boomin.

Fans joked that Future’s surprise release of a song with both Drake and Scott could threaten to overshadow album release day for Lil Baby, who shared his fifth album Fresh today. Future reposted Lil Baby’s album announcement post on his Instagram story in support. It’s a good thing there’s no one-song listening limit.
