items.author: Rolling Stone
paragraphs: Editor’s note, February 2024: In the two and a half years since Rolling Stone rolled out the all-new, fully revamped version of our 500 Greatest Songs list in September 2021, artists like Beyonce, Lana Del Rey, and Taylor Swift have all released classic tracks. So we’ve updated the list. We kept the update light; the 2021 list covered many decades of popular music, and was the result of a vote among more than 300 artists, writers, producers and industry figures; this update covers three years, from 2021 to early 2024.

In 2004, Rolling Stone published its list of the 500 Greatest Songs of All Time. It’s one of the most widely read stories in our history, viewed hundreds of millions of times on this site. But a lot has changed since 2004; back then the iPod was relatively new, and Billie Eilish was three years old. So we’ve decided to give the list a total reboot. To create the new version of the RS 500 we convened a poll of more than 250 artists, musicians, and producers — from Angelique Kidjo to Zedd, Sam Smith to Megan Thee Stallion, M. Ward to Bill Ward — as well as figures from the music industry and leading critics and journalists. They each sent in a ranked list of their top 50 songs, and we tabulated the results.

Nearly 4,000 songs received votes. Where the 2004 version of the list was dominated by early rock and soul, the new edition contains more hip-hop, modern country, indie rock, Latin pop, reggae, and R&B. More than half the songs here weren’t present on the old list, including a third of the Top 100. The result is a more expansive, inclusive vision of pop, music that keeps rewriting its history with every beat.

- Harry Styles, ‘As It Was’ The lead single from Harry Styles’ third album balances its agitated inner monologue, where the shape-shifting pop star picks at the details of a relationship in crisis, with spun-sugar synths that give cover to his torment. From its playful opening — Styles’ goddaughter Ruby giggling “Go on, Harry, we want to say goodnight to you!” — to its singsong bridge, during which Styles’ thoughts are ping-ponging around his head at “high-speed internet” velocities, “As It Was” paints an unusually vivid picture. Everything might seem fine on first glance, but it all becomes more troubling (“What kind of pills are you on?”) with each repeated glimpse.

- Townes Van Zandt, ‘Pancho and Lefty’ An epic story-song about a bandit and the friend who betrays him, “Pancho and Lefty” became a country hit thanks to Willie Nelson and Merle Haggard’s 1983 duet. But it’s the songwriter’s own forlorn reading, on 1972’s The Late Great Townes Van Zandt, that best conveys the doomed fates of the main characters. It begins with what might be one of the most descriptive opening verses in the country-folk canon: “Living on the road my friend/was gonna keep you free and clean/now you wear your skin like iron/your breath as hard as kerosene.” “It’s hard to take credit for the writing,” Van Zandt said in 1984, “because it came from out of the blue.”

- Lizzo, ‘Truth Hurts’ “That song is my life and its words are my truth,” Lizzo wrote at the time. She had to tack on a writing credit to British singer Mina Lioness, who had tweeted its iconic line “I just took a DNA test, turns out I’m 100 percent that bitch,” but the power of this gale-force breakup banger was pure Lizzo, uproariously swaggering and endearingly soulful. “Truth Hurts” was originally released in 2017, but the song got a big boost two years later, when Gina Rodriguez day-drunkenly sang it in the Netflix show Someone Great, and it became Lizzo’s signature hit.

- Harry Nilsson, ‘Without You’ “We did it because my career was on the wane and we wanted something to make a hit,” Harry Nilsson bluntly told an interviewer when asked why he covered Badfinger’s near-despondent ballad: “I heard it and searched through every Beatles album for two and a half weeks, trying to find out which one of their tunes it was.” Producer Richard Perry agreed, piling on the strings to showcase Nilsson’s desperate lunge of a vocal. Both were right — the song went to Number One and earned a Grammy nomination for Record of the Year.

- Carly Simon, ‘You’re So Vain’ The holy mother of all diss tracks, “You’re So Vain” contains one of the most enduring musical mysteries of all time. Just who is so vain that he probably thinks the song is about him? Simon previously revealed that actor Warren Beatty inspired the second verse of the song (“Oh, you had me several years ago/When I was still naive”), but speculation abounds regarding the other man (or men) behind the ire. Either way, the track — boasting omnipresent Seventies arranger Paul Buckmaster’s orchestration and Mick Jagger’s background vocals — is pure soft-rock fire.

- Cyndi Lauper, ‘Time After Time’ Cyndi Lauper was nervous about “Time After Time” — the aching ballad she wrote in the studio with keyboardist Rob Hyman to finish off her blockbuster solo debut, She’s So Unusual. “I asked them to please not put ‘Time After Time’ out as the first single,” Lauper said. “People would never have accepted me. If you do a ballad first, and then a rocker, that doesn’t work.” Her instincts were right: Following the jaunty “Girls Just Want to Have Fun,” “Time” became her first Number One.

- The Pixies, ‘Where Is My Mind?’ No song typifies the freakish pop instincts that made the Pixies stand out in a sea of gloomy Reagan-era bands better than “Where Is My Mind?” Joey Santiago’s lead guitar is catchier than most Top 40 hooks, and by the time Fight Club made this song iconic a decade after its release, it had already formed part of the DNA of countless alternative-radio hits in the years between, from Nirvana to Korn. When an interviewer in 1988 asked about his unique ability to crank out great songs, Black Francis’ answer was typically cryptic: “It’s nice to have space. How much can one brain deal with?”

- Kanye West, ‘Stronger’ Explaining the tighter, broader-reaching songs on his third album, Graduation, Kanye West said, “I applied a lot of the things I learned on tour [in 2006] with U2 and the Rolling Stones, about songs that rock stadiums. And they worked!” West found the inspiration for his most grandiose statement to date from Daft Punk’s “Harder, Better, Faster, Stronger,” which he sampled and reshaped. West is a big fan of the French duo: “These guys really stick with the whole not-showing-their-faces thing. Just amazing discipline — that’s straight martial-arts status.”

- Miles Davis, ‘So What’ It’s likely that no song on this list has soundtracked more dinner parties than Kind of Blue’s warm, welcoming first track. But at the time it was a jarring departure, trading bebop chord changes for a more open-ended modal style. According to pianist Bill Evans, the trumpeter worked up his material just hours before recording dates, but the all-star band here sounds like it’s been living with “So What” for years: Saxophonists John Coltrane and Cannonball Adderley turn in solos that have since become as iconic as any in jazz history, and the rhythm section of Evans, bassist Paul Chambers, and drummer Jimmy Cobb swings like it’s dancing on air.

- Bad Bunny, ‘Titi Me Pregunto’ “Tití Me Preguntó” is a showcase for Puerto Rican superstar Bad Bunny’s unbridled creativity and eccentric pop genius, mixing frantic dembow beats, a classy sample by bachata master Anthony Santos, and a coda with a dash of Latin psychedelia to the global mainstream. He does it all with panache and a healthy sense of humor. Using the archetype of the concerned Latin American aunt asking about her nephew’s potential girlfriends as a starting point, he launches into a hilarious tirade of salacious puns to a bouncy party vibe that — in typical Bad Bunny fashion — unexpectedly morphs into moody self-reflection.

- Lil Nas X, ‘Old Town Road’ Montero Hill was an Atlanta college dropout sleeping on his sister’s couch and looking to break into music when he came across a track he liked by a Dutch 19-year-old called YoungKio that was based around a banjo sample from a Nine Inch Nails track. “I was picturing, like, a loner cowboy runaway,” he told Rolling Stone. Within a year “Old Town Road” was the longest-running Number One song of all time, seeming to sum up eons of American cross-cultural love and theft in just one minute and 53 seconds.

- The Breeders, ‘Cannonball’ Notified by fax that her services in the Pixies were no longer required, Kim Deal called up her twin sister, Kelley, to be her new guitarist (never mind that she didn’t know how to play guitar) and had the last laugh when this absurdist gem became an MTV phenomenon in 1993. “When people were talking about the Breeders being a one-off,” Kelley told Rolling Stone, “I was like ‘No, actually … the Pixies are a side project.'” A little over a year later, the Breeders were on an extended break of their own, but the effortlessly fun trampoline bounce of “Cannonball” is one for all time.

- The Weeknd, ‘House of Balloons’ Far from the international superstar he’d become, Toronto singer-songwriter Abel Tesfaye didn’t even send out photos or do any interviews when he released the first Weeknd album. “The whole ‘enigmatic artist’ thing, I just ran with it,” he said. “No one could find pictures of me. It reminded me of some villain shit.” But the title track of House of Balloons nevertheless set the course for his career, both thematically — drugs and sex, meet depression — and musically, with its sample of Siouxsie and the Banshees’ “Happy House” announcing a new direction for R&B.

- Solange, ‘Cranes in the Sky’ In an interview with her sister Beyoncé, R&B innovator Solange Knowles described how this song was inspired, in part, by overzealous real estate development she noticed around Miami: “This idea of building up, up, up that was going on in our country at the time, all of this excessive building, and not really dealing with what was in front of us.” She turned the metaphor inward to examine her own feelings about change, self-doubt, and aspiration, finishing the song years after it was originally conceived with producer Raphael Saadiq to create a lavish moment of neo-soul introspection.

- Lil Wayne, ‘A Milli’ Producer Bangladesh looped the opening chords from Gladys Knight and the Pips’ “Don’t Burn Down the Bridge,” then segued to a drill-like volley of trap drums. He gave the beat to his friend Shanell — a onetime R&B singer on Wayne’s Young Money Entertainment — to pass along. Wayne initially had grand plans for “A Milli”: He wanted to use the instrumental as skits for rappers like Tyga, Hurricane Chris, Corey Gunz, and Lil Mama. In the end, though, “A Milli” is just Weezy solo, blacking out in the booth and dazzling everyone who hears him.

- Azealia Banks, ‘212’ In 2011, Azealia Banks was a teenage rapper-singer whose clear talent yielded a development deal with XL Recordings but little else. “She had been working on a collection of tracks and there was one Dutch house-sounding one that was just absolutely insane,” producer Jacques Greene recalled. Banks freestyled ferociously about her New York hometown and, uh, cunnilingus over the jittery beats of Belgian house duo’s Lazy Jay’s “Float My Boat.” Initially released in 2011 as a viral track, “212” was a hip-house banger that earned Banks a deal with Interscope and served notice that this uninhibited provocateur would not be constrained.

- Weezer, ‘Buddy Holly’ Never has geek been so chic as in Weezer’s 1994 breakout single, “Buddy Holly.” Written for frontman Rivers Cuomo’s girlfriend, the poppy ode to nerdy romance was almost left off the band’s self-titled debut, also known as the Blue Album, due to Cuomo and now-ex-member Matt Sharp’s reticence. “We had the sense that it could be taken as a novelty song, and people aren’t going to take the album seriously,” Sharp told Rolling Stone. After producer Ric Ocasek heard the receptionist at the recording studio humming it, he insisted they keep it in.

- The Four Tops, ‘I Can’t Help Myself (Sugar Pie, Honey Bunch)’ One of Motown’s most rousing anthems, “I Can’t Help Myself” was inspired by songwriter Lamont Dozier’s grandfather, who’d call the women his hairdresser wife fixed up “sugar pie” and “honey bunch.” During the recording, engineer Harold Taylor recalled, “People were banging on the door of the studio; they were so ecstatic about what they heard.” Nevertheless, Levi Stubbs asked Brian Holland if he could do another take. Holland promised him they’d do it soon — and Stubbs’ first pass hit Number One.

- Lady Gaga, ‘Bad Romance’ Shortly after Gaga had established herself as a star, she catapulted to a next level of weirdness with this Nadir “RedOne” Khayat production, which drew upon the electronic music Gaga had been inundated with while touring Europe. “I want the deepest, darkest, sickest parts of you that you are afraid to share with anyone because I love you that much” is how she summed up the idea behind the song. Fittingly, she debuted the hit-to-be at Alexander McQueen’s show at Paris Fashion Week.

- Robert Johnson, ‘Cross Road Blues’ The primal terror in the Mississippi bluesman’s voice, and his mystifying slide guitar playing, transfixed the Sixties generation of British rockers: “I could take the music only in very small measures because it was so intense,” said Eric Clapton. Recorded during a session at a San Antonio hotel room in 1936, two years before Johnson was murdered at 27, “Cross Road Blues” is a mythmaking statement of spiritual desolation and scorched-earth betrayal — even if the legend that it’s about Johnson selling his soul to the devil in exchange for his monster guitar chops is, as far as we know, apocryphal.

- Biz Markie, ‘Just a Friend’ Nobody beats the Biz (1964-2021), an impossibly good-natured DJ, rapper, producer, human beatboxer, and hip-hop personality who broke big with this ode to the friend zone off his second album. Built on a fat beat, plinking piano, and his charmingly off-key singing, “Just a Friend” interpolates Freddie Scott’s 1968 song “(You) Got What I Need” as Biz warbles about a love that will never come to pass. It was based on real life. As he told Rolling Stone in 2000, “I was talking to this girl from L.A., and every time I called her, this dude was at her house, and she’d say, ‘Oh, he’s just a friend.’ I hated that.”

- Santana, ‘Oye Como Va’ Growing up in San Francisco, Carlos Santana was shaped by the city’s psychedelic explosion. “You cannot take LSD and not find your voice,” he once claimed, “because there is nowhere to hide.” And while his early heroes were bluesmen, he changed history with this foundational Latin-rock reworking of a 1962 salsa number by Cuban percussionist Tito Puente. Santana kept the original’s cha-cha pulse but replaced its horns with Greg Rolie’s organ and Carlos’ lysergic guitar flares. Said Puente years later, “He put our music, Latin rock, around the world, man.”

- Juvenile feat. Lil Wayne and Mannie Fresh, ‘Back That Azz Up’ In the late Nineties, Mannie Fresh’s diamond-sharp productions for Cash Money Records helped put New Orleans in the center of the hip-hop map. The title of this hit was so reminiscent of local artist DJ Jubilee’s single “Back That Thang Up” that Jubilee sued (unsuccessfully) for infringement, and the beat rode the “Triggerman” rhythm that is foundational to New Orleans bounce. Juvenile freestyled his best shit-talking bounce rhymes, and Lil Wayne shut it down with a “drop it like it’s hot” hook. As Mannie said, “[He] immediately was just like, ‘Shit, I’m getting a piece of this.’”

- The Go-Gos, ‘Our Lips Are Sealed’ The radiant first hit of the Go-Go’s was influenced, according to writer Jane Wiedlin, by “the Buzzcocks and Sixties girl-group stuff.” It was also inspired by a clandestine relationship she was having with Terry Hall, of U.K. ska group the Specials, who got a co-writing credit because Wiedlin based the lyrics on some poetry he’d written her in a letter. “It was pretty personal,” Wiedlin recalled. “I mean he had a fiancee at the time — nowadays I wouldn’t touch that with a 10-foot pole, but I was 19, and I was like ‘fiancee shmiancee.’”

- Kris Kristofferson, ‘Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down’ The desolation of spirit in Kris Kristofferson’s “Sunday Mornin’ Comin’ Down” is so heavy, so apparent, that it’s almost hard to listen to. But that despair is exactly what drew Johnny Cash to sing it on his TV variety show in 1970. Kristofferson cut his own stunning studio version that same year for his debut album, Kristofferson. Cash’s interpretation, more shuffling and accessible, is the one most listeners turn to, but listen to them back-to-back if you can, and marvel at how Kristofferson’s lyrics about being hung over, alone, and desperate shake your soul.

- Janet Jackson, ‘Rhythm Nation’ Jackson’s socially conscious Number Two hit came together late in the sessions for her blockbuster LP Rhythm Nation 1814. Co-producer Jimmy Jam recalled being in the studio and “switching between MTV and CNN. Watching music videos on one side and watching atrocities on the other. Somehow they all merged together. The idea for ‘Rhythm Nation’ was you can dance, but we can also do something more intelligent.” When Jam heard Sly and the Family Stone’s “Thank You (Falettinme Be Mice Elf Agin)” at a restaurant, he raced to the studio to sample it.

- Curtis Mayfield, ‘Move On Up’ Mayfield’s irresistible “Move On Up” was politically empowering, morally demanding, and effortlessly propulsive, powered by swinging horns and tangy congas — the nine-minute LP version, with its powerful drum break, laid a foundation for disco and hip-hop alike. Mayfield’s message was just as steadfast: that pride and dignity were paramount for Black America to rise. “I’m not trying to say anything to make you think, ‘Well, this is the way, this is the only way,'” Mayfield said. “I’m trying to cover the whole subject.”

- Tammy Wynette, ‘Stand by Your Man’ From the start, this pledge of wifely devotion, the first song Wynette ever co-wrote, was a cultural lightning rod. Feminists recoiled from its pledge of unquestioning fidelity in the Seventies, and Hillary Clinton defined herself a modern woman by slamming the song during Bill Clinton’s first presidential run. But the recording itself steamrolls over ideological objections, as the catch in Wynette’s voice on the verses gives way to a vocal swell that rises to meet the epic sweep of Billy Sherrill’s production.

- Peter Gabriel, ‘Solsbury Hill’ Shortly after Gabriel quit Genesis in 1975, he climbed to the top of Little Solsbury Hill in Somerset, England, to reflect on his life-changing decision. It inspired his debut solo song, in which he explained to fans why he felt the need to go out on his own. Musically, it was a departure too, a pastoral tune with a 12-string acoustic guitar lead that was pointedly different from Genesis’ prog-rock. The song has since become ubiquitous in movies and film trailers. “Maybe I’ve let it go too much,” he admitted to Rolling Stone in 2011.

- The Animals, ‘The House of the Rising Sun’ “We were looking for a song that would grab people’s attention,” said Animals singer Eric Burdon. They found it with the old American folk ballad “The House of the Rising Sun.” In 1962, Bob Dylan had sung this grim tale of a Southern girl trapped in a New Orleans whorehouse. The Animals, from the English coal town of Newcastle, changed the gender in the lyrics, and keyboardist Alan Price created the new arrangement (and grabbed a composer’s credit). Price also added an organ solo inspired by Jimmy Smith’s hit “Walk on the Wild Side.”

- Gladys Knight and the Pips, ‘Midnight Train to Georgia’ Songwriter Jim Weatherly originally composed this as “Midnight Plane to Houston,” only to change it for Cissy Houston (Whitney’s mom) to something “more R&B … in order to get it onto Black radio.” Weatherly had already penned “Neither One of Us,” Knight and the Pips’ Number Two hit, and when they heard “Midnight Train,” they took it to the top. “I never really imagined writing R&B songs,” Weatherly admitted. “I really thought I was writing country songs.” It reflected the times; the 1970s were the first decade since after World War I in which more African Americans were moving to the South than leaving it.

- Dixie Chicks, ‘Goodbye Earl’ A murder ballad with a modern, feminist twist, this jaunty song about poisoning an abusive husband spawned disparate reactions. Some stations banned it, apparently concerned that it would spawn a rash of hubby offings; others shared the number for domestic-abuse hotlines. When the label reps listened to the Chicks’ Fly album, though, they were more concerned with another song: “Sin Wagon,” with its reference to “mattress dancing.” “You can’t say [that],” Natalie Maines recalls their manager’s relayed message from the execs, “but they love the song about premeditated first-degree murder.”

- Mazzy Star, ‘Fade Into You’ Singer Hope Sandoval and guitarist Dave Roback, the prime movers behind Mazzy Star, were active in the 1980s neo-psychedelic Paisley Underground scene in Los Angeles. After Sandoval replaced singer Kendra Smith in the band Opal, David Roback and Sandoval reconstituted the band under the name Mazzy Star. Their second album yielded this spaced-out hit, perhaps dream pop’s ultimate statement of blurry desire. “We’re not so concerned about the outside world,” said Roback. “[Each song] is its own world unto itself.”

- Nirvana, ‘Come as You Are’ “It’s just about people and what they’re expected to act like,” Kurt Cobain said. “The lines in the song are really contradictory. They’re kind of a rebuttal to each other.” The song is driven by a simple riff that Butch Vig goosed with a flanged, subaquatic guitar effect. Cobain apparently lifted it from a 1984 song by U.K. art-metal band Killing Joke, who Dave Grohl paid back 12 years later by drumming on their 2003 album. In the wake of Cobain’s suicide, though, the most haunting lyric would become, “And I swear that I don’t have a gun.”

- Luther Vandross, ‘Never Too Much’ The Eighties’ major male R&B balladeer’s solo debut was financed in part from money he made singing jingles for KFC and 7UP. Vandross had been pushed to do his own thing by Roberta Flack, for whom he’d sung background. Said Vandross: “She said, ‘Luther, you’re too comfortable sitting on that stool singing “ooh and aaah.”‘ Roberta was single-handedly responsible for me starting my own career.” What pushed her was hearing the demo of “Never Too Much” — one of the most buoyant love songs of the Eighties, with Vandross’ high notes as delicate as soap bubbles.

- Daft Punk feat. Pharrell Williams, ‘Get Lucky’ When Pharrell Williams volunteered to appear on Daft Punk’s fourth album, he told them he’d been thinking about Chic legend Nile Rodgers musically; fortuitously, the French dance producers could play him a track they had on hand that they’d made with Rodgers himself. The result was “Get Lucky,” which, as the lead single from their disco-flavored album Random Access Memories, rose like a phoenix to become the song that defined its year. “I think the robots are leading,” Williams told Rolling Stone. “Daft Punk, they’re definitely leading.”

- Joni Mitchell, ‘Help Me’ Mitchell’s 1974 album, Court and Spark, her biggest-selling ever, was also the one that she held the tightest amount of musical control over to date. “I guided everything into place on Court and Spark — even though I didn’t play it, I sang it, and then they played it from that, and it was pretty much as writ,” she said. (Her next album, The Hissing of Summer Lawns, was looser and more jazz-oriented.) “Help Me,” recorded with the jazz group Tom Scott’s L.A. Express, features one of Mitchell’s sultriest vocals and most brocaded arrangements, inspiring Prince, 13 years later, to pay the song lyrical tribute in his “Ballad of Dorothy Parker.”

- John Lee Hooker, ‘Boom Boom’ Hooker, whose canny blues boogie became a root integer for early rock & roll, said this swinging, swaggering bit of primal thump was inspired by his inability to get to a regular gig on time. “There was a young lady named Luilla,” Hooker said. “She was a bartender [at the Apex Bar in Detroit]. I’d always be late, and whenever I’d come in she’d point at me and say, ‘Boom Boom, you’re late again.’ One night she said, ‘Boom boom, I’m gonna shoot you down.’ She gave me a song, but she didn’t know it.” Keith Richards said of Hooker, “Even Muddy Waters was sophisticated next to him.” That was a compliment.

- Van Morrison, ‘Into the Mystic’ Delectably arranged, transportingly sung, this may be the definitive Morrison song — an evocation of “the days of old” that feels like a lover’s whisper. The highlight of 1970’s classic Moondance, “Into the Mystic” benefited from a new, more organic way of recording for him: “It was more like working with an actual band rather than a bunch of session guys,” Morrison said. As for the lyrics, he’d admit, “So many of my songs from that Seventies period, I haven’t a clue what they’re about. A lot of the time, I was just picking up on a vibe.”

- Roy Orbison, ‘Crying’ Orbison said he wrote this lush, dreamy ballad after an encounter with an old flame: “Whether I was physically crying or just crying inside is the same thing.” His near-operatic performance culminated in a high, wailing note, which Orbison never lost the capacity to hit before his death, in 1988. “He sounded like he was singing from an Olympian mountaintop and he meant business,” Bob Dylan wrote in Chronicles. “He was now singing his compositions in three or four octaves that made you want to drive your car over a cliff. He sang like a professional criminal.”

- Steel Pulse, ‘Ku Klux Klan’ The first great British reggae band — and some of the style’s finest songwriters — made their Island Records debut with this incendiary look at the rising tide of racist violence in late-Seventies Britain: “The Ku Klux Klan/Here to stamp out Black man.” They underlined the lyric by actually performing the song live — including a memorable BBC appearance — wearing white Klan headgear. “The hoods seemed extreme at the time, but that’s what we are in a way,” vocalist Michael Riley said. “When we wore them, people started questioning what the song was about instead of just dancing to it.”

- Sade, ‘No Ordinary Love’ Helen Adu’s small but fully inhabited range has been her secret weapon from the beginning. “I decided that if I was gonna sing, I would sing how I speak, because it’s important to be yourself,” she said. Her voice cracks before she reaches the first chorus of this 1992 hit, playing up the romantic drama of the lyric. Even better, so does Stuart Matthewman’s guitar; in the middle of this otherwise mellow groove, he overdubs a seriously moody and low-key noisy part that gives the whole thing a welcome edge. Sade — it’s not just the singer’s name, it’s also a band.

- Beck, ‘Loser’ In 1992, 22-year-old Beck Hansen was scraping by as a video-store clerk while performing bizarro folk songs at L.A. coffeehouses. After friends offered to record some songs, Beck cut “Loser” in his producer’s kitchen. It became the centerpiece of the album Mellow Gold. At first people took “Loser” to be a mere novelty hit, but Beck knew better. “You’d have to be a total idiot to say, ‘I’m the slacker-generation guy. This is my generation.… we’re not gonna fuckin’ show up,'” he said. “I’d be laughed out of the room in an instant.”

- Bon Jovi, ‘Livin’ on a Prayer’ Like his New Jersey model Bruce Springsteen, Bon Jovi concentrates on working-class heroes and heroines. “Livin’ on a Prayer,” co-written with guitarist Richie Sambora, pumped the everyday struggles of Tommy and Gina full of grandeur — guitar-pick slides, dramatic pauses, the inevitable key change — and continues to resonate today. “It’s great that we wrote songs so long ago that people can still relate to,” Bon Jovi said in 2005. “When I hear ‘Livin’ on a Prayer,’ I think to myself, ‘We wrote that. That song has really made its mark. I guess that works.'”

- Lana Del Rey, ‘A&W’ “A&W” is maximum Lana Del Rey: a sweeping, seven-minute epic that follows the sunburned, SoCal folk rock she’s perfected on recent albums back to the hip-hop-inspired pop productions of her early discography. That musical scope is paired with a narrative that’s no less ambitious — vulnerable and lurid, nostalgic and hopeless, funny and utterly bleak. And the bow tying it all together? The name of classic root beer brand, “A&W” used as shorthand for “American Whore,” because no one bends American iconography to their will like Lana Del Rey.

- Jefferson Airplane, ‘White Rabbit’ The song that brought acid rock to Middle America was a heady rock bolero written by vocalist Slick, reportedly after taking LSD and listening to Miles Davis’ Sketches of Spain. She first recorded it with her earlier band, the Great Society, before rebooting it with the Airplane. “Our parents read us stories like Peter Pan, Alice in Wonderland, and The Wizard of Oz,” Slick said. “They all have a place where children get drugs, and are able to fly or see an Emerald City or experience extraordinary animals and people.… And our parents are suddenly saying, ‘Why are you taking drugs?’ Well, hello!”

- Sister Nancy, ‘Bam Bam’ Nancy (a.k.a. Ophlin Russell) was the DJ (mic controller) for Kingston’s Stereophonic sound system when she met reggae producer Winston Riley in the late Seventies. “I really admired how he took recording serious,” Nancy said. “You couldn’t go into his studio and do any foolishness.” Their peak, “Bam Bam,” is one of the great early dancehall anthems, booming but bright, tough but playful — and it’s been sampled extensively by everyone from Lauryn Hill to Kanye West.
- Missy Elliot, ‘The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)’ As producers, Elliott and Timbaland had already made their rhythmic impact on hip-hop and R&B before Missy’s first single. And some high-profile features

items.author: Sophie Brookover
paragraphs: Poor Sam continues to go through it. Having just killed Jerry, he can’t face walking past Jerry’s empty concierge desk to go up to his room, but then when he rings Lenny’s bell, she gives him a very hard time. No waifs! No strays! The Battersea dog shelter is down the street, kid! Only the prolonged application of his best puppy-dog eyes and an earnest threat of self-harm softens up the old girl, but with caveats. He’s on his own in the kitchen and must hand over his gun until the morning, then he’s forced — pre-caffeinated — to speak with Patrick first thing. The indignities keep piling up as Patrick continues to convey both almost-genuine concern and menace simultaneously. He wants to make sure Sam is okay and to remind him how easily he can be gotten to (with a dash of “Yeah, I would kill your Work Granny, too, or even make you do it, if it was expedient for me to do so”). What a great guy to be associated with.

Patrick’s got this whole philosophical argument about how it’s not just that Sam loves Helen but that he believes her life is more important than Jerry’s because she’s a Black Dove. That’s the real reason he’s killing their agents; it’s all part of a grand, righteous plan to take down their entire rotten organization. Oh, does Kestrel have a nobler purpose? That hasn’t exactly come through loud and clear in their conversations so far. Give me Lenny and her ilk any day. I appreciate her brisk, amoral clarity.

Sam’s next target is Alexi Chernov, a hit Helen unknowingly assists him with when she tells him where and when she and Wallace will have dinner with Alexi and Katia that very evening. Watching Sam and Eleanor work as a team was a fun little twist. I really think they could team up with Helen, Williams, and Laila to form an assassin agency (which I have to physically restrain myself from describing as likely to be so successful that they would make a killing). I love that Black Doves continues to make a pragmatic case for the treasonous Helen being the oblivious Wallace’s political secret weapon. She helps him smoothly ignore Cecile Mason’s loud and reasonable objections to the Webbs’ meeting with the Chernovs, and with equal finesse, holds “the real meeting” with Katia in the ladies’ restroom. Katia and Alexi’s case for his giving some presummit remarks to the gathered dignitaries doesn’t seem unreasonable; he’s not there to represent Russia formally, but it could smooth feathers in the Kremlin for him to be there as a bridge between the summit and Russia. The war with Ukraine is very much the unspoken heart of Wallace’s summit, but the primary agenda item for the real meeting is Helen’s quest for what the Chernovs know about the robbery in their Paris hotel room; the murder of their Black Dove housekeeper, Ida Povetkin; and any echoes from Alexi’s KGB days in East Berlin. These appear to be dots Katia has not connected — maybe she hasn’t, and maybe she’s a good liar, too. Either way, Helen is satisfied enough.

Her being the power behind the throne is not a new trope by any means. I just appreciate that Helen’s power is of a type and on a scale that Wallace, bless him, can scarcely begin to imagine. That’s part of what MI-5 officer Jim Perryman is for, though. He was instrumental in increasing the Webbs’ home security last season and had some questions for Helen back then, too, but was satisfied enough with her answers that he didn’t dig any further. Now that Wallace is PM, there’s more background checking to do, and he’s sorry to have to ask her about details that don’t quite line up, but needs must. Helen once again snaps into Good at Lying mode to fend off his questions about where her parents are buried and if she recalls having a stepsister named Bonnie Weir. Perryman is good at his job — he’s got a bunch of new material to ask Helen about and doesn’t accuse her of anything straight-out. He just places pieces of evidence in front of her and hopes she’ll say something revealing, but though she’s surprised to be having this conversation, this is not amateur hour. Perryman will need stronger material than this, and now Helen knows she’s in his crosshairs and she is furious about it. The combination of details from her pre–Black Doves life finding their way into the hands of MI-5 and the video Kestrel is using to blackmail Sam is at least as dangerous for Kestrel as for her.

Plenty of Helen’s rage is driven by her resentment at the spy-wife label, of course. Would she be married to Wallace if she weren’t so married to her job? The flashback of Reed informing Helen that she’ll soon be the prime minister’s wife shows her clearly not being thrilled with the news. (N.B.: That conversation takes place just a few weeks after the end of last season and is a repeat/revision of a very similar scene in the first-season finale.) Would a spy-wife take the initiative to break into Dani’s grotty little apartment and convince her to team up to surreptitiously access the Black Doves’ on-site archives about Wildflower? Would a spy-wife have the presence of mind to prompt Dani to tell Conteh about Reed’s rendezvous/dead-drop bench in Battersea Park? Take that, Laila! Helen’s going to offer up a high-potential source on a silver platter! That’s actually a pretty solid gift to pull out of thin air, and better still, it provides an excuse to introduce Laila and Sam, who very, very believably declare themselves charmed to meet each other. I think both can sense that they’re working at cross-purposes to each another. They all need to find Reed but for different reasons. While Helen doesn’t exactly like Reed, they have a long history and Reed has never lied to her; she thinks Conteh hasn’t told her a truthful word even once. Laila is in Conteh’s crosshairs for whatever reasons are behind her being removed from active duty, and Reed could get her out of whatever that pickle is. Sam isn’t really sure why he’s along for this ride except for his reflexive need to help Helen, until the end of the episode, when he learns Reed is his final target for Kestrel.

As the episode closes, we’re on the verge of getting into 19th-century farce territory. Sam and Eleanor have poisoned Chernov, but now Sam has to watch his back even more than usual because Conteh has put contracts out on Sam and Laila. Someone has taken the contract for Laila, and the last we see of her, she has noticed a rifle’s laser sight on her chest. That does not bode well. Sam needs to get ready to take out Reed, whose location Laila has extracted from her kidnapped Black Dove, but to facilitate that job, he’ll be tagging along with Helen to assist in Reed’s rescue from wherever she’s now being held. That’s not a two-man job, now, is it? And how are things going to turn out for Williams and Eleanor? Williams sort of took Sam’s advice about confessing her feelings to Eleanor and almost instantly regretted it, so that could get very messy very quickly.
Strange Times to Be Nefarious

• No doubt Agnes O’Casey is quite capable of playing characters who are not squirrelly little minxes, but she has built up such an impressive résumé in roles like Dani. Off the top of my head, I can recommend three more performances that take advantage of this particular skill: Irina Morozova in Star City, briefly but memorably as Margaret Douglas in Wolf Hall: The Mirror and the Light, and the heroically steely (yet doe-eyed) Vivien Epstein in Ridley Road.

• Eleanor’s belief that “Just when I thought I was out, they pull me back in” is from The Hobbit had me first howling and then wondering if that was scripted or one of a variety of hilariously implausible films Gabrielle Creevy might have ad-libbed. When I asked Knightley and Whishaw, if there’s much improvisation on this show, both immediately said “there’s none.” Knightley went on to elaborate that Joe Barton puts his characters in “serious-ridiculous scenarios, but you’ll be on a tangent, like Helen and Laila in the lift [in Episode 1], where Laila’s talking about how she masturbates to the rabbit from Zootropolis [sic]. This why you work with a Joe Barton script!”

• Helen’s face when she recognizes Eleanor at the Chancellor Club is quite a moment. This may be the first time it has occurred to her that Wallace could easily be a target for assassination and that getting to him wouldn’t be so difficult.
• I know I’m not the only Black Doves viewer old enough to immediately start humming “Meeting in the Ladies’ Room,” by Klymaxx, in that scene with Helen and Katia. What a rich text that video is.

• How fun to see Ambika Mod and Ben Whishaw onscreen together again! They co-starred in 2022’s This Is Going to Hurt, an excellent and devastating limited series about how hard it is to be a dedicated medical professional in today’s NHS.

items.title: Black Doves Recap: ’Twas Ever Thus
items.description: Sam and Helen are having what is, at base, the same midlife crisis. After investing so many years in their illicit but exciting careers, they must now face facts: The jobs will never love them back, and they may be aging out of their related fields. At least H
items.author: Sophie Brookover
paragraphs: Sam and Helen are having what is, at base, the same midlife crisis. After investing so many years in their illicit but exciting careers, they must now face facts: The jobs will never love them back, and they may be aging out of their related fields. At least Helen’s work has forced her to create some aspects of a real life that can exist outside of espionage, but her loving relationships with Wallace and their children may not survive the next couple of weeks. The revelation that the woman they know as a loving (if often distracted and not always present) wife and mother has been committing treason almost daily for the entirety of their relationship with her could ruin it all.

Sam’s situation is even worse. He has no family (remember, he assassinated his own father to seal his commitment to the life). He has no friends outside of Helen, and it’s clear that prior to their call while she’s safecracking in Paris, the two of them haven’t spoken in months. He lives in a hotel where the staff has a betting pool going on what his career could be. His isolated existence is bleak, especially for such a bighearted person naturally inclined to love others.

At every turn, Sam is reminded of both his own mortality and his lack of a ready answer to the question of what he will do with the time remaining in his one wild and precious life. He’s already sort of taking a page from Lenny’s book by surrounding himself with younger colleagues to mentor and assign work to. This is a smart move, and there are bound to be more Williamses and Eleanors out there for him to mold into the next generation of triggermen. But will it be enough? When he goes to kill Spitfire, a.k.a. Melanie Ambrose, she tells him that choosing to retire early (rather than being retired) gave her about 20 more good years of life before he turned up at her door. She’s got the adorable flat to show for it, too — it’s a basement, but her kitchen gets lots of light and the balance of cozy to expansive is just right — yet has retained enough assassin-spy skills that she’s able to maneuver Sam into the living room and herself close to the gun she keeps by the door. His reflexes are better, though, so RIP Spitfire.

Helen is deeply vexed by this turn of events. Would it kill Sam to hold off on killing the people she needs to talk to before she can talk to them? Her ever-shortening list of agents associated with Wildflower leads her to attempt to team up again with Laila, who Conteh says was dropped from active duty about six months ago and has been AWOL ever since. The first one-on-one meeting between handler and agent isn’t promising. There has always been friction between Reed and Helen, but in the main, Reed has been successful in using a shifting combination of wheedling, scolding, complimenting, and threatening to ensure Helen fullfils her mission objectives. Conteh needs some practice in this area or at least to accept a certain degree of independent action from her. He clearly knows Helen well from Reed’s reports to the steering committee and from her file, but that’s a totally different experience from managing a field agent. The episode brings out an interesting tension in Conteh. He says he doesn’t think much of assassins because of their fundamental incuriosity; he always has questions and always wants answers. But does he really? Or does he mean he wants to be the one to find answers? He’s certainly not a fan of Helen’s seeking answers on her own. The fastest way to get her onside would be to show that she can trust him, but he seems more invested in asserting his authority over her. It’s too bad because if he strikes the right balance, their partnership could be very fruitful!

At one point, Helen remarks that as the prime minister’s wife, she has to be careful about whom she’s seen with, and this feels like a moment to wonder aloud about the advisability of the Black Doves meeting with their handlers in public in a city blanketed with CCTV cameras. There’s a funny nod to this in the episode’s big set piece, in which Laila reluctantly meets with Helen and they lead several teams of Black Doves security guys on a chase through Somerset House. The whole thing — Laila’s irritation at Helen’s spy-wife assumption that she hasn’t been followed, the ease with which she dispatches the guys who try to kidnap her, how their improvisational fighting style lets them escape, and all the banter in between — is the high point of the episode. Ambika Mod gets all the best lines, and her spiky chemistry with Keira Knightley is so much fun to watch.

It’s clear that Laila’s dismissal of her as a spy-wife continues to make Helen desperate to prove she’s more than that. So desperate, in fact, that she goes off and does a whole bunch of spy-wife things, such as summoning Laila to a meet where she didn’t notice she was being followed (while wearing a pretty useless disguise of a brown tweed baseball cap and large sunglasses). That wild chase through Somerset House only strengthens her reckless determination to get to the bottom of what’s going on with Reed and the Black Doves in general. In the end, Helen’s biggest challenge as a Black Dove that day turns out to be the most spy-wife thing she could do: follow Reed’s advice, digging deep into her arsenal as an accomplished liar to convince Wallace she doesn’t want an exit strategy from their marriage and certainly has never cheated on him.

If only Reed knew she had such good reason to be proud of her girl. She definitely enjoys learning about Helen’s exploits with Laila (another managerial challenge whom Reed clearly enjoys working with; I’m so curious about who her handler was and how she got pulled from active duty), but that’s the high point of Conteh’s visit. Otherwise, he’s all business; as far as he can tell, all roads of the murders of three Black Doves lead to her and this bizarrely underreported East Berlin mission from 1988. She’s the sole survivor and was the undercover asset there for five years, so Conteh knows there’s a much bigger story for her to tell. Now is the time for Reed to try to clear her name.

Of course, we know what Conteh does not (and perhaps Reed suspects), which is that Kestrel (through Patrick) is behind it all and that someone else must also have survived that operation. Poor Sam wishes he didn’t know about Kestrel, but under Helen’s curiosity-driven influence, he enlists Lenny’s help to track down Patrick and get some answers. For the third time in two seasons, Sam is forced to sever a relationship, and this one may be the most painful, the most cruel, because in killing Jerry, Sam is destroying potential. Maybe he and Jerry would have had a long, lovely life together; maybe it would have been only a romantic interlude, but he’ll never know. Whatever life Jerry had ahead of him, with or without Sam, as a concierge or something else entirely, is over because Sam got too curious and then had to choose between the love (or hell, even just the date at the nice shared-plates restaurant!) he might have had with Jerry and the love and protectiveness (and sometimes resentful obligation) he already shares with Helen. Once Patrick shows Sam the video of Helen shooting an older man in the head, it’s game over for Jerry. Once again, Sam feels he doesn’t have a choice, but Lenny’s right: He does have a choice; he just dislikes one of the options too much to take it.

Before heading out into the night to break his own heart, Sam tells Williams that she should tell Eleanor that she’s in love with her. She’s miserable carrying her love around like a big secret and waiting for Eleanor to notice, but if she tells Eleanor, she’ll know for sure what’s on the other side of sharing it. Assassins don’t have a superlong life expectancy, Sam reminds her, and does she really want to wake up one day years from now only to realize she has no one and nothing long-lasting in her life? Tell her!
Strange Times to Be Nefarious

• Three lines are in a dead heat for best of the episode: (1) Eleanor’s bewildered, mocking “What, are you gay Miss Marple and lesbian Poirot now?” (2) Laila’s up-to-here line with Helen, “It was nice knowing you — we’ll always have Paris. Don’t call me again!” and (3) Lenny’s (Kathryn Hunter can do no wrong) “If you came to kill me, you better fucking not have — I’ve got goulash on!”

• You don’t bring in Neve Campbell for just a couple of scenes, and I look forward to Cecile Mason making more of a pest of herself at No. 10 as we get closer to the Defense Summit. Joe Barton has written the United States’s Defense envoy to sound a bit like a mid-20th-century screwball heroine (via Texas, maybe?), which is both odd and tantalizing.

• My hat is off to the costume-design team. Lenny leaning all the way into cheetah print; Conteh’s luxurious, extremely buttoned-up layers; Laila’s belligerently cool streetwear — the personalities and priorities conveyed in the costuming are knocking me out.

items.title: Black Doves Season-Premiere Recap: I’ve Built My Dreams Around You
items.description: Welcome back to Black Doves, dear readers! We’ve got another season of quips, murders, and espionage for hire; rapidly shifting alliances; and getting by with a little help from one’s friends. When last we left Helen and Sam, they were enjoying a cozy Christma
items.author: Sophie Brookover
paragraphs: Welcome back to Black Doves, dear readers! We’ve got another season of quips, murders, and espionage for hire; rapidly shifting alliances; and getting by with a little help from one’s friends. When last we left Helen and Sam, they were enjoying a cozy Christmas together at Helen and Wallace’s home after taking down the London representatives of an increasingly international crime syndicate. They’d solved the mystery of Helen’s lover Jason’s murder, too (not a conspiracy, just the sad result of a crime lord’s nepo baby having accidentally killed the Chinese ambassador, could happen to anyone), and managed not to get themselves or any more of their colleagues murdered. Oh, and Reed told Helen that Wallace was likely to be rewarded for being untainted by scandal — next stop, ascending from secretary of state for Defence to prime minister. Everything was coming up roses, or pretty close to it.

These people are not made for long-term contentment, though. Black Doves has always wondered aloud about what it means to be a middle-aged spy-assassin. In any other field, Helen and Sam would be successful mid-career professionals, but in their line of work, happy retirements are basically unheard of. Last season, Dani (Agnes O’Casey) thought herself ready to step into Helen’s shoes should Wallace unexpectedly find himself widowed. Sam still mourns the end of his relationship with the very lovely Michael, who has gone on to embrace a very normal life, adopting a little girl. In this season, series creator-showrunner-writer Joe Barton (Giri/Haji, the Amadeus TV series) continues to excavate the theme while raising the stakes from the micro or personal to the geopolitically consequential (and still personal).

It makes sense to widen the scope and ratchet up the stakes at this point. When the second-season premiere opens, Wallace is about to become prime minister, so he and Helen are attending a gala dinner at a peace conference in Paris (Helen later refers to it brattily as a networking mixer). All looks exactly right with the power couple in their formalwear, and Helen should be positively giddy at the scope and significance of what she can pass along to Reed, but instead they’re both miserable. Wallace can feel that something isn’t right with Helen, but because he’s a normal person, his mind goes to infidelity, not the selling of state secrets and unrelenting, casual violence. (Okay, he can’t be fully normal — he is a Tory, after all. Nobody’s perfect.) There’s no way Helen can possibly engage in couples therapy honestly, and she also seems kind of bored, sitting at their table alone and fidgeting with her rings while Wallace works the room.

She may well be bored, but because Helen is always working, she uses it to segue smoothly into a conversation with Katya, the wife of Russian oligarch Alexi Chernov (who is chatting with Wallace). The two hit it off at once, and Helen offers to encourage Wallace to give Alexi a speaking slot at the defense conference he’s hosting in London next week. She also finds a moment to steal Katya’s hotel key card, duck out of the venue through a utility hallway (where she has already stashed a pair of sneakers), and zip over to the hotel where she links up with another Black Dove, Laila (played by the always welcome Ambika Mod, yay!). Like her spiritual kin Williams and Eleanor, Laila is somewhere in her mid-20s, a cheerful and judgmental motormouth, and a dab hand at merciless, quick-draw gunfights. I can’t wait to see the three of them together this season.

As if Helen were not already obviously out of sorts, her knowing less about the mission than Laila does and being wholly unprepared to crack a high-end safe makes the whole evening a bit much. Thank goodness for Sam calling her out of the blue! Her body language shifts instantly — can-do Helen is back! — and he walks her through the tricky bits to retrieve a laptop with files about Wildflower. There’s no further time for the lengthy catch-up session Helen would love to have with Sam, though, because she has to put in an appearance at the party the security goons are dying to throw for her and Laila is about to kick off. The fights on Black Doves are always a lot of fun to watch — the choreography is energetic and freewheeling, and at their best, the physicality is witty in a way that matches the dialogue. Helen and Laila have known each other for about five minutes, but they sync immediately, dispatching (by my count) ten security guys total, and by the end, neither has so much as a droplet of blood on her.

The job was a success, but Helen can’t shake how crummy it felt to be called a spy wife. Laila’s throwaway comment has touched a very sensitive nerve; Helen knows she was hired as much for her multilingual intelligence as for her moral flexibility regarding murder, so why does Reed keep her in the dark about so much of the purpose and consequence of her work? She wants to feel like “a real fucking spy, not a honey-trap idiot who can’t be trusted,” but Reed is too unsettled by the Wildflower files to grasp how deep this runs for her agent. Helen already knows plenty by Reed’s lights, and it’s possible that even her present level of knowledge is a danger to her. Better to “stay good at lying,” get her marriage back on track, and make the most of however long she winds up having to live behind the titular glossy black door at No. 10 Downing Street. Leave the messiest stuff to Reed. We know the mess must be horrific because Reed is visibly unsettled by a Russian-accented recording in the files. She describes Wildflower as “an echo of something from a long time ago,” but that echo seems deafeningly loud, especially once Reed is cornered by two cars as she walks back to wherever she’s staying. What a bravura little moment for Sarah Lancashire in this scene, as surprise, irritation, and resignation flicker across her face. She doesn’t say a word, but I heard loud and clear “Well, this was bound to happen eventually.”

Things that were bound to happen eventually also include Sam hitting the sauce before a dreary, low-end hit on an older fellow triggerman, then getting cornered by about ten armed Metropolitan Police officers the second he walks out of his victim’s tower block. That call Helen took from him earlier was Sam’s one postarrest call, which did not go the way he’d hoped. But not to worry: A man claiming to be his solicitor arrives, introducing himself as Patrick (Sam Riley), who represents an as yet unnamed “private entity” (surely nothing to worry about! Plenty of legit, completely untroubling organizations refer to themselves that way!) that wants to offer Sam his freedom in exchange for four murders at 20 percent above his usual rate. No hesitations, no refusals, tight timelines — sure, why not?

Sam returns to his quiet life as a long-term resident of a swanky hotel whose adorable concierge, Jerry, is also Sam’s fuckbuddy and deliverer of the dossier on his first target, Zeus. Zeus (a.k.a. Erik Klein) is living in a safe house with enough armed guards surrounding it that Sam needs to bring in some muscle of his own. Yes, it’s time to get the band back together: Williams and Eleanor are reporting for duty! They’re every bit the exuberant, sarcastic bowl of puppies you remember from last season, making a nuisance of themselves with the waitress at the tapas restaurant Sam has selected for them and lamenting the near unkillability of bodyguards these days. As if a wee wisp of a girl assassin doesn’t have enough to contend with in her line of work, now she has to shoot a target a dozen times and run over him with her car because he’s turning himself into Rasputin with all the steroids and cocaine at his disposal?

Their stakeout and invasion of Zeus’s safe house goes pretty smoothly (I didn’t keep a running tally of dead guys, so let’s ballpark it at eight) with Sam getting his polka-dot-undies–clad man in the upstairs bathroom. It takes a bit of grappling and scuffling to get himself into position to pull the trigger on Zeus, but the real drama comes from Helen leaving Sam a frantic voice-mail begging him to abort the mission. During her deeply unsettling command performance at the Black Doves’ swanky London office, she was assigned a new handler (the officious Mr. Robert Conteh) and used her little file-copying device to download Mrs. Reed’s details. Scrolling through the “known associates” section, she comes across Ida Povetkin, the Chernov family’s housekeeper found murdered in Moscow a few weeks ago, and … Erik Klein! Zeus himself is an active-duty Black Dove! Helen needs to talk to that guy, but that’s never going to happen because Sam is just too good at his job.
Strange Times to Be Nefarious

• Helen seems not to have a security detail? I recall the Webbs beefing up their security at home last season, and of course No. 10 is well guarded, but what about personal protection? How does this aspect of Black Doves’s fictional world compare with our reality? My limited understanding is that the prime minister has close protection from Royalty and Specialist Protection officers, but I am wholly unclear on what protection is provided for the PM’s family.

• During Helen’s visit to the Black Doves’ offices in some nondescript high-rise that looks like it could be next door to the old Pierpoint & Co. offices in Industry (now there’s a crossover I’d love to see), there’s a blink-and-you’ll-miss-it moment where we see Dani is now a desk jockey. Well, well.

• Jerry, the adorable concierge who could maybe possibly also become Sam’s boyfriend, is played by Samuel Barnett. To me, he’ll always be Dirk Gently from Dirk Gently’s Holistic Detective Agency. If you’re in the market for something quirky, exuberant, and not infrequently sinister, it’s well worth a watch (bonus: Fiona Dourif, a.k.a. Dr. MacKay from The Pitt, is outstanding as a holistic assassin named Bart).

items.title: The Lowdown Recap: Above the Law
items.description: It’s taken half a season, but — finally and with flair — a villain worthy of The Lowdown emerges from the cesspit of Woodrell. It’s not that Vela Thorne isn’t sinister enough in her own right. The ruthless county SHEriff has professional-grade acetone running
items.author: Amanda Whiting
paragraphs: It’s taken half a season, but — finally and with flair — a villain worthy of The Lowdown emerges from the cesspit of Woodrell. It’s not that Vela Thorne isn’t sinister enough in her own right. The ruthless county SHEriff has professional-grade acetone running through her veins. But The Lowdown is about plumbing the depths of Oklahoma’s political corruption. Everyone knows that TV cops are bad guys, but how far up the chain — and how low down into Oklahoma’s very foundations — does the graft go?

Jed Sallsman, Woodrell County’s oily judge, is the brains behind its prisoner diversion scheme, which exchanges prison sentences for work opportunities at a meat-processing plant. Based on the size of Jed’s cattle ranch — conspicuously vast for a man on a government salary — the judge is likely also the scheme’s principal beneficiary. But Jed’s not content to quietly enjoy the spoils of an exploitative labor arrangement. He wants to campaign on it. He has a sanitised promo video made to showcase Fresh Start Fine Foods, where Sheriff Thorne’s husband, Bob T (Clifton Collins Jr.), serves as factory foreman.

What’s more is that Jed — played by Deadwood star John Hawkes, always welcome — screens the film for Lee and Governor Donald Washberg even after Nathan Spence’s death, which we now know happened on site at Fresh Start. Jed’s not afraid of the law. “I am the law,” he tells Lee. Judge Sallsman’s so convinced of his own invulnerability, backed up by sky-high approval ratings, that he suggests the tone-deaf line would make a fine title for the hagiographic, rags-to-riches political profile he wants Lee Raybon, award-winning journalist, to write.

It’s staggering how much life Lee fits into 24 hours. He wakes up in county lockup, spends the day with Oklahoma’s preening elite, and still manages to make it home in time for his daughter’s birthday party. What could I accomplish if I never slept or bathed or ate proper meals? Surely Daymond could have facilitated Lee’s release from custody given he’s facing zero charges, so why does Lee call in a showy favor from Governor Washberg (the “Big D” tattooed inside his cowboy boot at the end of last episode)? Perhaps the point is to intimidate Vela and her henchman, but the move puts our Tulsa truthstorian in new and uncomfortable territory. Lee thrills to stick it to the man, but here he is fighting police corruption with personal favors. Lee and Donnie are sitting in a local diner fine-tuning the contours of their friendship of convenience when Judge Jed walks in.

There’s some history between Jed and Donnie, who starts saying goodbye to the judge before they’ve finished their hellos. But Jed’s here to give the out-of-towners a warm Woodrell welcome. Asked if he’s from Tulsa, Lee answers that he’s from Heartland, U.S.A. — from the land of chili dogs and Tastee-Freez. The forgotten places between the map dots that John Mellencamp writes songs about. There’s a persistent emphasis this season on Lee’s origins. Where does a man like this — tenacious, fiery, unapologetically crass — come from? If you ask Lee directly, he’ll tell you he comes from nowhere. He made himself, though; I think the more accurate answer is yes, sir, Tulsa.

Aware that Lee is planning a story about Woodrell, Jed invites the men on a whistle-stop tour, which Lee accepts over Donnie’s protests. Weirdly, though, all the stops are at Tallgrass, Jed’s ranch. This is a tour of the man who stands before us. First, they visit the big house, where Jed shows off his collection of taxidermied dead animals, the horns of said animals, and an original Dances with Wolves one-sheet. He’s got a pool and a grand piano and a loft brimming with cowboy-era Americana — antique rifles and Native American artifacts (of dubious provenance, we can be sure). Jed’s even collected the gavel of Judge Isaac Parker, who once presided over this frontier and earned the nickname “hanging judge” for the 160 men he sentenced to death.

“We should bring back the noose, to be honest,” Jed says, too honestly. The future is the past. The past is eternal. These men aren’t politicians. They’re kids playing cowboys — judges and sheriffs acting out their boyhood games of winning the West. Except, of course, the West has been won. Native American land is U.S. land. Native American culture is held hostage behind glass curios in the private collections of wealthy men who think they own whatever land they land on. At Jed’s insistence, the three men ride out on horseback to survey the expansive ranch that theft and expulsion made.

All afternoon, Donnie has been understandably eager to leave, but after watching the Fresh Start promo, he starts to see the value in a photo-op with the wildly popular judge. They don’t even have guards at the meat factory, the judge boasts; that’s how docile the forced laborers are! When Lee mentions Nathan Spence was meant to attend the program, Jed barely flinches, expressing sympathy for the boy’s confused and grieving mother.

Lee eventually leaves Woodrell with a rain check from Jed, who promises to give the reporter a tour of Fresh Start some other time. From Donnie, Lee gets warnings — stop asking questions and don’t call again — that he’ll never heed. You’d think the hard part of his day was behind him, but when Lee shows up to the bowling alley for Fran’s birthday party, he’s met by his dad, wearing a bowling shirt that’s been embroidered with “Grandpa.” Earlier in the episode, Francis swung by Sweet Emily’s, where Frog was once again holding court, telling Ray and Marty about how the antiquities trade really works in Oklahoma. Mining companies loot where they dig and quarry, then later, they establish sham excavation sites where the same artifacts can be re-discovered for the first time, washing them clean enough to be acquired legitimately by museums and universities. That explanation casts Frog as Robin Hood, stealing from the black market to return important relics back to the Caddo, assuming they were ever really important in the first place. One day, Frog says, someone will dig up this diner and sell his coffee mug as Christ’s chalice. You can’t beat the grifters, he seems to be saying.

Lee sulks through the party, more focused on his deadbeat dad than the guest of honor. Luckily, his ex is kind enough to give him a pep talk before Lee ruins the afternoon for everyone. “You can’t take my peace,” he tells his father, who gets under Lee’s skin less than a minute later. Still, the party is a success. Grandpa brings Francis some flowers and an IOU; her dad gives her a first edition of Slow Days, Fast Company, which is a legit cool gift for a teenage girl. Deidra terrorizes a teenage boy who dares to hit on her, and no one cries, not even the birthday girl.

By the time we meet up with Ginger at work, it’s been more than a day since she and Lee split up. I suppose she’s already learned not to panic every time he disappears. Or maybe she’s been too preoccupied to notice. Though Jeff assures Vela that Nathan’s mom stonewalled Ginger, the truth is that Deborah invited Ginger in to talk. She told Ginger that Nathan had called home from Fresh Start, where he supposedly never was. Deborah suspects the “medical emergency” that took her son from her was karoshi. The inmates are being worked to death. Vela is covering for her husband. McMann is covering for his cousin. And everyone, seemingly, is covering up for Jed.

When Lee finds out about Deb’s hunch, he suggests that he and Ginger head back to Woodrell to talk to her again. They leave right after Fran’s party, and still, they’re too late. As Lee pulls up, a fire truck leaves Deb’s house, sirens off. Her dead body is being loaded into an ambulance. Carbon monoxide poisoning, a neighbor says. Nathan Spence, Chili Franks, Deb Spence. Someone, or some collection of ones, is on a killing spree. They must be hiding something big to go after a mother in mourning, Lee posits, but Ginger is turned off by his appetite for the case. Where he sees the promise of a meatier story, she sees her own trail of destruction.

She asks Lee to drop her off at home, then runs to the mini-mart for cigs. While she’s out, Ginger calls Pookie, who’s been inside long enough to learn that Ginger’s been acting on old intel. According to Pookie, Mekko was at Fresh Start, too. And word around Boontill is that he’s the one who killed Nathan.

Ginger’s still stumbling over the revelation when McMann and Lonnie arrive to abduct her at gunpoint. Throughout “A Dog With Two Tails,” McMann’s been telling his partner-in-crime he has a master plan to clean up this mess. Part 1 was to dig up Chili’s body and bring it to the incinerator. Part 2, it seems, is to kidnap a public defender they know to be working closely with a bullheaded reporter. All in all, a cracking plan, and I see no reason at all for Vela or Jed to be worried.

With three episodes to go, there’s a sense that things are coalescing just beyond the limits of our understanding. We still don’t know why Frog has come to town, for example, but after touring Jed’s personal museum at Tallgrass, we can begin to imagine that father and son’s stories will collide. The number of bodies piling up in Woodrell is clearly no coincidence, but in a place as menacing as Sterlin Harjo’s Oklahoma, can all this evil really fall at the feet of a mere county judge? Whatever else is true, “Where is Mekko?” no longer seems to be the season’s operative question. I’m more curious to learn where Mekko’s been and, more consequentially, who put him there.

items.title: The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City Recap: Et Tu, Angie?
items.description: Angie is falling apart, and while she’s trying to keep it a secret, the cracks are starting to become so visible that everyone around her can tell that something is up … They just don’t know what yet. It all eventually comes to a head this episode in a truly d
items.author: Tom Smyth
paragraphs: Angie is falling apart, and while she’s trying to keep it a secret, the cracks are starting to become so visible that everyone around her can tell that something is up … They just don’t know what yet. It all eventually comes to a head this episode in a truly dark, painful way — but before we get to that, we’re given the treat of watching Lisa train with her vocal coach. She has her do vocal warm-ups on camera, which is a fate I wouldn’t wish upon my worst enemy, and somehow they manage to get Lisa’s fountain soda involved in the process. Lisa tells us that she’s gonna be big, and she doesn’t mean community theater; she means Gaga.

Speaking of pop stars, something that I’ll be thinking about until the day I die is John Barlow sitting down in the confessional seat to tell us that one of his favorite singers is Halsey and paraphrasing one of her songs to say that Lisa is a god. “And I’m happy to worship her,” he says, and I couldn’t agree more. I also worship her.

Somebody I don’t worship is Bronwyn, who shows up to shop at Kemo Sabe (Kyle Richards you are always with us) in a foul mood, which she expresses by wearing jeans. She repeatedly tells us that she only wears jeans if she’s in a bad mood, and does it over and over, really trying to make it a thing. It’s performative, like those people who store sweaters in their ovens to be like Carrie Bradshaw even though they’ve got drawer space. Enough already, just be pissed off.

She’s especially pissed at Angie, who she thinks was stirring the pot at the Jupiter Party and being “Lisa’s soldier” and doing her dirty work even after Bronwyn told her she didn’t want to hear it. Angie defends herself by basically saying she was being funny by telling her the gossip anyway and points out that Bronwyn was laughing about it in the moment. To quote Lisa Barlow: “Roll footage!” Sure enough, she was laughing it off in the moment, but it’s fair that in hindsight Bronwyn feels like Angie was being messy and acting out. It’s the overarching sentiment of the episode: Something is up with Angie.

This whole situation is especially frustrating for the viewer because we have more information than most of the cast. We know why Angie is acting out, whereas all of her castmates (save for Heather) lack that context. Would the context make them give her a free pass? Probably not, but at least they’d have the full picture. As of now, we just have to watch them confusedly surmise that something must be going on with her at home, like concerned guidance counselors when a middle-schooler randomly starts talking back. Plus keeping this secret in — though understandable — can’t be good for Angie. In fact, I think her acting out is more the result of her keeping this secret and not because of the split itself. But slowly and surely she’s starting to soft-launch the breakup, as we see her nervously tell her father.

But it’s not all bad news; she first proudly shows this elderly Greek man that she won the Grindr Award for Housewife of the Year. “This is the Grindr Award, because they love me and I’m funny, that was given to me by the gays,” she tells him, holding up the statue. This is clearly a broken woman. She says she’s a gay man trapped in a woman’s body, and honestly, seeing her desperately turn to Grindr for validation in her lowest moment makes me think she actually might be right. We make a sharp pivot to her crying as she tells her father about her marital problems, but fortunately he’s completely supportive, telling her that life is too short to be miserable. It’s a weight off her shoulders and hopefully a key step toward her opening up more to the group.

That is, if it’s not already too late. They’re all heading to a reiki session that Quai planned (Mary accidentally refers to it as “racketeering,” and honestly, given the history of Housewives, that’s not a bad guess), and on the way there, Bronwyn and Mary commiserate over their frustrations with Angie. Mary was particularly upset that, rather than check on her as she stormed out of the Jupiter Party, Angie opted to stay back and film a TikTok with Britani, who was the reason Mary was storming out.

When they arrive, Angie tries to pull Mary aside, sensing that they need to clear the air. But Mary isn’t interested in clearing the air; she’s interested in snapping at Angie for what she did. Angie is completely thrown and doesn’t understand where this is coming from, and quickly runs off crying after Mary tells her she’s got a “head of granite.” Knowing that Mary drove over with Bronwyn, Angie is convinced that Bronwyn got in her ear to rile her up, and when she returns, calls Bronwyn a snake for that. Her screaming is interrupted only by the reiki healer walking over with her little drum, just in time.

The highlights of the reiki session itself included the practitioner/medium not knowing that Heather was dating someone and then pretending that she actually did know, Lisa skipping the session because she was good with her energy as it was, and Mary later revealing that she prefers to use the bathroom completely nude like George Costanza.

When they sit down for lunch afterward, the drama picks right back up. Sure, Whitney and Lisa come to some kind of peace, but the vibe turns sour again when Angie once again takes the floor and starts fighting with Bronwyn over being called Lisa’s soldier. There’s also a weird dynamic here where each of them seems to think they have a leg up on the other by way of information they got via Todd and Shawn’s friendship. Angie knows (or claims) that Bronwyn is playing nice with Todd to get her $85,000 payout, whereas Bronwyn alludes to knowing more about Angie and Shawn’s split than she’s thus far shared.

But then something really bad happens. Mary and Angie get back into the same argument from earlier about Angie being self-centered, and Mary snaps, “What happened to your husband? What happened to your child?” And Angie, clearly not thinking, throws the question right back at her, saying, “What happened to your husband? What happened to your child? What are you talking about?” The room freezes. Whitney leaves to throw up.

Angie, seemingly still not realizing what words just came out of her mouth, just forges ahead — eventually explaining that she forgot what situation she’s in and meant it in the general sense to say that anybody being a mother shouldn’t mean they can’t take care of themself. But naturally, and understandably, it’s too late for Mary, who clings to the statement immediately. The misstep only makes Angie crash out even more; she stands up, fully sobbing and screaming and throwing utensils. “Somebody get Jen Shah out of here,” Mary says, using their former cast member’s name like a slur. As a complete sidebar, I do just want to say that I love that kind of self-referential shorthand … but they must be wary. I fear it may be a Beetlejuice-like situation where if they say her name three times she’ll appear.

After Mary storms off, Heather, Lisa, and Whitney circle around Angie — not to defend her but because they can clearly see that she’s in the midst of some kind of breakdown. Even Bronwyn doesn’t like seeing her, and the group, in this state — and they all put everything aside to try to throw water on the situation because nobody wants to see these two best friends fall apart for good. Angie keeps trying to explain herself through tears, and even tries to chase down Mary in the parking lot, but no dice. We know Mary and her ways, and (as Britani can tell you) once she makes up her mind like this, it’s almost impossible to bounce back. The whole thing is dark and sad on so many levels, but hopefully, with time, things can settle.

items.title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ Renewed for Season 4 at Netflix
items.description: “Nobody Wants This” has been renewed for Season 4 at Netflix, Variety has learned.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: “Nobody Wants This” has been renewed for Season 4 at Netflix, Variety has learned.
The news comes just over two weeks after the launch of the comedy series’ third season, which debuted on Netflix on Oct. 22.

“We are so happy and thrilled to do another season of our favorite show on television, which coincidentally is the one we run,” said series co-showrunners Erin Foster, Jenni Konner, and Bruce Eric Kaplan.

“Nobody Wants This” stars Kristen Bell and Adam Brody along with: Justine Lupe, Timothy Simons, Jackie Tohn, Stephanie Faracy, Michael Hitchcock, Paul Ben-Victor, Tovah Feldshuh, Andrew Rannells, Sarah Silverman, Shiloh Bearman, and Sherry Cola.
The official description for Season 3 states:

“That ‘first time’ feeling, all over again. After recommitting to each other at the end of last season, Joanne (Bell) and Noah (Brody) are moving into a home — and a relationship — that finally feels solid, embracing every exciting ‘first’ that comes with building their life together. Sasha (Simons) and Esther (Tohn) are thrust back into the dating world, whether they like it or not, stumbling through all the awkwardness (and unexpected thrill) of getting to know someone new, right as Morgan (Lupe) takes her career to the next level, on her way to becoming an (almost) media sensation. Meanwhile, Sasha and Morgan have been circling something neither of them has been able to admit to.”

“Great love stories never go out of style, and ‘Nobody Wants This’ has become a true cultural phenomenon,” said Tracey Pakosta, Netflix’s vice president of comedy series, US. “This incredible creative team has built a show that grows with its audience, and our members around the world have embraced it season after season. We cannot be more excited for Season 4.”

Erin Foster created the series and serves as co-showrunner and executive producer along with Konner and Kaplan. Bell is also an executive producer along with Sara Foster, Nora Silver, Steven Levitan, Danielle Stokdyk and Jeff Morton, as well as Oly Obst for 3arts. The series is produced by 20th Television and is filmed in Los Angeles.

“Nobody Wants This” originally premiered in 2024 and proved popular from the outset, spending eight weeks on the Netflix global top 10 English language TV chart. Season 2 followed in 2025, spending four weeks on the same chart. The show has reached 78.5 million views across all three seasons to date, with a view defined as total hours viewed divided by total runtime.

There was some controversy around the third season when Brody once again stated his opposition to recent Israeli actions in Gaza against Palestinians, describing it as “a genocide.” Feldshuh publicly disagreed with Brody, saying “to accuse the Jewish people of genocide is wild. It’s right out of Hitler’s playbook.” Feldshuh followed up on Threads to say that there was no tension on the set of the show and she “deeply” enjoys filming it.

items.title: Meghan Markle’s Father Arrested Over Allegations He Possessed Child Sex Abuse Images
items.description: Meghan Markle‘s estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., has been arrested over allegations he possessed child sex abuse images.
