items.author: Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: Meghan Markle‘s estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr., has been arrested over allegations he possessed child sex abuse images.
The 82-year-old was arrested in Florida on Friday in connection with allegations that emerged last month, as the Daily Mail first reported and CBS News confirmed.

“A Florida man was arrested today on a federal criminal complaint alleging he kept child sexual abuse material (CSAM), including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades,” the U.S. Department of Justice said in a statement. “Thomas Wayne Markle, 82, of Lakeland, Florida, is charged with one count of possession of child pornography.”

A DOJ press release said that the FBI searched the storage units, which Markle Sr. had kept since 2008, and “seized approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected CSAM.” The affidavit describes several images, two of which “depict an adult man – whom a witness identified as Markle – with a nude prepubescent girl. The third image depicts a nude prepubescent girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines,” the release continued.
Markle Sr. is expected to appear in court in Tampa, Florida on Friday.

Last month, a report in The Sun claimed that child sex abuse images had allegedly been found in his former home in the Philippines by his son, Thomas Markle Jr. Markle Sr. vehemently denied the allegations to the Daily Mail, calling them “a bunch of lies” and adding: “I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.”

In a statement at the time, the Duchess of Sussex said she was “deeply distressed” at the news. She claimed that in 2018, a letter about her father was sent to the Metropolitan Police and its Royalty and Specialist Protection unit and was “subsequently shared” with her.

“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said. “I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.”

The Metropolitan Police said at the time that they were “undertaking enquiries internally in an effort to confirm” that a letter had been passed from their officers to Meghan. It is understood that the Met has not and is not currently investigating Thomas Markle Sr.

Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018, when he failed to walk her down the aisle at her wedding. She was escorted by King Charles instead. Thomas Markle has never met her and Prince Harry’s two children. Last year, she sent a letter to him while he was in the hospital getting his left lower leg amputated due to a blood clot.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” Meghan concluded.

The FBI also issued a statement last month saying that they were “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law.”
Representatives for Meghan Markle did not immediately respond to Variety’s request for comment on Markle Sr.’s arrest. Variety has also attempted to contact Markle Sr. for comment.

items.title: Charlie Collier and Anjali Sud Exit Fox As New Digital Structure Set at Company
items.description: Fox is restructuring its senior executive ranks in the wake of its Roku deal closing.
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: Fox is restructuring its senior executive ranks in the wake of its Roku deal closing.
The changes will see some high-profile names exit the company, including Roku president of media Charlie Collier, and Tubi president Anjali Sud, who Fox says is leaving for another opportunity.
The changes were announced in a memo to staff from Anthony Wood and Paul Cheesebrough Friday.

Among the other moves will be elevating Mustafa Ozgen to CEO of Roku, with Pete Distad, CEO of Fox direct-to-consumer, adding Tubi and Roku’s Frndly TV to his oversight. Mike Bidgoli will become the new president of Tubi. Lisa Holme, head of content for The Roku Channel, will also report to Distad while also working with the programming team at Tubi.
Chris Handman, senior VP and general counsel at Roku, and Robyn Peterson, executive VP of AdRise, will also exit the company.
You can read their memo below.
Building FOX Digital Platforms

Lachlan shared this morning that FOX’s acquisition of Roku is complete. This is a big day for all of us. To our new Roku colleagues: welcome to FOX. And to everyone across FOX and Roku who made this possible: thank you.

Together we have premium live sports and news, a growing streaming portfolio, and a leading connected TV platform. More importantly, we have talented teams who know how to build, innovate, and deliver for viewers, partners, and advertisers. We have a lot to celebrate—and a lot to build.
With the inclusion of Roku, Tubi Media Group is now FOX Digital Platforms. It brings our digital businesses together around five goals:
1. Grow Platform Share and Engagement: Expand connected TV device sales and platform engagement through affordability, simplicity and creative partnerships.
2. Lead in Free Ad-Supported Streaming: Be a top destination for movies, TV shows, podcasts and creator content.
3. Lead in Premium Subscriptions: Build a compelling destination and bundling ecosystem for premium subscriptions.
4. Win in Performance Advertising: Invest in AdTech, data and go-to-market capabilities to become the premier advertising partner at scale.
5. Grow our Portfolio Globally: Use our combined strengths to expand on and off platform in the U.S. and internationally.
For our first 100 days, we’ll organize around three core teams while we identify the biggest growth opportunities and determine the right long-term structure.

Mustafa Ozgen will lead Roku as CEO. He helped grow Roku into a platform reaching more than 100 million households, and we’re excited to have him lead its next chapter. Roku’s open platform—central to its success with viewers and content partners—will remain open. We intend to protect and build on that strength.

Mustafa will continue to lead Roku’s Device, Product and Technology organization and will expand his scope across the business by taking on AdRise advertising product and engineering, the Roku Channel, Streaming Services Partnerships, Roku Subscriptions, Howdy, Roku Pay, and Roku Brand and Creative.

Pete Distad, CEO of FOX Direct-to-Consumer, has built a strong team and has developed, launched, and grown FOX One into a formidable consumer offering. Effective today, Tubi and Frndly TV will join his portfolio. Bringing free and subscription services together creates opportunities to better serve viewers, connect audiences, and build smarter bundles.

Anjali Sud, CEO of Tubi, is taking on a new role outside of the company but will be helping us through the transition. She and her team have helped take Tubi from a challenger brand to a free streaming force. We want to thank her for her extraordinary contributions and wish her every success in her next endeavor.

Mike Bidgoli is being promoted to President of Tubi, reporting to Pete. An early Tubi investor, Mike has led its product and engineering teams with a focus on innovation and execution. The Tubi leadership team will report to Mike.
Andy Karofsky, co-founder and CEO of Frndly TV, and the Frndly team will also join Pete’s group. Welcome to FOX.

Lisa Holme, Head of Content for The Roku Channel, will report to Pete and work closely with Adam Lewinson and the Tubi content team. Together they will coordinate content investments, strengthen our programming, and help us compete more effectively for free streaming audiences.

Melody Hildebrandt will continue as our CTO, leading IT, cybersecurity, and cloud infrastructure governance, while coordinating AI adoption across FOX. Jeff Dow, EVP of Platform and Media Technology, will retire at the end of the fiscal year, and the Tempe broadcast and distribution facility will move into Melody’s organization.

As Lachlan noted, all advertising sales across the portfolio will continue to report to Jeff Collins, President of Advertising Sales at FOX. Gil Fuchsberg will serve as Chief Strategy Officer, reporting to both of us. He will lead group strategy and continue to oversee major retailer and OEM deals.

Supporting the whole group: Finance, led by Andy Croxson, CFO; Human Resources, led by Pooja Dalal, SVP of HR; Legal, led by Angie Park, EVP, General Counsel of FOX Digital Platforms; and Communications, led by Seana Sullivan, SVP of Corporate Communications. Some members of legal, finance and HR will also become part of the wider corporate functions across FOX, and those teams will hear more directly.
Red Seat Ventures and Credible

Red Seat Ventures, led by CEO and co-founder Chris Balfe, is growing quickly in the creator economy, with two shows currently in YouTube’s top five. Credible, led by CEO Robert Humann, is making financial decisions simpler and more transparent through technology. Both businesses will continue to report to Paul and have our full support.
Thank You to Three Valued Leaders

We’re also saying goodbye to three leaders who have made major contributions to these businesses. Charlie Collier, President of Roku Media, has had a major impact on Roku’s advertising and content businesses. Chris Handman, SVP and General Counsel at Roku, has been instrumental in Roku’s success. And Robyn Peterson, EVP of AdRise, helped FOX unify ad inventory and measurement across the portfolio. We’re grateful to each of them and wish them the very best.

We won’t have every answer on Day 1. We’ll share decisions as they’re made, be clear about what’s still open, and keep moving. Our priorities remain the same: build great products, serve our viewers and partners, and support each other.

We’ll host Town Halls in San Jose and San Francisco on Monday; the FOX Lot and Santa Monica on Tuesday; Austin Wednesday and New York Thursday with international offices to follow. Here we’ll go deeper on the strategy, meet colleagues across the combined business, and answer your questions directly. You can expect invites shortly.
This is the start of an exciting chapter. We have the opportunity to build something special together, and we’re ready to get to work.

items.title: Melania Trump Dismisses Media as “Noise” in Trailer for ‘Melania’ Doc Follow-Up
items.description: Melania Trump isn’t especially impressed by her media coverage in the trailer for Melania, the two-part docuseries from Prime Video about the first lady that dropped on Friday ahead of a Nov. 20 premiere.
items.author: Etan Vlessing
paragraphs: Melania Trump isn’t especially impressed by her media coverage in the trailer for Melania, the two-part docuseries from Prime Video about the first lady that dropped on Friday ahead of a Nov. 20 premiere.

“The media, they want gossip. For me, it’s noise,” Melania Trump says in the teaser for the two-parter follow-up to the Melania documentary released earlier this year, made from bonus footage shot by director Brett Ratner as his cameras followed her in the days after President Donald Trump‘s second inauguration. Of course, Melania Trump got more serious press coverage after she recently brokered a local and six-day ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the occupied city of Oleshky.

But the docuseries will focus on Melania Trump as a wife and mother, especially to son Barron Trump, who she insists in the trailer is her priority. “The honor of serving as first lady comes with an immediate call to action. Moments after the inauguration, first lady Melania Trump sets her mission in motion for the American people,” a synopsis from the producers states about the second episode, entitled Pride & Honor.

Prime Video will stream Melania worldwide after the earlier theatrical release of Melania, the movie, which grossed around $16.6 million at the box office. Amazon’s $75 million deal for Melania included two additional episodes of bonus footage not included in the theatrical documentary that also streamed on Prime Video.

Melania the follow-up docuseries was produced by Amazon MGM Studios, Muse Films, New Element Media and RatPac Entertainment. Melania Trump and Marc Beckman executive produce the docuseries directed by Brett Ratner, who also produces along with Fernando Sulichin.

items.title: ‘Stranger Things’ Spinoff Series ‘Other Worlds’ Set in the 1950s Ordered by Netflix
items.description: Stranger Things is returning to Netflix.
items.author: James Hibberd
paragraphs: Stranger Things is returning to Netflix.
The streamer has officially ordered a live-action prequel series to its massive sci-fi hit (see announcement video below).
Titled Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure, the new series will be set in the 1950s, with production taking place in New Mexico.

Original series creators and showrunners The Duffer Brothers will serve as co-creators, but have otherwise handed over creative duties to longtime Stranger Things writer Kate Trefry, who also penned the Stranger Things: The First Shadow stage play, and Golden Globe-winning director Joe Wright (Atonement), who will helm the first three episodes.

The series will feature an all-new cast and story. Details are being kept under wraps, but the title, 1950s New Mexico setting, and one hint by the Duffers in their statement (“watch the skies”) sure do suggest the show has a UFO/aliens/outer space theme.

“We’ve been dreaming of Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure for many years now, and to see it become a reality is surreal and exhilarating,” said Matt and Ross Duffer in a statement. “We’re so grateful to our incredible team of collaborators: our showrunner Kate Trefry, who has been in the trenches with us since season two and wrote Stranger Things: The First Shadow; and our director, Joe Wright, a brilliant artist whose work we’ve long admired. We can’t wait for you to see what they’re cooking up. It’s Stranger Things, but also thrillingly fresh, with a new setting, new heroes and villains, and new… actually, we’re not allowed to say any more. Now, on to casting. In the meantime — watch the skies, nerds!”
Last year, Duffers signed a deal to officially jump from Netflix to Paramount as part of a four-year deal with the studio which covers film, TV and streaming projects.

“Stranger Things has always belonged to the fans, and their passion made it a worldwide phenomenon,” said Netflix scripted head Jinny Howe. “Today, on Stranger Things Day, we’re honored to partner again with Matt and Ross Duffer and Kate Trefry to give fans a new dimension of this universe to step into. Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure takes us to the 1950s with new heroes and all the heart, mystery, and spectacle of the original series.”

Added Trefry: “The Duffer Brothers gave me my first paying job in Hollywood, and it has been a joy and a fever dream ever since. Now, it is my insane honor and privilege to be bringing this new chapter of Stranger Things to life alongside them and our incredible director Joe Wright. With the support of Netflix and 21Laps, we have had the time of our lives returning to all the horror, wonder and mystery of the flagship, while also telling a wholly new story, one we hope will blow your minds and break your hearts all over again.”
Executive producers include The Duffer Brothers via Upside Down Pictures, Shawn Levy and his 21 Laps company, and Paul Dichter, Shelley Meals, Andrea Sperling and Pavlina Hatoupis.
Stranger Things debuted in 2016 and became Netflix’s biggest show, delivering 1.2 billion views globally during its first four seasons. The show aired its series finale earlier this year.

items.title: Jordan Firstman (Sort Of) Grows Up With Debut Feature Film ‘Club Kid’
items.description: At the tail end of this year’s New York Film Festival, on an early October Saturday night, several A24 staffers were busy shuffling the gorgeous, multigenerational cast of the distributor’s recent Cannes acquisition down the red carpet set up inside Lincoln Ce
items.author: Kevin Dolak
paragraphs: At the tail end of this year’s New York Film Festival, on an early October Saturday night, several A24 staffers were busy shuffling the gorgeous, multigenerational cast of the distributor’s recent Cannes acquisition down the red carpet set up inside Lincoln Center.

Nathan Fielder and Vera Wang chatted briefly as the crowd waiting to enter Alice Tully Hall grew, while Julia Fox and other beautiful downtown and Brooklyn nightlife fixtures fanned out around the auditorium. The night’s star, Jordan Firstman, was one of the last to arrive on the carpet, in the moments just before the hometown premiere of Club Kid, his quantum leap from Instagram comic impersonator-turned-TV writer to auteur filmmaker. With his tight brown curls and perma-grin, Firstman was an absolute natural with the press and the crowd, delivering genuine New Yorker bravado and razor-sharp replies — some perhaps locked and loaded — as he worked a line of news outlets and broadcasters eager for time with the it-boy of the moment and toast of the festival circuit.

Club Kid, Firstman’s debut feature, landed at A24 — perhaps the most fitting home for it — after a bidding war that followed a lengthy standing ovation at its Cannes premiere in the festival’s Un Certain Regard section. The perpetually-hip New York distributor appears to be grooming the film as an awards-season dark horse; it was recently submitted for Golden Globes consideration in the drama categories, rather than the less competitive musical or comedy race. The film plays perfectly in both but the decision speaks for itself.

“Forty-two percent,” the filmmaker joked with The Hollywood Reporter when asked how much of Firstman, the real-world human, is in Peter, the wayward lead he plays in his debut. The film is his entry into an admittedly well-trodden category: comedies about a childless urbanite or misfit who suddenly becomes a single parent. The genre has given us classics like Paper Moon, sentimental favorites like Disney’s The Kid; broad modern takes like the Diane Keaton vehicle Baby Boom, the inevitable Adam Sandler version, Big Daddy, and arthouse spins like Mike Mills’ C’mon C’mon. With Club Kid, the genre now has an unflinchingly queer entry, one that doubles as a coming-of-age drama about an adrift man emerging from the haze of the NYC party scene and the arrested development that such a lifestyle can foster.

“I already liked the genre, and I felt like a queer addition to the canon was actually not superfluous. It was actually meaningful, and there was something to say there because of how queer men grow up,” Firstman told THR just before presenting the film to his home city. “Because we don’t get pressure to get married or have kids. We have this kind of prolonged adolescence. So, everything kind of just started clicking into place at that point.”

Coming from someone with Firstman’s signature deadpan delivery and nice-Jewish-boy-from-Long-Island charm, that 42 percent figure feels like a modest understatement of how much of his own life experience shapes Peter — a club fixture in his 20s who, in the film’s opening moments, has a drug-fueled encounter with a British woman he meets in a club’s darkroom, only to never speak to her again.

After a smash cut to 10 years later, Peter has graduated from club fixture and life of the party to adrift, half-tuned-out party promoter, and a 10-year-old son he never knew he had is dropped into his life after the boy’s mum dies suddenly.
Firstman ultimately betrays his lowball estimate by copping to the many ways in which Peter may be more him than that figure suggests.

“I think [Peter has] my loneliness and the way I navigate the world, and feeling like I’m this person that brings people together. And then I go home and I feel alone. I think that’s a very real thing for me, and I think Peter has that too,” Firstman explained. “He is like a caretaker, but he doesn’t take care of himself. And I think if you saw, like, my car, for instance, you’d say, ‘You need to, like, take care of yourself.'”

Firstman’s longing, that caretaker instinct, and his tangible sense of today’s nightlife scene in lower Manhattan and Brooklyn stem from the winding path that brought him to the cusp of fame. The son of two Newsday journalists, he grew up in the suburbs outside New York with two sisters, both of whom are lesbians (“Three for three!” he exclaims). His teen years, during which he emulated Kurt Cobain for a spell and got into musical theater, eventually gave way to a love of comedy. He pursued it in earnest after a brief stint in the University of Cincinnati’s undergraduate musical theater program, dropping out to move to L.A., where at 23 he landed a job writing for the cult hit Search Party.

His early TV writing and comedy career was punctuated by a move to Berlin, where he partied at Berghain and lived the German version of the Club Kid lifestyle, in which ketamine and cocaine fly onto the backs of toilet seats faster than the relentless, four-on-the-floor beats at the notorious club’s main dance floor. In Berlin, he fell in love and partnered, twice — having gone and retired for relationships that, as he explained to THR’s Scott Feinberg at a recent event at Chapman University, eventually left him brokenhearted. The fatigue of such heavy heartbreak is felt in Peter and runs as an undertone through Club Kid, a film rooted in both loss and redemption.

“I was at a phase in my life where I knew what I wanted to talk about was my own personal change, and I think I also wanted a way to change,” Firstman told THR. “And through art, I find, in writing, that’s the way I can figure out what I’m feeling the most. I was at this impasse and partying too much and doing too many drugs. And so I just started writing the story, and then the kid kind of just became the clearest representation of what is going to make this character grow up really fast.”

If you don’t yet know Firstman from his acting turns in shows including Ms. Marvel, The English Teacher and, currently, I Love LA, you’ve probably crossed paths with him online, whether you realize it or not. His first breakout came when his Instagram impressions series went viral, thanks to one Ariana Grande, who turned his goofy COVID lockdown fun into a sensation on the platform. He’s still trying to shed the followers the pop star sent his way back then, Firstman quipped at the Chapman event. His career has progressed steadily since with various short films entering prestige festivals and a writing gig for the Independent Spirit Awards that led to the Gay Men’s Chorus of Los Angeles delivering his brilliant musical ode to LGBTQ+ representation at the 2020 event. It all pushed him toward becoming a full-fledged filmmaker, and last year he boldly stepped into the director’s chair.

“I knew this guy had something to him that was interesting, and he had a voice, a perspective. He was willing to kind of take his artistry to places that he wanted, and was always willing to go,” Club Kid producer Alex Coco told THR at the NYFF premiere.

Coco was already familiar with Firstman’s work when the filmmaker’s team reached out with the Club Kid script — he’d seen his acting, particularly in Sebastián Silva’s 2023 dark meta-satire Rotting in the Sun, in which Firstman plays an exaggerated version of himself on holiday at a gay nudist beach in Mexico. While speaking of the man of the hour, Coco draws several connections between Firstman and his own longtime collaborator, writer-director Sean Baker; the two have made multiple films together, and in 2025, Baker’s modern take on the Cinderella story, Anora, swept the Oscars. Both writer-directors have a talent for taking a universal concept and dropping it into a specific setting that hinges on providing a lived-in experience, he said.

“Even though he’s a first-time feature filmmaker, he’s been exposed to the business and he’s worked on a lot of sets. So he’s not green, you know. But nonetheless, there were a lot of things that we needed,” Coco said.

For one, attaching the perfect director of photography for the project was going to be crucial, so to capture the film’s kinetic club scenes and the vibe of present-day lower Manhattan and north Brooklyn. They found him in Adam Newport-Berra, whose work on prestige TV series Euphoria, The Studio and The Bear was preceded by stunning music videos for Kanye West, Dirty Projectors and Kendrick Lamar. His work elevates every scene of Club Kid, and after the shoot he shared a telling observation about the first-time filmmaker with Firstman himself.

“You know, my DP, Adam Newport-Berra, is a genius,” Firstman said as the red carpet was about to wrap and his film’s first New York screening was set to begin. “He said to me at the wrap party, ‘I’m very impressed with your patience.’ And I have never thought of myself as a patient person — quite the opposite.”

As he continued, his young co-star, the perfectly cast Reggie Absolom, was ushered away from the carpet; Colleen Camp, the character actor and producer (and Yvette the maid in the 1985 classic Clue) who plays Peter’s downstairs neighbor, gazed around with her signature smirk at the pre-screening hullabaloo; and a scrum of photographers corralled the film’s ensemble of downtown hipsters, club kids and actors for a series of group shots that Firstman soon joined.

“But then I thought, the way I worked with Reggie, and child actors, and non-actors, party kids,” he said as the group gathered for what was perhaps their biggest moment as a cast, and certainly one of Firstman’s biggest nights as he enters the next phase of his career. “I think I did give them space to find it, and give them time to find it. So I think I learned that I may be more patient than I thought.”
Club Kid opens today in New York and Los Angeles and nationwide later this month.

items.title: What to Wear to a Job Interview, According to Hiring Experts
items.description: Looking for a job can be a grueling marathon of resumes, cover letters, and HR acronyms—and that’s before you ever get into the room with your would-be future employer (or their AI proxy, as may be the case). Once you’ve secured an interview, the finish line m
items.author: Jeremy Freed
paragraphs: Looking for a job can be a grueling marathon of resumes, cover letters, and HR acronyms—and that’s before you ever get into the room with your would-be future employer (or their AI proxy, as may be the case). Once you’ve secured an interview, the finish line may feel tantalizingly close, but the race is far from over. Before you get the chance to wow them with your articulate and highly considered insights into your personal strengths, weaknesses, career goals, and salary expectations, however, you’ve got to make a good first impression, and that starts with what you wear. So what, exactly, should one wear to a job interview in 2026? Aside from “probably not pajama pants,” the right answer depends on the job. Despite the loosening of office dress codes across the board in recent years and the rise of remote work in the post-pandemic era, every industry has its own answer to that question, from the traditional suit and tie to “whatever makes you feel the most creative.” For advice on getting the right look for the job, we consulted a bunch of folks who ought to know.

“The interview and the job are very different things,” explains Atlanta-based personal stylist Joshua Davis. “A tech founder might wear a T-shirt to a meeting with a VC, but even if all your research says the office is pretty casual, you should still go more conservative for the interview.” Davis suggests researching the company on LinkedIn to see how employees present themselves and even perusing their individual social media accounts for further insights into their style and presentation. “People expect that a lawyer will arrive in an E-Class and wear a black suit. A trial attorney might, but an attorney who specializes in tech IP will usually dress more like their client,” he adds. “The same is true for most bankers, consultants, and accountants who are client-facing – they have learned to research their client and make sure their image is usually only slightly more conservative than the person they are trying to sell to.”

Whether you’re applying at a disruptive startup or a firm with centuries of history, your clothes are an important means of determining how well you’ll fit into the corporate culture and represent the company to the world. “We get a fair number of calls from HR departments that have found a great candidate, but they don’t feel like they can fully recommend that person because of their wardrobe,” Davis says. “The most common reason is that a candidate is dressing too casually or they don’t dress for their body. To translate, that means too sloppy or too sexy.”

At the most formal end of the spectrum are law firms, and the longer a firm has been around the more traditional its dress code is likely to be. “Law firms in New York are still conservative workplaces and interviewees hoping to land a position as an attorney should still wear a suit with leather shoes,” says Jessica Chin Somers, Esq., a managing director at Kinney Recruiting, an NYC-based legal recruiter. “For men, the uniform of a blue suit with brown shoes or a gray suit with black shoes exists for a reason, but more important than color is the fit.” Aside from that, Chin says, there’s only one big rule to remember: “Lawyers do not show up to interviews wearing sneakers, no matter how “cool” you think the firm is or how expensive the shoes.”

Unless it’s a firm specializing in crypto, the finance field’s dress code remains similarly conservative. “First impressions are important, especially for a job interview in the finance industry, and the candidate needs to convey a sense of seriousness, competence, and trustworthiness,” explains J. Daniel Chi, Ph.D., the chair of the finance department at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. “The dress code has relaxed quite a bit over recent years, however, as a job candidate, unless the firm gives clear instructions on dressing casually, dressing formally is a safer bet.”

The tech world’s reputation for preferring hoodies and sneakers over suits and brogues turns out to be well deserved. “What I see with a lot of different [tech] companies is a more casual approach to being at the office,” says Sam Fricker, the head of recruiting at Philo, a streaming service with offices in the Bay Area. “Because our company is bi-coastal, employees who are based on the East Coast sometimes are sometimes dressed more formally,” adds Maryland-based Philo Recruiter Alexis Fagin. “Departments may differ as well, like finance teams might require a little bit more of a buttoned-up look for meetings, for example.”

At Toast, a tech company serving the restaurant industry, things are similarly relaxed. “We encourage employees to wear whatever makes them feel most comfortable and confident to do their jobs, and the same goes for those interviewing,” says Toast's chief people officer Mike Gutner. “That said, our recruiters will suggest something in the realm of business casual. The bulk of our interviews are virtual at this point, so I’m sure I’ve talked to more than a couple of applicants in formal tops who are also wearing sweatpants and slippers below the camera. I won’t blame them; I do the same from time to time.”

At the other end of the spectrum are creative agencies, whose commitment to out-of-the-box thinking extends to personal presentation. “[Your] experience and portfolio far outweigh [your] presentation,” says Matt Johnson, the founder and chief strategy officer of LA-based creative agency Haymaker. “At the end of the day, we’re investing in the person and their abilities, not their appearance, so I’d say dress to represent your best and most true self. The more authentic you can be, the better.”

“NGOs value humility and authentic alignment with the cause, and your outfit should communicate authenticity, cultural sensitivity, and reliability,” says Sam DeMase, a career expert at ZipRecruiter in NYC. In other words, the safest play at your NGO interview is business casual, i.e. a blazer and button-up shirt with trousers or dark jeans, or a sweater, a collared shirt, and dress pants or chinos. Depending on the role and the organization, you should also steer clear of anything too flashy or obviously expensive-looking, the better to reinforce your focus on the mission.

Jobs in media—a range that covers everything from journalism to social media management to advertising planning—are extremely diverse, as are the dress codes at media organizations, but most media companies fall on the more casual end of the spectrum. “You want to wear something you feel genuinely comfortable in so you can focus on the conversation and be yourself,” advises Rich Kleiman, the CEO and co-founder of Boardroom, a sports, business, and entertainment network. “But comfort shouldn’t come at the expense of fit. Whatever you wear, make sure it fits well and feels intentional.” Despite this latitude, Kleiman cautions against confusing casual with careless, and advises investing in alterations to nail the fit. “Sometimes, investing a little in your presentation is worth it, especially if it helps you walk into the room feeling confident.”

Dress codes can vary widely between academic institutions and the departments within them, so the best course of action is to act like an academic and do your research, says Jocelyn Coalter, senior director of career and leadership development at St. John’s University in NYC. Beyond that, she advises candidates to err on the side of formality when in doubt. “It’s a lot easier to remove a blazer that you may not need than to put one on that you didn't bring,” she says. “I also recommend professional yet comfortable shoes for academic interviews, as there’s often a component that involves meeting different people on different parts of campus, or getting a tour.”

items.title: Is 'The Only Living Pickpocket in New York' Immediately the Best Watch Movie Ever?
items.description: There are plenty of great movie watches: James Bond’s OG Rolex Submariner, Hans Gruber’s Cartier Tank, or even Hamilton’s made-for-Interstellar Murph. But there are very few great watch movies that dig into the myriad layers of meaning that compel real-world c
items.author: Alex Garofalo
paragraphs: There are plenty of great movie watches: James Bond’s OG Rolex Submariner, Hans Gruber’s Cartier Tank, or even Hamilton’s made-for-Interstellar Murph. But there are very few great watch movies that dig into the myriad layers of meaning that compel real-world collectors. In that way, The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, which rolled out to theaters nationwide on October 30, is a timepiece-lover’s dream movie.

In the film, John Turturro gives an Oscar-buzzy performance as Harry Lehman, an aging New York hustler who has scraped by for decades without evolving with the world around him. He doesn’t have a phone, dances to vinyl records, pays at diners with cash, and rents Barbara Stanwych movies (“tapes,” he calls them) from the public library for his wife.

Naturally, Harry is drawn toward watches, both for his personal use as items to steal. Along the way of The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, there’s a cornucopia of watches and Easter eggs for collectors to appreciate: Director Noah Segan meticulously selected a watch to fit every character’s personality. It matters deeply to Segan whether a character is wearing a vintage Rolex Explorer 1016 or a modern Hublot; and the movie even gets deep into the inner workings of timepieces. A pawn shop owner, played by Steve Buscemi, deems a Patek Philippe “fugazi” and shows Harry the lack of jewels in the movement. Watches, as totems of an analog world imbued with personal and cultural history, aren’t just a detail, but a vital motif.

It’s clear that The Only Living Pickpocket in New York could only come from a writer-director embedded in the hobby themselves. And, in the future, Segan, along with the dealer Adam Golden who sourced the pieces for the film, plans to bring these essential watches to auction for charity. GQ talked with Segan about how he chose the film’s array of timepieces, the state of his own collection, and why he would make a terrible watch salesman.
GQ: After I watched your film, I found myself thinking that I’m not sure I’ve ever seen a better watch movie. I’m curious if anything comes to mind for you?

Noah Segan: That’s a great question. I wouldn’t presume to jump on anybody else’s intent in terms of watches. I think obviously there are a lot of watches in movies that have become iconic. The first kind-of-nice watch I ever got myself was a TAG Heuer Monaco because I was such a huge fan of Steve McQueen and Le Mans. There are obviously a lot of watches that are worn. I don’t know how often they get woven into a story, but in our case, our story is not just about time, but time changing, time running out, and that in combination with very physical things, tactile things. We’ve got a pickpocket, he’s tactile. He touches you. The idea of a totem and an object representing those things started feeling very important to me, and watches do that for me.
You have said that you would be selling watches if you weren’t a filmmaker. What is your personal connection to the hobby?

I would probably be a very bad watch salesman simply because I would want to keep all my favorites. So I think maybe collector is where I should stay, but I’ve always been a very, for lack of a better term, sort of analog guy. I still shoot film with a camera. I spin records. I live in an old house. The classic car in the movie is my old car.

I was lucky enough to grow up in an environment that appreciates the marriage of engineering and art and history. To me, that Venn diagram is a solid circle when it comes to wristwatches. These are objects that can be beautiful, they can be sophisticated, they can represent personal historic endeavors and also the macrocosm of historic feats.

The idea of what a watch means when you think of it in terms of The Dirty Dozen [a WWII-era field watch for soldiers commissioned by Britain from 12 iconic Swiss watchmakers] being there for the military or [Paul] Newman’s Rolex Daytona and its engraving on the back that says, “Drive Carefully Me.” All of a sudden you’re talking about something bigger than us, a celebrity, probably one of the biggest celebrities of all time who did something absolutely crazy, which was not being a movie star, but being a race car driver. And yet his wife still said, “Drive Carefully Me.” So there’s the personal, there’s the promotional, there’s the macro and the micro, and they all are fascinating to me.

In your film, there’s a very personal connection that the character of Harry has with his Rolex Explorer 1016, considered one of the great vintage watches among collectors. What led you to choose that as Harry’s watch?
Well, a close friend of mine is Adam Golden, who has a company called Menta, is actually a watch dealer who deals in very specific, unique vintage watches of great provenance.

In considering the watch for Harry, I really wanted something that could bridge the gap between a very useful tool and something of value. And that watch represents a lot for people in that respect. There was a time when Harry was a younger man, and that would have been a really good, valuable, useful tool for him to have. It’s an understated watch. It’s easy to read. It can last through whatever you throw at it on the streets in New York.

And yet today it’s something of incredible value financially and also incredible value to him because it is his watch. It has been a tool for him. And I couldn’t think of a better example than that Rolex 1016 to represent that combination of factors. And so Adam found us that watch and loaned it to us to wear.
Did that level of thought go into other characters’ watches?

We built the other watches in the movie around [the 1016]. Giancarlo Esposito plays Detective Warren, [Harry’s] foil and mirror image. He both helps Harry and is keeping an eye on him. He wears a Tudor Tuxedo, which shares a lot of, as we say in the watch game, DNA with something like a Rolex Explorer. In fact, it was made by the same company, and yet it’s just a little different.

Steve [Buscemi’s character] wears a thin, gold Rolex Cellini on a gold bracelet that, again, is something that would have been definitely a luxury item back in the day and is an even bigger luxury item today, but still represents something of an older time. Meanwhile, the watch Dylan [a young mobster played by Will Price] has, the Hublot, is considered today to be a very flashy, modern watch. It has a modern chronograph movement. It’s made with very present-day materials. And in fact, he’s not wearing it. It’s stuffed into his gym bag, and he says, “I only wear that when I go out to flex,” because it doesn’t represent a daily tool to him.

All of these things were designed and lent to us by Adam Golden to talk about who these characters were and to reflect something about the characters in a world where the physical items and the physical representation matter.
Looking back on the movie and looking ahead to talking to you, I was thinking, I am sure there are watches I missed.

I can walk you through all of it! We also had some interesting newer watches. We worked with an incredible team at Oris, a brand that’s been around forever, but remains really relevant. Victoria Morolis, who plays Eve, wears Oris. She’s a sort of younger hero in the movie and a punk computer hacker. She’s wearing the Oris Roberto Clemente, which is a watch that is very old-school in a lot of ways, but made with very 2026 technology.
Was Moira (a surprise cameo from Jamie Lee Curtis) wearing a watch?
She was wearing her very own gold Cartier tank. She said, “I am going to do this.” And we all said, “Of course you are, because you are the boss.”

The character of Dylan makes a very explicit comparison in the movie between Harry’s Rolex Explorer 1016 and his Hublot. How do you see the spiritual and aesthetic differences between a vintage watch and a very hyper-modern watch?

Well, I have a personal feeling about that because I have a lot of knowledge of this stuff. This is my hobby, right? So to me, when I look at a 1016, I see history, I see Tenzing Norgay summiting Everest, whether that’s the actual truth or not. I am applying that to my perspective. And I’m also thinking about elegance in terms of what I like to wear. I’m thinking about how it sits on my wrist. I’m thinking about the simplicity in the design. And I can also see how someone else would appreciate the exact same thing about the Hublot: the work that went into skeletonizing that dial, the complication of a chronograph movement, and the mixture of metals and materials to make it. So I see both sides of it. I think because it is something so personal, it goes on your body. I think what ends up mattering is how you interpret that and whether you believe that one is of more value to you than the other stylistically.

In one scene, Harry pickpockets a Patek Philippe that turns out to be fake. We don’t spend tons of time with the character who owned that piece, but enough to understand he is a wealthy businessman “with platinum cards,” as Harry says. What does it mean for that character to have a fake watch?

Well, I think it sort of speaks to Harry’s world quite a bit. Harry comes from a world where if someone looked like they had money, they probably had money, right? And if they had nice shoes, they probably had a nice watch. And if they had a nice watch, they probably had money in their pocket. And you could do that math, and maybe it wouldn’t always be right, but these were educated guesses. And now we live in a world where a gold watch is not necessarily a gold watch. A Patek Philippe, presumably one of the most recognizable objects of value, is not necessarily an object of value. And to put that on Harry, to put that on a guy whose job it is to steal watches is, among other things, really a statement about him. And I guess in a wider sense that the world is not always what we think it is.

I think for the businessman at the beginning, he obviously has lots of nice suits and lots of nice shoes and he lives in a tall building on the Upper East Side and he’s got a camel hair coat and works in a fancy office. There are all these reasons to think that this guy is fancy and makes money. He doesn’t carry cash. You know what I mean? He wears Aldens, as we know, a fancy shoe, but he wears a fake watch. I think it speaks to where the world is right now, which is that it isn’t about honesty or dishonesty. There are shades of gray, and we exist in a bit of a gray world.
Does that character know it’s fake, or does he just not care?

Great question. I think he knows that it’s fake. I think there is a world now where people—and I don’t think it’s just for watches, I think it’s for a lot of things—where people believe that getting most of the way toward something is enough. So somebody says to this guy, “Hey, you made partner. Isn’t it time to buy a $20,000 watch?” And then the guy next to him goes, “You can buy a $400 watch that looks just as good as a $20,000 watch.” And this guy goes, “Great.” And that’s it—that’s as far as they go.
What’s in your personal collection right now? How many watches do you have?

“Too many” is the answer to how many watches I have. But most of what is in my collection that’s important to me are watches that are not [necessarily] of significant financial value. I have a watch that belonged to each of my grandfathers that I had restored. And I did not have fancy grandfathers. These are watches that cost more to restore than they were worth, but are of incredible value to me. And a couple of my friends who I’ve worked with many, many times, my friends and mentors in movies have given me watches, and those are important to me because of that, because of where they came from and what they mean and the consideration that went into them.

Watches like Benrus, which is, again, not a Rolex-level name, but Benjamin Lazarus founded that company in New York, and that means something to me as a guy from New York. So there’s something significant there. There are a lot of newer watches that I’m fascinated with, whether it’s companies like Oris or smaller brands like Haven or Bernhardt, which I appreciate.
And do you have any grail watches?

I mean, listen, I don’t own an Omega Speedmaster. I’d love to own a Speedmaster. I love what they’re doing with modern watches now, actually. I’d love to own a gold Rolex. I think there’s something really cool about a gold Rolex.

I don’t know what I would do if I had a Rolex 6542, a Bakelite Bezel GMT [from the ’50s], because those are the coolest-looking watches. But if you sneeze at it wrong, does the bezel crack? I can’t worry about that.
Just to have it sit in the box.
Yeah, and I don’t believe in that! I want to wear my watches.

items.title: Can Hermès Make a Watch as Iconic as the Birkin?
items.description: I arrived in Miami expecting to see the latest watches from Hermès. But as representatives of the historic Parisian luxury house led a group of us through the Rubell Museum, there was no sign of the timepieces. After passing through rooms showcasing Basquiat,
items.author: Troy Barmore
paragraphs: I arrived in Miami expecting to see the latest watches from Hermès. But as representatives of the historic Parisian luxury house led a group of us through the Rubell Museum, there was no sign of the timepieces. After passing through rooms showcasing Basquiat, Keith Haring, and Anselm Kiefer on the walls, we came into a room that looked more like an art classroom than a luxury-watch launch. Instead of being shown new editions of the H08, which Hermès has been slowly sculpting into an icon, I was handed a paintbrush.

Present in the room was Cuban American artist José Parlá, along with tables covered in paint, brushes, and scraps of paper torn from street advertisements. On the walls hung canvases Parlá had already begun and which would serve as the starting point for our own creations.

Delighted by the surprise arts-and-crafts, I happily donned my apron. Later that day, Hermès would unveil two new versions of its distinctive H08, the sporty model it debuted in 2021 and has been carefully building up. The latest pair introduced into the catalog both feature ceramic bezels, one in blue and another in white. They share a shimmering fiberglass case coated in aluminum that gives the watch the look of a tumultuous, gray sea.

When it was first released, the H08 garnered immediate praise from the collector community and broader market. Such rave reviews out of the gate are nearly unheard of for a completely new collection. The H08 is defined by its vaguely rectangular case with soft, sloping edges; the straight lines of the watch are contrasted by a round concentric dial. Paired with colorful, complementary rubber straps or the occasional bracelet, the H08 is a collection clearly intended for an active lifestyle without veering into the realm of the tool watch.

Hermès is a Goliath in the luxury world with a massive multibillion-dollar business across leather goods, handbags, and silk scarves. But amid all of its exceptional offerings, watches were never a primary focus; they were something one might add in while buying a Birkin. The H08 is an opportunity for Hermès, a maker of icons, to establish one in a category where it’s still establishing its reputation.

Inside the museum workroom, I set about the task of customizing my canvas. I chose one reminiscent of a rich, red sunset. I sorted through the sheets of torn paper that resembled craggy mountaintops, glued them down, and began to paint. I felt like I was transported back to my childhood art classes.

I realized that this was not simply an activity to fill the time but was actually a sophisticated metaphor for how Hermès views the creative process itself, especially as it applies to the development of pieces like the new H08s. The work is collaborative, iterative, and builds on the concept of what came before to create something new. The base is familiar enough to collectors at this point, but new colors and approaches round out a growing army of H08s so everyone can choose their flavor.

“We understood that our way to make this line grow would be to animate it and go deeper into materials,” Laurent Dordet, CEO of La Montre Hermès, the house’s Swiss watchmaking subsidiary. “It’s part of the playground of H08.” While the H08 already comes in a host of colors and accents, from bright teals and oranges to blues, greens, and yellows, the new bright blue and white variants bring a fresh, almost resortwear vibe to the collection.

H08 has given Hermès a foundation to build its limitless creativity on top of. The fundamental design hasn’t changed at all, but Hermès has continuously renewed it through new colors and materials. Hermès has played with satin brushing, DLC or colored PVD-coated titanium, and carbon composites coated with graphene powder. There are also skeletonized versions of the watch as well as ones with a chronograph (or a stopwatch function). As the H08 was always intended to be the brand’s far-reaching sport offering, opening up Hermès to new clients and lifestyle applications, the collection quickly became the vehicle for such innovation.

But even if Hermès isn’t primarily a watch brand, the house’s world-class artisans never passed off second-rate design. And the playfulness that pervades the house is essential to the watches too. “That’s what our clients expect from us. Hermès is obsessed with making a beautiful object that will bring comfort and pleasure to its owner,” Dordet says. “We are not obsessed with having something fun or playful every time. It's a balance between style, elegance, sobriety, subtlety, colors.”

Later that evening, at Hermès’s Miami Design District boutique, I encountered another expression of the company’s creative imagination: a smaller version of Jean-Simon Roch’s kinetic sculpture Mysterious Mechanics, which had appeared at the industry’s flagship trade show Watches and Wonders earlier in the year. Its elaborate system of ropes, pulleys, and moving frames was a theatrical interpretation of mechanical timekeeping, part of the broader cabinet of curiosities that informs Hermès’s creative universe.

As I stood before Mysterious Mechanics, I realized it would be all too easy for Hermès to tap into this same type of whimsy to create an H08 that was loud or multicolored in some obvious embodiment of abstract art. But that just isn’t how Hermès works. The brand understands that a signature watch is forged over generations. Look at a model like the Rolex Submariner—one of its most valuable assets is that the base design is largely unchanged over 70 years. There’s a beautiful juxtaposition between the very serious, capital-L luxury done at the highest levels of capability and concept, and the fun-loving, whimsical approach to how Hermès creates. Perhaps that’s why the brand has endured for nearly 200 years. And also why the H08 may just be its next iconic creation.

items.title: Democrats Sweep Republicans in Nearly Every Race That Matters
items.description: Democrats stormed through key battleground races across the US in their battle to capture the House and Senate on Tuesday night, marking a decisive repudiation of President Donald Trump’s second term.
items.author: Hugo Lowell
paragraphs: Democrats stormed through key battleground races across the US in their battle to capture the House and Senate on Tuesday night, marking a decisive repudiation of President Donald Trump’s second term.
The scale of victory for Democrats—in some races, the party flipped seats that Trump won by double digits just two years ago—marked a historic night that exceeded the party’s highest expectations.

Democrats pulled off arguably the greatest upset in Texas, where James Talarico defeated scandal-plagued Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton and where Gina Hinojosa defeated Greg Abbott for the governorship, despite the millions and millions of dollars spent by billionaire Elon Musk on behalf of the Republicans. No Democrat had won a statewide seat election since 1994.

Democrats also seized other critical Senate races on election night, including in Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa, and North Carolina, while retaining control of seats in Georgia and New Hampshire, according to the Associated Press.
At the White House, stunned Trump officials tell WIRED that high gas prices and the increased cost of living brought on by the Iran war were the principal reasons for widespread GOP losses.

“If any good comes out of tonight for the Republican party, it’s that no Republican president will ever listen to imbeciles like Mark Levin and Marc Thiessen again,” one source close to the White House said of two commentators who had urged Trump to prolong the Iran war.

Exit polling showing massive defections from other parts of the 2024 Trump coalition show there was more to the losses than that, with Latino voters turning to Democrats as the administration pursued brutal and unpopular immigration policies.

Some officials, who were granted anonymity to speak candidly, privately laid the blame at the feet of the president for taking the nation into the Middle East conflict, which he wrongly assumed would be over in a matter of weeks and has continued with no clear end in sight.

“President Trump was not on the ballot, and it’s proven that Trump voters show up when he is on the ballot,” a White House official said in a statement, even as Trump had implored his base on the trail to pretend that he was on the ballot.
“Also, candidate quality matters, and President Trump did a better job promoting many of the candidates on the ballot than the candidates did themselves,” the official added.

Many of the losing candidates were hand-picked by Trump, who forced out incumbents like Texas senator John Cornyn and blessed candidates like Darline Graham (sister of late senator Lindsey Graham), who ran a dismal campaign in South Carolina.
Still, other Trump officials have cast about for other scapegoats, blaming a failed redistricting effort as well as candidate quality.

Republicans embarked on a strategy earlier this year to redraw numerous congressional maps as part of a gambit that White House aides thought could yield 10 to 15 House seat pickups if Trump voters turned out. The downside, political scientists pointed out, was that it made seats harder to defend, as while there were more Republican districts, each was less Republican.
On election night, the strategy failed to yield results. Democrats won at least three House seats in Florida that Republicans had redrawn, as well as the seat in North Carolina.

The closest thing to a bright spot for Republicans came in the Senate race in Florida, which became abruptly competitive in the final days of the midterm campaign. In the end, Ashley Moody barely fended off the progressive candidate, Democrat Angie Nixon.

As the likely control of the House and Senate became clear, top House Democrats separately ended the night relishing the prospect of mounting an aggressive oversight campaign against the Trump administration.
Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, issued a two-word statement: “Lawyer up.”

items.title: ‘Sometimes You’re an Alien Who Looks Like My Mom’
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Elna Baker
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
It started when Simone was 4 years old. She would take two fingers, run them down the center of her mother’s face, from forehead to chin, and say “Zup.”

At first her mother, Rachel, thought it was just one of those strange, cute kid things — like when a child invents a secret language or suddenly decides they’re a cat. Then one day she asked Simone what she was doing. Simone answered matter-of-factly, “I’m unzipping your mask.” When Rachel pointed out that she wasn’t wearing a mask, Simone’s response dumbfounded her: “Sometimes you’re not my mom,” her daughter said. “Sometimes you’re an alien who looks like my mom.”

As far as I know, Rachel is not an alien. She’s a single mom in her early 40s who teaches fiction and memoir at Bard Early College and writes short stories and novels, often about troubled women and including weird sex scenes. She and her two daughters live in a house upstate. Camille, 13, wears 30 beaded bracelets on each arm and a multicolored raccoon tail; collecting bones is her favorite hobby. Simone is now 10 and has short Ramona Quimby brown hair. She can more readily pass as “normal,” at least until you get her talking. Within minutes of meeting her, I heard about her ex-husband, Dexter, a helium balloon she met at a party and fell in love with—until, one day, he flew away, leaving Simone heartbroken.

I have known Rachel for two years, and I love her for her morbid curiosity, which makes her a great conversationalist and a slightly unconventional mother. She finds most forms of traditional momming tedious: having to fake an interest in Paw Patrol, praising bad art. Instead, Rachel and her daughters have their own repertoire of bits; she’ll happily chase the girls around the house in a Korean face mask and put ice down their shirts, acting as a character they know lovingly as Panther.

But Alien Mom is different. It appears out of nowhere, and, over the past six years, it has become a regular, somewhat bewildering feature of their lives. Every few months, without warning, Simone will look at Rachel and accuse her of being an alien wearing a skin suit.

As a fiction writer, Rachel values imagination, and she encourages it in her children. She’s a big proponent of allowing your mind to go to scary or strange places. “I’m entertained by Alien Mom in a very genuine, spiritual, philosophical, and existential way,” she told me. But Rachel has often wondered What, exactly, is provoking it? Simone can be an anxious kid, what Rachel calls a “big feeler.” When she accuses Rachel of being an alien, she sometimes appears genuinely afraid. Plus, Rachel admitted, it can get a little maddening, almost like a real test of her humanity. No matter how many times Rachel tells Simone that she is her real mother, Simone responds, “That’s exactly what an alien would say.”

When Rachel first told me about Alien Mom a year ago, it struck me for a particular reason. In 2008, I nannied for a 5-year-old named Roman who would occasionally back away from his mother, Carmen, and look at her sideways, as though her very presence alarmed him. In those moments, he wasn’t sure, he said, if she was his real mom or an impostor. The accusations were regular enough that they eventually developed a shorthand. Whenever Roman got scared or suspicious, he would ask, “Real mom or impostor mom?” Carmen would always say “real mom,” which was enough to put him at ease.

The similarities between the two stories gnawed at me: How many other kids had, at some point, felt this way? So, four months ago, I posted on social media and asked if, growing up, anyone else had thought their parents were impostors of some kind. Several people wrote to say “yes.” One friend said his mother went to get a haircut and didn’t come back the same. Another friend told me that after seeing Vincent D’Onofrio rip his skin suit off in Men in Black, he had a dream that his parents were aliens with bits of metal and insect shells showing through the gaps where their skin suits didn’t quite fit. He couldn’t make himself go near his mother the next morning; she was clearly an alien. Another believed his parents were both aliens but that they were only in their alien form when he wasn’t looking. He spent the next 14 months whipping his head around suddenly to catch them and sneaking into their room when they weren’t expecting it. He never found them in alien form but did nearly give them multiple heart attacks.

What could make the most familiar person in the world suddenly seem like a stranger? Over the years, Rachel looked for a pattern. But there wasn’t one. It could happen at dinner, on the way to piano lessons, when Rachel was in a good mood or a bad one, when she was wearing makeup or bare-faced. Maybe it was just a phase that had gone on for an unusually long time. Or maybe Simone was clocking something real.

Once I started looking for alien parents, they were everywhere. Just last month, there was Other Mommy, a movie about a 7-year-old whose mother — Jessica Chastain — is increasingly distracted by work and whose parents’ marriage is coming apart. An entity identical to her mother begins visiting her when her real mother is away, asking to be let into her heart. In the new Hulu show Phony, a teenager wakes up from a car accident to discover his mother has been replaced by an impostor.

This isn’t a new genre, and in most examples, the child is the first to notice. In Goodnight Mommy, twin boys become convinced that their mother, who comes home from cosmetic surgery with her face bandaged, is a creature wearing her skin. Invasion of the Body Snatchers begins with a little boy running down the road screaming that his mother isn’t his mother. And in Philip K. Dick’s short story The Father-Thing, a boy finds the husk of his father’s empty skin in the garage and realizes that whatever is sitting at the dinner table is not his dad. Dick later said the story was inspired by seeing his own father after his parents divorced.

When I described Simone and the others to Trudy Goodman, a child and family therapist and founder of the meditation center InsightLA, she told me she wasn’t at all surprised by how many examples I’d come across. Of course, some children simply are letting their imaginations run wild. But kids are also drawn to creative explanations as a means of making sense of disruptions or events in their lives—which, she added, is a perfectly normal way for them to explain an uncanny feeling. “They know things, but they don’t know what they know,” she said.

Dan Siegel, a psychiatrist and author of Mindsight, sees “variations of this all the time.” Our brains are storing information about the world long before we have the language to describe it, he said. “The mind is this fantastic symbolic machine. And it creates ways of trying to make sense of what it’s going through.” Those experiences shape our expectations of how people behave, how they respond to us, what feels familiar and what doesn’t—what Siegel calls mental models. And sometimes, when something doesn’t fit, children turn it into a story. “When children play, the themes of their games and the stories they tell are often arising from those mental models,” Siegel said. “In this way, we try to ‘make sense’ of life by making the implicit explicit.” Which means the truth of what a child is feeling is often hidden in the games they play, in what they draw, in the books they ask for over and over again.

Siegel noted that there is an extremely rare psychiatric condition called Capgras syndrome in which someone becomes convinced that a familiar person has been replaced by an identical-looking impostor. A 2024 review in General Hospital Psychiatry found only 38 published cases involving children and adolescents over the previous century; in 84 percent of those cases, the person the child believed had been replaced was a parent. One theory for what causes Capgras is a disconnect between the brain’s facial-recognition system and its emotional-response centers. There is no reason to believe Simone or any of my friends had suffered from Capgras, but the distinction seemed to underscore their experiences: Recognizing someone and feeling that they are there are two different things. In other words, children can sense when a parent is present physically but mentally absent or when they’re being inauthentic. “If adults could see and know what children see and know,” Goodman said, “they might be a little heartbroken.”

I asked those friends who’d shared stories about their own impostor parents what else had been happening in their lives at the time. The friend who had whiplash from trying to catch his parents in alien form told me his mother would fall into long depressive spells and that his parents, both Mormon, would simply avoid talking about it. He initially suspected his mother of being an alien and later added his dad by a logic that’s hard to argue with: They were together all the time, so how could he not know?

A famous experiment gets at what he was seeing: In 1975, the developmental psychologist Ed Tronick wanted to know whether babies were actually reading their mothers’ faces or just responding to being held and fed. He had mothers play normally with their infants and then, on cue, go blank — no expression, no response, for two minutes. The babies tried everything to get them back: smiling, pointing, shrieking. Then they gave up, turned away, and went slack. Stretch that experience out sporadically over years, to a kid old enough to need a theory, and my friend’s alien parents start to make sense.

The friend who dreamed his parents were aliens after seeing Men in Black said it happened just as he began to notice problems in his parents’ marriage. His dad would leave the house late at night without saying where he was going. His mom acted like everything was fine. In reality, his father was having one of several affairs. Looking back, he thinks his impostor theory was, in some ways, right. “You kind of are somebody who I don’t know, and there is somebody hiding behind you that I can only see little glimpses of,” he said.

Roman, the boy I used to nanny, is 22 now and just out of college. A few months ago, he came over and sat on a trundle bed while I asked what he remembered about Impostor Mom. He worked the tassels of a throw blanket between his fingers while he thought. The accusations, he said, were usually triggered by his mother doing something out of character — staring blankly or switching to a chipper voice when she answered the phone. Curious if anything else had been happening at the time, we both started reconstructing the timeline, and we realized we’d forgotten something. When Roman was 5, his aunt — his mother’s only sister — died by suicide. His mother had changed overnight, becoming distracted and harder to reach. “I felt like it was her trying to convince me that she was the same person she’d always been without being convinced herself,” he said.

Roman’s mother, Carmen, has remained a close friend. When I told her what Roman and I had pieced together, she immediately started to cry. “I was in a blackout with them. I was just functioning and doing everything I could, but I don’t even remember. I genuinely don’t remember who I was.” She searched for the word. “It was like I was a robot. Or something — not a robot, but …”

What she does remember is dropping Roman off at school while getting calls about her sister’s suicide attempts, kissing him good-bye as though everything were normal, then running to the hospital. And she remembers that after her sister died, she waited weeks to tell the kids, meeting with therapists to figure out how. “There were weeks that I was existing as if she was still alive,” she said. “Preparing to tell them.” All Roman was eventually told was that his aunt had a “brain sickness” and that she’d died of it. Carmen wondered whether Impostor Mom had started in those weeks, and what Roman had been reacting to — the grief or the effort of hiding it.

One night, Rachel stumbled on a theory for what was causing Alien Mom. It was the end of the day, and Rachel was a little stoned — she felt relaxed, unhooked from all her daily stressors. As she tucked her daughter into bed, Simone grabbed her face, looked into her eyes, and said, “Oh, you’re my real mom.”

Rachel was startled. It was as though Simone were seeing some core part of her spirit that existed outside all the stresses of young mothering — a version of herself she wished she could give Simone all the time. Rachel has always known that Simone would prefer her to be more into momming — to answer her questions in the voice people use when they talk to children, to let her buy a squishy toy without bringing up capitalism and climate change. Given the nature of her work, Rachel knew she could often get lost in her own world, become temperamental or distant.

She thought back to what had been happening in her life when Alien Mom began. It was the height of COVID, and she was mothering two young children, feeling like she was losing herself and in a marriage that would eventually fall apart. Every week brought some new thing to be afraid of. Rachel was wearing an actual mask; she had moved out of her bedroom and into the nursery, where she dragged in a mattress and cleared everything out. “I had become the baby of my own family,” she said. She would lie there at midday, “unsure if I was awake or asleep for minutes or hours, fully dissociated.” At night she’d sneak up to the roof and read the complete short stories of Alice Munro. “Daytime I was the baby, taking midday naps, and nighttime I was the teenager, trying to find myself in her short stories.”
A terrible thought began to haunt her: When Simone accused her of being an alien, was she actually just seeing her worst self?

Once, fed up, Rachel tried agreeing with Simone. “Yes,” she said, when Simone accused her of wearing a skin suit. “I am an alien.” Simone seemed slightly alarmed; she asked where her real mom was. “In a dog crate in the barn,” Rachel snapped.

When I finally interviewed Simone, on the couch in their living room, she’d just come in from dressing the chickens in bonnets and tutus; she insisted on showing me every outfit she’d made for them before we could start. l asked about the dog-crate comment, what Simone had made of it. Had it scared her, her mother saying that? “No,” she said — she knew it was her real mom the second she said it. “My real mom’s dark,” she told me, “and my fake mom’s not.”

The rest of her system worked the same way. If, at the playground, Simone got on the monkey bars and her mom climbed them with her, “then I know she’s an alien,” she said. “My mom doesn’t climb.” Another test: Alien Mom let Simone get away with things. Real mom knew her bedtime and didn’t let her do things that were dangerous. Alien Mom used a fake happy voice and would let her have ice cream for breakfast.

Rachel appeared to have it almost backward. Simone wasn’t looking for a mom who baked cookies and kept her voice even. She was looking for the mom she knew. The funny, wry mom who could always be counted on to say the weird thing. “It’s actually very relieving,” Rachel told me. “I think I had this script that real mom was when I was trying really hard to participate in a way that was maybe challenging. To force myself into presence versus being in my own odd mind. And I think what Simone is saying is making me think that she really is clued into the authentic me.”

Siegel says part of what these kids may be tracking is something called synchrony: the tiny, patterned back-and-forth that happens when two people genuinely interact. If Simone says something, she expects a Rachel-shaped response: the comedic timing, the face, the familiar pushback. The overall effect isn’t Mom heard me. It’s Mom got me. “When you don’t show up with presence, and you’re not attuning to me,” Siegel said, “my way of translating that is to say, ‘You’re not familiar to me.’”

When I described this to Goodman, she brought up another finding by Ed Tronick, the psychologist who created the Still Face experiment. He filmed ordinary mothers and babies interacting and tracked how much of the time they were really attuned to each other and how much of the time they were each doing their own thing. Even in healthy pairs, Goodman told me, they were in sync only about 30 percent of the time. “I think this is really essential for parents to know,” she said. “A parent can, and does, fail to be there moment to moment.” What matters isn’t being present all the time, she added. “It’s coming back.”

items.title: Russell Brand Was Found Guilty of Rape and Sexual Assault
items.description: Russell Brand, the former comedian and current right-wing spiritual podcaster, was found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday. Brand, who was on trial in the U.K., was found not guilty of two other counts of rape and one c
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: Russell Brand, the former comedian and current right-wing spiritual podcaster, was found guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday. Brand, who was on trial in the U.K., was found not guilty of two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault. Judge Joel Bennathan of Southwark Crown Court in London told Brand that he will receive a “significant custodial term.” Brand has been remanded in custody until Monday’s sentencing.

The jury deliberated for eight and a half hours before reaching a unanimous decision. Brand was being tried for incidents that occurred from 1999 to 2009. He was found guilty of raping a woman in 2009; groping a female MTV employee at a London bar in 2004; groping a woman at her workplace in 2004; and sexually assaulting a different woman in 2009 after forcing her to give him a massage.

Brand has denied all allegations of rape and sexual assault. In 2023, several women came forward with allegations of sexual abuse (and, in one instance, rape) in Russell Brand: In Plain Sight, an investigative documentary from Channel 4, the Sunday Times, and the Times of London. None of those women were part of this trial, but prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said the documentary moved the women in the trial to come forward. Karmy-Jones told the court that the women had “realized they are not alone and have bravely come before you to tell the truth.”

The only person to testify in Brand’s defense was his wife, Laura Brand. She called him an “amazing husband” who is “caring and kind” and “a wonderful father to our children.” Judge Bennathan shut down the line of questioning when Laura was explicitly asked about the allegations against her husband.

In a statement, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London’s Metropolitan Police Service called the verdict “a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them.”

“Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women,” Furphy said. “As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement. I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be.”

items.title: I Spent My Childhood Summers In Japan — Here's How I Rediscovered Tokyo
items.description: All products featured on Refinery29 are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links.
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa
paragraphs: All products featured on Refinery29 are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links.

Growing up, I spent my summers in Japan with my grandmother (aka my obaachan) in a quiet suburb outside of Tokyo. And even though those memories are like prized treasures to me now, as a teenager, I begrudgingly endured the 13-hour flight from Washington, D.C. to Tokyo with basically negative enthusiasm about being away from friends, the nearby mall, and American TV for two months. (Nobody should feel bad for me, and I've since apologized to my parents for being a brat.)

I'm 33 now, and no matter how many times I've visited Japan, I always manage to find something new. But during my most recent trip this fall, I got to experience Tokyo like I never have before: Through the eyes of a true local.

As part of AC Hotels' 20-Minute Edit, I got to see my favorite city via the ultimate fashion-person itinerary, curated by Japanese fashion designer and creative director of CLESSTE Ryo Takashima. (Writer's note: Marriott covered my travel and accommodations for this trip, but opinions are all my own.)  After touring the brand's boutique and atelier — and leaving with the coolest leather jacket — I stopped for a matcha nearby at Zen Punk, less than a 10-minute walk from the AC Hotel in Ginza. Then we walked over to Dover Street Market, one of the best places to shop Japanese designers like Rei Kawakubo and Junya Watanabe. (I left with a Comme des Garçons PLAY mesh tee that I wore later that night to dinner layered over a Skims bralette, pictured above.)
