items.title: Is This What Hope Feels Like?
items.description: The air began to feel electric around 9 p.m. on Election Night. Polling locations in most states had closed, and early results were making the electoral map look quite blue already. My group chats started lighting up, cautiously weighing how much excitement we
items.author: Andrea González-Ramírez
paragraphs: The air began to feel electric around 9 p.m. on Election Night. Polling locations in most states had closed, and early results were making the electoral map look quite blue already. My group chats started lighting up, cautiously weighing how much excitement we should feel. But it was too early to read into the vote count — plenty of time for everything to still go to hell yet again.

By 10:15 p.m., I was full-on libbing out. “I feel insane,” we texted each other back and forth, alongside clips of NBC News projections and memes of the Blue Man Group. Georgia had elected Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, making her the first Black woman to become governor in U.S. history. Democrats were projected to retake the House in what was looking like their biggest victory in years. And Democrat Annie Andrews had pulled a stunning upset, flipping the Senate seat in ruby-red South Carolina. The blue wave was actually here; now it was just waiting to see how big it would be. “Is this what hope feels like????” a friend wrote.

By 11 p.m., Democrats had gained enough seats to retake the Senate; Texas had gone blue for the first time this century, electing a Democratic governor and senator; and even Mississippi seemed like it could be in play. Wave? More like an actual tsunami — in coastal cities, in the prairie lands, in the Midwest, in the Deep South.

In some ways, no one should be shocked: The polls were consistently projecting a Democratic sweep. But the polls have also been horrifically wrong before, and given President Donald Trump’s election-interference attempts, skepticism felt like the safer bet. We’ve become so accustomed to feeling disappointment and heartbreak that it’s like our nervous systems have forgotten how to process optimism and joy. But despite the $474 million broligarch Elon Musk poured into GOP candidates this cycle — more than any other donor in history — he had embarrassingly nothing to show in return. And the Republicans’ blatant attempt at rigging the electoral map via last-minute gerrymandering failed as their decades-long control of certain House districts, Senate seats, and governor mansions evaporated before our eyes.

Every demographic in the country shifted toward Democrats, even in states that Trump carried in the 2024 presidential election, by double digits. Trump’s gains with young men, Latinos, and Black voters were wiped away — the “realignment” of his 2024 coalition was a mirage. Even white working-class workers, who have been a reliable Republican voting bloc for the past decade, had swung about 15 percentage points left as of last night’s estimates. It’s the kind of generational shift I doubted I’d ever see.

A few months ago, I wrote about how some of the people who were most politically active in the Trump 1.0 days now seemed to be numbing out, paralyzed by the constant stream of horrors and opting to disengage. It concerned me that there was a sense that the fast slide into fascism was inevitable — that there was no way to stop the Trump administration’s madness, just slightly mitigate its effects. This, of course, serves the authoritarian playbook: Moving fast and breaking things overwhelms people to the point they can’t even keep track of what new nightmare the administration is cooking up. Someone who feels terrified, helpless, and like nothing will change as a result is unlikely to rise up against a regime. Would people even show up to the polls if they felt like it’d be pointless? Thankfully, voters chose another path. Numbing out is easy, but they did the hard thing instead, stepping up to the plate when the time called for it.

Trump repeatedly told Americans to vote like he was on the ballot, so that’s exactly what they did. For 21 months, communities have seen up close MAGA’s brand fascism and everything that comes with it: the unnecessary wars, the tariffs and cuts worsening our financial future, the campaign of terror against immigrants, the corrupt self-dealing, the carte blanche being given to billionaires, the gleeful cruelty. On Election Day, they decisively rebuked all of it.

Democrats’ wins nationwide open a world of possibilities. By ending two years of one-party rule in Washington, they’ll now be able to keep Trump in check. They have a long wish list of things to accomplish: undoing some of his most harmful policies, aggressively investigating wrongdoing in his administration, finding creative ways to address the crises that voters have tasked them with tackling. Even Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito’s decision not to retire may come back to haunt him, as the Democratic majority in the Senate will now have the power to reject Trump’s judicial nominees. Downballot wins in governor and state legislature races will have an even more immediate impact on voters’ daily lives, from addressing the affordability crisis to restoring reproductive rights. These state-level victories will also create yet another firewall against Trump’s federal overreach, as they can take him to court to challenge his policies.

But the Democratic Party, which so often snatches defeat away from the jaws of victory, would do well to remember that voters are a fickle thing. A seismic change like this is not set in stone — for the next two years, they need to rise up to the occasion and deliver on the promises they made. This is not the time to fall back into the old way of doing politics; nationwide, the desire for change is bigger and deeper than that. Anything less than being brave is unacceptable. After all, voters delivered a clear message: This imperfect, heartbreaking, remarkable country is worth fighting for. Time to get to work.

items.title: Are Your Parents Hiding Their Money From You?
items.description: Most Americans do not have rich parents. But if you suspect your family may be more well-off than you’ve been led to believe, it’s worth asking questions. “A lot of boomers have more money than they need and certainly more than enough to help their kid with th
items.author: Charlotte Cowles
paragraphs: Most Americans do not have rich parents. But if you suspect your family may be more well-off than you’ve been led to believe, it’s worth asking questions. “A lot of boomers have more money than they need and certainly more than enough to help their kid with their wedding or student loans or a down payment for a home,” says AJ Ayers, a certified financial planner and co-founder of BKFi, a money-management firm based in Brooklyn. “The least you can do is ask. But I find that a lot of people are afraid to.”

Perhaps you’ve heard about the “Great Wealth Transfer”: Boomers — the richest generation in American history — are expected to pass an estimated $84 trillion to $124 trillion to their heirs by the mid-2040s, resulting in the largest transition of family money to date. Many of us assume we won’t be on the receiving end. But what if you are? One of the many pieces of advice Ayers gives in her upcoming book, Creative Money: New Financial Rules for Artists, Innovators, and Misfits, is how to address the question of “secret family money” — especially if your parents are squeamish about discussing their finances. (She also tackles the opposite scenario — what to do if you find out your parents will be financially reliant on you.)

Ayers believes we should all talk to our families more often about our money — and the sooner the better. “Sometimes parents think they’re protecting their adult children by not telling them about their finances, but that just makes it harder for their children to make an informed plan for their future,” she says. Below, she shares her tips for bringing it up, asking for help, and dealing with miserly relatives.
So do you have secret family money? And if so, how did you learn about it?

I grew up in an upper-middle-class family. But my parents had a very contentious divorce that lasted for most of my childhood, so money became this explosive topic. Someone wasn’t getting the money they deserved, someone was withholding money — it was a big source of conflict. I knew we had money and it bought us beautiful things like nice houses, but it also threatened happiness. It was very confusing.

After college, I went into book publishing, which doesn’t pay very well. And it was obvious among my friends who was getting support from their parents and who was not. I did not get regular support. That said, I remember my dad once coming to visit and seeing the state of my apartment and giving me $400. Another time, I had a bad breakup and needed $1,000 for a security deposit on a new apartment. My dad helped me then, too. So there was a safety net, absolutely, but there wasn’t a steady drip. Frankly, I resented that. My thinking was, Hey, I graduated from college. I’m not spoiled. I’m working two jobs because I have student loans and rent to pay. If my parents could spare $300 a month, it would dramatically change my life right now and it would make no difference to them. If it was difficult for them to spare that money, then that’s completely different. But for them and so many boomers, they could have helped me a lot and they didn’t.
How did you finally approach the topic of money with them — and express that you would appreciate their help?

I switched careers and started making more money, so that changed things. I also got much more comfortable talking about money with them and in general. But I find many parents are more likely to help out for big milestones. When I was getting married, I went to my dad and said, “Hey, it would be amazing if you could contribute to our wedding.” And he did. But I don’t think you should have to hit a life milestone for that to happen. I think if a parent has extra money and a good relationship with their adult children and they’re happy with where those adult children are in life, they should transfer wealth to them now instead of waiting until after they’re dead.

What I see a lot with older generations is they think, Well, I worked really hard for this money and I might need it, so I don’t want to give it away. Which might be true. But a much better approach is for them to go to a financial planner who can tell them, definitively, how much money they have to spare. A lot of boomers don’t even realize how much money they have tied up in real estate and 401(k)s, and they’d get a lot more enjoyment out of those assets if they transferred at least some of them to their loved ones before they pass away. The stock market has done extremely well for the past decade and a half, and that has benefited older Americans more than anyone. Meanwhile, millennials have struggled with student loans, low wage growth, and high home prices, among other things. Plenty of boomers have more money than they need and certainly more than enough to help their kid with their wedding or student loans or a down payment for a home. They may just not realize it or know how to talk about it.
I think many people are nervous to ask their parents for money. They’re worried their parents will say “no” or the money will come with strings attached. How do you recommend going about it?

I’d start by asking about your parents’ financial plans. But be patient when you’re waiting for an answer. They may not have a plan — and they may be embarrassed that they don’t. They may not have as much money as they want you to think they do. It might take six months for them to respond. It might take two years or five years. But start now.

At the very least, you want to avoid the situation where your parent gets sick or passes away and nobody knows what’s going on, and there’s no will or the estate is complicated for no reason. At that point, not only have you lost your parent but you’re fighting with your sister over who gets to keep the lake house. Who wants to deal with a ton of legal paperwork and conflict when you’re mourning a parent and trying to manage your regular life stuff, like a job and kids? What a terrible legacy for a parent to leave behind. That’s what you want to avoid.

I have a list of questions every adult should ask their parents as soon as possible. You don’t need to sit your parents down and do it all at once, but don’t drag it out, either. I like to give my clients three months to complete the list. The key is to do it before there’s a crisis. Like, where are all your financial documents? Do you have an up-to-date will? Where’s the deed for your home? What’s your plan for long-term care? Are there investment accounts? Who manages them? How do I contact that person? Get that manager’s email address and send them a note that says, “Hey, I’m the child of so-and-so. Here’s my contact if you ever need me.” And you should have this conversation even if your parents don’t have a lot of money.

If your parents do have money, though, and you’re hoping they’ll be open to sharing some of it, try explaining some of your own financial challenges to them. A lot of people in their 30s and 40s are not having kids because they can’t afford them. And that’s really sad, especially if they have parents who could help. I think it’s perfectly reasonable to have a conversation with your parents about that, especially if they want grandkids. You can’t always assume that your parents know what you need; sometimes you have to tell them. You could say, “Hey, in the event that I wanted to buy a house next year with my partner where we could raise our family, would you be willing to help us with a down payment?” They might say “no,” or they might say “maybe.” And then, six months later, you could send them the Zillow link and a really mature email that says, “Hey, Mom and Dad, my partner and I found our dream house. It’s about $78,000 out of budget. Here’s the spreadsheet where we broke down all the costs. If you have anything to spare, it would make a huge difference to us.” That’s not going to work for everyone, but a lot of people don’t even try because they’re afraid.
I also think people are scared, with good reason, of their parents saying, “We didn’t raise you to ask for a handout.”

Or the opposite. Sometimes their parents are secretive because there is no family money and they’re embarrassed. In certain cultures, it’s expected that you, as the child, will be taking care of your parents when they age. But if you aren’t expecting that, it can be quite shocking — and really disruptive to your financial plans. So you need to know what their plans are, whether they involve you or not.

Another reason parents may not want to talk to their kids about money is that they don’t trust their kids’ judgment. Or maybe they do trust their kids but not their kids’ spouses. Or they trust one kid but not another. There’s a fine line between helping your kid and protecting them. How do you deal with that?

That is really tricky. I do believe that when people need help and you’re in a position to give it, you should. So if, for example, you have twins and twin A is a happily married, well-employed person with two beautiful children but twin B is kind of a fuckup, do you divert money from twin B to twin A? I think the answer is no. But it’s complicated. Of course, if someone has an addiction and you don’t want to enable it, that’s a different story.

Regardless, I think people need to reevaluate what their definition of “spoiled” is and maybe put that aside. How do you raise your kid to be a good citizen who isn’t entitled? Sometimes parents go overboard. I really resented everyone in my family when I was in my 20s and coming home at 4 a.m. from working my barback job in Gowanus. I was like, It doesn’t have to be this hard. At the end of the day, if your kid is going to benefit from your support and you can give it, the least you can do is talk about it with them.
Email your money conundrums to mytwocents@nymag.com (and read our submission terms here.)

items.title: Allison Williams Is "Not F*cking Around" When It Comes To Skin Care
items.description: Allison Williams Is “Not F*cking Around” When It Comes To Skin Care
items.author: Rachel Lapidos
paragraphs: Allison Williams Is “Not F*cking Around” When It Comes To Skin Care
The Girls star opens up about eczema, her beloved fanny pack, and millennial tendencies.

“It’s so nice to meet you. Come sit in my beautiful apartment.” That’s how Allison Williams greets me as I walk into a lavish hotel suite overlooking Central Park. She flashes a big smile as I join her on the couch.

At first glance, Williams looks like the Marnie Girls fans know and (sometimes) love: long brown hair, a cream sweater, and an air of quiet luxury. But she's considerably cheekier than her on-screen alter ego. I'm there to talk with her about eczema, an inflammatory skin condition she's finally found relief from thanks to a treatment she's partnered with Sanofi and Regeneron to raise awareness about. Despite the personal nature of the subject, the 38-year-old actor is refreshingly candid — and frequently hilarious — throughout our half-hour conversation, which also covers her beauty routine, self-care habits, and rather unusual fanny pack contents.

The treatment, Dupixent, involves giving yourself an injection every two weeks. And though Williams has never been a fan of needles (“to put it extremely mildly,” she explains), she's developed a routine that she now actually looks forward to. The secret? “I always watch an episode of whatever the unscripted show is that I’m watching, so the minute the injection’s over, I’m just in a world that is filled with joy and nothing very serious, and it immediately takes my mind off it,” she says. “It’s become a kind of meditative moment in the day.”

Her current unscripted obsession is The Real Housewives. She's been working her way through each franchise and is currently on Atlanta. “I have ‘Tardy for the Party’ stuck in my head pretty permanently,” she says.
Ahead, Williams opens up about her emotional support beauty products, her fanny pack essentials, and why she’s at peace with being a millennial.
How would you describe your beauty philosophy these days?

I’m out of the in-it toddlerhood, so I’m devoting a little bit more time to my beauty routine. I’ve always experienced it as a feedback loop of self-esteem — you’re investing time, and you’re being deliberate, and the self-care of it all at the beginning of the day sets the tone for the rest of it.

Mine is as quick and low-maintenance as possible while also being hopefully effective. Bang for my buck, I guess, is my philosophy. I don’t have a morning shed or anything like that. I’m just trying to keep everything healthy and producing collagen.
What is something you understand about your skin now that maybe you wish you’d known 10 years ago?

Well, I always knew I had eczema. I just lived with it. The thing I know now is that I didn’t have to tolerate what I was experiencing to the extent that I was. And that has genuinely changed my experience of being alive.

Everyone’s flavor of eczema is different, but mine always showed up on my calves. I have four pairs of shorts and 1,000 pairs of summer pants for that exact reason. After a while, I adjusted to that being a part of my life. Then, when it started showing up in other places on my scalp, suddenly it triggered me to actually address it.

That’s when I talked to my dermatologist about it, and she recommended that I try Dupixent. And for my friends and family, people who've known me forever and know how I feel about injections, when they hear that I'm doing that to myself on purpose every two weeks, they're like, "Oh, you must really like this medication." I'm like, "Yes, I'm also partnering with Sanofi and Regeneron to talk about it. That's how much I like it." And so that honestly is knowing the kind of skin you have feels like knowing your blood type. It's something that I feel like we should all learn very early in life.
“If I see a split end, I cut it. My hair is like a bonsai, basically.”
What is something in your routine that would surprise most people who know you?
Oh, my gosh, what a good question. See, here's the thing — people who know me, they really know me. I'm pretty predictable and consistent. I'm so on brand that I don't do anything against my type.
Fair. What is something you wear to feel instantly more put together?

I feel like a belt, weirdly. I can be in a kind of schlumpy everything, but then if I’m belted for some reason, I’m ready. I also am always wearing a fanny pack, so sometimes I feel belted anyway. I wear one around the house all day, every day. That’s also something no one would be surprised by, because everyone in my life knows that I do this. That's not saying that it makes me feel chic — it just makes me feel like I'm ready and I can take on whatever's coming.
What's in your fanny pack?

Hardwired headphones, hand sanitizer, Listerine strips, AirPods. Hair scissors, because I cut split ends — another thing that no one in my life will be surprised by, because they all know that I do it. If I see a split end, I cut it. My hair is like a bonsai, basically. I just cut split ends as I see them. It's like a meditation. And I recently posted it on my Instagram. The number of people who do this is shocking.
What? I've never heard of this before in my life.

If you get in a certain light, you just see a split end, and then you have scissors in your fanny pack, and you cut it. That whole scenario. I found that you can fly with them if the blades are short enough because airplane light is among the best light. So I'll bring a tiny lint roller so I don't make a huge mess.
I'm unwell. So the scissors are in there, my license and a credit card, and what am I forgetting? Hand lotion, cuticle oil, and a lip gloss, usually. And I think that's it.
“If you have taken nothing else away from this interview, it's just, in general, I'm not f*cking around.”
What is the last beauty product that got you genuinely excited?

I recently went down a rabbit hole of looking online to see if there are things that can help eye cream penetrate better and get rid of bags under my eyes. This is how I ended up with basically a vibrator for my eyes.

It's a product from a company called Foreo, and it is exactly what I'm describing. There's zero way that anyone who sees my toiletry kit display is not going to be like, "And there's her vibrator with her other facial products for some reason." Every time I use it, I'm not adult enough to be mature about it. But it is this thing that vibrates and undulates, and it really feels good. It smooths the bags under my eyes, and I do it every morning.
Is there a beauty trend that you've tried that did not work for you?

Most of what Gen Z has offered us, I can't achieve. And that's OK. The middle part is kind of as far as I can go. I can't really do the clean girl thing. I haven't really figured out lip contour. I just end up looking like I had ice cream and didn't use a napkin.
You just have to own being a millennial.
I feel like I'm pretty solidly locked to that generation in a way that is OK. I'm at peace with it.
What is the most chaotic thing you've gotten into lately, beauty-related or otherwise?
Most of what I do, as I'm saying it, is deeply chaotic. I feel I’m very calm and predictable and type A. I don't love chaos, so I avoid it. I’m trying to think if there’s anything.

I'm not a big wellness girlie. I prefer to be unwell. Well, I would say that my houseplant situation is getting chaotic. I have over 50 houseplants. I don't have a natural green thumb. I used an app called Planta to help teach me how to take care of them. Now I'm addicted. I have several arriving today that I don't have places for, but the emails got me.
Has playing a character ever made you want to change something about your beauty routine?

Well, I will say one of the weirdest beauty routine-ish experiences I had was on Fellow Travelers. I aged up and down for the show, and that was very odd because it was an emotional roller coaster. It was also very interesting to just see my face in the past and also in the future-ish. I mean, we can't really know for sure. I literally wear two sunscreens every day, so the sun spots in my makeup [on that show] made me double down on the sunblock.
You're not f*cking around.
I'm not f*cking around. If you have taken nothing else away from this interview, it's just, in general, I'm not f*cking around.
Is there a beauty look from one of your projects that you still think about?

Yes, because people also talk to me about it a lot. My character's makeup on Girls when she got married is something I still think about a lot. It was heavy makeup, and I am proud to say that I applied most of it with the inspo I got from Instagram and watching really intense makeup tutorials. It was sort of the beginning of that era, and I realized that if you combined all the tutorials into one face, it would look insane.
Well, I mean, it's not a brag when you see it.
What is something that instantly improves your mood no matter what kind of day you're having?

This is so trite, but I got this advice from so many different sources, and then I finally applied it, and it's true. If you're feeling bad and you do something for a different person, it changes your mood entirely.

Yesterday I was grumpy because of hormones, and then my friend whose husband is recovering from surgery was talking to me about how stressful it is, and I sent her food — and literally the act of sending her food took away my grumpiness, either because it distracted me and I'm Dory and I forgot to be grumpy, or because it does something to you energetically to do something for someone else. It takes you out of your own, I don't know, myopia and makes you think about somebody else.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

items.title: Hulu's New Romantasy Series Is Perfect For Fans Of 'Bridgerton'
items.description: Dreaming of a swoony period romance that blends the palatial trappings of Bridgerton with high-fantasy magic and shape-shifting? Hulu’s The Remarried Empress may just become your next obsession.
items.author: Grace Wehniainen
paragraphs: Dreaming of a swoony period romance that blends the palatial trappings of Bridgerton with high-fantasy magic and shape-shifting? Hulu’s The Remarried Empress may just become your next obsession.

Of course, for many fans worldwide, it already is. The new Korean series (streaming now) is based on a viral webtoon of the same name and follows Empress Navier as she finds love with a prince in the wake of her husband’s infidelity.

Bustle got an early peek at The Remarried Empress during a recent press trip to Seoul, where leads Shin Mina and Lee Seyoung — who play Navier and her husband’s mistress, Rashta — opened up about taking on the highly anticipated project at an explosive moment for romantasy.

For Lee, the genre’s popularity comes down to “curiosity, vicarious satisfaction, and the desire to experience something,” she says. “I think it really stimulates the imagination, and there’s a pleasure in satisfying that as you watch.”
As Shin puts it, “I think it may be because the original fantasy romance [stories] being loved right now are about self-determined women, which many female fans around the world relate to and want.”

Indeed, while the very premise of The Remarried Empress sets Navier and Rashta at odds, their stories both center on themes of female agency and self-preservation. Over the course of the series, viewers will watch their layers unfurl.

“When I read all the comments on the webtoon, I saw one that said, ‘Rashta craves Sovieshu’s love, and Sovieshu is her true love, but maybe she actually loved and admired Navier, and that’s why she tried to get close to her,’” Lee says. “Since I’m the one portraying her, I thought that could be possible, because Rashta is a girl who came in wanting to survive, wanting to be acknowledged and adored and to stay alive. So [my performance leaves] room for that.”

It wasn’t hard for Lee to play her character’s wonder at her new environs. “When we filmed the scenes of her wandering around and taking in the imperial palace, I felt the same wonder and joy as Rashta,” she says. “And even when we filmed on sets, the design, the interiors, the furniture, and the props were so beautiful and impressive that I filmed in a state of admiration, happy and amazed.”
After The Remarried Empress’ four-episode premiere on Nov. 4, two new episodes will drop on Wednesdays through Nov. 25.

I literally shed tears of joy when the Georgia gubernatorial election was called for Keisha Lance Bottoms. A woman elected governor of Georgia for the first time AND the first Black woman elected governor in the entire nation? Yes, there were tears. And somewhere between wiping my eyes and listening to her victory speech, I realized I also needed a fuchsia suit.

For the victorious occasion, Bottoms stood out in an electrifying pink ensemble that practically radiated through the screen. Dedrick Thomas of Hideoki Bespoke designed the look, according to Vogue, and while we might not have her exact outfit hanging in our closets, that doesn't mean we can't join in on the pink power fun.

After all, a night like that gives you a little more hope for the moments still ahead. The glass ceilings waiting to be shattered. The doors we'll walk through and hold open for someone else. The big ideas we'll finally give ourselves permission to pursue. And while an outfit can't do the work for us, I'm very much here for manifestation dressing.

Whether you're preparing to nail your next big presentation, interviewing for your dream role, or launching your own business, a pink blazer brings a bit of that baddie feminine energy along for the ride. Go all in with matching trousers, or let the jacket do the talking with the jeans and white tee already in your rotation. Either way, there's something satisfying about putting on a color that has absolutely no intention of disappearing into the background.
Ahead, shop the pink blazers and suits I’m eyeing for my next ambitious endeavor.
