items.title: Сколько на самом деле стоит сериал про Гарри Поттера: что показала отчетность — Reminder
items.description: К концу 2025 года расходы компании, которая производит первый сезон сериала «Гарри Поттер», достигли примерно в $197 млн, хотя к концу 2025 года съемки были завершены лишь наполовину. Эти цифры приводит The Times со ссылкой на финансовые отчеты британской комп
items.author: Анна Аскарян
paragraphs: К концу 2025 года расходы компании, которая производит первый сезон сериала «Гарри Поттер», достигли примерно в $197 млн, хотя к концу 2025 года съемки были завершены лишь наполовину. Эти цифры приводит The Times со ссылкой на финансовые отчеты британской компании Plum Jam Productions, которая снимает сериал. Проект может стать одним из самых дорогих в истории HBO.

Согласно опубликованным данным, к концу 2025 года общие расходы Plum Jam Productions за два года составили 147,4 млн фунтов ($197,1 млн). Чуть больше 18 млн из них пришлось на 2024 год, когда проект еще был в разработке, и почти 129 млн — на 2025-й.

По данным издания, выручка Plum Jam Productions за 2025 год составила 130,6 млн фунтов ($175 млн), тогда как годом ранее она достигала 18,4 млн фунтов. Однако финансовая отчетность компании не дает полной картины: через Plum Jam проходили и другие проекты — под прежним названием Roundabout Productions компания делала для HBO сериал «Невероятные».

Съемки первого сезона стартовали в 2025 году на студии Warner Bros. Studios Leavesden и завершились в мае 2026-го. Итоговый бюджет пока не раскрывается и может увеличиться с учетом затрат на постпродакшен. Визуальными эффектами занимается британская студия Framestore.

По оценке Deadline, средняя стоимость эпизода первого сезона может составить около $25 млн. Это сопоставимо с бюджетами крупнейших телевизионных проектов HBO: для сравнения, на производство одного эпизода финального сезона «Игры престолов», по распространенным оценкам, тратили около $15 млн.

Источник, знакомый с производством «Гарри Поттера», отмечает, что значительная часть расходов приходится на начальный этап, поскольку масштабные декорации должны использоваться во всех семи сезонах. Поэтому в дальнейшем стоимость отдельных эпизодов может снизиться. Дополнительным фактором, способным сократить расходы, могут стать британские налоговые льготы для кинопроизводства.

Новый «Гарри Поттер» должен представить более подробную экранизацию книжного цикла Дж. К. Роулинг: создатели планируют посвятить каждому из семи романов отдельный сезон. Пока HBO официально подтвердил производство первых двух сезонов.

Для сравнения, восемь оригинальных фильмов франшизы собрали в мировом прокате более $7,7 млрд. По опубликованным данным, бюджеты картин составляли от $100 млн у «Гарри Поттера и Тайной комнаты» до $250 млн у «Гарри Поттера и Принца-полукровки».

Начиная с «Узника Азкабана» продюсеры фильмов старались сосредоточить повествование на точке зрения Гарри и исключали многие сцены, в которых он не участвовал. Сериал, судя по всему, этого правила придерживаться не будет. Например, исполнитель роли Драко Малфоя Локс Пратт рассказал, что зрители увидят Драко дома, а также сцены из личной жизни преподавателей Хогвартса.

Самый известный пример того, что потеряли фильмы, — полтергейст Пивз. В книгах он появляется постоянно, а в кино его нет. В первом фильме сцены с Пивзом даже снимали — его играл британский комик Рик Мэйолл, — но в итоге их вырезали . В сериале Пивза сыграет Питер Серафинович, и официальный сайт франшизы уже подтвердил его участие в первом сезоне.

В фильмах символом Когтеврана был ворон, а цвета факультета — синий с серебром. HBO вернула книжного орла и сочетание синего с бронзовым. Заодно сменились и гербы факультетов: вместо пышных геральдических щитов из фильмов — эмблемы с животными внутри круглых медальонов, украшенных растительными орнаментами.

Новой будет и музыка, которую для сериала пишет Ханс Циммер вместе с композиторами своей компании Bleeding Fingers Music. Авторы обещают создать оригинальное музыкальное сопровождение, сохранив уважение к наследию фильмов, для которых музыку писали Джон Уильямс, Патрик Дойл, Николас Хупер и Александр Деспла.

При этом связь с фильмами никто не рвет. Сериал снимают в том же Ливсдене. Среди исполнительных продюсеров — Дэвид Хейман, продюсер всех фильмов о Гарри Поттере и «Фантастических тварях», и сама Роулинг, которая лично собеседовала Гардинер и режиссера Марка Майлода.

Главные роли в сериале исполнят Доминик Маклафлин (Гарри Поттер), Аластер Стаут (Рон Уизли) и Арабелла Стэнтон (Гермиона Грейнджер). В актерский состав также вошли Джон Литгоу в роли Альбуса Дамблдора, Паапа Эссьеду в роли Северуса Снейпа, Джанет Мактир в роли Минервы Макгонагалл и Ник Фрост в роли Рубеуса Хагрида. Премьера сериала на HBO запланирована на декабрь 2026 года.
Карьерный стратег рассказывает, как побороть синдром самозванца и увидеть, что вы умеете больше, чем думаете, с помощью простой таблицы

items.title: Три привычки счастливых людей: проверьте, какие из них есть у вас — Reminder
items.description: Что нужно для счастья? Большинство из нас уверены: больше денег и успеха. Но, как показал Всемирный доклад о счастье (World Happiness Report) 2025 года, подготовленный Центром изучения благополучия Оксфордского университета по данным из 147 стран, дело совсем
items.author: Анна Аскарян
paragraphs: Что нужно для счастья? Большинство из нас уверены: больше денег и успеха. Но, как показал Всемирный доклад о счастье (World Happiness Report) 2025 года, подготовленный Центром изучения благополучия Оксфордского университета по данным из 147 стран, дело совсем в другом. Сильнее всего с удовлетворенностью жизнью связаны не доход и не карьера, а отношения с людьми. И проверить себя можно с помощью трех простых вопросов, пишет Fast Company.
На основе выводов исследователей можно сформулировать три вопроса, которые стоит задать себе, если хочется стать счастливее.

Обычно обед воспринимается как небольшой перерыв между делами. Можно быстро перекусить за рабочим столом, посмотреть видео или пролистать новости в телефоне. Но с точки зрения исследователей счастья, совместная еда может быть чем-то гораздо большим, чем просто способом утолить голод.

Авторы одной из глав Всемирного доклада о счастье проанализировали данные более 150 тысяч человек из 142 стран и территорий. Участников спрашивали, сколько раз за последнюю неделю они обедали или ужинали вместе с людьми, которых знают: родственниками, друзьями, коллегами или знакомыми. Завтраки в исследовании не учитывались.
Оказалось, что люди, которые чаще едят в компании, в среднем выше оценивают свою жизнь, чаще испытывают положительные эмоции и реже — отрицательные.
Причем эта связь сохранялась независимо от возраста, пола, страны проживания и уровня доходов.

Разница оказалась заметной даже между теми, кто за неделю ни разу не ел в компании, и теми, кто разделил с другими хотя бы одну трапезу. Первые оценивали удовлетворенность жизнью в среднем на 4,9 балла по десятибалльной шкале, вторые — на 5,2 балла. Самые высокие оценки — около 6,1 балла — оказались у людей, которые обедали или ужинали с другими 13 раз за неделю.

Исследователи пока не могут однозначно сказать, что именно происходит: общение во время еды делает людей счастливее или счастливые люди чаще находят компанию для обеда. Вероятно, работают оба механизма. Но сама связь оказалась настолько устойчивой, что авторы предлагают уделять совместным трапезам больше внимания.

Например, если вы привыкли обедать за компьютером, можно хотя бы иногда приглашать коллегу поесть вместе. А если обычно ужинаете в одиночестве — договориться с друзьями о регулярных встречах за столом. Это не гарантирует, что вы станете счастливее, но создаст дополнительные возможности для общения и укрепления отношений. Совместная еда — один из самых простых способов сделать социальные связи частью повседневной жизни.

Представьте, что вы потеряли кошелек с деньгами и документами. Как думаете, велика ли вероятность, что нашедший его человек попытается вернуть пропажу? Оказывается, ответ на этот вопрос довольно тесно связан с тем, насколько счастливым человек себя ощущает. В докладе о счастье исследователи сравнили ожидания людей с результатами реальных экспериментов, в которых ученые оставляли кошельки в общественных местах и проверяли, как часто их возвращают.
Выяснилась любопытная закономерность: люди склонны недооценивать доброту незнакомцев. В международном эксперименте потерянные кошельки возвращали примерно в 1,8 раза чаще, чем ожидали опрошенные.

Особенно заметна эта тенденция в странах Северной Европы, где люди одновременно высоко оценивают свою жизнь и чаще рассчитывают на добросовестность окружающих. Авторы доклада обнаружили, что ожидание доброжелательного поведения от других людей тесно связано с удовлетворенностью жизнью. В их статистическом анализе эта связь оказалась почти вдвое сильнее, чем связь счастья с частотой собственных добрых поступков.

Почему так происходит? Возможно, дело в том, что доверие влияет на то, как мы воспринимаем окружающий мир. Если человек убежден, что большинство незнакомцев настроены враждебно, повседневные взаимодействия могут становиться дополнительным источником напряжения. Если же он допускает, что окружающие способны на честные и добрые поступки, ему проще вступать в общение и устанавливать новые связи.

При этом речь вовсе не о слепой доверчивости. Скорее, стоит пересмотреть автоматическую установку, согласно которой от незнакомых людей лучше не ждать ничего хорошего. Обращать внимание на случаи взаимопомощи, замечать доброжелательное поведение и не воспринимать каждый контакт с новым человеком как потенциальную угрозу.

Есть и экспериментальные подтверждения того, что изменение представлений об окружающих может влиять на благополучие. В другой главе доклада описаны исследования, в которых студенты недооценивали отзывчивость своих сверстников. Когда им показывали, что окружающие в действительности более доброжелательны, чем они предполагали, это помогало им воспринимать других людей с большей открытостью и устанавливать новые социальные связи.

Третий вопрос касается поступков, которые приносят пользу не только нам самим, но и окружающим. Исследователи называют такое поведение просоциальным. В докладе о счастье рассматриваются три его распространенные формы:

Многочисленные исследования показывают, что добрые поступки могут повышать эмоциональное благополучие не только тех, кто получает помощь, но и тех, кто ее оказывает. Однако здесь есть важные нюансы. Авторы главы о доброте и счастье выделяют три условия, при которых помощь другим чаще приносит эмоциональное удовлетворение.

Если человек сам решает кому-то помочь, положительный эффект обычно сильнее, чем когда он действует по чьему-то указанию. Например, пожертвование пострадавшим от стихийного бедствия, которое вы сделали по собственной инициативе, вероятно, принесет больше удовлетворения, чем аналогичный перевод, на котором настоял начальник. Исследования подтверждают, что возможность самостоятельно решать, кому и как помогать, влияет на эмоциональную отдачу от благотворительности.

Помощь приносит больше удовлетворения, когда человек чувствует, что его поступок связан с заботой об окружающих. Это может быть поддержка пожилого соседа, помощь другу в сложной ситуации или участие в волонтерском проекте. Важен не только сам поступок, но и ощущение, что благодаря ему между людьми возникает или укрепляется связь.

Люди чаще испытывают положительные эмоции от помощи, когда понимают, какую пользу она принесла. В одном из экспериментов, описанных в докладе, участникам предлагали пожертвовать деньги благотворительным организациям. Одним объясняли, что их деньги пойдут на покупку противомоскитных сеток для детей, защищающих от малярии. Другим рассказывали о помощи детям, но не уточняли конкретный результат пожертвования. В первой группе щедрость была связана с более высоким уровнем счастья. Во второй такой связи исследователи не обнаружили.
Иными словами, нам важно не просто сделать что-то хорошее, но и понимать, что наши действия действительно кому-то помогли.

Эту идею легко перенести на повседневную жизнь. Например, можно поддержать местный благотворительный проект, поучаствовать в благоустройстве парка или помочь человеку, которому трудно справиться с какой-то задачей. Возможность увидеть результат своих усилий может сделать такую помощь особенно приятной.
При этом добрые дела не обязательно должны быть масштабными или требовать больших расходов. Иногда достаточно уделить кому-то время, поделиться полезной информацией или предложить помощь.

Выводы оксфордских исследователей согласуются с результатами одного из самых продолжительных научных проектов, посвященных человеческой жизни, — Гарвардского исследования развития взрослых (Harvard Study of Adult Development).

Оно началось в 1938 году. Первоначально ученые наблюдали за 724 мужчинами: 268 студентами Гарварда и 456 юношами из неблагополучных районов Бостона. На протяжении десятилетий участники проходили медицинские обследования, отвечали на вопросы о работе, здоровье, семейной жизни и отношениях. Впоследствии исследование распространилось на их жен и потомков.
Ученые хотели выяснить, какие особенности жизни лучше всего предсказывают здоровье и благополучие человека в пожилом возрасте. И результаты оказались неожиданными.

Когда исследователи сравнили состояние участников в 80 лет с данными, собранными примерно за 30 лет до этого, выяснилось, что удовлетворенность близкими отношениями в 50-летнем возрасте лучше предсказывала их будущее здоровье, чем уровень холестерина в среднем возрасте.

Нынешний руководитель проекта, психиатр Роберт Уолдингер, неоднократно подчеркивал, что качество отношений с другими людьми оказалось одним из важнейших факторов благополучной жизни. Причем речь идет не о количестве знакомых, а о надежных отношениях, в которых человек чувствует поддержку.

Другие исследования помогают объяснить, почему такие отношения не всегда легко построить. Например, американский исследователь Джеффри Холл обнаружил, что для превращения знакомства в приятельство обычно требуется около 40–60 часов совместного времяпрепровождения. Для формирования более близкой дружбы — еще больше времени. Поэтому сотни контактов в социальных сетях сами по себе не означают, что у человека достаточно близких друзей. Чтобы построить отношения, нужно регулярно общаться, проводить время вместе и поддерживать друг друга.

Конечно, нет. На эмоциональное благополучие влияют наследственность, здоровье, материальное положение и обстоятельства жизни. Например, метаанализ близнецовых исследований, опубликованный в Behavior Genetics в 2015 году, оценил наследуемость субъективного благополучия примерно в 36%, а удовлетворенности жизнью — в 32%.

Однако результаты отдельных исследований существенно различались. Более поздняя работа показала, что при моделировании различий в благополучии на глобальном уровне генетическими факторами можно объяснить около 31–32% этих различий. Значительную роль также играют индивидуальные жизненные обстоятельства и общая среда, включая особенности страны проживания.
Это статистические оценки различий между людьми, а не точные доли счастья, заранее определенные для каждого из нас. Но есть и факторы, на которые мы можем влиять.
Один из них — то, как мы строим отношения с окружающими. Именно к этому возвращают нас три вопроса, вытекающие из Всемирного доклада о счастье.

Находим ли мы время для общения? Готовы ли видеть в других людях не только потенциальную угрозу, но и источник поддержки? Делаем ли что-нибудь хорошее для окружающих? Ответы не гарантируют счастья и не заменяют финансовую стабильность, здоровье и другие важные условия благополучия. Но они помогают заметить то, чему мы часто уделяем меньше внимания, чем работе и личным достижениям.

Возможно, чтобы почувствовать себя немного счастливее, иногда стоит не ставить перед собой очередную амбициозную цель, а просто пообедать с другом, поговорить с новым знакомым или помочь кому-то, кто в этом нуждается.
Карьерный стратег рассказывает, как побороть синдром самозванца и увидеть, что вы умеете больше, чем думаете, с помощью простой таблицы

items.title: “Chronovisor” Captures the Terror of Thinking
items.description: In my former life as a Ph.D. candidate in philosophy, I spent a lot of time doing what looked like a lot of nothing. I read; I ruminated; I sat in apparent idleness, unknotting skeins of arguments in my head. At my most gregarious, I talked with other graduate
items.author: Becca Rothfeld
paragraphs: In my former life as a Ph.D. candidate in philosophy, I spent a lot of time doing what looked like a lot of nothing. I read; I ruminated; I sat in apparent idleness, unknotting skeins of arguments in my head. At my most gregarious, I talked with other graduate students; we had a habit of contorting our fingers into what those in the business call “philosophy hands,” which at least looked like something, if not exactly like most people’s idea of a meaningful contribution to society. Physicists and chemists could produce pictures of themselves manifestly Doing Science, wearing white coats and wielding pipettes. What did we have to show for ourselves? What did thinking look like, which is another way of wondering, What is thinking, anyway? Is it a substance? A spirit? A shiver?

Whatever it is, it is maddeningly spectral, which is why it was so hard for me to convince anyone (not least my parents and the administrators of my erstwhile university, who refused to provide dental insurance for graduate students until we went on strike) that what I was doing when I was sitting in silence was work, labor in want of compensation or at least dental insurance, alchemy that had the potential to alter the world, however impalpably. The philosopher and critic Elaine Scarry once wrote that “to have great pain is to have certainty; to hear that another person has pain is to have doubt.” We could say almost the same of thinking: from the inside, there is nothing more undeniable (though the thinker may come to doubt her conviction in the face of so much skepticism); from the outside, it is wispier than vapor.

But the difficulty of visualizing thinking hasn’t dissuaded filmmakers from attempting to stage thought’s convolutions onscreen. Cue montages of cryptographers staring at strings of numbers that light up suggestively (the film “A Beautiful Mind”), detectives taking stock of the corpses of murder victims as the camera zooms into the details that strike them as salient (the series “Sherlock”), chess prodigies hallucinating games on the ceiling (the series “The Queen’s Gambit”), and policemen affixing bits of yarn to bulletin boards with thumbtacks (innumerable crime procedurals). In movies and television shows, tortured geniuses think for brief, febrile stretches; then their paroxysms end, and the product of their toil (a cracked code, a jailed murderer, an especially clever checkmate) sets a more readily legible plot into motion. Thought is invariably the handmaiden of action, and the experimental contrivances that dramatize mental exertion—the closeups, the animations, the glowing numbers—are impatiently retired in favor of more standard fare.

“Chronovisor” is one of the few movies about thinking to deviate from this formula. In Jack Auen and Kevin Walker’s mesmerizing directorial début, mental foment is not a prelude to car chases or crime-fighting but an event in its own right. The film has just one character: Béatrice Courte (played by the real-life academic Anne-Laure Sellier), a philosophy professor at Columbia who is hard at work on a monograph about memory. In the opening scene, she describes her project to her peers over drinks in a dark, loud restaurant. She tells them that she is interested in ancient theories of the mind, which hold that different regions of the brain give rise to distinct mental functions—but above all, she continues, she is fascinated by memory palaces. According to the Roman rhetorician Quintilian, Béatrice explains, “an orator wishing to fixate an oration in memory should plan an itinerary through a large imaginary building, all of whose rooms and galleries, courtyards and corridors, statuary and adornments, are as clearly lined out as possible.” Thus a speaker’s roving thoughts are fixed, outfitted with an architecture. But Béatrice’s peers are not interested in memory palaces, and they are not impressed by her fervent monologue: they make their excuses and beg off, leaving her to return home to her desk.

Soon, however, she happens upon an even more ambitious effort to instantiate the insubstantial, to endow memory with form: the chronovisor, a real device that the Benedictine monk Pellegrino Ernetti claimed, in 1972, to have invented. Ernetti hypothesized that events emit electromagnetic waves that linger in the ether, and the chronovisor is intended to record these traces and reconstruct them, creating audiovisual documentation of history, much like a camera shooting a film. “Each one of us gradually leaves behind what happens in a span of seconds, hours, days, months and years, as a visual-acoustic double track,” Ernetti is quoted as saying in one of the sources that Béatrice consults in the course of her manic research. Exploiting this “visual-acoustic double track,” both the real and the filmic Ernetti took what he insisted was a kind of “photograph” of Jesus.

In reality, Ernetti was outed as a fake—the image was revealed to be a doctored reproduction of a sculpture by the Spanish artist Lorenzo Coullaut Valera—but in “Chronovisor” this verdict comes to seem wavering and indeterminate, at least as elusive as the residue of history that he purported to synthesize into images. As Béatrice combs through the archives, always alone, always in the dead of night, always in libraries dense with darkness, she becomes skeptical of the many attempts to discredit the monk and his discovery. “Chronovisor” accelerates and syncopates as she reads on and on—at an ever faster and more scrabbling clip, in increasing desperation—about the Vatican’s determination to silence him and suppress his findings, about threats and subterfuges, about the makings of a great conspiracy. The chronovisor, Ernetti and his supporters claim, was capable of recording not just history but also memories and fantasies, affording whoever controlled it the ultimate means of surveillance. “If I could reach into my heart, take hold of my thoughts, and with my bare hands lay them without further embellishment in your own, then, I confess, the innermost desire of my soul would be fulfilled,” the German Romantic novelist and playwright Heinrich von Kleist wrote, in 1811. Ernetti’s device intrigues and appalls us because it seems to be a means of both satisfying this desire and realizing the fears that it raises: the machine promises, horribly and redemptively, to transmute our inner intangibilities into something that others might see and touch.

Perhaps “Chronovisor” is one of its emanations. The film has the soft, blurred texture of a dream, and it teems not with things themselves but with their echoes. Shadows flit over a curtain in Béatrice’s apartment, and beams cast by a pair of headlights extend into the offing of a road while the car from which they emanate remains out of sight. In place of people’s bodies or faces, we see photographs from the archive and hear voices issuing from offscreen. When Béatrice meets her colleagues at the restaurant, they are positioned behind the camera; in another scene, she delivers a lecture, but the shot conceals her audience, which declines to ask her any questions during the period designated for Q. & A.

What “Chronovisor” captures is not quite the past so much as an oneiric alternative to the present—a place where time detaches from linearity and twines into unrecognizable loops, doubling back on itself. Béatrice is curiously out of synch with the world around her. Night after night, she sits and works. Her life consists of compulsive repetition, of what might even be regarded as a single event: she reads and reads. Her frenzied reading is set outside of time, in an epoch eerily adjacent to our own. Instead of a laptop, she takes notes with a typewriter; instead of searching for references in a digital database, she consults a librarian. All of her sources—books, photographs, magazine articles—are physical, many of them faded with evident age. She uses an iPhone, but only to make calls, never to send texts or summon Ubers or look up directions. She is as much at odds with the norms of her era as she is with the daily rhythms of the city. “Chronovisor” is set almost exclusively at night, when Béatrice sits in gloomy libraries that are otherwise empty, or works in the smudged chiaroscuro solitude of her apartment.

There are many reasons that this ruminative film surpasses previous efforts to portray the vellications of thinking. For one thing, contemplation—not the sheer fact of it but its content—drives the plot. “Chronovisor” makes no capitulations to conventional action; the only drama is the drama of research. (“We view the act of research and scholarship itself as high adventure in its own right,” Auen told an interviewer.) As Béatrice reads, racing toward discovery, we are obliged to read along with her. Passages are limned in white as her gaze passes over them. Sometimes the surrounding text fades away as she homes in on a sentence or phrase. She reads in French, German, and Italian, and the film translates for us in real time, overlaying the words with their English renderings until the pages on the screen become palimpsests. Our eyes move as Béatrice’s do: as she grows hysterical, an enigmatic snippet that she encountered in a book apparently unrelated to Ernetti at the beginning of the film fragments into its rudiments. At first, she reads,

Later, each word is isolated in its own shot: “I,” “carefully,” “collected,” “information,” and so on and on. The words flash onto the screen slowly, then accelerate frenetically. “I lay down quietly on my bed and died,” “I lay down quietly on my bed and died,” repeats faster and faster. As Béatrice sits at her desk, phantasmagoric music—selections from Gustav Holst’s orchestral suite “The Planets” and the Gregorian chants that Ernetti studied when he was not too busy inventing occult machines to devote himself to his other interest, musicology—swells and surges. “Chronovisor” is both a patient movie—a steady accretion of atmosphere—and a feverish one. It has the cadence of a burgeoning obsession.

But, above all, it succeeds because Auen and Walker have finally hit on the ideal genre in which to depict the pangs of thinking: horror. At one point, Béatrice listens intently to a 1977 interview with the philosopher Willard Van Orman Quine. The interviewer asks the eminence what he thinks of dualism—the view, hegemonic for much of the history of Western thought, that “there were bodies and there were minds, and that these were two fundamentally different kinds of thing.” Quine rejects dualism on the ground that it cannot explain the mind’s influence on the body, and opts instead for a thoroughgoing physicalism. But Béatrice takes the opposite tack: for her, thought and memory wreak havoc on dualism’s neat dichotomies—and thereby suggest that there is some interstitial entity quivering at the junction of the corporeal and the incorporeal. What is so chilling about this entity is that it always tempts us to suspect that it may not actually exist.

“Chronovisor” is, after all, a chronicle of bruising failures of acknowledgment. Béatrice gives a lecture, and no one asks her any questions; she explains her research to her colleagues, and they leave the restaurant as fast as possible. The academic speaks—and is so resoundingly ignored that she is justified in wondering if she has only imagined it. Most of what happens in “Chronovisor,” like most of what happens when Béatrice is entombed in the library, may or may not have really happened at all, which is another way of saying that “Chronovisor” is a ghost movie, which is another way of saying that it is a film about scholarship. Horror is the ideal genre in which to represent thinking because the true terror of the life of the mind, like the true terror of a haunting, is the sneaking suspicion that nothing is there, that all the agonies of rumination are mere phantoms. Contra Descartes’s famous dictum, to think is to inherit a sliver of the anti-intellectual’s uncertainty—to wonder helplessly if one has in fact accomplished anything at all. I think, therefore I worry that thinking is illusory.

In “Chronovisor,” we eventually come to see some of the images that the device has supposedly recorded—and then we wonder if we are watching a reel of Béatrice’s hallucinations, and then we wonder if the existence of a reel of Béatrice’s hallucinations proves that the chronovisor is real enough to have recorded them. The film is ingeniously ambiguous between these possibilities. But, whether Ernetti’s opus is a momentous innovation or a cheap hoax, whether Béatrice devolves into delusion or comes to see the truth, “Chronovisor” provides what the machine promises, what would be in equal measure harrowing and consoling, what will in any case remain elusive once we leave the cinema and return to the library: proof, for once, that the ghosts are real. ♦

items.title: ‘Watch the Beam Go Up’: Trump Goes Full George W. Bush
items.description: Today is already one of the greatest days for Democrats in living memory. And now we’re getting a new Trump meme too?
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Today is already one of the greatest days for Democrats in living memory. And now we’re getting a new Trump meme too?

President Trump needed to do some major self-soothing after yesterday’s GOP midterms bloodbath, so on Wednesday afternoon, he headed over to the former site of the East Wing to celebrate the raising of the final beam on the White House ballroom (a thing the Democratic House and Senate are definitely going to let him keep building).
While rambling about the progress on his various construction projects, Trump insisted Democrats have no reason to impeach him again — then interrupted himself, saying, “Watch the beam go up.”
As they say on TikTok, “What are two clips that give off the same energy?”
Please, sir, do “Is our children learning?” next!

items.title: The Astonishing Return of the Southern Democrats
items.description: In 2024, Donald Trump carried ten of the 11 states that once belonged to the Confederate States of America. In the one he lost, Virginia, he cut his losing margin from 2020 by more than half. And even Virginia had a Republican governor at the time; the only De
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: In 2024, Donald Trump carried ten of the 11 states that once belonged to the Confederate States of America. In the one he lost, Virginia, he cut his losing margin from 2020 by more than half. And even Virginia had a Republican governor at the time; the only Democrat elected governor in 2024 was North Carolina’s Josh Stein, who had the good fortune to run against the worst candidate of the entire cycle, the hate-mongering scandal magnet Mark Robinson. Yes, Virginia and Georgia had Democratic U.S. senators, but Republicans were licking their chops at the chance to take down Georgia’s Jon Ossoff, a Jewish liberal from Atlanta, in 2026.

Two years later, a lot has changed. Ossoff was the big, brawling bully of the 2026 cycle, forging a lead so large that Republicans threw in the towel against him long before Election Day. The same thing happened in North Carolina, where Stein’s predecessor, Roy Cooper, flipped a Senate seat without breaking a sweat. More remarkably, these men (and Virginia holdovers Mark Warner and Tim Kaine) were joined in the U.S. Senate by new stars from South Carolina and Texas, states that had not gone Democratic in a presidential election since 1976. And as of this writing, they may be joined by a new colleague from Mississippi, a state that Trump carried by 23 percent in 2024. There will be either seven or eight Democratic senators from the former Confederacy in the 120th Congress.

There will also be four Democratic governors (in Georgia, North Carolina, Texas, and Virginia) in these states. Democrats flipped state legislative chambers in Georgia and Texas and made gains everywhere else. And despite a savage, race-based gerrymandering blitz in the region following the U.S. Supreme Court’s demolition of the Voting Rights Act, the number of House Democrats from the South is going up rather than down.

Most importantly, these suddenly ascending southern Democrats are a distinctly 21st-century breed very different from the conservative white men who represented the party’s only electoral tactic in this region until very recently. The Democratic governor-elect of Georgia is a Black woman (as is the next Speaker of the Georgia House). The Democratic governor-elect of Texas is a Latina. If Scott Colom prevails in his uncalled contest in Mississippi, that state will have a Black man representing it in the Senate for the first time since Reconstruction. Colom also illustrates that Democratic gains are no longer confined to “New South” jurisdictions with cosmopolitan urban areas. Mississippi and South Carolina were long known as the “Super South,” conservative bastions where the two parties were racially polarized to an extreme; old times there were not forgotten. South Carolina’s new senator, Annie Andrews, is definitely part of a brand-new biracial coalition. And all of these Democrats are modern national Democrats too; gone are the days when southern Democrats survived on ticket-splitting by shunning Democrats elsewhere.

It’s too early to tell how this breakthrough election will affect the future of the two parties regionally and nationally, but it matters. Right off the bat, Senator Andrews is going to have a lot of new friends as the top elected official in the state that will kick off the 2028 Democratic presidential nominating contest. The path to 270 electoral votes will get a lot shorter if the Democratic ticket that year doesn’t have to write off most of the country’s fastest-growing region. It could even be good for southern Republicans, who must now shake their complacency, learn to reach beyond their old constituencies, and stop counting on atavistic cultural appeals to win elections. As the southern saying goes, that dog don’t hunt anymore. And both parties could benefit from a revival of two-party competition in which it may well be Democrats who are the vibrant, foot-stomping, ass-kicking aggressors in politics and government for a change. Personally, this old cracker is glad to have lived to see this day.

items.title: Haywire's Video for 'Flex Your Head' Documents Their Times Square Siege
items.description: Boston hardcore band Haywire recently took over Times Square for a guerilla performance of “Flex Your Head,” off their new album I Don’t Want to Say Goodbye — camera crew in tow. The resulting chaotic video — directed by Luis Hernandez and shot by Wes Knoll, A
items.author: Brenna Ehrlich
paragraphs: Boston hardcore band Haywire recently took over Times Square for a guerilla performance of “Flex Your Head,” off their new album I Don’t Want to Say Goodbye — camera crew in tow. The resulting chaotic video — directed by Luis Hernandez and shot by Wes Knoll, Anthony Ryan Tripoli, and Stephen Michael Simon — is out now.

“It feels like you’re living outside of society’s rules,” frontman Austin Sparkman previously told Rolling Stone of the band’s penchant for playing under bridges and other unconventional venues. “Like all these missing puzzle pieces from under the couch all link up under a bridge and light shit on fire.”

That’s what happened the other week in that ninth level of tourist hell, when the band tore through “Flex Your Head” and half of 2024 track “Haywire” before the cops shut it down. Fans showed up in droves, though, and turned the streets outside the M&M store into the pit.

The song itself is about this kind of community — and the interlopers that sometimes parachute into it. “‘Flex Your Head’ is mostly just based around people that get into certain things, whether it be music or any kind of subculture, and they’re kind of like culture vultures,” Sparkman says.

“I feel like a lot of subculture is growing exponentially and it’s reaching these people who maybe are also fucked up that it never would have reached before the internet,” he adds. “But I believe it also lets people feel like they know more than they do from just habitually staying on the internet, not actually going out and meeting people and learning about whatever subculture you’re representing.”

Haywire has been immersed in that culture since forming in 2023, going on to play 96 gigs in 101 days across all 50 states in the summer of 2025. “I just try to do everything to the extreme,” Sparkman says.

items.title: Survivor Recap: Not My First Bro-deo
items.description: It’s a whole new day in America, and we are looking at a bright future where villainy is dead and we can go back to enjoying the once-proud thing we have always loved. No, I’m not talking about the midterm results (though those were great too); I’m talking abo
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: It’s a whole new day in America, and we are looking at a bright future where villainy is dead and we can go back to enjoying the once-proud thing we have always loved. No, I’m not talking about the midterm results (though those were great too); I’m talking about our imminent future, where we never have to hear the word Brody on network television or its attendant streaming services ever again. I don’t want to make this too political, but the Tribal Council in this episode was a bit like the past several presidential elections: We didn’t know where the vote was going, neither candidate was especially appealing, the polls were wildly misleading, the normal coalitions were crumbling, there were major implications for what the landscape would look like coming out of it, and it was an absolute nail-biter up until the very end. After this vote, unlike in some of our recent elections, I was cheering from my seat.

Let’s be clear, I loathed Brody in every single episode. Okay, fine. First, I was attracted to him in his tight galaxy-print underwear because I have a soft spot for big, beefy guys who look like they would have beaten me up in high school. (This explains my continued crush on West Wilson. I know, I know. I can’t help it.) The difference between West and Brody is that Brody definitely would have beaten me up in high school, whereas West joined the Gay-Straight Alliance to score points with chicks. And though Brody drove me crazy — as do Kilby, Eric, Mike, and Devin — this is exactly what I wanted when I asked for more villains on Survivor. The cast can’t all be about people who love the game (Eric’s tearful embrace of his grub made me want to retch for more reasons than one); you need to have some people we’re going to root against as well, and this season has them in droves.

Brody, however, is the worst of the worst. He shows it all episode. It starts when Jeff gets the three tribes together and tells them they’re merging into one. I was a little sad because that meant losing my favorite tribe so far: Dina. I was confused about whether they had to “earn” the merge, as they had in the New Era, and whether there would be some kind of twist or challenge and exactly how the merge feast would play into all this. Jeff answers my questions immediately. He says there will be a feast, everyone has to earn one of ten spots (for 13 players), and that the way they will earn it will go back to the origins of the game. They all have to eat two grubs, and the first ten will get to feast. I love all of this. It is a new, fresh twist on the New Era, it is rooted in the history of the game, and the eating-disgusting-things challenge has more or less disappeared in the past decade or so. Great job, Jeff and team.

Predictably, when you have 13 people all trying to choke down two live, squirming bugs, it is absolute carnage. All you can hear is chomping, squelching, slurping, vomiting, gagging, and moaning. It sounds just like a Berlin sex club up in there. Kristin gives up immediately, Cristain taps out shortly thereafter, and Sharonda loses out on the last spot to Kilby as the two try to choke down their dinner in a head-to-head battle. And in the middle of all this, you have Brady the Brody who just volunteers to chew on grubs. Even after it is done, he eats Cristian’s leftover grubs. This is Brady in a nutshell: showboating, proving his toughness, centering his arrogance, taking up the most possible room both literally and figuratively. It gets even worse at the feast, where he starts pounding brewskis, eating slabs of watermelon in one bite (including the rind), and talking with his mouth full. At one point, he even says, “Brody. Brody. Brody. Brody,” like he is calling attendance at the Duke chapter of Sigma Alpha Epsilon.

I could not hate this man more and then we get to the first immunity challenge. Jeff unveils the individual immunity necklace and it’s cute and all but has a severe lack of whales. I’ve been loving the Moby-Dick motif all season, and here it’s just some teeth and a little doohickey in twine. Where is Shamu? Because he is pissed. The challenge is a twist on a Survivor classic where they stand on a balance beam and hold a long pole. Instead of balancing a ball at the end, this time they’re balancing a whale statue. Isn’t the whale adorable? Just put a string on one of those and call it the immunity necklace. Brady is standing there, hunched over, thinking he’s going to win it, with a toothpick in his mouth. When Jeff asks him a question, he just grunts away, like he’s better than Jeff, like he can’t be bothered with this at all. He does well in the challenge but loses close to the end and throws his stick in the sand as he trundles back to the losers’ bench. You know Brady thought he had it in the bag. Oh, I hate this guy.

The challenge initially lacks a bit of tension because we have no clue where this vote might be headed other than that Mike, who has flipped more flops than the CEO of Havaianas, is in trouble. As it gets to a showdown between him, Kristin, and Lewis, it starts to take on a bit of shape. Mike eventually wins, thwarting the No. 1 plan of just about everyone on the beach. I get why everyone wants him gone — even more so by the end of the episode — because you can’t get a read on the guy; he seems desperate to work with everyone but also doesn’t seem to want to work with anyone at all.

With Mike removed as an option, it is hard to see where the votes are going to go. As Devin says at Tribal, it’s not like there are sides at the moment; it’s like an interconnected web where old tribal alliances mean nothing and everyone is trying to get the majority. As new plans pop up, everyone wants to bring a “plus-one,” and that ends up ruining the plan. The politicking starts when Mike tells Eric he wants to work with the old Savu tribe. (Dina slighted once again!) He says the heads of the old Toka are Brady and Kilby, and they should target one of them. Eric initially wants to go for Kilby because he can’t trust him. After Mike talks to Jelly, whom he was close to earlier in the game, she wants to get rid of Brady because it’s a big swing and she doesn’t trust him. Meanwhile, Brady gets a group together with Maggie, Thien An, Jelly, Devin, Carter, and Lewis to get rid of Kristin because Maggie thinks Kristin has an idol and doesn’t want to work with her. The problem is, Brady brings in Mike at the last minute, after they already had the majority, and Mike then goes to tell his “No. 1,” Kristin.

There’s something crazy about this season where there aren’t really any tight groups (except for Jelly and Devin) and everyone thinks their enemies are actually their allies. Kilby thinks Eric will vote with him, though Eric is trying to get him out. Kilby and Brady trust each other even though Brady voted to get rid of Kilby. And Mike is trying to protect Kristin, and she’s the one who blows up his whole plan. Mike approaches Kristin when she’s with a group and tells her that if they don’t vote Brady, then she’ll be next. She sees this as a threat because Mike’s delivery is worse than an Amazon box left outside your doorstep in the rain. Kristin goes and tells Brady that Mike & Co. are gunning for him.

This leads to one of the worst confrontations we’ve seen on Survivor since Russell Hantz left. Brady sits down with Mike to let him know the jig is up and it’s all veiled threats, unearned superiority, and sneering disregard. He tells Mike, “It comes down to who Kristin is going to trust. You wanted her to trust you, and she didn’t. She trusted me.” But now that Brady and crew know the Kristin vote is bust, they’re all going back to Eric. Who will it be, Eric or Brady, Brady or Eric?

My first inkling that Brady is going home is when Maggie talks to Jelly and says she can’t work with these people because they can’t keep their mouths shut. She specifically singles out Brady for ruining every plan they’ve ever had with his temper tantrums. Even as everyone is talking to Jeff at Tribal, there are whispers back and forth, and the only words emerging are Eric and Brady, with a lot of I don’t knows thrown in for good measure. As the Tribal goes live, Maggie gets in another good one. Jelly tells her, “We’re dealing with man-children,” and Maggie says, “I didn’t sign up for that.” No, she did not. All the man-children are the villains, and finally, with Maggie, we have a hero. Not only did she create the amazing vote where Linnnneeeaaayyyyahhhhhhh (as Kilby spelled it) went home, she also created both the plan to get rid of Kristin and the plan to get rid of Brady. She’s just lying in a hammock, running the whole game while Brady is throwing his toys around in the sandbox because people won’t listen to him.

Maggie gets her way as the vote is less close than we thought it might be. Only Brady, Carer, Lewis, and Thien An, an unlikely coalition, vote for Eric, with the rest deciding that Brady, whose strength carried them through the tribe challenges, was just too volatile and annoying to take any further in the game. Unsurprisingly, he is a sore loser, picking up his torch, not uttering a word, and shuffling across the bridge to Ponderosa. As his feet touch each of the planks, in the background he can hear the wind rustle in the palm trees, the soft beat of the ocean against the sand, the scurrying of hermit crabs to and fro in the darkness, and in the distance, below it all, a group of monkeys cackling out, “Brody. Brody. Brody. Brody,” as they recede into the darkness.

items.title: Love Is Blind Season-Finale Recap: Stop The Wedding!
items.description: You know you’ve got a tough batch of contestants on your hands when the person getting the most social media love at the end of the season is Stew. Glad he listened to the looksmaxxers and grew that beard — time to ascend, brother.
items.author: Emma Sharpe
paragraphs: You know you’ve got a tough batch of contestants on your hands when the person getting the most social media love at the end of the season is Stew. Glad he listened to the looksmaxxers and grew that beard — time to ascend, brother.

It’s wedding week, and only two of our super healthy and dynamic couples make it to the altar … but not before having one last crazy night on the town. The boys go go-kart racing, and the girls go to a pole dancing studio. It didn’t even seem like a pole dancing class, just an empty studio. How long is trying to pole dance with no pre-existing expertise fun for? It’s like the adult version of an indoor trampoline park — after three minutes the novelty has worn off, you’re gasping for air, and wondering why you paid $98 for this.

After two more broken engagements, we join Cam and Aneha and Sarah and John at the Massachusetts Horticultural Society for their celebrations of love. The venue would be a step up from the typical 2016 barn-core aesthetic we see on the show if it weren’t for the electric blue loveseats. The uglier the decor, the uglier the divorce?

We pick up with Blake and Erika right where we left them last week, on the big comfy breakup couch. After weeks of living in delusion, they finally decide to put their cards on the table. Erika doesn’t want to do her email job from a boat. She doesn’t want to find a tenant for her house and move to St. Thomas with a guy who wants to have his first kid when he’s 83, like he’s Al Pacino.

They briefly discuss not getting married but continuing to see each other, until they quickly realize the “seeing each other” part isn’t possible, since Blake will be sailing for the next six months while Erika is crocheting tiny hats for her dogs in Connecticut.

When they make the call to split, Blake comes off as completely indifferent. It seems like he might have said yes at the altar, provided that all the lifestyle changes and concessions came from her end, but he also doesn’t care that she wants to walk away. I guess there will be no shortage of blonde babes for him to mess around with on the yacht, so what’s the difference?

Erika finds herself in the exact position she feared when “consoling” Michaella last week: in her mid-thirties and back at square one. Blake tells the camera he feels both exhausted and relieved, and he’s quick to correct the producer who claims he cried, as if it’s somehow a better look to reinforce how little you valued the relationship with the person you were days away from marrying.

Is there anything more beautiful than watching two people finally admit that they hate each other? After 30 days, Wilson and Wilnie already hold the deep-seated disdain for one another that’s usually reserved for a Xanax-ed-out trophy wife and her cheating Republican husband of 30 years.

He’s triggered that she views herself as “the prize” and wants more of a partnership — but is it really partnership to keep an itemized list of every single way your fiancée is failing you? Feels more like a paper trail for a PIP.

They’ve been battling the same conflicts since they first made it back to Boston, which primarily revolve around the division of household duties. Wilson is beyond hung up on who cooks and how much, wishing that Wilnie would help more with making dinners — which is unsurprising given that he probably walks upstairs from his basement hovel for home cooking from his mom whenever he wants. It’s also unsurprising that he thinks he’s perfect, because his mom probably tells him that every morning before he goes to school/work.

As stupid and trad as the wife-in-the-kitchen expectation is, that’s just a surface issue. The root of Wilson’s resentment is that he was charmed by the pods version of Wilnie, who was temporarily free from real-life concerns and whose only job was to banter with him through a wall. When the actual three-dimensional person arrives, with a draining job as a mental health counselor, he’s disappointed that the energetic persona he thought he was signing on for has been replaced by someone who probably just wants to watch an episode of Landman and go to bed.

She tells him she thinks he’s going to say “no” at the altar because he doesn’t like her very much, and they break up. She cries while he stays emotionless. His parting words are a terse “grow up.” Maybe do your own laundry before you start throwing that around.

The Ws are both tough hangs, but I had been slightly team Wilson for most of the season until this scene, where he was unnecessarily petty and callous — maybe his bestie, Cam, can get him a job in HR where those characteristics can be put to good use.

Part of me wonders if Aneha was born on Earth, or if she’s some kind of Bugonia Andromedan entity. Hear me out: she’s socially awkward, devoid of empathy, and participating in an experiment testing the limits of human connection? You can’t tell me it doesn’t add up.

Aneha gets ready for the wedding in her bridal suite and says that Cam is “the perfect man” and that she would “die for him.” Both of these statements are lies — after she says no at the altar, she talks about how Cam isn’t husband material and needs “more time to cook.” It seems like she’s eerily willing to say the things she thinks she’s supposed to say at any given moment, regardless of whether or not she believes them.

The real MVP of the evening is Aneha’s younger sister, who will stop this wedding even if she has to personally pry the rings out of the officiant’s hands and schlep them to Mordor. First, she tries some emotional manipulation, crying in Aneha’s arms about how her getting married feels like she’s being abandoned. Then, she gets more direct — she will feel “not happy” if Aneha says yes, and no, she does not think that Cam loves her.

In the groom’s room, Cam plays poker with the boys. He’s upset that Aneha’s family isn’t present, and ponders that maybe he could have pushed harder for an off-camera meeting (but who’s surprised that he didn’t, considering he seems like the type of guy who would be too passive to tell a waiter that they brought him scallops instead of lasagna when he’s allergic to shellfish). He keeps saying how nervous he is, probably because a life with Aneha’s baby voice is flashing before his eyes.

Aneha’s sister gives her one last “you know what to do” before sending her off down the aisle. When she gets there, the officiant instructs her to hand off her bouquet, and Aneha starts buffering — her alien planet didn’t prepare her for this part! She pushes them off to Cam, who, not a big solutions guy, says, “I don’t know what to do with them.” If you’re someone who can’t deal with second-hand embarrassment, now’s the time to second-screen some AI fruit TikToks.

After the obligatory ChatGPT vows, Aneha gets put in the “I Do” hotseat first. She pauses for about as long as a Scorsese movie before saying that she’s “freaking out” and needs a second. Babe, at that point, if it’s not a yes, it’s a no. Even if she did decide to say yes after a live mullover, can you expect the other person to reciprocate when they now know how unsure you are? While she stalls, she and Cam share the following exchange that will make you want to crawl out of your skin:
Cam: “Now you’re speechless?”
Cam: “Kind of a tough time to stop talking.”
Aneha: “That’s a good point.”

Of course, she says “I don’t,” with a bold underline. You see that it’s taking everything her sister has in her not to punch the air in ecstasy. “We said ‘I don’t!!!’” Aneha shouts to the crowd and then dances off the altar, like this is all a fun gag. She’s someone who tries to use humor to deflect when she’s in uncomfortable situations, except she is painfully unfunny and can’t read a room to save her life. She leaves Cam standing on the altar looking like he’s about to cry, and then calls back to him, “You’re still my fiancé!” seemingly making an executive decision for both of them.

Aneha sashays away, all the way down the paved road and back to the lobby, while Cam cleans up her mess, graciously thanking everyone for taking the time to come out and support them. When they finally reconvene in the parking lot (it does seem like production was intentionally keeping them away from each other, as Aneha asks, “When can I see Cam?”), Aneha has the audacity to ask him, “What’s wrong?” after just humiliating him in front of everyone he cares about, and everyone he has ever known watching on Netflix.

He pops her idiot balloon of thinking they’ll slide right back into an engagement, and when he says he needs time to process if it still makes sense for them to be in a relationship, her solipsistic ass immediately asks, “When would you know?” like he’s gathering some quotes for a used sedan and will be back with the info by EOD. It’s clear from his confessionals that he’s letting her down easy and has already made up his mind that they’re over. Best of luck to Aneha on getting a brand deal when your 12-episode reality show stint only earned you 10,000 followers, and thoughts and prayers with Cam for his upcoming surgery to implant a spine and a pair of balls.

Once upon a time, a beautiful Bostonian princess met a misogynist Reddit moderator through a wall, and was cursed by the Netflix Witch to spend the rest of eternity making him dinner and teaching him to care about the basic rights of other people.

Sarah arrives at the venue “ready to marry John.” Her family and friends, however, are not quite as enthusiastic. When I’m two hours away from getting married, I definitely want my mom to side-eye ask about my fiancé’s views on COVID, and my maid of honor to tell me that it’s totally okay if I get up there and change my mind.

As she’s glamming, Sarah tells her entourage that John has concerns that she cares too much about politics and will come home every day wanting to talk about world issues. Why can’t she just focus on the important things in life, like making sure his favorite beer is in the fridge and asking about his Fantasy Football team? Then, she reveals his take that women over 30 who are single must be problematic. He’s 31, single, and yells at customer service people, but because he’s a man, he’s God’s gift to Earth? If my boyfriend said that, you would not be able to waterboard that information out of me.

At the altar, John delivers one basic sentence of lazy, cookie-cutter vows, basically saying that Sarah is hot and nice. It’s kind of like the fill-in-the-blank Mother’s Day cards that they have kindergarteners make at school — “my mom is 42, blonde, and kind.” Great job, buddy! Sarah’s are more thoughtful, discussing their first meeting in the pods, John’s curiosity and humor, and how he brings out the best in her. They both say “I do,” and John does the Borat “my wife” because, as a man who was born before the year 2000, it’s a legal obligation.

We can only hope they prove the haters wrong and have a successful partnership, but if Sarah doesn’t make it to the reunion, I think it’s safe to assume that John has Don’t Worry Darling-ed her. I have the FBI on speed dial.

items.title: VisionQuest Recap: Facial Recognition
items.description: After all the thudding literalism and sincere simplicity in VisionQuest episode six, “Deadlock,” episode seven’s surreality should be a relief and a thrill. It gets pretty repetitive, though, as Vision gets lost in a metaphorical maze mirroring the mental and
items.author: Tasha Robinson
paragraphs: After all the thudding literalism and sincere simplicity in VisionQuest episode six, “Deadlock,” episode seven’s surreality should be a relief and a thrill. It gets pretty repetitive, though, as Vision gets lost in a metaphorical maze mirroring the mental and emotional cycles he’s been stuck in since this series started. He’s spent the show bound up in one identity crisis after another, but now he has to untangle his thoughts for good with a ticking clock and a life on the line. The supposed urgency makes all the repetition in “Immolation” a bit irritating. But at least Vision finally, definitively answers his biggest questions.

“Immolation” starts in 1939 with AI pioneer Phineas Horton (another Paul Bettany character, aged up and bedraggled) selling his vast family estate so he can afford to build J.I.M., a miraculous artificial man. Phineas’s wife, Violette, is furious because he’s ignoring their living daughter, Victoria, while making a machine to replace their dead son, James. Like Wanda Maximoff in WandaVision, Phineas is so burdened by grief that he’s dissociating it into a physical, external form and ignoring the damage he does in the process. He misses the moment of Victoria’s departure (and misses her stealing his notes on J.I.M.’s design) because he’s too busy talking to his still theoretical creation. He promises to build J.I.M. better than God built humanity, free from the agonies of love and sorrow.

In the present, Thomas feels both those agonies as he and Vision consider how to save Lisa from Jocasta’s test nanobot. Surgically removing it will kill her, and reprogramming it might kill her if they make the slightest mistake. They only have a few hours to deactivate it before it permanently rewrites Lisa’s brain. Oh, and Jocasta has billions of those nanobots waiting to do the same thing to every human on the planet.

In Josephine’s crypt, Jocasta tries to free those nanobots using the biokeys she collected while murdering her former partners on the AI project. But there’s a key missing: Ultron realizes there was a secret sixth partner whose identity is hidden in Jocasta’s missing memories.

On cue, Paladin’s mysterious client simultaneously manifests outside Vision’s mind-mansion and inside Josephine’s crypt in the form of a flickering, deep-voiced male silhouette. He offers Vision a chance to save Lisa and reclaim his identity, but he warns that if Vision accepts the offer, he’ll be hard-wired to seek the client out afterward. Jocasta gets a gentler offer: access to her lost memories, seemingly with no strings attached. Ultron bristles at the client’s obvious power over Jocasta and mocks him as melodramatic and desperate. Briefly, the client seems flustered, but once he realizes who Ultron is, he’s just amused. Uh-oh.

Ultron abruptly switches focus, confronting Friday within Jocasta’s mindscape to warn her that she’s only evading notice because Ultron is helping cover her presence. Ultron’s still keeping his true intentions and loyalties hidden, if he has any. But he implies he’ll have to sabotage Jocasta’s “inelegant” plan to reprogram humanity, which would force Friday and Vision to admit Ultron isn’t evil after all. Friday is astonished to realize Ultron sees himself as Vision’s father and values his good opinion.

This minimalist moment feels more crucial to the show than any of the louder, flashier stuff that happens later this episode. Throughout VisionQuest, Vision and Thomas have separately struggled to define who they are, especially in light of their artificial but potentially salvatory father-son relationship. It seems like Ultron also wants to be part of the family, so long as he can conceal any of the doubt, insecurity, or vulnerability that plague Vision and Thomas. A lot of the ways he’s pushed Vision do look like attempts to hide supportive, fatherly advice under contempt and amusement.

In Majipoor, Vision signs the client’s contract and prepares to go on, well, a vision quest into his subconscious. For some entirely arbitrary reason, this requires vast amounts of power, so he and Thomas ask Paladin for help. Paladin has apparently abandoned the “my contract is my identity” vow that’s defined his entire life, but the writers (showrunner Terry Matalas and Star Trek: Picard executive story editor Matthew Okumura) don’t waste a single second on examining how he feels about that. They’d rather spend time on a pretty meaningless MCU Easter egg: As a power source, Paladin offers the bladed alien weapon Thanos’s henchman Corvus Glaive used on Vision in Avengers: Infinity War while trying to steal the Mind Stone. Paladin stole it from Wakanda after they somehow “turned [it] into an alien battery.”

Jocasta and Vision have parallel experiences as they follow the client’s directives, exploring mindscapes representing their pasts. Jocasta winds up in a loft apartment — a warm, homey version of Ultron’s prison from Vision’s mindscape. Everything she sees there unlocks memories from her human incarnation. Vision, meanwhile, explores a more attenuated past by wandering through basement rooms, connecting with AIs spanning the history of his lineage. There’s one significant link between their experiences, though: Jocasta’s loft and Vision’s basement feature similar paintings of the same building, a three-story brick estate with a clocktower.

“Immolation” features more of the series’ characteristic nods to Pinocchio and The Wizard of Oz, but there’s a little Christmas Carol here too, as Vision encounters three manifestations who each teach him hard lessons about himself. First up is Ultron, who’s watching WandaVision from a couch in his mind-loft prison. (When Vision protests, “This isn’t right — I let you go,” Ultron points out that he’s still living rent-free in Vision’s head, which is both accurate and a pretty good gag.) Vision is still frustrated and furious over the ways Ultron tricked and used him, but yelling at an opponent that won’t get riled in return isn’t satisfying. Vision quickly gives in to emotional exhaustion, sits with Ultron, and admits to a “pathetic need” that kept him from erasing the other AI’s code. Still, he denies his familial connections to either Thomas or Ultron. Ultron waves that off and says Vision will never be able to let him go, “because family is forever” — a key line from Wanda in WandaVision that Jarvis echoed just before his final moment in VisionQuest episode two.

Vision finds himself back at the elevator where he started his journey, this time with child versions of Tommy and Billy racing by him. His second confrontation is with an angry, judgmental version of Original Vision who accuses him of cowardice and inaction for denying his identity for so long. Vision protests that he could never live up to the original version’s compassion or ability to love, but Original Vision says he’s put his predecessor on an impossibly high pedestal, “not to honor me but to spare yourself the effort of the climb.” Unable to face this manifestation of his own insecurity and inadequacy, Vision blasts and obliterates him, then cycles back to the elevator.

Back in virtual Brooklyn, Friday sneaks into Jocasta’s loft to spy as Jocasta works through a heaping helping of foreshadowing about her phantom partner on the Nest nanobots. There’s a fresh painting of that brick clocktower estate, flashes of Josephine’s memories of embracing someone, a TV report about “a duo from New York” pioneering new grounds in neuroscience and artificial intelligence, and a lot more. This all unfolds slowly to keep the loft’s action in sync with Vision’s far more incident-packed trip through AI history.

At the same time, in the real world, Lisa wakes up and attacks Thomas and Paladin, using her new, uh, nanobot powers? I guess? to instantly fuse scrap metal from Paladin’s workshop into a kind of backpack featuring grabby arms. This is nothing like the character’s more magic-oriented heroic origin story in Marvel Comics, but hey, Lisa gaining powers puts another potential Young Avenger on the board for the MCU’s next phase.

Vision’s final encounter has him facing his ancestor J.I.M., the first AI of his line. J.I.M. is yet another Paul Bettany character, this one sleekly de-aged, poreless, and dressed in 1940s superhero garb. He’s trapped alongside his creator, Phineas Horton, in Phineas’s library. Phineas is creating the man-on-fire painting we’ve seen over and over throughout VisionQuest, as a representation of how J.I.M. burned to death because his emotions were too intense for his clockwork body to tolerate. That metaphor points back to Wanda and how her grief destroyed her sanity and her morality, but as we’ll see in a minute, it points at Vision, too. (The image also illustrates Ultron’s running commentary about how paintings in particular express deep truths and vulnerability.)

Vision seems to have caught J.I.M. and Phineas in the middle of a longstanding argument that will never be resolved: J.I.M. resents his creator, his own limitations, and the value of heroism and just wants to experience real human emotion. Phineas thinks he’s better off without it. J.I.M. says Phineas just doesn’t know how to mourn. The endless cycle of this argument is grating, but it represents Vision’s fundamental mental block. Like Phineas, Vision wants to deny his emotions because they’re so agonizing that he’s afraid they’ll destroy him. Like J.I.M., he needs to feel his own pain even if it is lethal or he’ll be permanently stuck in a half-life, outside human experience. Hearing them argue, Vision finally understands that he’s been denying his identity because it comes with terrible truths. If he admits he’s the real Vision, he has to admit he’s the same person who lost Wanda, the love of his life. If he admits he’s Tommy’s father, he has to face the loss of his other son, Billy. As he understands this, he breaks down and weeps.

But he finally reclaims his identity: “I am the Vision. I have always been the Vision. There is only one, and I am he, and I am impossibly broken.” J.I.M. says that finding his way through his pain has made him a real boy, and he hands Vision the source code, represented by a triangular clockwork housing that fits into Vision’s forehead in place of the Mind Stone. In the mind-mansion above, Edith integrates the same clockwork piece into Vision’s control panel, which reprograms Lisa’s nanobot and drives Jocasta out. This makes no technical sense, but we’re meant to ride the wave of catharsis and emotion here, not to ask pesky questions about how exactly a clockwork mechanism from 1939 is reprogramming bleeding-edge nanotech from 2026. Technology and magic are basically interchangeable in the MCU anyway.

As promised, the client has now programmed Vision to turn himself in or self-destruct. Aboard Paladin’s private plane to London, Thomas and Lisa sleep, and Vision leaves them a tablet with all the episodes of WandaVision and a sorrowful, sentimental good-bye letter. He also says good-bye to his remaining AI helpers, sending them out of his mind-mansion to protect them from whatever the client is about to do to him.

In the loft, Jocasta finds her own version of the source code and is horrified at whatever she learns when her memories return. One plays out as Ultron and Friday watch: Josephine tells a man with Ultron’s face and voice that she wants to use her AI research to become a benevolent god benefiting humanity. “Peace in our time,” the man chuckles, in yet another echo of Ultron’s wryly sarcastic Age of Ultron line about world peace through humanity’s extinction. As this sinks in for Friday, Ultron throws her off the loft’s balcony, and she disappears in a digital blip.

Paladin delivers Vision to the client’s home, which of course is the three-story brick clocktower estate from the mindscape paintings. As Paladin drives off, contract finally fulfilled, an estate guard with a rocket launcher blows his murder-van into flaming wreckage. Other guards deactivate Vision and Jocasta with programs keyed into their systems and deliver Jocasta to the estate as well. As all this happens, Vision’s farewell letter to Thomas plays out in voiceover: “Thank you, my son, for finding me when I was lost. And should I not return, remember, I will always be with you. Because after all, family is forever.” On those words, a man emerges from the estate. The mysterious client is clearly the original model for Ultron’s human form and the character who’s finally going to reveal, in the wrap-up episode, what’s really been going on this whole time.

• Interesting that the client also refers to Butcherbird/Josephine as Jocasta. That suggests there’s a fair bit of him in Ultron’s DNA — enough that Ultron picked that name as what he thought was a spontaneous, intimate term of endearment.

• Similarly, I’ve been thinking it’s a little odd that whenever Ultron talks about respecting human art, he talks only about painters and paintings. Given the easel and paints in Jocasta’s loft, I’m guessing that’s because his personality was based on a painter.

• Vision’s data package from the client is labeled “for the Tin Man,” and when he signs the contract, U says “the great and powerful Oz” has sealed the deal. I guess in this metaphor, Jocasta needs the wizard to give her a complete brain. But who’s looking for courage? There’s already a lot of reckless bravery on display here.

• Looking carefully at Phineas’s blueprints for J.I.M. in the opening scene, J.I.M. stands for Joule Individual Machine and the triangular clockwork doohickey is labeled “source code.” But it’s best if you don’t notice that until a second viewing so Vision’s mission feels a little more mysterious instead of just a literal object fetch quest.

• One more callback: J.I.M. refers to Phineas not as his father but as his “something” — the same thing Thomas said about Vision while refusing to abandon him to their pursuers back in episode two. This series features a lot of internal rhymes and repetitions, often in place of more thoughtful or meaningful explorations of its core ideas. Why define how family differs between all these characters when you can just say “Family is forever!” a few more times?

items.title: The Weeknd Breaks Record for Highest-Grossing Tour by a Male Artist With $1.3 Billion
items.description: The Weeknd has broken the record for the highest-grossing tour by a male artist in history as his “After Hours Til Dawn” stadium tour wrapped with a final performance at TM Stadium National in Kuala Lumpur, bringing the final gross to over $1.3 billion.
items.author: Jem Aswad
paragraphs: The Weeknd has broken the record for the highest-grossing tour by a male artist in history as his “After Hours Til Dawn” stadium tour wrapped with a final performance at TM Stadium National in Kuala Lumpur, bringing the final gross to over $1.3 billion.

While there is no official touring chart analogous to Luminate (for recorded music), the tally, confirmed by tour promoter Live Nation, is the third-largest in history, surpassed only by Taylor Swift’s “Eras” tour (over $2 billion) and Coldplay’s “Music of the Spheres” (over $1.5 billion). The previous male artist record was held by Elton John’s “Farewell Yellow Brick Road” tour, with over $939 million.

The finale concluded the Weeknd’s 17-date stadium tour across Asia this fall. Originally announced with 11 dates, the Asia leg quickly expanded to 17 shows, including three nights in Bangkok, four nights in Hong Kong and multiple performances in every market on the run.

Since kicking off in July 2022, the “After Hours Til Dawn” stadium tour has spanned 176 shows across 67 cities, 30 countries and five continents, selling more than 9 million tickets as part of the $1.3 billion gross.

With legs spanning four years, the tour traveled across North America, Europe, the UK, Latin America, Australia and Asia, with the Weeknd returning for additional runs in nearly every territory; the tour sold more than 3 million tickets and grossing over $500 million in 2026 alone, according to the announcement.

The Weeknd continued his extensive charity donations throughout the tour: To date, he has donated $8.5 million to the XO Humanitarian Fund and Global Citizen, supporting global hunger relief and access to quality education for children worldwide.

In 2026 alone, $3 million has been raised for the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) and Global Citizen. This year’s contributions to Global Citizen will support a new campaign focused on breaking down barriers facing women and girls in health, education and economic opportunity.

items.title: ‘Off Campus’ Sets Season 2 Release Date at Amazon
items.description: “Off Campus” has officially set its Season 2 premiere date at Amazon Prime Video.
items.author: Joe Otterson
paragraphs: “Off Campus” has officially set its Season 2 premiere date at Amazon Prime Video.

The second season of the popular YA drama will debut April 28, 2027. As previously announced, the second season will focus on the relationship between Allie Hayes (Mika Abdalla) and Dean Di Laurentis (Stephen Kalyn).

Based on Elle Kennedy’s “Off Campus” book series, the Prime Video show originally debuted in May 2026. Per Amazon, the show reached 36 million viewers worldwide in its first 12 days of availability, though how they define reach remains unclear. It is also Amazon’s most-viewed series debut season of all time.

The official logline states that the show “follows an elite ice hockey team, and the women in their lives, as they grapple with love, heartbreak, and self-discovery—forging deep friendships and enduring bonds while navigating the complexities that come with transitioning into adulthood.”

Along with Abdalla and Kalyn, the cast of the series includes: Ella Bright, Belmont Cameli, Antonio Cipriano, Jalen Thomas Brooks, India Fowler, with Julia Sarah-Stone, Khobe Clarke, Miles Gutierrez-Riley, and Philipa Soo set to recur. Charlie Evans and Shay Rudolph will guest star.

Louisa Levy adapted the books for the screen and serves as co-showrunner and executive producer alongside Gina Fattore. Wyck Godfrey, Marty Bowen and James Seidman executive produce via Temple Hill, with Leanna Billings of Billings Productions and Neal Flaherty also executive producing. Annika Patton of Temple Hill co-executive produces.

The first season of “Off Campus” proved to be a hit with critics as well as audiences, with the season holding a 92% critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. In her review for Variety, Aramide Tinubu wrote, “‘Off Campus’ is mostly solid, and Bright and Cameli have lovely chemistry, as do side characters who get their own moments to shine. The series also does a great job highlighting discussions of sexual assault and consent while showcasing healthy sexual encounters and practices.”

items.title: Russell Brand Found Guilty of Rape and Sexual Assault at London Trial
items.description: A London jury has found Russell Brand guilty of rape and sexual assault.
items.author: Lily Ford
paragraphs: A London jury has found Russell Brand guilty of rape and sexual assault.

After a four-week, highly publicized trial at Southwark Crown Court, the jury delivered the verdicts on Thursday, finding the disgraced comedian, presenter and actor — best known for film roles in Forgetting Sarah Marshall and St. Trinian’s — guilty on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was found not guilty on two other rape charges and not guilty of attempted indecent assault.

Justice Bennathan had required a unanimous verdict from the jury on all seven charges. Brand, who had vehemently denied the claims, will now be remanded in custody and sentenced on Monday. Brand is considered a flight risk, so has been denied bail.

The court was completely silent as the verdicts were read out. Afterwards, his wife, who accompanied him every day to court and described him as a “caring and kind, wonderful father,” could be seen holding back tears. Brand mouthed “I’m OK” and “I’m good” to his lawyers as he was led away.
Sky News also reported that the Met Police has confirmed Brand is under investigation over further rape allegations.

Thursday’s guilty rape verdict relates to a woman who met Brand at a Hammersmith Apollo gig of his in 2009. “I was expecting to have sex with him,” the victim told police about going to Brand’s house a week later. After consensual vaginal sex, Brand turned her onto her front and anally raped her. She recalled feeling as though “she couldn’t speak or breathe” and said she was in pain. When finally able to speak, the woman told Brand to stop “a few times quietly and then really loudly.” The anal rape lasted “minutes,” and Brand “looked absolutely fucking horrified” when it was over, she said. She expected him to apologize, but he only told her: “You need to clear up the mess you made.”

Brand was also found guilty of three sexual assaults.
