One was his grabbing a victim’s breasts at a bar in Soho in 2004; another was an incident in 2004/2005 at Capital Radio where he pushed a victim up against a wall, kissing her and grabbing at her body, breasts, sides and buttocks “aggressively”; and lastly, an incident where he put his head and nose in the “vaginal area” of a female colleague in 2009.

He was cleared of oral rape and also found not guilty of raping a woman in a Bournemouth hotel room after the Labour Party conference in 1999. He was also absolved of an attempted indecent assault, in which a woman had claimed he tried to drag her toward the men’s toilet at the MTV offices in 2001.

The Hollywood Reporter followed the court proceedings closely. The jury watched police interviews with all six complainants, whose identities were kept anonymous throughout the trial. The jury was also shown multiple police interviews with Brand, in which he read from a pre-prepared statement. Brand also testified at the trial, maintaining: “I know what ‘no’ means. … Consent is a fundamental, essential and necessary and in many ways more important than sex itself.”

Brand said he was unable to persuade anyone to testify on his behalf, confirming his lawyer’s statement that “no one will touch [him] with a bargepole.” His wife, with whom he shares three children, did however tell the court that Brand is a “caring and kind, wonderful father” and that she feels “very seen by him.”
Laura Brand confirmed that her husband had been baptized in April 2024, after the rape and sexual assault allegations against him came to light.
The court also heard from his former personal assistant, Helen Berger, who had described Brand’s “insane sexual appetite.”

Over the course of a month, the prosecution sought to expose Russell Brand as a “ruthless, sexual predator” who allegedly understood that these women weren’t consenting. None of them “sought the limelight” or “any kind of publicity,” said lead prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones in the closing arguments on Friday, Oct. 30. “None of these women has anything to gain — except perhaps some closure,” she said. “[Russell Brand] didn’t listen when I said no, he didn’t listen, he didn’t care. … In the rape cases, he just kept on going until he achieved his ultimate aim and ejaculated.”

Russell Brand’s legal team, on the other hand, rejected the claim from the prosecution that his defense was “a lot of half-truths, spun into lies.” His lawyer Ian Winter had told the court of the “devastating impact” of Channel 4’s Dispatches documentary, in which rape and sexual assault allegations against Russell Brand first came to light and kick-started a police investigation in 2023. “There is nothing random at all about these people coming forward. … They have all come forward because they have been brought at the invitation of that program,” said Winter. He also told the court that Channel 4 and Sunday Times journalists “poisoned the well of justice” by prompting these women to speak up and denying Brand a fair trial.

That sentiment was palpable in a heated exchange outside the court after Brand was taken into custody. His lawyer confronted a Sunday Times journalist who worked on the Dispatches investigation that alleged crimes by Brand. “I hope you are pleased with yourself,” Winter said. “I’m pleased justice has been done,” she was heard responding. “Well, it wasn’t. You f***ed it,” Winter replied. “Congratulations.”

items.title: Six Hollywood Consequences of Tuesday’s Democratic Blockbuster
items.description: The massive showing by Democrats in Tuesday’s midterm elections enmeshes in the lives of all Americans. But the entertainment industry has a particular role to play, given its charge to tell stories — to explain America to itself.
items.author: Steven Zeitchik
paragraphs: The massive showing by Democrats in Tuesday’s midterm elections enmeshes in the lives of all Americans. But the entertainment industry has a particular role to play, given its charge to tell stories — to explain America to itself.
And now, suddenly, there’s a whole new chapter to write.

But man, that sounds awfully high-minded. There are far more concrete examples of how politics will change the entertainment industry. Here are six realms that could look a lot different after Tuesday’s domination.

The federal film tax credit has had a little bit of momentum with both Republican lawmakers like Tim Scott, Brian Jack and Nathaniel Moran and Democrats such as Adam Schiff, Laura Friedman and Linda Sanchez, all of whom introduced a bill last month to establish the 20 percent credit for certain labor costs. Where does Tuesday leave it?

Well, the good news is all the lead champions in Congress have won re-election and will be back to work next session (though Scott may have to spend a few extra minutes in the morning wiping egg off his face for his “unequivocal” assertion that Republicans would maintain Senate control).

The question is whether they can rally enough fellow lawmakers behind it. Theoretically Republicans would want to join the cause, as it’s a win for them at a time when those won’t come easy. Doubly so for President Donald Trump, who will be eager to crow about…something, and bringing some jobs back to the U.S. allows for the chirp.

The snag is that the tax credit reduces the U.S. tax base at a time of both a massive deficit and when many Democrats are promising a restoration of benefits — i.e., the kinds of things you need a deep tax base for. Supporters will argue that this is tax revenue that wouldn’t have happened anyway if productions are shipping overseas (sometimes but not always true) and that it will benefit workers (yes, it will trickle down, but the actual rebate goes to producers, not all of whom need the cash). On paper this should still stand a decent shot. But Congressional turnovers can mess with priorities. Put this in the unknown column.
Texas artists saw it all along

No one around the cable-news dial could quite believe that Texas had elected a Democratic senator for the first time in 38 years or governor for the first time in 32. Harry Enten was so in disbelief he almost got into a fight with his accent.

We should have paid closer attention to creatives. They’ve been telling us how it’s possible — telling us of another Texas — all along. Natalie Maines of The (then-Dixie) Chicks famously and at the expense of her career told a London audience at the start of the Iraq War in 2003 that “we do not want this war, this violence. And we’re ashamed that the president of the United States is from Texas.”

But the idea has been creeping into plenty of other Texans’ work too — in the films of Richard Linklater and his anti-exploitation 2006 movie Fast Food Nation and the arched-eyebrow-to-false-jingoism Last Flag Flying in 2017. Or Mike Judge, pushing back against George W. Bush-era compliance in 2006’s retroactive documentary Idiocracy. Or even just the work of an Austinite like David Modigliani and his 2019 nonfiction piece Running with Beto. (Actually, Beto walked so James Talarico could run.) We haven’t always paid attention.

No doubt we’ll soon start hearing other artists around the country tell us a place is a lot more Democratic than its Republican politicians want to project. After Tuesday, it’s worth listening to them.
You know how you’re going for some minor medical procedure and the doctor’s like, “In the short term, it will hurt like hell, but then you’ll feel a lot better?”

I suspect we’ll get a whole lash-out at mainstream media figures by Trump and members of his administration after Tuesday’s drubbing. “Outlets are failing,” “hosts should be fired,” you know the lyrics. But lame ducks tend to get lamer as their term wears on, and I suspect once Trump sees how little effect this is having — the meager few days of Jimmy Kimmel suspension’s after the Charlie Kirk joke last year will practically look like a Colbert canning by comparison — we’ll start seeing these instances fade as his attention turns elsewhere.

Spasms from the FCC are still possible, Brendan Carr writing letters to this media company or that asking them to drop by for a not-so-friendly visit. But how hard do you want to go on these when — oh yes, you’re not a presidential cabinet department but an agency overseen and funded by….Congress? The Carr witch hunts and saber rattles of the past two years are going to get a lot quieter. Who knows? Maybe the media companies will stop quaking in their boots and even restore a DEI program or two.
David Ellison’s true colors

For months we’ve been told by Ellison apologists — and David Ellison — that the new owner of Warner Bros. wasn’t actually a Trumper; he just played one at UFC fights. Ellison needed Trump to get his deals through, so it was all realpolitik. Well, now he doesn’t need that — in fact, if anything, a Trump association hurts him with a new Congress. So does he reveal himself to be the pragmatist his defenders say (or even the liberal on many issues that he says he is)? Or, with his Trump cover falling away, does he just unmask as the conservative he’s been all along? First test: Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, coming in a few months on HBO. Does Ellison still release it despite its targeting of the leading GOP donor? Musk just paid a lot of money to Skydance, potentially so HBO doesn’t air it, though he has bigger challenges to worry about right now.

And there will be all sorts of other markers — films to buy, TV shows to air, news divisions to revamp — for one of the bigger moguls operating today. We’ll see what he’s really made of soon enough. At the very least John Oliver can rest a little easier today.

Speaking of Musk, and of getting things right, Alex Gibney’s idea that if we just pull back the curtain his weakness will be revealed was practically borne out verbatim on Tuesday as Musk’s half a billion went for naught. “The Great and Terrible Oz kept people in check because they were afraid of his visage that loomed over everybody, and he used that power to exert an enormous amount of control,” Gibney told THR last month. “But when a little dog pulled aside the curtain, and you can see a frumpy man operating gears and levers, suddenly he wasn’t so terrible and he wasn’t so great.”

One loser in this Democratic midterm surge: Rob Bonta and the AGs who garnered a…modest settlement from Ellison over his WBD acquisition as pressure mounted from various politicians and leaders. Had the attorneys general just held out six more weeks, they would have had all of Congress and a whole new vibe on their side.

The Hollywood model this electoral season has been really interesting. Many people you talk to around the entertainment business and beyond in recent weeks have suggested some version of “Hollywood’s been sitting this out.” That’s not exactly true. Entertainers lent plenty of financial muscle to these midterm campaigns — see under: all the fundraisers thrown by A-listers, from Damon Lindelof for James Talarico to Shonda Rhimes for Jon Ossoff, along with all the donations from the likes of Chuck Lorre, Sally Field and Casey Bloys. Don Henley alone gave a half-million dollars to various candidates in Texas.

What happened a lot less were public campaign appearances. Celebrities did that nonstop in 2024, and it either didn’t help or got them (and their Democratic candidates) pulverized. If your party’s message is “return power to the people,” then some very rich red-carpet types standing there telling the people how to do it sort of jams the signal and generally casts an elitist cloud over your message. We ain’t in 2004 anymore.

No doubt 2028 will bring plenty of big names stumping for candidates. People want to help, and famous people want to help famously; nothing wrong with that. But after the stark contrast between 2024 and now, we might see a different tack. Maybe a candidate doesn’t turn down Beyoncé who wants to show up at a campaign event. But maybe also Beyoncé thinks better not to offer? It’s not like stumping makes celebs’ lives easier, either.

One other change: the idea of celebs running for office. A time-honored tradition. But Michele Tafoya just rode her Sunday Night Football popularity to the Republican nomination for Senate in Minnesota — then got trounced by 14 points. I mean, if a celebrity can’t get elected in Minnesota…
That said, if McConaughey scratched his political itch and tossed his cowboy hat in the ring for, say, Ted Cruz’s seat in four years, how many of us would object?

What kind of actual regulation we’ll get on AI remains to be seen. Ed Markey may have promised all those subpoenas for tech executives, and there’s a general air of bring-Big-Tech-in, but actually stopping Silicon Valley from developing new models and products is hard. It would be like trying to stop politicians from issuing press releases — it’s what they do. Also, there’s a pacing misalignment, with Congress moving slowly and writing laws and tech companies moving fast and writing code. Also also, tech companies have a lot of money and a lot of lobbyists.

All those caveats said, the winds blow differently now. Many of next term’s roughly 259 House and 54-56 Senate Democrats got there by promising tougher oversight on AI, particularly on data centers, and they’ll be incentivized to make some moves. And even if Trump won’t sign bills of that ilk, the numbers are now lopsided enough that Senate Democrats would just need to peel off a few Republicans to get a 60-vote filibuster. (Josh Hawley, John Curtis and John Kennedy of Missouri/Utah/Louisiana come to mind; they’ve all expressed Big Tech-skeptical leanings.)

All of this could slow down how quickly the models get developed and thus how fast they get adopted by studios/consumers. Good news for creatives, most of whom are fine with AI as a limited-use tool, less so as a soul- and job-destroying blunt instrument of automation.

items.title: Nithya Raman Wins Los Angeles Mayor’s Race, Defeating Karen Bass
items.description: Nithya Raman will be the 44th mayor of Los Angeles, unseating incumbent Karen Bass, a fellow Democrat who struggled with credibility as constituent anger surged over various municipal ills, including housing and affordability, the entertainment production exod
items.author: Gary Baum
paragraphs: Nithya Raman will be the 44th mayor of Los Angeles, unseating incumbent Karen Bass, a fellow Democrat who struggled with credibility as constituent anger surged over various municipal ills, including housing and affordability, the entertainment production exodus and her response to the Palisades wildfire. A win for the leftist city councilmember, running as an outsider against the local party machine, would be a significant victory for the region’s progressive movement, which heavily skews toward younger voters who rent instead of owning their homes.

Independent election polling site Decision Desk H.Q., which partners with Ballotpedia, announced it was projecting a Raman victory. Raman is currently up more than 4 percent, with nearly three-quarters of expected votes now tallied. The full count may not be in for a week or longer, as any mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day are still valid even if they arrive by early next week.

During her election night party on Nov. 3 at the Greek Theatre in Griffith Park, Raman denounced the “cynicism” which “started to make us believe that L.A.’s problems weren’t just bad, but they were permanent.” She avowed that the city “is worth fighting for every single day of our lives.”

Raman, 45, is a Harvard- and MIT-trained urban planner who founded a L.A. homelessness nonprofit and served as executive director of Time’s Up, the ill-fated advocacy organization focused on workplace sexual harassment, before winning her City Council seat in 2020. The industry-heavy district spans the southern swath of the San Fernando Valley, from Sherman Oaks to Studio City, across the Hollywood Hills to the Eastside enclaves of Los Feliz and Silver Lake. It includes the Hollywood Bowl, the Hollywood Sign and NBCUniversal.

Through each of her campaigns, Raman, who was born in India and will be the city’s first Asian American mayor, has generated Hollywood support — particularly from its TV comedy scene. Donors to her mayoral race have included Tina Fey, Mike Schur, Mindy Kaling and Cord Jefferson. She’s married to Vali Chandrasekaran, a writer-producer who has worked on 30 Rock, Modern Family, My Name Is Earl and The Four Seasons. They have twin 10-year-old children.

During their campaigns, both candidates said they’d back unlimited film and TV credits at the state level, and champion a federal tax incentive to make the U.S. more internationally competitive. Raman has attacked Bass’ handling of the issue, including her tardiness in appointing a film liaison to the industry. Still, despite her closeness to the industry, Raman’s record of advocating for Hollywood’s needs has been called into question, even as the city and state continued to experience its historic runaway production. (The effects of the entertainment free fall have been felt across the local economy.)

In office, Raman’s key policy focus has been on housing, first championing Measure ULA, known as the “Mansion Tax,” then criticizing the unintended consequences of the legislation once its ruinous impact on apartment construction became clear. She’s since pushed for reform. (The issue has been a recurring subplot on Netflix’s real-life drama about L.A. real estate, Selling Sunset.)

Bass, 73, was Los Angeles’ first female mayor and second Black mayor. A former community organizer turned veteran elected official, she spent years ascending to the top of California’s state assembly before spending more than a decade in Congress, representing a largely African American and Hispanic section of South L.A., which has been her political base. Joe Biden reportedly took her under serious consideration to be his running mate while he was the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee in 2020.
Bass has long maintained Hollywood ties. Her most prominent supporters in her mayoral re-election campaign included Jane Fonda, J.J. Abrams, Samuel L. Jackson and Anthony Anderson.

Raman ran to the left of Bass. Her campaign included a sit-down interview with the controversial leftist streamer Hasan Piker, as well as a fraught relationship with the Democratic Socialists of America. Once a dues-paying member of the organization’s local chapter, citing its commitment to housing affordability, she was censured by DSA L.A. in 2024 for not fully adopting its policy positions against Israel. In the mayoral race, the local chapter ultimately backed her, while the DSA’s national leadership challenged that endorsement.

Raman’s last-minute insurgent run against the local Democratic Party machine put her at odds with a bloc of her fellow progressives on the City Council, who had already endorsed Bass. The top sitting L.A. politicians to endorse her were County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath, who considered her own run against Bass and represents a swath of the Westside affected by the Palisades wildfire, along with City Controller Kenneth Mejia. Now Raman, Mejia and newly elected L.A. City Attorney Marissa Roy, who’s a member of the DSA, constitute a triumvirate of progressivism at the highest reaches of City Hall.

The general election followed a heated primary race defined by the reactionary-populist run of the former reality TV star Spencer Pratt. He drew national attention for his high-energy campaign of grievance politics after he lost his house during the Palisades wildfire due to what he argued was government negligence.

Another key figure through the cycle has been the local billionaire real estate developer Rick Caruso, a center-right Democrat who lost to Bass in 2022. He declined to run again but has remained a prominent and influential presence in the city’s political conversation. Despite having fiercely criticized Bass during her term, including over her handling of the Palisades disaster (his own Palisades Village luxury shopping center was damaged), he announced in October that he would be voting for her.

Raman’s term will overlap with L.A.’s hosting of the 2028 Summer Olympics, a global spectacle offering the city an opportunity to reboot its tarnished image. The former Lucasfilm head Kathleen Kennedy recently took the baton to oversee the ceremonies after Peter Rice, who had been running the effort, became Netflix’s chief content officer.
Story updated on Nov 5 at 11:50AM PT to reflect latest results.

items.title: The Real-Life Diet of Christian McCaffrey, Who Thinks Cold Plunges Are a Metaphor for Life
items.description: The last time Christian McCaffrey was featured in this magazine, in 2020, he posed poolside, ogling the camera in nothing but a pair of crisp white Calvin Kleins. The All-Pro running back still looks like Adonis, but a lot has changed in six years. For one, he
items.author: Jake Nevins
paragraphs: The last time Christian McCaffrey was featured in this magazine, in 2020, he posed poolside, ogling the camera in nothing but a pair of crisp white Calvin Kleins. The All-Pro running back still looks like Adonis, but a lot has changed in six years. For one, he's a 49er now, and at the midway point of the 2026 NFL season he and quarterback Brock Purdy, a popular MVP candidate, have San Francisco sitting pretty atop the NFC. McCaffrey, now in his 11th NFL season, also recently became a father, a development that's thrown the demands of professional football into stark relief. “I want to spend all day with my kids,” he confesses. “But obviously I play football, so it's not always like that.”

When McCaffrey's not chasing after his springy 15-month old daughter, his days consist of morning prayer ("it puts me in the right head space"), film study (he goes through “a bunch of notebooks every year”), cold plunges ("a good metaphor for life, actually"), and meditation, a practice he embraced this past summer under the auspices of the movement coordinator and spiritual guru Ido Portal. “Some days were great,” McCaffrey says. “Some days were crippling.”

But the week we spoke, the 49ers happened to be on their bye, which meant the typically scrupulous 30-year-old could permit himself that rare indulgence: a slice of his wife Olivia Culpo's carrot cake.

Christian McCaffrey: It's funny, even on the bye week, you can never just take a week off. You always have to do something. For me, you get a good week in the middle of the season to just get your body back, get your mind back. I think a lot of it is just being with my family. It's so good for your mind, your body, your soul. And then in the mornings, I'll do whatever workout—the team gives us different workouts to do throughout the week so that you stay up to date or you're at least moving a little bit. And then recovery work, any treatment you have to do, and later in the afternoon you'll do another mobility recovery session just to stay moving so you don't get stale.

I think the first thing that I did right was marry correctly. When you play in the NFL, it just takes all of your energy and time, frankly. I mean, I want to spend all day with my kids, but obviously I play football too, so it's not always like that. So to be able to still do my job and know that they're taken care of—my wife's a super mom, so I still do everything I need to do. And when you come home, to be able to look at my daughter's face and hold my son and just spend time with them, it makes those moments so much better.

My son is a month old, but my daughter—she's 14, 15 months now, and she's all over the place. If there's something to play with, she'll play with it. She is obsessed with that little Roomba. She won't stop. She'll just click the button on the Roomba 24/7, and then when it starts moving, she gets scared and runs to me. She likes climbing and moving, and we just try to keep her moving as much as possible, and she loves it. Just watching her smile and enjoy life is the greatest thing ever.

For me, the staples are nutrition. Those are things you can control, always. So if I'm eating healthy, if I'm getting the correct amount of sleep, if I have my Dymatize shake after my workout or my prehab session or whatever it is, getting those positive calories into your system at the same times every day is something everybody can control. That's why partnering with them was easy for me, because it was a product that actually helped me and also tastes good.

I like the Fruity Pebbles. I'm still a kid at heart, so anything that tastes like an old cereal, I'm going to go ahead and do that. But I mean, there's so many things out there now. It's almost overwhelming how many modalities and recovery tools and different things you can do. But I think the thing I've learned most, as somebody that's experimented with all of that stuff, is your mindset and your ability to just stay moving is critical. I think you can try all of the different tools, but if you're not doing the staples—moving, recovering from moving, eating correctly, having the right nutrition, sleeping correctly—then a lot of this stuff is not going to move the needle as much as you think.
I used to, and then I got way too obsessed over it. But I had an Oura ring for a long time, and I'll track my sleep in the offseason with that.

Well, it's fascinating. After the season, you think you're sleeping well, but your body and your mind go through a lot over an NFL season. So you think, “Oh, I can rest now.” But I was looking at the sleep scores early in the offseason and they were horrible. Maybe I slept eight hours, but it's the worst sleep ever. You're detoxing… I mean, the reality is that you take a lot of drugs to help you play. You have to do all these things to help you get back on the field on Sunday, with all the hits you're taking. So it takes a while to get back to a good sleep score. But then once I get the ball rolling it’s like, "Okay, I'm in a good place now.”

I don't think anyone loves getting into the cold plunge. But everyone loves it after. The cold plunge is a good metaphor for life, actually. The things that are usually the most challenging are usually the most beneficial. So yeah, I've learned to like it. And again, when you're playing and it's in season, you're so focused on the practice and the game and getting your body right that the things that you think just become routine and habit.

I always start my morning with prayer. That's been a staple, and if I can connect with God as much as possible, it just puts me in the right head space. It reminds me why I'm doing this and it eliminates a lot of distractions. I meditated a lot this offseason, especially in the summer. I worked with a guy, Ido Portal, who's a legend and has had a massive influence on me. And for six weeks straight, we did one hour of stillness every morning. That was a huge challenge, but a really moving experience. I still do that all the time. I don't have time to do it for an hour anymore, but if I can get 20 minutes in the mornings, or even throughout the day at a random point where I have a little window, I try to do that as much as possible. That just helps your nervous system get back to where it's supposed to be, especially in a high-stress week.

Yeah, I'd never done that before until this summer. And Ido, he's a character, man, but he's a beautiful person and an unbelievable human being. It was very moving working with him for a summer, and it wasn't negotiable. We were doing it, starting at seven o'clock every morning, one hour straight, complete stillness, can't move, nothing. It's only something you can explain through experience. It wasn't about whether or not you turned your brain off. There was no shot. For six weeks, I didn't shut my brain off one time. It's more about, can you focus and refocus on the task at hand as best as possible? Some days were great. Some days were crippling. Some days you're cramping because you're in a seated crisscross position and you're like, "I'm in so much pain." And then you get done and you're like, "Wait a second, I wasn't in as much pain as I thought." It was such a moving experience because, again, you said you were going to do something, therefore you need to do it. You're going to find out what your purpose is through this six-week experience. It might be different than the guy next to you. It might be different than Ido's, but you're going to go through it, and you're going to learn a lot about yourself and you'll be better for it.

You watch so much film with the team all the time, but people think we just go out and practice and play. But really, we have a job. We're sitting in meetings taking notes all day. I mean, you go through a bunch of notebooks every year in the NFL and you're watching film all the time. I've watched less film as I've gotten older, but I'll watch a lot of blitz tape to make sure I'm prepared for different tells, when they're blitzing, when they're not. But running back is such an instinctual position, so I try to train the instinct more than predict things based on what you're seeing. There are certain things you can pick up on, but that can also be a crutch, so I try to find the middle ground.

Look, I try to eat as clean as possible, but there's a time to indulge. If you're feeling great and you have a couple of days off—if my wife's going to make a dessert, I'm going to eat it. It's good for the soul.

She makes a carrot cake and, to this day, there's not a better one I've had. Or my mom will be in town and cook something. Or her mom will be in town and cook something. So I'll definitely indulge every once in a while, but throughout the week I eat clean.

In Real-Life Diet, athletes, celebrities, and other high performers talk about their diet, exercise routines, and pursuit of wellness. Keep in mind that what works for them might not necessarily be healthy for you.

items.title: Our Favorite Loafer Now Comes in Menswear’s Favorite Leather
items.description: A store I worked at in the 2010s used to stock dozens of styles of well-known shoe brands, and while our inventory was well-stocked, the rare cordovan loafers that popped up were almost mythical. There would be murmurs of a possible restock and by the time I s
items.author: Reed Nelson
paragraphs: A store I worked at in the 2010s used to stock dozens of styles of well-known shoe brands, and while our inventory was well-stocked, the rare cordovan loafers that popped up were almost mythical. There would be murmurs of a possible restock and by the time I showed up for my shift they’d be gone. In other words, cordovan loafers aren’t always easy to come by. I bring this up because Meermin’s 25th Anniversary Unlined Penny Loafer is now available in a gorgeous burgundy shell cordovan—one that, considering the nature of both the material and the build, should hold up for another 25 years of consistent wear.

First, a quick little primer on Meermin: the Mallorca-based, family-owned shoemaker started in, you guessed it, 2001. They decided to put decades of luxury industry experience into their own, less-marked-up, dexterously-made products. 25 years later, and the Unlined Penny Loafer is the catalog’s crown jewel—tenaciously timeless, super versatile and as comfortable as loafers come—and thus the bedrock the brand has riffed-upon for the anniversary.

We should also note that shell cordovan leather is very much not like the other leathers. For starters, it can only come from horsehide, and specifically from the underlayers of the rump, which is the (actual) technical term for the ass and also a very finite region of hide. Cordovan is notoriously sturdy. Like, damn-near-indestructible, will-outlive-the-cockroaches, kind of durable. And, like many long-lasting materials, it develops an inimitable character with age, such that one could argue it gets more beautiful with each scuff.

And if you’re worried about the bottoms of a pair of shoes designed to last decades—and millions of steps—the flexible chestnut bark-tanned leather outsoles Meermin employs are affixed with a resoleable Goodyear welt, so you won’t need to fret about the inevitably asymmetrical wear-and-tear. If there was a single nit to pick with the endeavor, it’d be that these are a limited release and don’t allow for a whole lot of waffling. So, if you’re in the market for some forever loafers, your search could be over in a matter of minutes. Head on over to Meermin to check ‘em out in all their glory.

items.title: Particle Physicists Are Getting a First Glimpse Into the ‘Zeptoverse’
items.description: The Large Hadron Collider has been slamming protons together for years. But recently, a proton collision produced an improbable result that is the first step toward exploring the so-called “zeptoverse”—a scale of reality many, many times smaller than an atom.
items.author: Jorge Garay
paragraphs: The Large Hadron Collider has been slamming protons together for years. But recently, a proton collision produced an improbable result that is the first step toward exploring the so-called “zeptoverse”—a scale of reality many, many times smaller than an atom. This would be the smallest scale of the physical world ever explored and may defy our expectations of how physics works.

While crashing protons together at nearly the speed of light, scientists at CERN found evidence of one of the most improbable decays of matter—so unlikely that it’s a phenomenon physicists have been hoping to observe for more than four decades. The collision produced numerous particles, including some known as neutral B mesons, and scientists found signals indicating that one of these had decayed into a muon and an antimuon.

Mesons decay all the time. These tiny particles, smaller than atoms, arise from collisions between other particles and exist only briefly before transforming into other particles. Muons, on the other hand, are similar to the electrons found in atoms, but about 200 times heavier. Scientists study these particles and their decays to test the predictions of current physics and search for clues to unknown particles.

The standard model—the sort of bible of particle physics—predicts that for every 10 billion decays of neutral B mesons, this transformation will occur once. In other words, even if scientists were to observe 10 billion of these particles decaying, they would expect to find, on average, only a single muon and antimuon. This discovery is the first time an experiment has obtained evidence of this phenomenon, the details of which the researchers have made available in a preprint on arXiv.

“Physicists have been chasing this decay for more than 40 years,” Marco Santimaria, who co-led the international analysis team, said in a press release from CERN. “Extreme precision is required to pick the muons out of the overwhelming background.”

The extraordinary rarity of this process explains why it’s taken decades of research to arrive at this discovery. But upgrades to the Large Hadron Collider in 2024 also made observing this phenomenon possible. The revamp enabled faster data collection, and new machine-learning techniques allowed researchers “to suppress the vast background of processes that would have otherwise swamped the signals from these rare beauty-particle decays,” as CERN described it in its statement.

This decay opens a new avenue for investigating the limits of what scientists have been able to observe. For now, the results are consistent with current physics predictions, but future measurements could reveal phenomena unique to the zeptoverse, which describes the scale where distances are measured in zeptometers (equivalent to one quadrillionth of a meter). To put this unit into perspective, a typical atom is about 100,000 million zeptometers in diameter. That’s also about the difference in size between you and one of your skin cells.

Beyond the zeptoverse lie even smaller scales, such as the Planck length, which is about 60 trillion times smaller than a zeptometer and the smallest theoretically possible unit in physics. Scientists still don’t know whether anything truly exists at that level, but it’s generally believed that physics as we know it completely breaks down on that scale. However, if scientists could gain access to this micro world, it could help us understand the first infinitesimal fraction of a second after the Big Bang, when the whole universe was such a size.
But, for now, much of what might happen there remains in the realm of speculation.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

items.title: Chernobyl’s Dogs May Be Evolving, but Scientists Don’t Know Why
items.description: The dogs living near the disaster site of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant are not like other dogs—at least as far as their genomes go. In recent years, researchers uncovered a unique genetic profile among this population, but what’s driven this distinction r
items.author: Jorge Garay
paragraphs: The dogs living near the disaster site of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant are not like other dogs—at least as far as their genomes go. In recent years, researchers uncovered a unique genetic profile among this population, but what’s driven this distinction remained unclear.

The explanation that’s perhaps most tantalizing to a sci-fi author is that the persistent radiation at the nuclear site has caused mutations to accumulate in the dogs’ genomes. But there are other ways a population’s genetics can change over time, such as random drift or natural selection. A recent study published in the scientific journal Genes revisited these pups, searching for genetic patterns pointing to one of these processes.

The researchers compared the DNA from dogs living in the area right around the nuclear plant with genetic material from dogs living in the city of Chernobyl, about 16 kilometers away. They also compared these canines to other global dog populations. The contrast alone was extreme. The dogs in Chernobyl city “are more genetically similar to dogs in the Galapagos Islands than they are to the dog population” at the nuclear plant, said Megan Dillon, a postdoctoral researcher at North Carolina State University and first author of the study.

But more striking still, the comparison revealed that random chance alone could not explain the differences between the dog populations. Instead, it seems the dogs at the nuclear site have been experiencing natural selection.
“When I was first doing those analyzes, I had to kind of pause and was like, ‘Wow, I have to make sure I'm doing all of this right,’ because this is very interesting, very surprising,” Dillon said.

Not only did the dogs seem to be evolving, but some of the genomic regions under the highest selective pressure were associated with functions such as DNA repair, immunity, and cell survival. In other words, certain genetic differences in the dogs from the plant could be relevant for coping with environmental stress.

Instead of being mutations, these genomic variants likely already existed among local dogs but became more common in the population over the past 40 years. “These dog populations already had this high degree of genetic diversity,” Dillon said. “Maybe this founding population at the power plant had the kind of genetic toolkit to endure and survive in these harsh conditions. It’s not necessarily that they were being bombarded with new mutations.”

Taken together, the results support the hypothesis that natural selection contributed to the difference seen in the dogs at Chernobyl compared to other populations. What remains unclear is which environmental factors favored these variants and whether they provide any specific advantage. “Even though we found this evidence of selection and it is around these biologically relevant genes, we still cannot say that this is tied to the exposures that the dogs have faced,” Dillon noted.

Radiation at the disaster site might seem like the easiest explanation to point to, but there are many other selective pressures this dog population has faced since nuclear meltdown. Chernobyl’s dogs are descended from pets left behind during the evacuations. Since then, they’ve persisted through Ukraine’s harsh winters and weathered other pollutants including heavy metals and pesticides also deposited in the area. “A lot of these contaminants have similar signatures and similar pathology,” Dillon said. “There are just too many different things to really be able to tease apart a single variable.”

The researchers also don’t have access to longitudinal samples that would show exactly how this population has changed over time. “It's almost like looking at a single still image and trying to figure out what came before it,” said Matthew Breen, a professor of genomics at North Carolina State University and the study’s senior author. “Those first few years were probably the most critical period—if they were selected, that's when that selection process would have happened.”

It’s not possible to go back and get samples from the dogs who lived there in 1986, a time when no organism—not even a bacterium—had its full genome sequenced. Breen was a graduate student in England then. “I was involved in a project driving around the Welsh mountain hills, collecting sheep from the pastures because the radioactive cloud had blown over Western Europe,” he recalled. There wasn’t anything to see in the data gathered then, but the technology has evolved, and those sheep had also not been living at the center of a nuclear meltdown for generations.

Nearly four decades after the accident, the Chernobyl exclusion zone has also become a refuge for wildlife. Wolves, deer, wild boars, and lynx now roam the area—a return that researchers largely attribute to the decline in human activity. Among some of these residents, such as the wolf population, researchers have also observed similar genomic distinctions to those seen in the dogs.

“It really demonstrates the resilience of nature to catastrophic events caused by humans,” Breen said. “You push something in one direction, it can respond to that and either push back or deviate its path going forward. I think this is what we're seeing here.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.
Additional reporting from Anna Rogers.

items.title: Casey McQuiston Manifested Blexas
items.description: When writer Casey McQuiston published Red, White & Royal Blue, a romance novel about the bisexual First Son of the United States president falling in love with the gay prince of England, in 2019, readers couldn’t get over the far-fetched plot. Specifically, th
items.author: Sam Reed
paragraphs: When writer Casey McQuiston published Red, White & Royal Blue, a romance novel about the bisexual First Son of the United States president falling in love with the gay prince of England, in 2019, readers couldn’t get over the far-fetched plot. Specifically, they couldn’t get over the idea that in the book’s alternate 2020 timeline, the state of Texas flipped blue to reelect the country’s first female president, a Texan Democrat. As if, they said.

Obviously, McQuiston is feeling smug today after the state of Texas turned blue in the midterm elections. On Instagram Stories, they shared a series of memes, including an incredibly apt photo of Zendaya from Challengers wearing her “I Told Ya” tee. After Greg Abbott conceded the governor’s race to Democrat Gina Hinojosa, McQuiston wrote “Blexas not so silly now, is it” alongside a meme of Kuzco from The Emperor’s New Groove holding a “license to lib out.”

McQuiston, who was born in Baton Rouge and attended Louisiana State University, also began engaging with fans who reposted stills from the Red, White & Royal Blue movie adaptation that premiered in 2023. “It was all in the binder,” they commented under a film still of Taylor Zakhar Perez, who played First Son Alex Claremont-Diaz, posted by Vulture. (In the book, “the binder” refers to Claremont-Diaz’s strategy to flip Texas.)
On a more serious note, McQuiston reminded their followers “to love and celebrate and empower progressive leftists in the historically red states and especially the South.”
“I didn’t pull Blexas out of my ass 10 years ago,” they said. “I simply looked around and saw it.”

items.title: Luxury Gifts Under $50 That’ll Impress Anyone (Without Breaking The Bank)
items.description: Luxury Gifts Under $50 That’ll Impress Anyone (Without Breaking The Bank)
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa; Victoria Montalti
paragraphs: Luxury Gifts Under $50 That’ll Impress Anyone (Without Breaking The Bank)
Piecework Puzzles Happy Hour Puzzle

2026 emphasized more than ever our craving for analogue activities and hobbies that pull us away from our phones. So puzzles, especially ones as beautiful as the artwork from Piecework Puzzles, make for thoughtful gifts. It's a relaxing, time-consuming activity that leaves your giftee with a stunning piece of art. There are numerous designs to pick from, but we're eyeing this colorful cocktail tablescape.
Quince Lightweight Cotton Cashmere Crew Cardigan

If you want to impress your gift recipients with high-quality yet budget-friendly gifts, you have to look to Quince. The selection of under-$50 gifts spans accessories, home decor, and, our favorite: cashmere sweaters. Consider a cozy cardigan that's a bit more versatile and can be worn across seasons.
Anthropologie Bistro Tile Stoneware 24k Gold Accent Pitcher

The entirety of Anthropologie’s Bistro Tile collection is stunning with its mosaic look and artisanal feel, making tons of items perfect for gifting to your holiday party hosts… or yourself. This under-$50 pitcher is a classic style for holding Thanksgiving gravy, signature Christmas cocktails, or flower bouquets year-round.

Lush's viral massage bars are viral for a reason. I myself got persuaded and purchased a citrus scent over the summer and couldn't get over the super-moisturizing formula, which left me with glowing skin, or the invigorating scent, which gained me many compliments. There are many many scents to pick from, including calming and meditative scent combos. (Tip: Purchase a $5 oval tin online to hold the bar too. They're usually sold out in-store!)
JW Anderson X Uniqlo Wool Cashmere Stole

Uniqlo knows how to do a designer collab right, and its latest with JW Anderson is full of high-quality pieces at reasonable prices. Gift these wool-cashmere scarves in multiple color combos, stamped with the JWA logo. This functional and fashionable unisex design is great for nearly everyone on your list.
GloryByAbbey Custom Photo Strip Wood Frame

It was truly the year of photo booths. Friends and couples scoured their cities for the best photo booths, leaving with vintage-style photo strips. Because of this, we've also noticed an influx in photo strip frames. Whether you DIY one or support a small business on Etsy and customize it online, there are tons of designs available to display you and your giftee's favorite shared memories.
Nécessaire The Hand Cream + The Tube Key

Anyone would be delighted to be gifted anything from bodycare brand Nécessaire. We recommend the bestselling hand cream, but elevating it more with the brand’s stainless steel tube key to help squeeze out every last drop of the moisturizing goodness.
Lululemon Metallic Nano Crescent Bag

For the Lululemon lovers on your list, consider this new metallic mini bag-keychain hybrid. It can be hooked onto a larger Lululemon bag for extra personalization. The festive design is small but practical (it can fit your coins, earbuds, lip balm, or house keys).
Staub 16 oz. Petite Tomato Cocotte

This mini heirloom tomato-shaped cocotte doubles as a mini Dutch oven and statement serving bowl (perfect for side dishes) that’ll instantly enhance any meal or tablescape. It’s so beautiful, no one will guess how much (or little) you spent on it.
Fotofoto Zero Waste Recycled Disposable 35mm Film Camera

Whether you're shopping for a Gen Z giftee, a nostalgia lover, or a frequent traveler, a disposable film camera is a great under-$50 option to help them document special moments in an instant without taking 30 identical photos on their phone. Even better, this particular camera is made from up-cycled materials and comes with a mailer from Fotofoto to send the camera back to get photos developed (and recycle the camera after the fact).
Free People Frostbite Fur Pillbox Hat
Your giftee will look like they're stepping out of a luxe '80s ski resort with this retro faux fur pillbox hat. Pick from leopard print, caramel, or cream designs to best fit your giftee's style.
Fishwife The Spicy Trio with Gift Tin

Tinned fish lovers assemble! Fishwife’s gift tins — like this smoked salmon, albacore tuna, and sardines trio spicy olive oil and hot pepper — will delight foodies. Because who doesn’t love unwrapping niche treats during the holidays?
BaubleBar Bubble Letter Custom Necklace

Baublebar’s custom charm jewelry was a reader-favorite last year, so we had to spotlight it again. Opt for a more modern and youthful version of a nameplate necklace with these puffy letter charms in either gold (for $48) or sparkly gold pavé (for $50).
Godonlif Candle Warmer Lamp with Timer

A candle warmer is one of the best gifts I’ve ever been given. It quickly fills up my space with my favorite scent, and doesn’t wear down my candle like a flame does, so I can reheat it over and over again. And from the gift-giver perspective, it's a low-lift, high-reward option!
Julie Pedersen The Bread Baker's Seasoning Kit

At this point, we probably all know someone who has taken up sourdough bread-making in the last couple of years. We think an ideal gift for spicing up their baking is this bread seasoning kit, which contains 15 jars of sweet and savory seasoning blends like Tuscan Tomato, Green Tea Sesame, and Dill Caraway.
Ugg Men's Suede Clamshell Logo Gloves

Who knew you could find Ugg gloves under $50. Well, you can at TJ Maxx, and these men's suede gloves are calling our names. Cart them up for your father, brother, partner, or friend and leave them in awe over the very generous gift.
Kylie Cosmetics Mood Stones Mini Trio Gift Set

Kylie Jenner knows a thing or two about viral moments, and her fragrances are no exception. The mogul released these new mood stone scents over the summer and got everyone hooked. On the chance that your giftee hasn't already carted up one of these perfumes, consider buying this mini trio scent so they can test out their favorites. They're also the perfect travel size for throwing in weekender bags and suitcases.
Charles & Keith Croissant Charm

A bag charm that's also a coin purse that's also a croissant? What more do we have to say? We're loving this design, but Charles & Keith has so many adorable bag charms to pick from that'll put a smile on your giftee's face.
Crocs Classic Cozzzy Slipper

Unless you look closely, you’d never know these faux-fur shearling slippers are from Crocs. Super cozy and plush, they’re the perfect option for the homebody on your list! And even better, they’re currently on sale!
Lilly Pulitzer 2027 Large 12 Month Agenda

Just because your budget is $50 doesn't mean you need an inexpensive version of a luxury gift. Instead you can get a super luxe version of an ordinary gift, like an agenda. And this chic zebra-print 2027 agenda calendar is just that! It'll add a bit of whimsy to your giftee's everyday routine.
Maison Balzac Hand Cake Server

From chrome fortune cookies to sparkling ornaments, Coming Soon offers some of the most unique and elevated under-$50 homeware gifts. But we’re eyeing this kitschy hand-shaped cake server for the baker, host, or sweets-lover on your list.

items.title: JORDAN FIRSTMAN - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: The first-time director tries to keep his mouth shut
paragraphs: The first-time director tries to keep his mouth shut

Jordan Firstman (American, 35 years old, completely fabulous) might be familiar to readers from his brassy internet memes, or his brilliant leading role in ‘Rotting in the Sun’, 2023’s crime thriller set in sexy Mexico. Or from the news that his debut as a director ‘Club Kid’ (which he also wrote and plays the lead in) was heralded with a seven-minute standing ovation at Cannes earlier this year and triggered a fierce bidding war between the biggest studios in Hollywood. A star was born.

Because he does so much, Jordan often struggles with knowing what to call himself. Luckily, help is at hand from Luca Guadagnino, Jordan’s friend of close to ten years and the director of ‘I Am Love’, ‘Call Me by Your Name’, ‘Queer’, ‘Challengers’ and so many other cinema highs. Here, Jordan gets some handy life advice from his fellow multi-tasking director, who also photographed and interviewed him for this story. The following Q&A has been edited for maximum readability and pleasure. Ready?
From Fantastic Man n° 43 – 2026
Text and photography by LUCA GUADAGNINO
JORDAN — Did I get too sunburnt?

L — A little bit. You’re a bit red, like a lobster. One second, baby, that’s not the beginning of the interview. It should start this way: Okay, Jordan Firstman has always been at the forefront of the most up-to-date things: the most up-to-date behaviour, the most up-to-date public persona. You have been directly and indirectly commenting on the state of the world and making fun of it and finding a way to showcase your personality and individuality. Eventually this has allowed you to be perceived as who you actually are. Not many people succeed in that. How do you see that in the face of the way the world works right now, the way in which authority expresses itself, the way in which parts of the world are in flames but not for the right reason?

J — Well, thank you. That’s a compliment, I think. I’ve always just tried to go from the inside out, and I’ve always known I’ve had a problem with saying everything that was on my mind, and I think it took, from high school, about a decade to figure out how to say that in a way that worked for me and didn’t hinder me. I remember my high school theatre teacher told me that I had special powers, and he said, “But you have to use your powers for good and not evil,” because I think he saw me. He saw that I was capable of both.
L — What kind of evil were you capable of at that stage in your life?

J — I’m able and have since I was a kid been able to see through things and speak honestly about them. He saw that I’ve always felt a strong sense of justice, and when people weren’t treating me or my peers right, I would be outlandish.
L — Is this something that comes out when you deal with power, or people in positions of power?

J — Until very recently this is how I have felt with a lot of people, where I think there is something hidden in their actions. Maybe they feel like I’m going to corrupt the system they have made, so they want to take my voice or my thing away from me, and I often respond very strongly to that.

L — I don’t know anyone, or at least haven’t met anyone in the last ten years, who has been able to express themselves through so many different mediums and through so many different types of performance in the way that you do. Whether that’s movies, or YouTube videos, or TV, or acting as an actor or writing as a writer or directing as a director. Is it possible that it’s a sort of victimisation of the self that helps propel you?
J — I believe I have been very, very lucky, but also, you know, I had to go to the internet because I had eight years of trying to develop ideas for TV that I just kept hitting walls with.
L — But do you agree with me, Jordan, that if you’d had fame and success, let’s say at the age of 22, 23, 24, just after theatre school, you would have become a horrible person?
J — I think it wouldn’t have been great for me. I don’t know if I would have become a horrible person, but I think I would have potentially self-destructed.
L — It’s so important to understand that maturity and success are better allies than success and youth.
J — Well, they say youth is wasted on the young, do they not?
L — I agree. Do you like younger men, men your age, or older men?
J — I usually like my age or older. Young people just end up annoying you in some way or another.
L — Do you despise people that are not fit, particularly men?
J — Of course. I envy you for many, many reasons.
L — No, no, I think the only reason you envy me is my belly and my lack of muscles.
J — I like your belly. I mean, I like a belly. I think it’s a classic gay thing, too, where we like to feel a body with some fluff on it, but we don’t want it for ourselves. I like a bigger guy.

L — One day, many, many years ago – I was very young – I met David LaChapelle, and I shot a tiny little documentary about him that I never edited. It must have been 1994, something like that, and David was super fit, and I was, like, 23 and he said to me, “Listen, as a gay man, I make sure that I’m very fit, because I have to offer something that someone else will recognise as attractive to them.” Do you think these politics are still valid?

J — I think so. It’s not only gay men, though. I mean, maybe it’s not straight men, but I don’t know. I feel we’re at a place in culture where everyone is being objectified. Male movie stars are being objectified purely for their appearance in ways they never have been, which I guess is a good thing. It’s great for women to kind of reclaim that gaze, but then it’s also got some sides that are not so positive. Every- where you look in Hollywood, everyone is bone thin, or every guy is on steroids.
L — What happened to body positivity?
J — I think it ebbs and flows. Everything that was cool in 2019 became not cool in 2022 and then whatever was cool then became not cool in 2025. Things just move very fast now.
L — How many categories of men are there? If you had to take me on a journey through the labyrinth…

J — I’ve never subscribed to the whole “gay animal” thing. I think it’s very weird that we compare ourselves to animals. I don’t really understand that. A lot of people fall in between categories. I’ve always thought of myself as just a normal-looking gay guy.

L — When I met you, I thought you looked like a straight-acting gay guy. For a moment, I actually thought you were straight. Now I would say, first of all, you’re very handsome and very attractive, and it’s interesting because you’ve kept being so throughout the ten years that I’ve known you, which is great, so congratulations.
L — But I have to ask, would you see yourself in the otter category?
J — No! I don’t think I’m an otter, because I think of otters as a little thinner framed than I am. I think I’m a little bit bulky. I think I’m supposed to be… God wants me to be fat.
L — God wants you to be a bear.
J — Yes, God wants me to be a bear. Honestly, I hate these categories. It actually makes me feel sick.

L — One of the things that comes to mind when I think about you is your very emotional investment in autobiography. Everything is autobiographical: even in Rachel Sennott’s show, you appear as a version of yourself, which I think is a great thing, because, as you know, I love Bernardo Bertolucci, and Bertolucci always said movies should be documentaries about the actors playing the characters. Do you think this will always be the case for you, or do you think that – after these long apprenticeship years of expressing yourself through movies, through acting, through performing, through writing and directing – you will try to test yourself with a more transformative way of presenting yourself?

J — But you know, in ‘Club Kid’, there’s a lot of me in it but it’s not me or my story. With my favourite artists and film-makers I get this sense that I can tell what they are going through in their personal lives when I see their work. I think you are like that, even if you maybe don’t agree. I feel like Paul Thomas Anderson is the same way. Stephen Sondheim, not to be a total faggot about it, but, you can tell he wrote ‘Sweeney Todd’ when he hated the world, he wrote ‘Company’ when he was a single man and in his forties. So, I would like to be the type of artist that finds different stories to tell, based on where I’m at in my life.
L — You are already there. You know that, right? Even the movie that you did as an actor with the director whose name I constantly forget…
L — ‘Rotting in the Sun’, by…?

L — Exactly, Sebastián Silva. Sebastián Silva is a mega cult director, he has an incredible following, he’s beloved by the most sophisticated critics, and he has a very, very strong personal voice as a film-maker.
L — And then the movie ‘Rotting in the Sun’: it’s as much yours as it is his.
J — I couldn’t tell if you liked it when I sent it to you.

L — I think the movie pushed buttons in me that made me feel that I hated it, and then I watched it a few years later, because people kept saying how great the movie was, and I can see the greatness now. Sometimes you need to hate things in order to understand them.
L — Okay, so you are now thinking, maybe next time I’ll put on a mask to cover myself, but I will still try to express the inside of myself, the inner emotions.

J — Yes. I’m interested in doing projects without me appearing in them. I think maybe for the next one I would still like to be in it, but then with the one after that I would like to explore something else. You know, what would my emotions and POV look like from a 60-year-old woman? I’d like to put my filter through different types of characters, and see how that lands.
L — ‘Club Kid’, a tear-jerker story of a father and a son, truthfully starts from an anguish-filled and tear-jerking experience in your life with a man, correct?
L — Why did you feel that a father-and-son relationship was the best metaphor to tell the story of this lost love?

J — The movie really started from the very simple thought that me next to a kid is funny. I wanted to take my life – the way I live, the way I talk – and see what happened when there’s a ten-year-old boy suddenly there. But then I went through a break-up in the middle of writing it, and it became about something else, and when I watch it now, I can really see the metaphors of being both the parent and the child to someone you’re dating, and vice versa. There’s a lot of transference happening. I think it happened in a really natural way: just the more I worked on it, the deeper it got.
L — I think every character is you, particularly the two main characters. Or let’s say the main character, Peter.

J — I really love Peter, and there’s so many parts of Peter that I wish I was more like. I definitely pushed back on myself a couple times, wondering whether the characters in my movie were too good or too idealised. And I came to a place where I kind of wanted the characters to be good people. I feel that right now you don’t really see that so much. I feel like we’re in the anti-hero movement. It’s very in vogue.
L — What is the anti-hero movement?

J — In a lot of films currently every character needs to be a bit of a shitty person for it to be palatable, or to create a bit of distance between the audience and the character. I don’t want to name movies, but I think it’s very millennial, and very, very my generation to have this detached distance from the characters – almost as a protective shield.
L — I want you to name these movies.
J — I’m not… Luca, I told you, I’m growing up and learning how to keep my mouth shut in interviews, unlike some people… ‘F1’, is that the movie you shit-talked?
L — That was Jodie Foster. Jodie’s amazing. Do you know her?
J — But didn’t you say something about ‘F1’ too?
L — No. Jodie Foster made remarks about ‘F1’. She said that ‘F1’ seems to be a movie made with AI. What do you think of Jodie Foster?
L — Have you ever met Jodie Foster?

J — I have never met her. She’s the aunt of one of my dear friends and I’m scared to meet her because either she’s gonna love me or hate me, which is often the case with lesbians. But I think she’s a legend and amazing, and I hope she would like me.
L — But don’t you think the liking or the not liking will depend on how you present yourself?
J — Yes, but as you know, maybe I would get nervous and say something off-putting.
L — It seems to me that Jodie Foster is one of the brightest people you can meet in Hollywood. What would be off-putting to say to Jodie?

J — I don’t know, I would probably end up being, like, “Oh, you know, lesbians sometimes are like this or don’t like me,” and then she would be, like, “Oh, you think all lesbians are like that?” and I’d be, like, “No, no, not all lesbians, I’m sorry,” and then I would just put my foot in my mouth.
L — Next question. Do you have children?
J — I do. I have a child, and I have to be a little bit careful. I just can’t say any proper names.
L — Okay? Do you think you’re the father?
J — No, I’m the…uncle. Right now, I’m the uncle who gave my cum away.

L — Wait, I just realised you have already told me this story and how personal it was, and it’s my bad that I asked you about it. It was unconscious because I was thinking of the character in ‘Club Kid’ – this gay man who discovers one day that he has a ten-year-old child. I was wondering if you think you could have a kid of around ten somewhere in the world that you are not aware of?

J — Sometimes I think I would be such a great dad, and I would love to have a kid to hang out with, and then sometimes I think I would be a horrible parent and ignore my kid and go off and eat at Erewhon by myself. One of the questions at the core of ‘Club Kid’ is: “What makes a kid?” Is love enough, or do you need to raise them in a traditional way for them to be all right? I think a lot of parents have kids when they are a bit stuck and they use the kid as a way to move to the next thing and hope that they will figure out, or learn, who they are through that, but often that doesn’t work. So I wanted to give Peter, the dad, the gift of time to not have drugs in his life, to not have partying, to have some form of stability.
L — That is your conservative side coming out.

J — I knew you were going to say this, because we’ve talked about it before together, and I’ve thought about it a lot since you said it. You said to me: “You’re a very conservative person,” but I think, no tea no shade, Luca, I’ve been in it, and when you’re in this hyper specific scene that I am just now kind of exiting, I think anyone who sees this movie that has experienced the G and the drugs and the state of it now knows it is not sustainable, you can’t end up there.
L — What were Jordan Firstman’s first five years of life like? Do you remember them? Where do you come from, what’s your hometown?

J — I’m from Long Island, a nice Jewish family with some bubblings of darkness underneath. It seemed nice to me at the time, and then, you know, you find out things. I guess, like any family, mine had their secrets.
L — What’s the dark secret of your family that you want to disclose?

J — I really can’t say at this juncture, but hopefully I will be able to, I don’t know, make something about it one day. But just a lot of lies, a lot of financial stuff that was being lied about and some familial generational trauma kind of stuff. But I can’t really talk about it.
L — You grew up in the ’80s, right, or in the ’90s?

J — In the ’90s. I was born in ’91. I do remember it being very, very nice, very, very peaceful. I was very shy, I was very sweet, I was smiling a lot. I started to be kind of funny around, like, five. I would watch ‘Seinfeld’ with my parents and do Kramer impressions, so I think that’s when that started. I think people are surprised when they meet me, and I can sometimes be a little shy. I’ve learned how to be an extrovert, but I think my true self is a bit shy.
L — Like pretty much all the comedians and, I would say, all the talented people.

J — I think creative people often have a lot going on in their minds, and it can be very overwhelming or overstimulating when they meet people. Especially as a somewhat public person, people come up to me all the time, and they have some sort of perception of me, so they want to have a certain vibe.
L — Do they all want to have sex with you?

J — No, the ones who want to have sex with me talk shit about me on Twitter and don’t come up to me in real life, and the ones who do come up to me are, like, usually very, very nice, but they want to banter. I think, through the nature of my work, I’ve created that lack of boundary, maybe, especially when I was doing this stuff online. People just come up and want to immediately have a rapport with me, joke around, and most of the time I’m not in the place to want to do that.
J — I don’t know. I think joking is such a personal thing; you have to be with someone that you trust. For me, I can’t just joke around.
L — So at the age of five, you started to exhibit some comedic tendencies. But when would you say you started to realise it was something really fundamental about yourself?
J — I would say I honestly started getting what comedy was when I started watching Woody Allen in high school.
L — You know Woody Allen is not mentionable as an artist.
J — But I was in high school! I didn’t know the things that I know now.
L — You are gonna be in trouble quoting Woody Allen in an interview.
J — You can’t say you watched Woody Allen as a high schooler?
L — I already had a lot of shit with making my movie ‘After the Hunt’, having the title sequence paying homage to his movies. How do we get off of the Woody Allen?
J — Okay, okay, I’m gonna think of something else…
L — No no, Woody Allen is now within the interview; we can’t remove him. But how do we reassure the readers that we are good people?

J — I do not condone anything that ever happened in his personal life. I think he genuinely is a sick person and I genuinely do think that he became disturbed at some point. But when I was in high school and was someone who didn’t know anything about his personal life, the way he wrote characters was very new to me, and I found it very interesting. When I was in high school all I wanted to be was affluent.
L — Did you like Brian De Palma when you were growing up?
J — I didn’t watch any De Palma until my early twenties.
L — Okay, so that didn’t have any power or influence on your upbringing?

J — No, but when I discovered Paul Mazursky, that was the real wake-up call for me as an artist. Because even Woody Allen, his dialogue is very arch in a lot of ways; it’s very pointed, it’s very sharp. But Paul Mazursky, when I saw that, I was, like, “Oh my god,” because it had a naturalism that not many funny movies I loved had, but it still had this edge of observation and humour. But the edges were really soft. The dialogue felt very soft to me, and when I saw ‘Bob & Carol & Ted & Alice’ I just fucking lost my shit. That really shaped the way I’ve written. That and ‘Enlightened’, the Mike White show. Those were the two things I saw in my early twenties where I was, like, “Okay, this is the type of writing I would love to do.”

L — I think that the idea that you quote Paul Mazursky is fantastic. I love that director. There was another Paul that I love, which was Paul Bartel, and there is one movie called ‘Scenes from the Class Struggle in Beverly Hills’ that I think you’ll love very much.
L — I’m offering you an idea to watch the movie, love the movie, and maybe remake the movie, because it’s one of the great movies of the late ’80s, and it’s very Jordan Firstman, so watch that.
J — Okay, I want to watch.

L — Now that you’ve done ‘Club Kid’, and since I saw the movie, I don’t think of you as an actor or as a comedian anymore. I think of you as a director, and I think that will be forever. Did you want to be a director forever?
J — No, I think I would say a film-maker. I hate to say it, but film-maker feels like the right term to me.

L — No darling, that’s wrong. “Directed by” is the most noble thing you can think of when you go to the cinema. “Directed by John Ford.” He’s a director, and the director is the quintessential personality of cinema.
J — The person that gets all the autonomy is the director, but I think the writing is so important, and they very rarely write.
L — How do we deal with the fact that many of the greatest directors of all time, and many of the greatest movies, have been directed by directors who didn’t write?
J — I don’t know how to deal with that.
L — Would you work with a script that you’ve been handed but didn’t write yourself?
J — It’s tough for me. I’m new right now. It doesn’t feel so appealing to me. I’m definitely getting scripts sent to me but they just don’t do it for me.

L — I think the fact that you aren’t getting any good scripts is normal, because 90 percent of scripts are not good, or not good enough: they are too formulaic, they don’t have a real point of view, they are derivative, and so on. But that has been the same since forever. When you meet a great writer with a great script, that’s the moment in which you, as a director, are completely freed. So, I want Jordan Firstman to consider the possibility of working with a writer in the future, and to be a director: “Directed by Jordan Firstman.”
J — I’m open to it right now.
L — I don’t think you’re open to it.
J — I’m open to a world where I’m open to it.
L — When you were in Cannes, did you think, “Damn it. Why didn’t they put me in the competition?”
J — No, I promise you. Not for one second. How could I feel anything but, “What the fuck is happening?”
L — Were you upset that you didn’t win Un Certain Regard?
J — I think I was upset for three hours.

J — Genuinely, I was bummed for three hours. But you know, I understood the decision. You know, you can never really be sad about losing something. I’ll probably say this 20 more times in the course of the next year, but this is the first time I’m saying it: genuinely, when we wrapped production on ‘Club Kid’, I felt so lucky for the experience and what it opened up in me and for getting to not only do it but do it my way, that everything else feels like a bonus.
L — How will you prepare yourself for the award season?

J — Stay in the gym. Try not to drink. I want to figure out how to be myself, but not say anything too outlandish. I want to stay on people’s good sides. I don’t know, it’s gonna be my first release, so I just…I want to stay present, I want to stay alert, I want to be able to do this again, so I want to do everything I can to ensure that I’m able to, you know, make another movie the way I want to make it.
L — Can I give you a tiny little bit of advice? I don’t want it to sound paternalistic, or like I’m patronising you, though.
L — Shoot your next movie within the next ten months.
J — Can you give me an extension…
L — Twelve months, 14 max.
J — Okay, 14 months from now.
L — It means basically you being on set in March. Can you do that?
L — Are you writing something?
J — I am. I have the idea, but I don’t want to give a timeline.
L — All the people who are reading this interview are completely rooting for you and want you to keep going without the industry timelines. Make a movie in a year.
J — I am going to try to go as fast as I can. But I want it to be good. I want to have time to rewrite it and work on it. You know what I mean.
L — I do, absolutely. Jordan, have you ever used your smile as a weapon?
L — When did you realise your smile was a weapon?
J — I think honestly pretty young, and I definitely used it romantically a lot in my twenties.
L — Have you ghosted lovers that you charmed with your smile?
J — I’m not a ghoster, believe it or not. I’m pretty open, and I think I’m very clear with what I’m looking for in people.
L — Let’s enact a scenario where you break up with me.
J — I have had so much fun spending time with you, and I hope we can keep spending time. I think romantically I’m not really looking for this right now, but I think you’re amazing.
L — What are you looking for?

J — I don’t know, I don’t know, but I think I just need to keep my options open right now, and I hope we can still hang out. I’m a huge fan of everything you do. I think you’re so handsome and beautiful, and I know I really believe that. I swear, Luca, I really believe this.
L — Jordan, you are full of shit. And you’re using the smile. This is on the record: he’s using the smile to kill me!
J — That is how I would do it. Don’t you think that was a very kind way to break up with someone?
L — No, I think it’s formulaic. It’s a bad script.
J — I believed it, though.
L — It was a very good improvisation. I think the people will love it.

Photographic assistance by Jacopo Vimercati and Nicolò Rampazzo. Digital operation by Emanuele de Rossi. Styling assistance by Ilaria Taccini. Hair by Alessandro Rebecchi at Artlist Paris. Tailoring by Camilla Masi. Set design by Flavia Manacorda. Production by Frenesy.

items.title: Palace Built Itself a Palace For Its London Flagship (Exclusive)
items.description: Real streetwear heads will know this legendary lore: in the late 2000s, a dilapidated, slightly skuzzy South London flat — affectionately nicknamed “the Palace,” and occupied by the Palace Wayward Boys Choir skate gang — became the unlikely origin point for wh
items.author: Chris Erik Thomas
paragraphs: Real streetwear heads will know this legendary lore: in the late 2000s, a dilapidated, slightly skuzzy South London flat — affectionately nicknamed “the Palace,” and occupied by the Palace Wayward Boys Choir skate gang — became the unlikely origin point for what’s become one of Britain’s biggest brands.
The brand, if you hadn’t already sussed it out, is Palace Skateboards.

It’s been 17 years since co-founders Lev Tanju and Gareth Skewis first launched the label, churning out small-batch skate decks and T-shirts riffing on luxury fashion house logos, and a lot has changed. Including, crucially, their digs. On November 5, Palace opens the doors to a new flagship that lives up to the brand’s name: the sprawling 8 Poland Street location occupies nearly 2,700 square feet and feels as much a store as a cultural landmark.

Inside, an amalgamation of design inspirations — from the British Museum to English churches to historic local skate spots — adds up to something that feels fit for the legacy Palace has built in less than two decades. Visitors will find archival imagery next to stained-glass windows, alongside the brand’s signature Tri-Ferg transformed into a raw oak bench and stool.

And product, of course. So, so much product. Alongside its regular wares and skate decks, Palace went all out for its London launch: its surprise banger of a Burberry collaboration will be exclusively available in-store, alongside an extra set of store-exclusive merch centered around the number 8 — a nod to the location’s address, rotated 90 degrees to become an infinite symbol.

The Poland Street store may sit within the same city limits as the original crash pad in Waterloo, but these two points in the brand’s history feel worlds apart. Palace may have stores all around the world, but there’s something about growing into its own in the city it calls home that feels fitting, especially as it nears its 18th anniversary. Ahead of the flagship store’s launch, we caught up with Tanju to talk about paying architectural homage to the London skate scene and how that legendary Burberry link-up actually happened.
This interview has been condensed and edited.
Why frame a skate shop as a museum, and how do you keep it from feeling precious or inaccessible for the kids who actually skate?
