items.title: With Michigan Victory, Abdul El-Sayed Becomes Nation's First Muslim Senator
items.description: All eyes were on Michigan on Tuesday, as the state’s 2026 midterm election led to a national debate over the Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers. As polls closed at 8 p.m. local time (four of Michigan’s northwestern counties
items.author: Eve Batey
paragraphs: All eyes were on Michigan on Tuesday, as the state’s 2026 midterm election led to a national debate over the Senate race between Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers. As polls closed at 8 p.m. local time (four of Michigan’s northwestern counties observe Central Time, while the rest are on Eastern), El-Sayed was projected to win—a triumph that, if confirmed, would move the Democratic Party toward its predicted goal of flipping the Senate. Early Wednesday morning, the Associated Press confirmed El-Sayed's victory, making him the nation’s first Muslim senator.
“You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed told supporters at a rally in Detroit on Wednesday. “Thank you. This is all yours.”

The battleground state’s 13 seats in the House of Representatives are also up for grabs in 2026. Key races include the Fourth Congressional District, where Democrat Sean McCann is neck and neck with Republican incumbent Bill Huizenga. In the Seventh District, Democratic challenger William Lawrence declared victory against Republican incumbent Tom Barrett on his Facebook account; and in the 10th District, it’s between Republican candidate Michael Bouchard Jr. and Democratic candidate Christina Hines.

Also at stake was the governor’s house, with the current governor, Democrat Gretchen Whitmer, at the end of her second of two legally allowed terms. Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, a Democrat, defeated Republican US Representative John James, according to the Associated Press.

items.title: Maine Senator Susan Collins Has Reportedly Conceded Race to Democratic Challenger Troy Jackson
items.description: One of the most closely watched states during the run-up to the 2026 midterm elections has been Maine, where incumbent US senator Susan Collins, a Republican, faced a significant threat from upstart candidate Graham Platner. Allegations of misconduct toppled t
items.author: Eve Batey
paragraphs: One of the most closely watched states during the run-up to the 2026 midterm elections has been Maine, where incumbent US senator Susan Collins, a Republican, faced a significant threat from upstart candidate Graham Platner. Allegations of misconduct toppled the Democrat’s campaign, but his replacement, former logger and state senator Troy Jackson, has had a strong showing in the polls, and posed the first actual competition Collins has faced in nearly three decades. A little more than three hours after Maine's poll closure at 8 p.m. ET, Collins reportedly called Jackson to concede the race, even as most news outlets were reporting that the race was still ongoing.

Susan Collins was running for a sixth term, and was the only Republican representing a state President Donald Trump lost in 2024. As votes rolled in on Tuesday and into Wednesday morning, Jackson's lead continued to grow. According to outlets, including Maine broadcast station WMTW, Collins called Jackson shortly after midnight to congratulate him for his win. In an address to supporters early Wednesday, an ebullient Jackson celebrated his win. At the time of publication, the New York Times was forecasting that “Jackson is almost certain to win," and NBC had projected him the winner as well.
“20 minutes or so I spoke to Senator Collins and I thanked her for her service to Maine,” Jackson said. “I wished her and her family well.”
“To every Mainer who voted for her or supported her, you can count on me to be your senator now.”

Elsewhere in Maine, Democrats kept the governor’s office blue, as term-limited governor Janet Mills will be replaced by Democrat Hannah Pingree, the Associated Press said when they called the race Tuesday night. She bested Republican candidate Bobby Charles, according to the AP.

Maine only has two congressional districts, both of which are up for election every two years. The state’s First Congressional District is known as a Democratic stronghold, with Hannah Pingree’s mother, Chellie Pingree, expected to retain the seat she’s held since 2009. Its Second District is considered a battleground region, with former state secretary of state Matthew Dunlap, a Democrat, still locked in a tight race against Republican former governor Paul LePage as of publication time.

items.title: Cynthia Erivo to Play Tupac Shakur's Mother in Snoop Dogg Biopic
items.description: Cynthia Erivo has been tapped to portray Afeni Shakur, the mother of Tupac Shakur, in the upcoming Universal Pictures biopic about Snoop Dogg, as The Hollywood Reporter reports.
items.author: Althea Legaspi
paragraphs: Cynthia Erivo has been tapped to portray Afeni Shakur, the mother of Tupac Shakur, in the upcoming Universal Pictures biopic about Snoop Dogg, as The Hollywood Reporter reports.
Erivo joins a cast that includes Jonathan Daviss, Myles Bullock, Lauren London, Camron Jones, Algee Smith, Tre Hale, Laya DeLeon Hayes, Olly Sholotan, Corey Champagne, Jonica Booth, and SwayvoTwain.

Afeni Shakur was a former Black Panther and political activist, and was the subject of several of her son’s songs, including the 1995 single “Dear Mama.” A year after the song was released, Tupac was gunned down in Las Vegas and died a week later. Afeni Shakur launched the Tupac Amaru Shakur Foundation one year after her son’s death, and oversaw the late rapper’s estate. She died in 2016 at age 69.

Daviss (Outer Banks) stars as Snoop Dogg and Jones (Panic) stars opposite as Tupac Shakur. SwayvoTwain — the musician born Michael D’Angelo Archer II to late legendary artists D’Angelo and Angie Stone — will portray Notorious B.I.G. in the film. Bullock plays Dr. Dre, Hale stars as Suge Knight, London plays Snoop’s mother Beverly Tate, and Laya DeLeon Hayes as Snoop’s wife, Shante.

The Craig Brewer-directed film is currently in production in California and producers include Snoop Dogg and Death Row Pictures president Sara Ramaker, alongside Imagine Entertainment’s Allan Mandelbaum and Brian Grazer, who was behind Eminem’s 8 Mile. The film is expected to arrive in theaters in August 2027.

Erivo’s next upcoming movie is the film adaptation of the Broadway play Prima Facie, for which she also serves as an executive producer. The drama recently premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival. It hits theaters in the U.K. and Ireland on Nov. 13.

She is also starring in upcoming action-thriller Karōshi. The Takashi Doscher-directed and written film hits theaters on Feb. 5. “Every empire fears rebellion,” Erivo teased on Instagram Wednesday, sharing the film’s poster and revealing that its trailer will be released Thursday, Nov. 5.

items.title: The Real Housewives of New York City Recap: Invite Only
items.description: I love it when Real Housewives get arrested on camera, get caught in fraud scams, and return from prison for their fourth DUI and then totally deny having an alcohol problem, straight to Andy Cohen’s ever-improving hair. (Seriously, which devil did he make a d
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: I love it when Real Housewives get arrested on camera, get caught in fraud scams, and return from prison for their fourth DUI and then totally deny having an alcohol problem, straight to Andy Cohen’s ever-improving hair. (Seriously, which devil did he make a deal with?) But this episode has just the kind of low-impact fights that I want to deal with. There is an expanding fight about who has a better fish market, and while Sai has publicly repped Fish Tales in Brooklyn, Daisy has yet to name-drop her preferred seafood purveyor, even as she insists that it’s better and Fish Tales gets their fish from hers. Then we move right on to not being invited to a party. Then we move on to talking about that party in front of the person who wasn’t invited. Take us back to the good old days of petty squabbles and none of this dark legal bullshit.

Well, there is that part where Carole and Erin are walking down the street eating pizza, and someone yells at her about the Epitein Files. Okay. Fine. We’re still dealing with that, but it does give Erin “Mew Mew” Lichy a moment to shine. She needs it after failing to parallel park the most famous jalopy in Manhattan, Carole’s 1996 Jeep Cherokee. Who taught Erin how to parallel park? John Barlow? The two have a little chat in the park about how Carole doesn’t like Sai and then go to get a slice to alleviate their hangovers after Abe’s party the night before. As they’re walking, someone yells at Carole about the Epstein Files and then ducks into a bodega. Erin, a true New Yorker, still has her slice in the grease-splattered paper plate as she goes and yells at the lady that it’s not nice to just shout random accusations about people on the sidewalk. I talk plenty of trash about Erin, but she had her friend’s back more than Bethenny ever would have.

Carole seems a bit unruffled, but in her confessional, it is probably the most emotional we’ve seen her in her long tenure. She is grappling with something that Hailey said, about how her involvement with Ghislaine Maxwell will forever be a footnote to her story. I understand this. Even if Carole thinks that their relationship was minor, because of what Ghislaine did, it’s going to have an outsized impact on Carole for the rest of her life. Despite what you think of Carole and her involvement, it must sting that after all of her accomplishments, she’s going to be stuck with a black mark because of someone else’s evil.

The first part of this episode goes around and checks in on the ladies in their personal environments, which is fascinating. We first watch an argument slowly unfurl between Erin and Abe in front of their absolutely adorable tiny baby, Jack. Abe doesn’t like that Erin scolded him at his party about spilling his drink and not helping with the kids, and Erin is frustrated that none of her children will listen to her. Earlier in the season, it was her daughter, and now it’s one of her sons. I have never parented, so feel free to just put a piece of tape over me and ignore me as Hailey did with the surveillance cameras on her terrace, but if two out of four of the kids (one of whom is still an infant) aren’t listening to her, maybe it has something to do with the way she and Abe parent? I don’t know. She was selling it as if her daughter was really tough, but it seems like she’s struggling in general. I don’t think Erin is a bad mother, but maybe she could use Super Nanny or something?

Next, we see Sai and Jessel go to lunch, and Jessel is bitching about Pavit. Not only is she upset that he isn’t making much money, but she says that he “despises” her. Really? Of all the husbands we have seen on these shows clearly hating their wives, Pavit does not seem to be one of them. I can see how he ignores her. She points out that after the kids are in bed, they’re on their own screens and he doesn’t even say goodnight to her. But despise? I don’t know. Jessel tries to bring this up to her mother, Nilam, who is visiting, but she’s not hearing any of it. Nilam was set up in an arranged marriage, and Jessel says that she’s always taking Pavit’s side. I don’t know about that, but it does seem like she is giving the man in the relationship the right of way and putting it on Jessel to make it work out. Wait, I also did the same thing. Are we both right, or are we both brimming with internalized misogyny? Maybe both? When Jessel tells Nilam that Pavit doesn’t take an interest in her or her career, Nilam points out that Pavit asked Jessel how a meeting went, and she said, “Fine,” and shut it down, so maybe there is enough blame to go around.

Next it’s off to Orville Reddenbacher Village to visit Daisy’s popcorn ceiling and meet her sister Samona, who is the Bizarro World version of Ramona Singer. Samona is visiting from her home in Boca, and Daisy tells us that she and her sister are super close even though they fight all the time, which is exactly what I would expect from Daisy and her sister, Fake Ramona. Daisy is now upset because Samona left her “doctor husband” for a 28-year-old Cuban firefighter. Daisy asks if the “D is that good” and, well, we get to meet Anthony, the Cuban firefighter in question. I can guarantee that, yes, the D is that good, and I fully support Samona and all the decisions she has made in relation to this fire hose. Daisy also asks if she couldn’t have just had an affair, and I think that is a very good question. To paraphrase the Baker’s Wife from Sondheim’s genius Into the Woods: “Have a child for warmth and a baker for bread and a big-dicked Cuban fire man for … whatever.”

On to the gorgeous-looking Crane Club where Erika is going to commit the absolute hate crime of eating a whole pizza on camera while still having a stomach flatter than the Alex Jones thinks the Earth is. She’s upset that they met with a potential surrogate and they might get rejected again, that their embryos aren’t good enough, and that she’ll never have the child she dreamed of. (Wow, this is all very Baker’s Wife.) Her husband, Ankur, is incredibly reassuring, telling her that it will all work out, and of course he thinks that. He’s the billionaire son of a billionaire. He knows that they have the resources and the power and the will and that they can pay their way out of any single problem they might ever face. As if he just wrote a check to heaven itself, Erika gets a text at dinner that their potential surrogate accepted their offer and they’re going to work on implanting an embryo soon. Why did this make me so emotional? We barely know this Erika, so no, I’m not crying, you’re crying.

The more I learn about Erika, the more I love her. She invites the entire cast, minus Daisy, to her birthday party. Daisy, instead, has some dog charity gala she’s at with Samona and Anthony the Hose. Jessel stops by and says she has to leave to go to Erika’s birthday party. She assumes that Daisy knows about it, and Daisy says she wasn’t invited. (She also wasn’t invited to dinner with King Charles and her boss, Martha Stewart.) Then Daisy goes to Erin and asks if she was going to the party. Erin says no, but makes it clear, in that mean girl way of Erin’s, that she was totally invited. Daisy, we know, is someone who likes to be included and likes to be asked to things, even if she can’t go. She’s pissed, but she should have been thinking about all the future invites when she shit all over Daisy’s private island for three days in a row. We see some Insta stories and cellphone footage of Erika’s birthday, with Jessel, Carole, and Hailey all whooping it up. Wait, she had a birthday party during filming, and the crew wasn’t even invited? How did she get away with that? We need to see this party!

When they all convene at the end of the episode for a comedy show in a pizza restaurant (seriously, I have more questions than Anthony the Hose has inches), Carole, Hailey, and Erika are all talking about the party in front of Daisy. Erika could have taken the easy out. Daisy invited her to the gala, and Erika declined, saying it was her birthday. She could have just said, “I didn’t invite you because I knew you had the gala,” but she didn’t. She just lets Daisy sit there and fester in her own juices. I get it. I’m just like Daisy. I hate being left out and have incurable FOMO, and to have to listen to this dispatch while she suffered at Chelsea Piers, objectively the worst event space in Manhattan, at a boring dog benefit with her Floridian sister and her boytoy must be absolute torture.

Just then, in the backyard of a Brooklyn pizza restaurant turned comedy club, they all looked up as a black cat jumped from the roof to the fire escape, scurrying its way up through New York. Daisy wished it were her at that moment. She wanted to scamper away, but also have the best seat in the house. She wants everyone to look at her in awe and want to touch her, but to be so removed that they can’t possibly. She wanted the freedom to go wherever she wants, be invited everywhere, part of every group, but also so aloof that they all wonder what she’s up to when she’s not around. Just as Daisy entered back into her body on that fairy-lit back patio, she wished that she were a cat again because Sai just loped into the joint, and Daisy could tell that she was ready to pounce.

items.title: Dancing With the Stars Recap: We’re All in This Together
items.description: Bibbidi-bobbidi-boo, bitch — it’s “Disney Night”! This week usually feels like a special blend of corporate synergy and childhood nostalgia, but I don’t know, Dancing friends … this evening felt a little lacking in the magic of it all, no? It’s a tough time in
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: Bibbidi-bobbidi-boo, bitch — it’s “Disney Night”! This week usually feels like a special blend of corporate synergy and childhood nostalgia, but I don’t know, Dancing friends … this evening felt a little lacking in the magic of it all, no? It’s a tough time in the season. Everyone’s exhausted physically, mentally, and emotionally — and I’m talking about our dancers and your recapper. Little cracks are starting to show. But people need to lock in. There are only eight couples left and all of them have put in at least a few great routines. Anyone could go home and anyone could win, and that’s both exciting and terrifying if you have personal favorites and a weak stomach.

This season we’re celebrating not just Disney, but Disney on Broadway, which means DWTS has brought in Broadway performers to sing live during some of the routines — Tony Award winner Heather Headley, the original Aida, singing in the ballroom? Bless this show! — and recruited Cynthia Erivo to be our guest judge. She and Bruno match each other’s energy perfectly, and they should go out on the road together. But after all the Disney-and-Broadway fun is over, including our first team dances of the season, we’ll still have to send one couple home. I’m calling on all the Fairy Godmothers right now to not let the elimination break my heart.
Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov
Quickstep // “A Star Is Born” from Hercules

Blast those muscles, ladies — you work hard for them! And it’s what Amber Glenn is doing in her Hercules-inspired Quickstep in which both she and Pasha are playing the titular demigod and trying to out-muscle each other. (She even leads in certain sections.) Amber looks like she’s having fun out there — these two truly seem so happy to be dancing together each week — but the routine is kind of forgettable. The judges knock her for a small misstep, but Carrie Ann still found it “clean, crisp, and smooth.” Amber and Pasha have been on a bit of a plateau these past couple of weeks, but I have faith they’re going to break through on their way to the finals. When these two get the perfect score they deserve, their little blond heads are going to explode and honestly, I’m looking forward to that.
Carrie Ann: 8 // Derek: 9 // Cynthia: 8 // Bruno: 9
Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas
Jive // “You Can Fly! You Can Fly! You Can Fly!” from Peter Pan

Maura describes herself as being “in Tinker-hell this week” with Jive, a style that needs to be fast and sharp and calls for a whole lot of stamina. None of these are Maura’s strengths and she knows it. Now, did I almost tear up when she looked defeated in rehearsal and Mark got right in her face and told her that she could do this? Of course I did; I’m a human woman. Maura is so easy to root for. I also appreciated that instead of Mark playing Peter Pan, the obvious pairing for Maura’s Tinkerbell, he said, Fuck that, I’m that curly-haired diva Captain Hook, because that feels so, so right. Anyway, this Jive is unfortunately lacking in both energy and sharp footwork and is generally kind of sad, but Maura and Mark still manage to get eights.
Carrie Ann: 8 // Derek: 8 // Cynthia: 8 // Bruno: 8
Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik
Contemporary // “Easy As Life” from Aida

I’ve been stoked all week since this performance was announced. Contemporary is Jan’s forte and they’re doing it to Aida? With Heather Headley performing live?! It does not disappoint. Tatyana is so full of passion and emotion when she dances, and that’s exactly what this routine calls for. The musicality here? Off the charts. I don’t give a flying fuck about how far she’s extending her lines, a critique not one but three of our judges used their entire time to harp on. Other people aren’t extending their arms as far as Cynthia Erivo’s nails, and I don’t hear judges complaining. Tatyana and Jan dance so beautifully together, and that they’ve been underscored more than once keeps me up at night. This week, however, Tatyana and Jan give Carrie Ann chills, and I thought she might weep right there at the judges’ table. At least she gets it!
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 8 // Cynthia: 8 // Bruno: 8
Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson
Jazz // “Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious” from Mary Poppins

I am but a simple woman who likes to ooh and ahh from time to time, so yes, the way Harry and Jenna utilize that giant screen behind them to give us a little Mary Poppins magic did, in fact, work for me. Though at times the choreography does seem to highlight Jenna more than Harry, it’s so freaking fun. Harry wanted to pay homage to Dick Van Dyke’s physical comedy in his movement, and he does just that. Also, that toe-touch? I cannot stop thinking about that toe-touch. I don’t want to stop thinking about that toe-touch. That toe-touch is my life now.
Carrie Ann: 10 // Derek: 10 // Cynthia: 10 // Bruno: 10
Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach
Samba // “Under the Sea” from The Little Mermaid

At the beginning of the season, Daniella and Ezra decided the Samba would be a no-go because there would be no way for Ezra to get the classic Samba bounce going. Then they start dancing and Daniella realizes Ezra can do everything she’s asked him to do, so Samba was back on the table. When Ezra talks about how Daniella believed he could do it, so he believed, I did indeed need to bite a pillow. And guess what? He can pull off a Samba, one accompanied by Broadway star Michael James Scott no less. (Also, yes, Ezra looks so much like Prince Eric, it’s wild.) He moves through the classic Samba content — the walks, the rolls, the hip actions — with such ease. There was nothing to worry about here!
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 10 // Cynthia: 9 // Bruno: 9
Julia Stiles and Ezra Sosa
Paso Doble // “Satisfied” from Hamilton

Oof, Julia’s rib injury looks so painful, and it’s flaring up again following a week where you could tell it affected her performance. Her Hamilton Paso Doble is definitely an improvement on the Argentine Tango last week, but you can see her holding back still. Julia nails the intensity of the dance — despite the fact that I wouldn’t necessarily match this dance style with this song, Ezra’s choreography is great — but her shaping leaves a whole lot to be desired. She also has some stumbles with the footwork, but Carrie Ann appreciates how deep Julia is clearly digging to survive each week.
Carrie Ann: 8 // Derek: 8 // Cynthia: 8 // Bruno: 9
Jenna Dewan and Val Chmerkovskiy
Quickstep // “Be Our Guest” from Beauty and the Beast

Jenna invites her Tony-winning partner Steve Kazee to rehearsal for some Broadway-related advice, and I can’t believe Jenna hasn’t danced something to a Once song yet. Make us bawl, Jenna! Quicksteps, unfortunately, aren’t known for being emotional, but they are known for being fast and fun, and this one hits those marks. It’s not the most original or memorable of dances, but it is full of content and so precise and clean. Carrie Ann is amazed at how in sync Jenna and Val were, and Derek is overjoyed at how much they used the entire dance floor in this routine — they were moving. It’s about as technically perfect a Quickstep as you can get.
Carrie Ann: 10 // Derek: 10 // Cynthia: 10 // Bruno: 10
Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold
Waltz // “I See the Light” from Tangled

Connor gets to try out a new piece of fake facial hair for this routine, and I’m beyond happy for him. I hope he saves each one and puts them on a shelf like in a creepy little trophy case. Facial hair aside, his Waltz technique could use some work. Last week, Connor was brimming with confidence; this week, he seems hesitant again in his movement. Derek can really see improvement in the way Connor is articulating his feet and ankles, but his frame remains a rough point. Bruno, too, points out the collapsed frame and lack of sweep in his footwork, but he does find Connor’s dancing “light and bright” and appreciates how honest the connection between Connor and Rylee feels. Speaking of: When Rylee started tearing up talking about how Connor has made this season so great for her? Gah! I’m too emotionally attached to everyone on this show, and it is not going to end well for me.
Carrie Ann: 8 // Derek: 8 // Cynthia: 8 // Bruno: 8
Team Slaytopia: Alfonso with Tatyana and Jan, Amber and Pasha, Maura and Mark, and Julia and Ezra

I feel unmoved by team dances in general, but this one especially is a snooze. Of all the Disney songs you could choose, this team is given “Zoo” from Zootopia 2? I love this team — Tatyana, as one of the lowest scorers of the season, got to choose the members — but this music is so awkward, and everything just looks too slow and a little limp. Amber and Julia are the standouts, but I don’t think anyone will be talking about this routine after tonight.
Carrie Ann: 9 // Derek: 9 // Cynthia: 9 // Bruno: 9
Team Wildcats: Julianne with Connor and Rylee, Harry and Jenna, Ezra and Daniella, and Jenna and Val

Honestly, DWTS should hire Connor Wood to be a team captain every season from now on. He hypes up every single person on his team and also makes the stakes very clear: “We can’t drop Julianne! There’s no show without Julianne!” Even without Connor, you give a team “We’re All in This Together” from High School Musical and more often than not, they’re going to crush it. It’s bright and fun and goofy, and they don’t drop Julianne.
Carrie Ann: 10 // Derek: 10 // Cynthia: 10 // Bruno: 10

The team dances don’t affect the leaderboard too much — the three couples at the bottom were all on the same team anyway — but they do give Julianne Hough an opportunity to make a solid “No thank you, Alfonso” joke and it’s almost enough to make me forget whatever is happening with her bangs tonight. Almost. So, alas, you had to know it is most likely going to be someone from Team Slaytopia going home tonight, and it is: Julia Stiles and Ezra Sosa are eliminated from the competition. It never looked like she really got into the groove of this whole thing, but it does seem like she got a lot out of it emotionally. May her ribs take time to rest and heal.

items.title: Below Deck Recap: Mess With the Bull, Get the Horns
items.description: Deckhand Matt may just be the most audacious toe-stepper to debut in this franchise since Alesia, who, in the last season of Down Under, managed to rearrange the interior team according to her own proclivities. Matt might be able to pull a similar move and est
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: Deckhand Matt may just be the most audacious toe-stepper to debut in this franchise since Alesia, who, in the last season of Down Under, managed to rearrange the interior team according to her own proclivities. Matt might be able to pull a similar move and establish himself as bosun — Joe Bradley, watch and weep — if Alex doesn’t get his ass up and work.

That said, the second charter of the season is rough for every department. Last week, I wrote that Fraser was dropping his service standards, but toward the end of the charter, it was mostly the guests’ unappeasable attitudes that were ruining the vibe. Well, let us not generalize: Acro-yoga inventor Jason is a good time. All he wants to do is spin grown men in the air. He even gets to “fly” Kerry, who looks extremely uncomfortable the entire time but is game enough to help secure a good tip. We know Jason is a nice guy because, leaving the boat, he says with ignorant bliss: “I’m going to miss the crew! We’re gonna hang out with them after; they love us.” Sir, you will never see these people again.

This week’s episode picks up right where we left off with steam coming out of Kerry’s ears after Alex doesn’t react quickly enough to Sen dropping the Jet Ski strap in the water. Matt says they lost the only strap they had onboard, which I found hard to believe. Surely, things must fall into the ocean all the time? To make matters worse, Alex screws up again when Kerry, Fraser, and Kaylee leave with the guests for an excursion at the elephant sanctuary. They get tendered there, and before leaving, Kerry asks Alex to make sure they didn’t leave anything behind. Alex gives him a go-ahead, not realizing he forgot to pack towels. Fraser notices it when they’re already on the way. “I’m gonna end up getting sacked,” Alex laments when he gets Kerry’s furious text. Alex sends Matt over with the towels, and even though Matt sprints down the dock where the guests are waiting — it’s only 15 minutes, but to these people, it might as well be 15 hours — Kerry still yells at him. The captain scolds him with his favorite expression: He’ll “have to make changes” if the team doesn’t get their act together. One of the guests chuckles with evil delight when Kerry confirms that someone got in trouble.

Back on the boat, Matt is angry about having taken the heat for Alex’s mistake. He muses that Alex probably sent him because Alex didn’t want to get chewed out again so soon after the Jet Ski strap fiasco. All of this adds to Matt’s frustration with the bosun. Earlier, while putting out the slide, he complained to Sen and James that if working on deck is like driving a car, he is a “race car driver” while Alex “rides horses.” In a confessional, he says that the job is “not that hard” and Alex should be able to “do it in his sleep.” This is aggravating because Matt’s arrogance is extremely annoying, and Alex keeps giving him reasons to talk.

Still, Alex at least takes full accountability for his mistakes. He apologizes to the captain for underperforming and explains, as he did to Matt, that the sleep deprivation is getting to him. Kerry worries Alex won’t be able to manage the stress of the job, but gradually, Alex turns things around. He comes up with a solution for the lost Jet Ski strap by MacGyvering an old one he found in the laz. He tests it out with the deck team and one non-cast engineer; they nearly drop the Jet Ski in the water, but manage to haul it up. The next day, when Kerry sees the Jet Ski safely tied down on the sun deck, he praises Alex for a job well done. Later, heading into a windy marina with strong tides, Alex leads a smooth, competent docking. Kerry is relieved to see Alex prove that he does have what it takes, even if he’s on his back foot for now.

Kerry has his doubts, especially after talking with Matt when they return from the excursion. Matt comes up to the wheelhouse to apologize for the deck’s screw-ups and to say that Alex is falling short. In no uncertain terms, he tells the captain that he is ready to “step up” should he need to. Kerry appreciates the talk and tells Matt he’ll think it over, but he doesn’t seem at all disturbed by Matt’s shameless attempt at a coup d’état. Matt’s frustrations are understandable, but there are a hundred other approaches he could take, not least among them having an open discussion with Alex. The bosun has reassured his team time and again that he is open to collaboration and feedback, and rather than take that to heart, Matt is content to stab him in the back.

Of course, that’s because Matt is not really concerned with the success of the team — he just wants to be the loudest voice on deck. As they’re hauling the anchor to depart for the marina, he repeatedly asks Sen to take down the anchor ball before the anchor has been locked in. Sen insists on waiting until Alex is done guiding the chain up, “so [Alex’s] hand doesn’t get chopped.” Matt keeps pushing, but Sen holds her own and waits until Alex is done, as she said she would. In a confessional, she says that Matt is “ignorant, arrogant, and a manchild,” while Matt insists that as a green deckie, she should do as she’s told and not talk back. That’s how he puts it, which is as red a flag as I’ve seen when it comes to the way a man speaks to and about women.

Kaylee, bless her, is hoping Matt won’t be another “lesson” in her life. “I’m sick of lessons!” she pleads. To his coworkers, Matt jokes that having a captain is like having a girlfriend: “You can be nice to her for three years, then you cheat once…” Rainbeau gets it: She tells Moe that her current boyfriend is the only one she has never cheated on. Later on, after the guests have left, this cheating convention makes Kaylee nervous. Rainbeau asks to sit next to Matt at dinner, so she can “get to know him better.” Probably not thinking much of it, Matt agrees. Later Rainbeau tells Kaylee, in her weird fake English accent, that she hopes it’s okay that she asked to sit next to “her man.” This puts Kaylee in a bad position: If she says she does care, she comes off looking like a jealous type, which she is, because she’s been cheated on in the past. The stress makes her cry. Oh, Kaylee. It’s been four days.

Rosa reassures Kaylee that she’s not crazy for being jealous of Rainbeau. Regardless of how thoughtlessly Rainbeau might be acting, Rosa has had it out for her since day one. Rainbeau is trying her best to connect with Rosa, but she feels like Rosa runs hot and cold. At least when it comes to James, Rosa has put in a more explicit effort. After Kaylee tells her that James has a thing with a girl at home, Rosa asks him explicitly if he is seeing someone. James replies that he is “fully single,” which is good enough for Rosa, but should set off alarms. Where is my red button? Fully single? Last week, he told us that he was in an open relationship with ground rules that include no cuddling! It’s starting to look like it’ll be Rosa, not Kaylee, who will be taught a lesson, if she can find it in herself to speak more than two words to James.

Still, out of all of this drama, it is probably Moe who has the worst charter. He makes mistakes, it’s true, but as Fraser says to Kerry, it also seems like the guests decided before they came onboard that they would take issue with the food. Kerry offers to have dinner with the guests on their last night, hoping his presence will temper their complaints. The last dinner is a “big deal” because it’s Melani’s birthday, and Melani has proved to be nothing but understanding and flexible, ha, ha. She calls a meeting with Fraser, Moe, and Carolyn — it’s amazing how the most difficult guests are almost never the primary — to go over the menu. When Moe offers to make her a birthday cake, she says she would prefer a cheese course instead. I’m sorry to anyone out there who “hates cake,” but that’s as strong an indicator of a rancid personality as hating dogs or children.

Moe’s military training prepared him to keep cool under pressure. He turns out two beautiful courses, though he forgets to include the glass noodles Carolyn had requested during their meeting. Worse, he puts a dollop of strawberry jam in Melani’s cheese plate dessert. Melani is, as we’ll all remember, allergic to strawberries. Seeing the cheese plates before they went out, Fraser suggested they add some jam, but neither he nor Moe remembered the allergy in time. It’s a silly mistake, and Melani is, of course, rude when Rainbeau comes to take away her jam dish. “They’re trying to kill me,” she says, but doesn’t throw as big of a tantrum as I expected. Apparently, she cares less about a potential anaphylactic reaction than she does about not having her bedside wine.

Kerry’s presence at dinner works well as a complaint-shield, but the guests resume their shit-talking as soon as they’re back in their cabins. Carolyn is annoyed that Moe came up to the dinner table in his blue uniform, which she calls “a dirty T-shirt.” I’m sorry, lady; he didn’t have time to change because he was busy making you food. “Dinner sucked,” Robby says, sounding like a kid who was forced to eat broccoli. The next morning, Robby talks to Fraser about the noodles. Fraser was in the meeting with Carolyn and Melani, too, and he also seems to have forgotten about the request. He apologizes and encourages Moe to do the same. When he does, Moe is met with a lukewarm “It’s okay.”

Amazingly, given how much, how often, and how stridently they complained, the guests leave a whopping $33,333 tip. It might seem like an act of generosity, but I think the really difficult guests leave huge tips not because they want to make up for being difficult, but because they want to show off their wealth. At the tip meeting, Kerry acknowledges it was a rough charter for Moe — leaving the dock, Robby says that he had “a little problem with the food here and there” — and for the deck team, and they probably don’t deserve such a fat tip. If that’s so, it makes no difference to the crew, who are each happy to be $2,777 richer.

Before going out, Moe talks with his teenage daughter on the phone. He tells us that as a girl dad, he feels protective over young women; we’ve watched him develop a loving relationship with the stews. That’s probably why he gets so aggravated when, leaving for their night out, a random drunken douchebag starts messing with the girls. They mostly ignore him and then ask him to leave, but he keeps trailing them. So, while all the other men in the crew stand around doing nothing, Moe steps in to tell the guy to leave — once calmly, then more aggressively — and then takes off his belt and wraps it around his hand. The episode ends on a “to be continued” cliffhanger, but we all know that Moe won’t actually get into a physical fight with these people.

items.title: The Gilded Age Season-Premiere Recap: Love in This Club
items.description: Sign up for The Gilded Age Club, a subscriber-exclusive newsletter where writers and editors obsess over season four.
items.author: Alice Burton
paragraphs: Sign up for The Gilded Age Club, a subscriber-exclusive newsletter where writers and editors obsess over season four.

The Gilded Age is alive this season. People are out there doing things and having human emotions. I am thrilled. They’ve been sitting in parlors having sedate conversations for three seasons, and now the winds of change seem to be upon our characters. But also if you, like me, were staring bewildered at some of the cast and remembering them along the lines of “Oh, there’s Bertha’s daughter,” then allow me to provide a refresher.

The Russells have been fully accepted by society but are falling apart as a family. George is shot near the end of the season but survives and believes his old second-in-command, Mr. Clay, was involved in the shooting. George moves out of the Russell home because he is furious with Bertha for manipulating their children for her own ends (George is being a butt). William Kirkland and Peggy are engaged. Oscar and Enid Winterton are engaged. Larry and Marian get engaged, then break up, then get back together. “Bertha’s daughter” is Gladys, married to Hector, and she is pregnant and happy about it. Jack (“Clock Twink”) buys an expensive house and is moving up in the world thanks to his alarm-clock invention.

Everything seemed very wrapped up at the end of season three, minus George’s temper tantrum. Fortunately, though, we’re shoved right into some drama at the top of the first episode. This show has always suffered from an overly stilted atmosphere, so I appreciate anything that breathes life into it. Enter Oscar and Enid’s wedding.

Yes, the show tries to trick us into thinking it’s Marian and Larry, but little did the show know that I did not remember Larian got back together last season. Enid and Oscar are having their lavender wedding, which is really a best-case scenario for Oscar. Enid knows what she’s getting into, and the only fear here is that she falls in love with the gay guy she’s married to. A real Judy Garland move.

Gladys’s pregnancy has moved into terrifying 1880s childbirth. Bertha is with her at Gladys’s English ducal estate, as is her lady’s maid, Adelheid. Gladys screams, and Adelheid tells her to “be strong.” I’d say this isn’t helpful, but when my wife gave birth, I mainly contributed by telling her she was crushing it. Even at the time, I knew this wasn’t a top move. Gladys is in danger because the baby is breech (ah!), and the doctor tells Hector the Duke that it may come down to saving Gladys or the baby. Hector’s sister, Lady Sarah, says, “The child, surely” (Sarah!), but Hector fortunately says, if it comes down to it, to save the Duchess. A low bar but great job, Hector — you cleared it.

The baby is alive and Gladys is alive. She doesn’t seem nearly wrecked enough for having delivered a breech baby, but then Adelheid finds a giant amount of blood in the sheets (this is par for the course for a period drama). I really thought they might kill off Gladys, but the doctor performs a hysterectomy, so instead the drama is that she wants a big family but now will only have one child. At least it’s a boy, right, British aristocracy? Hector has to tell Gladys about this because why would they have talked to her about it before? Why would the doctor communicate with her at all? No, I’d be surprised, but a main plot of the 1970’s smash hit Love Story is that the girl has terminal cancer and the doctor tells her husband, and the husband doesn’t tell her. Hector doesn’t tell Gladys right away, but she is recovering from a near-death experience, so I’m giving him a pass until next week.

At the Oscar-Enid wedding, Agnes is delighted that Oscar is marrying a woman but particularly that he’s marrying a wealthy woman. The Ada and Agnes household will soon be entertaining the president, who is unfortunately Grover Cleveland. As a Cleveland hater, I was 100 percent thrilled when Peggy stopped by and mentioned that he sucks and she wrote about it for the paper. Ada asks Peggy to send her the article, then says she will not provide any more funds for Agnes to keep upgrading the event. Agnes is exasperated because he is still the president. Et tu, Agnes? Would you visit the White House after your soccer team won, Agnes? (Yes.) Side note, who is this new and hilarious footman? He’s anyone with anxiety clearing glasses at an event. “I can …? Unless you’re not done?” Bannister has to tell him clearing glasses is a silent event. But what if they’re not done, Bannister? This is Erin and the pens all over again.

Things seem to be going well for Peggy. Suspiciously well. What invisible ax is about to fall on our enterprising journalist? Right now her biggest foe is her seemingly reformed mother-in-law, who is not being as much of an overt asshole anymore but is now tormenting Peggy through overinvolvement in the wedding plans. She invites Peggy and Dorothy to join her ladies’ club, the Daughters of Friendship, then schedules a hair appointment for Peggy without asking. Could Peggy say, “I’m sorry, I have plans already,” i.e., “I have to meet with my publisher to discuss publicity for my book”? Yes, she could. But she does not. Maybe because you don’t say no to Phylicia Rashad.

Back to Marian and Larry. So yes, they got back together at the end of last season, but apparently, they “couldn’t get it right,” and he’s been away in Chicago until this wedding. Marian says they have both moved on. This is vague and unconvincing, Marian. Oscar and Enid invite her to the after-party downtown. Oscar and his soul patch say Marian should think of it as an adventure. She agrees to go and changes into something sleeveless. Larry shows up and says he’s missed her. Aw, I like these two kids. There’s been a supreme lack of chemistry on this show as of late, especially with the Russell parents fighting. I am pro–these two. They dance to “a kind of a mazurka,” and we see Oscar and Enid doing the best choreography I’ve ever seen in my life. Why didn’t I do this at my wedding? Are Oscar and Enid the best pairing on the show now?

Marian and Larry have a slow-motion dance moment, and when they get into the same carriage after, you’re like, Are they gonna make out? The vibe is more Are they gonna bang? but this is The Gilded Age and not Bridgerton, so I set my expectations accordingly. The carriage horses get spooked by the storm, and a wheel breaks. The two run to a hotel (ooooooooooooooooo) and go to their separate rooms. You think, Wait, they’re not gonna bang? No, they’re gonna bang. Why else would this hotel moment happen? I’ve read fanfic. Larry obviously knocks on the door as soon as Marian is down to her undergarments. He says he wanted to make sure she was all right, which is 1880s for “u up?” We see them make out through gauzy curtains, and that’s all this show will give us. Fine.

The next morning, Marian is racked with guilt and tells Larry she is probably ruined. Larry starts crying. Wow, what is this, my Christian high school? Peggy comes over to talk about getting the first printing of her book. Ada says they’ll have to put a plaque on the house saying she once lived there. Aw, that’s nice, Ada. Marian pulls Peggy aside so she can tell her she messed up, to which Peggy responds that Marian’s being too hard on herself because Peggy is a good friend. Marian says she is not who she thought she was. Relatable. It’s easy to judge other people until you also fuck up. No one’s “the kind of person” to do something. They’re just a person.

After the after-party (I do hope there was also an after-after-party), Oscar and Enid return home, still mazurka-ing and still drunk. They decide to define what society means to them and start holding a salon at their home. Enid low-key propositions Oscar, who similarly low-key says “no.” Enid! Don’t mess up this sadly necessary situation for yourself! Just find a dude you like who also likes ladies. Agnes later finds out about Enid’s past as the help but seems to get over it when Enid offers to front the rest of the cost for the presidential hosting.

And what of George? George is being extremely unpleasant toward everyone and seems to be moving toward a breakdown. He’s mad about Rockefeller, he’s mad about Bertha, he’s mad about Chicago and steel, he’s mad about Grover Cleveland (but not for the right reasons). The sexily confident robber baron is now the fuming, impossible-to-deal-with robber baron who hasn’t kissed his wife in way too long, and I am annoyed about it. Bertha is coming home, and he is moving back to the club. The Pinkerton detectives are possibly closing in on two suspects in the assassination attempt. If one of these suspects is Emma Goldman, then I want her to get away.

I know all the Clock Twink fans have been waiting, and I’m sorry to give him short shrift, but Clock Twink is not at the top of my list. He’s very cute! But his story line is usually isolated from all other events. We learn that Jack has invented an electric mixer with varied speeds, making it different from others on the market. The businessmen he talks with are obsessed with what school everyone went to because they can’t move past that part of their lives, so Jack feels awkward. Also, he doesn’t know how to eat an artichoke, and they are judgy about it. Bannister tells him he can teach Jack how to move in society. It’s very Barney teaching Vivian which fork to use. Bridget is frustrated because she thinks Jack is going to marry some society woman. I do like how we initially dealt with Bertha’s forced entrée into society, and now we’re seeing it in season four from Jack’s perspective. Enid snuck in there as a former servant, but Jack has to negotiate past all the fraternity bullshit purely based on having really good ideas. Will he triumph and retain his doe-eyed charm? One can only hope.
Gossip Items for Mrs. Astor’s Next Ball
• (Is Mrs. Astor still hosting balls?)
• Can someone forcibly shave Oscar’s soul patch, and can it be Mamie Fish who does it?
• Do we all have to learn the mazurka? It seems fun, so we should.
➼ What do you think of Marian and Larry?
We know you have thoughts. Comment your response below for a chance to be featured in The Gilded Age Club newsletter.
Sign up for The Gilded Age Club here or below to continue discussing season four with writers and editors from Vulture, The Cut, and all across New York Magazine.
