items.title: Big Daddy: How Jordan Firstman Turned ‘Club Kid’ Into a Glorious, Gay, Oscar-Worthy Crowdpleaser
items.description: It’s 3 p.m. at the Sunset Tower Hotel, the purgatory hour between lunch and dinner at one of Hollywood’s favorite places to hammer out deals and gaze at stars.
items.author: Matt Donnelly
paragraphs: It’s 3 p.m. at the Sunset Tower Hotel, the purgatory hour between lunch and dinner at one of Hollywood’s favorite places to hammer out deals and gaze at stars.

Jordan Firstman decides it’s late enough in the day for his first Aperol spritz, which leads to some reminiscing. It was a decade ago that über-producer Greg Berlanti invited the then-25-year-old Firstman to the Tower Bar to discuss the trajectory of his career. Berlanti, who became the showrunner of “Dawson’s Creek” at age 27, has served as a coach for more than one young queer creator, and Firstman had just sold a series to the cable channel Sundance TV, based on his romantic intergenerational short film “Call Your Father.” He was getting pushback from the network about casting a 50-year-old out gay actor in the lead.

“He wasn’t an unknown; he was a great working actor,” Firstman recalls, declining to give his name. “The studio was like, ‘We would love to cast a gay actor, but there’s just no one that even touches the level of fame we need to justify you doing the show at this budget.’”

Firstman stabs Aperol-soaked ice with his straw, tensing at the memory. “I got to a place where I told them, ‘I’m not doing this if the actor isn’t gay.’ I was a little bit threatening, like, ‘You guys don’t want to look homophobic.’” Sundance TV ended up passing on the show, prompting Berlanti to attempt to rescue it for the nascent HBO Max. It would languish there for years, and then disappear altogether in that company’s revolving door of mergers and executive changes.
My, how times have changed.

Firstman, 35, does not resemble the typical filmmaker whose career launched into the stratosphere out of the Cannes Film Festival. His baggy jeans, chest-hugging polo and Oakley raver sunglasses lend themselves better to the hipster neighborhood of Silver Lake. (Not coincidentally, that’s the setting of Rachel Sennott’s HBO comedy “I Love L.A.,” on which he co-stars as a stylist and BFF to Sennott’s aspiring talent manager, Maia.) Impishness is Firstman’s trademark — he’s all easy crooked smiles and bouncing brown curls. That quality is what’s made his “Internet Gay” persona travel so readily — as evidenced by his more than 1 million followers on Instagram and TikTok. Yet in May, Firstman took the French Riviera by storm with “Club Kid” — his feature debut as a writer-director and first turn as a leading man on the big screen — where the project inspired a heated bidding war. Indie giant A24 beat out Focus Features, Searchlight, Netflix and Mubi for a global rights deal worth $17 million, instantly solidifying Firstman as a force to be reckoned with.

“Club Kid” tells the story of nightlife promoter Peter (Firstman), who has blinked and lost 10 years of his life to hard partying (ketamine, cocaine and GHB are supporting characters in the film), a circuit of on-demand lovers and a deep indulgence in modern queer life in New York City. Depression and low self-esteem hover over Peter like buzzing drones, swatted away by late nights and early mornings and Uber Eats and laptop porn. That cycle is disrupted when 10-year-old Arlo (newcomer Reggie Absolom) shows up at the door of Peter’s SoHo apartment announcing he is his son. Both father and child are saved and tested in equal parts, as we learn that truly happy endings never come home with us from the club.

The magic trick of “Club Kid” is Firstman’s ability to sell a broad, humorous story about the kind of love that fundamentally changes us — all while being firmly rooted in the digital, unapologetically gay culture that formed his artistic sensibilities. Firstman is the creative love child of Judd Apatow and Nicole Holofcener, delivered unto a Gen Z cohort who’ve become obsessed with watching movies in theaters.

“It’s been amazing to see the kinds of people that relate to this film, but it really is a movie about growth,” says Firstman. “In Telluride, I watched a 75-year-old conservative man leave the theater in tears. Then we took it to the New York Film Festival, which I was very nervous to do, and showed it to the 35-year-olds who do drugs. I built the story to work on levels, with the top being a layer of warmth that feels like a hug. I explore some of my more transgressive ideas beneath the surface. If you don’t get it, there’s still a story that will make you laugh and feel something.”

For those not familiar with Firstman, he’ll seem like an overnight sensation. To others, he’s a veteran comedic force for the chronically online. From the tiny town of Northport on the North Shore of Long Island, Firstman made the pilgrimage to Manhattan that countless hopeful queer people had before him. While building his social following with razor-sharp snark, Firstman worked in writers’ rooms for cult comedy series such as “The Other Two,” “Search Party” and “Big Mouth.” He also wrote a now-legendary sketch for Aubrey Plaza when she hosted the 2020 Independent Spirit Awards, highlighting gay representation among that year’s nominees that might not be obvious to the straight eye; it ended up becoming a tribute to an astonished Laura Dern, who tearfully stood up and cheered.
Starting out, Firstman didn’t dare dream of ascending the stairs to the Grand Palais or carving a path to the Oscars stage.

“It was the era of the TV auteurs,” he says of his early idols. “Phoebe Waller-Bridge, Donald Glover, Lena Dunham: I had a voice and felt confident I could do that. They are storytellers. The directing part has always been scary to me, because I’m not as versed in images. I’m the person at the museum who has to ask why the painting is good. Words are the way I get my point across.”

Firstman overcame that fear to shoot “Club Kid” in just 26 days last year. With a production budget just shy of $5 million, Firstman sacrificed his own fees as writer, director and star in exchange for two nonnegotiables: There had to be a pivotal location shoot in London, and the movie had to be shot on pricey film stock — a decision he defends with the weariness of a seasoned auteur.

“That was vital; we shot on 35mm. We want prints of this movie made,” he says with a kind of reverence. Not for his own ego, but for his vision of how “Club Kid” needs to exist in the world of cinema. Two-time Oscar nominee and longtime Firstman mentor Richard LaGravenese (“The Fisher King,” “Behind the Candelabra”) isn’t surprised the debut director is calling his own shots.

“What makes Jordan special is that, like any good artist, you don’t wait for an invitation,” LaGravenese says. “You create the space for yourself in the culture. He’s done it by sticking to who he is.”

When I spoke with Firstman at Cannes after “Club Kid” exploded, he told me that the script began as a frothy experiment meant to evoke the dreamy wish-fulfillment films of the early aughts like “Uptown Girls,” starring Brittany Murphy, and “Big Daddy” from Adam Sandler. “That’s how I was pitching it, and once I started writing, it got a little ‘Kramer vs. Kramer,’” he said.

The movie also had to be decidedly, gloriously gay. It’s not lost on Firstman that “Club Kid” sits alongside other 2026 releases that represent some of the most elevated queer stories that mainstream Hollywood has produced in years, with several of them sitting in the awards conversation with Firstman’s film: Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s “La Bola Negra,” Andrew Scott’s tearjerker “Elsinore,” Jane Schoenbrun’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” and Lukas Dhont’s fellow Cannes player “Coward.” Queerness is integral to these movies, but not exclusively the point — they are portraits of soldiers propping up unjust wars, artists defying heteronormative conventions to find themselves and, in Firstman’s case, a fading party boy belatedly becoming an adult.

“I feel like there hasn’t been a defined generation of new filmmakers since the Safdie brothers era began,” Firstman says. “Los Javis and Jane and Lukas and I are all around the same age. Our collective is so queer, and people are responding, and the movies are doing well.”

At the Tower Bar, we cave and order french fries to soak up the spritzes. Firstman is recognized by a musclebound music producer dining nearby with a woman of equitable attractiveness. “He’s hot,” Firstman says, “but he’s a really nice guy. And he has a great kid!”

If Firstman is indeed part of a new wave of queer storytellers, some might say it took a minute for him to ingratiate himself to that community. Prior to his Cannes breakthrough, his brand was, well, messy. Firstman excels at highlighting the absurdity of celebrity and the pretension of coastal media types. Last year, he criticized the crossover sensation “Heated Rivalry” for what he called a narrow depiction of gay sex (he said that’s “not how gay people fuck,” and that the show eroticized two closeted athletes falling in love under deep cover). The show’s rabid fans descended, and Firstman made it right by deploying his online instincts and recruiting “Heated Rivalry” star Hudson Williams for a TikTok post satirizing the whole blowup. In the clip, Williams lip-synched Nicki Minaj’s 2015 MTV VMAs acceptance speech, in which she aggressively called out host Miley Cyrus for remarks she’d made about the rapper in an interview (“Miley, what’s good?”). Firstman played Cyrus, claiming she’d been taken out of context. This Minaj-Cyrus exchange also appears in “Club Kid,” as Firstman’s character sells drugs to a group of shrill gay guys locked in a bathroom stall.
Much of the press tour for “Club Kid” has been a reframing of Firstman’s intentions, especially as it relates to his fellow queer people.

“You really can’t try to steer the narrative within the gay community. But I’m speaking to them from my heart, and I feel confident in what I’m showing them. I’m also doing my best to be a good friend, and to protect my cast,” he says. “It’s been amazing seeing messages from people who say they feel seen by the movie — even the judgy-ass bitches in the nightlife community. They were like, ‘You did that.’”

Josh Hutcherson, Firstman’s co-star on “I Love L.A.,” who describes him as his brother, says the filmmaker is “one of the most sensitive people I know. He has an abrasive and controversial mask he wears, and it’s very funny. His humor shakes up the right people. But he’s also got an amazing sensor for humanity.”

That “Club Kid” leads with its heart might confound Firstman observers, but the movie’s sentimental value is why A24 made its big bet. Because on the other side of that LBTGQIA+ embrace is the rest of the moviegoing market, and the eight-figure check cut by the boutique studio means “Club Kid” must leg out at the box office through the holiday season and beyond to reach profitability, after opening in limited release this weekend. Firstman is personally involved in the marketing, recruiting famous DJs to spin at premiere parties in Paris, Rome, London and New York, while rolling out merchandise like “Club Kid” cropped T-shirts that resemble one his character wears in the film (“I Love Björk and Bareback,” it reads).

Some of his peers have suffered the slings and arrows of failed crossovers. In 2022, Universal Pictures backed comedian Billy Eichner’s noble attempt to program a gay romantic comedy for wide audiences in the Apatow-produced “Bros.” That film grossed only $14 million worldwide on a $22 million budget, not accounting for the significant marketing cash the studio spent. While Firstman’s film is quite different, the projects may invite an inevitable comparison.

A24 and Firstman are betting on word-of-mouth, which also has its consequences. Conservative rage-baiters could latch on to “Club Kid” for its depiction of a child spun into the chaos of a druggy NYC underbelly. The film’s 100% Fresh Rotten Tomatoes score (based on 65 reviews), however, is a good indicator that audiences are receiving Firstman’s intended message. After all, the kid in “Club Kid” is often the one doing the child-rearing.

“The world of this movie isn’t sensationalized: I don’t put a positive or negative lens on the party scene. I just try to show these people for their beauty and their flaws and their creativity,” says Firstman. “I wanted to explore what felt universal. A general millennial malaise, like, what are we doing? The pandemic was six years ago, and we still feel like we’re in our 20s — but we’re not. This has permeated our culture. So many friends of mine wanted to stop partying and didn’t know how.”

But for a movie about generational sadness, “Club Kid” is riotously funny, filled with Easter eggs for meme lovers and culture queens. During a dance sequence, Firstman and a friend do choreography to the chant “No arms! No legs! No eyes!,” a reference to a 1998 micro-scandal caused by Claire Danes, who used those words to describe the people she saw in the Philippines while filming the prison drama “Brokedown Palace.” (When a character expresses confusion about the dance, Peter screams, “Google ‘Claire Danes Philippines!’”)

One of the film’s best jokes was sacrificed for a leaner run time, Firstman laments. On his second day of daddy duty, Peter takes little Arlo to brunch at the glitterati staple Balthazar. He asks if his son, born and raised in the U.K., likes the spot because it was founded by another Brit (celebrity chef Keith McNally). Peter jokes that “James Corden isn’t even allowed in here anymore,” referencing a nasty 2022 beef between McNally and the late-night host over the latter’s alleged rudeness to the staff. “Who is James Corden?” the boy asks. Peter sighs with jealousy and tells the kid he’s so lucky not to know.

“If I want a bunch of gays to be screaming the Nicki Minaj speech, the gays will like that. But a straight guy will still get the message — you’re trapped in the bathroom with annoying gays,” Firstman says with a laugh. There’s also the script’s parade of memorable nicknames for drug use, with “Sniffany Haddish” as the moniker for cocaine. Want to mix that with ketamine? Then you’re having “a little Charlie, a little Kirk.” Administering your drugs in the rectum for faster results? That’s a “Benson Boof.”

A millennial born on the tail end of his generation, Firstman grew up with the competitive noise of friends posting their best, most successful lives minute by minute on social media. As the sweet orange liquid in our glasses turns to slush, he says he’s grateful that fame and artistic praise didn’t come so fast or easy. Whatever fate the box office and the Oscars hold for “Club Kid” and Firstman, he’s leveled up as both an artist and a man.

“Life gives you what it gives you when it does,” he says, imagining a world where that Sundance TV show had actually been made. “I don’t know where I’d be now. My voice and vision are more fully formed because of my experience.”

At the last second, I try to tempt Firstman with another round, but he declines. After all, he’s on his way to the first L.A. screening of his film, to be moderated by “Anora” Oscar winner Sean Baker.
He bids me farewell when, half in his car, Firstman springs out and runs back to the valet stand. “This is for you,” he says, handing me a lighter emblazoned with the words “Club Kid.”

items.title: Blue Wave Sweep: What Does Democratic Shift Mean for Hollywood and the Media?
items.description: The Democratic rout in the midterms was a referendum on President Trump, prices and the war in Iran. But it will have impacts that go well beyond the determinative issues — touching topics of key interest to Hollywood studios, broadcasters and their teams of g
items.author: Gene Maddaus
paragraphs: The Democratic rout in the midterms was a referendum on President Trump, prices and the war in Iran. But it will have impacts that go well beyond the determinative issues — touching topics of key interest to Hollywood studios, broadcasters and their teams of government relations professionals.
Here’s a quick rundown of some of the key open questions as Washington adjusts to a new, blue reality for the final two years of Trump.

Hollywood’s top legislative priority is to pass a federal tax incentive by the end of the year. The bill is bipartisan — uniting Trump and Adam Schiff — so in theory, a looming change of party control shouldn’t affect it.

But any disruption — and the election was a massive disruption — probably doesn’t help build momentum. It also doesn’t help that Trump seems to be wavering, telling a rally last Friday that people in Hollywood are “all calling me kissing my ass” for tax credits. “I’ll probably do it. Should I do it?” he asked the crowd, which booed. “We’ll have to think about it.”

The industry is putting stock in that “I’ll probably do it,” but it wouldn’t be the first time Trump had let someone down. Congressional Republicans, meanwhile, are in shock, and are turning their attention to recriminations and to a leadership race. They could still get Hollywood tax credits done, but it’s not top of mind. For their part, House Democrats may want to hold off on any bipartisan deals until the next Congress, when they will hold all the leverage.

Democrats are more supportive of Hollywood than Republicans are, so the odds may improve in the 120th Congress. But that would require starting over. Out of the 31 Republican cosponsors in the House and Senate, 10 will not be back next year. The bill also benefits from the idea of a crisis requiring immediate action — which could be hard to sustain over a longer legislative process. “The iron is very hot right now,” Schiff said in September. “We’re all very focused on this. The president is focused on this. I wouldn’t want to see that bleed into next year.”

Democratic control of Congress won’t flip the Federal Communications Commission. But it will lead to greater oversight of chairman Brendan Carr, who has spent the last two years jawboning broadcasters over Jimmy Kimmel’s jokes and launching inquiries into political commentary on “The View.” Democrats in Congress see Carr as a manifestation of Trump’s impulse to squelch opposing views, and are likely to use subpoena power to investigate past and future controversies. Whether that adds light or just heat is very much TBD.

The Corporation for Public Broadcasting went out of business last year when Congress stripped $1.1 billion in funding. That in turn threatened the budgets of hundreds of local stations, some of which have been forced to consolidate, and eliminated a significant source of funding for PBS and NPR.

With Democrats in charge, there’s at least the possibility of restoring the funding, though it would require a sidequest into the culture wars, as conservatives see NPR and PBS as vehicles of leftwing bias and indoctrination.
Supporters want more than just to recreate the CPB, which was built for the media environment of 1967. They hope to reinvent federal support for public media in a way that goes beyond broadcasting.

“We urge the incoming Congress to renew federal investment in public and community media after the loss of the Corporation for Public Broadcasting and build a system around what communities need today,” said Rima Dael, CEO of the National Federation of Community Broadcasters, in a statement. “Universal access to fact-based news, trusted local information, and cultural programming means reaching people on air and online, in the languages they use, at a time when reliable internet access remains uneven and AI can amplify misinformation and disinformation.”

The House Oversight Committee will have a full plate of corruption investigations to pursue. It may or may not want to use its time to dive into the media capitulations of 2025 — the “Melania” documentary deal and the payouts over Trump’s “60 Minutes” lawsuit, his George Stephanopoulos lawsuit, his deplatforming lawsuits against Twitter, YouTube and Meta. Committee members may also take a hard look at the Ellison family’s efforts to win Trump’s blessing for the Paramount-Skydance and Paramount-Warner Bros. mergers. Any such efforts may lead to prolonged battles over executive privilege. But if Congress goes down that road and is successful, it could open up a trove of internal communications revealing how major media companies approached their dealings with the president at the peak of his powers.

items.title: ‘The Pitt’ and ‘ER’ Are Similar Enough to Allow Crichton Suit, Appeals Court Rules
items.description: An appeals court ruled on Wednesday that “The Pitt” is similar enough to “ER” to allow Michael Crichton’s widow to pursue a lawsuit over the Emmy-winning show.
items.author: Gene Maddaus
paragraphs: An appeals court ruled on Wednesday that “The Pitt” is similar enough to “ER” to allow Michael Crichton’s widow to pursue a lawsuit over the Emmy-winning show.
In a unanimous opinion, a three-judge panel denied an appeal from Warner Bros. Television, which has argued that the two shows are unrelated.

“There are clear and numerous similarities between ‘The Pitt’ and ‘ER,” the court ruled, citing the emergency room setting, the fast pace, the medical jargon, the graphic depictions of injuries, and a young, incompetent doctor fresh from medical school. “We find the details here suffice for a prima facie case.”

The appeals court did dismiss a claim against key creators of the show — Noah Wyle, John Wells and R. Scott Gemmill — finding no evidence that they were aware they could be violating Crichton’s contractual rights.

Crichton was a creator of “ER,” which was based on a 1974 script he wrote about his experiences as a medical student. His contract with Warner Bros. Television included a “frozen rights” provision blocking the studio from making any spinoffs or reboots without his approval.

Sherri Crichton, his widow, filed the suit in August 2024, months before “The Pitt” debuted, alleging that Wells and Wyle had originally wanted to reboot “ER” and only changed course after failing to secure her permission.

Warner Bros. has argued that “The Pitt” is a completely different show, and filed a motion to throw out the suit under California’s anti-SLAPP statute, which is meant to deter frivolous lawsuits that stymie free expression. Judge Wendy Chang denied the motion last year, finding that Sherri Crichton had offered enough evidence to proceed.

The appellate ruling allows the suit to move forward at the trial court. The question of whether “The Pitt” is in fact a derivative work of “ER” could ultimately be up to a jury to decide unless the parties reach a settlement before it gets to that point.

“I am deeply gratified by the Court of Appeal decision and look forward to discovery and to our case, which affects writers, creators, and their families and estates, being presented to a jury,” Sherri Crichton said in a statement.

items.title: Variety’s 10 Comics to Watch for 2026
items.description: Since the turn of the century, Variety has scoped out the next generation of comedy stars through our annual 10 Comics to Watch franchise. The inaugural lineup in 2000 included future industry favorites Zach Galifianakis, Maria Bamford, Patton Oswalt and Louis
items.author: Ethan Shanfeld
paragraphs: Since the turn of the century, Variety has scoped out the next generation of comedy stars through our annual 10 Comics to Watch franchise. The inaugural lineup in 2000 included future industry favorites Zach Galifianakis, Maria Bamford, Patton Oswalt and Louis C.K. And 15 years later, this magazine identified Nate Bargatze and Nikki Glaser as burgeoning comedy titans — now, they are two of the top-selling stand-ups in the world. Over the years, Wanda Sykes, Fred Armisen, Dane Cook and Michael Che have been named Comics to Watch, as well as more recent breakouts Ayo Edebiri, Hannah Einbinder, Caleb Hearon and Julio Torres.

The comedy industry is bigger than ever in 2026, and this year’s list represents the bold breadth of those currently making us laugh, from slacker-provocateur talk show host Adam Friedland to the musical satirist Kyle Gordon, who has been dubbed the “Millennial ‘Weird Al.’” Some stand-ups are straddling the stage and the small screen, like “Overcompensating” star Wally Baram, while others like Lucas Zelnick have built huge online followings off viral crowd-work clips.
Read on to see the full lineup of Variety’s 10 Comics to Watch for 2026, plus the more veteran comics endorsing them, from Glaser and Hasan Minhaj to Tim Robinson.

You can also see the comedians perform live at a New York Comedy Festival showcase on Nov. 12, taking place at the Hard Rock Hotel in Times Square. More information, including how to buy tickets, can be found on the New York Comedy Festival website.

- Wally Baram Wally Baram! Wallifer Aniston, as I call her on set of “Overcompensating” at 3 a.m. on a soundstage in Toronto! I met Wally for the first time on Zoom when I was interviewing writers for “Overcompensating.” I am not being dramatic when I say it felt like fate. She entered the Zoom and I thought, “That’s Carmen.” She was exactly what I wanted for the role. But what I didn’t know was that she would be more funny, brilliant, creative, and sparkly than anything I could have dreamed of. She was vulnerable and deeply honest for the entire hour we chatted. I wanted to tell her my life story (which we would eventually act out on the aforementioned soundstage in Toronto) and felt like I knew her forever. EVERYONE who encounters her feels this way. At the end of the Zoom, I noticed that something moved in the background. I said, “Oh, do you have a dog?” to which she replied, with no ceremony, “No, that’s my pet boa constrictor named Jersey Mike.” I was in love. After the meeting, I devoured her stand-up and devastatingly funny script and hired her for the writer’s room immediately. I knew full well that she was going to get the role of Carmen when we opened auditions. I am forever lucky that I get to make a show with her by my side, and I will forever be in the front row of anything she does with Jersey Mike around my neck. — Benito Skinner My job before comedian was… A ball python snake breeder (in my defense, I was a teenager in college). The hardest I bombed was… Opening for Jeff Garlin in the Improv Lab when I was 20; I earnestly asked to start over. My pre-show ritual includes… I text my mom to tell her I love her before I go onstage … every single time. Is that embarrassing or what?

- Olivia Carter When I discovered Olivia Carter’s clips on Instagram I had the same feeling I felt back in 2002 when I first discovered Sarah Silverman: here was a comic who was just for me. That’s not to say that she’s not for everyone else, but there was something about her dry wit, precise joke writing, and fearless delivery that made me feel like “not only do I want to consume everything she does forever and ever, but I also kind of want to be her.” The thing that astounds me about Olivia is that she knows exactly who she is on stage even though she’s just six years in. It’s said that it takes ten years for a comic to “find their voice” on stage, but when you watch Olivia, I’m almost certain she never had to search for it. Her material is jarring and biting, but rarely offensive because her delivery is so self-assured. Sure, her jokes might make you uncomfortable, but that’s your problem, because Olivia is right at home in the tension. When I guest judged the roast episode of Netflix’s “Funny AF,” I watched Olivia deliver incredibly well-written jokes about subject matter that I know she had been told by higher-ups to steer away from. I couldn’t believe the tenacity it took for her to break the “rules” on a show she was trying to win just so she could tell the best jokes possible, and more importantly: the truth. This is the moment I knew that Olivia wasn’t just a comic to watch, but the kind of comic we should all aspire to be. — Nikki Glaser The weirdest place I’ve ever performed was… A women’s prison. I made fun of the security guard and got a standing ovation. Crushed so hard they arrested me. The best advice a comic gave me was… “Get sleep if you can.”
My favorite thing about comedy is… People love to tell you there are rules, but actually there are no rules.

- Aaron Chen Do yourself a favor and watch a clip of Aaron Chen at the 2019 Melbourne Comedy Festival. That’s how I first got introduced to him. His mullet, every single word choice and his quiet, calm but confident delivery had me dead. My favorite joke from one of his YouTube specials is: “When people say let’s meet for a coffee, what I’m hearing is let’s go do a poo poo.” His comedy is silly but smart, weird and completely unpredictable. He’s truly one of the most exciting new voices in stand-up, and I cannot wait to see what he does next. — Ali Wong The hardest I bombed was… At a private club for wealthy elites. I saw some things I should not have seen. It was hard to get laughs as people were more interested in some disturbed rituals. The one thing I’d never joke about is… The ethnic and political tensions of Singapore in the 1960s. My parents think I… Don’t give a damn what anyone even says and they are correct. The most misunderstood thing about comedy is… The microphone is not actually on; it’s an optical illusion.

- Adam Friedland Who the hell is Adam Friedland? I didn’t know. My manager says he’d like me to do his podcast, and as one who doesn’t say “no” to anything, I agree. He says he wants this show to be like “The Dick Cavett Show.” It’s nothing like the “Cavett Show.” We talk a lot, make each other laugh. I throw crap at him. He throws it back. We have a great time. He has me read a ridiculous three-page script and then we talk about Nazis. Then I leave. I had a great time. He’s funny, likeable, smart, and we really get along. A few weeks later, my son calls me from college. “Dad, how do you know Adam Friedland?” I don’t. “I heard you on his show. That guy is hilarious.” I walk down the streets. One kid after another says, “You were great on Adam Friedland’s show.” And yet, I still ask: Who the hell is Adam Friedland? — Richard Kind The weirdest place I’ve ever performed was… A women’s rally six months into comedy. My job before comedian was… Paralegal, my true passion. The strangest fan interaction I’ve ever had was… An old man asked for a picture thinking I was Sarah Sherman from “Saturday Night Live.” My favorite thing about comedy is… That it’s not important.

- Kyle Gordon The first time I heard Kyle Gordon shout, “If you want parties to be making, have some noise” in his European foam-bar anthem “Planet of the Bass,” I felt like Salieri reading the sheet music for Sonata for Woodwinds in “Amadeus.” What a cruel trick, that God had given me the power to recognize when someone as bonkers as Kyle Gordon would come along. Kyle’s albums are entitled: “Kyle Gordon is Everywhere,” “Kyle Gordon is Great” and “Kyle Gordon is Wonderful.” All of these statements are true, but Kyle Gordon is also bonkers. Kyle Gordon is crushing it in a new arena of song comedy, a genre that has been pretty upbeat for the past hundred years. While Kyle has some upbeat comedy songs (“Selekta,” “Myrtle Beach,” “Mr. Jambo”) he’s also written some of the darkest comedy songs in years: “Crawl to Me,” “If You Break Up With Me,” “I’m a Whore.” Kyle asked me if I’d like to be in the video for his hit “Irish Drinking Song.” I said, “Of course, Kyle!” Then I listened to the lyrics. A hilarious song, yes, but I knew I could never be in a video with almost any of those words in it. But Kyle wasn’t worried; that’s what makes his stuff so special — Kyle doesn’t worry, he commits. Kyle is breaking new ground in song comedy all the time. He’s a force of nature, and if it were perfectly accurate, Kyle’s next album would be called: “Kyle Gordon is Unafraid.” — Thomas Lennon The most misunderstood thing about comedy is… Comedy isn’t funny because it’s true. It’s funny because it feels true, whether it’s actually true or not. The strangest fan interaction I’ve ever had was… I signed a Ziploc bag filled with a fan’s mother’s ashes. The weirdest thing I’ve ever done for a laugh is… Got naked and ran on the subway tracks.

- Shapel Lacey Shapel Lacey? You mean the kindest man in comedy? Please hold while I gush about my baby. *Cracks knuckles* Believe me when I tell you Shapel is the type of comic who has the audience by the balls within five words or less. There’s a rawness to his delivery that feels effortlessly personal and refreshingly candid. While watching him perform, you’re sure to find yourself completely immersed in his story. And let me add: It’s one hell of a story. What makes Shapel a star (yeah, I said it) is that he isn’t trying to fit a familiar comedic mold. He’s developing a style that’s distinctly his own. Also… you haven’t lived until you’ve had a 1 a.m. post-show recap with Shapel Lacey at Swingers Diner. Many have applied; few have received the invite. — Joe Dombrowski My pre-show ritual includes… Watching skateboarding or cheerleading videos on YouTube. The hardest I bombed was… My fourth time doing stand-up ever, at a dance club while the DJ was taking a break. My favorite thing about comedy is… Being able to laugh at the things that used to make me sad.

- Eilise Patton I am a massive fan of Eilise’s work. She makes me excited and hopeful for the future of comedy. Her ideas and characters feel so inspired and brand new. — Tim Robinson The last thing that made me laugh was… I was visiting my mother and she heard a noise outside, and I saw her type into ChatGPT: “What was that boom?” The weirdest place I’ve ever performed was… On a Zoom during COVID for a shipping company. Everyone had their camera and mics off. The title of my memoir will be… “Eilise on Life” (like “A Lease on Life”!), but now I’m sure some bitch with the normal spelling of Elise will take it. The one thing I’d never joke about is… No such thing! The most important thing on my rider is… A Celsius. Must consume for energy as well as ritual. Not sponsored just deeply superstitious. The best advice from a comic is… Steve Martin’s “Never show doubt” has been my North Star forever. Just being fearless and fully going for it every time.

- Usama Siddiquee Usama Siddiquee is a true comic’s comic, grinding, hustling and building an undeniable act for years. I’ve known Usama for nearly a decade, and I’ve watched him work his way up from open mics to the biggest stages. When Kevin Hart crowned him live on stage at the Village Underground during his “Funny AF” taping, it may have appeared to be kismet, or a “lucky night” but it wasn’t. It’s what so many comics have known for years — Usama is undeniable, and he’s here to stay. He’s got it all. The charisma, charm, the smile, the act outs, the hair. My God, the waves in the hair. Look, I want him to get married, but he told me he’s married to the game. (I still don’t know what that means.) During the finale taping of Kevin Hart’s “Funny AF,” I remember seeing videos of the entire theater chanting his name before he even hit the stage. It made me emotional. Because he’s not a burgeoning “Comic to Watch” — he’s arrived, and we can’t stop saying his name. — Hasan Minhaj The weirdest place I’ve ever performed was… A strip club that was named Strip Club. The heckle I still think about is… I was killing on stage when out of nowhere an old Irish lady in the crowd told me to “get over myself. Enough is enough.” Almost quit comedy that day. The most misunderstood thing about comedy is… How long it takes to get good. Whatever time you think it is, it’s double that.

- Josh Ocean Thomas I met Josh in Chicago at a Don’t Tell Comedy in some dingy dive bar, after which he would not stop trying to be my friend. He is so nice to a point where it’s suspicious, and I have to ask myself, “Is this guy for real?” Aside from being a decent human, Josh kills every time he steps on stage and offers a respite from the standard comedy you might be used to. I truly believe Josh has everything it takes to be one of the top performing comics of all time, and I say that emphatically. — Morgan Jay My job before becoming a comedian was… A Kayak & Snorkel Tour Guide at La Jolla Kayak in San Diego. The most misunderstood thing about comedy is… That all comedians are miserable people. My favorite thing about comedy is… Meeting other comedians who, despite being strangers and coming from completely different walks of life, share one of the most important parts of life with me. I also just love getting to do it. The best advice a comic gave me was… “Be kind, stay funny, and you’ll be all right” – Conan O’Brien, when I met him at 14 years old at Comic Con San Diego.

- Lucas Zelnick I think what’s been most impressive about watching Lucas’ rise is him taking on subjects that are unique to him and historically not funny at all. Most comics would avoid talking about coming from money or their mom dating Epstein (when she was an adult!). Lucas leans into it and it’s hilarious and my favorite material of his. It’s always cool to see comics get more honest as the stakes get higher and the rooms get bigger. Hollywood should call him soon before his dad makes him run the diamond mines in Botswana. — Andrew Schulz The weirdest place I’ve ever performed was… A church (I’m Jewish). The most misunderstood thing about comedy is… You can be edgy as long as you’re not mean-spirited. The strangest fan interaction I’ve ever had was… A fan let me write “I watched Lucas Zelnick bomb” on their arm and then got it tattooed. My favorite thing about comedy is… You can say exactly what you think and everyone acts like you’re kidding.

items.title: Cynthia Erivo to Play Tupac Shakur’s Mother in Snoop Dogg Biopic
items.description: Tony, Grammy, and Emmy winner Cynthia Erivo has joined the cast of Universal’s upcoming Snoop Dogg biopic and is set to portray Tupac’s mother, Afeni Shakur.
items.author: Jazz Tangcay
paragraphs: Tony, Grammy, and Emmy winner Cynthia Erivo has joined the cast of Universal’s upcoming Snoop Dogg biopic and is set to portray Tupac’s mother, Afeni Shakur.
Jonathan Daviss leads the cast of “Snoop,” which is described as the “definitive biopic of the entertainment mogul and icon,” Snoop Dogg.

Erivo joins the film’s starry ensemble, which also features Myles Bullock Be (as Dr. Dre), Lauren London (Snoop’s late mother, Beverly Tate), Camron Jones (Tupac Shakur), Algee Smith (Warren G), Tre Hale (Suge Knight), Laya DeLeon Hayes (Snoop’s wife, Shante Broadus), Olly Sholotan (Kurupt), Corey Champagne (Nate Dogg) and Jonica Booth (The Lady of Rage).

Afeni Shakur was a prominent member of the Black Panther Party. Born in North Carolina as Alice Faye Williams in 1947, she moved to the Bronx with her mother as an 11-year-old. She joined the Panthers after hearing Bobby Seale speak in 1968, and married fellow Black Panther member Lumumba Shakur soon after.

Craig Brewer (“Hustle and Flow,” “Song Sung Blue”) is directing “Snoop,” which Universal dated for theatrical release on Aug. 6, and it’s based on his rewrite of Joe Robert Cole’s (“Black Panther,” ”Wakanda Forever”) original script.

Snoop Dogg is producing “Snoop,” which will incorporate music from his vast catalog, alongside Imagine Entertainment’s Brian Grazer (“8 Mile”), Allan Mandelbaum and Death Row Pictures president Sara Ramaker. “Snoop” is the first project under Death Row Pictures’ overall deal with NBCUniversal Entertainment and Studios. Senior VP of production development Ryan Jones and director of development Tony Ducret will oversee the project for the studio.

Erivo recently hosted “Saturday Night Live: U.K.” and starred in “Wicked” and “Wicked: For Good.” She earned her Golden Globe, SAG, Critics’ Choice, NAACP, BAFTA, and Academy Award nominations for her portrayal of Elphaba. Up next, she executive produced and stars in the film adaptation of “Prima Facie.” The film premiered at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival. She also stars in “Children of Blood and Bone,” directed by Gina Prince-Bythewood. The film includes Viola Davis, Chiwetel Ejiofor, Idris Elba, Amandla Stenberg, Damson Idris, Regina King and Lashana Lynch, and it will open on Jan. 15.
Erivo is represented by UTA, Entertainment 360, The Lede Company and Peikoff Mahan Law Office.
The news was first reported by The Hollywood Reporter.
