items.title: Best Memes and TikToks After Midterms’ Blue Wave, From Regina George to ‘The Office’ References
items.description: The internet has not been disappointed with its reactions to the blue wave during the 2026 midterms on Tuesday, when Democrats flipped both the U.S. House and Senate.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: The internet has not been disappointed with its reactions to the blue wave during the 2026 midterms on Tuesday, when Democrats flipped both the U.S. House and Senate.

It was a tough night for Republicans as Democrats flipped Senate seats in several battleground and ruby-red states, including Texas, North Carolina, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and Maine, and held on to seats in Georgia and Michigan. As for the House, they also flipped more than two dozen districts.

As conservatives grapple with what went wrong, liberals are reveling in their big wins, specifically with memes and TikTok flooding social media. Some people are even using clips from popular movies and TV shows — such as The Office, Avengers: Endgame, Breaking Bad, Mean Girls and Step Brothers — to express their euphoric feelings as well as take jabs at President Donald Trump, who is undoubtedly frustrated.

Some are also taking a moment to shout out some of the notable Democratic winners, including James Talarico, who won the Texas Senate race; Sen. Jon Ossoff, who was reelected in Georgia; Abdul El-Sayed, who won the Michigan Senate race; and Annie Andrews, who won the Senate race in South Carolina; among others. Others are celebrating history-making wins, such as Chris Pappas becoming the first openly gay man elected to the Senate and Keisha Lance Bottoms becoming the first-ever Black woman elected governor in any state with her win in Georgia.
Below, The Hollywood Reporter is rounding up the most memorable social media reactions.

items.title: Skims Centimillionaire Emma Grede Shares Her Best Money Advice
items.description: Welcome to Profits & Losses, GQ’s questionnaire about money that asks someone of note how they made it, lost it, spent it, grew it, and think about it.
items.author: Rebecca Dolan
paragraphs: Welcome to Profits & Losses, GQ’s questionnaire about money that asks someone of note how they made it, lost it, spent it, grew it, and think about it.

A luxury that’s worth its price: Being able to holiday on a boat. I’ve been a guest on many people’s beautiful boats over the years, but there is nothing quite like being able to charter one for you and your family and your friends.

A luxury that’s not: I can’t really imagine spending ridiculous amounts of money on a car. Growing up in London, the Tube was the best way to get anywhere. For me, after a Range Rover, it all goes downhill.

The best $50 I’ve ever spent: It will always be food. Yesterday I was on Sawtelle [LA’s Japantown] and queued to get into the ramen place, and it was a $38 bowl of ramen, and I thought it was the best thing I’ve ever eaten.
Something that I own multiples of: Vintage Levi’s—I have hundreds and hundreds and hundreds. If I find a wash or a rip pattern that I like, I’m buying it.

The wage at my first job: I worked in fashion production. I was a production assistant on the shows, and my salary was £18,500 [about $25,000]. I negotiated that up from £16,000, which is what I was offered. So I was really proud of myself that I got a bit more money. I just asked.

My first big purchase: A Gucci diamanté thong, and it was the light of my life. I wore the “G” outside my jeans, and I thought I was the absolute shit. It was £165 [about $225]. At that point, that was like spending £1,500 [about $2,000]. It was so much money. I was young. I was interning and working in stores and hustling away. When I’d get a Christmas bonus, I was straight down to Gucci. That was all I cared about.

What I splurge on today: Tabletop glassware, beautiful ceramics. Wherever I go in the world…. I can be on an island, I will find the ceramic shop, and I will ship plates from a random place in Greece. That is my little splurge arena that I think is so worth it—because you eat off of plates every single day.

My first big payday: I sold my first company in my mid-20s, and I thought it was a billion dollars. It certainly wasn’t, but, to me, the freedom that gave me to then make decisions was wild. I could step back and for the first time in my life have a moment to breathe and to think and to decide. My ambition went through the roof.

“I feel rich when…” My aim in life was to never have to look at the price on a menu, because I felt like I was always totaling things up to make sure I could afford it. I grew up really poor.… I grew up in a house that had an electricity meter and I knew how long £30 would last. I’m still that kid deep down inside. I actually think that’s what makes me good at my job.… I’m very, very careful about how I use money and how I think about it.

The best money advice I ever got: The thing that’s really stuck with me is never outsourcing any of your decision-making. The more money you get, the easier that becomes because you’re surrounded by wealth managers and business managers and people who are experts in places that you might not be. I think that trusting myself is probably the single best thing that I’ve ever done. I didn’t inherit anything. Nobody gave me anything. Every penny I have is of my own making and it’s mine to look after.

The best investment I’ve ever made: Is in myself. I invest in countless companies, but I have worked without taking a paycheck on multiple occasions in my own companies, and those have been the best investments I’ve ever made.

The best thing I own that I didn’t buy for myself: My husband buys me beautiful jewelry and he’s very considered. He finds things with meaning and things that have come from specific dates or periods that would mean something to me. He bought me a vintage Rolex from the year of my birth. I was like, “That’s so beautiful. What an amazing thing.”

[Prenup] one million percent. I got married before I had money. I still made sure I had a prenup because I believe in myself. When you get married, you are entering into a legal contract anyway. Why wouldn’t you protect your assets and protect your future ability to earn and to look after yourself?

I’m really lucky. I married a Swedish man, and Sweden is an extremely matriarchal society. He has no problem having a powerful woman in his life and sharing responsibility. I don’t think that my husband ever came into the relationship thinking that I was going to be passive in our decision-making or in my ability to earn.
For sure. I’ve worked in this industry since I was 17 years old. And so somebody who didn’t say hi to me when they were 20, they don’t get a meeting with me now.

I’ll tell you what I’ll tell you: Childcare is one of the single biggest luxuries that I afford myself. It is a necessity, it is something that I’m willing to pay for, it’s something that I think we need to speak about more, and it’s something that I am unapologetic about.
I hate to be boring, but I don’t think I did. I don’t do risky shit.
A version of this story originally appeared in the October 2026 issue of GQ with the title “Profits & Losses with Self-made Centimillionaire Emma Grede.”

items.title: Adam Friedland’s Secret Weapon? An Unapologetic Cold Call
items.description: Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.
items.author: Alyssa Bereznak
paragraphs: Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.

In a world of texters, Adam Friedland is a self-described phone-call guy by necessity. Since launching his irreverent Dick Cavett–style conversation show in 2022, he’s earned critical acclaim for cajoling a wide range of interview subjects into revelatory exchanges. (It’s the only program where you can see California governor Gavin Newsom tear up and 2 Chainz share a joint with the host.) He’s also racked up over 100 million views on YouTube and can now summon the booking power of his cable counterparts. But his ascent has required some grind. “Late-night talk shows have hundreds of people working for them,” says Friedland. “We’ve had to bootstrap a lot.”

That means Friedland plays a hybrid role—not just as onscreen talent but also as the behind-the-scenes talent booker. “I’ll be working the phones a lot of the day,” he says. “I call people all the time, whether it’s to bother them—Do you have this person’s number? Can I get them on the show?—or just to get information. It feels very 1990s Hollywood.” The Cum Town podcast alum is aware that his methods can often be unwelcome in a culture that has normalized the pre-call-alert text. “People behind my back characterize me as just firing off intrusive phone calls out of the blue,” he says.

But hey, it works. Last season, when he wanted to interview the journalist Olivia Nuzzi, he admittedly rang her so many times that she finally acquiesced. “Most things get done when you’re on a phone call,” he says.

The day I speak to him on, yes, the phone, he’s prepping for three consecutive interviews. To do so, he draws from the extensive research his staff compiles and maps out a game plan. He took, for instance, a whole two weeks to “go crazy” on the concept of Alec Baldwin. “Half of it is, What’s a way to talk to a person that no one has?” he says. “The other half is, How do I accommodate someone that I’ve never met in order for them to be disarmed?” Friedland is sometimes up late, on the phone, fiddling with the puzzle pieces of his subjects or refining material with collaborators—tasks not suited for email. “You know if something’s funny,” he says, “if it makes someone whose sense of humor you respect laugh.”
We chatted with Friedland about how he prepares for his interviews, his love of sports, and how he got over the fear of giving something his best shot.
Adam Friedland: No problem. I hope this’ll be not the most boring interview you’ve ever had, but we’ll see.

The show’s grown pretty much since its inception, so it’s just continuing that trajectory. First and foremost, it’s a comedy show, so I want everything to be at least interesting and to speak to something more cultural than political. I know I’ve kind of veered from that territory in a couple of instances, but the happy medium is kind of like the Gavin Newsom episode we had, which was sufficiently funny and weird and substantive at points. But I think when comedians go politics, you stop being funny. So if I can’t find something interesting or compelling or something that speaks to a cultural moment, then I’m not too keen on going in that direction, but we’ll see. I mean, this has kind of just happened. When I say I’m in preproduction, it’s not like I’m looking at a map of Europe and deciding when to invade Poland. I don’t know why I used Hitler as an example. I’m not Hitler. I don’t know why I said that.
Yeah. Okay, fine. But I’m not doing what Hitler would. Exactly. The point stands. Okay. Yeah, I’m not Hitler.
Yeah. The goal is to disarm the guests. There’s a lot of research that goes into the show.

I try to do extensive work beforehand, and I have people that I work with that are researchers, and I try to have a game plan that’s a little bit more considered than people may realize or maybe it comes across. But the primary consideration is what kind of person it is. And the neat part about that is that it’s a person I’ve never met, so I’m kind of piecing together information that I find and [from] people that I’ve talked to. It’s kind of like a puzzle.

Half of it is, What’s a way to talk to a person that no one has? The other half is, How do I accommodate someone that I’ve never met in order for them to be disarmed? So it’s a pretty boring answer, but it’s fun sometimes with a bigger guest. Like with Alec Baldwin, there’s this notion of him being a hothead and all this stuff. But I could tell that’s kind of tabloidy and maybe there’s more depth to people than just what you hear. There’s more depth to people than the way that they’re gossiped about or characterized. And what I find is that the show is a good opportunity to show people as they really are.

Some of them have been pretty extensive. There’s various elements that go into it. You also have to consider the audience. You don’t want to talk above people’s heads. You want to take what a normal person would know about something or someone and find a way for the guest to connect with that. So instead of building it out from a biography, you kind of build it out from an audience member and then how could this guest speak to those things that this person knows.

Sometimes it could be really fast, depending on people’s schedules. I prefer it to have some runway where we can really get into it, especially if it’s a more interesting guest. I keep thinking of Alec Baldwin, but yeah, that one we had two weeks to go crazy on. I have a researcher that reads multiple books, and he’s just a psycho, and he’s really…. Shout out to Justin, the best guy I’ve ever met. Justin. He’s got a real future ahead of him.

We’ve been working together for a while, and through doing the show, I’ve developed a language for the interviews and for the comedy. And that really is half prep and then half postproduction, I would say, and editing and telling a story, I guess. These are really boring answers.

No, it’s really cool that I get to do this. I think it’s totally different than if your boss is telling you to do something. I feel very fortunate that I get to do it, so I work really hard. And also it’s really cool and fun. I really like what I’m doing, and I think most people hate their job. So if you find a way to like what you’re doing, it’s really fucking rare. And I don’t want to take that for granted. So yes, because it’s interesting to me, I bust my ass. It’s not finding motivation. It’s more so it’s kind of there. Plus I didn’t really work hard for most of my life. So it’s like when you find that you start working hard, you don’t want to go back to lazy. You kind of feel like you just wasted a lot of the time. I think I kind of want to work forever.

It’s not so structured. I would say it’s deadline-oriented. But the benefit is that there’s so much to do that you can’t really dwell on what people think about…. I mean, if my friends like it, that’s pretty cool. But I don’t really dwell on where this exists. People say it’s going well. It sounds like false modesty, but I am just at a studio with three guys that work with me, and then I’m at home and I’m with my wife. I found a way that in order to maintain productivity, you have to streamline your life.

I go to the studio and then I come home and I have dinner. If I have an interview the next day, I’ll probably be up prepping and stuff or on the phone. I’m on the phone a lot. I’m a phone call guy. I call people all the time, whether it’s to bother them—Do you have this person’s number? Can I get them on the show?—or just to get information. It feels very 1990s Hollywood. People behind my back characterize me as just firing off intrusive phone calls out of the blue.
Fuck them. I’m sorry. If I’m trying to actually have a productive conversation, a text takes so much longer. And also you could make jokes and goof around a little bit. It’s fun.

Yeah, totally. I’ll be working the phones a lot of the day. You know if something’s funny if it makes someone whose sense of humor you respect laugh. So it’s easier if you’re making a comedy show to surround yourself with people who you trust. That’s how I work well. I bother people until I get the answers I want. Most things get done when you’re on a phone call. If you send an email or a text, the success rate of figuring out the thing that you want to figure out is less successful, I would say.
I liked Howard Stern a lot.

He was able to be your best friend immediately. He was able to really disarm the [guest]. It’s like magic when you watch him. But within 90 seconds, you’re his best friend and you’re open. And he’s just the master of that. And he would have interviews where you saw people that you thought you knew or that were super famous or you’d see them in an entirely different light.

The inspiration for the set and everything was Dick Cavett, who had this long-form interview show where you’d watch John and Yoko or Orson Wells, and they’d communicate and you’d see them in a way that you never really got to see them. So that’s the objective of the show, I’d say. I’ll put it this way. You watch late-night talk shows, it’s like the way that they communicate with the guests is fucking weird. They’re like, “Tell me an anecdote and then what’s the movie?” And then they play a clip. It’s a six-minute conversation that’s not really a conversation. It’s kind of just all set up. Instead, I have people, usually it’ll be 90 minutes to 2 hours. I think that you can explore and find really interesting things that you can’t otherwise.

I don’t know. I think the objective isn’t just to do Between Two Ferns. There’s more of a substantive aspect to it. And I feel like if I have a substantive framework, I can find ways to fill in the gaps comedically. I’ve been doing comedy for a long time. And also that’s just how I am when I meet people or talk to people. I’m annoying. So that to me is just less of a concern than having actually something interesting to talk about. I could fucking do the bullshit.
Well, yeah, I’m an incredibly superficial person.

I wouldn’t say that she gets mad at me, but yeah, it must be annoying if she hears me on the phone. I’m trying more so not to take my work home with me, less staying up till 2 a.m. to prep. Late-night talk shows have hundreds of people working for them. We’ve had to bootstrap a lot. But I’m 40. I need my sleep. I’m not 40; I’m 39. Let’s clarify. For the record, on the record, I’m 39. It’s a pathetic age. It’s really horrible sounding.

Thirty-eight’s fine; 39 is like, “You should kill yourself.” Forty is like, “That guy doesn’t give a fuck.” No, 39 is like, “That guy’s a loser. He’s about to be 40.” But at 40, you’re like, “Oh, that guy’s just living life.”
Yeah. There’s a zen in it. Thirty-nine stinks.

I’m probably just working or at least trying not to. I don’t know. I don’t really think so deliberately about those kind of things. Perhaps, I don’t know, I just spend time with my friends and family.

Yeah. Books about history and golf. Yeah, just pretty much a middle-aged white guy. I think there’s an inflection point in every middle-aged Jewish man’s life where you go Zionism or you go golf, military history. So I’m going that way.

The method is refined and evolved. I think that if I watched anything I’ve ever done, I would be like, “I’d change this, this, this, and this.” People that do something and they’re like, “I’m a genius,” I think they’re probably just not. Usually you only get better if you just struggle against something and then put it out and then put it out of your mind.

I don’t know, if it felt good. Sometimes it didn’t feel good and it ends up being good. When I had that guy from Barstool Sports, Dave Portnoy, in the room, it was awful. And I think the episode was pretty good. But at the time I was like, “That’s terrible.” He didn’t know what to make of me. And then he found out I knew more about sports than him and stuff, and his brain was short-circuiting. He was like, “What the hell kind of guy is this? I don’t know how to classify this kind of guy.”

So that’s an example of even though the feelings in the room or the vibes were off, it turned out to be really good. I’m a stand-up comedian, so if it’s not getting a laugh, I’m like, “Was that bad?” But for the most part, I’m kind of used to it by now. So it’s like, “Oh, let’s see what we get back in the footage.”

I don’t know. Are there other things that are like this? I don’t know. I feel like I’m so lucky I get to do it, and I have come up with something that works for me, but I don’t know. What’s Joe Rogan do? I don’t know. He’s probably eating elk and fighting guys or something. I don’t know if it’s unique or if it’s incredibly boring, but the way I’ve negotiated my life has just kept me grounded and just productive.

I go to work and then I come home and I have dinner and watch a movie maybe with my wife, or I work if I have something the next day. I have three interviews in a row this week. So I’ve been making sure that I’m not going to kill myself this week, but in three consecutive days. I’m not going to the Chateau Marmont.

It’s just be normal. And this is going to sound corny, but who cares? At the end, what matters is just the time you spend with the people you love, and you just need to remember that. I’m not going to remember the fucking…. I mean, maybe I will, but I’m not going to remember the Chet Hanks episode when I’m on my deathbed, but I’ll remember hanging out with my grandkids. For me, it’s a matter of challenging myself and devoting myself to something and being driven and feeling like I’m taking life seriously, but it’s not as important as your family.

Yeah, I watch soccer. I’m obsessed with this team, Arsenal. It’s really embarrassing. Being an American soccer fan is just one of the lamest kind of guys you could be. It’s just this being like a Ted Lasso loser.

That’s kind of what I’m thinking about at night. It’s so pathetic how much…. I’m not even from England. That’s kind of how I unwind. I have this one guy that knows as much as me, and we yell at each other on the phone. This guy, Sam. And I scream. We scream at each other on the phone.

Yeah, I just know everything. It’s like astrology for boys. It’s a way that I can meet some guy I’ve never met. If I’m on a double date with one of my wife’s friends, you’re basically on a date with the other guy. They’re talking and then you’re sitting there with some guy. And if they can’t talk about sports, then I’m just done. On the car ride home, I’m like, “Well, thanks a lot for nothing. I don’t know what this guy does with his time.”
I probably have had a lot, but I don’t…. Do you do that? You’re like, “I had a learning moment?”
Are you overly therapized?

Yeah. I’ve done a good amount myself. I haven’t in a while, but I find that at a certain point, if your life is medium or regular, it could oftentimes prompt one to navel gaze, perhaps, or kind of ruminate more. My new mantra is just That’s some shit. I feel like I’m saying this and something terrible is going to happen, I’m going to start therapy next week. But I think I’m equipped enough as an adult to navigate. Shit happens, and I feel like I’ve been equipped enough as an adult to navigate those things. But I will say in various other moments—I lost my mother—[therapy has] been like a godsend. It’s been so helpful.

Incredibly good for the other difficult moments that have happened. I mean, he told me in the first session I had, he said, “You’re the smartest man I’ve ever met.” He said, “You should be the teacher.” I said, “I’m here to learn, sir. Okay?”
Yes, it did. Put it in your column. Because if there’s anything that I take seriously, it’s being honest to Gentlemen’s Quarterly.

No, it’s not about introspection. You should definitely be introspective. I think that one should trust themself to say that I’m capable of navigating whatever crap happened, the bumps along the way. I don’t think it’s good to just fixate on oneself.
It’s not a cosmic joke, because I’ve found that I actually may have some sort of, I don’t know, some modicum of talent. I didn’t think I did before, I would say that.

I don’t know. When I decided I was going to try at being a talk show host, I think that something just came over me. I think I’ve said this before a million times, but it’s really scary to try at anything, because if you try as hard as you can and someone’s like, “That stinks,” you’re like, “Hey, man, I tried as hard as I can.”

In the old podcast we used to do, we trafficked in irony. So the conceit was like, “Hey, it sucks, but that’s because we’re not trying. And if you’re listening, fuck you.” But really that’s kind of like you insulate your feelings. I’m cutting myself off, but it’s like when you see Susan Boyle on Britain’s Got Talent; the reason it makes you cry is because she’s singing as hard as she can. You want her to do good because everyone laughed at her. And then she sings Les Mis perfect.

So that’s what I’m describing. It’s really scary to do that. And I think it took me until 35 to do that for the first time. And then I’ve gained a tremendous amount of purpose and direction, and it makes me feel great that I didn’t know that I could do. I’m not even that good. I want to get better. But I know that I’ve worked really hard at something, and I think I’ve gotten better, hopefully, and I want to keep getting better. It’s just as simple as that.
A version of this story originally appeared in the October 2026 issue of GQ with the title “Routine Excellence with Talk Show Host Adam Friedland.”

items.title: The GQ Guide to London
items.description: For the Fall 2026 issue of GQ, we shot Sense and Sensibility star George MacKay across various London locales. We also asked Murray Clark, British GQ’s head of editorial content, to give us all his best tips for places to hit up for a weekend in the capital. C
items.author: Tyler Chin
paragraphs: For the Fall 2026 issue of GQ, we shot Sense and Sensibility star George MacKay across various London locales. We also asked Murray Clark, British GQ’s head of editorial content, to give us all his best tips for places to hit up for a weekend in the capital. Clark sees London as a city filled with messy contradictions, at once “creaking and weird and chaotic and cosmopolitan and idyllic.” And he hits all of the above notes, plus even more, with his personal recs for how to do it right.

Once a 1920s car park (Brit-speak for parking lot), now a hotel that still has all its Art Deco charm. A stay here, Clark says, is “like being in a bit of a film.” Loosen up at the spa—enjoy all the temperatures, courtesy of a steam room, sauna, and cold plunge—before dining at Rosi, helmed by acclaimed chef Lisa Goodwin-Allen.
A menu with beef and ale pie and ox cheek mushroom pudding lets you know you’re eating classic British—but steeped in easy opulence.

With all due respect to the National Portrait Gallery, this is the more interesting (and less-crowded) location to see Old Master paintings, with underrated B-sides from Rembrandt to Rubens. Dulwich has “got all that historic side to it as well—but in a much calmer, quieter, more peaceful space,” Clark notes.
This non-touristy pub is tucked into a residential neighborhood—not that it’s sleepy: The scene is “a raucous Irish version of Cheers,” Clark says.
The renowned spot reopened after a long renovation, and, thanks to a more mature crowd, it’s always bumping without being “scuzzy.”
Four can’t-miss stores in London.

A vintage-clothing shop absolutely stacked with esoterica, from ’90s movie apparel (like a Kids promo tee) to archival Comme des Garçons. You might just snag something that would’ve otherwise ended up in Paul Mescal’s next red-carpet fit.
As much an art gallery as it is a boutique, Clark says, this spot is both “where serious people buy their clothes” and one of the “most peaceful shops” in London.
Even if your home isn’t stacked with rare LPs, Clark says this independent record store’s nonjudgmental staff won’t make you feel like a “dickhead for taking an interest.”

Held every other Sunday, this bazaar is basically a flash mob tag sale with 100-plus sellers offering up everything you can imagine—much of it sold from the trunk of their cars. That’s only half the reason for stopping by. The “people watching is better than Fashion Week,” says Clark.
A version of this story originally appeared in the October 2026 issue of GQ with the title “The GQ Guide to London.”

items.title: Actually, You Can Wear a Gold Watch Every Day
items.description: We get it: A gold watch can seem scary. It speaks loudly on your behalf, and you’re worried it might say something to make you look like a prick. But when a gold watch is done up just right, the effect is less Gordon Gekko, more Danny Ocean. You get elegance a
items.author: Cam Wolf; Bowen Fernie
paragraphs: We get it: A gold watch can seem scary. It speaks loudly on your behalf, and you’re worried it might say something to make you look like a prick. But when a gold watch is done up just right, the effect is less Gordon Gekko, more Danny Ocean. You get elegance and flair in a way no run-of-the-mill steel sport watch can match.

So what separates a glorious gold timepiece from a gaudy one? Simplicity. Omega’s new Constellation Observatory takes that mantra to extremes: A whisper of a bezel. No complications or subdials. Not even a seconds hand. Just 18-karat Moonshine gold wrapping the hyper-precise movement (to the right). It is flawlessness and flash in perfect equilibrium.

The thing about a gold watch this good is that it deserves plenty of time to shine. Wear it with your matching cuff links for expense account sushi with clients…but also to Zoom meetings and on burger runs. Because the only dull gold watch is the one stuck sitting on a nightstand.
Don’t have the dough for real gold just yet? Try a gold-toned timepiece on for size instead, which’ll deliver almost as much flash for a fraction of the price.
Rendered in yellow gold, the most hallowed models in the watch world somehow feel even more covetable.
These luxed-out sports models are proof that you should always go for gold.
Photography by Bowen Fernie
Styling by Haley Gilbreath
Manicure by Nori using Chanel Le Vernis
Special thanks to Nobu Downtown
A version of this story originally appeared in the October 2026 issue of GQ with the title “A Solid-gold Watch That Wears Like a Beater.”

items.title: The Wallabee Goes Gorpcore
items.description: Clarks has been on one lately. Over the past few weeks, Moncler worked up the British footwear brand's signature Wallabee, while A.P.C. took on the Desert Boot and the Weaver. Now, Clarks has called in Italian shoemaker Diemme to drag three of its biggest silh
items.author: Adam Cheung
paragraphs: Clarks has been on one lately. Over the past few weeks, Moncler worked up the British footwear brand's signature Wallabee, while A.P.C. took on the Desert Boot and the Weaver. Now, Clarks has called in Italian shoemaker Diemme to drag three of its biggest silhouettes up a mountain.

(In case you don't spend all day thinking about Italian hiking boots, here's a primer: Diemme was founded in Montebelluna, a town in northern Italy with a very serious footwear-making history. The brand is best known for taking the kinda boots originally built for mountains and making them nice enough to wear with your very best trousers. Every pair is still made at its factory in Veneto, and the upcoming Clarks collection is, too.)

The main event is the Wallabee, of course. Diemme reworked the familiar moccasin-shaped shoe and covered it in pale “champagne” suede from Charles F. Stead, the British tannery responsible for some of the nicest fuzzy leather in footwear. So far, so classic. But then you get the thick rope laces and rubber mudguard wrapped around the bottom. Underneath, the OG crepe sole has been swapped out for the chunky, lugged unit found on Diemme's Roccia Vet and Cornaro boots. It makes the whole shoe sit higher and gives it enough tread to deal with more than a slightly sticky pub floor. Your ’Bees are now ready to hit the trails.

There are two more styles in the cross-branded collection. The Desert Boot comes in the classic “cola” brown suede, only now it's been fitted with a heavy-duty sole. Then there's the Desert Trek, which has been transformed into a mid-cut boot and made from black full-grain leather. It keeps the signature center seam and little Trek Man logo, but it's easily the biggest and baddest of the three, with metal D-rings running up the lacing system and a beefed up ankle for extra support.
The Diemme x Clarks collection is set to drop on November 5, purchasable through Diemme, Clarks, and select stockists globally.
A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

items.title: Derek Blasberg Looks Back at His Life in Parties
items.description: Derek C. Blasberg’s origin story is “pretty typical,” he says: “Small-town boy moves to the big city with dreams and stars in his eyes.” Born and raised in St. Louis, the 44-year-old decamped to Manhattan in 2000 to attend New York University and was instantly
items.author: Claire Valentine
paragraphs: Derek C. Blasberg’s origin story is “pretty typical,” he says: “Small-town boy moves to the big city with dreams and stars in his eyes.” Born and raised in St. Louis, the 44-year-old decamped to Manhattan in 2000 to attend New York University and was instantly fascinated by the fashion world. He began his career as an intern at W and at Vogue, then quickly became a man-about-town, as likely to write about the best parties as he was to attend them. Since then, Blasberg has enjoyed many careers, from New York Times best-selling author to YouTube’s first-ever head of fashion and beauty.

These days, he juggles a few jobs: He’s a senior director at Gagosian, a special correspondent for Vanity Fair, a columnist for Harper’s Bazaar, and a Substacker. In July, he published Fast + Louche, a collection of Interview magazine nightlife columns he wrote from 2009 to 2012. With his point-and-shoot camera, he captured everyone from Phoebe Philo at the CFDA Awards to Nicole Richie at Mr. Chow for the column. “I still get giddy when I get invited to any of these fancy parties,” he says. “Honestly, sometimes I also still get nervous, because there’s a little part of me waiting for someone to tap me on the shoulder and say, ‘Excuse me, sir, you’re not supposed to be here.’”

With hundreds of soirées under his belt, Blasberg has theories on what makes one work. “A great party needs three things: people you love, people you don’t know, and at least one person you probably shouldn’t be talking to,” he says. Ultimately, “the best, most memorable nights of my life were the spontaneous ones. I’ve been lucky enough to go to some of the most fabulous places with some of the most fabulous people—but you can’t manufacture a great night. You can plan a party down to the flowers and the seating chart, but you can’t plan the magic. That’s the whole point.”

Top: Two-year-old Blasberg is pictured sleeping at his family’s kitchen table. “I’ve lived in New York for longer than I lived in Missouri, but I still identify as this Midwest kid trying to make it in the big city,” Blasberg explains. “So many of my core memories are vividly suburban: riding bikes around the neighborhood and never locking them, a social life that revolved around the mall. Of course, I couldn’t wait to get the fuck out of there, but the older I get, the more I cherish those memories. That’s probably why I’ve always maintained a little bit of an outsider’s perspective on this industry.” Bottom: He’s pictured celebrating his third birthday at McDonald’s, an event with Happy Meals, paper crowns, and a giant chocolate chip cookie cake. “For a 3-year-old in suburban America, it was as glamorous as you could get.”

Blasberg (bottom left) in 1985 with his brother, Chris (behind Blasberg), and the children of his mother’s Beta Sigma Phi sorority sisters at a party on the Lake of the Ozarks, or “the Hamptons of the Midwest,” as he calls it. Blasberg still returns to the lake every summer, for “long days on the water, waterskiing, tubing, and sunburns.”

Blasberg with his friend Maja Heyduk at their senior-year homecoming, themed “One Moment in Time.” Blasberg rented a tuxedo from Desmond’s, at Crestwood Plaza mall, and the dance was held in the high school gym, which was decorated by the student council. “It was all very sweet and small-town and homemade. At the time, it felt like the biggest night in the world.” He loved his vinyl black and white rental shoes so much that he begged the girl at the shop to let him keep them. “I still have them, of course.”

Top: Blasberg with his high school best friends, Maria Zemen (left) and Heyduk, in Zemen’s childhood bedroom. Growing up in St. Louis, the trio shopped at thrift stores, put together “wildly avant-garde outfits,” and went on late-night picture-taking adventures. “We were basically proto-influencers—we just didn’t have anywhere to post the content.” Bottom: They’re at their high school graduation, in 2000. Blasberg had a perfect attendance record from kindergarten through senior year. “It made the local news. I was a huge overachiever in high school because I knew I’d have to pull every trick I had to chase my dreams.”

“I attended NYU in 2000, and it felt like my real life could officially begin. I finally met other gay men— I didn’t meet an openly gay person until I was 18—and found a community of people who were as obsessed with fashion and art as I was.” When he spent a year abroad in London, he “fell even deeper under fashion’s spell.” Above: His student ID from his time in Europe.

In 2006, models Lily Donaldson (left) and Gemma Ward brought Blasberg to a French Vogue party hosted at the Gramercy Park Hotel. He got in as a plus-one, “a role I happily fulfilled for most of my early 20s,” he explains. “What’s the opposite of a nepo baby? My dad was an accountant, and my mom worked for a medical journal—in Missouri. Tagging along with these girls gave me a front-row seat to this world I was still figuring out how to become a part of.”

In 2008, Blasberg went to Moscow with (from left) artist Olympia Scarry, socialite Eugenie Niarchos, gallerist Larry Gagosian, Zhukova, and activist Barbara Bush. They all attended “For What You Are About to Receive,” an exhibition the Gagosian gallery staged in a 28,000-square-foot Soviet-era chocolate factory. “Afterward, we drank approximately a zillion gallons of vodka,” recalls Blasberg, who met Gagosian socially years before working for him. “He continues to be a source of inspiration.”

In 2012, Blasberg and Emma Watson (below, right) attended a party in London thrown by Gucci celebrating Blasberg’s book Very Classy. It was an expanded edition of his first book, Classy, a collection of comedic essays about etiquette. Very Classy carried the unofficial tagline “Be a lady, not a tramp.” As he says, “Some of the etiquette advice has aged better than the tagline, which makes me cringe a little now.” Blasberg met Watson in 2008, when the actor attended her first fashion show—Chanel, no less. “I have to confess that I never read the Harry Potter books, and I still haven’t seen the films, but the fashion gods brought us together. I remember being completely bowled over by how clever and well-read this young woman was. She was a teenager reciting sonnets!”

“I love Celine Dion—who doesn’t?” In 2012, Blasberg flew to Las Vegas twice to see her residency. He recalls sitting in the audience and “thinking over and over again: This person was put on this planet to do this one thing.” Afterward, he visited her dressing room, “with its billowing white curtains and scented candles.” He sat there “enraptured as she morphed from pop diva into wonderfully kooky, completely unfiltered Celine.”

During Couture Week in 2013, Blasberg attended a dinner Valentino Garavani and his business partner, Giancarlo Giammetti, hosted for Anna Wintour. The festivities were held at Château de Wideville, Valentino’s 17th-century estate outside of Paris. “Nobody did decadence quite like these two: beautiful rooms, beautiful tables, beautiful people, incredible food, and always a sense that the evening could go anywhere.”

From left: Miley Cyrus, Karen Elson, Emma Roberts, Karlie Kloss, Cara Delevingne, Rita Ora, and Blasberg at the 2013 Met Gala—one of the 15 or 16 he estimates he’s attended. The theme was “Punk: Chaos to Couture,” for which Blasberg had a makeup artist apply neck tattoos at the Carlyle hotel a few hours before. Blondie was performing when he snapped this picture, which may or may not be the first group selfie at the Met Gala. “This ould be my greatest contribution to fashion history. Put it on my tombstone!”

Blasberg with (from left) entrepreneur and podcaster Sara Foster, art collector Dasha Zhukova, Nicole Richie, and Naomi Campbell at an Oscars afterparty in 2016. “You have to understand that the Oscars were a national holiday in my house,” says Blasberg. “My parents would let me stay up late to watch them—but I’d record them on VHS anyway so I could watch them again. Yes, I was one of those kids. I still am, by the way.”

In 2019, Blasberg celebrated the Fourth of July in Paris at the house of Lauren Santo Domingo (third from left), along with (from left) his partner, Nick Brown; filmmaker Simon Kinberg; filmmaker Fabiola Beracasa Beckman; poet Cleo Wade; and actor Jessica Chastain. Blasberg met Santo Domingo when she was a market editor at Vogue and he was interning in the accessories closet during his senior year at NYU. “She was already one of the most glamorous women I’d ever met, a title she continues to hold.” Her Paris home, decorated by the late François Catroux, has been the site of countless soirées.

From left: Blasberg, Margherita Maccapani Missoni, Coco Brandolini d’Adda, Santo Domingo, Simmons, Kelly Sawyer, and Beracasa Beckman visiting Vistorta, the Brandolini family estate in Friuli, Italy, for Brandolini d’Adda’s 40th birthday, in 2019. The night featured a giant cake covered in tiny strawberries (Blasberg’s favorite food) and an outdoor disco that ran until the wee hours.

In 2021, Blasberg and a group of friends, including (from left) designer Lazaro Hernandez, editor Kristina O’Neill, fashion editor Katie Grand, stylist Tabitha Simmons, and designer Jack McCollough, stopped for a nightcap at the Carlyle hotel. Mariah Carey happened to pull up in a limo. “We watched her sort of wiggle out of the car and float into the hotel. Naturally, we followed.” O’Neill trailed her into the bathroom and persuaded her to sing. Minutes later, Carey was serenading the group. She requested to take this photo. “This was back when I carried a digital camera with me everywhere—for moments just like this one.”

Blasberg with Dua Lipa in 2021 at the afterparty for “Fendace,” when Versace’s and Fendi’s designers swapped houses for a collection shown in Milan: “Kate Moss on the runway! An afterparty in Gianni Versace’s old apartment on Via Gesù!” Later that night, a few stragglers gathered around a grand piano in a hotel lobby for an impromptu performance by Lipa.

Blasberg with Giammetti (center) and Valentino on the dance floor at Château de Wideville. As Blasberg recalls, whenever anyone complimented the designer on his style, he’d reply, “I love beauty; it’s not my fault.”

Blasberg with jewelry designer Jennifer Meyer (left) and actor Kate Hudson at their joint birthday party in 2023, held at Hudson’s home in the Pacific Palisades. The joint-party tradition began in 2015, when the three realized their birthdays fall within a week of one another’s: “Why not combine forces?”

In 2023, Blasberg co-curated “Avedon 100,” an exhibition at the Gagosian gallery marking the centennial of Richard Avedon’s birth. Above: He’s with Hillary Clinton in front of Avedon’s portrait of her. For the photo session, Clinton arrived in one of her trademark pantsuits. Avedon told her he’d seen enough pictures of her wearing that, so he handed her the sweater off his own back. When Clinton ran for president in 2016, Blasberg canvassed for her and joined her at New York’s Javits Center on election night. “That remains one of the saddest and most surreal nights I can remember. I’d gone there expecting to witness one kind of history, and instead witnessed another.”

Brown and Blasberg getting ready for the 2022 Met Gala with their twins, Noah and Grace, who were born in 2021. “Suddenly, I’d swapped popping bottles for baby bottles,” says Blasberg. “A very different kind of pregame. Becoming a father has been the greatest choice and most fulfilling ride of my life.”

items.title: The 12 Biggest Fashion Trends From the Spring 2027 Runways
items.description: The spring 2027 runways in New York, London, Milan, and Paris proved one thing: that it’s safe to say quiet luxury has left the chat. In its wake, maximalism bursts onto the scene, amid a flurry of fur, feathers, paillettes, and glittering beads. There were to
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: The spring 2027 runways in New York, London, Milan, and Paris proved one thing: that it’s safe to say quiet luxury has left the chat. In its wake, maximalism bursts onto the scene, amid a flurry of fur, feathers, paillettes, and glittering beads. There were tons of fabulous trends from the collections hewed by such designers as Matthieu Blazy for Chanel, Jonathan Anderson at Dior, and Michael Rider’s Celine. Below, we’re highlighting the 12 ready-to-wear fashion trends that caught our eye this season.

Say hello to the new Hawaiian shirt. The fact that Loro Piana, one of the key brands to helm the stealth-wealth style movement, created a take on an aloha button-down means this trend has staying power. There were cheeky nautical takes of all forms on the runways, including Miu Miu’s rash-guard tops layered with bejeweled bras and sporty mini-shorts. At Loewe, Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez designed beaded dresses inspired by the way one drapes themselves in a towel after going for a swim.

Every season, we see a different take on decade dressing. There were a number of riffs on ’70s styles, but our favorites were the ones that reflected the aesthetic of Southern California—more specifically, Venice Beach. Let’s call it elevated bohemian: at The Row, a pair of perfectly cut slouchy slacks was paired with an intricate sequin fringed antique fabric that was draped over the model as a top. In contrast, there was also August Barron’s lovable bungalow bro. And we adored the bright-sunshine dress at Celine, which was paired with exaggerated glasses and a monogram bag.
Itty-Bitty Titty Committee

The girls are wearing bras as shirts now, and it’s official. We went from the no-pants trend of the last couple of seasons to this new take: the no-top trend. Bras were everywhere, in every form—as daywear, and eveningwear, in all shapes and textiles, including satin, metal, and embellished.

We lost a true original this year: Dolly Parton, whose music and idiosyncratic signature look inspired designers for decades. For spring 2027, it was clear some looks on the runways were made specifically with Ms. Dollywood in mind. You could practically picture Parton on stage singing “I Will Always Love You” in Schiaparelli’s glamorous pink satin suit with jeweled buttons.

From glossy finishes to sculptural silhouettes, plastic is having its moment in the spotlight on the spring 2027 runways. Prada surprised audiences with a collection where every look was a variation on a skirt, including one crafted from a technical pink fabric. Chloé reimagined the classic trench with a rigid plastic overlay, while Maison Margiela’s own plastic skirt resembled a floral apron.

For spring 2027, subtlety is out and clashing prints are very much in. Florals ran headfirst into plaids at Polo, while Chanel’s Matthieu Blazy created a masterwork in patterns from head to toe. And your favorite art teacher appears to have had a nervous breakdown—albeit a pretty chic one—at Prada and Jil Sander.

While we’re on the topic of more-is-more, ornate beading made a major statement in this season’s collections, both on ready-to-wear fashion and accessories. Chanel made a play on its own classic with a yellow two-piece set done entirely in beads, while The Row worked black beading onto a flowing blue top. Loewe took things into three dimensions with beaded florals that seemed to bloom right off the dress.

Consider this trend the cousin of the one before it, especially when it comes to the ultra-luxe feel of each look. Saint Laurent delivered what felt like an entire collection of gold outfits, including the one shown here, which combined both gilding and brocade. At Gucci, the outfit was styled with a pussy-bow blouse and major sunglasses.

This season, designers put skirts under the microscope in a major way, remixing the garment into as many variations as there are women who wear them. First up was Miuccia Prada and Raf Simons at Prada, who devoted their entire spring 2027 collection to skirts: knee-length, mini, A-line, pleated, embroidered, and everything in between.

It seemed like every kind of plaid walked the spring 2027 runways: houndstooth, plain check, you name it. Duran Lantink transformed a classic picnic blanket print into an ’80s-esque blazer and skirt set for Jean Paul Gaultier, while Marni kept things in a ’60s kind of mood. Nicklas Skovgaard’s fierce checked skirtsuit had a furry friend on its right shoulder.

Designers imagined the full spectrum of a true 365 party girl’s perfect night out. Picture the scene: you arrive to a rager in a glamorous outfit, then start to get a little sweaty on the dance floor. Perhaps your dress is rumpled or your hair’s gotten caught in a stray streamer. Hours go by. What happened? Once daylight breaks, you find yourself heading back home in last night’s clothing.

If you’re currently having a 365 party girl-worthy hangover, don’t worry. Unplug your steamer and feel confident shoving that T-shirt to the bottom of your dresser drawer, because wrinkles are so in. Don’t even think about buttoning a sweater all the way, or fully fastening a belt! You think you need a tailor? Absolutely not. Let your seams be undone.

items.title: NASA’s Swift Observatory Is Falling to Earth. Here’s What to Know About the Impending Impact
items.description: After 22 years in orbit and a failed rescue mission this summer, it is highly likely that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will crash into Earth sometime next week. It is not known where on the planet the spacecraft—which is roughly as big as a large elevato
items.author: Javier Carbajal
paragraphs: After 22 years in orbit and a failed rescue mission this summer, it is highly likely that the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will crash into Earth sometime next week. It is not known where on the planet the spacecraft—which is roughly as big as a large elevator—will fall. Despite its size, experts say the risk to the public is relatively low.

What is now a useless piece of space junk was for a long time extraordinarily valuable to the scientific community. Launched on November 20, 2004, Swift was a space observatory equipped with three telescopes. It was designed primarily to detect and study gamma-ray bursts, which are among the most energetic explosions in the universe. Swift would locate these events and transmit their positions to observatories around the world for further study.

The observatory was designed to operate for a few years in low Earth orbit, but it far exceeded its expected lifespan, helping to make many important discoveries about the evolution of the cosmos, including the study of supernovas and the destruction of stars by black holes. However, in 2024, increased solar activity heated and expanded the upper layers of Earth’s atmosphere, increasing the drag on the satellite and accelerating its descent. Without a propulsion system capable of correcting its orbit, its days were numbered.

In July 2026, NASA launched a special $30 million mission to rescue Swift. A robotic spacecraft called LINK was supposed to drag Swift away from Earth by 150 miles, giving it a higher orbit and thus extending its operational life. Unfortunately, LINK failed. In August, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman explained that the difficulties that led to the mission’s cancellation were due to problems with the spacecraft’s control system, which made it impossible to keep it properly oriented and stable in space.

On October 26, NASA announced that Swift was less than 170 miles from Earth’s surface—a very low orbit for a satellite. According to the agency, the telescopes on board could no longer maintain stable observations of their astronomical targets. Swift conducted its final observation on October 20, then the operations team based at Pennsylvania State University terminated its operational status.

“Swift delivered an incredible, lasting return on investment for the nation, designed for a two-year primary mission but productive for more than 10 times as long,” Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of the Astrophysics Division at NASA headquarters in Washington, said in a statement. “In that time, Swift played a major role in advancing our understanding of the changing universe and was part of a revolution in astrophysics that showed how critical rapid-response observations are to the entire community.”

In its lifetime, the satellite observed over 2,000 gamma-ray bursts and nearly as many supernovas, data from which contributed to more than 7,000 research papers. And its contributions are far from over. “Swift leaves us with an extraordinary archive of multiwavelength observations that will fuel new discoveries for decades more,” Domagal-Goldman added.
What to Expect From the Reentry?

The US Space Force estimates Swift is likely to crash on or around Friday, November 6—or at least whatever remains of the satellite will. Most of the space observatory is expected to disintegrate as it reenters the atmosphere. However, some pieces made of tungsten and parts of the mirrors could survive that chaotic process, Brad Cenko, NASA’s chief scientist for the mission, told the Associated Press.

“The most likely survivors are its six heavy reaction wheels, the spinning flywheels it used to aim itself, along with tougher telescope parts such as lenses and mirrors,” Dean Sladen, a quality manager and aerospace engineer at Accu Components, said to Space.com. “Only a handful of small, scorched fragments are expected to make it down—nothing recognizable as a telescope.”

Where exactly will that debris fall? Large areas of Africa, Australia, India, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America fall within the reentry zone monitored by the Space Force. If there is a more precise calculation, that information has not been made public, but it’s most likely that all Swift’s remaining pieces will end up in the ocean.

“NASA's own orbital debris requirements state that the risk of human casualty from surviving debris shall not exceed one in 10,000, so it is highly likely this work has been completed but not published,” Sladen said regarding the risk assessment. “Personally, I believe it should be published, as NASA has done with previous satellites. The risk is almost certainly very small, but it would give people a clear, factual picture rather than guesswork.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

items.title: Ancient Meteorite Found in the Sahara Holds Secrets About Mars’ Watery Past
items.description: In 2022, a strange rock was found in the Sahara Desert, and now a new analysis reveals that it’s even more valuable to science than it first appeared. This fragment, weighing about two pounds, came from Mars’ crust. It was likely ejected by an impact, flying t
items.author: Jorge Garay
paragraphs: In 2022, a strange rock was found in the Sahara Desert, and now a new analysis reveals that it’s even more valuable to science than it first appeared. This fragment, weighing about two pounds, came from Mars’ crust. It was likely ejected by an impact, flying through space until it eventually reached Earth. The rock is one of the oldest known samples from our neighboring planet, estimated to be at least 4.1 billion years old. At that time, Earth was a young planet with intense geological activity, likely with oceans but no animals, plants, or any other complex life.

The location is not what makes this finding surprising. The Sahara has long been a kind of natural archive of the history of Earth and the solar system. Among its sands, scientists have found 40-million-year-old fossils and other meteorites. In 2019, for example, a 4.5-billion-year-old fragment was recovered that, according to recent research, may have come from an ancient, now-vanished protoplanet, possibly as large as the moon.

The meteorite, named Teghaza 001, might have remained just another entry in the collection of Martian fragments found on Earth. Although these rocks are extraordinarily useful for studying Mars’ composition and geological history, they often provide limited information about the environmental conditions of its distant past. However, a series of studies published in the journals Science and Science Advances revealed that Teghaza 001 is not like other samples. In addition to being exceptionally old, it has preserved chemical traces of the interaction between materials in the Martian crust and its ancient hydrosphere.
“One of the paper’s reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars,” Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory said in a press release.

Tiny crystals of a mineral called apatite preserves signatures of two sources of hydrogen: one originating from the interior of Mars and the other related to its ancient hydrosphere. In other words, the meteorite contains material that was altered by a water-rich environment. For years, there has been considerable evidence that Mars once harbored liquid water on its surface. Today, some of the big questions about the planet are whether that water allowed microscopic life to emerge and what happened to change this once hospitable environment.

This meteorite reveals that there was an exchange of materials between the magma deep within Mars and a watery surface. Since the rock comes from just about 500 million years after Mars and the rest of our solar system formed, this volatility occurred very early in the planet’s existence.

“This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we’ve never had a sample of before,” added Lee Saper, another NASA scientist who contributed to the research. “It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water.”

Today, Mars is a cold and barren planet, but it was not always that way. Evidence gathered by space missions suggests that it once had rivers, lakes, and possibly large bodies of water. But how that transformation happened over billions of years has remained a mystery. Answering that question is part of the reasoning behind sending probes, rovers, and perhaps, one day, crewed missions to Mars. But sometimes science is about serendipity, and answers arrive in the form of extraordinarily unlikely meteorites.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

items.title: The White House Chose the Wrong Day to Piss Off Adéla
items.description: President Trump’s White House is once again using music made by musicians who hate him to promote the MAGA agenda on social media. On the eve of Election Day, the White House TikTok account shared a heavily filtered pro-Trump video featuring an airplane, milit
items.author: Sam Reed
paragraphs: President Trump’s White House is once again using music made by musicians who hate him to promote the MAGA agenda on social media. On the eve of Election Day, the White House TikTok account shared a heavily filtered pro-Trump video featuring an airplane, military men, and many different angles of Trump in his favorite baseball hat. The video was set to the song “Nicole Kidman” by the Slovak singer Adéla, which features lyrics like “Every single night I pray that my tits are sittin’ right.” Nothing says patriotism like symmetrical cleavage! (You can watch the video here, but Adéla advises against giving any more attention to the White House’s “flopping” accounts.)

The 22-year-old singer wasted no time sharing her thoughts on the unauthorized usage of her song, which she likened to “rage bait” given how often it happens to her and other artists. With her pink hair still pinned in curls, the singer filmed a video telling followers that Trump’s use of her song is “obviously so fucking wrong on so many levels.” She added that there is “zero” overlap between her values and the values of the Republican Party.

Because Adéla is an immigrant, she can’t vote against the Republican Party in the midterm elections. However, she can reach millions of American voters and encourage them to vote against Trump et al. “Let me use this attention to give you a message of my own,” she said. “I would love to vote for a party that loves immigrants and that believes in accessible and safe abortion.” She also advocated on behalf of politicians that foster “an environment where people can be free and be themselves and feel safe.”
“Please, please, please, go out and vote in the midterms,” she concluded. “And fuck you guys for using my song.”

items.title: Haley Stevens Doesn’t Want You to Blame Her Fiancé
items.description: According to Representative Haley Stevens, it’s sexist to assume her fiancé was behind the decision that ruined her political career. She can do that all by herself, thank you very much. On Sunday, Stevens shocked Democrats across the country by endorsing Repu
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: According to Representative Haley Stevens, it’s sexist to assume her fiancé was behind the decision that ruined her political career. She can do that all by herself, thank you very much. On Sunday, Stevens shocked Democrats across the country by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan’s Senate race. Some of Stevens’s colleagues and former staffers have wondered if she was persuaded to abandon her party by her fiancé, Jason Turkish, who announced he’d be voting for Rogers just a few days before she did.

Turkish, a lawyer and prolific Democratic donor, was quite involved in Stevens’s failed Senate campaign. Former staffers told CNN he would berate and belittle them with one person saying he was “extremely overbearing, controlling, arrogant — a misogynistic personality.” Sources inside the campaign said Turkish would send negative social-media comments directly to Stevens, even after she told staffers to only show her important news. “He would wind her up, and then we’d have to wind her down,” one aide said. It’s unclear when things turned romantic between them, but this past spring, the couple got engaged on the campaign trail via FaceTime.

On October 28, Turkish told the Detroit News he planned to vote for Rogers, specifically because of El-Sayed’s stance on Gaza. “I’ve just seen an escalation in his rhetoric since the primary, and it makes folks unsafe. Every time he talks about genocide (in Gaza), Jews get death threats,” Turkish said, adding that El-Sayed was acting “recklessly toward the safety of Jews.” At the time, Stevens said they were “a house divided” and she would still be voting for El-Sayed.

The day before Stevens endorsed Rogers, her former campaign consultant Caitlin Legacki claimed on X that Turkish was “vaporizing Haley’s future so that he can be a main character in this moment.” She said he was “an extraordinarily toxic presence, was verbally abusive to staff and had some of the worst political instincts I’ve ever witnessed.”

After Stevens’s endorsement, other people close to her expressed concern about how much Turkish had been involved. Former representative Susan Wild wrote on X, “If this is because of her new relationship … all I can say is that any woman who abandons her friends when a new guy comes along is no friend at all.” Michigan state senator Mallory McMorrow said it was “hard to watch” Turkish try and speak for Stevens.

Former Michigan governor Jim Blanchard told Gongwer News Service that Turkish was “working [Stevens] over” when he hosted the couple for dinner last Friday. “The way he was saying it was, ‘Everyone is disappointed in you, they did everything they could to help you and then immediately after you lose the primary, you endorsed him,’” Blanchard said. The former governor tried to defend Stevens for being a “team player” and later said he told her he thought Turkish was a “bad influence.”

Stevens and Turkish, however, have strongly denied he had anything to do with her choice to endorse Rogers. In an interview with the Free Press on Monday night, Turkish said if anyone thought he was controlling Stevens, “they’ve obviously never met Haley.”

In her own lengthy statement shared to X, Stevens took umbrage with the idea that Turkish was involved in her decision. “A woman can serve in Congress, run statewide, and fight for her convictions, and still be told that when she makes a choice people dislike, someone else must be pulling the strings,” she wrote. “That is sexism dressed up as political analysis.”
“My fiancé has his own views. I have mine,” she continued. “I made this decision, and I am proud of it. Do not question my independence simply because you disagree with my conclusion.”

Hear that? Women can make bad decisions of their own accord! This is what the suffrage movement was all about. In honor of those women, Stevens showed up to the polls Tuesday in a comically large hat. Turkish was also there, lurking in the background.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 4, 2026
items.description: This morning, Venus and Jupiter (in Libra and Leo, respectively) are likely to put you in a warm, sociable mood. You’ll feel generous and cordial with everyone you encounter. The sun also aligns today with Mercury, the planet of thought and communication, in p
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: This morning, Venus and Jupiter (in Libra and Leo, respectively) are likely to put you in a warm, sociable mood. You’ll feel generous and cordial with everyone you encounter. The sun also aligns today with Mercury, the planet of thought and communication, in perceptive Scorpio, which means you might experience some important emotional revelations. Just remember that both Mercury and Venus are still retrograde until mid-month, so do your best to keep the focus on inner reflection rather than outward action.

You tend to make up your mind about people quickly — and your first impressions are usually reliable. Today, though, is a good time to revisit your opinions about the people around you. Maybe you were right about them when you first met, but it’s possible they (or you) have grown up or evolved since you first met. Set aside your preconceptions for now and give people a chance to change your mind about them.

When you’re trying to build (or maintain) relationships with people, it might seem prudent to focus on your similarities and downplay any disagreements. You can almost always find some sort of common ground, and that’s often a good place to direct your energy. But today, remember that there’s value in your differences too. Other people have skills you lack and vice versa. Your relationships will get stronger if you can make a point of recognizing and appreciating the ways your friends are different from you — and how you can complement one another.

You feel a responsibility to be aware of what’s going on in the world around you. But you also enjoy being up to date on things. You want to know everything that’s happening in your community and be tuned in to the dramas in your friend group. The more you know, the more full and exciting life feels. Today, though, your challenge is to recognize that some things simply aren’t your business. Give yourself permission to stop paying attention so you can refocus your energy on what truly matters.

Today, you’re likely to encounter some laziness in those around you. Even if everyone can agree on what needs to be done, no one will want to be the one to actually do it. If everybody around you is hesitating to take action, it might fall to you to step up and be brave right now. You don’t need to seek out opportunities to be the hero, but if the chance comes your way, trust in your ability to rise to the occasion.

Initiating new projects and embarking on new relationships is always exciting to you. You love the feeling of possibility — anything could happen! But after a while, what was once thrilling and new can start to feel dull and commonplace and you might be tempted to find another new source of entertainment. But today, resist the urge to do this. It’s important that you focus on finishing (or maintaining) what you’ve already started. That endurance will serve you well in the long run.

You’ve encountered plenty of people who don’t seem to respect you or your dreams — but their disapproval means little to you. You take your own life seriously, and you treat your ambitions like they’re worth fighting for. However, be careful to not get so laser-focused on your goals today that you lose your sense of humor or your ability to laugh at yourself. Joking around can actually help you let off steam so you don’t burn out. That in turn will help ensure that whoever underestimates you continues to be proven wrong.

If you feel stuck and unable to make any progress on the projects before you today, consider that you might be overcomplicating things. Maybe you’re thinking too many steps ahead or trying to consider too many angles at once. The solution right now is to simplify, simplify, simplify. Your job isn’t to figure everything out at once or understand the problem in its entirety — all you need to do is determine your immediate next step, then take it.

You know everyone makes mistakes sometimes — but part of you feels that you shouldn’t. It’s fine for other people to be wrong about things, but you don’t offer yourself the same grace. Today, try to recognize when your expectations for yourself are unreasonable and make a point of treating yourself with more compassion. The people who love you don’t need you to be perfect. Your genuine effort is enough for them; let it be enough for you too.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You’re someone who values honesty and open communication. You consider being forthright a sign of respect. But today, remember you don’t need to be fully transparent with everyone. It’s one thing to be honest and direct — even vulnerable — with the people you trust and care about, but you needn’t bare your soul to every random person you meet. Save your deepest thoughts for the people you’re closest to; with everyone else, it might be wiser to hold back for now.

If other people’s expectations feel unreasonable today, remember that you don’t have to live up to them. When the unspoken norms of your social circle feel restrictive, you’re allowed to break them. Other people might insist that you have to follow their rules, but in many cases, this isn’t true. Right now, what’s more important is that you follow your own rules. You have the freedom to decide what truly matters to you; set your own moral code, then follow through.

You’ll have the ability to charm just about anyone right now. But the key is to make sure you’re not squandering that gift on people whose opinions you don’t actually value. If you try to please people you don’t even like, you’ll be wasting your time; if you indulge people who don’t share any of your values, you’ll betray the ideals you care most about. If you’re going to put in the effort to be liked by someone, make sure it’s somebody you truly respect.

Today, try to step outside of your usual routines. You needn’t do anything impressive or dramatic — if anything, it’s probably best to avoid grand gestures for the time being. The point isn’t to transform your whole life but to remind yourself that the world can still offer some surprises. You aren’t locked into your habits; if you need a change, it’s as simple as deciding to switch up your schedule, start a conversation with a stranger, or test out a new activity just to see if you like it.
Buy Claire Comstock-Gay’s book, Madame Clairevoyant’s Guide to the Stars, here.

items.title: Abby Phillip Has a Very Cute Reason for Skipping Election Night
items.description: Election Night is as big as it gets for the cable-news cohort, but CNN anchor and political correspondent Abby Phillip had the best — arguably, the only — excuse for skipping the big night. Phillip welcomed her second child, a son named Maxwell Elias Richardso
items.author: Sam Reed
paragraphs: Election Night is as big as it gets for the cable-news cohort, but CNN anchor and political correspondent Abby Phillip had the best — arguably, the only — excuse for skipping the big night. Phillip welcomed her second child, a son named Maxwell Elias Richardson, on October 27, and spent November 3 with her family.

“Missing our Election Night coverage today for a very good reason 👶🏾🩵,” Phillip wrote on social media alongside a photo of her family of four. “But I’ll be watching and cheering on my colleagues from afar. Hope you tune in also!” She helpfully added a link to CNN’s All Access coverage, because she’s a team player, even on maternity leave.

Phillip shares Maxwell and her 4-year-old daughter, Naomi, with her husband, Marcus Richardson, whom she married in 2018. Earlier this year, she shared with People that her and Richardson’s “journey to a second child looked a little different from our first.”

“Like so many families, we were able to conceive with the help of IVF,” she said. “The process was challenging to manage, both emotionally and physically, but I’m thrilled to say we arrived at a beautiful place.” Phillip wasn’t on the ballot, but she’s a winner today!

items.title: 5 Spicy Friends-To-Lovers Books ‘Nobody Wants This’ Fans Will Swoon Over
items.description: The central love story of Nobody Wants This may be the star-crossed pairing between “hot rabbi” Noah and sex podcaster Joanne, but in Season 3, a new fling enters the chat. And friends-to-lovers fans... this one’s for you.
items.author: Grace Wehniainen
paragraphs: The central love story of Nobody Wants This may be the star-crossed pairing between “hot rabbi” Noah and sex podcaster Joanne, but in Season 3, a new fling enters the chat. And friends-to-lovers fans... this one’s for you.

Brought into each other’s orbit by their respective siblings’ relationship, Morgan and Sasha have spent several seasons developing their own special friendship — one defined by playful banter that even they’re rarely sure is friendly or flirty. (As Morgan told Sasha in Season 1, “Stop saying that it’s not weird when we both know that it kind of is.”)

In the latest entry, they finally hook up, and while fans might debate the specifics of their fling, there’s no denying that the friends-to-lovers trope brings a special kind of buzz. That built-in intimacy can lend itself to sweet, humorous repartee — there’s no need to play brooding or aloof when you know someone that well.
Need some more? Here are seven spicy friends-to-lovers books that echo the playful passion and relationship conundrums of Nobody Wants This.
The Roommate Risk by Talia Hibbert

After sharing a passionate night in college, Jasmine and Rahul decide to be just friends. Best friends. But seven years later, a plumbing emergency forces them into close proximity — leaving them to reckon with feelings that never really went away.
Funny Feelings by Tarah DeWitt

Stand-up comedian Farley is best friends with her manager, Meyer. When a career opportunity prompts them to begin a fake relationship, their closeness takes on a new (and deliciously passionate) form.
When Javi Dumped Mari by Mia Sosa

Though he’s had feelings for her since college, Javi’s insecurities lead him to believe his best friend Mari is unattainable. By the time he feels worthy of her, Mari’s engaged — and he’ll have to make his feelings known before she says “I do” in a countdown to the altar sweetly reminiscent of My Best Friend’s Wedding.
Hook, Line, and Sinker by Tessa Bailey

Much like Morgan in Nobody Wants This, Hannah meets Fox through her sister’s relationship, and the two become good friends. But when actor Hannah moves to Fox’s coastal town to shoot a movie, they discover a romantic tension that’s too reel to ignore.
Romancing Mister Bridgerton by Julia Quinn

There’s a Bridgerton book for every trope, and friends-to-lovers is executed beautifully in Romancing Mister Bridgerton. Penelope has long nursed a crush on her family friend, Colin, and while their union brings some obstacles to work out (including Pen’s secret gig as the ton’s juiciest gossip), all those years of pining have some seriously steamy payoff.

items.title: Here’s Your November Horoscope
items.description: November opens in the deep end. The new moon rises in uncompromising Scorpio on Nov. 9. Prepare to get real about what you want. What are you finally ready to release in order to get it? This isn’t the time for half-measures or surface-level intentions. The ch
items.author: Alexandria Lettman
paragraphs: November opens in the deep end. The new moon rises in uncompromising Scorpio on Nov. 9. Prepare to get real about what you want. What are you finally ready to release in order to get it? This isn’t the time for half-measures or surface-level intentions. The choices you make now carry a lasting weight, so consider them carefully.
The fog finally lifts on Nov. 13, when Mercury retrograde ends in Scorpio. It may feel easier to pick up the thread of a conversation, decision, or idea you have been circling since late October.

The next day, Venus follows suit when it stations direct in Libra. The culmination of this retrograde is the exhale you’ve been waiting for. Notice what has changed about what you are willing to give and receive to sustain a relationship.

After all of Scorpio season’s intensity, the sun’s ingress into Sagittarius on Nov. 22 swings open a window and lets the light back in. Adventure and hope are back on the table. Look forward and aim high.

Electric energy buzzes around the full moon in Gemini on Nov. 24. Uranus, the planet of innovation and change, links up with the bright supermoon. A breakthrough could be on the horizon, the kind that leads you to finally share what’s on your mind. However, one thing remains uncertain: how other people will respond. Don’t let this stop you from speaking your truth.

When motivated Mars enters precise Virgo on Nov. 25, effort, discipline, and methodical action beat impulsivity. The goals that have been gaining momentum now require focus and a plan of execution. Roll up your sleeves and dive into the real, productive work — then relax the next day with some turkey and cranberry sauce.
Happy birthday, Sagittarius!

Good news, Aries! The words you couldn’t find in October may spring to mind with clarity this month. That conversation you’ve been dreading could turn out to be the one that actually frees you. Don’t be afraid to revisit a situation that has tested your honesty, trust, and ability to be vulnerable.

Whether you are hashing out a shared financial burden or getting intimate with a partner, you could walk into Sagittarius season (beginning on Nov. 22) feeling optimistic about what lies ahead. Rather than letting your thoughts fester, speak up in the moment. Luck is on your side.

All relationships have ups and downs, but they shouldn’t feel permanently exhausting. After the intimate Scorpio new moon on Nov. 9, you may have a clearer idea of what’s worth fighting for. How can you turn over a new leaf?

By mid-month, complicated issues at work can be resolved through stronger collaboration. Remember your worth and think twice before you pick up other people’s responsibilities again.
