items.title: «Ерунда, все пройдет». Что скрывается за диагнозом «остеохондроз» и почему это важно знать | Такие дела
items.description: «Ерунда, все пройдет». Что скрывается за диагнозом «остеохондроз» и почему это важно знать
items.author: Алексей Семенов
paragraphs: «Ерунда, все пройдет». Что скрывается за диагнозом «остеохондроз» и почему это важно знать

Хроническая боль беспокоит 43% россиян, чаще всего она локализуется в спине. До половины тех, кто обращается по этому поводу к врачам, получают диагноз «остеохондроз» без дополнительных обследований. Но этот термин означает определенные изменения, которые есть у многих, кто вообще не жалуется на спину. Использование остеохондроза как универсального диагноза приводит к риску пропустить по-настоящему серьезные заболевания: инфекции, переломы и даже опухоли.

По данным ВЦИОМа, 43% россиян всех возрастов сообщают о хронической боли. В 37% случаев эти симптомы связаны со спиной. До четверти пациентов, обращающихся в поликлинику, приходят к врачам именно из-за такой боли.

Исследование 2020 года показало, что за прошедшие 30 лет количество людей, испытывающих такую боль, во всем мире выросло на 60,5%. Через 30 лет распространенность боли в спине, по прогнозу ученых, вырастет еще на 36%. За всю жизнь с этим сталкивается до 80% человек.

Зимой 2024 года у 26-летней москвички Карины впервые в жизни заболела спина. Девушка ведет активный образ жизни и не ожидала, что столкнется с этим. «Я пошла к неврологу, которая была очень незаинтересованной и выписала нестероидные противовоспалительные и миорелаксанты», — рассказывает Карина.

Ее состояние немного улучшилось, и девушка отправилась в запланированный отпуск в Китай. Там ей снова стало хуже, ее госпитализировали и сделали МРТ, на котором увидели грыжу. «Сказали, что надо делать операцию, но это только дома», — рассказывает девушка.
По возвращении в Москву она снова обратилась к врачу, и ей без дополнительной диагностики поставили диагноз «остеохондроз позвоночника», назначили ЛФК, физиотерапию и плавание.
Карина строго выполняла рекомендации, и через пару месяцев боль прошла, но вскоре вернулась. Невролог заявил, что не видит никаких проблем:

На повторных снимках врачи заметили также протрузии, но сказали, что все это не может быть причиной боли в спине. «Я спрашиваю: “А почему у меня тогда болит спина?” И мне пишут в заключении — остеохондроз», — рассказывает девушка.

В итоге причину боли в спине Карины так и не нашли, а рекомендации врачи давали прямо противоположные. «То можно мне плавать, то нельзя. То можно идти в поход, то можно только с определенным весом, то совсем нельзя. То нужна ортопедическая подушка, но неизвестно, какого вида. Надо худеть, но не бегать. Ничего мне никто нормально не сказал. Нет никакого решения, что именно вызывает эти боли и как не допускать обострений».

До середины XX века боль в спине связывали с воспалительными заболеваниями. В шестидесятых годах прошлого века советский врач Яков Попелянский, основываясь на исследованиях немецких коллег, заметил связь между болевым синдромом и изменениями в позвоночнике.

Такой подход стал основой вертеброневрологии — направления в советской медицине, объясняющего боль в спине дегенеративными проявлениями в позвоночнике. В восьмидесятые годы эта концепция закрепилась в рекомендациях Минздрава СССР. С тех пор практически любую боль в спине стали связывать с остеохондрозом.
«Доктору достаточно было увидеть на рентгене возрастные изменения, и пациент получал готовый диагноз», — объясняет основатель Клиники Ткачева невролог Александр Ткачев.

Остеохондроз действительно существует в МКБ-10, использующейся в России. Такой диагноз получает более половины пациентов, которые обратились в российские поликлиники с костно-мышечными заболеваниями. Это значительно больше, чем, например, в Германии, где врачи физической и реабилитационной медицины ставят этот диагноз только в 10% случаев.

Дело в том, что в зарубежной практике под остеохондрозом чаще всего понимают определенную группу заболеваний, связанных с нарушениями развития костной ткани у детей, но не с болью в спине у взрослых. В МКБ-11, на которую перешли многие страны, но не Россия, остеохондроз позвоночника у взрослых вообще не указан.
«Если говорить простыми словами, “остеохондроз” в том виде, как этот диагноз часто используют у нас, — слишком общий термин», — комментирует невролог клиники «Три сестры» Александра Грибова.

Статистики, насколько часто за диагнозом «остеохондроз» скрывается другое заболевание, в целом по России нет. В исследовании, описывающем практику неврологического стационара Ярославля, с остеохондрозом поступило 70% пациентов, но у всех, кому позже назначили дополнительные обследования, диагноз изменился на более точно описывающий их состояние.

Сами по себе разночтения в терминологии не слишком важны для пациентов, отмечает Грибова: «Проблема возникает, когда словом “остеохондроз” объясняют любую боль в спине или шее и на этом обследование заканчивается. Иногда за такой болью действительно могут скрываться более серьезные состояния: перелом позвонка, опухолевое поражение, инфекция, воспалительное заболевание позвоночника, сдавление спинного мозга или нервных структур».
В 2011 году у 20-летней петербурженки Ульяны заболела спина. Девушка около полугода ходила по разным врачам, и в итоге ей диагностировали остеохондроз.

«Некоторые говорили: “Ерунда, что у вас там может быть в ваши годы? Делайте гимнастику, и все пройдет”. Из исследований меня направляли только на рентген. В итоге боль стала такая, что было невозможно спать», — рассказывает Ульяна.
После одной такой ночи она без направления врача отправилась в платную клинику, чтобы пройти МРТ.

Через три недели девушке сделали операцию. Новообразование оказалось доброкачественной невриномой. «После операции лечащий врач сказал, что если бы я затянула с обращением, то могли начаться дегенеративные процессы в нижней половине тела, вплоть до паралича», — добавляет Ульяна.

При этом сразу после первых признаков боли в спине делать МРТ не нужно, предостерегает Грибова. Это исследование с высокой долей вероятности покажет какие-то изменения в позвоночнике, но они встречаются у 37% человек в возрасте от 27 лет и у 96% — в возрасте от 80 лет. Большинство из них не связано с болью в спине.
«Изменения на снимках и боль — не одно и то же. У двух человек может быть почти одинаковая картина на МРТ, но один живет без каких-либо жалоб, а другой испытывает сильную боль», — поясняет Ткачев.
К врачу нужно обращаться, если боль в спине не проходит больше месяца. В группе риска — люди, которые часто поднимают тяжести, курят, имеют большой вес или находятся в депрессии.

Сначала доктор должен определить, что именно происходит: есть ли поражение нервного корешка, грыжа диска, стеноз, воспалительные изменения, мышечная боль или речь идет о неспецифической боли в спине, при которой невозможно уверенно назвать одну поврежденную структуру. Если никаких серьезных причин не нашлось, лечение включает физическую активность, местное разогревание, обезболивающие и миорелаксанты.

В этом случае врач сосредоточится на особенностях позвоночника, которые не приносят дискомфорта, рискуя пропустить настоящую причину, объясняет Грибова. «Поэтому лечить нужно не снимок, а человека и его симптомы», — добавляет она.

По-настоящему тревожными симптомами, при которых нужно дополнительное обследование, она называет слабость в руках и ногах, проблемы с ходьбой, мочеиспусканием и дефекацией, лихорадку и резкую потерю веса. Дополнительное обследование оправдано и тогда, когда боль долго не проходит, несмотря на лечение. По данным исследований, угрожающие симптомы были примерно у 10% россиян, обратившихся к врачу с болью в спине.

«Остеохондроз нельзя превращать в универсальный ответ на любую боль. Он не объясняет автоматически, почему у конкретного человека болит спина, и не может заменить полноценный клинический диагноз», — говорит Ткачев.
Врачу нужно не просто увидеть изменения на МРТ, а собрать анамнез, провести полноценный неврологический осмотр и только тогда поставить диагноз и назначить лечение, заключила Грибова.
Каждый день мы пишем о самых важных проблемах в нашей стране и предлагаем способы их решения. За девять лет мы собрали 300 миллионов рублей в пользу проверенных благотворительных организаций.

«Такие дела» существуют благодаря пожертвованиям: с их помощью мы оплачиваем работу авторов, фотографов и редакторов, ездим в командировки и проводим исследования. Мы просим вас оформить пожертвование в поддержку проекта. Любая помощь, особенно если она регулярная, помогает нам работать.

Оформив регулярное пожертвование на сумму от 500 рублей, вы сможете присоединиться к «Таким друзьям» — сообществу близких по духу людей. Здесь вас ждут мастер-классы и воркшопы, общение с редакцией, обсуждение текстов и встречи с их героями.
Станьте частью перемен — оформите ежемесячное пожертвование. Спасибо, что вы с нами!

items.title: Republicans Are Calling It the Worst Campaign of All Time
items.description: By the time Texas was close to being called for James Talarico, the texts were coming in fast and very furious. Closely mirroring the attitude of the voters, Republican operatives saw a group of out-of-touch party elites getting rich while the rest of them sta
items.author: Jake Lahut
paragraphs: By the time Texas was close to being called for James Talarico, the texts were coming in fast and very furious. Closely mirroring the attitude of the voters, Republican operatives saw a group of out-of-touch party elites getting rich while the rest of them staggered under catastrophic losses. “Susie Wiles, James Blair, and Chris LaCivita have proven themselves to be historic: losing South Carolina, Texas, and Kansas,” one GOP strategist said, naming three of the key members in President Donald Trump’s inner circle. “Trump has truly hired the dumbest people.”

Republican staffers are mortified by a president they readily admit couldn’t have been more distant from voters’ concerns, which revolved around high prices stoked by an unnecessary war in Iran. Another Republican operative, who had been conducting polling in just about every competitive House district, laid the blame at the feet of NRSC director Richard Hudson, who lost his North Carolina seat in a shock upset to Richard Ojeda, a veteran who previously ran for Congress in West Virginia in 2018. “Absolute embarrassment for Richard Hudson, Hudson’s NRCC, and the White House,” said this operative, who like others requested anonymity to speak candidly. “They hand-picked a lot of their candidates, took huge swings, such as starting the redistricting war, and it all blew up in their faces.”

One Trump-aligned strategist said, “It’s easy to point fingers, but I think it boils down to significant messaging failures across the board, failing to understand what’s important, in some cases just bad candidates, which I guess goes back to the consultant class. Significant unforced errors.”

A Republican pollster described a “criminal laziness” permeating the party, a slavish devotion to the president that resulted in god-awful candidates and poor messaging. On the bright side, the midterms acted like a cleansing wave, ridding the party of many of its worst representatives, like Ken Paxton in Texas. “Well, we’re at rock bottom,” the pollster said, “but there’s a lot fewer guys around to dig.”

The bottom began falling out after Labor Day, coinciding with the president’s midterm convention in Dallas. “I don’t think it was because of the convention, but that convention coincided with when voters started paying attention and what they saw was Trump focusing on everything except their own bottom lines and what would make their lives and their families’ lives better,” said the GOP operative involved in competitive races. “Across the board, I would also give a lot of credit to Democrats.”

Trump’s closing speech in front of the Reflecting Pool, where he spent most of his time musing about various forms of marble and grass, was a little too on the nose. “I think things like that are emblematic of what voters are frustrated by, not that it specifically was a factor,” the operative said. “Trump focused on vanity projects instead of continuing to focus on affordability and growing the economy.” A Republican official leading one of the top Senate campaigns sent me a text simply saying, “Really something.”

Not even independent men, one of Trump’s strongest demographics, came to his party’s aid. “Across the board, the shift among this demo that voted strongly for Trump is alarming, 30 to 40 points in a lot of places,” an operative said.

The Republican pollster who joked about being at rock bottom said the election should be a reckoning for Trumpworld. “In any civilized society, we would set them on an ice float and push it out into the middle passage,” they said. “But they’re like cockroaches.”

items.title: Abdul El-Sayed Called His Shot
items.description: It had been a bumpy flight, she said. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez had flown from New York City, changed planes in Chicago, and landed in Escanaba, Michigan. She blamed rain for the turbulence, but AOC had also just traveled through some choppy poli
items.author: Chris Smith
paragraphs: It had been a bumpy flight, she said. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez had flown from New York City, changed planes in Chicago, and landed in Escanaba, Michigan. She blamed rain for the turbulence, but AOC had also just traveled through some choppy political meteorology.

On this day in mid-October, she was standing in the Miracle of Life Pavilion, a livestock-birthing barn on the state fairgrounds in Michigan’s rural Upper Peninsula, a region that went for Donald Trump over Kamala Harris by 18 points in 2024. Days earlier, AOC had been standing in front of a crowd of cheering liberals, including Michael Stipe and former New York mayor Bill de Blasio, who paid as much as $57,000 to gather in a swanky downtown Manhattan hotel for a campaign fundraiser.

Both those efforts were on behalf of Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed — and for the larger project the two of them represent. “What we do is that we break open the entire political calculus in America, period,” AOC told the New York crowd. “If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere. Anywhere.”

On Tuesday night, the first goal came to fruition. The brash El-Sayed easily defeated Republican Mike Rogers; at press time, he was leading by almost exactly the seven-point margin he’d predicted. After a series of shocking Democratic victories in deep-red states, El-Sayed will join a new Democratic Senate majority that might swell as high as 56 seats, higher than just about anyone expected.

In his boisterous victory speech during the early hours of Wednesday morning, El-Sayed relished in cataloguing — and rebuking — the barrage of often straightforwardly Islamophobic attacks he faced from his opponent, as well as Trump and other powerful Republicans. He will become the first Muslim senator in American history. And with his considerable charisma, El-Sayed will continue to be an attention magnet, especially with Michigan moving to an earlier slot in the 2028 presidential-primary calendar.

Cara Tobe, who leads the Detroit chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, is quick to point out that El-Sayed is not a DSA member. But she believes his forceful championing of Medicare for All, a top DSA priority, was key to his Michigan win and would be a galvanizing issue nationally. Jamal Simmons, who grew up in Detroit and became an adviser to Vice-President Harris, is considerably more cautious in his interpretation. “We’re arguing over what ideological car Democrats should take, but we haven’t actually agreed on where we’re going as a party,” Simmons says.

Extrapolating nationally from Michigan is tricky. The state includes an unusual concentration of Arab, Jewish, and Black voters. The Senate race also featured a weird soap opera starring El-Sayed and Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic primary and initially endorsed El-Sayed before bitterly denouncing him and backing Rogers.

But the Michigan race foreshadowed two things for 2028, when Democrats will have their first truly open primary field since 2008: continuing division over Gaza and a renewed battle between the party’s liberal and centrist factions.

Stevens claimed her anger was based in dismay over El-Sayed’s staunch support of Palestinians and criticism of Israel. The party’s generational and ethnic split over the issue, which already fuels intense passions in Democratic circles, is likely to grow more inflamed as presidential candidates take to the primary trail. One critical piece of the argument will be just how widely the subject resonates with voters nationally. A Democratic strategist who worked on midterm races in the South says Gaza never came up in focus groups.

That hints at the second, larger way in which the Michigan race prefigures the 2028 Democratic presidential contest. It not only increases the chances of AOC mounting her own White House bid but also stokes the seemingly endless war between the party’s Establishment pragmatists and economic populists. “A progressive winning in Michigan, a legitimate battleground state, is a big deal,” says Mark Longabaugh, who was part of the team that delivered Bernie Sanders’s upset win there in 2016. “I think the candidates are all sensing which way the wind is blowing inside the Democratic Party.”

The party did so well Tuesday night across the country that every faction can claim at least some level of success. Still, the bulk of Democratic winners were moderates; an operative for one of them calls El-Sayed, who wants to abolish ICE and eliminate private health insurance, “an outlier.” El-Sayed lost the Upper Peninsula by large margins, weakening the argument by AOC and other progressives that culturally conservative voters can be swayed with economic arguments. Relative to the national environment, he was not an electoral overperformer on the order of James Talarico in Texas or Josh Turek in Iowa.

Lis Smith, the consultant who steered Pete Buttigieg’s surprisingly competitive 2020 presidential run, had a big midterms night with her firm’s candidates winning everywhere from the New York City suburbs (Cait Conley) to Kansas (Adam Hamilton), Texas (Talarico), and, likely, Alaska (Mary Peltola). Smith also has recent, unhappy expertise in Michigan, where her client Mallory McMorrow dropped out of the Senate Democratic primary early on and endorsed El-Sayed. Smith’s victors are all moderate Democrats. “What Abdul El-Sayed has done is impressive,” Smith says. “But it’s dishonest to say just because someone wins in Michigan they can win in red states. God knows we’ve seen this kind of left-resurgence talk before. We saw it after 2018. But we’re just not going to be able to build a durable majority that way.”

Cornell Belcher, a pollster for both of Barack Obama’s White House wins and a top adviser in Keisha Lance Bottoms’s stunning Georgia gubernatorial triumph, sees a big-picture demographic change lifting Democrats, one driven by an erosion of rights under Trump. “A big part of this story is college-educated white women moving fairly consistently away from MAGA. And I think you’re seeing the floodgates burst on that movement,” Belcher says. “We have not seen such a dramatic shift of white voters for Democrats in a long, long time. How Democrats are doing in the South and in typically red places, I think that’s a more telling story than a progressive one in Michigan.”

One clear midterm lesson is that fielding compelling candidates, many of them younger political newcomers, has helped boost the Democrats. The danger is in giving the party too much credit for creating the 2026 blue wave and thinking it can easily be surfed back into the White House. “There will be all these Democrats who think we won because of something we did,” says John Anzalone, a Michigan native who was a top adviser in Gretchen Whitmer’s winning 2018 race for governor, Joe Biden’s successful 2020 race for president, and Roy Cooper’s Senate victory last night in North Carolina. “And we did have really good midterms candidates. But voters aren’t rewarding us; they’re punishing Trump.”

items.title: Talarico’s Demolition of Paxton Is the Crown Jewel of the Democrats’ Win
items.description: In a night full of incredible victories for Team Blue, none was more remarkable or significant than Texas state legislator James Talarico’s landslide win over Attorney General Ken Paxton for a U.S. Senate seat that Republicans had held since 1961. This was the
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: In a night full of incredible victories for Team Blue, none was more remarkable or significant than Texas state legislator James Talarico’s landslide win over Attorney General Ken Paxton for a U.S. Senate seat that Republicans had held since 1961. This was the most expensive non-presidential political contest in U.S. history, and the winner, himself an incredible fundraising machine, was outspent overall by about a two-to-one margin. That was in no small part because the richest man in the world, Elon Musk, spent an incredible $168 million in a rescue effort for Paxton that from a distance felt irresistible in its sheer demonic weight. Not just Musk but Republicans all over and far beyond Texas made saving this Senate seat job one. And because the scandal-plagued Paxton was so powerfully unlovable (even being mocked to his face by his friend Donald Trump for his slovenly appearance), that meant smearing the seminarian Talarico as a predatory menace to small children, a blasphemer and heretic, an unmanly vegan, and, of course, a “radical leftist.” Near the end of the campaign, Republicans even spread the rumor that the flu-ridden Talarico had actually been committed to a mental institution. No holds were barred.

The Democrat kept on keeping on with a message that took a moderate problem-solving approach to cost of living concerns, but with a distinctive populist edge. He benefited from a public backlash to the state’s unpopular data-center boom and took advantage of Paxton’s long history of self-dealing and ethical lapses to make him the poster boy for Texas GOP corruption. Yet Talarico never pandered to conservatives nor abandoned even the most vulnerable Democratic constituencies. And in the end, it all worked.

A contest expected to go down to the wire instead turned into an unlikely blowout. Talarico won by 12 percent of the vote — by nearly 1.2 million votes — and led a ticket that crushed the long-dominant Texas GOP up and down the ballot. His share of the vote in Texas’s urban areas and also along the Rio Grande Valley (famously part of Trump’s 2024 coalition) was astounding: 72 percent in Dallas County, 66 percent in Harris County (Houston), 67 percent in Bexar County (San Antonio), and 79 percent in his Travis County (Austin) base. In Zapata County in the Valley, where Trump won by 22 percent in 2024, Talarico won by 41 percent. In nearby Webb County (Laredo), where Trump won by 2 percent in 2024, Talarico won by 47 percent this year. It was a historic ass-kicking for an exceptionally arrogant Texas Republican Party and its supremely arrogant commander in the White House.
Talarico’s Election Night victory message understandably focused on Musk, who added his unique brand of arrogance to the Paxton effort:

“The people of Texas delivered a crystal-clear message to the world’s first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale,” Talarico said. “The power in this state, in this country, belongs to the people and we’ve got to make sure it stays that way….”

“He wanted a senator who was going to do his bidding, who was going to sell off Texas land to his data centers, who was going to give our Texas water, who was going to give our taxpayer dollars,” Talarico said. “And I think he knows that I have a history of standing up to billionaires in state government. I have a history of tackling corruption and cleaning up government, and that’s exactly what we’re going to do in the U.S. Senate.

Now the 37-year-old senator-elect will take his place cheek-by-jowl with that living symbol of the old Texas GOP, Ted Cruz. He will share the post-midterms spotlight with a lot of instant sensations after this remarkable night, including his new colleagues Adam Hamilton of Kansas (another progressive Christian minister), Annie Andrews of South Carolina, and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, as well as Texas’s new governor, Gina Hinojosa. But no one will quite equal Talarico as a survivor of every terrible weapon the opposition could deploy, and as a reminder that sometimes hope and faith actually can vanquish hatred and greed.

items.title: How Democrats Unleashed a Blue-nami
items.description: That was the message delivered to Sherrod Brown, the three-term senator from Ohio until he was bounced out of office by the Trump surge in 2024. Brown was thinking of running for governor or, at 73, retiring from public life altogether, not least because the s
items.author: David Freedlander
paragraphs: That was the message delivered to Sherrod Brown, the three-term senator from Ohio until he was bounced out of office by the Trump surge in 2024. Brown was thinking of running for governor or, at 73, retiring from public life altogether, not least because the state where he had made his mark as a rumpled avatar of Rust Belt populism had rapidly shifted red over the last decade.

Chuck Schumer, the leader of Senate Democrats, in a series of lunches in Brown’s hometown of Cleveland, told him that he understood how appealing retirement sounded. That, sure, the governor’s mansion would be a shorter commute.

But, he said, if Brown didn’t run for the Senate, and the Democrats fell one seat short in their quest for the majority, Brown would never be able to enjoy his retirement. And Schumer made the same pitch to others — like Mary Peltola, a former congresswoman from Alaska who also lost her seat in 2024 but outperformed Kamala Harris by ten points. And Roy Cooper, the popular two-term governor of North Carolina, who Schumer called the day his term ended.

These conversations were in the summer of 2025, back when Democrats were still flattened, run over by the Trump electoral steamroller in 2024 and then overwhelmed by his administration’s assault on Washington in the first few months of his second term. The map for a Democratic takeover of the Senate ran almost entirely through states Trump won in 2024, and the party’s donors were dispirited after spending nearly $2 billion in Harris’s loss.

A year and a half later, Cooper flipped a state that hadn’t elected a Democratic senator since 2008, winning it with enough ease that the party was able to shift resources into races elsewhere on the map. That allowed Democrats to spend some of the record $600 million they raised this election cycle on states that looked like fantasy pickups even a few weeks ago, states like South Carolina, Kansas, and Texas that have not elected a Democrat this century — and have now done so. The Democrats on Tuesday not only took the House, which was broadly expected, but the Senate, which was viewed as a near-impossibility not long ago.

“From the beginning Chuck thought this was winnable and he practically willed it into existence,” said one Democratic operative familiar with the dynamics of 2026 Senate campaign, one of a dozen who spoke to me for this story and were granted anonymity to discuss internal party strategy.

For much of 2025, Senate Democrats were in a familiar state: Disarray. Trump was laying siege to the edifices of the federal government, destroying international alliances, and turning his tenure into both a get-rich scheme and a personal retribution campaign. Democrats seemed powerless to stop him. Schumer resisted calls in March of 2025 to shut down the government, figuring that it didn’t make sense when Trump retained decent approval ratings. A mutiny among left-leaning Democratic senators began to grow, with some openly wondering if time had passed the longtime Democratic leader by. Instead, Schumer rallied the party to fight on more favorable terrain: extending Obamacare subsidies, and later opposing the excesses of Trump’s immigration enforcement regime

By that point, Trump’s favorability had begun to nosedive. His “Liberation Day” tariffs were starting to pinch consumers, farmers and manufacturers, particularly in the northern states along the Canadian border. Still, few Democratic operatives, even those working on Senate races, believed the party had much of a chance.

“It was like, ‘Holy shit, this is 2006 all over again,” said another senior Democratic campaign aide, referring to the midterm where Democrats, buoyed by George W. Bush’s unpopular war in Iraq, gained 31 House seats and — led by Schumer — six seats in the upper house.

Still, many would-be candidates sat on the sidelines this time around, which allowed little-known figures like Adam Hamilton in Kansas and Annie Andrews in South Carolina to run virtually unopposed. Meanwhile, progressives were on the march in swing states like Maine and Michigan, where firebrand leftists Graham Platner and Abdul El-Sayed vowed to depose Schumer should they win. Schumer had recruited Janet Mills, the sitting two-term governor, into the race in Maine, a move that even some of Schumer’s most ardent supporters felt was misguided since she was clearly a reluctant candidate. In Michigan, he had less success luring Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg into the race, backing Congresswoman Haley Stevens only when it seemed like she was the best vehicle to defeat El-Sayed, a public health official whose outspoken leftist views were likely to be a drag in November.

When Platner ultimately imploded in Maine in a flurry of sexual assault allegations, many Washington Democratic strategists felt relief, figuring that his baggage would have kept the party from the winning the seat. Troy Jackson became the Democratic nominee, which allowed Democrats to run a campaign that focused less on their own candidate and more on Trump’s perfidies. And after El-Sayed won the primary in Michigan, the Democratic campaign arm embraced him, rushing out a heartwarming digital ad of him over the soundtrack to Journey’s “Don’t Stop Believin’” (“Just a city boy/Born and raised in South Detroit”) that signaled that the party establishment was behind the insurgent.

People close to El-Sayed have never quite forgiven the next Senate majority leader for backing Stevens, but the two talk several times a week, both of them trying to keep the focus not on intra-party drama but on defeating Donald Trump and his MAGA acolytes. A spike in gas prices arrived after Labor Day, which gave voters a reason to be receptive to Democratic campaign messages across the country.

That message, according to Schumer, was simple: chaos, corruption and costs. Despite being outspent, Democrats tend to spend early in Senate races, before ad rates spike, and the party buried Republicans under a relentless barrage of ads that blamed the party for defunding rural hospitals, stripping away Medicaid funding for the neediest, and rising costs.
“We are in a super-majority mindset,” said Morris Katz, a leading Democratic strategist. “It’s where we need to be every year.”

But of course, this election in the end had little to do with Chuck Schumer, or even any of the candidates he picked or didn’t pick. It was a race about Donald Trump, who not only anointed uniquely awful candidates from Texas to South Carolina, but bogged down the Republican ticket across the country. The Democratic majority was made by a number of factors, but the Republican majority was lost by only one.

items.title: Los Angeles Libbed Out as a Blue Fever Seized Hollywood
items.description: Ta-Nehisi Coates (Vanity Fair senior staff writer) recently said that if he reads “another scene from a DSA party in Brooklyn where people are drinking beer and doing whatever, I’m going to scream.”
items.author: Maxwell Adler
paragraphs: Ta-Nehisi Coates (Vanity Fair senior staff writer) recently said that if he reads “another scene from a DSA party in Brooklyn where people are drinking beer and doing whatever, I’m going to scream.”

But I can report that there were a lot of ecstatic and tipsy socialists in oversized vintage jackets at the DSA election party on the edge of Skid Row in Los Angeles Tuesday night. And, boy, did these socialists have a lot to celebrate.

Democrats were trouncing Republicans nationally. Democratic socialists were projected to take at least seven seats in the House, up from two. And in Los Angeles, the DSA’s preferred mayoral candidate, Nithya Raman, appeared poised to unseat Karen Bass. The incumbent Democratic mayor held a less than 1% lead in early returns, but ballots are expected to skew toward the more progressive candidate, Raman.

“Karen Bass said that she would need to be up 10 points on election night to be comfortable,” one DSA-LA leader told the crowd. He gestured at a graphic showing Bass’s narrow lead and said, “I’m not good at math because I’m gay. Is that 10 points? I don’t think so.” (Bass didn’t actually say that, but a pundit on KTLA did say something to that effect.)

At the DSA party, people cheered victories elsewhere in the country by socialists and establishment Democrats alike, but they booed when Bass appeared on television, and laughed when a Fox News commentator suggested the economy was doing well. At one point, organizers put on Hasan Piker’s livestream, and at another they played an AI-generated video showing Raman dancing while wearing a traditional Russian fur hat with ear flaps and a red star. When local TV station KTLA suggested Raman would likely win and Mayor Bass’s face appeared onscreen, someone shouted, “Whoa, get fucked, Karen.” It kind of encapsulated the strongest force animating the DSA members I talked to in this mayoral race: their dislike for Mayor Bass. They even called her the C-word onstage: “conservative.”

The DSA and Raman have had something of an on-again, off-again relationship. The organization helped propel her to an upset City Council victory in 2020, only to reprimand her over disagreements about Israel, housing policy, and the city’s mansion tax. The local DSA chapter endorsed her candidacy late in the campaign, but the national organization almost stripped it from her at the eleventh hour. The national DSA voted last week to preserve its Los Angeles chapter’s endorsement of Raman by a single vote, after a dispute over her refusal to embrace the movement to boycott Israel.

“I think people here have varying levels of begrudgingness about supporting Raman, but I think everyone here voted for her,” said one DSA-LA member at the party who worked on the chapter’s video team and declined to give her name.

Still, the DSA members at the party seemed to think this mayoral race offered another encouraging sign for their organization, even if Raman isn’t quite New York mayor Zohran Mamdani. She was attacked consistently by her opponents—mainly Spencer Pratt—as a dangerous extremist, but with the help of the DSA (it said members knocked on more than 110,000 doors this election cycle) she might be the first LA mayoral candidate to defeat an incumbent in over 20 years.

Meanwhile, at the Raman campaign’s official election night party at the Greek Theatre in Los Feliz, there weren’t any signs calling to “Tax the Rich” or to implement “Medicare for All,” as there were at the DSA party, but comedian Guy Branum from Apple TV’s Platonic sounded pretty similar to those socialists. He argued that Raman’s coalition reflected a class divide within Hollywood.

“Nithya has way more of entertainment’s middle class,” Branum said, describing workers worried about their next job. And Raman’s husband, television writer Vali Chandrasekaran, understands the industry’s problems firsthand, he argued.

Branum, who hangs with the couple socially, also wanted voters to appreciate one of her lessdiscussed qualifications. “They lead with the master’s in urban planning, and the Harvard, and the MIT,” he said. “But what you really need to see is that [she can dance]. You really need to see that hair let loose.” (Vanity Fair did not stick around at the party long enough to verify Raman’s dancing skills.)

Raman’s campaign manager, Ian Manheimer, was pretty psyched when he took the stage outside the Greek. “Holy shit! What is good, Los Angeles?” he shouted. Nearly three quarters of his campaign staff had never worked on a political campaign before, he told the crowd. Regardless, they managed to knock on over 100,000 doors, according to Manheimer.

The campaign’s grassroots operation had apparently become a bit of a competition. Volunteer Leo Blain, 25, told VF he’d knocked on more than 300 doors, putting him near the top of the campaign leaderboard. But the person to beat was Raman’s father, whom volunteers said had knocked on more than 1,000. All of that knocking was crucial, especially since Raman didn’t have a lot of institutional support or name recognition. Many of California’s most prominent Democrats stayed on the sidelines, because most of them would do anything to avoid the choice between an establishment incumbent and a rising DSA-endorsed challenger. But their neutrality didn’t necessarily mean indifference. A high-ranking official in Sacramento told me that plenty of state legislators were privately rooting for Bass, who had served as Speaker of the California Assembly before heading to Congress.

John, a DSA member who volunteered for Raman after having worked on Tom Steyer’s gubernatorial campaign, expected strong support for Raman among the local socialists, arguing that her independent thinking was a positive.

Raman’s party also included some unlikely converts. Kathleen Jensen, a Toluca Lake resident who previously supported Republican Rick Caruso, told me she considered Raman brilliant and wanted a “doer” in City Hall. Although she said some of her Democrat friends remained uneasy about Raman’s DSA association.

By 10:30 p.m., Bass’s election night party at the Loews Hotel in Hollywood had grown considerably quiet as her supporters began to digest the initial results. But the people who remained were still getting down to Snoop Dogg. The demographic differences between the parties were striking. Raman’s crowd skewed whiter, and more Asian, and the music was more alternative and disco. Bass’s crowd was notably more Black, reflecting the mayor’s decades of relationships in the city’s African American community.

Vaval Victor, 28, a member of Alpha Phi Alpha, the historically Black fraternity with which Bass has worked, remained confident that she would pull through. “She started the LA Black Dems Club in her kitchen,” he said, invoking her long history of organizing. “People are thirsty for hope.”

Bass had spent the campaign defending her record on homelessness, city finances, and last year’s catastrophic fires. Caruso, whom she defeated four years earlier, had swooped in at the end to say that he was voting for her, giving some of the city’s more conservative voters permission to support the incumbent. But early election-night returns were not the decisive advantage her campaign hoped for.
For all the divisions this mayoral race exposed, the three parties shared something that had been in short supply among Democrats lately: liberal joy.

items.title: The Midterms' Biggest Loser Is Elon Musk
items.description: Elon Musk tried to buy an election. Several elections, in fact. All told, the world’s richest man pumped around $474 million into Super PACs working on behalf of Republican candidates around the country in the 2026 election cycle, most of it focused on Texas.
items.author: Jack Crosbie
paragraphs: Elon Musk tried to buy an election. Several elections, in fact. All told, the world’s richest man pumped around $474 million into Super PACs working on behalf of Republican candidates around the country in the 2026 election cycle, most of it focused on Texas. But on Tuesday night, in that state and basically every other battleground, he lost — and he lost big.

Musk’s plan for the midterms was simple: Funnel massive amounts of cash into super PACs that could overwhelm elections with relentless ad spending, sending voters a constant deluge of negative information about Democrats like James Talarico in Texas and Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan in a blatant attempt to exert all the power and influence money could buy into the democratic process. On Tuesday night, it failed.

As of this morning, current voting totals have Talarico up by 13 points. In Michigan, El-Sayed overcame rampant racism and Islamophobia to win by around eight percent. Sherrod Brown regained a seat in Ohio. Gina Hinojosa will become Texas’ first Latina governor. So many House districts flipped that the Democrats may have as much as an 81-seat majority in the lower chamber. They will certainly run the Senate, with at least 53 seats and more, perhaps, to come. Shares of SpaceX and Tesla, Musk’s two biggest companies, started falling as soon as the markets opened this morning.
Musk, after seething and catastrophizing for weeks, tried to laugh it off. “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time,” he wrote at 1:13 a.m. today.

By 9:30, he was back to making mundane tweets about the Qualcomm technology in his Starlink systems and his Grok AI’s new shopping feature. But Musk won’t be able to wriggle out of the shame of defeat that easily. With majorities in the House and Senate, Democrats now have an enormous latitude to weaponize the investigative powers of Congress. House Democrats have been indicating for weeks that if they were to regain control of these powerful weapons, they’ll turn them right onto Musk.

“Elon Musk and his DOGE cronies stirred up chaos, ruined careers, and played a large role in illegal grant cancellations and firings of civil servants,” Rep. Zoe Lofgren of California, the top Democrat on the Space, Science and Technology Committee, said in a statement last month. “He helped orchestrate the systematic destruction of government programs and services over the last nearly two years. The sheer number of conflicts of interest are astounding.”

Tesla and SpaceX depend heavily on their relationship to the government, both through direct contracts for things like satellite launches and the tax breaks that both the federal government and individual states offer for electric cars and energy products.

Part of the reason Musk got spanked so badly is that Democrats in Texas and around the country specifically planned for his deluge of cash. Shortly before election day, Democratic strategists in Texas told Rolling Stone that Talarico’s entire campaign strategy was structured around limiting the potential harm of a massive cash dump, mainly by building the candidate’s own communication channels with voters through social media and earned appearances, rather than being forced into the battleground of ad-versus-ad spending in the final days of the race. Musk’s money bought plenty of AI-powered attack ads calling candidates names, but it couldn’t buy the Republicans better candidates themselves (and in Texas, at least, it did the opposite — Musk’s cash was a major factor in the openly corrupt, scandal-prone Ken Paxton ousting incumbent stalwart John Cornyn in the Republican primary earlier this year).

But Musk’s real defeat, at least symbolically, was his utter rejection by his adopted home. Musk and many other tech moguls, including Amazon CEO Jeff Bezos, have made a big show of moving parts of their businesses — and often their personal residences — from liberal states like California to Texas in recent years. Texas’s conservative leanings, they maintained, made it a friendlier place for their brand of cut-throat capitalism and edgy free speech. The beauty of America, of course, is that no amount of money can ever make you truly safe from the will of the people, who turned Texas just as blue as California, at least for now.

items.title: The Real Housewives of Potomac Recap: For Better Or Worse
items.description: I’ve repeatedly said that amongst all of the franchises of the greater Housewives universe, Potomac has shown one of the unvarnished looks at the pitfalls of women placing their validation and identity within the construct of marriage, and episodes like this w
items.author: Shamira Ibrahim
paragraphs: I’ve repeatedly said that amongst all of the franchises of the greater Housewives universe, Potomac has shown one of the unvarnished looks at the pitfalls of women placing their validation and identity within the construct of marriage, and episodes like this week are exactly why. Yes, the theatrics may be hard to stomach at times, but amidst the hysteria and chaos of these women are some genuinely uncomfortable truths about the institution of marriage, as their unions slowly shift from proud partnerships to something resembling a prison sentence one at a time.

While the rest of us may not be curating our personal lives on camera, if you are a single woman over 30, you likely have had a front-row seat to the demise of a couple whose self-mythology has become impossible to maintain, and that is exactly what we are seeing play out with Karen, Wendy, and Tia. And despite the show’s absurdities, these ladies lay plain the pitfalls of your social status, identity, and security being predicated on a man you committed to for life having his shit together. (Newsflash: they don’t really have the best track record).
But first things first: the tagline report cards have arrived. Let’s review, shall we?

- Gizelle Bryant: “I can honor my past and still read you in the present.” What does this even mean? The woman has spent a decade establishing herself as Potomac’s premier distributor of unsolicited opinions, and this is the best she could come up with? 2/10

- Stacey Rusch: “Talk about depth, talk about truth, talk about Stacey.” We’re stretching the limits of a viral moment here, but at least it’s on brand. Stacey has never met an opportunity for self-branding that she wasn’t willing to seize, but that’s probably why she was doing so well with QVC for all those years. 5/10

- Wendy Osefo: “All eyes are on me, so I might as well give them a show.” We’re only four episodes in, and I’m already exhausted by Wendy’s insistence on presenting herself as the victim of the court of public opinion. But I’ll give her credit for the wordplay. 6/10

- Ashley Darby: “I’m no one’s sugar mama, but I still make life sweet.” Ashley has somehow managed to continue to publicly humiliate Josh through her tagline in a manner that is neither particularly clever nor especially flattering, which I suppose is at the very least consistent. Somebody, please return this man’s self-respect to him — and while we’re at it, let’s pray Ashley manages to locate some of her own before the season is over. 3/10
- Tia Glover: “I may speak the King’s English, but I will never entertain a jester.” Dry, cheeky, and delivered with exactly the right amount of English disdain. No notes. 7/10

- Courtney: “I came to spread the word, and maybe a little gospel.” Did nobody inform Courtney that Gizelle is already the proprietor of the Word on the Street? Jokes aside, it’s cute enough for a first-season effort. 6/10

- Karen Huger: “I found my higher self, but humbling you? No problem.” True to form, Karen has delivered a tagline that is equal parts grandiose and incoherent, but at least she’s finally retired the fence metaphors. I’ll take the victories where I can. 3/10

Before we get into everyone’s marriages, we finally got to see a little more of Courtney’s dynamic with the girls as she tags along with Ashley and Karen to what I can only describe as a group shopping trip for lingerie, purportedly to help Karen celebrate her freshly singed-off bootyhole with Ray. I’m not entirely sure the leadership of the AME Church would share Courtney’s enthusiasm, but hey: the Lord works in mysterious ways, and perhaps sometimes that involves a great matching set of bra and panties.

But one thing is for certain: Courtney is not one to let a sheer lace teddy stop her from spreading the gospel. When Ashley inquires about the viral videos circulating of Courtney beseeching her IG Live followers to heed her prophecies, Courtney embraces it without skipping a beat, informing the pair that she can see everything from angels and demons to the ghost of Christmas Past with breezy assurance; Ashley and Karen look on in shock.

For what it’s worth, she said in the clip that “machines will stop working, cars will fail, and people will be unable to access their money.” — and AI, Elon Musk, and the cratering economy have definitely taken a hit to all three. Perhaps she truly is gifted; if so, hopefully she can bibbidy-bobbidy-boo and save these women from the purgatory of their marriages. And anyone is desperate for some divine intervention; it is certainly Karen Huger.

For years, the Hugers have maintained a carefully cultivated image, more for their own self-delusion than for anyone else. But with Karen newly sober and the couple attempting to adjust to life after her incarceration, the cracks aren’t being smoothed out by the blurriness of beer goggles. They are essentially passing ships in the night, sleeping in separate beds; the emotional distance between them has become difficult to disguise. In a revealing moment, Ray shockingly admits that he misses drunk Karen, who was more aggressive, sexual, and fun, complicating the sympathetic portrait of Ray that has emerged over the years. He expected a wife who was ready to swing from the pole after six months in the pokey and got a house filled with incense and candles instead, and apparently isn’t all that interested in supporting that.

Ray’s relative silence has long helped reinforce his image as Karen’s long-suffering husband while viewers have filled in the blanks with their half-baked assumptions. His confession, however, indicates that he is less concerned with his wife’s well-being than with the loss of the version of Karen he found most entertaining. Even in his admission that he nearly called off their wedding because of her drinking — suggesting the problem has been present for far longer than the couple has publicly acknowledged, as everyone suspected — he still seems to be more interested in enabling Karen than supporting her shifting to a different lifestyle, which, amongst other things, is remarkably selfish and shortsighted. None of this absolves Karen of responsibility for her actions, and sober counselors will readily tell you that the process of recovery can and often does fundamentally alter a relationship’s dynamics. Nevertheless, I was troubled to watch a husband openly expressing disappointment that his wife is no longer as sexually available as when she was drinking, as opposed to focusing on finding a new path to reestablishing their connection altogether.

In the harsh light of sobriety, Karen and Ray appear to finally be confronting a possibility that neither has been particularly eager to entertain out loud outside of that one time Karen was knocking back Fireball shots in the basement: they may still love each other, but they don’t seem to enjoy each other’s company very much. What do you do when the person who claims to love you most may not actually like the person you’re becoming? That public confession may end up becoming considerably more destabilizing to their union than any rumor Gizelle could have circulated throughout the seasons. And as the oldest member in the cast, Karen’s marriage will always be an ominous warning to the other ladies of what their future could be like if they continue to prioritize the status that marriage affords them over being truly fulfilled and supported.

While Karen continues her spiritual journey to save her marriage, Tia continues to mull over how she wants to handle the unexpected speed bump in her marriage, with varied input from friends and family, and Tia and her mother’s chat about the state of her marriage revealing a delicate tension in their dynamic. Watching them both, it’s clear that her relatively stiff upper lip isn’t just a charade for the cameras; while I’m sure she does a bit of Vanderpump-style English theatrics, her mother’s similar demeanor suggests that she grew up in a household of studied restraint and repressed secrets, which we see when Tia admits she feels she’s not allowed to be too wounded by Robert’s disloyalty because of the depth of betrayal her mom withstood.

In her confessional, Tia admits that over the years, she has learned to reduce her expectations to appreciate the mother she has instead of what she isn’t. Reader, if that isn’t the well-worn battle cry of an eldest daughter who has spent years on a therapist’s couch attempting to untangle her relationship with a difficult mother, I don’t know what is. But one thing is for sure: Tia will continue to struggle to admit how hurt she is by Robert’s failed attempts at infidelity as long as people like her mom keep suggesting to her that the betrayal isn’t that big of a deal.

Back over at the Osefo household, Wendy and Eddie are continuing to navigate their fractured marriage amidst the fallout from their legal troubles, to mixed results. Listen, I’m no one’s body language expert — I leave that sort of pseudoscience for Love Island fans — but while Wendy is largely saying the right things on camera, everything about her composure suggests that Wendy is actively withdrawing from Eddie. She says she loves him when prodded, but there’s little warmth or reassurance behind any of the words; as Eddie gingerly pointed out, she paused before saying it. Eddie seems to be in a constant state of anxiety that he poorly tries to mask by plastering on a forced anxious smile whenever the cameras are on him, as if he’s terrified to say the wrong thing.

Wendy has decided, in true Catholic fashion, that she will be redeemed by loudly proclaiming her suffering. In every scene we see her in, she seems to be carrying thinly veiled rage that she only releases via clipped, flat jabs. She suggests that Gizelle is more gung-ho about preserving her marriage than she is in the moment; she brings up Tia and Robert’s lack of intimacy as a not-so-subtle way to make it known that she and Eddie are similarly romantically disconnected. Every scene makes me just as uncomfortable as I get when I watch Couples Therapy, except Dr. Orna isn’t there to reset the room when the tension becomes too thick; their double date with Tia and Robert is no exception.

Almost from the moment the couples sit down, Wendy goes on the offensive, directing a barrage of questions toward Tia and Robert about the state of their relationship. It’s a transparent attempt to steer the ship: if she controls the conversation, she can dictate how much of her own marriage she’s willing to disclose while forcing another couple to account for theirs. Tia recognizes the maneuver almost immediately, but the train has already left the station, as Wendy’s four degrees continue to pester Robert. Unsurprisingly, Robert doesn’t have much to say beyond mumbling about the usual platitudes about the trials and tribulations of marriage, which does nothing to assuage Wendy’s uncomfortable questioning.

At one point, she begins interrogating Robert about the loneliness he claims drove him to dating apps, going so far as to suggest that Tia’s frequent solo travel may have contributed to the distance between them. The implication is particularly galling, and despite her insistence that she’s doing this to advocate for Tia, it all feels less like an act of friendship than an attempt to redirect scrutiny away from herself. Not only is Wendy obscenely overstepping here with this ham-fisted audition for a revival of Iyanla: Fix My Life, she knows full well that she wouldn’t accept receiving a similar third degree.

Tia, on her end, handled the ambush skillfully, parrying jabs without raising her voice to prevent Wendy from having any opening to feign victimization. When Wendy has the gall to sit there in her hot pink floral choker and suggest that Tia contributed to this issue with her constant travels, she mentions that she regularly travels to London and Nigeria to stay connected with her family, subtly reminding Wendy she has more ties to their shared homeland. When Wendy attempts to wrap up the tit-for by assuring the couple that she and Eddie are “rooting for you both,” Tia responds with a perfectly cheeky “We’re rooting for you guys too!” The message in the response isn’t subtle: I see exactly what you’re doing, and I’m not impressed. (As a general word to the wise, you are rarely going to win a battle of passive-aggressiveness with an English person. These are people who say “fuck off” by signing texts with a single dismissive “x” rather than the more affectionate “xx.”)

Faced with the potential collapse of her professional reputation and marriage, Wendy has decided that the best way to protect herself is to redirect attention toward everyone else’s problems. It’s an aggressive strategy that ultimately may prove spectacularly counterproductive: if the people around you come to believe that you’re willing to push them into the line of fire, you can’t reasonably expect them to stand beside you when the chips are down. Nevertheless, Eddie begins laying the groundwork for what we all suspected would become the Osefos’ central defense of their current legal troubles, insisting that Wendy was largely unaware of the details of their finances and was blindsided. Only time will tell if her narrative will prevail under scrutiny from her castmates (and viewers watching the bevy of extravagant purchases we’ve seen her invest in this season alone), but one thing is for certain: the only thing more exhausting than working through your declining marriage is having Wendy Osefo volunteer to work through them for you.
That’s all for now. Next week, the women head to Bethany Beach, Wendy and Stacey’s on-again/off-again dynamic kicks back up, and the Eileen Davidson accords are finally lifted. See you all there!

• Whenever Gizelle isn’t waist-deep in mess, I’m confused by exactly what we’re watching. It’s great that she’s taking her advocacy work with the National Brain Tumor Association to Capitol Hill (although it’s not really clear why Ashley isn’t involved when GNA is a joint partnership … or why she continues to feel she is the steward of her father’s legacy after everything continued to play out with the will), but with the kids out of the house, the distance she keeps from viewers feels more painfully obvious than ever.

• Stacey is a great addition to the group, but her little Amelia Bedelia homemaker family act runs thin quickly. That said, I hope Arabella gets to plan out a K-pop Demon Hunters-themed wedding of her dreams for her parents; whatever she comes up with will likely have a higher taste factor than her mom’s affinity for an A-line skirt and a sensible shoe. (Also, the dormant Black auntie in me absolutely whipped my head around like Willow Smith when she started calling her parents by their first names).

• Wendy insists that only their eldest son, Karter, is aware of what’s happening with her and Eddie, which is almost laughably delusional. Siblings have group chats too, and children are infinitely more perceptive than adults tend to give them credit for.

• For all of Ashley’s flaws, I admire her determination to ensure that the younger members of her extended family have a degree of stability that she didn’t necessarily enjoy growing up. If there’s one thing Ashley is going to do, it’s turn her house into a temporary residence for a rotating cast of relatives navigating life’s transitions.

• I cannot pretend to care about Ashley pretending to look for a vacation house in someplace as overrated as Bethany Beach, Delaware. It takes a solid three hours to get to from DC in good traffic, just to sleep in single beds in a drafty house that was last renovated during the Clinton administration; in other words, it will be exactly like the last time they tried to do a group trip there.

• Courtney opening up about her fertility struggles was touching. It’s truly underappreciated how Housewives is one of the few shows that gives a relatively naked glimpse at how women cope with everything from struggling with fertility to transitioning into menopause.

items.title: Saturday Night Live Recap: Inde Navarrette Leaves SNL Obsessed
items.description: If you were home this Halloween, either because you’re a parent, a teen staying up too late, or a 30-something in a sugar coma from eating all her niece’s Halloween candy, I hope you were watching Inde Navarrette, the breakout star of the horror movie Obsessio
items.author: Rima Parikh
paragraphs: If you were home this Halloween, either because you’re a parent, a teen staying up too late, or a 30-something in a sugar coma from eating all her niece’s Halloween candy, I hope you were watching Inde Navarrette, the breakout star of the horror movie Obsession, crush her first time hosting Saturday Night Live.

Considering that Navarrette is a relative newcomer, I wasn’t sure what to expect going into the episode. Navarrette proved to be a deft performer in Obsession, delivering a terrifying performance while also being genuinely funny. But no matter how talented a host is, there are always other factors at play. Would she be nervous? Would the writing give her enough to work with? Luckily, the Halloween episode is ideal for a first-time host because there’s so much infrastructure built into it: past Halloween sketches to call back to, excuses for guest cameos, the magic of spooky decor and lighting, and an audience hopped up on Nerds Gummy Clusters. A Halloween episode would provide a cushion for Navarrette, if she needed it.

But she didn’t. Navarrette started her monologue with a magnetic charm and confidence, guns blazing, with a smirk: “I’m gonna be in a Marvel movie … so every morning, I put on my little whore outfit, and I hit the gym.” Well, yes! I was wondering how the show would acknowledge the Shane Gillis episode fallout, and Navarrette delivered the callback perfectly. She held court the rest of the episode, slipping in and out of characters like they were Halloween costumes. She did well because she’s a good actor, but her performance was also buoyed by her incredible physical comedy instincts, notably as a blonde ghost child from the 1930s, which featured her hitting her head and crossing her eyes, a telenovela star who barrels off of furniture, and a curt Paw Patrol SVU captain lightly roughhousing her team of useless dogs. In addition to more out-there roles, she also adapted nicely to playing straight character roles, like in a Dan Bulla pretape, where she played a somber widow whose dead husband leaves her a robot that does, ultimately, rip her date’s penis off and shoot it to the moon. At the end of the night, when she took a backseat in the ensemble in the Plates sketch, it felt well-deserved. It almost made me sad that we don’t get a universe where Navarrette is a cast member, but perhaps whenever it is next year that Lorne wants to ask Shane Gillis back for the seventieth time, perhaps someone could float Navarrette instead.

And it helped that Navarrette had a lot of good material to work with. After a rocky start to the season, this episode’s writing was the best it’s been in a long time. The game show, Delta pre-tape, and the telenovela sketches were top-notch, and across the episode, there really wasn’t a bad sketch. I don’t usually care for the cold open, but Tom Hanks reprising David S. Pumpkins was a nice little cameo, and I really liked seeing Grace Reiter and Saidah Belo-Osagie right up at the top. Even the Queen Mary Ghosts sketch, which I’d put at the sleepiest, was still pretty funny (and a nice way to immediately introduce us to Navarrette’s physical comedy). At the season premiere, I had hoped the team would brush off the summer cobwebs, and you know what? Consider them brushed off. Between a compelling first-time host, sharp writing that revealed genuine playfulness and surprise, and a cast hitting a stride in their chemistry with one another, it was hard to go wrong. It’s early in the season, but this episode could be a contender for one of the best we’ll see in the next few months.

In this pre-tape, we learn about Delta Disruptive, a new part of the cabin dedicated to unruly passengers. The only rule is that you can’t stab anyone with pens, but “almost everything else is fine.” We meet passengers who are clipping their toenails and fighting, to more extreme characters, like a conspiracy-minded passenger trying to open the plane’s emergency exit (played by a kooky-eyed Mikey Day). Navarrette, with a delightful conviction, plays a gum-chewing, pantless woman named Sondra who’s straight from the Jersey Shore. I also love this universe where these insane characters willingly act normal for the talking heads for about two seconds before going back to their upsetting behavior, which also made for fun reveals once the camera panned out (like Sarah Sherman’s Debbie duct-taped to the seat, or Tommy Brennan’s character, a quarter-zip-clad rich guy who looks like he’s been airdropped from Delta One, reading Mein Kampf). This sketch moved fast with a delightful chaos and a million jokes a minute.
Uninterested Woman Game Show

A classic game show premise, where our contestants are three scuzzy-looking men (Inde Navarrette, Jane Wickline, and Sarah Sherman) who really cannot just leave a married lesbian named Kelly (Saidah Belo-Osagie) alone. The notes I took during this sketch just say “everyone is so funny in this.” So joke-dense, and some especially memorable lines read from Wickline (“Do you want to get a drink right now? I know all the spots that are open in the morning.”) The contestants are so exasperating that even our host Sephora Outlet (Ashley Padilla) loses her cool by the end (“She is a lesbian! She said that!”). Shout out to Navarrette’s choice to hop and cling to the podium like a koala, and also to Belo-Osagie’s subtle and hilarious facial expressions, especially when the boys declare “Kelly’s a bitch!”
Telenovela: El Corazón Que No Siente

A telenovela shoot gets interrupted by two execs from Sprite (Mikey Day and Ashley Padilla) who want the stars (Marcello Hernandez and Inde Navarrette) to promote a new, particularly nasty Sprite flavor. So many laugh-out-loud lines (“It’s bad but they paid for this,” “The Sprite has made me hit a woman”), and between a devastating spit take and fully lobbing herself off of a couch, Navarrette’s physical comedy here is incredible. Padilla’s character losing her composure at the end (“We wanted it to taste good and it doesn’t! We know … for the first time in history, AI screwed up!”) and the reveal that Day’s character has been a double agent for 7Up the whole time land the plane. I also really enjoyed the sub-game of the director (Kenan Thompson) declaring, apropos of nothing, whether or not each take felt erotic to him.
Weekend Update: Ben Marshall as Pennywise the Clown on Gen Z Wellness Parties and Bobby Moynihan as Drunk Uncle on the Milwaukee Brewers’ World Series

Pennywise (Ben Marshall) as a tech bro living in an Austin loft with “three other motivated young Christians” … that’s the kind of imaginative world-building I like to see this Halloween. And call me simple, but I laughed at the honking sound from Michael Che squeezing his arm. Ending it with an intervention for Che felt clever (and, in perhaps a win for Colin Jost, one of the few times his participation in a bit at the desk ends with him being likeable).

I was delighted that Moynihan was back at the desk after his brief cameo in the cold open. “There’s only one gender” and “Yeah, I do voter fraud” were two favorite lines out of many! And congrats to the Brewers. I didn’t know baseball was happening, so this was also informative for some of the most unobservant among us!

If there’s anything you can rely on in this one life, it’s an Ashley Padilla character sketch. In this one, Denise (Padilla) is out to dinner and determined to maintain her chill reputation after the server (Mikey Day) accidentally drops a bunch of plates on her head. When everyone at the table tries to check if she’s okay, she deflects by cracking plates against her head. Eventually, Denise reveals that she can no longer see after all that blunt force trauma. Thinking that everyone’s left her, lets out some of the most egregious farts, which sound so cartoonish and surprising that even Padilla breaks. If you don’t like poop humor, lines like, “I can smell my blood, and I can feel my bones, and at one point I saw the Ninja Turtles walk into the room” still make it worth it.
• “Pass out then! Come on!”
• Both Gracie Abrams performances? Ethereal.
• A sweet Patrick Stewart tribute at the end.
• “I’m six-foot-negative three.”
• For a second during the credits, I thought that Sarah Sherman had quickly changed into one of her classic clown outfits, only to realize it was Tommy Brennan dressed as Sherman for Halloween.

items.title: Dexter: Resurrection Season-Premiere Recap: Generation Dex
items.description: There’s a certain irony in Dexter Morgan having a midlife crisis. Yes, it feels a little late — like Michael C. Hall, Dex is now 55 — but it’s more that Dexter the series is thriving. The first season of Dexter: Resurrection (really just the tenth season of De
items.author: Louis Peitzman
paragraphs: There’s a certain irony in Dexter Morgan having a midlife crisis. Yes, it feels a little late — like Michael C. Hall, Dex is now 55 — but it’s more that Dexter the series is thriving. The first season of Dexter: Resurrection (really just the tenth season of Dexter) was a wildly satisfying return to form for a show that had long ago lost its footing. Let us forget the dreadful Dexter: New Blood, the uneven Dexter: Original Sin, and yes, that whole lumberjack thing. Last year, the franchise hit heights not seen since the Trinity Killer stalked Miami in 2006, and while that makes for a tough act to follow, we’re off to a promising start with the season premiere. Dexter himself might feel aimless and underappreciated, but Dexter is in a creative renaissance, and long-suffering fans can remain grateful.

Aside from setting up the presumably seasonlong thread of Dexter’s discontent — he’d like a little recognition for 35 years of saving lives through serial killing, please! — “Risky Business” ties up loose ends and gets the new plots moving. Dexter is still plagued by nightmares about Batista’s death, even as Harry generously insists, “Angel’s death wasn’t your fault.” And the work of the Bay Harbor Butcher isn’t hitting the way it used to. Following the NYPD’s discovery of Leon Prater’s vault, Dex has been tracking down and offing the remaining members of the serial-killer club. He reasons that taking out the Midnight Mangler and the Yonkers Slayer saved over 50 lives, but what good is that if he’s not getting any credit for it? “This is hardly the life I imagined I’d have in my 50s,” he laments.

It doesn’t help that Dexter’s day job is shuttling around entitled assholes for UrCar. When a particularly obnoxious passenger hits him with a “What a life you live, boomer,” all Dex can offer is a weak “Generation X, dipshit” once he’s out of earshot. (The Code precludes further intervention, even for bros who rate him two stars.) The one bright spot in Dexter’s life is Harrison, who is now 21 and graduating from the police academy. The two are closer than ever, in fact — Dex even suggests they share their locations with each other (terrible idea) and promises he’ll be there for Harrison’s gun-and-shield ceremony. We know he’s almost certainly going to flake, but let’s appreciate this healthy father-son bond while we can.

Prater’s vault has also forced the NYPD into action, namely by revealing the identity of the New York Ripper to be Don Framt. (Remember when we thought he might be a character we already knew? We were so young once.) When we catch up with detectives Wallace and Oliva, they’re interrogating Framt for the ninth time. The iconic Brian Cox joins the Dexter: Resurrection cast to play the Ripper, who has put down his manhole hook but is still leaving taunting voice-mails for his victims’ loved ones. Though this isn’t the first time Cox has played a serial killer — his Hannibal Lecter remains tragically underrated — Framt feels like something we haven’t seen from him before. There’s a real sense of whimsy to this monster who gleefully spits in his coffee cup in case the cops want to test his DNA again. We meet Captain Mixon, played by new regular Bokeem Woodbine, as he reminds Wallace and Oliva that they need real evidence to put the Ripper away. For the time being, they’re going to have to stop hauling in Framt, especially after his lawyer calls the repeated interrogations “full-blown harassment.” But Wallace, who has been working this case for 23 years, is determined to put the Ripper behind bars while he’s alive. There’s some compelling overlap between Dexter and Wallace, both of whom worry their decades of effort won’t amount to anything.

It turns out the NYPD has more urgent problems than a retired octogenarian in an electric wheelchair. There’s a new serial killer in town: the self-proclaimed Five-Borough Killer, played by newcomer Dan Stevens. While I’ll admit to feeling trepidatious about all the series regulars Dexter: Resurrection has added, I’ll never complain about a show making room for Stevens, who is at his best when he’s playing a homicidal psychopath. (And also his hottest. Watch 2014’s The Guest if you don’t believe me.) FBK — I feel like we’re already on an abbreviation basis — calls the precinct and informs them he’ll be killing one New Yorker at tomorrow’s baseball game. “Consider yourself warned,” he says. But despite the extra two dozen officers Wallace sends to Citi Field, the fledgling serial killer easily follows through on his threat. Is this the show’s progressive commentary on more cops not making the city safer? When the game is rained out, FBK wanders through the parking lot wearing pervert glasses (I don’t think this is official Meta Glasses sponcon) and shoots a woman getting into her car. “Nobody cares” is the only hint he offers as to motive. Later, he AirDrops his snuff film to unsuspecting parkgoers, and we see him cross Queens off a map. There are at least four more murders on the horizon — unless somebody stops him. Will the NYPD or Dexter get there first?

Given the show we’re watching, my money’s on Dex, but our hero seems determined to let himself get distracted by side quests. To be fair, he’s had a Rapunzel problem ever since Al bailed on the second act of Hamilton and left town last season. Once Dexter realizes Al is still actively murdering women and stealing their ponytails, he tracks him down and hightails it to Pennsylvania. There are a couple of problems here. One, Al is on an extended cross-country RV trip with his family, which will make killing him a challenge. Two, Dexter has promised to be at Harrison’s police-academy graduation. When Harrison clocks his dad’s location — told you that was a bad idea — he calls to confront him directly. To his credit, Dex is up-front about what he’s doing in the Keystone State, but he insists he’ll be back in time for the gun-and-shield ceremony, an obvious impossibility. Both Harrison and Harry try to convince Dexter he’s being overly impulsive about killing Rapunzel. “It just feels like you’re taking on more risks than necessary, especially for someone …” Harrison says, letting the unspoken “your age” linger in the air. But as Dexter later reminds Harry, “I’m not even supposed to be alive, Dad. Let me live a little.”

And yes, Rapunzel is going to kill again. When Dexter arrives at the campground, he finds Al enjoying a bike ride with his family while also covertly eyeing a possible next victim. I’m glad to see Eric Stonestreet back on the show, however briefly, and he gets to play a different side of the character here. The moment he sees “Red,” his guard is up — the members of Prater’s serial-killer club knew better than to impinge on one another’s personal lives, and that was before the added danger brought on by the vault discovery and Prater’s disappearance. Dexter, still pretending to be Red, tries to smooth things over by telling Al he’s been scared and misses connecting with like-minded individuals. There’s probably a bit of truth to this and to his admiration for Al’s apparent ability to be a loving husband and father. “I hope to find out his secret to a happy family life tonight,” Dex admits to Harry. On that front, it would help to not bail on Harrison’s graduation at the last minute. I’m confused how Dexter thought he could be in two places at the same time, but surely, he realized he was going to flake well before sending Harrison — seconds from graduating! — an all-caps “NOT GOING TO MAKE IT, BUDDY” text. It took so long for these two to find their way back to each other, and Dex is already blowing it.

At least he didn’t drive to Pennsylvania for nothing! Dexter lures Al to an abandoned auto body shop that he’s transformed into a kill room. After a brief moment of friendly banter, Al drops the mask. Turns out he’s more like Trinity than Dexter realized, revealing himself to be exactly the kind of sociopath his crimes would suggest. When asked how he persuaded his family to hop in the RV for an endless vacation, he coldly answers, “I tell them what to do, and they do it. Basically they’re mine.” Al’s also no dummy, and he knows Red has rummaged through his RV and stolen his ponytail trophies. Dexter is completely unprepared for a fight, and the situation looks dire as Al knocks the etorphine needle out of his hand and tackles him with a “You fucked with the wrong cheesehead, motherfucker!” Dex is eventually able to get the upper hand, though, revealing his true identity as the Bay Harbor Butcher and hanging Al with a hydraulic chain rather than following his standard M.O. In another change of pace, he decides to leave Al hanging in the shop. “Fuck it,” he reasons. “I’ll let the world know Rapunzel is no longer a threat.”

But Dexter’s true motives here aren’t as noble as he’s pretending. Once he’s back in New York, it’s clear the lack of credit for his crimes is driving him to be noticed. He bristles when a Google search for “rapunzel serial killer dead” comes up short. “It’s like you’re trying to prove something, that you’re as good as or better than you’ve ever been,” Harry tells him. “I am,” Dexter answers. And no one (minus the audience at home) knows it. His slides are works of art he can’t display. His kills are a net good for which he’s never been thanked. Instead, he’s living an anonymous life and getting two-star ratings as a rideshare driver — can anyone blame him for this midlife crisis? Harry is right, however, that no matter how justified Dex’s attention-seeking behavior may be, it’s a dangerous path to go down. Just because Wallace and Oliva already have two serial killers in their sights doesn’t mean they can’t also pursue the Bay Harbor Butcher — particularly given the sudden arrival of Miami Metro’s Joey Quinn.
