items.title: Dominic Fike Might Be Growing Up, But He's Angsty as Ever
items.description: Across How to Quit Smoking, it’s clear that Dominic Fike has mastered the art of a distinctively Dominic Fike sound. It’s in his distorted, sunburned guitars, in the quake of his voice as he sing-raps, in all of the Florida nostalgia baked into his lyrics. Thi
items.author: Julyssa Lopez
paragraphs: Across How to Quit Smoking, it’s clear that Dominic Fike has mastered the art of a distinctively Dominic Fike sound. It’s in his distorted, sunburned guitars, in the quake of his voice as he sing-raps, in all of the Florida nostalgia baked into his lyrics. This is his third album, but it doesn’t feel so far removed from the 22-year-old kid who sparked a label war after uploading low-fi songs to SoundCloud in the late 2010s — and who went wildly viral for hits like “3 Nights” and “Babydoll,” the latter of which is still sitting high on the charts. The angst and anguish and the ability to come up with a damn good hook are still there, even if the pressures and the stress of adulthood have taken on aching new heights.

How to Quit Smoking finds Fike at 30, now a dad and still figuring a lot of things out. Throughout his past albums, he’s detailed pretty clearly what he’s gone through: Fike recorded his first EP while under house arrest for battery of a police officer; when it started blowing up, he was in jail for violating his parole. Once Columbia won the label bidding war and signed Fike for a reported $4 million, he used a lot of that money to bail his mom out of prison, where she was serving time on drug charges. (“Everybody looking at me like I’m not invested/Bitch, you know how hard I was stressing?” he raps on “How Much Is Weed,” the jittery track that opened 2023’s excellent Sunburn.)

He’s outlined his journey with sobriety and addiction in his music, all while dealing with loneliness and some highly public breakups. His lyrics dwell on the things that he misses or wishes had gone differently, and How to Quit Smoking circles the same existential anxieties as Fike tries to kick bad habits and own up to mistakes. “I don’t even go up the street for a cup of ice,” he sings on the surprisingly sunny “Pangea.” “If I fuck it up, I’m going back to the hood.” On the dreamy “Cabby,” with Emma Ogier and Love Spells, he admits, “I’m not sanctified, I’m not Jesus Christ/But if this wine was water, I’d feel fit to drive.” It’s especially thrilling to see him pull in different guests across the album; Ogier also appears on the bouncy “Small Town” with Gabriel Jacoby; Grace Ives hops onto the smoky “Honeylove.”

There’s a void as he tries to give up his vices, and Fike is trying to find anything that’ll fill it: past memories, late-night drives, relationships he knows didn’t work out. But a lot of Fike’s songs can feel fleeting, like he’s too itchy to fully sit in whatever emotion he’s conjuring up. He traces a mood and moves on before revealing too much. He’s struggling on “Casting Call,” trying to reconnect with anyone who can help him escape for a while. “I’m sobrie, I’m sobri- I’m sober for right now,” he stammers on the song, suggesting he’s anything but — yet he doesn’t go any further into his turmoil. Most tracks barely hit the three-minute mark; a large majority end up as quick, two-minute sketches.

And yet, even in their brevity, the songs are good, layered, and surprisingly upbeat. The opener, “Wallflower,” welcomes fans right in, with tons of intricate guitar work and rich textures folded into the production, not to mention endlessly catchy ways into each verse. “Squeeze” is infectiously bright; “White Keys” gets stuck in your head immediately. Fike is a particularly good live performer; a lot of these are begging for the gritty makeover he often gives his songs onstage. They’re indebted to alt-rock and especially Weezer, who joined Fike on Sunburn’s standout “Think Twice.”

When Fike does lean into deeper, heavier feelings, he can land a serious gut punch. “Spotlight/Inner Child” closes the album, and it finally lays out everything he’s been searching for a way to say. He sets it up as a conversation with the artist Tay-K, who raps from prison, where he’s serving an 80-year sentence on multiple counts of murder and aggravated robbery. Fike lets it out as he invites him onto the song: “We been moving throughout the world, I just had a son,” he says. “We been touring a lot, I’m feeling disconnected from my home, um/And I’m growing up at the same time/And so it’s just, I don’t know, being 30, the culmination of all these things, being 30/I don’t know where you’re at with life right now/But I’d be curious to hear it.” Tay-K raps about his childhood hardships, his mom, and trying to stay connected to his inner child in his darkest moments. The two of them seem to land on a central idea that Fike sings about earlier in the song: “Whatever happens, up next, I will do my best.” Throughout the losses and grief and tantamount fuck-ups, he finds a way to get through.

items.title: Outlander: Blood of My Blood Recap: The Homecoming Committee
items.description: You know that thing where you go off to war where there’s a high likelihood you’re going to die, and then your own father betrays you to join the enemy, and then you have to infiltrate an English prison, kill multiple people, save your friend from drowning whi
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: You know that thing where you go off to war where there’s a high likelihood you’re going to die, and then your own father betrays you to join the enemy, and then you have to infiltrate an English prison, kill multiple people, save your friend from drowning while watching another guy drown in front of you, and then you return to safety just to be informed of the worst news of your life? Yeah, that’s what happened to Brian Fraser. My greatest wish for this man is that he finds two hours to go stare at a wall in a dark room and dissociate for a while. He’s earned it.

But Brian does not get to dissociate! The man doesn’t even get to bathe, and you know he smells awful. He and Murtagh deliver Dougal back to Castle Leoch, and as a thank-you for saving their brother and the War Chieftain’s life, all Brian wants is to go see Ellen. Of course, when he does find Ellen, she’s in bed crying and still in pain. This whole scene is heartbreaking. From Ellen telling Brian that she hoped for a girl and prays she is with Janet now, to her breaking the news that it was Brian’s father who did this to her and the doctor doesn’t think she’ll ever be able to have children, to her assuming if she can’t have kids, Brian won’t want to be with her anymore. The depths of despair on this show know no bounds.

And while I get Ellen’s insecurity about her (possible) infertility — I mean, her brother is in the next room freely uttering phrases like “a woman with no womb is worth nothing at all,” fucking Colum — we (and Ellen) also know that Brian and Arch Bug are constantly duking it out for biggest wife guy on Blood of My Blood. He would never leave her. Well, emotionally speaking. Literally speaking, he does immediately tell her that he loves her always and then walks out the door. But guys, don’t worry, he’s just running off to kill his dad. Oh, wait, on second thought, maybe do worry a little bit.

Brian, understandably, wants Lovat to die. In a truly boss move, he walks into Castle Leathers, slams Balloch’s face into a table, and asks, “Do I have your attention, Father?” I wish Ellen was there to see it because it is honestly very hot. Lovat doesn’t try to deny anything and instead tells his son quite forthrightly that he did it because of the prophecy. He wants that baby to be king, so he had to make him the last of his bloodline. Brian’s disgusted by that, but it’s not until Lovat calls Ellen a “barren MacKenzie whore” that he takes his father by the throat and slams him against a wall. He thinks about cutting off Lovat’s dick, which would do a lot of people a favor, but then Julia and Davina arrive to beg Brian not to kill Lovat. If he does, he’ll be hanged. Think of Ellen, they tell him. And so he does. Instead of revenge, Brian demands a piece of land and the promise that Lovat will never set foot on it. If Lovat ever touches Ellen again, Brian will not hesitate to kill him. And then he’s gone.

Brian returns to Ellen safe and sound, and he hands her a rock from the bridge where they had their first meeting — “Our bridge,” he says — and tells her that this stone will be the hearthstone that he builds their home around. My heart wishes them peace and joy in this new home even though my head knows it is impossible on a show like Blood of My Blood.

If that was Brian’s welcome home from Sheriffmuir, you should hear about Dougal’s. Holy hell, could Colum be any angrier with his brother? I get Colum has had to bury so many MacKenzie men, and it was Dougal who pushed their clan to the Jacobite side, but you’re not even a little relieved to see your brother still alive? Colum is falling deeper and deeper into the clan above all else, and it’s frustrating to watch. He berates Dougal in front of their sisters and Maura and lays the blame for every single MacKenzie death at Dougal’s feet. He also calls him a “selfish cunt,” so you know he’s big mad. Since Dougal just escaped from prison, the English will surely be coming after him, so Colum banishes him to a cottage away from Castle Leoch.

Dougal, by the way, has barely said three words. He looks haunted by everything he’s endured. Colum didn’t even need to blame Dougal for all the men who died; Dougal is already walking around with that guilt. It’s wild to see him so still. He doesn’t fight back.

Before he leaves Leoch, Colum allows him time with his wife, which he accepts because come on, Dougal’s always gonna Dougal. And yet … he can’t really, um, Dougal? We find him and Maura in bed, and the sex looks terrible? No one is enjoying it, and Dougal can’t even look at Maura. He stops and sits on the side of the bed. She sits next to him. He still can’t even speak about how he’s feeling, so she takes his face in her hands, kisses him, and whispers, “Be with me.” She wants him to focus on her; she wants to give him a reprieve from how he’s feeling. And he kisses her back. It is, maybe, the first actual kiss they’ve shared? He takes her onto the bed, and this time they can’t look away from one another. Is it possible this husband and wife have — gasp — fallen in love with each other? It remains astounding that somehow it’s these two who are giving us the most achingly romantic moments in this entire series.

Sure, Henry and Julia can be romantic, too; it’s just that their story is getting a little ridiculous and drawn out at the moment. Right now, they’re writing letters, and Henry’s trying to procure three gemstones so they can time travel again, and the plan is to … rappel down a gorge and chisel three pieces of amethyst from a rock formation? He can’t just nick some jewelry from the affluent Grants, who he lives with, and make a run for it? At the very least, after almost dying while getting into that gorge, he only takes three tiny pieces of amethyst? No backups? Some to sell in case he or Julia needs money? This is why Julia should be head of all time-travel operations from here on out.

But Henry and Arch Bug — at the insistence of Murdina, who believes if Arch brings some amethyst, which is tied to stories of the Fair Folk, back, maybe the faeries will grant them another child — do go to that gorge, and Henry does come out of it with three pieces of stone. Henry brings those gemstones to Julia, and they decide they will make their escape in a few days’ time when all of the lairds of Loyalist clans, including Lovat and Uncle Grant, will be convening at the Duke of Sandringham’s for investitures by invitation from the king. Both Julia and Henry will be there, and they’ll be able to slip away while everyone is distracted. A solid plan!

There is one tiny problem. After blissfully leaving Henry at the wall, knowing that soon they’ll be together and they’ll get to the stones and back to Claire in just a few days, Julia finds that Maisri has returned to Leathers. When Julia asks if she’ll ever see Claire again, Maisri dumps some news on her that we’ve all pretty much known was coming since the season-two premiere: Julia can’t time travel, and the only reason she traveled the first time was that she was pregnant with William, who does have that ability. Julia is stuck 200 years in the past forever. Yeah, they’re going to need a new plan.

• In one happy bit of news: Murtagh and Grace tell each other how they feel, and then they have sex in a barn, and it is sweet, if a bit awkward. But I still fear for Grace’s life. Perhaps now more than ever!

• Is Murtagh actually the most romantic character in all of the Outlander-verse? When Grace stops herself from kissing Murtagh because she fears “wanting too much,” he replies with “Too much? How will it ever be enough?” before kissing her.

• Arch tearfully opens up to Henry about him and his wife losing their baby. Their son died before they could give him a name, but Arch called him “Wee Bug.” He and Murdina love each other so much. I think I like them now? Don’t tell Jamie, Claire, or Young Ian, okay?

• We get a flashback, er, forward maybe, that shows us Henry and Julia out on a date after getting married and running into Henry’s terribly snobbish ex. It’s both a way to explain how Henry knew about the amethyst (Julia talked about the supply in the Highlands because her wedding band has an amethyst in it) and to remind us how much they loved each other from day one.

• When Colum learns that Brian didn’t kill Lovat and there’s no real recourse for what Lovat did to Ellen, he seems angry that he’s taking yet another loss as laird so soon after the Sheriffmuir disaster. I’m worried he’s going to go all unhinged on us soon. Is Colum going to do something reckless?

items.title: What Election Day Commentators Are Saying: Trump Rants, Hasan Piker Wonders if MAGA ‘Cult’ Is Over and More (Updating)
items.description: It’s Election Day in America, which means that pundits were falling over each other to discuss the day’s results as soon as the polls opened. At stake: all 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 Senate seats and plenty of high-profile state races. Here’
items.author: William Earl
paragraphs: It’s Election Day in America, which means that pundits were falling over each other to discuss the day’s results as soon as the polls opened. At stake: all 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 Senate seats and plenty of high-profile state races. Here’s what some of the country’s loudest and most influential talkers had to say about America’s big vote day.

Trump started his Election Day rants early, taking to Truth Social to say, “Abdul El-Sayed Hates Jews and Hates Blacks. Don’t feel bad, he also Hates Whites. Only fools would vote for him in the Michigan race for the U.S. Senate! He will, 100%, do you in!”
He called into “Fox & Friends” later in the morning to go on a lengthy diatribe about everything on his mind, including why the war in Iran isn’t a big deal.

“Iran had threat of a nuclear weapon,” Trump said. “Iran is No. 1 state sponsor of terror in the world. They are the meanest. They are very tough. I see why Middle East was afraid of them. They’re very tough, but they have been decapitated. They have no Navy. They had 159 ships.

“Every ship is at the bottom of the sea, every airplane is laying in small pieces, tiny pieces all over the runway. No anti-aircraft, we took some out last night,” he continued. “Minor attack, wasn’t war. They built an anti-aircraft facility, it took them about two months. We watched it get built. We hit it last night nicely, not big war. You talk about war, this is not really war. We have — hit them hard at the beginning, but that was it. We knocked out their nuclear capability and dust, thousands of tons of rocks, we have that under surveillance, if anyone went there we’d hit it again. We have Space Force I developed my first term. We can see the badge, name tag on man’s chest from outer space. It’s the most unbelievable stuff you’ve ever seen.”

Later in the day, Trump again took to Truth Social to document his dislike of Fox News and Jessica Tarlov’s voice. “I can’t stand Jessica Tarlov’s voice — DUMB AS A ROCK, but it’s the voice that gets me,” he wrote. “Have to go somewhere else until that LOSER is off the air — I’ll be back later!” Back later he was indeed, this time to attribute the network’s ratings to their “spending too much time covering the Trump Deranged Dumocrats.”

He continued: “All of those people who used to watch Fox, and no longer do, get it. It’s them, not me — My numbers are better than they have ever been. The new CNN Poll stated that “TRUMP” is at 99% among Republicans and, among Republican Presidents, “TRUMP” is at 53%, compared to Ronald Reagan at 18%, and Abraham Lincoln at 8%! Fox knows this, and so does everyone else! Also, why is Fox Corp. spending so much money donating to the Worst of the Worst, including Hakeem Jeffries, Jamie Raskin, Ted Lieu, Pete Aguilar, the California Dumocratic Party, the Dumocratic Congressional Campaign Committee, the Dumocratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, the Congressional Black Caucus PAC, the CHC Bold PAC, and the New Dumocrat Coalition Action Fund, among others? No wonder FoxNews Ratings are collapsing, and they’re going to go down a lot further. They’re way down, not because of me, but because they are AGAINST me! This happened once before, and Fox almost collapsed. It’s happening again!”

In an interview with CBS News conducted just before polls closed, Trump told the outlet he is prepared to use his “tremendous powers” if Democrats flip the house. According to the outlet, Trump said that he is prepared to veto Democratic legislation if necessary. “The presidency, our presidency, is considered a strong presidency. You can do a lot,” Trump said.

After Democrats won control of the U.S. Senate and the House of Representatives, Trump congratulated the party, per a phone call with CBS News. “My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country,” he said. “I know a lot of Democrats, I have total veto power and I’m sure we’ll be able to work things out. I think they’re gonna want to work with me… Otherwise, I’d just veto everything, and they’re not gonna want that.”

Jimmy Kimmel took to the stage for “Jimmy Kimmel Live” Tuesday night and delighted audiences with a humor-filled monologue about Election Day happenings. “After all of the talk about Nicki Minaj’s ass, John Husted’s ass, the only ass on Trump’s mind tonight is the one that got handed to him,” said the host.

Following the news that democrats have won the House, Ben Shapiro joined the “All-In” podcast during their live election coverage and said that this is “not an evening to remember… It’s a wipeout for Republicans; there’s no way to sugarcoat that. And again, if you’re looking at it across the map, that bodes pretty ill for 2028.”

Shapiro also noted that Trump had said that the election was going to be a referendum on him, and “I think that the president was kind of on the ballot.” He continued: “If this were just the case of a few outstandingly bad Republican candidates losing, like Paxton in Texas, for example, or if it were just a matter of an outstanding Democrat candidate winning somewhere, like Josh Turek in Iowa, but the fact that South Carolina is going… you basically have an empty suit in South Carolina losing. Or the fact that Florida stayed red, but very, very, very closely… Angie Nixon is a full-scale nutcase, and Angie Nixon is going to lose that senatorial race by about two points.”

The outspoken Twitch streamer took to X early in the day to muse about some big questions, writing, “we’re abt to find out how much ‘cult’ still remains in maga today. Is it over? Is it still strong? how well does racial polarization & pure vitriol work on Americans after experiencing negative real wage growth?Can Trump truly reverse every single campaign promise & still maintain the cattle vote?”
Click here to watch Piker’s Election Day Twitch stream.

On the Election Day morning edition of the podcast, the trio of hosts were bullish on a blue wave. When Jon Favreau asked if not winning both chambers will feel like a loss for Democrats at this point, Jon Lovett gave a passionate response.

“In this environment, with a President this despicable, with an illegal war, with the tariffs, with a Republican Congress rubber-stamping this ridiculous, vile, lawless administration, if we can’t win both chambers, then yes, that will be a loss,” Lovett said.
Later in the evening, Alex Wagner was joined by Stacey Abrams, who spoke about Keisha Lance Bottoms’ historic victory after she was projected to become Georgia’s first Black woman governor.

“I feel like the gains we are seeing tonight in the Peach State are a result of the work you and Fair Fight Action have been doing for so long, and just the way you taught us that Georgia could become a blue state,” said Wagner as Abrams joined her. When asked how Abrams was feeling (John Ossoff also won re-election in the state), the former state representative replied, “I’m excited. We also just picked up the attorney general seat, which means that Georgia will be on the right side of lawsuits for the first time in more than a decade,” she said. “We’re delighted to be making history… We saw record number of people of color show up and vote, and we’ve been building at this since 2018 and 2022 and 2024, and now it’s coming to fruition. But you’re seeing that across the country.”

Abrams continued: “So while I’m incredibly proud of Georgia, I’m also so proud of what we’re seeing across the South, what we’re seeing around the nation. As more and more people who were left out of this conversation, who did not believe their voices matter, they believe their votes should count, and they are showing up in droves. And that’s what’s changing the composition not only of Congress, but it’s going to change the composition of state legislatures, of governors’ offices, the secretaries of state who will be responsible for defending us because we don’t have a voting rights act, and attorneys general who will be responsible for fighting back when they weaponize whatever new crazy they come up with next year because their voter suppression in 26 is a test run for 28, and now we have new champions and new sentinels who are ready to go to work and ready to go to war to defend democracy.”
On MS Now, Joe Scarborough called the Republican Party’s closing arguments “astronomically stupid.”

“You have Ramaswamy talking about Communism, right?” Scarborough said. “And there is no Communism here. Amy Acton has no Communist views, Donald Trump does … It’s not what the Democrats are doing, but they’re talking about Communism instead of talking about the price of the cost of gas, Communism instead of the cost of diesel, Communism instead of the cost of groceries. I’m not good at this political stuff, but I think that and a reflecting pool doesn’t add up to victory for Republicans today.”

Following the news that Bottoms was elected as Georgia’s first Black woman governor, MS Now’s Symone Sanders gave an emotional reaction to the historic win. When asked how she knew Bottoms would win, she responded: “Well, one, I know Keisha Lance Bottoms, but two, because the people in Georgia have been organizing.”

She continued: “And to be very clear, we just take it all the way back to the New Georgia Project, way back when, and Stacey Abrams, when Stacey Abrams set out and said there are voters in Georgia to be organized. There are people who have yet to be touched, and if you just speak to them, if you just talk to them, if you just talk to voters about their power, they will participate. And cycle after cycle, we saw some gains and some moves. And today, America has elected its first Black woman as governor in this country.”

Sanders explained that while Bottoms made history tonight, she didn’t run on history alone. “She ran on the issues, and I think that resonated with folks in the state… It is no small thing that Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the governor of Georgia during the next presidential election. It is Keisha Lance Bottoms who will make sure that the election is certified for whoever the winner is. It is Keisha Lance Bottoms will be on the other side of the phone if Donald Trump picks up the phone and calls. It is remarkable. And so whatever else happens tonight, this is a reminder that in America the people have the power, and Georgia has a governor named Keisha.”
The incendiary former Fox News talking head took to her YouTube show to accuse Amy Acton, the Democratic nominee for governor of Ohio, of sounding intoxicated when she speaks.
“There’s apparently a drunk lady about to become governor potentially in Ohio,” Kelly said. “Why does that Amy Acton sound completely hammered in every clip you see of her?”
Kelly later said, “At a minimum, we can be comforted if she wins by the thought that she’ll have a designated driver taking her around and will no longer be behind the wheel.”
Watch Kelly’s analysis below.

items.title: Jason Statham and Guy Ritchie Reunite — Again — for Netflix Revenge Action Movie ‘Dogfight’
items.description: The Jason Statham–Guy Ritchie partnership is set to extend into a seventh film.
items.author: Alex Ritman
paragraphs: The Jason Statham–Guy Ritchie partnership is set to extend into a seventh film.

“Dogfight” — announced by Netflix — is described as a “stylish revenge actioner” set in the London criminal underworld. No other plot details have been revealed, but it’s safe to presume there’ll be guns, blood and — probably — some mean-looking faces. Production is due to commence n early 2027, with filming taking place in the U.K.
Like almost all of their previous collaborations, Ritchie will write, direct and produce, while Statham will star.

Production companies on “Dogfight” are Black Bear Pictures, behind most of Ritchie’s recent titles (including his latest releases “In the Grey” and “Wife & Dog”) plus Ritchie’s own Toff Guy Films and Statham’s Punch Palace Productions. Producers include Ritchie, Statham, Ritchie’s Toff Guy partner Ivan Atkinson and John Friedberg from Black Bear.

“Dogfight” lengthens a long-running and hugely successful relationship between the director and his action star, which began when Ritchie gave Statham his first film role in his 1998 directorial debut “Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels.” This partnership would continue with “Snatch,” “Revolver,” “Wrath of Man” and “Operation Fortune: Rose de Guerre.”

The pair’s latest feature together, announced last year by Variety, is the action-thriller “Viva La Madness,” based on J.J. Connolly’s novel and the author’s sequel to “Layer Cake,” which was adapted into the 2004 film by Matthew Vaughn. However, while plot details have been kept under wraps, “Viva La Madness” has been described as a standalone film and not a continuation of previous work. Principal photography on the film wrapped earlier this year, with Black Bear distributing in North America and Amazon MGM Studios holding rights to most international territories.

items.title: James Wan and Jason Blum Unveil New Company Name: Blumhouse Atomic
items.description: James Wan and Jason Blum have unveiled a new umbrella title for their merged horror production companies, Blumhouse and Atomic Monster: Blumhouse Atomic. Blumhouse and Atomic Monster will continue to operate as distinct production labels, and their respective
items.author: Jack Dunn
paragraphs: James Wan and Jason Blum have unveiled a new umbrella title for their merged horror production companies, Blumhouse and Atomic Monster: Blumhouse Atomic. Blumhouse and Atomic Monster will continue to operate as distinct production labels, and their respective creative teams will develop and produce film and television projects under each banner.

“When we merged our companies, we believed the whole would be greater than the sum of its parts and that is exactly what has happened,” said Jason Blum, Co-Founder of Blumhouse Atomic. “Blumhouse Atomic is a natural evolution of what we’ve built together. ‘The Conjuring’ franchise, ‘Insidious,’ ‘Saw,’ no filmmaker has created more horror franchises than James Wan, and together we’ve brought some of the genre’s most recognizable properties under one roof. Bringing ‘Saw’ back to James, with a new chapter on the way, is a perfect example of what we can do together. We have the output of a studio with the creative freedom and financial discipline of an independent company, and more opportunities than ever to take these stories beyond the theater and into television, games and live experiences.”

Wan and Blum merged Blumhouse and Atomic Monster in 2024, bringing together two of the most productive and successful production houses and execs in the horror space. The combined banners have since generated more than $2.5 billion in worldwide box office against combined production budgets of less than $330 million. In 2026, Blumhouse Atomic pulled in $1.3 billion, riding the wave of two of the year’s biggest hits in Curry Barker’s “Obsession” ($520 million worldwide) and Kane Parsons’ “Backrooms” ($400 million worldwide).

“The future of horror comes from new voices, and Blumhouse Atomic gives us more ways to find them and support them for the long haul,” added James Wan, Co-Founder of Blumhouse Atomic. “I got my start with a small film and people willing to take a chance on it, so creating those opportunities for others is personal to me. Working with filmmakers like Kane Parsons, Curry Barker, Josh Giuliano and Dylan Clark is a big part of that. We want to give them the freedom to make something distinctive and build relationships that last beyond one film.”

Blumhouse Atomic’s mission of cultivating blockbuster horror hits from undersized budgets was further bolstered this year with the appointment of Sam Zimmerman as senior vice president of development and acquisitions, who was tasked with developing a slate of genre features with budgets of under $5 million. The company also recently inked a first-look deal with Divide/Conquer to develop high-concept projects for an economical rate.

Blumhouse Atomic’s 2027 film slate includes “River,” “The Revenge of La Llorona,” “The Exorcist: Martyrs,” “Anything But Ghosts,” “Paranormal Activity,” “Molepeople,” “Blair Witch,” “Sleepover” and “Seasons.”

items.title: U.K. Celebrity Loses Injunction Bid to Prevent Sexual Misconduct Allegations From Being Published, but Will Remain Anonymous Pending Appeal
items.description: An anonymous U.K. celebrity has lost his injunction bid to prevent two news organizations from publishing sexual misconduct allegations against him and therefore revealing his identity.
items.author: Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: An anonymous U.K. celebrity has lost his injunction bid to prevent two news organizations from publishing sexual misconduct allegations against him and therefore revealing his identity.

Earlier this month, it was reported that an anonymous celebrity had applied for a permanent injunction at London’s High Court to try to stop ITN and The Guardian from publishing a story containing allegations that he abused his power to engage in “inappropriate sexual activities with a large number of girls and young women,” according to BBC News. The celebrity denies the allegations.

Judge Mr. Justice Nicklin rejected the injunction request on Tuesday, as reported by BBC News, but the celebrity will remain anonymous for the time being to allow him a chance to appeal the judgement.

“The claimant’s claim for an injunction was dismissed,” Nicklin said in his ruling. However, he added: “The court did not determine whether the allegations, or any of them, were true, and the dismissal of the claim does not amount to approval of any publication the defendants may decide to make.”

The lawyer for the celebrity told the court earlier that should he lose the injunction and the stories publish, it was “highly likely” he would attempt to commit suicide. According to his lawyer, he has already attempted to do so twice before.

ITN and The Guardian’s lawyer, on the other hand, argued that publishing the allegations and the man’s identity is in the public’s best interest. He said that the news organizations had spoken to over 100 people in their investigation and that many of the women “have been traumatized by the claimant’s alleged conduct and have suffered mental health crises and mental illness as a result,” according to BBC News.

The unusual case has sparked much conversation in the U.K. amid widespread speculation about the celebrity’s identity, as well as concern for potential ramifications on press freedom. on Monday, Variety spoke with defamation lawyer Paul Tweed about the likelihood that the celebrity’s request would be approved due to his mental health.

“The court don’t grant that very lightly — they’ll be very thorough in their examination of whether there is a genuine risk of suicide, or whether that is being used just an excuse, basically,” Tweed said, though he acknowledged that a “threat to life” is one of very few “main grounds that are remaining” for an injunction such as this in today’s world.

items.title: Pierce Brosnan Approves of Callum Turner as James Bond: He’s ‘So Strong’ and I’m ‘Eager to See’ Who Becomes the Next 007
items.description: Pierce Brosnan has given his James Bond seal of approval to Callum Turner.
items.author: Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: Pierce Brosnan has given his James Bond seal of approval to Callum Turner.

The Irish actor — who played 007 across four films from 1995 to 2002 — told Vanity Fair in a new interview that he is “eagerly” awaiting the announcement of the next Bond like the rest of us, and could see Turner taking the role. Brosnan previously shared the screen with Turner in 2017’s “The Only Living Boy in New York.”

“Oh, I’m just an audience member now. I’m just the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history,” Brosnan said when asked if he’s keeping up with the Bond chatter. “All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire. Callum Turner is someone I’ve worked with, and he’s so strong. They all have a voice and a physique, and a presence on film. They all have longevity as actors, all of these young men.”

As Variety reported, the other frontrunner appears to be “Slow Horses” star Jack Lowden and final auditions are believe to be taking place in London. Other names that have previously been floated include Josh O’Connor and Jacob Elordi.

Asked his advice for the next actor to don Bond’s dapper suit, Brosnan said: “Whoever plays the role, I wish him the very best of life and strength and courage. You know, it’s hard to tell who it would be, but I eagerly await to hear the news and the celebration of the next James Bond.”

Brosnan is particularly excited to see “Dune” director Denis Villeneuve’s take on the spy franchise. “I think we are going to be blown away. I really do,” he said. “[Villeneuve] is such an iconoclastic director. His work is visionary, and his stealth and imagination of camera work and storytelling is so visceral and sensuous. It’s going to be great. It’s going to be truly magnificent.”
Read Brosnan’s full Vanity Fair interview here.

items.title: Xavier Becerra Defeats Steve Hilton to Become California’s First Latino Governor in 150 Years
items.description: Democrat Xavier Becerra will be the next California governor, according to the Associated Press, defeating Republican Steve Hilton to become the state’s first Latino governor in more than 150 years.
items.author: Carly Thomas
paragraphs: Democrat Xavier Becerra will be the next California governor, according to the Associated Press, defeating Republican Steve Hilton to become the state’s first Latino governor in more than 150 years.
The AP called the race just after the polls closed in the Golden State at 8 p.m. on Tuesday. As of 9:30 p.m., with 49 percent of ballots counted, Becerra had a substantial lead over Hilton.

“What a great night to be a Californian. What a great night to be an American,” Becerra said in his victory speech. “To be the son of immigrants from a union household to be standing in victory with all of you. Now, I’m not gonna sugarcoat it. These past two years have been tough: higher prices, more wars, corruption and lawlessness. But we hung in there; fought back. It felt like Mission: Impossible. We knew it was mission necessary.”

He added, “And tonight, sisters and brothers, because of your tireless work, we can proudly utter the inspiring battle cry of our beloved and departed sister and warrior Dolores Huerta: ‘Sí, se puede.’ Yes, we can! Yes, we did! We fought and we won!”

Heading into election night, the odds were already against Britain-born Hilton, as California hasn’t elected a Republican to any statewide office in two decades. The last Republican to lead the Golden State was Arnold Schwarzenegger, whose term ended in 2011.

Given that registered Democrats outnumber Republicans by 4.6 million voters in the state, any Republican starts at a disadvantage. For Hilton specifically, receiving an endorsement from Donald Trump also likely didn’t help, as the Republican president is widely loathed outside his conservative base in a state he often criticizes (Most recently, Trump was slammed in October for suggesting Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if it were allowed to develop a nuclear weapon.)

In attempts to win over California voters, Hilton, a former Fox News host, also leveraged his media-savvy background with some headline-making campaign ads, specifically his “Just Try It, California” ad that featured two young women making sexual innuendos and his viral “Barstow street taco” blunder from his video outside the original Del Taco location.

When it came to policies, while Hilton focused his campaign on targeting government waste, high living costs, education reform and public safety — such as wanting to eliminate state income tax on the first $150,000 earned by residents, lower gas prices to $3 per gallon, implement statewide homeless encampment bans and propose a film tax credit as high as 60 percent to save Hollywood — it ultimately wasn’t enough to overcome Becerra.

On Tuesday night, Hilton conceded to Becerra. “Maybe this isn’t the best year to be running for office as a Republican. Well, when we see what’s going on around the country,” he said in a speech following his loss. “But I tell you what, this is the best place to be running for office as a Republican, because there is nowhere better than California. This is the greatest place in the greatest nation on earth. And it has been an honor and a joy to travel this beautiful state of ours.”
“I just want to tell you right now, the change we hoped for may be delayed, but the change is coming,” Hilton added. “Our fight goes on, and I’ll be there with you.”

The Sacramento-born Becerra, who previously served as California’s attorney general and the 25th U.S. secretary of health and human services under President Joe Biden, had a slow start early in his primary campaign. But after Democratic contender Eric Swalwell suspended his campaign amid sexual misconduct allegations, Becerra consolidated support and utilized a seven-figure ad blitz to surge past Democratic rivals like Tom Steyer just weeks ahead of the primary election in June.

While his campaign centered on lowering the cost of living, expanding healthcare and investing in state infrastructure, he now has his work cut out for him to deliver for Californians, who have expressed concerns surrounding affordability, housing and homelessness. Specifically, Becerra aims to double the rate of home building in the state, work toward a universal single-payer health care system and propose a tax on the state’s highest earners.

As for Hollywood, which has faced a significant production exodus in the state, Becerra wants to propose a law that studios/streamers must provide performance data to everyone and expand entertainment tax credits based on specific areas “where we are losing work.”
Becerra is set to be sworn into office on Jan. 5, 2027, succeeding Gov. Gavin Newsom.

items.title: Kimmel Bashes Trump After Democrats’ Midterms “Tsunami”: “The Only Ass on His Mind Is the One That Just Got Handed to Him”
items.description: Jimmy Kimmel became the first late night host to take on the results of the 2026 midterm elections late Tuesday night.
items.author: Hilary Lewis
paragraphs: Jimmy Kimmel became the first late night host to take on the results of the 2026 midterm elections late Tuesday night.

While none of the major late night shows went live on election night, ABC’s Jimmy Kimmel Live! reportedly taped later than usual on Tuesday night to react to some of the early returns. Comedy Central’s The Daily Show was the only other major late night show to air a new episode Tuesday night, but that was taped before many of the polls closed. Stephen Colbert regularly took his Late Show live on election nights, but, of course, CBS canceled his show last year and it came to an end in May.

Kimmel’s late taping allowed the host to get in some early jokes on a night that saw the Democrats projected to win both the House and the Senate amid historic, surprise victories in Georgia, Texas, Ohio, South Carolina and Kansas.
And Kimmel had plenty of barbs ready for President Donald Trump, with whom he has long feuded.
Early in his monologue he homed in on Trump’s recent fixation with complimenting people’s rear ends.
“It seems to be after all the talk about Nicki Minaj’s ass, Jon Husted’s ass, the only ass on Trump’s mind tonight is the one that just got handed to him.”
Kimmel even revived the false 2024 rumor about Vice President J.D. Vance once having sex with a couch.
“The Democrats took so many seats, J.D. Vance can’t even find one to have sex with him,” Kimmel said.
Returning to Trump, Kimmel joked that he spent the day watching Fox News coverage of the results “trying to give himself an insurrection.”

“Word from the from inside the White House is he’s already run out of dipping sauce containers to throw at the television set,” Kimmel joked. “Man, oh man, would I hate to be the Door Dash driver who delivers Trump his Papa John’s tonight?”
Kimmel went on to recap where some key races stood at the time of his show taping and paid tribute to outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson with a compilation of some of his funniest moments.

items.title: Texas Turns Blue: How James Talarico, Gina Hinojosa Broke Dems’ 36-Year Losing Streak
items.description: For the first time in 38 years, a Democrat has been elected senator in Texas.
items.author: James Hibberd
paragraphs: For the first time in 38 years, a Democrat has been elected senator in Texas.
And for the first time in 36 years, a Democrat has been elected governor of Texas.

Riding a blue wave of anti-Trump sentiment, James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton in the traditional red state, fulfilling a decades-long dream come true for Democrats, while Gina Hinojosa beat Greg Abbott to take the governor’s mansion.
“David wasn’t as big or as strong as Goliath but he had hope, he had faith and he had a slingshot.” Talarico told supporters at around 11:30 pm local time. “You were my slingshot.”

With final election results still coming in, both NBC and CNN called the race for Talarico. About 85 percent of the votes have been tallied as of late Tuesday night, and Talarico is up some 12 points. With the same count in, Hinojosa is up seven points, and CNN and NBC have now called that contest too.
The candidates’ performance was the result of a perfect storm of circumstances (as CNN’s Alyssa Farah Griffin said early in the evening, “If Texas were ever going to go blue, it’s now”).

There was, clearly, some of the strongest tailwinds for Democrats in years given widespread dissatisfaction with President Trump, who currently has some of the worst poll numbers of his political career.

There were the candidates themselves. Talarico is an unabashed Christian, telegenic and charismatic, making himself rather hard to dislike — even as the GOP spent an estimated $221 million on negative attack ads to brand him as a progressive radical. While Hinojosa ran a populist campaign focused on lowering household costs, raising teacher pay and challenging corporate influence in state government.
And finally, there were their opponents.

Paxton was considered a weak, scandal-prone candidate, one who’s been accused of corruption and adultery, and ran a low-energy campaign. Earlier this year, Paxton won a primary runoff against long-serving senator John Cornyn after Trump gave Paxton his endorsement, a move that was against the advice of GOP establishment insiders. It was an obvious error by Trump, as it would have been much tougher to imagine Talarico defeating Cornyn in November.

Abbott has served for nearly 12 years, and it’s tough to find Texans — even conservatives — who feel particularly warm towards him. Abbott has governed with so-what-who-cares style, yet until now managed to fend off challengers by presenting himself as the more practical choice.

The GOP rushed to Paxton’s defense, pumping a whopping $316 million in Republican-aligned outside spending into the Senate race to help him ward off Talarico, while the White House reportedly micromanaged his campaign remotely. Republicans also spent heavily to protect Abbott, whose campaign outspent Hinojosa’s nearly eight-to-one — $281 million to $36.8 million — according to The Texas Tribune. Elon Musk played a big role in both races, donating $158 million to a GOP Senate super PAC helping Paxton and another $5 million to Abbott’s campaign. Musk relocated to Texas in 2020 (and has since brought much of Tesla with him).

Even as voters nationwide cited affordability as their top concern, Republican attack ads heavily pushed culture-wars issues like transgender rights. Local news viewers — even in the liberal “blueberry in the tomato soup” city of Austin — were bombarded with two commercials for the senate campaign: One suggested Talarico would help make your kids trans, the other that Paxton would “protect” your kids. The ads had a stale quality — trying to re-run a GOP strategy from 2024 when Republicans made electoral gains.

Mailers sent to residents likewise declared that Hinojosa would introduce a state income tax “to pay for her socialist agenda.” And after Talarico took a highly publicized 12-day break from in-person campaigning due to the flu, Paxton’s campaign sent a mailer showing Talarico on a milk carton blazoned with “MISSING: Where’s James Talarico been? With the defund-the-police radicals in Austin.”
And so Texas voters crossed ideological lines to elect their first Democratic U.S. senator since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988 and their first Democratic governor since Ann Richards in 1990

If you’ve spent some years in Texas (I’ve spent most of my life here since 1991, back when Ann Richards, the state’s last Democratic governor, was in office) you come to realize that much of Texans’ longtime reluctance to vote for Democrats has to do with contentment with the status quo as much as it has to do with conservative vs. liberal policies.

Since 1990, the population of Texas has grown 87 percent — 15 million residents — more than any other state in the union (including 8.6 million Hispanics, a statistic that’s helped fuel Dem dreams of flipping the state). But many people who move to Texas, or have always lived in Texas, are here because they like Texas. They like that there’s no state income tax, that authorities are tough on crime, that regulators are pro-business and that, in general, the government plays a distant background role in their everyday lives.

In other words, part of the reason Democrats have faced uphill battles in Texas is because Democrats run on advocating dramatic change, and most Texas voters aren’t looking for dramatic change. It’s always tougher to sell something people don’t feel they need.
This year, however, was different.

Trump’s dual unforced errors — his tariff policy and the ongoing Iran War — caused the cost of living to surge nationwide, all while coming across as callously indifferent to Americans’ economic suffering.

The average Texas voter may not love everything Talarico and Hinojosa stand for, but one suspects that plenty wanted to push back — punish, even — Trump and his polices, which Republicans in Congress have declined to stand up to. Anonymous GOP insiders have been in the press this last week preemptively blaming Trump for the expected electoral blowout. But when a fearful Congress doesn’t check and balance the executive branch, they’re arguably at fault too and should expect voters to give the other party a shot.

At an Oct. 24 rally, Trump made his latest comment expressing a lack of concern about the cost of living, saying he did not “give a damn” about high gas prices resulting in negative headlines because the oil and gas industry is “making a fortune.” That’s a pretty big misstep given high diesel prices have hit Texas particularly hard due the state’s trucking, agricultural and energy industries (Abbott even declared a statewide disaster over the prices in September). While it might not be typical Texas to vote Democrat, casting a vote that throws a punch at a president for having such a dismissive attitude about working people’s financial hardship? That’s about as Texas as it gets.

items.title: Nobody Wants to Have a Baby Boy Anymore
items.description: It began, innocently enough, with a cake. In 2008, American blogger Jenna Karvunidis threw a party to announce the sex of her unborn baby. The reveal came when she cut a slice and found pink inside. She wrote about the experience online, the post went viral, a
items.author: Sam Parker; Karolina Burlikowska
paragraphs: It began, innocently enough, with a cake. In 2008, American blogger Jenna Karvunidis threw a party to announce the sex of her unborn baby. The reveal came when she cut a slice and found pink inside. She wrote about the experience online, the post went viral, and a new ritual was born.

Nearly 20 years later, we all know the drill. If it isn’t a cake, it’s a balloon or a cannon. Friends and family gather. Someone counts down; something explodes in blue or pink; the parents-to-be hug; a grandparent enters the frame looking thrilled and slightly confused. And, of course, there’s a camera rolling, meaning my daughter could have in theory earned her first “like” long before she drew her first breath.

For the first time in a century, nearly less than half of parents are circumcising their newborns. New dad Kevin Lincoln investigates how America’s favorite elective surgery became as debated as childhood vaccines—and considers his own decision.

The gender reveal has evolved from a modest party trick into a full-blown genre of internet spectacle, complete with its own newborn industrial complex. Private ultrasound companies now sell “gender-reveal experiences,” with rooms that glow pink or blue and teddy bears containing recordings of an unborn baby’s heartbeat. Online, the reveals have become more elaborate: smoke bombs, pyrotechnics (one of which started a wildfire in South California in 2020), choreographed dances, skydivers and, in one particularly memorable case, a Louisiana alligator called Sally biting through a blue jelly watermelon.

But the spectacle has moved on. A new kind of gender-reveal video is becoming a genre of its own, one in which a particular reaction is the main event. A recent compilation racked up 33 million views and three million likes on TikTok. Expecting couples do not scream with delight when the color appears. They scream in horror. They collapse and cry. The reason is nearly always the same: it’s blue. They’re having a boy.

What looks like internet absurdity may actually point to something much bigger. Last year, The Economist published data showing that in mostly higher-income countries, the centuries-old preference for sons is starting to reverse. And in some countries, the data shows that opinion has fully flipped: Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Portugal and the Czech Republic are showing evidence of a preference for girls.

In the US, the same trend appears among adoptive parents. According to the National Bureau of Economic Research, prospective parents were willing to pay an average $16,000 more for a girl than a boy. Among couples having IVF in the US—where, unlike the UK, sex selection is legal— leading clinics have reported that 75–80% of patients want a girl.

This is a big demographic plot twist. On one hand, it’s what progress looks like. For most of human history, boys have been the prize. They inherited the family name and property. They were expected to earn money and carry the family line into the future. Girls, in turn, were generally expected to marry out or care for relatives.

In the worst cases, the preference for sons has had lethal consequences. In China, where a one-child policy enforced by the government lasted 35 years, and in India, sex-selective abortion and the killing or abandonment of female babies has led to generations with far more boys than girls. Misogynist discrimination has been so pervasive that in 1990, the Nobel Prize–winning economist Amartya Sen estimated that more than 100 million women were “missing” from world history. (Researchers have since questioned the precise figure and methodology, but the point still stands.)

But there is another, stranger side to the reversal. You don’t have to spend long reading the 20,000-plus comments beneath a viral gender-reveal video to realize that some of this isn’t simply about girls finally being valued properly. There is a growing and increasingly open distaste for boys—a sense that they are inherently problematic, undesirable by default.
Having a son, in certain corners of modern parenthood, has become unfashionable. A curious society might ask itself why this is—and where it might lead.

Ruth Whippman is the mother of three boys. She grew up in England but now lives in America, in what she describes as a “progressive area of the country [with] very progressive school districts”. As she writes in her 2024 book, BoyMom, friends and neighbors kept saying versions of the same thing: “I hope for your sake this one is a girl.”

“We were a year into the [first] Trump presidency,” she tells me. “There were incels on the news. There was just this huge backlash against toxic masculinity. So it wasn’t even just a sense of, ‘Oh, boys, their clothes aren’t as nice; you don’t get to play Barbies.’ It was this sense that boys are actively toxic and harmful.”

When Whippman’s first son was due, she had the standard worries about raising a child of the opposite sex. Would they have enough in common? Would she know how to navigate experiences she hadn’t had? As a lifelong feminist, she tells me, the additional sense of cultural disapproval made everything worse. “It was really horrible, because nobody likes to be pitied,” she says. “Nobody likes to think that their children are second best. But I think it played into something in me as well, if I’m totally honest. I had my own fears and feelings about [having boys], and hearing everybody else’s reaction just made it much worse.”

Nearly a decade on from #MeToo, with Donald Trump back in the White House and male chauvinism metastasizing across the internet, it’s unusual to hear the word “masculinity” without the word “toxic” prefacing it. So parents can end up feeling—even if they’re guilty about it—that having a son is more complicated than it was for previous generations.

“When you hear about boys at the moment, at best, they’re this underachieving lunk who won’t go to college, is doing badly at school and will fail to launch,” says Whippman. “And at worst, he’s deep in the manosphere, commanding his AI girlfriend to let him choke her, or whatever. It gets to this wider consumerisation of parenthood. [The idea that] girls are better consumer products, in a way—which is a terrible, terrible way to talk about human beings.”

I’d be lying if I said it hadn’t crossed my mind, when I discovered I was having a daughter, that if I could raise her to be a confident, secure, kick-ass girl, I’d win the approval of the types of circle I move in. “Girl dads” who let daughters paint their nails are the subject of endless kind TikTok videos.

Parents of boys, not so much. Whippman, who has heard more and more fathers say they would prefer daughters, recognizes the problem. “Parenting a son is almost seen as a harm reduction project, rather than anything empowering,” she says. “That’s really at odds with our modern parenting culture, which is about encouraging [our kids] to reach for the stars and be happy and access all the world has to offer.”

And like everything else in 2026, the random, happy event of your unborn child’s sex can somehow thrust you into the us-versus-them culture war. “In the States and in the UK, there’s a sense that if you are on the progressive left, you are on the side of girls and women… any time you’re defending boys and men, it has this sniff of something right-wing, or being a bad actor,” says Whippman. “That’s a really hard thing to hold as a progressive, feminist parent of a son.”

There are other theories for why parents in Western countries, in particular, are increasingly downbeat about having boys. Millennials are having fewer children than any generation in history, and we’re doing it later in life. In other words, by the time it happens, we’re already exhausted. And boys are often perceived as more work, especially when they’re little: more physical, and harder to keep occupied and under control.

Lara Miller has been a midwife for more than 20 years. She uses social media to demystify pregnancy and childbirth. She thinks there is some truth to the idea that older parents may be wary of boys. “When you see older people having babies, they tend to be more controlling about everything to do with it,” she says. “I say this without judgment—I was an older mum myself—but you become used to doing things your own way and to your own routines.”

Of course, it would be silly to assume every girl will be content quietly coloring in while every boy spends his childhood trailing dog shit through the house. But according to Alex Trippier, a kids’ club leader who runs the social media account Be A Happier Parent, there can be real differences in behavior. “You get testosterone surges around age two, which I really see with the kids that I look after in my groups,” he says. “All of a sudden the boys come in and they’re going crazy. Parents who are on the quieter side can be overwhelmed by the sheer energy. Some people insist this is all nonsense, and [boys being more boisterous] is completely socialized. I think it’s a mixture of both. You’ve got that developmental layer going on, and you’ve got all the socialization on top of it.”

Trippier, who has two boys and a girl, thinks culture has shifted. Parents have always worried about teenage girls. But now, they have a whole new list of concerns for boys: porn, gaming addiction, exam results, algorithms. “There are all these fears we have for our sons, this kind of moral anxiety about the impossibility of raising good men,” he says.
In 2024, Zach Baron documented his long journey to fatherhood via IVF in GQ. Now, he reports on the mind-altering chaos (and occasional brilliance) of life with two walking, talking young boys.

Miller, who had similar feelings when she was pregnant but is now the happy mother of two sons, thinks there’s another factor: Schools aren’t always very good at accommodating boys. “We have changed as a society and we’re not as accepting of boys,” she says. “Boys don’t tend to fit the school model. You get worse reports. [Our school] gives the boys set days to be allowed to kick a football. Well, you don’t remember that at school, do you?”

She recalls being summoned by a headmaster after her son made a gun sign with his fingers. “The girls do better at school,” she says. “They’ve read 20 books; my boys have only read two. The teacher’s gone, ‘Well, if you buy a football magazine, do you think they’d read that?’ You’re like, ‘Oh, fuck off. Just fuck off.’”

There’s something else unusual about today’s parents, beyond grappling with the manosphere and Parkrun injuries. We’re the most psychologically literate generation to have ever lived. If we haven’t done therapy ourselves, we’re at least sufficiently fluent in the language of therapy to take a stab at self-reflection (or, as Boomer parents might call it, self-absorption). We know about childhood trauma. We know about attachment styles. We know that our parents’ behavior has consequences. We know that our childhoods don’t simply disappear when we become adults. It gives us an enormous number of things to worry about.

One of the most interesting conversations I’ve had on this subject is with a colleague who is expecting a son. He’s delighted now, but initially, the prospect of having a boy unnerved him—as it did me, before I knew the sex of my baby. We both agreed this probably came from remembering difficult experiences with our own fathers, and being afraid of repeating them. For me, it may have gone a step further. The idea of having a son scared me because I had a pretty broken relationship with myself.

Dr. Chrissy Jayarajah is a psychiatrist and the author of the world’s only academic paper on “gender disappointment.” She’s quick to point out that the term is not a clinical diagnosis, but what you might call a “known phenomenon” (particularly on TikTok, where thousands of videos are tagged with it).

“Something I always say is that becoming a parent will undoubtedly make you reflect on the way that you were parented,” she says. “Whether it was a good relationship, a bad relationship, an indifferent relationship or a non-existent relationship—they all play a part. An absent father is still very present in your mind. We are more psychologically minded and reflective compared with, maybe, the generation before. But I also think we don’t know what to do with that reflection.”

This can manifest in different ways, explains Jayarajah. “Working predominantly with mothers, I would say they fall into two camps,” she says. “They either want to emulate exactly how their mother was, from recreating those childhood memories, making those family favorite meals on a Sunday, and so on. Or they’re: ‘Oh my God, I’m turning into my mother.’”

That can produce powerful feelings about your baby’s sex. “We see that with women who have experienced abuse of some kind,” says Jayarajah. “Some absolutely do not want to have a girl, because they don’t want their daughter to experience what they went through. On the other hand, I have had women who say, ‘No, I definitely want a girl. I don’t want to have a son,’ because a son [would remind] them of the perpetrator.”

The sex of your baby, in other words, can become a vessel for all sorts of fears that existed long before the baby did. Then, there’s the demographic problem. There just aren’t enough babies. A rapid collapse in birth rates and fertility is playing out across the world. In 1990, global fertility was about 3.3 children per woman. Today it is around 2.2 to 2.3. More than half the countries in the world are already below “replacement level.”

The consequences will be huge. Labor shortages. Pressure on pensions. Rising social and healthcare costs. Less of the innovation and forward momentum traditionally associated with younger populations. In that context, favoring one sex over the other seems beyond counterproductive.

Maybe we are retreating into old, narrow assumptions. “We’ve never thought about gender more as a society than we do at this present day,” says Jayarajah. “Ideas about gender are in our face all day long. There was no such thing as a gender reveal party 20 years ago, let alone putting it online. What’s happening, in my opinion, is gender essentialism. This sexist idea of what it means to be a man, what it means to be a woman, is playing out in what we expect for our children.”

The following week, I saw this in action. I took my 19-month-old daughter to a soft-play morning, where she likes to roll around on the multicolored shapes and go down the slide on my lap. A few minutes after we arrived, I heard a scream. “Aaaargh!”

At one end of the ball pit, a little boy was staring at his own reflection in a mirror. “Aaaargh!” he went again, hammering his fists against the perspex and making the entire frame shake. A few feet away, my daughter watched him quietly. I made a mental note to keep them as far apart as possible.

The boy’s parents were nearby, deep in conversation. They seemed oblivious, or perhaps simply immune, to their son’s King Kong routine. A dozen judgmental thoughts zipped through my head. Why aren’t you keeping a closer eye on him? What kind of irresponsible shit are you pulling at home for him to do this? If he harms her, I swear to God…

I took a sip of my coffee, scrolled through my phone, then turned around, ready to rescue my sweet, innocent little girl. The boy who had been screaming a moment ago was now shyly handing her a dumper truck with a missing wheel. She closed her eyes, grinned, and took it with both hands.
A version of this story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of British GQ with the title “For Centuries, Everyone Wanted Boys. Now, Not So Much”
