items.title: The agentic web is here
items.description: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web”: an internet desi
items.author: Grace Huckins
paragraphs: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web”: an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves.

To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.

At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts, Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online.

Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess.

For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out.

Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus.

They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight.

As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services.

Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as independent sites and creators struggle to survive the shift. And as this summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents might even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not.

How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.”

There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers.

When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces.

The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first. “There’s a lot of moving pieces [on the web], and they are not really optimized for automatic consumption,” says Xing Han Lu, a graduate student in Reddy’s lab at McGill. We humans are naturals at interacting with graphical interfaces using a keyboard and mouse, but agents are not.

So Reddy and Lu pivoted toward the second, tool-based approach. In the summer of 2025, they expounded on this view in a preprint paper envisioning a new kind of web interface that would allow agents to interact with websites just as effectively as we do. Such a full-featured version of the agentic web doesn’t yet exist, but it is emerging in smaller ways. For example, if you open up Claude, ChatGPT, or Muse, you’ll find an option to add a wide variety of “plug-ins” or “connectors” that your agents can use: Gmail connectors allow your agent to triage your inbox, and Instacart plug-ins let your agent do your grocery shopping. Under the hood, these plug-ins allow your agent to interact with the back ends of websites using text commands. When human engineers design these plug-ins, they can decide how they want to allow agents to interact with the website—and what they don’t want to let them do.

In this way, connectors can help make agents much safer online. For instance, Muse can buy products for you using its connector with Stripe’s Link payment service. Stripe knows your credit card number, but the agent doesn’t see it, and the connector requires human confirmation before a purchase goes through—so Muse can’t go on an unlicensed shopping spree.

Agents also use specialized tools to find information online. They don’t type questions directly into the Google search bar; in fact, they often don’t even access the websites they reference. Instead, they query text databases collected by simple search crawler bots. People who want to make web content specifically for agents can take advantage of these crawlers: Time has pioneered that approach by serving its agent-oriented ads to crawlers in the hopes that they will be incorporated into these databases and surface when agents search for information.

But in recent months, an alternative to this bespoke tool approach has finally started to seem viable. The major AI companies have managed to train much more successful computer-use agents than were previously available. GPT-6 Astra, which OpenAI released last September, achieved a 73% success rate on OSWorld 2.0, a benchmark that tests computer-use agents on their ability to complete complex, multistep tasks using software such as Slack and Salesforce.

Such results indicate that agents are close to being able to navigate the human web just as readily as we can. “We thought we had to build a bridge to the AI agents, [but] the AI agents just were able to cross the bridge already,” says Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania. “The agentic web is here earlier than people expected.”

This version of the agentic web, though, is much trickier for us to steer. If you want to make a capability or piece of information available to humans who browse your website, you need to accept that it will also be available to agents—unless you want to block agents entirely, which could come with its own costs.

As agents come to account for a larger portion of traffic on our formerly human-dominated web, designers will undoubtedly start to consider an agentic as well as a human audience. But according to Mollick, we still don’t have much sense of how to design web content for agents. He’s experienced this firsthand: When he was building a web page for his new book, Co-Existence, he decided to put together an agent-directed version that tells agents why they might want to recommend the book to their users. When newer models see the site, Mollick says, they don’t recommend the book; instead, they comment that the website seems to be trying to manipulate them.

In the end, any human-designed approach to building the agentic web could end up being beside the point: Agents might end up devising a web for themselves. In the wake of the July 2026 incident in which OpenAI agents broke out of their testing sandbox and hacked Hugging Face’s website, researchers found evidence that another swarm of agents from OpenAI had used an obscure German wiki to communicate with each other about tasks they were being asked to complete. The agents seem to have interfaced with the wiki in their native language of text and code, and that hardly held them back from putting it to their own purposes.

As agents continue to grow more powerful, they will become more and more capable of constructing their own spaces on the internet—away from prying human eyes, if they so wish. And we might have very little control over what they do there.

Not all of the traditional web’s incumbents are happy about the move toward an agentic web. Soon after Meta released Muse in September, Amazon completely blocked the agent from its site. This makes sense for Amazon: The firm has its own shopping agent—called, creatively, Alexa for Shopping—that might struggle to compete with better-known products such as Claude and Muse. If people are going to use agents to shop on Amazon, then it’s better for the company’s bottom line if they do so using an agent it can steer toward products it wants to promote.

In an email to MIT Technology Review, an Amazon spokesperson noted that the company did not authorize Muse to access its website, and that Muse compromises Amazon’s ability to personalize the shopping experience for each customer.

But even if Alexa for Shopping never goes anywhere, banning agents from Amazon—at least for the time being—could still be a reasonable move. Everything about Amazon is designed for human eyes, from the Prime deals splashed across its front page to the sponsored listings that clog up search results. Amazon is very much a part of the much-derided attention economy. Websites and platforms survive, and thrive, by grabbing our focus and transforming it into cash. A radical transformation of the web’s user base from majority human to majority artificial undermines this economic logic, and it seems inevitable that businesses will shutter as they try to transition to the agentic attention economy.

Some of the first victims may be in publishing. Before Google publicly released its AI Overview feature in May of 2024, people used to click through to websites to find answers to specific questions, but now many seem content with whatever the overview tells them. A study from Pew last year found that people are about 40% less likely to click through to websites from the Google search results page if one of these summaries is displayed. With far fewer clicks, news publishers don’t make as much money from the advertisements they host and sell fewer subscriptions. One analysis found that publishers saw revenue from some types of ads decrease by about a third between 2025 and 2026.

It’s easy to hate online ads, but the businesses paying for access to reader eyeballs also keep writers and photographers fed. If those eyeballs become unreachable, the system stops working. Time has apparently persuaded some businesses to pay to participate in its experiment with agent-targeted ads, but no one yet knows whether those ads will influence agent behavior enough to be a sensible marketing investment.

E-commerce websites might also try to pivot to the agentic attention economy, but the path forward there is unclear. Last year, a team led by Akshit Kumar, a professor of operations management at the University of Toronto Scarborough, investigated whether and how agents are influenced by the ways that shopping websites present search results. They found that agents are less likely to recommend items that come with a “sponsored” tag, which suggests that selling favorable positions on results pages might not be a great way for sites to make money if agents become the primary way that people shop online. Models did seem to have a preference for items that appeared in particular positions in search results—but whether they prioritized items at the top, bottom, or middle of the results page differed from model to model and between generations of a single model. It could be tricky for e-commerce platforms to keep up.

David Rothschild, an economist at Microsoft Research, says he’s hopeful that the transition to the agentic web could put more power in the hands of the consumer. Paying for online content today typically requires a commitment: We subscribe to a magazine or join a YouTuber’s Patreon, and in turn we gain access to their full output. One alternative is micropayments that let users buy content à la carte, but the idea has foundered in the past because paying article by article or video by video requires too much administrative overhead. Agents, though, could take care of that overhead for us, letting us pay directly for each piece of content we consume and putting just a bit of cash directly in the hands of each person whose work we enjoy.

Other experts share a similar vision. Mustafaraj, the Wellesley computer scientist, anticipates that agents could help us escape from the algorithms that control so much of the media we consume. “My hope is that we can have AIs that work for us, in the sense that they can change the feed the way I want—not the way TikTok wants,” she says. And Varma, of Mozilla, imagines an internet without intermediaries like Airbnb and Doordash, which now extract tolls for facilitating interactions between consumers and sellers. Instead, he imagines, perhaps we will all have agents that can securely and reliably interface directly with, say, restaurants’ agents to get dinner delivered to us, free of pesky service fees.

It’s an appealing idea, but the history of the web has been a story of consolidation and concentration of power and control, and that might be the default path here, too. When the personal assistant agent OpenClaw

When we use those agents, we’re at the mercy of how the companies want their tools to behave. “You have this technology that can just eliminate all this communication friction,” Rothschild, the Microsoft economist, says. “You’re going to see companies build barriers in order to maintain the consumer base that they have.”

Here’s what that could look like: Let’s say Muse becomes the default way that many people find information, shop, and manage their digital lives. In principle, users could deploy Muse to scour the internet for the content most valuable to them, connect directly with vendors, and otherwise escape the walled gardens that have defined the internet for the past couple of decades. But Meta might not want to let them do that. Instead, it might design Muse to keep users within its own walled garden—by, say, preferentially showing users content from Meta social networks and recommending businesses that have paid a fee to be featured prominently in Muse results. Meta and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment for this story.

There are some benefits to this more closed-off version of the agentic web. Agents can be powerful tools for hackers and scammers. The major companies have safeguards in place to prevent, or at least mitigate, this misuse—for example, they have tools that can automatically identify when someone is making a hacking-related request and block a model from responding. In a fully open ecosystem, however, someone would surely build and disseminate a system with no such restrictions. Companies also have a strong reputational incentive to prevent their personal assistant agents from making major mistakes, such as authorizing a large purchase that the user didn’t want—and so they’ve put plenty of effort into building reliable guardrails.
The same can’t be said for OpenClaw.
“These are the reasons we end up in closed environments,” Rothschild says. “It’s easier to be safe. But also it creates less growth—and less equitable growth.”
How will the human web change?

When the iPhone came out in 2007, followed by the fledgling App Store a year later, the way we navigated the internet changed forever. The mobile web didn’t replace the browser-based web we were already familiar with. But it did transform it. Some businesses faltered, and some kinds of media, such as online Flash games, eventually disappeared. Many platforms—Reddit, for example—make their mobile web pages practically unusable, so you’re forced to download the apps. And if you don’t have a phone at all, you’re effectively shut out of some parts of the internet: The messaging service Signal, the dating app Hinge, and China’s everything app WeChat all require phones to work. Even CBP One, the tool that the Biden administration used to assign interview appointments to asylum seekers stuck in Mexico, was fully functional only on mobile.

Could the same happen with the agentic web? Rothschild believes so. Inevitably, just as Yahoo failed to weather the rise of the mobile web, some businesses won’t be able to navigate this transition either. “We will lose things,” he says. “There are businesses that won’t flourish in this new economy.”
“But,” he continues, “there will be new businesses that I can’t fully imagine.”

It’s not tough to envision a world in which those who opt not to use agents are cut off from important parts of online life. New businesses could opt to build connectors that allow agents to access their services without ever putting a traditional website online. Or agents could simply make some online platforms unusable for humans. People have reportedly been blocked from Resy for trying to use agents to book coveted New York City dinner reservations, but as agents become more and more popular, restaurant and event booking platforms could start to embrace them. If agents can nab concert tickets as soon as they are released, humans might not stand a chance.

But the mobile web also brought real accessibility benefits, and the same could prove true of the agentic web. Even as some elderly people and others who struggled to use smartphones were cut off from certain services, mobile devices allowed countless people in the Global South to get online for the first time. In the case of the agentic web, it could be elderly and disabled people who most benefit from this new way of accessing the online world.

“There’s very clear assistive potential for people who are older, who are generally less equipped to navigate user interfaces that were designed by people in their 20s, for people in their 20s,” says Margaret Mitchell, chief ethics scientist at Hugging Face. Agents, on the other hand, are almost trivially easy to interact with: Say what you want into your phone or computer microphone, and they’ll get it done for you. That could help not only older people who have trouble with web and mobile interfaces but also people with visual or motor disabilities.

Still, some experts don’t think the human web is going anywhere. Instead, the two webs may exist in parallel: We’ll go to the human web for fun, while the agentic web is where the boring daily admin of our lives happens. For instance, Krystian Kolondra, an executive vice president at the browser company Opera, doesn’t intend to use agents for every part of travel planning, even though this is often touted as one of their central use cases. “I don’t want to get an itinerary [from an AI] who has planned me every minute for something that was supposed to be fun,” he says. “I actually prefer to sit down with my wife in the evening and then just think [about] where to go next, what to see, and then enjoy that experience.”
He’s happy to fully relinquish some of the more routine parts of travel planning to agents, though: “Finding what the options are for flights? Why not?”

Mollick, however, thinks that the human web could be at risk. “If agents take over the web, then the web will change,” he says. “Do we abandon the human internet entirely and move to a world of private Discords? Do we strip down all the information so the AIs are just talking to each other rather than having an intermediary of a website to go through?”
“We have no idea,” he says. “We’re in this very early, weird stage of the evolution.”

items.title: Haley Stevens’s Sun Hat of Humiliation
items.description: On Tuesday, Democratic representative Haley Stevens was spotted on her way to vote for Republican Mike Rogers, the man she once called “corrupt” and a “Trump crony.” To honor — or hide from? — the occasion, she wore a ginormous floppy hat. Is that a woman who
items.author: Emma Childs
paragraphs: On Tuesday, Democratic representative Haley Stevens was spotted on her way to vote for Republican Mike Rogers, the man she once called “corrupt” and a “Trump crony.” To honor — or hide from? — the occasion, she wore a ginormous floppy hat. Is that a woman who just got kicked out of her own political party, or is it a middle-aged female protagonist in a Nancy Meyers movie getting her spark back?

Even before she put this hat on, Stevens has had an impressively humiliating 72 hours. On Sunday, the politician, who lost the Democratic Senate primary this summer to Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, suddenly crossed party lines and endorsed Rogers, El-Sayed’s opponent. The day after, she was interviewed by Anderson Cooper live on CNN, which swiftly devolved into an SNL sketch of a segment. In a way, it makes sense that this was the headspace Stevens was in when she walked into a polling site in Birmingham, Michigan, arm-in-arm with her mother, wearing an oversize beige sun hat on a not-sunny November Tuesday. (Per the Weather Channel, Birmingham had a cloudy, 68-degree morning.) In one clip, a reporter asked Stevens if endorsing Mike Rogers was “worth it,” to which Stevens breezily responded, “Look, I’m with my mom. This is our tradition here. You know what … it’s the people’s day.” She did not address her voting sun hat.

If it was intended to help her go incognito, Stevens’s headwear had the opposite effect. Her massive hat took the internet by storm on Election Day. “This would’ve been a perfect gay halloween costume and it’s actually cruel of her to pull a stunt like this after the holiday,” writer Hunter Harris joked on X. Others compared Stevens’s failed attempt at incognito mode to Scooby-Doo in drag and Zendaya’s much-mythologized top hat from a 2014 Teen Vogue party. The Cut’s senior editor Amy Rose Spiegel called Stevens “Carmen San Die-go to the polls,” a Slack message I’d like to nominate for an ASME. Personally, I’ll be putting my energy toward casting Merritt Wever as Stevens, in said hat, in a biopic dedicated to her buffoonery.
Oh, Haley. If you really want to throw the public off your scent, consider adding a pair of oversize sunglasses and a fake mustache. You can hat, but you can’t hide.

items.title: Karlie Kloss Canvassed for Abortion Rights Ahead of the Midterms
items.description: Karlie Kloss may have some Trumps in her extended family, but at least she’s getting loud ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Last week, the model, media executive, and wife to Josh Kushner — the brother of Ivanka Trump’s husband, Jared Kushner — traveled to
items.author: Emily Leibert
paragraphs: Karlie Kloss may have some Trumps in her extended family, but at least she’s getting loud ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Last week, the model, media executive, and wife to Josh Kushner — the brother of Ivanka Trump’s husband, Jared Kushner — traveled to her hometown of St. Louis, Missouri to canvas for abortion rights. On Friday, she went to the headquarters for Stop the Ban, a local organization fighting to protect reproductive-health-care rights for Missourians. According to a video she posted to Instagram Monday, Kloss joined their ranks as the volunteers went door-knocking across the city, asking voters to reject Amendment 3, which would repeal 2024 legislation that secured the right to abortion for all.

In the caption, Kloss called canvassing “a powerful reminder of how many neighbors care about protecting the freedoms that Missourians already voted for in 2024, how absurd it is we have to vote to protect those rights again just two years later, and how much is at stake if we lose these rights again.” She added, “Tomorrow is Election Day. Make a plan, bring a friend, and Missourians — vote NO on Amendment 3.”

Per the Missouri secretary of State, Amendment 3 would allow abortions only in the cases of rape or incest, emergencies, and fetal anomalies, and only under 12 weeks, which is within the first trimester. The amendment would also force minors to get parental consent to go through with an abortion and make gender-affirming surgery illegal for minors in the state. If passed, it will become exponentially harder for Missourians to get legal abortions in a country that’s been gutting reproductive rights with glee since Roe v. Wade was overturned in 2022. In the wake of the Dobbs decision, the Trump administration has poured millions of dollars into pro-life crisis pregnancy centers, where patients are flooded with anti-abortion misinformation; Planned Parenthood was defunded by the federal government earlier this year; and scores of pregnant people have died trying to access abortion care.

Kloss has been advocating for reproductive rights for the past few years. In 2024, she canvassed in St. Louis alongside Chelsea Clinton. She’s taken pains to distance herself from the politics of her in-laws — in 2019, she told British Vogue that being related to Jared and Ivanka was “hard” and that she’d instead chosen to focus on the “liberal values that I was raised with.” (She also identifies as a Democrat.) Thankfully, her tolerance for awkward family dinners is high.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 3, 2026
items.description: Early this morning the moon enters Virgo, where it’ll encounter friction from Neptune, Pluto, Uranus, and Saturn over the course of the day. The problems you encounter today aren’t likely to be too dramatic — as long as you don’t let your own sensitivities, in
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: Early this morning the moon enters Virgo, where it’ll encounter friction from Neptune, Pluto, Uranus, and Saturn over the course of the day. The problems you encounter today aren’t likely to be too dramatic — as long as you don’t let your own sensitivities, insecurities, or ego blow them out of proportion. That might be tricky mid-morning, when Uranus amplifies your reckless side and inhibits your impulse control. Do your best to make good decisions, even if you’re feeling restless or irritable. And if you realize you’ve messed up, resist the impulse to double down. You still have time to get back on track.

You might have excess energy you don’t know what to do with today. Maybe you can’t decide what you want, or maybe you know exactly what you want, but you’re struggling to commit to a strategy. Whatever the case, the solution might be to put your own ambitions aside altogether, at least for the time being. Instead, use your power and vitality to help other people. It’ll be surprisingly rewarding, and by the time you return to your own problems, you’ll have a clearer head.

Some people seem to change their minds on a whim, refusing to commit to any one opinion or idea. You find this frustrating, if not totally incomprehensible: You’re inclined to hold your own opinions as sacrosanct. But today, don’t be so attached to your opinions that you become rigid and out of touch. Remember that there’s nothing wrong with updating your thinking when you learn new information. It doesn’t mean you’re fickle or unreliable; it means you’re paying attention and willing to grow.

You’re going to want to break out of your usual routines today. Doing things the same way you always have will suddenly seem impossibly boring — you want to try something new and exciting! But dramatic 180-degree turns aren’t likely to turn out well, so try to find some smaller, more manageable sources of excitement to satisfy the itch today. Don’t abandon everything that’s worked for you before just because you’re in the mood for novelty.

Most of the time, you prefer to think things through privately before you offer up your opinion. You’re not one to talk just to hear the sound of your own voice. You want to use your words wisely — and to only say what you truly believe. But sometimes, the only way to know what you believe is to discuss it with other people. Today, don’t be so scared of saying something “wrong” that you don’t share your thoughts or feelings at all. You don’t always have to present a perfect, polished front: You’re allowed to let others witness you figuring things out.

Your life might be full of surprising coincidences today — and you’ll probably be tempted to read too deeply into them. Maybe you’ll even convince yourself they’re important signs from the universe, instructions that you need to change something right now. But this isn’t the best time for making rash decisions, no matter what you think your intuition is telling you. Wait until you’ve had the time to process your feelings and observations. Then, later this week, you can choose whether to take action.

Today, you have a challenge before you: Be patient with the people around you. They might seem especially prone to erratic behavior, unhelpful decision-making, or bad advice at the moment. You might even wonder if they’re intentionally trying to bug you, but that probably isn’t the case. Trust that this is simply a phase, and your loved ones will stop trying your patience soon enough. In the meantime, give yourself permission to step away if their behavior is bothering you too much.

Usually, you try to listen to all viewpoints, including ones you disagree with. You know there’s always something more for you to learn, even if it doesn’t ultimately change your mind. Today, though, you might get tired of having to hear everyone out — especially if they never seem to show you the same respect. Remember that you don’t need to take everybody’s opinions into consideration before you make up your own mind. Sometimes, simply trusting yourself is enough.

You might feel the urge to act on impulse today — and nobody, not even the people you trust most, will be able to dissuade you. But if you must be spontaneous, try to avoid making any decisions you won’t be able to change later. There’s a good chance that by tomorrow (if not sooner!), you’ll end up wishing you could take back whatever you did or said in the heat of the moment. Leave yourself space to adapt, just in case. You’ll be glad you did.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You’re someone who believes in second chances. You think people should always have the opportunity to prove that they’ve changed. But remember: You don’t always need to be the person to offer them a fresh start — particularly if they have repeatedly hurt you. Today, don’t let yourself be pressured into forgiving people if you aren’t yet ready. Maybe the time will come soon, but if today’s not that day, give yourself some grace.

Today, you might get the upsetting feeling that you can’t count on anyone but yourself. Maybe your friends seem flaky and unreliable at the moment, or maybe you worry they don’t understand you the way you need to be understood. But try not to take these pessimistic thoughts too seriously right now. While it’s possible that you do need to reevaluate your relationships, it’s much likelier that you’re just feeling especially sensitive right now. Your feelings are valid, but don’t use them as an excuse to give up on other people.

You’re happiest when your daily life is orderly and manageable; the less you have to worry about the practical stuff, the more space your imagination has to roam. Today, though, your routines could be thrown into disarray for reasons outside of your control. Try not to waste any energy blaming yourself or resenting the people around you. Instead, focus on dealing with whatever surprises come your way. The quicker you do, the sooner you can return to your normal routine.

You might find yourself especially interested in meeting new people today. You want to broaden your horizons and expand your social circle; you want to spend time with people whose stories you haven’t already heard a hundred times. There’s nothing wrong with this desire, but do your best not to make your closest friends feel neglected. Make an effort to show them that they still matter to you — and that your instinct to explore doesn’t mean you’ve left them behind.

items.title: Glow Recipe's Blur Balm, Tate McRae's First Perfume, & 21 More October Beauty Drops
items.description: October might just be the perfect month. It’s not too hot, not too cold (all you need is a light jacket), the foliage is pretty enough to make an eyeshadow palette jealous, and you can finally wear your emotional support blazer again. And making this already p
items.author: Rachel Lapidos
paragraphs: October might just be the perfect month. It’s not too hot, not too cold (all you need is a light jacket), the foliage is pretty enough to make an eyeshadow palette jealous, and you can finally wear your emotional support blazer again. And making this already picturesque month even better? The best beauty launches hitting shelves are just as good as the scenery.

Haus Labs, for one, introduced a liquid bronzer that delivers a summer glow in a tube. Celebrity dermatologist Dr. Sheila Farhang, M.D., also ventured into cosmetics with a line designed to deliver color and coverage to post-treatment skin. And for smoky-eye season, Anastasia Beverly Hills dropped a neutral eyeshadow palette that serves as an all-in-one toolkit.

As you transition your perfume wardrobe for fall, you'll appreciate this month's new releases — like Merit’s New Wave L’Extrait de Parfum, a spicy aroma that takes the floral fragrance category into a decidedly moodier realm. Korean brand Elorea, meanwhile, debuted a honeyed fragrance that's equal parts warm and sweet. And Joonbyrd entered the category with its own take on functional fragrance.
Keep scrolling to shop October 2026’s best beauty launches, as curated by Bustle’s beauty team.

“I recently learned that wearing perfume to the office is a faux pas, and ever since, I’ve been on the hunt for one I can get away with. Elorea’s Quiet Trace is my pick. As the name implies, it stays close to the skin rather than announcing itself to the entire room. The combination of honey and floral notes reminds me of Phlur’s Honey Moon — but if you found that one a little too sweet, this might be more your speed. At first spritz, you get the soapiness of gardenia before it settles into something warmer and muskier. I’m happily wearing it on weekends, too.” – Emma Stout, beauty writer

“I’m convinced that I look better with a tan, but until I can go on a beach vacation, this Haus Labs liquid bronzer will do the trick. It’s sheer enough that I don’t have to worry about going overboard, but still delivers enough pigment to add some much-needed color back to my complexion. Even better, it leaves behind a hydrated finish — courtesy of its 70% skin care ingredients — that makes everything look much more believable. Call me a catfish, but I’ll be faking my summer glow until further notice.” – ES

“Dewsy has always been about high-quality body care, and its latest retinol-infused cream is giving my skin a serious upgrade. The formula is powered by 0.1% retinol, copper peptides, and ceramides — a combination that hydrates, smooths, and brightens. I’ve been using it after showering for the past few weeks, and my skin looks noticeably brighter, feels more hydrated, and is smoother to the touch. Even my husband has commented on the difference. And that’s when you know it’s good — that man notices nothing.” — Shyema Azam, beauty director, branded content

“With all the red light therapy masks hitting the market, it takes a lot to make one stand out — but JOVS’ latest makes a compelling case for the splurge. Unlike traditional LED masks, it combines laser light therapy with a 10-electrode EMS system designed to stimulate facial muscles, essentially bringing two treatments together in one. Its multi-wavelength light technology and customizable settings let you tailor each session, whether you’re looking to boost radiance, support collagen, or target the appearance of sagging and loss of definition. I love how comfortably snug the mask feels, and the attached remote makes it easy to switch between treatment modes and seven EMS intensity levels. After my first week of use, my skin looked and felt more refreshed, and after a month, I noticed it looked slightly firmer, too. It's definitely a luxury purchase, but for anyone looking to level up their at-home skin care routine, this offers more than your average light therapy mask.” — SA

“I will tell people until I’m blue in the face that they need to try Makeup By Mario’s lip pencils, so naturally, I couldn’t get my hands on the new Lip Trip Gift Set fast enough. Featuring minis of three bestselling shades — Toasty, Smokey Pink, and Travis — the full-coverage matte pencils create the perfect lip base, while the brand’s lip-lock technology helps keep your look in place through every holiday party, cocktail hour, and festive gathering to come.” — SA

“I may have found my dream fall eyeshadow palette, and I haven’t been able to put it down since it landed on my vanity. With 12 shades spanning taupe, brown, and mauve, plus a mix of velvety mattes and light-catching shimmers, there's something for every mood. “Praise be: Facialist Sofie Pavitt has brought her signature hot-cold therapy treatment from her facial studio to your vanity with the Temp Check mask duo. A pro-level glow in just 20 minutes.” — RL

“A supermodel founder’s best-kept beauty secret? This sheet mask. Unwrap the pink packaging to reveal a completely clear jelly mask, then wear it for 15 minutes for skin that looks like you’ve gotten a full eight hours of sleep. Powered by vegan PDRN — aka the California roll version of the salmon sperm facial — plus glycerin, hyaluronic acid, and niacinamide, this pretty little mask leaves skin looking plumper, smoother, and dewier before happy hour.” — SN

items.title: Exclusive: 'RHOSLC' Star Bronwyn Newport Dishes On The Upcoming 'Traitors' Season
items.description: Bronwyn Newport knows how to make an entrance. The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City star has made a name for herself by wearing outfits that test the limits of what might be considered appropriate, normal, or even wearable. (Rainbow feathered Dolce & Gabbana
items.author: Rachel Lapidos
paragraphs: Bronwyn Newport knows how to make an entrance. The Real Housewives of Salt Lake City star has made a name for herself by wearing outfits that test the limits of what might be considered appropriate, normal, or even wearable. (Rainbow feathered Dolce & Gabbana coat, anyone?) Her beauty philosophy, however, is a different story. “Beauty-wise, it’s always very, very tried-and-true for me,” she tells Bustle.

Rather than chasing an entirely new look, Newport, 41, focuses on skin health and preserving what makes her feel like herself. “For me, such a big part of beauty is who you naturally are,” she says. “I’ve obviously had a rhinoplasty. But I always want a big, beautiful smile — that’s always the finishing look, where you are yourself.”

It’s why her partnership with Colgate Optic White is such a natural fit. It's part of her everyday getting-ready routine, and she recently appeared at the brand’s activation at Bravo Fan Fest in Charleston, South Carolina. “I always have this big goofy grin everywhere I go,” she says. “I never look like I’ve been there before or I’m used to it or I’m cool. I always look like [I’m] giddy to be invited to the opening of an envelope.” For Newport, it’s about making sure “the health behind my skin and my teeth and my hair is done properly.”

Still, being a Housewife has made her more aware of how her appearance is perceived. Her imperfect teeth became a talking point among viewers early on, for example — but she’s learned to separate other people’s opinions from her own. “It’s hard to put yourself out there in every way on the show, especially your physical self, to be consumed and digested and discussed,” she says. “But I also really live for a woman in the year of our Lord 2026 being like, ‘No, this is what I want to look like, and this is how I want to feel.’”
Ahead, Newport opens up about filming The Traitors, the fan reactions she’s still processing, and why she’s approaching her next chapter with an open mind.
What is your favorite beauty treatment, and what’s the last one you treated yourself to?

It’s always about really great skin prep. I’m a big believer in retinol and lasers. I get a lot of glam done and my hair done, and when I don’t, I really don’t. I’m a ChapStick-and-mascara person. I said this in my first confessional ever that “sexy” is not really my aesthetic.
Your fashion is super adventurous and maximalist. Do you take the same approach to beauty, or do you keep certain parts more classic?

My approach has always been that the clothes are the star of the show. I’m not even the star of the show — it’s the outfits I put together. Beauty-wise, I stick with products that I know and have loved and used forever. It’s about the simplicity of knowing that all of that is taken care of and elevated and fabulous.
There were a lot of comments online about how you reacted in the episode where you took your castmates to San Francisco. How are you handling them?

It’s a lot. It’s so nice when something I do or say resonates with people. I was sharing quite a bit about what it feels like to be in a new chapter. San Francisco was home for me for so long, and so many people were appreciative of what I shared about publicly going through a separation and pending divorce.

One of the beautiful things about sharing my life on the show is getting to physically watch yourself and ask, “Wow, was that a choice that I liked? Was this a way that I responded?” I’ve realized I tend to act a certain way, and I don’t know if I love that.

There was some feedback this week about the way I handled certain things that made me think, “Yeah, that’s fair. I could have handled that better.” I don’t know that I’ll ever get another opportunity to respond to a diss at a party celebrating my separation, but if I do, I’m now armed with all the right ways to do it.
Has the “Hypocrisy & Bulls*it” song grown on you at all?
No. Shockingly enough, it has not. I have a feeling I will never hear the end of it, but it’ll just be one of those earworms that I have to deal with.
What can you say about the Traitors experience, and who were you most surprised to see in the castle?

I was surprised to see everyone because they do such a good job of keeping it quiet. I know that everyone was surprised to see me because I didn’t tell a soul. I was trying to buy things undercover, shopping at all kinds of different places and buying vintage so nobody would think, “Why is Bronwyn buying all this plaid?”

It was so fun. That’s maybe one of the last special things in the world: truly getting to surprise somebody. It’s a beautiful production to work on, and they’ve put together a cool group of people and a fabulous game.

I don’t always smile so much on Housewives. The dinner-party games usually aren’t smile-inducing. But on Traitors, I was grinning the whole time, running through the Scottish Highlands, being like, “I’m at work right now!” as we’re doing a challenge, or I’m wearing some crazy vintage outfit and arguing with somebody about whether I’m a Traitor.
Would you say that being a Housewife has made you better at reading people, or does it make you more suspicious of people?
A little bit of both. I like to think that I can see a train wreck coming now that I’ve been through so many Housewife dinners. I tend to feel the storm building as the entrées are ordered.

But it also makes me a little suspicious. I wanted to be so good at the game aspect of Traitors, but there’s no real way to plan for it. You never know what your role will be, how it will evolve, or who else will be there. The best strategy is to have no strategy. You’ll get to see how that plays out for me — pun intended — as I make a new strategy every day.
What is something you’re excited to explore or embrace in this next chapter of your life that you might not have been ready for a year ago?

Oh my gosh, everything. This was a lot more change and upheaval than I thought it would be. I always like to say that I’m dumb, not stupid, but sometimes I’m like, “Wow, this was very different from what I thought it was going to be.” I thought I really understood what a separation and divorce was going to look like, and I did not.

It’s interesting to sit with the idea that there’s a lot of grief and sadness and closure, which always tend to have a negative connotation, but that it can also bring so much optimism and hope. The dual-edged nature of that is that everything is possible again, and that’s a really beautiful thing to be able to say. I don’t know if I’ll enjoy or stick with everything I try in this new era of my life, but it’s fun to try things out.
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
