items.title: How psychology’s classic studies misled us about the self | Psyche Ideas
items.description: Imagine a creature that is like humans in every way, except that it has no enduring inner self. The behaviour of this hypothetical species – which we will call Homo vacuus – would be driven not by their private beliefs and inclinations, but rather by knee-jerk
items.author: Jack W Klein; William B Swann
paragraphs: Imagine a creature that is like humans in every way, except that it has no enduring inner self. The behaviour of this hypothetical species – which we will call Homo vacuus – would be driven not by their private beliefs and inclinations, but rather by knee-jerk responses to their immediate environment. Lacking an enduring web of preferences, attitudes and proclivities, the contents of the H vacuus character would be filled by whatever situation they find themselves in. As a result, their behaviour would vary dramatically as they moved from one situation to the next.

Scrutiny of H vacuus would reveal a host of curious behaviours. Their attitudes towards others would be shaped by random factors that unconsciously influence their thoughts. They might feel ‘warmer’ toward others when they handle a hot cappuccino, and ‘colder’ when clasping an iced latte. Their political decisions would hinge on seemingly innocuous details. For instance, turnout in their elections would surge if they were affirmed as being ‘voters’, rather than merely people who vote. And on morality, their views on topics from abortion to pornography could depend on something as mundane as whether they had washed their hands, making them feel ‘cleansed’ and in the mood for judging others.

Given the inherent fluidity of H vacuus, trying to predict their behaviour beyond the present moment would be pure folly. H vacuus would be so mercurial that when they wed, they would effectively be marrying a stranger. In the end, being the pawns of powerful environmental forces would compromise their ability to effectively plan and adapt. Others would recognise the impossibility of holding them responsible for their actions, as they could refuse to accept responsibility for their behaviour by claiming: ‘I was just responding to the situation!’ At the end of the day, religious, ethical and judicial systems would be largely irrelevant.

In light of the many challenges facing H vacuus, it may be surprising to learn that this fictitious creature is based on an implicit assumption about human nature suggested by the work of numerous influential behavioural scientists. This assumption is that if you were to peer into the contents of people’s selves, you would discover little that isn’t susceptible to the random influences of the situation. Indeed, the peculiarities of H vacuus life described above – including the ideas about ‘warm’ attitudes, election turnout and moral cleansing – are based on claims that have been made about real humans.

We label this view of human psychology the empty-self metaphor. Although it has fostered an erroneous understanding of human nature, the empty-self metaphor has inspired a large following. These followers embrace an optimistic view in which human foibles can be readily vanquished through systematic manipulation of the social environment. However alluring it may be, we suggest that it is time to replace this Panglossian view with one that acknowledges the importance of enduring psychological structures.

The empty-self view has a long history in psychology, arguably tracing its origins to the behaviourist movement at the beginning of the 20th century. The behaviourists were almost entirely focused on ‘the situation’, eschewing speculation about what they considered the ‘black box’ of the mind. This emphasis on the situation was influential with founding social psychologists, who defined social psychology as the study of how individual thoughts, feelings and behaviours ‘are influenced by the actual, imagined, or implied presence of other human beings’.

An emphasis on the power of the situation, and its propensity to overwhelm or displace personal agency, has dominated social psychology ever since. Examples abound. In the 1970s, the author of self-perception theory argued that, rather than beliefs guiding behaviour (as common sense might imply), situations cause behaviour, and people generally infer their own beliefs by taking note of how they behave. Others made the corollary argument that personalities effectively do not exist. In fact, the term ‘fundamental attribution error’ was coined to describe an allegedly flawed tendency to attribute someone’s behaviour to their personality. Elsewhere, including in sociology, impression management research and the dramaturgical movement suggested that all the world’s a stage, with people portraying whatever character best suits a given scene. This focus on the situation reached a fever pitch with the ‘situationists’, who explicitly placed the influence of the situation on human behaviour far above any possible internal motivations.

Although situationism has lost some of its lustre, the empty-self metaphor has remained at least implicitly popular within certain circles. This is particularly true in the field of social priming, which deals with the impact of seemingly inconsequential environmental cues on human behaviour. In examples of this kind of research, seeing words related to old age seemed to make university students walk more slowly, and plotting dots on paper further apart appeared to make people feel more distant from their family.
Classic evidence for the primacy of the situation has lost force

In recent years, however, the evidential tide has turned against the empty self. Social priming and other areas of social psychology have struggled in the wake of the ‘replication crisis’ – the unfortunate realisation that a surprising number of psychological findings could not be independently replicated. Many such findings are likely to have been false positives, stemming from tendentious statistical decision-making and other questionable research practices. The authors of one report found that when a number of social priming studies were carried out again, only 17 per cent of the findings were successfully replicated. A much smaller proportion of empty-self-style research has been dismissed as simply fraudulent – such as the celebrated finding that people are more honest when filling out forms if they sign at the beginning, rather than at the end.

In our own research, we’ve compared studies that were or were not premised on the empty-self assumption that behaviour is unexpectedly shaped by subtle, seemingly irrelevant environmental factors, as opposed to pre-existing beliefs and dispositions. We found that studies reflecting an empty-self view were far less likely to hold up.

Classic evidence for the primacy of the situation has also lost force. Take, for instance, Stanley Milgram’s obedience studies, in which participants were asked to administer electric shocks to someone until the victim seemed to be unconscious or dead. These classic studies have been taken as evidence that authority can override individual will. However, subsequent research has found that personal traits associated with diligence and helpfulness predicted an increased willingness to administer the electric shocks. This reframes the experiment as demonstrating not mindless obedience, but often wilful collaboration – participants who gave the shocks were ostensibly helping an experimenter in the service of ‘science’.

Consider also the Stanford prison experiment, led by Philip Zimbardo, where students acting as guards in a fake prison (with others acting as prisoners) appeared to succumb to their temporary role, becoming belligerent. Attributing this behaviour to the roles the students were assigned is jeopardised by several design flaws, including a selection bias that likely caused dispositionally authoritarian individuals to be overrepresented in the study. The upshot is that participants’ unique, personal identities seem to have mattered far more than the authors of these classic examples of situational influence would have us believe.

The idea that the human mind is so fickle should have attracted more scepticism than it has often received. First and foremost, it is at odds with other evidence. The entire field of personality psychology – which investigates the unique qualities of people that persist across situations – informs us that the self is not empty at all. Measures of personality such as the Big Five traits (openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism) are remarkably stable and predictive of behaviour and long-term life outcomes. In fact, research suggests that the average effects of personality and situations on behaviour are similar in magnitude. Elsewhere, there is ample evidence for an enduring self: for example, self-esteem is largely steady over the lifespan, and attempts to break habits frequently fail, highlighting that personal tendencies impede many people’s efforts at self-change.

It is not difficult, though, to understand the appeal of the empty-self metaphor. The idea that our thoughts and behaviours are dictated by banal aspects of daily life, such as the temperature of our coffee, offers a tantalising glimpse at ‘hidden’ causes of behaviour. This is probably why social priming occupied a full chapter of Daniel Kahneman’s bestselling book Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011), why mentalists like Derren Brown attract large TV audiences by showing how the ‘power of psychology’ can be used to control and befuddle, and why exciting ‘counterintuitive’ findings are published in top journals.

The empty-self metaphor also lends itself to an admittedly admirable progressive agenda (popular among social psychologists) that is focused on addressing inequality in the social environment and avoiding victim-blaming. If the plight of the have-nots is primarily attributable to the harsh social conditions that society unwittingly thrusts upon them, then the obvious solution is to change those social conditions. Ultimately, the empty-self metaphor teases the provocative possibility that society could be righted if only we determine how to control the social environment. But reality is much messier.
There is considerable evidence for human consistency, agency and a remarkable propensity to shape our situations just as they shape us

The good news is that psychology appears to be slowly moving toward increased acceptance of what’s called ‘interactionism’: the view that the person and the situation interactively dictate behaviour. Many people have heard of nudging, in which subtle changes to the presentation of choices can systematically influence behaviour (eg, placing fruits and vegetables more conspicuously, to increase healthy consumption). The idea of nudging has proven enormously popular, with multiple governments around the world setting up ‘nudge units’, but initial results were lacklustre. Happily, research has moved to second-generation, interactionist nudges that tailor the intervention to the beliefs and preferences of the individual. For example, recent research suggests that personalised nudges to make healthier food purchases might be more effective than generic ones.

Interactionism likewise paves a more realistic path forward for social change. Rather than assuming that one size fits all, an interactionist approach acknowledges that individual differences inform the way people respond to social situations. Any social movement to reduce harmful behaviour or improve wellbeing needs to meet people where they are at. That means acknowledging that different individuals will respond to the same policies and political messages differently, and in accordance with their own perspectives.

Rebuking the empty-self view recognises that, far from being the dithering shells that psychology studies have often suggested we are, most of us are loyal to a reasonably clear and coherent self-concept. We do not ‘marry strangers’, nor do our relationships hinge on irrelevant details of the moment. On the contrary, there is considerable evidence for human consistency, agency and a remarkable propensity to shape our situations just as they shape us. Although imputing this degree of agency and stability to the self may lack the intoxicating simplicity of Homo vacuus, we are confident that it will pave the way to a deeper understanding of Homo sapiens.

items.title: 20 Questions with Kali Malone
items.description: The composer and musician on the transcendent properties of music-making and how revenge is a dish best served with two scoops of gelato
items.author: Sam Elliott Connor
paragraphs: The composer and musician on the transcendent properties of music-making and how revenge is a dish best served with two scoops of gelato

It feels impossible to write about the work of Kali Malone without reaching for the grandest of terms and ideas. Her output is of huge scale and ambition, and it is thrillingly unfussed about adhering to the conventional bounds of most music.

Over the past few years the Stockholm-based Coloradan has built a reputation as one of the most exciting experimental musicians in the world. Her discography incorporates dark ambient, drone and choral forms, each recording pushing listeners into a musical terra incognita where recognisable sound signatures are purposely de-emphasised. In their place are impressionistic tones, textures and harmonies. Put simply, if you ever want to listen to something that makes you feel like you’re hovering an inch above the ground whilst moving at a thousand miles an hour, Kali’s got you covered.

Malone’s brilliantly transportive new album, Burning Song, was recorded in St Thomas’s Church, Leipzig, using the Bach Organ – an instrument completed in 2000 and titled in honour of its namesake, who served as a musical director of the space in the first half of the 1700s. On the recording, Malone is joined by British cellist Lucy Railton and Sunn 0))) guitarist Stephen O’Malley – likeminded souls who inherently understand the restraint and nuanced instrumental articulation her pieces require. Shortly before the release of the new LP, Malone took some time out to answer 20 questions for AnOther.
1. What is your earliest memory?
Picking all of the neighbour’s tulips to give my mom, then returning them in tears.
4. What is the best part of the songwriting experience?
Right before a song emerges, when it’s pure boundless, burning potential.
“I swear he [Bach] whispered in my ear and fixed the music” – Kali Malone
5. Speaking of which, your new album is entitled Burning Song. What is the most important thing for people to know about it?
I somehow got the keys to the most sanctified classical music institution and made an album of precious songs with my beloved collaborators on top of Bach’s grave in the dead of night.
6. Can you tell us about the relevance of the album’s title?
7. How would you classify the music on the album? Do you consider it music in the classical tradition, or is it purely experimental?

I am not a classically trained organist coming from the Bach tradition. As an outsider in that very conservative world, I often claim the experimental musician card. It gives me the liberty to obscure the codes and find my own path.
8. You recorded Burning Song on the Bach Organ. What can you tell us about the history of the instrument?

It’s a historical replica of an organ built by JS Bach’s uncle, an instrument he was heavily influenced by as a child and referenced throughout his life. The replica is built by one of my favourite living organ builders Gerald Woehl. He also built an organ in northern Sweden that I recorded on my album The Sacrificial Code. I’ll take any chance to play his instruments.
9. The organ uses a “bespoke tuning and temperament system”. Can you explain what that means?

Temperament is how you divide the octave to create the intervals between the notes, establishing precise frequency relationships that characterise the personality of the harmony. We take it for granted now, but before equal temperament became widely standardised in the 19th and 20th centuries, there were many types of temperaments that had drastically different emotional effects. This is all important to me because I see tuning as a fundamental extension of artistic expression.
10. Aside from his professional connection, JS Bach is buried in St Thomas’s. Did it weird you out having that kind of musical history attached to the space?

Playing there alone at night was actually quite comforting. I swear he whispered in my ear and fixed the music a few times. But these historical churches carry complicated and traumatic histories beyond the music. There’s beauty and violence held in the same space, and it can be intense to reckon with that. I have my own techniques for navigating it. Once I commit to the music, I can create a kind of psychic forcefield and transform that pain into something that breathes with relief. As a kid, I was always afraid of going down into basements until I figured out that nothing could get me as long as I was singing.
11. What’s your best on-stage experience?

One preserved memory was performing my album All Life Long at Lincoln Center in New York. I was conducting a crescendo of brass musicians extending the final ecstatic chord of my organ piece No Sun To Burn. I turned around from the console to face the musicians who were positioned in the darkness and slowly raised my arms out wide over the course of five minutes. As the brass grew louder and louder it felt like we were edging towards sublime collapse. I sensed my family in the audience, my eyes and cheeks were wet.
12. What’s your weirdest on-stage experience?

I was playing an electronic show in an active crematorium in the most haunted cemetery in Chicago. I didn’t know what I was getting myself into until I showed up for soundcheck and was taken to my green room, which was a mausoleum in the basement next to the cremator. My modular synth was broken and I was preoccupied with a screwdriver, so I didn’t really clock where I was until a hearse rolled up. We brought my gear to the altar using the coffin elevator and raised my table to standing height with fire-resistant bricks, generously supplied by the crematorium workers. I was playing in the middle of a thunderstorm in front of a giant American flag and the chapel was strobing with lightning. The acoustics were so bizarre and hallucinatory, I was completely possessed while playing. Afterwards, I found a soaking wet security guard searching the mausoleum with a flashlight. He thought someone was in there, and explained he was clairsentient, coming from a long lineage of clairvoyant family members. He was all shaken up and I gave him some chocolate.
13. What’s the best piece of advice you have ever been given?
[Portishead singer and lyricist] Beth Gibbons told me “better done than perfect”. It stung the first time and still makes me shudder.
14. What is your worst nightmare?
Not being able to save the people I love.
15. What are you most proud of?
Moving to the other side of the world [to Stockholm], alone as a teenager.
“Music has always been my inner companion. It’s not a career choice, but a necessity” – Kali Malone
16. Most treasured possession?
17. What is your greatest hidden skill?
My sense of direction, although I’m sure some friends would beg to differ.
18. What’s the most satisfying act of vengeance you’ve ever enacted?
Smashing a double scoop of gelato into a misogynist’s face.
19. If you weren't a musician what would you be?

Music has always been my inner companion. It’s not a career choice, but a necessity. Ten years ago I slipped while climbing up some rocks in Stockholm and broke my jaw in a few places, including the small bone that connects to the ear. My hearing temporarily disappeared upon impact, and in the shock of the moment, I feared I’d never be able to make music again. I saw this alternate reality of having to move back to the Rocky Mountains, live in my dad’s basement, be a caretaker by day and drive a snowcat by night.
20. Are there any mantras you live by?
Burning Song by Kali Malone is released 30 October by Ideologic Organ

items.title: Marie Kreutzer and Léa Seydoux on Looking Beyond the Villain Stereotype
items.description: “It’s a film that asks questions, nothing more,” says director Marie Kreutzer of her new feature film, Gentle Monster, a disorienting provocateur about truth, denial and never really knowing someone, starring Léa Seydoux
items.author: Rose Dodd
paragraphs: “It’s a film that asks questions, nothing more,” says director Marie Kreutzer of her new feature film, Gentle Monster, a disorienting provocateur about truth, denial and never really knowing someone, starring Léa Seydoux

“Look into my eyes, can’t you see they’re open wide?” sings a dirty-blonde-bobbed Léa Seydoux from behind a piano in the opening scene of Austrian director Marie Kreutzer’s new feature, Gentle Monster. “Would I lie to you, baby, would I lie to you?” Seydoux plays the French pop-classical musician Lucy Weiss, whose enchanting mezzo-soprano voice is soon interrupted when her partner, Austrian filmmaker Philip (Laurence Rupp), arrives home to their Munich apartment, crumbling to the floor in a panic.

Kreutzer’s film opens as the couple relocate with their young son to Bavaria, seeking a slower life after Philip suffers from burnout. All seems well as the family settle into their spacious farmhouse reno in the verdant German countryside, which becomes the backdrop to an unfolding horror when police detective Elsa (Jella Haase) and a squad of uniformed officers arrive at the door with a search and seizure warrant. After Elsa informs Lucy, who speaks limited German, that Philip has been implicated in a heinous and unthinkable crime, Lucy must grapple with denial, the agony of doubt and the haunting possibility that she may never really have known this man, the father of her child, as she thought.

“Lucy is a really grounded and relatable character,” says Seydoux, talking to AnOther with Kreutzer ahead of the film’s screening at London Film Festival. “They are a very ordinary couple. They’re in love. They still have sex. Everything seems to be perfect on the page, right?” Ordinary and relatable, and in many ways aspirational, was how Kreutzer intended them to be. “Lucy and Philip were written as a combination of real people,” says the director. “I wanted them to be creatives because I relate to that way of living, with that passion for your job but at the same time the insecurity in it. I wanted them to feel like they could be friends of mine.”

Gentle Monster, which premiered at Cannes Film Festival, asks what we are willing to believe about the people we love, spotlighting the disconcerting capacity a person has to be good and bad – gentle and monstrous – at once. “That’s what the film is about for me, that people are not only one thing,” says Kreutzer. “A good person can be a bad person, too. And the worst people can be people we trust, or at least, think we can trust. We view a perpetrator as someone distant from us, never close to us, and we can be quick to judge, to only see darkness, to only see the bad. But when that perpetrator is close to us, if it’s someone we know, it’s much more complicated. That person is certainly a bad person, but he, Philip, has sides that Lucy can love, sides she thought she knew.”

Kreutzer, whose 2022 historical drama Corsage, about the Empress Elisabeth of Austria, received critical acclaim, here holds up a magnifying glass to the simple distinctions we give to both perpetrators and victims. “In fiction, it’s easier to see the bad guy and the good guy definitively, without ambiguity,” Kreutzer says. “In real life, it’s not black and white like that.” She critiques the stereotypes we use to imagine what a villain might look like as a means of distancing them from ourselves. “Often the perpetrators are people we know,” says Seydoux. “Those with the greatest capacity to harm us can be those closest to us.”

The film confronts the unequivocally condemnable while inviting viewers to consider the complexities that orbit it. The idea for the story came to Kreutzer in 2020, when she read about a police investigation into child sex abuse in a German newspaper. The subject later became more personal when an actor she had worked with was charged with possession of child pornography, only fuelling the urgency of the story. Her experience offered her unique insight for the character she was writing. “At first I felt like I couldn’t go on making Gentle Monster because it would always be associated with this case,” Kreutzer said previously. “But it didn’t take long before I realised that this was precisely why I had to – and wanted to – make this film.”

At no point in the film does Kreutzer reproduce images of abuse. Likewise, Lucy never witnesses the very thing her partner has been accused of. Instead, it exists for her and the audience to imagine, adding to the terror while inflating space for doubt. “Without the imagery, just your imagination, it’s very powerful,” says Seydoux, whose agents were apprehensive as to whether she should take the role, considering the film’s sensitive nature. “I was scared to read it at first. My agents said, ‘It’s a beautiful script but you have kids,’ and I thought maybe not, but I was moved to tears when I read it and I fell in love with Lucy. There was no question about it, I had to do it.”

The story is observed through Lucy’s perspective, through her shock and isolation, her denial. “I like that it’s told this way, not via the perpetrator, or the victim; it’s very much [about] how Lucy reacts, and how she deals with all these contradictory emotions,” says Seydoux. The severity of her secret prevents her from feeling like she can talk to friends and family. Lucy lives in a country that isn’t her own and must deal with the authorities in broken German. “She’s a foreigner, she’s away from her home country and she has to deal with this terrible thing in secret,” says Seydoux. “Linguistically, she can’t express her pain, which is very isolating.”

Philip’s own denial soon morphs into excuses and lies – “This isn’t what it seems, Lucy,” he says – which Lucy wants desperately to believe. “I love you so much it hurts,” she says, paralysed in a fraught no-man’s-land between what she hopes to be true and what the evidence suggests to be true. Her mother (Catherine Denueve), who at first she cannot tell, insists she severs ties. But Lucy finds she cannot simply turn her feelings off at will, even when the relationship becomes impossible to sustain.

“I’ve had traumas in my life,” says Seydoux, “but never something as terrible as this. I don’t know how I would have reacted, honestly, but I had an immense empathy for the character, and I think a lot of that was due to how Marie wrote her.” Seydoux’s performance is extraordinary, and her preparation for the part was practical – she took piano and singing lessons, and learned German phonetically. “Léa has this unpredictability with timing; there’s something very mysterious about her,” says Kreutzer. “I always say that casting is very intuitive and emotional, and that’s what I felt with Léa – she’s unique.”

Kreutzer hopes her audience won’t have gone through what Lucy experiences in the film, but recognises that on some level everyone will have been disappointed by someone, lied to, manipulated, dishonest with oneself, or wrong about who a person really was. “I want people to engage and to feel something, to question their own stereotypes, to go with their gut a little more. [...] We’ve all heard – or maybe even spoken – the sentence ‘he could never do that’,” says Kreutzer. “We have so many things programmed in our head by society, by our own worst fears, that can we end up missing things.”
Gentle Monster releases in select UK cinemas on 30 October and streams on Netflix UK from 18 November

items.title: Has Kim Jones designed the ultimate hotel merch?
items.description: ‘One of the first things I do is go to the hotel shop, and buy everything,’ says the British fashion designer Kim Jones, who – having held roles at Louis Vuitton, Fendi and Dior Men – is well-versed in the business of travel. And, indeed, in the collection of
items.author: Jack Moss
paragraphs: ‘One of the first things I do is go to the hotel shop, and buy everything,’ says the British fashion designer Kim Jones, who – having held roles at Louis Vuitton, Fendi and Dior Men – is well-versed in the business of travel. And, indeed, in the collection of rare and obscure objects: his west London address houses first-edition books and century-spanning artworks; when we meet, in Tokyo, he has spent the day trawling the city’s second-hand shops for research garments to take back to his London studio (he has just announced the launch of an eponymous label, Kim Jones, which will begin with an A/W 2027 collection next year).

We are in the 33rd-floor lobby of Aman Tokyo, the hotel group’s vertiginous outpost in the city, which occupies the upper six floors of the Otemachi Tower in the Chiyoda business neighbourhood (the impressive view stretches across Tokyo, from the imperial gardens at the hotel’s base to the Tokyo Tower in the south, and even – on a clear day – the snow-capped peak of Mount Fuji on the horizon). Jones is what is colloquially known as an ‘Aman junkie’, the name given to those who have visited more than five of Aman’s 36 properties, though he has far overshot this milestone; by his estimate, he has visited ‘about 30’, and is in the top-two worldwide customers.
The story behind Kim Jones’ collaboration with Aman Essentials

‘Every detail is considered and already done before you get there,’ he says of Aman, which was founded by hotelier Adrian Zecha in 1988 as a riposte to the gaudy excesses of other luxury resorts of the era. In the decades since – now led by owner and CEO Vladislav Doronin – Aman, which began with the Ed Tuttle-designed Amanpuri in Phuket, Thailand, has honed a vision of serene minimalism (linear planes of limestone and marble; floor-to-ceiling glass; meditative gardens and pools) and arresting locations (several are in, or in close proximity to, Unesco heritage sites; the Tokyo outpost is a rare city-centre Aman). The name ‘Aman’ itself is derived from the Sanskrit word for ‘peace’.

‘Every Aman that I stay at, I know the people that work there – some of them for ten, 15 years,’ Jones continues. ‘So it’s just like coming home. I have the same room, I have the same set-up, and I can relax. And they are all so beautiful in different ways – here, [in Tokyo], you are looking out to concrete and glass; in Aman-i-Khás a tiger can walk past your tent.’ (The latter is located in Ranthambore National Park in Rajasthan, India and comprises a series of Mughal-inspired canvas tents for guests.)

So when Kristina Romanova, the CEO and creative director of Aman Essentials, the hotel’s lifestyle arm, which spans clothing, leather goods, fragrance and beauty products, approached Jones about a collaboration, it took little soul-searching. ‘We met at a masked ball in Venice, in around 2018,’ says Jones. ‘Kristina knew how much I loved the Aman, so I think she just asked me, and I said yes. It took about a year and a half to get to the point we are now.’ (The collection has now launched in selected Aman outposts and online, as well as at a handful Dover Street Market locations, including Ginza, Tokyo.)
‘It was the first collaboration of this magnitude that we had undertaken,’ adds Romanova. ‘When we started thinking about collaborating with a designer, we were just like: it’s got to be Kim.’

And, while hotel merch is certainly having a moment, Aman x Kim Jones goes far beyond the gift-shop branded caps and tote bags that have become increasingly ubiquitous among the style set. ‘There’s the whole merch aspect of Aman that people love,’ says Jones, referring to collectibles like the leather luggage tag you receive after your stay (they are unique to each property, and have become a subtle status symbol for those in the know). ‘But I was really thinking about what you wear at the Aman – you know, the things that you might have left behind when you packed in a rush, or what you might want when you’ve been at the resort for a while.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
‘I always end up going to the shop and buying stuff, and then just wearing it the whole time,’ he continues. ‘So it all just felt very organic, and real.’

So what are Jones’ travel essentials? There are those items one might expect to be able to purchase at a hotel store: pyjama sets (here constructed from silk in mineral-blue stripes or a deep ‘kombu’ green), swimwear (bikinis edged in woven cord; board-style shorts; sleek swimming costumes with visible zip fastenings), and slippers (ultra-padded with a fleece interior and toggle fastenings). But there are also garments made for traversing a new destination: a series of ‘technical tailoring’ captures Jones’ knack for pragmatic luxury (think: tailored abaca city shorts; zip-up Harrington-style jackets), while activewear comprises base-layer tanks, leggings and bralettes. Completing the line-up is a draped silk dress, should one be without an outfit for an evening at the hotel bar.

‘There’s a functional utilitarianism to the clothes, but there’s also something sexy to the silk story. I was thinking about the Aman couple, and obviously we have one part of the ultimate Aman couple here,’ Jones says, gesturing to Romanova (she is the partner of owner and CEO Vladislav Doronin). ‘I was talking to Vlad, and I was talking to you, and thinking about how we could make [these pieces] become reality.’
‘It’s got to be versatile, functional, but it has to have this understated elegance, and I think that’s what Kim is very well known for,’ says Romanova. ‘He is the master of that.’

The accompanying campaign was photographed in Aman Tokyo and across the city, with the launch marked by a sprawling eight-course dinner in the hotel’s restaurant (local attendees included rapper Verbal and designer Yoon; international guests were shuttled in by Japan Airlines’ luxurious new flagship vessel, the Airbus A350-1000). ‘I’ve been staying here since before it was open, it just feels like being in the future,’ says Jones about the choice of location. ‘Then you go up to the rooms, and they are so beautiful and spacious. And the baths – [I love] getting in that bath and just staring out at all of the lights.’

‘Tokyo was our first urban destination for Aman, and it was the first place I stayed in the city,’ adds Romanova. ‘I came for the opening, and it was such a defining moment for my personal taste to experience Japan and all the attention to detail. Everything has its purpose, and I think it really defined the way that I look at things.’

Aman Essentials launched in 2022, after an initial beauty line revealed a desire among guests for items they could take home with them to remember their stay (or, indeed, for those yet to spend a night but simply wishing to indulge in the lifestyle). ‘When we were going through options for names, we were like: what do we call it? It had to capture that essence of what we represent, and it’s really the essentials on your trip, or on your holidays, and this [is the thinking] behind every product,’ says Romanova. ‘Like, what do I need during my stay? Whether it’s a piece of clothing, pyjamas, a hat, a perfume, or a face mask, we are basically building that perfect traveller’s wardrobe.’
The collection is available at selected Aman resorts, and on Aman’s website, and selected Dover Street Market locations.

Jack Moss is the Fashion & Beauty Features Director at Wallpaper*, having joined the team in 2022 as Fashion Features Editor. Previously the digital features editor at AnOther and digital editor at 10 Magazine, he has also contributed to numerous international publications and featured in ‘Dazed: 32 Years Confused: The Covers’, published by Rizzoli. He is particularly interested in the moments when fashion intersects with other creative disciplines – notably art and design – as well as championing a new generation of international talent and reporting from international fashion weeks. Across his career, he has interviewed the fashion industry’s leading figures, including Rick Owens, Pieter Mulier, Jonathan Anderson, Grace Wales Bonner, Christian Lacroix, Kate Moss and Manolo Blahnik.

items.title: 10 new remote-working gadgets for modern road warriors
items.description: A couple of decades ago, in a world before pandemics and video calls, the now achingly Gen X phrase ‘road warrior’ was coined to apply to the new breed of perpetually mobile workers. Enabled and emboldened by tech – both in terms of gadgets and the soaring sco
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: A couple of decades ago, in a world before pandemics and video calls, the now achingly Gen X phrase ‘road warrior’ was coined to apply to the new breed of perpetually mobile workers. Enabled and emboldened by tech – both in terms of gadgets and the soaring scope of the industry itself – road warriors saw themselves at the vanguard of the new post-office landscape.

The pandemic put paid to any lingering glamour and the vast majority of modern remote workers have swapped the road for the kitchen table, with the occasional coffee shop if funds allow. But the idea of being rootless and restless, whilst remained tethered to co-workers and a career is still an attractive one, even if it often comes out of necessity rather than desire.

We’ve scoured the stores to find the best tech accessories for keeping up to date and on the ball when you’re out and about, whether it’s the perennial problem of having enough battery life on hand, or the myriad promises of AI-powered productivity boosts. Here’s our guide to gear for running an office on the move.

One of the thinnest and lightest laptops on the market, the new Acer Swift Blade 14 weighs in at just 799 grams. With a 14” OLED screen, 50Wh battery and Intel Core Series 3 processors (up to the Core 7 processor 350), along with 512GB of storage and 12GB of memory, the Swift Blade 14 is our choice of ultra-lite, providing you’re able to live with one of the two finishes, Marshmallow White and Marshmallow Blue.
There’s also four-speaker audio, three USB-C connectors and an easily switchable webcam. The 14’s overall thickness of just 12.9 mm makes this an easy addition to the smallest of bags.
Acer Swift Blade 14, from £1,049.99, Store.Acer.com

Pairing well with the Swift Blade 14 is the Krafted Edge, an ultra-slim laptop powerbank designed to slot beneath the device itself. Just 12mm thick, the Edge has 20,000mAh capability, enough for up to three full laptop charges or four phone charges. Charging the Edge itself should take around two hours and there are two USB-C slots and two USB-A slots for simultaneous device charging.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

The battery itself is modular and replaceable, while the casing combines an aluminium alloy base with a top panel made from OBP-certified ocean-plastic (i.e. waste that would otherwise have been ‘Ocean Bound Plastic’). The design cleverly incorporates a braided USB-C cable that slots into one end of the case so you’re never without a means of charging. Perfectly shaped to slot into a laptop sleeve alongside your computer, you won’t even know that it’s there.
Krafted Edge power bank, £149.99, Kraftedtech.com
Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD

The new Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD from Lexar is designed to bulk up the data capability of your smartphone. Described as the world's thinnest portable SSD, this pocketable storage measures just 8cm by 4.8cm by 3.8mm – it’s only 1 mm thick at some points). Available in 512GB and 1TB sizes, it weighs in at 26.5g and there’s a magnetic sleeve accessory for clipping it to the back of your phone.
Lexar Muse Ultra-Slim Portable SSD, available soon, Lexar.com

Timekettle have a pair of AI-equipped earbuds out in the wild, the W4 Plus and the LiveTalk. The former more focused on translation, while the LiveTalk is the choice for everyday translation and conversation summaries. Like all products of this ilk – and there are now a lot of them – there’s a certain amount of commitment required to get the best performance. LiveTalk consists of a pair of 6.9g open-ear earbuds that offer real-time AI translation, along with with AI-powered conversation summaries.

They do work, after a fashion, although the system struggles to keep up with the speed of casual conversation and works best when translating a piece of recorded speech. The sci-fi dreams of genuine real-time, UN-grade machine-driven simultaneous translation are not here yet, but they will be. LiveTalk can be used via your phone’s microphone or by joining in on a phone call.

Battery life is an impressive 35 hours (with the relatively hefty case) and as always there’s a subscription service for heavy users who need more than the basic 200 free minutes a month. Occasional travellers will find the LiveTalk’s arsenal of 54 languages (all European languages along with including Chinese, Japanese and Hindi and many more) spans most of the globe.
Timekettle LiveTalk AI Translation Earbuds, $109, Timekettle.co

Adopting a new workflow doesn’t always feel intuitive, plus there’s the very real danger of switching over to a system or technology that flails, fails or gradually fades into obsolescence. That’s why we’re only giving a cautious nod to the new Flowtica Folio, a luxury notebook folder designed to be used with the Flowtica Scribe AI note-taking pen. We can already sense your hesitation.

Essentially, the Scribe is another form factor for the increasingly common AI-driven Dictaphone model, a pen that contains a microphone, 32GB of onboard storage and the ability to export recordings to the Flowtica app, where they’re automatically transcribed.

There’s no additional trickery, save for a button that adds a bookmarklet into the recording when you want something highlighted. The Folio simply acts as a smart way of combining the pen with your favourite notebook. In this age of E-ink tablets and hyper-capable smartphones, Flowtica’s set-up feels like a step too far, and having a relatively discrete recording device in meetings, etc., is a potential legal red flag.

The company’s newest product, the Verso, is a more practical piece of portable technology. Superficially similar in function – it’s an AI notetaker – the Verso clips on the back of a Smartphone and has its own E-ink touchscreen, so memos and notes can be read straight away. Orders are open now.
Flowtica Scribe Field Kit (Pen + Folio Notebook), £144, Flowtica.ai
Flowtica Verso E-ink AI notetaker, more information at Flowtica.ai

If you’re the kind of person who can keep hold of a travel adaptor for more than one trip, it’s worth splashing out on a quality unit that does it all. That’s certainly the case for Anker’s newest 4-in-1 universal charger, a hefty but compact travel accessory with inbuilt UK, US, and EU plugs - Type G, Type A and Type C, for those keeping track. With enough sockets to charge up to four devices at once – and 100W power for laptops – it’s a one-plug solution to almost every travel and remote working use case.
Anker Universal Charger, £69.99, Anker.com

The Power Keyboard from Clicks is a really truly tiny, tiny keyboard. Those with long memories will remember the Blackberry, once heralded as the ultimate device (peak road warrior, in fact), but somewhat elevated in status by the passing of time. The Blackberry had a physical keyboard, you see, something that Steve Jobs’s new-fangled touchscreen couldn’t hope to surpass.

You’d be hard-pressed to find a modern human being who isn’t well-versed in high-speed smartphone text input, and even harder pressed to find someone who still uses their Blackberry. Clicks reckon there’s enough enthusiasm out there for their Power Keyboard, however, a battery pack combined with a slide out keyboard that adds power, bulk and the delight of tapping away on tiny little keys. The large fingered need not apply.
Clicks Power Keyboard, £109, Clicks.tech
ProtoArc XK01 Foldable Keyboard

Another way of transforming a tablet or smartphone into something a little more practical is a folding keyboard. We particularly like ProtoArc’s tri-fold XK01 unit, which offers a full-size 105-key layout, including a host of multimedia keys and a number pad, and an onboard battery for up to 120 days of standby power. The company also offers a version with an onboard trackpad.
ProtoArc XK01 Foldable Keyboard, £44.99, ProtoArc.com

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: Zaha Hadid built just two private houses; one’s now for sale
items.description: It's exactly ten years since Dame Zaha Hadid passed away unexpectedly at the age of 65, leaving an unassailable legacy in her Issey Miyake-clad wake. In a strange piece of synchronicity, there’s now an incredibly rare chance to own one of her buildings in the
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: It's exactly ten years since Dame Zaha Hadid passed away unexpectedly at the age of 65, leaving an unassailable legacy in her Issey Miyake-clad wake. In a strange piece of synchronicity, there’s now an incredibly rare chance to own one of her buildings in the heart of London.

Constructed from 2014 onwards, this house in Belgravia’s Grosvenor Crescent Mews has the distinction of being one of only two private residential projects completed by the studio (the other being the Capital Hill Residence outside Moscow).

A unicorn in the London property market, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews isn’t just a rare example of Hadid’s work but it’s also a 3,980 sq ft house with integral garage just a stone’s throw from Hyde Park Corner, located in what is Belgravia's only private gated mews.

Gaining permission for such an avant-garde structure in the midst of a thicket of Conservation Areas and listed buildings was no mean feat, even for an architecture of the calibre of Zaha Hadid. The site had boundaries with no fewer than nine different neighbours, placed in such a way that the only public-facing façade was just six metres in width.
That element, a rippling curtain of back-lit brickwork lattices and patterned glass, belies the scale of the house behind it, which extends over four generous 1,000 sq ft floorplans.
Basement kitchen, dining and living area
Basement kitchen, dining and living area

The garage was a planning condition, but it was fitted out to a residential specification so that it can be used as a study area if needed. It adjoins the main reception room, a space bounded by the curved interventions of the polished balustrade rail and the custom-designed staircase, formed from polished concrete and shaped to wind sinuously between the floors.
Atrium views from the lower ground floor
Atrium views from the lower ground floor
Atrium views from the lower ground floor

Like many London mews and conversion projects, the house goes down as well as up, with a kitchen and sitting room located in the basement, beneath a double height space which in itself is topped by a glazed terrace at first floor level. With windows, parapets, courtyards and walls arranged so as to avoid overlooking from surrounding properties, the entire house is cleverly folded into its site, making the most from the available space.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Utility, plant and stores are tucked away in the basement behind the kitchen, another area that is defined by a trademark Hadidian swoop, this time in the form of a polished kitchen counter that projects out from the wall like a geological form.

From here, the two-storey atrium rises up to the gauzy light that filters through the glass roof, with the polished balustrade playing off the curved concrete stair risers contained behind a glazed wall.

The first floor houses the principal bedroom suite, complete with curved glass and sole access to the terrace. A living wall flanks the perimeter of the property (it’s joined by a brown roof system designed to improve the house’s insulation), while the glazed stair tower rises up beneath the fluted forms of another skylight. On the second floor there are two further ensuite bedrooms, each winding around a central dressing room space.
The artistry and style of 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews is sadly unrepeatable, making this project a rare opportunity to acquire a functional work of art in the heart of London.

In the decade since her death, the firm Hadid established in Studio 9 of a former school on Bowling Green Lane in Clerkenwell has gone all out into making her wildly exuberant approach into a clearly defined architectural style, Parametricism, translating Hadid’s wild, analogue forms into a heady, AI-infused cocktail of data-shaped aesthetic adventures.
Design details, 6 Grosvenor Crescent Mews

items.title: This winter’s menswear is all about ‘crafting characters’
items.description: The changing of the fashion seasons gives one a chance to craft a new persona. For winter, menswear designers posited their own takes on character dressing, one which riffed on the tenets of traditional sartorialism with a preppy, sporty – and oftentimes colou
items.author: Jack Moss
paragraphs: The changing of the fashion seasons gives one a chance to craft a new persona. For winter, menswear designers posited their own takes on character dressing, one which riffed on the tenets of traditional sartorialism with a preppy, sporty – and oftentimes colourful – twist.

Such was the starting point of our November 2026 menswear fashion story, which saw London- and Paris-based photographer Luke Gooden and stylist Guy Miller capture A/W 2026’s spirit of easy elegance – where classic tailoring and outerwear meets elements of utility, from toggle fastenings and parka-style hoods, to a proliferation of pockets.
A/W 2026’s menswear is all about character dressing

Through it all, elements of colour and play: the vivid red of a Dries Van Noten overcoat, cut with oversized storm flaps; the exaggerated cuff of a Prada shirt, peeking out from beneath the sleeve of a technical parka; or the easy, sporty cut of tailored trousers from Loro Piana and Wooyoungmi, the latter featuring the kind of zip pockets one might find on track pants.

Gooden, who says he uses ‘the shapes, sounds and conversations’ to influence his photography, says the story was about ‘crafting characters and narratives’. ‘It’s all part of the act,’ he says. ‘The images are the final result of a built up symphony, orchestrated long before they reach the pages, and sung once seen.’

Models: Gideon Adeniyi at Next London, Arthur Vaughan at Elite. Casting: Concorde Casting. Hair: Michael Harding using Bumble & Bumble. Make-up: Sarah Edenborough. Photography assistants: Sam Robbins, Tommy Aucott. Fashion assistants: Minna de Bagota, Leonie Dennett. Production assistant: Danielle Quigley.

items.title: Discover Ellis King, the artist making sense of women's experiences
items.description: ‘I became a parent and had a really difficult journey getting there,’ says British painter Ellis King, who is examining the quiet spaces where unresolved trauma lives in her debut exhibition at London’s SQFT: Space Gallery.
items.author: Hannah Silver
paragraphs: ‘I became a parent and had a really difficult journey getting there,’ says British painter Ellis King, who is examining the quiet spaces where unresolved trauma lives in her debut exhibition at London’s SQFT: Space Gallery.

It makes sense that King turned inwards when creating her paintings, which are both deeply autobiographical and highly charged. Her scenes capture the mundanity of existence, yet sizzle with the tension inherent in a moment when experience briefly catches up with you, unawares – in King’s paintings, women freeze at the sink, or in the bath, lost in a recollection.

‘It changes something inside you when you have a baby, and I think that, coupled with the stress of my experience, switched something in me that I hadn't been aware of before,’ King says. ‘It was a bit like the blinkers were removed and I suddenly saw, on a small scale, how many women experience these huge, life-changing things, and then you're just kind of left to crack on. It was all of that we go through that's just never seen or heard.’

King’s distinctive style sits somewhere between reality and abstraction, her self-portraiture a foil rooted in realism, jarring against the sharp graphics and flat planes upon which she sits. ‘Working in self-portraiture meant I could be honest about the emotions I'd actually felt – disgust, shame, pity, exhaustion – rather than softening them,’ says King. ‘Those quieter moments are so often set at home, too. It holds some of the best and worst moments of our lives, and yet so much of what happens there stays unseen. A lone figure in a domestic space can carry a huge amount without anything dramatic happening at all. The quiet moments are where so much of women's private experience lives, unremarked on, easy to miss, but often where the real weight sits.’

For King, the paintings become a way to explore and consider her own anger, at a system which lets women down, and at the expectations women are held to. Ultimately, though, she wants the works to begin a conversation, rather than an argument. By rooting these scenes in her personal experience, King opens the doors for a dialogue in a new medium. ‘Quite honestly, I think I came back to painting partly out of rage at the system, and partly because I needed somewhere for all of that experience to go. I'd always painted portraiture, so it was the natural language for me to return to. I didn't fully realise it at the time, but painting became a way of processing what had happened. That experience has stayed at the centre of my practice. It's what made me interested in the things women carry quietly.’
Spilt Milk at SQFT: Space Gallery until 5 November

items.title: Making a Show, Sabine Marcelis
items.description: Making a Show is a photobook with Dutch artist and designer Sabine Marcelis, published on the occasion of her first museum exhibition at Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, Sabine Marcelis—Light and Color, on view from October 30, 2026 to April 4, 2027. Photographed
paragraphs: Making a Show is a photobook with Dutch artist and designer Sabine Marcelis, published on the occasion of her first museum exhibition at Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, Sabine Marcelis—Light and Color, on view from October 30, 2026 to April 4, 2027. Photographed by Mattia Balsamini inside Sabine’s Rotterdam studio in the months before the opening, the book documents an exhibition in transit: light, colour, and material stretched, poured, altered, and refined until they reach the simplicity that is Sabine’s fingerprint. Smashed mirrors, pink resin slabs, perfect droplets—all part of a symbiotic world, where the work produced inside the studio is in constant conversation with the hands that supply it from outside. Alongside, curator Damian Fopp grounds the book with a written introspection on living inside her universe as the show took shape, declaring by the end that ‘what appears effortless is anything but’. Punctuated by WhatsApp messages and email snapshots between Sabine’s team and the museum’s, Making a Show distils the incantatory movement of an exhibition in the making and the infrastructure of people behind it.

Sabine Marcelis is a Dutch artist and designer based in Rotterdam. Working across installations, objects, and spatial projects, she explores light, colour, and material, collaborating closely with a network of local manufacturers to push each to its limits. For the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival 2026, Sabine designed one of the headlining large-scale art installations, an immersive temporary installation titled Maze. She has also received multiple Designer of the Year honours (2020–2024) and her works are part of permanent museum collections worldwide, including MoMA, the Stedelijk Museum, and the Vitra Design Museum. Sabine Marcelis was previously featured in Apartamento magazine issue #21. Find her story from our digital archive here.

Mattia Balsamini is an Italian photographer based between London and Milan. After joining David LaChapelle’s studio in 2010 as a studio assistant and archivist, Mattia went on to develop personal and editorial projects through collaborations with institutions including MIT and NASA. His work has been exhibited at the Triennale di Milano, MAXXI, the Sandretto Re Rebaudengo Foundation, and the Italian Cultural Institute in San Francisco.

items.title: Meet the Shoe Brand That Takes “Nothing New” as a Compliment
items.description: Every good idea has already been had. All the best hiking shoes have already been designed. Everything that's come after has been, quite literally in the latter case, a retread.
items.author: Jake Silbert
paragraphs: Every good idea has already been had. All the best hiking shoes have already been designed. Everything that's come after has been, quite literally in the latter case, a retread.
So says od.A, a young footwear brand proud to produce "nothing new."

od.A's shoes are beautiful to behold, streamlined slabs of nappa leather and waxed nubuck that look as much like trail shoes' future as they do their past. (The debut Launch Collection is naturally available exclusively at progressive retailer Dover Street Market.)

Because, as artful as the shoes may be — od.A co-founder Albert Arenas tells me that inspiration came from the restless ingenuity of Issey Miyake, the material genius of Stone Island founder Massimo Osti, and the lived-in feel of interior designer Axel Vervoordt — they're also steeped in historic design cues visible only on closer inspection. The shoes were already seeded to a handful of discerning gents in the outdoorsy-style space and each was duly impressed (or maybe just glad to be sent something fresh).

Founded towards the "end of 2023," Arenas says, and "based between Barcelona and Shanghai," od.A's mission is to bring a little humanity back into a realm that lost it long ago. The great functional footwear of yesteryear was beautifully inelegant: clunky, bulbous, and defined entirely by purpose over aesthetic. And you saw the makers' hands in everything from the silhouettes to even the finishing, where nothing was necessarily perfect. And, yet, they were.

More importantly, they lasted, both as objects and as stylistic touchstones. Attempts to reinvent the trail shoe as something wholly new have largely failed — we circle the same few shapes to this day.

od.A knows this. It seeks to reclaim the untamed edge that's since been focus-grouped out of the realm of performance (not performative) outdoor shoes. Its debut silhouettes appear familiar but are actually not quite: an approach-style shoe's handsewn upper makes it look more like a gentleman walking sneaker than a badass hiker. Vibram's Gironda sole renders the 002 classically tough but the refined upper, made even sleeker by a zippered sheath, is unexpectedly elegant. There's even a convertible outdoor loafer.

It's singular stuff, a welcome breaststroke against the tide of an overcrowded footwear market lousy with microplastics and polyesters. Because the best part of these rugged but sensitive shoes is that, like the trail shoes of old, they're destined to only get better with age.
Let's go back to the beginning. What's od.A origin story?

Albert Arenas: We had worked together in the creative, fashion, and footwear industries for years. We started as [sneaker] collectors. As students, we sought out the shoes we loved and learned from them. We researched the history of each brand and took the shoes apart to study how they were built and understand why some worked, or looked, better than others. That research is still the part we enjoy most.
The brand name feels open to interpretation. Is it?

In a way, yes, although its original meaning is quite specific. The name comes from oda, Spanish for "ode": a tribute. The brand is an ode to the outdoor silhouettes of the 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s, and to the design solutions passed down from one generation of shoes to the next. It also honors ancestral ways of making shoes, and a way of manufacturing built around long-lasting objects.

The name is also an acronym. od.A was born from Outdoor Archive, with the A deliberately set apart so it could take on new meanings over time. Outdoor Artefacts, Outdoor Assembly, Outdoor Anatomy, Outdoor Atmosphere, Outdoor Allegory, and others yet to be defined. We borrow that from wabi-sabi: the acceptance that things change.
So, the name is not open because its meaning is unclear. It is open because it is designed to evolve.
Evolution by looking backwards. Right now, it feels like everyone is looking backwards — the market is saturated with outdoorsy footwear. Does that sort of thing bother you?

The market is a challenge we embraced from the start. We began while "gorpcore" was at its height. We make outdoor-inspired shoes, so we are part of that conversation, but our focus has not changed since: od.A has an anthropological basis. We focus on why certain designs and techniques have lasted, and pay little attention to the shoes going viral. A trend needs a name behind it. A shoe that lasts doesn't.

We call it a denial of fashion egotism. For us, that means no single designer or creative director takes the credit. od.A is teamwork. Each of us does our best in our own field, and none of us needs that credit.
That relates to your mantra of "nothing new," i.e. every shoe walks a trail blazed by every previous shoe. Can you talk more about that mentality?
We don't put history on a pedestal; we rework it. Every design starts from a reference. There is a right kind of newness: the kind you can trace back.

Before we drew the 002.1, we saw how ski boots evolved at an exhibition of historic ski equipment in the Vall de Núria in the Pyrenees. They started as laced mountain boots with a sole shaped to fit the binding. Then, to keep snow and water out, the closure moved to a diagonal, and a single piece of tough leather came to protect the front of the foot. The 002.1 keeps that logic, with a hard ripstop panel over the instep and a sealed, waterproof YKK zip.
Speaking of the process, what was the biggest learning curve?
What we underestimated was time: getting the shoe we had in mind took nearly three years.
Time, indeed. Three years later, how do you define a "good" shoe?

The one you want to wear every day, or the one you miss when you are wearing something else. To get there, comfort comes first; aesthetics always come second. A shoe you wear every day, exposed to the elements, should age well and look better, or at least more personal, with use.
So, it must perform, and the performance we care about most is durability. The form is never finished: the person wearing it completes it.
Let's go a step bigger. Why shoes at all?

Because a shoe is never only an object. Each design began as a tool shaped by what a community needed and came to say something about who wore it. Studying shoes closely taught us that every construction carries that history: the problem it was solving and the people it was made for. That is what captivates us.
We come from different cultures, and a shoe is a shared language, the meeting point where we understand each other.

items.title: В Австралии потратят миллионы долларов на защиту от нашествия жаб
items.description: В Австралии создадут безводный барьер для защиты от вторжения жаб
items.author: Александра Копылова
paragraphs: В Австралии создадут безводный барьер для защиты от вторжения жаб
В австралийском регионе Пилбара на западе страны создадут безводный барьер для защиты от нашествия жаб-ага. Об этом пишет ABC.

Реализация проекта Toad Containment Zone («Зона сдерживания жаб») начнётся в 2027 году и коснётся территории площадью около 7,5 тысячи кв. км. Предполагается, что жаб лишат доступа к искусственным водоёмам. Стоимость составит около 19,5 млн долларов.
Жабы-ага являются для Австралии чужеродным видом. Из-за их неконтролируемого размножения миллионы местных животных оказались лишены своих зон обитания и погибли.

Регион Пилбара изобилует животными и растениями, которые не встречаются больше нигде в мире, заявили в Университете Кёртина. Нашествие жаб представляет серьёзную угрозу для флоры и фауны. Предполагается, что создание барьера займёт от двух до пяти лет.
Ранее «Сноб» писал, что в Германии власти на четыре месяца перекрыли дорогу для строительства подземных переходов для жаб. До этого волонтёрам приходилось вручную переносить животных каждую весну.

items.title: Швеция отказалась играть с россиянами на чемпионате мира по хоккею в 2027 году
items.description: Швеция отказалась играть с россиянами на чемпионате мира по хоккею в 2027 году
items.author: Екатерина Палкина
paragraphs: Швеция отказалась играть с россиянами на чемпионате мира по хоккею в 2027 году
Сборная Швеции намерена бойкотировать матчи с российской командой в рамках чемпионатов мира в 2027 году. Федерация хоккея Швеции приняла это решение сегодня, заявил глава организации Андрес Ларссон.

Ларссон подчеркнул, что шведские спортсмены не отказываются полностью от участия в турнирах: они просто не выйдут на лёд против россиян. Позиция федерации заключается в том, что участие РФ в международных соревнования «остаётся немыслимым», пока не завершился конфликт на Украине, сказано в публикации. Позднее аналогичное решение приняли Финляндия, Норвегия, Дания и Латвия.

На прошлой неделе спортивный арбитражный суд (CAS) обязал Международную федерацию хоккея допустить российские команды до участия в международных турнирах, в том числе в Чемпионате мира и Молодёжном чемпионате мира в сезоне 2026/2027. Решение не подлежит обжалованию.

Ранее стало известно, что Финляндия намерена в следующем году закрыть въезд в Шенгенскую зону для российских спортсменов, которые собираются принять участие в соревнованиях. Еврокомиссия занимается разработкой соответствующих механизмов.

items.title: Eлена Цеплик: Давайте знакомиться
items.description: Мне 56 лет, и, наверное, я живу свою лучшую жизнь. У меня есть все, о чем, кажется, может мечтать человек: прекрасная семья, лучшая в мире работа, которую я обожаю, жизнь в православной церкви, замечательные друзья и увлечения, для которых я всегда нахожу врем
items.author: Eлена Цеплик
paragraphs: Мне 56 лет, и, наверное, я живу свою лучшую жизнь. У меня есть все, о чем, кажется, может мечтать человек: прекрасная семья, лучшая в мире работа, которую я обожаю, жизнь в православной церкви, замечательные друзья и увлечения, для которых я всегда нахожу время.

Начну все-таки с работы. Примерно 15 лет назад по стечению разных обстоятельств я завершила корпоративную карьеру, складывавшуюся более 20 лет довольно успешно. Я руководила подразделениями пиара и маркетинга в финансовых компаниях, но наступил момент, который сейчас называют выгоранием, а тогда я просто каждой клеткой почувствовала, что больше не могу. Не могу вставать в шесть утра и ехать через пол Москвы в любую погоду. Не могу носить офисные костюмы и есть офисную еду. Не могу видеть ни своих начальников, ни своих сотрудников, ни весь этот офисный антураж с ковролином, опенспейсами, переговорками, курилками и прочими радостями. Я устала существовать от отпуска до отпуска как во сне, бесконечно защищая бюджеты, стратегии и проектные планы. Я ушла в никуда, чтобы подумать, а что я вообще хочу? Где во всем этом водовороте зарабатывания денег я и мои настоящие желания?

Первый месяц я гуляла с собакой. Просыпалась когда угодно, пила кофе, а потом брала поводок и нашего 60-килограммового маламута Тима и шла с ним в парк. Мы ходили по полтора-два часа, я ни о чем не думала и постепенно начинала чувствовать, как ко мне возвращается обычная жизнь — погода, запахи, звуки, эмоции. В чуть освобожденную голову внезапно залетела случайная мысль, что я все же хочу работу, но ту, в которой будет смысл и которая точно будет нужна многим людям.

Никаких конкретных планов у меня не было. Но к тому времени я волонтерила в благотворительном фонде «Подари жизнь» (мы с мужем покупали какие-то расходники и продукты для онкологического отделения РДКБ), поэтому я просто написала письмо директору фонда, что у меня теперь много времени и я готова помогать больше. К моему величайшему изумлению, директор мне ответила, и меня пригласили на работу. Копирайтером! Обычным, рядовым, на рядовую зарплату. Это была очень классная работа.

И был момент, убедивший меня, что я на правильном пути. Однажды я написала текст про девочку с лейкозом, которой были нужны дорогущие лекарства. Его опубликовали на сайте, и деньги собрались за сутки. Это было невероятное чувство, вот я сама, своими руками сделала работу, набрала буковки! — и она принесла абсолютно осязаемый результат, спасла жизнь человеку (девочка выздоровела, выросла, вышла замуж и сейчас у нее уже двое детей!). И я решила, что у меня должен быть собственный благотворительный проект.

В конце 2013 года мы с мужем и близкой подругой зарегистрировали благотворительный фонд «Найди семью», и с этого момента каждый день у меня есть работа мечты. За почти 13 лет фонд вырос из крошечной частной инициативы, за которой стояли три немного сумасшедших человека и не стояло ни собственных больших денег, ни богатых спонсоров, в большую организацию, где работают более 70 человек. Мы помогаем детям-сиротам и семьям с приемными детьми.
Как родилась эта тема? Тоже довольно сиюминутно.

Тогда был принят Федеральный закон № 272-ФЗ, неофициально называемый закон «Димы Яковлева», серьезно ограничивший иностранные усыновления. Закон вызвал бурю обсуждений в прессе и среди российской общественности. Было много публикаций о том, как могут пострадать от его принятия дети в детских домах. И мы с мужем сходили на согласованный митинг, который был организован против принятия данного закона. Пришла домой я с чувством глубочайшего разочарования. Потому что поняла: все это — вообще не про помощь детям. Про что угодно, только не про них. И мне захотелось сделать что-то совсем иное. Что точно поможет именно детям — и сделать это через свой благотворительный фонд.

Когда я только придумывала, как это будет, я хотела только одного: чтобы в детских домах оставалось все меньше и меньше детей, чтобы те маленькие люди, которым очень не повезло на жизненном старте, получали другую жизнь и другое будущее. Чтобы у них появились мамы и папы, чай по вечерам, любимые блюда по выходным, прогулки в лесу и походы в кино, обнимашки на ночь и горячее молоко с медом, когда сильно болит горло. Чтобы их любили, о них заботились и защищали от жизненных невзгод. Понятно, что это очень широкий замах и серьезная заявка, но именно это и делало замысел интересным: как выстроить работу так, чтобы помощь приходила не к отдельным детям, а ко многим? Как превратить разовую помощь в систему поддержки? После консультаций с разными экспертами постепенно концепция стала проясняться, фонд — наполняться людьми, мы росли и расширялись.

Как именно устроена наша помощь, я расскажу отдельно, потому что это очень сложный и некороткий разговор. А сегодня в качестве знакомства просто скажу, что сейчас «Найди семью» — это та самая система комплексной помощи с подтвержденной эффективностью, которая помогает тысячам детей ежегодно.

А еще я обязательно расскажу, каково это вообще — работать в благотворительном фонде директором. Это отдельный и очень непростой путь, который, я надеюсь, будет интересен моим читателям. Ну, и, конечно, в моем блоге точно будут рассказы про наших подопечных, про то, как из волчат из детских домов получаются мамины и папины пирожочки и принцессы. И про то, что это вообще ни разу не похоже на сказку. А вот на рукотворное чудо — да, похоже часто. Подписывайтесь. Тут точно будет любопытно и живенько)))

items.title: В Испании футболист умер после столкновения с другим игроком на поле
items.description: В Испании футболист «Тенерифе» погиб из-за столкновения во время матча
items.author: Александра Копылова
paragraphs: В Испании футболист «Тенерифе» погиб из-за столкновения во время матча

В Испании футболист клуба «Тенерифе» Хесус де Мигель умер после того, как столкнулся с вратарём «Андорры» Хесусом Овоно на домашнем матче второго по силе дивизиона чемпионата Испании по футболу. Об этом сообщили в ФК в соцсети X.

Инцидент произошёл в центре поля в компенсированное время ко второму тайму. Де Мигель пытался принять мяч, но Овоно ударил его коленом в грудь. Футболист «Тенерифе» потерял сознание, его госпитализировали. Позже он умер в больнице.
Хесусу де Мигелю было 30 лет. Он выступал за «Тенерифе» с лета 2025 года. До этого он играл в нескольких других испанских клубах.

Национальная полиция Испании начала расследование в связи с инцидентом. Оно направлено на то, чтобы установить все обстоятельства произошедшего как на поле, так и после госпитализации футболиста. Дело передано в суд.

items.title: Древние художники могли раскрашивать наскальные рисунки в Португалии
items.description: В Португалии нашли краски возрастом 27 тысяч лет рядом с древними изображениями животных
items.author: Виолетта Ефимова
paragraphs: В Португалии нашли краски возрастом 27 тысяч лет рядом с древними изображениями животных

Археологи обнаружили сотни фрагментов минеральных пигментов возрастом более 27 тысяч лет во время раскопок в Пенаскосе, в португальской долине Коа. Регион известен тысячами изображений животных, вырезанных на скальных поверхностях. Новая находка позволяет предположить, что древние жители могли не только гравировать рисунки, но и раскрашивать их.

Исследования проводит фонд Côa Parque под руководством археолога Тьерри Обри. На участке площадью около восьми квадратных метров учёные нашли жёлтые, красные, чёрные и коричневые пигменты, изготовленные из оксидов железа и других природных минералов. Их обнаружили в слое, относящемся к позднему этапу граветтской культуры верхнего палеолита.

Датировка тоже оказалась важной — следы человеческой деятельности в Пенаскосе оказались старше 27 тысяч лет. Ранее считалось, что люди появились здесь около 26 тысяч лет назад. Помимо пигментов, археологи нашли каменные орудия, инструменты для охоты, следы обработки шкур и остатки очагов.

Пока неизвестно, для чего именно использовали краски. По одной из версий Обри, ими могли окрашивать шкуры или добавлять их в клеящие составы. Другая гипотеза предполагает, что пигменты применяли в наскальном искусстве. Некоторые изображения могли сначала раскрашивать, а затем дополнять гравировкой. Однако прямых доказательств этого пока нет.

В следующем сезоне исследователи планируют продолжить раскопки и выяснить происхождение пигментов. Лабораторный анализ частиц поможет определить, контактировали ли они с камнем, шкурами или другими материалами. Это позволит точнее восстановить повседневную жизнь обитателей долины Коа и понять, как выглядело их искусство более 27 тысяч лет назад.

items.title: «Я уже полысел, но все еще играю в йо-йо». Как игра продолжает развиваться в России
items.description: «Игра в йо-йо, или в чертика на веревочке, — вот чем грезит каждый осведомленный подросток этой весной», — писал в 2007 году «Московский комсомолец». Тогда у каждого был тот самый одноклассник, который на переменах разучивал трюки, а после уроков тусовался с д
items.author: Афиша Daily
paragraphs: «Игра в йо-йо, или в чертика на веревочке, — вот чем грезит каждый осведомленный подросток этой весной», — писал в 2007 году «Московский комсомолец». Тогда у каждого был тот самый одноклассник, который на переменах разучивал трюки, а после уроков тусовался с другими йоэрами на центральной площади своего города. По стране проходили соревнования, сходки, а на первом Пикнике «Афиши» и вовсе дебютировал российский йо-йо-бренд Fakel с моделью FKL-01.

Прошло девятнадцать лет. Массовый бум остался в 2000-х, а йо-йо у всех непричастных всплывает то в ностальгических промокампаниях брендов вроде Jacquemus, Valentino Garavani и Bottega Veneta, то в стендап-выступлениях как пример «бесполезного навыка, который отнимает время и никогда в жизни не пригодится». Казалось бы, игрушка осталась где-то в воспоминаниях о детстве миллениалов и поздних зумеров. Но российская сцена продолжает жить.

В Москве каждую субботу в КЦ ЗИЛ или «ГЭС-2» собираются участники Response. Команда проводит бесплатные мастер-классы, где новички знакомятся с йо-йо, а опытные игроки тренируют сложные трюки. В сентябре 2026 года у Response была даже собственная площадка на празднике в честь Дня города на ВДНХ.

Основатель творческого объединения «Сегмент 44» и игрок международной команды Atmos Projects Женя Кочергин подчеркивает, что костяк участников соревнований меняется не так сильно, но новые игроки все-таки появляются. На российском чемпионате 2025 года, например, выступали совсем юные участники, 10–12 лет, которые недавно взяли йо-йо в руки.

Филипп Курс, профессиональный игрок и участник Response, тоже замечает приток новичков. По его наблюдениям, за 2024–2026 годы в игру пришло больше новых участников, чем за предыдущие пять лет. В октябре 2026 года в Казани прошел контест, собравший рекордное количество участников, а в августе в Японии состоялся чемпионат мира, который Курс называет крупнейшим за всю историю соревнований.
Почему люди продолжают играть в йо-йо

«Мне 32 года, я уже полысел, но все еще играю в йо-йо. И в какой-то момент я понял, что готов заниматься этим и в 40 лет просто потому, что в йо-йо столько всего разного, что мне до сих пор интересно пробовать новое. В этом году я начал осваивать стиль игры, которым раньше почти не занимался, — и у меня даже снова появился спортивный интерес. Я захотел выступить на чемпионате России, хотя не участвовал в нем с 2022 года».

«Я играю с 2009 года, и это давно перестало быть просто хобби. Сначала были чемпионаты в России, потом сцены по всему миру — от Японии до США. Йо-йо дало мне комьюнити, которого больше нигде нет, — где бы я ни оказался, там найдется друг, с которым можно встретиться. И это никогда не заканчивается: всегда есть трюк, который надо дожать, комбо, которое надо собрать, новые люди и куча моментов, ради которых все это стоит делать».

«Я начал играть в йо-йо в 2010 году, и сейчас это скорее привычка: играю уже практически на автомате. Кто-то после работы играет в „Доту“, кто-то катается на велосипеде или скейте, а я беру йо-йо, чтобы немного отвлечься. На выходных можно встретиться с друзьями и поиграть вместе. Больше всего меня в йо-йо держат люди.

За столько лет появилось огромное количество друзей и знакомых по всему миру. Это, наверное, самое крутое во всей этой истории. Всегда есть повод куда-нибудь съездить, встретиться со старыми друзьями, познакомиться с новыми. Часто само йо-йо становится просто поводом для встречи».
Игрушка, к которой не относятся всерьез
