items.description: Если задуматься, фитнес-клуб — довольно странное изобретение. Люди платят за возможность бегать, никуда не перемещаясь, поднимать тяжелые предметы и снова опускать их десятки раз или крутить педали велосипеда, который стоит на месте. В общем, выполнять тяжелый
items.author: Ксения Зернова
paragraphs: Если задуматься, фитнес-клуб — довольно странное изобретение. Люди платят за возможность бегать, никуда не перемещаясь, поднимать тяжелые предметы и снова опускать их десятки раз или крутить педали велосипеда, который стоит на месте. В общем, выполнять тяжелый физический труд, который не дает видимых результатов здесь и сейчас и не оплачивается — более того, люди сами готовы платить за такое времяпрепровождение.

Идея тренироваться в специально оборудованных местах появилась задолго до беговых дорожек и абонементов. Древние греки занимались в гимнасиях, римляне — в палестрах при термах, а в XIX веке открылись залы, куда люди приходили уже за плату. Как места для подготовки атлетов и воинов превратились в современные фитнес-клубы?

Именно древним грекам мы обязаны современным словом gym, которым называют фитнес-клубы. Это сокращение от gymnasium, в свою очередь образованного от греческого gymnos — «обнаженный». Атлеты в Древней Греции тренировались без одежды: так было удобнее двигаться, а со временем нагота и вовсе стала частью спортивной традиции. Перед занятиями мужчины натирали кожу оливковым маслом — оно помогало защищать ее от пыли и солнца. После тренировки масло, смешавшееся с потом и грязью, соскребали изогнутым металлическим инструментом — стригилем.

Первые гимнасии представляли собой преимущественно открытые площадки, где можно было бегать, бороться и готовиться к состязаниям. Со временем вокруг тренировочных пространств появились дорожки, помещения для занятий, места для отдыха и общения. Гимнасий стал частью городской жизни и одним из учреждений, в которых молодые мужчины получали физическое воспитание.

Однако в гимнасиях занимались не только ради спортивных достижений. В классическую и эллинистическую эпохи они постепенно становились центрами общественной и интеллектуальной жизни. Здесь могли встречаться ученики и философы, обсуждать вопросы образования и политики, слушать преподавателей. Афинские гимнасии, в том числе Академия и Ликей, оказались тесно связаны с философскими школами.

Никто не приходил в гимнасии с целью купить абонемент на месяц и составить план тренировок для ягодиц. И все же сама идея выделить специальное пространство для регулярных упражнений появилась именно тогда.

В Древнем Риме физические упражнения были частью ритуала, в который входило и посещение общественных бань — терм. При них устраивали палестры, открытые дворы, где посетители могли бегать, бороться, заниматься гимнастикой и играть в мяч. Термы были важной частью городской жизни.

Римские врачи считали физическую активность, купание, массаж и питание важными составляющими здоровья. Поэтому посещение терм могло включать целую последовательность процедур: сначала упражнения, затем банные процедуры и отдых. Исследователи античного спорта отмечают, что в I–II веках нашей эры помещения для упражнений стали полноценной частью многофункциональных банных комплексов. В этом легко узнать некоторые черты современных клубов, где тренажерный зал соседствует с бассейном, сауной и зонами отдыха.

В конце XVIII века в Европе начал меняться подход к физическому воспитанию. Педагоги и военные все чаще рассматривали гимнастику как организованную систему упражнений, которой можно обучать по определенной программе.

В 1799 году датский педагог Франц Нахтегаль открыл в Копенгагене частный институт физического воспитания молодежи. Он также руководил военным гимнастическим институтом и участвовал в развитии физического воспитания в датских школах. Нахтегаль считал, что упражнения должны стать частью регулярного образования и не быть занятием исключительно для спортсменов.

Примерно в те же годы похожие идеи распространялись в немецких землях. В 1811 году немецкий педагог Фридрих Людвиг Ян открыл в берлинском парке Хазенхайде специальную площадку для гимнастики — Turnplatz. Там молодые мужчины занимались на перекладинах, лестницах, канатах и других снарядах, развивали силу и ловкость. Для Яна физическая подготовка была тесно связана с воспитанием граждан и национальным движением в Пруссии после поражения в войне с Наполеоном.

Постепенно и в США немецкие иммигранты стали создавать клубы Turnverein, объединявшие гимнастику, общественную жизнь и политическую деятельность. К началу Гражданской войны в США существовало около 150 таких объединений с десятками тысяч участников.

Именно в этот период появляются учреждения, которые уже напоминают предшественников современных спортивных центров: регулярные занятия, определенная программа упражнений, инструкторы и оборудованные площадки. Но до фитнес-клуба, в который человек приходит ради собственного здоровья и внешности, оставался еще один шаг.

В середине XIX века в европейских городах начали появляться коммерческие гимнастические залы. Их возникновение совпало с индустриализацией и ростом городов: у части населения появлялись свободное время и деньги на занятия, которые не были связаны напрямую с их работой или военной службой.

Одним из ранних примеров стал Grand Gymnase, который французский силач Ипполит Триа открыл в Париже в 1849 году. Это был большой зал с гимнастическими снарядами, канатами и другим оборудованием. Посетители могли приходить на организованные занятия и платить за возможность тренироваться под руководством инструкторов. Историк Эрик Шалин называет его одним из первых коммерческих гимнасиев современного типа.

Триа начинал как силач, выступавший перед публикой, и сумел превратить свою известность в предпринимательский проект. Его зал отвечал растущему интересу к физическому развитию среди городских жителей, которые хотели укреплять тело и улучшать физическую форму. В таких учреждениях можно было регулярно заниматься, осваивать разные упражнения и наблюдать за собственным прогрессом.

Постепенно гимнастические залы перестали быть исключительно местом подготовки спортсменов и военных. Они предлагали человеку возможность заниматься физическим совершенствованием как отдельной частью жизни — за определенную плату, по расписанию и с помощью специального оборудования.

Важную роль в распространении организованных занятий сыграла YMCA — христианская ассоциация молодых мужчин, основанная в Лондоне в 1844 году. Ее создали, чтобы помогать молодым людям, которые переезжали в индустриальный город в поисках работы и сталкивались с плохими жилищными условиями и опасностями уличной жизни. Организация предлагала им место для общения, обучения и отдыха.
Со временем при отделениях ассоциации начали открывать гимнастические залы. Первые здания YMCA в США, специально построенные с такими помещениями, появились в 1869 году.

В 1881 году сотрудник бостонского отделения Роберт Дж. Робертс разработал программу физических упражнений, которые стали предшественниками современных фитнес-тренировок. С ним же YMCA связывает популяризацию термина body-building — бодибилдинг, «строительство тела».
В этих залах занимались гимнастикой, работали со свободными весами, осваивали упражнения на снарядах. Вокруг тренировок формировалась среда, где люди могли регулярно встречаться и заниматься вместе.

Именно в YMCA в 1891 году преподаватель Джеймс Нейсмит придумал баскетбол. Руководство тренировочной школы попросило его разработать игру для зимних занятий в помещении, чтобы ученики могли поддерживать физическую активность в холодное время года. Нейсмит закрепил на балконах два персиковых ящика и предложил студентам забрасывать в них мяч. Так спортивный зал стал местом рождения нового вида спорта.

К концу XIX века физические упражнения уже стали частью массовой культуры. Одним из тех, кто помог превратить спорт в образ жизни, был Юджин Сэндоу — знаменитый силач и культурист, выступавший перед публикой и демонстрировавший возможности человеческого тела.

В 1897 году Сэндоу начал открывать в Лондоне институты физической культуры. Эти заведения уже во многом напоминали современные фитнес-клубы: посетителям предлагали персональные занятия, свободные веса, отдельные помещения для переодевания и купания, а также программы физического совершенствования. В них могли заниматься и мужчины, и женщины. Позже Сэндоу создал сеть таких учреждений и одним из первых превратил тренажерный зал в узнаваемый бренд.

Сэндоу продавал не только тренировки. Он выпускал книги, производил спортивное оборудование, предлагал программы упражнений и использовал фотографии собственного тела для рекламы своей системы. Современники видели в нем пример того, как регулярные занятия способны изменить физическую форму, а предприниматель понял, что на этом можно построить целый бизнес.

Теперь человек приходил в зал уже не только ради спортивной подготовки или общения, но и с какой-то конкретной личной целью — стать сильнее, изменить фигуру или улучшить самочувствие. Тренировки постепенно становились услугой, которую можно было приобрести и встроить в распорядок дня.
Отходить от образа мест исключительно для силачей и культуристов спортзалы начали в первой половине XX века. Одним из пионеров направления «фитнес для всех» стал американский тренер Джек Лалэйнн.

В 1936 году он открыл в Окленде собственную студию физической культуры. Лалэйнн разрабатывал собственное оборудование, составлял силовые тренировки и продвигал идею о том, что физические упражнения должны быть частью повседневной заботы о себе. Калифорнийский музей называет его студию одним из первых современных health clubs — клубов, ориентированных на поддержание физической формы и здоровья.

В 1951 году Лалэйнн начал вести телевизионную программу с упражнениями, которая позже стала выходить по всей стране и продержалась в эфире десятилетиями. Он показывал зрителям упражнения, которые можно было повторять дома, и помогал сделать физическую активность привычкой для людей, далеких от профессионального спорта.

Параллельно росла индустрия коммерческих залов. В 1940–1950-е годы предприниматели, в том числе Вик Танни и сам Лалэйнн, развивали клубы, в которых могли тренироваться мужчины и женщины. Такие пространства предлагали более комфортные условия, разнообразное оборудование и регулярные программы занятий. Впоследствии эта модель привлекла крупные компании, которые начали развивать сети фитнес-клубов.

В 1965 году американский культурист и предприниматель Джо Голд открыл небольшой тренажерный зал Gold’s Gym в Калифорнии. Голд тоже сам проектировал и собирал оборудование для силовых тренировок. Его зал стал местом встреч культуристов и спортсменов, которые приходили туда работать с тяжелыми весами и готовиться к соревнованиям. Со временем Gold’s Gym получил известность далеко за пределами штата.

В 1977 году вышел документальный фильм «Качая железо», рассказывавший о подготовке бодибилдеров, в том числе Арнольда Шварценеггера, к соревнованиям. Фильм помог сделать бодибилдинг частью массовой культуры и укрепил связь между тренажерным залом, физической формой и образом мускулистого тела.

В 1970–1980-е годы стала набирать популярность аэробика. Групповые занятия под музыку, телевизионные программы и видеоуроки привлекли в фитнес-индустрию людей, которые не обязательно хотели наращивать мышцы. Аэробика вышла за пределы фитнес-клубов благодаря книгам и видеокассетам актрисы Джейн Фонды, которые в 1980-е стали бестселлерами. Именно тогда фитнес-клуб стал коммерческим пространством для регулярной физической активности, рассчитанным на широкую аудиторию.

Сегодня под одной крышей могут тренироваться профессиональные спортсмены, любители зумбы и латины, адепты силовых тренировок и те, кто просто хочет поплавать в бассейне после работы. За несколько столетий спортзал превратился в пространство для самых разных целей — и именно эта универсальность сделала фитнес-клуб неотъемлемой частью городской жизни.

items.title: The Family of Nolan Wells Still Wants Justice
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Albert Samaha
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
Entering the high-school football stadium, Christine Wells-Wonsley and Elmore Wonsley could feel the stares.

It was late August, the first game of the season, and thousands from around Ocean Springs, Mississippi, had gathered to cheer for their boys on the city’s brightest stage. A marching band boomed. Cheerleaders danced. The public-address announcer introduced the starting lineup. Amid the spectacle, heads turned toward Wells-Wonsley and Wonsley, eyes following them up the bleachers. “No one really spoke when we walked in,” Wells-Wonsley said. “It was very surreal.”

Eight weeks earlier, on July 4, their 18-year-old son, Nolan Wells, had joined a group of friends on boats out to Horn Island, a roughly ten-mile strip of sandy wilderness where hundreds of locals gathered to swim, fish, and party. Wells never made it back home. His body was found washed up on the island two days later.

Wells had been a pillar of the Ocean Springs High School community. “He had an electric vibe to him,” said his friend Skylan Hunter, a 19-year-old who played football and basketball with Wells. “He’s always smiling. He’s real giggly.” He seemed to find friends everywhere: “You could put him with the smart kids. You could put him with the athletes. You could put Nolan with all the wannabe thugs. You put him with all the hood dudes. You put him around the band kids. He knew everybody. Everyone knew him.” A star wide receiver, Wells helped Ocean Springs win three straight district titles, scoring six touchdowns his senior season, before going off to Southwest Mississippi Community College, a two-and-a-half-hour drive inland, where he hoped to play his way to a Division I scholarship.

His parents were regulars in the bleachers at Greyhound Stadium, familiar faces in a tight-knit community, and now they returned to support Wells’s two younger brothers on the team. Those who purchased a game-day program could flip it open and see a page honoring Wells. But otherwise, nothing at the stadium indicated a beloved alumnus had recently died. There was no ceremony memorializing the tragedy that had rocked the community, no announcement recognizing Wells’s brothers, not even a moment of silence before kickoff. “There was no mention of him,” Wells-Wonsley said. “I feel like Ocean Springs as a whole wants this to just go away.”

But the questions surrounding what exactly happened to Wells on Horn Island have not gone away. The story ricocheted around social media, fueled by suspicions that his death echoed Mississippi’s history of racist violence. It sparked conversations about the safety of Black people in predominantly white spaces. The last known photo of Wells showed him sitting on a boat next to three white friends. Witnesses on the island said they last saw Wells flirting with a white woman. Ben Crump, the prominent civil-rights lawyer, signed on to represent Wells’s family. Al Sharpton spoke at his funeral. Colin Kaepernick paid for an independent autopsy. Terrell Owens and Tyler Perry contributed to the $125,000 reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction in connection with Wells’s death. Within days, facts and falsehoods swirled. Online sleuths and pundits started digging. Death threats flew in every direction. Some accused Wells’s white friends of murder; others blamed Wells’s family for inflaming racial tensions without proof his death was anything but an accident.

On September 21, the district attorney’s office announced that a grand jury declined to issue any indictments for Wells’s death, stating in a report that there was “no credible evidence to support the public allegations” against the friends on the boats and that the “public attacks” against them “are malicious, false, and have no truth in fact or evidence.” In a 15-minute statement, Jackson County district attorney Angel Myers McIlrath condemned those who “have attempted to exploit Nolan’s death to divide and create chaos here.”“The family, the Crump team, and anyone close to Nolan knew his disappearance and death were not the result of racial hate or violence,” she said, “yet the flames of that narrative set against the backdrop of Mississippi’s terrible history were fanned by both people who knew the truth and those who didn’t.” Wells-Wonsley and Wonsley have held firm to their suspicions. At a news conference after the grand-jury report was released, Wells-Wonsley accused McIlrath of prioritizing a “need to get this case done and over with” at the expense of a thorough investigation. “Elmore and I do not believe Nolan simply and accidentally drowned,” said Wells-Wonsley, who, speaking through tears, concluded that “our son’s life does not matter to those who hold positions that are supposed to serve and protect the public.” McIlrath responded in a statement expressing “complete confidence” in the investigation and the grand jury’s decision and blaming Wells’s family for allowing “Nolan’s friends to be publicly accused and have their lives and their family’s lives threatened and reputations ruined.”

When I visited Ocean Springs in September, I found a city struggling to process a tragedy that has shattered the sense of racial harmony many residents take pride in. The circumstances of Wells’s death are still unclear, blocking any path to closure for a grieving family demanding answers in a place where many locals just want to move on.
“Nobody talks about it, but everybody knows about it,” Hunter said. “They talk about it everywhere else but here.”

They talk about it 150 miles up the highway in Summit, a small town surrounded by woods and farmland where Wells attended college. His SMCC football teammates bused down to the Gulf Coast for his funeral. At a team meeting discussing the tragedy, the players dedicated their season to Wells. Their helmets bear NW stickers. “He should have been here with us,” said Nero Taylor, 19, a sophomore offensive lineman. “He was gonna be a big part of it.”

As the players on Wells’s college team took the field on a hot night swarming with lovebugs, the bleachers in John I. Hurst Stadium filled with students familiar with the story. D. J. Cagins, a 19-year-old freshman from Hinds County, about a three-hour drive from Ocean Springs, said he hadn’t intended to follow the investigation but the case seemed to follow him, regularly cycling into his feed, his algorithm serving up fragmented facts and breathless opinions. It was the same for the classmates sitting around him sharing their unfounded theories.
“He was chillin’ with some girl, white dude got mad,” said freshman Jalik Trim, 19.
“They beat the shit out of that man,” said freshman Von Miles, 20. “He could’ve been a star.”
“I feel like they were jealous of him or something,” said Draco, 18.

Cagins grew up in a town where most people are Black. He could count on two hands how many white kids went to his high school. His few encounters with white folks included a traumatic memory: One evening, as he rode bikes with a couple of friends, a group of white teens in a passing pickup truck shouted the N-word at them, then turned their way and accelerated. He and his friends leaped into the bushes to escape. Only once he got to SMCC, which has around the same number of Black and white students, did Cagins find himself regularly interacting with white people.
He and his classmates began to feel wary about Wells’s death when they saw the photo of him on the boat with the white boys.
“Me personally,” Cagins said, “I wouldn’t hang out with that many white people by myself.”
“Oh, nah, that’s not happening,” Miles said. “I’m not hanging around a group of white people.”
“I got white friends, but being the only Black person? Nah,” Trim said.
But it’s different in Ocean Springs. Cagins had been to the Gulf Coast a few times for high-school football games and it felt like another world compared with where he grew up.
“You gon’ see that more down there,” Cagins said.

Down on the bayou, halfway (geographically and spiritually) between New Orleans and the Florida Panhandle, Ocean Springs has developed a distinctive reputation around the state. “Like if Mississippi had Beverly Hills,” said Taylor, who grew up in nearby Gulfport. “Basically, the place you go if you feel like you’re moving up in the world.”

In Ocean Springs, where the median income is roughly $23,000 above the state average, big brick houses sprawl across neat subdivisions along the waterfront. With waters rich in oysters, shrimp, crabs, and catfish, the Gulf Coast became home to a thriving seafood industry. Biloxi got an Air Force base, and soon casinos went up, too. Pascagoula has one of the region’s biggest ports. Ocean Springs was where people went to escape the bustle. The city’s population more than tripled from 1960 to 2000, and in the years after Hurricane Katrina, a wave of development spurred new boutique hotels, an “urban renewal” plan, and debates over gentrification.

Locals describe Ocean Springs as a good place to raise kids or retire, as it offers a suburban backdrop for fishing, shrimp boils, fireworks on the beach, and Mardi Gras celebrations — a taste of Cajun culture “but in a white sort of way,” said Noelle Nolan-Rider, an organizer with the social-justice advocacy group Mississippi Rising Coalition. She moved to Ocean Springs 11 years ago after growing up in Natchez, going to college in Baton Rouge, and living in New Orleans. “It doesn’t include any of the Black culture that makes those places special. It’s more of a white party destination,” she said. She called the city “Bro-cean Springs.”

Slowly, though, more non-white people have made their way there, growing from around 12 percent of the population in 2000 to roughly 20 percent in 2020. Vietnamese and Latino diasporas have moved in. Black families from around the Gulf Coast come for the well-resourced schools, plentiful strip malls, and minuscule crime rates. “Most people from Ocean Springs are not born in Ocean Springs,” Hunter said. “They come here for a better life.”

Wells-Wonsley and Wonsley had grown up elsewhere on the Gulf Coast. Wells-Wonsley was born in the Philippines to a Filipina mother and a Black American father serving at a U.S. Air Force base; they moved to Three Rivers in southern Mississippi, where her father’s family had lived for generations, when she was 3. Wonsley’s grandparents had moved south from the Jackson area for jobs in the shipbuilding industry. They settled down in Moss Point, where the Wonsleys gained a reputation for producing football stars. Three of Wonsley’s uncles played in the NFL, and Wonsley won two state championships at Moss Point High School before playing college ball at Mississippi State. Nolan was a baby when Wells-Wonsley met Wonsley. She was working at a Sprint store in Pascagoula when Wonsley strolled in looking to buy a new phone. They got to talking, started going to the gym together, and developed a friendship that bloomed into romance. Their first home together was in Biloxi. Wells-Wonsley commuted across state lines to Mobile to study for her nurse-practitioner license. Wonsley got a job as an operator at a chemical plant, working the swing shift. They moved to Ocean Springs for the school district.

Wells was the fourth of six children in a blended family. His parents said he had Wells-Wonsley’s “goofiness” and Wonsley’s “attention to detail.” They noticed his peers gravitating to him from an early age. In middle school, his math teacher emailed his parents to relay an anecdote from class: When a special-needs student raised his hand to answer a question, “Nolan got everyone to put their hands down,” Wells-Wonsley recalled, and when the child got it right, “the room just erupted,” with Nolan “hyping everybody up, hyping up the kid.”

Skylan Hunter’s parents saved up for more than five years to buy a house in Ocean Springs just before he started high school. Skylan had been growing up one town over, in Gautier, though the distance felt greater than a few miles. The roads in his neighborhood were bumpier, and people he knew had been killed by gun violence, including a close friend in middle school. A couple of his cousins had already gone off to Ocean Springs.

Skylan had only ever been there to watch the fireworks on the beach and play on the local youth basketball team. He didn’t want to move. “I was nerve-racked,” he said. “What if somebody tried to try me or someone called me the N-word? That was the biggest thing.”

On his first morning in the school cafeteria, he found his cousins sitting with someone who looked vaguely familiar. “I was like, ‘Damn, bro, do I know you?’” Skylan recounted. “And he was like, ‘Sky?’” When Nolan reminded him they’d played grade-school basketball together, the memories clicked into place. Nolan was the quiet point guard with the bald “peanut head.” How could he ever forget that day he and Nolan showed up to practice with new haircuts? One teammate was known to christen fresh cuts with a slap to the back of the head. Nolan got hit early in practice, but when the teammate sneaked up behind Skylan during a scrimmage, it was Nolan who shouted, “Look out!”

Skylan hadn’t seen Nolan since they were 12. He barely recognized him at 15. No longer bald, Nolan now sported a crisp low-cut Afro, and no longer quiet, he held court across campus, the athlete who seemed to be friends with everybody. “He was just real happy,” Skylan said. “If Nolan came up to speak to you, he could know nothing about you, but by his voice, his tone, he would draw you into a conversation for, like, 20, 30 minutes and you wouldn’t realize you don’t know this man.”

On the school bus to football practice, Skylan and Nolan greeted each other with jokes about their respective outfits, Skylan ribbing Nolan about his short shorts, Nolan firing back about Skylan’s skinny jeans. After basketball practice, a group of players often ended up at the McDonald’s down the street from campus, usually in the same seats at the same high-top table, filling the sleepy fast-food joint with howling punch lines. Nolan seemed fluent with anyone he encountered. Hanging out at a white friend’s house, he was known to sometimes slip away from the group to chat with one of the parents. Taylor, his college classmate, marveled at how comfortable he appeared when persuading professors to grant him an extension on an assignment. “He didn’t act Black or white, he acted like Nolan,” said Skylan. He still laughs thinking about how easily Nolan would walk up to a girl at a party, ask her name, inquire about her interests, and next thing you know, they’re chatting like old friends and exchanging numbers. “He switched his voice up,” Skylan recounted, attempting an impression before conceding that he couldn’t do justice to Nolan’s charm. “He was smoother with it than how I’m putting it because I don’t know how to talk to white girls.”

At SMCC, Wells joined several high-school teammates. Every player on the football roster had just one or two years to earn a scholarship to a university, inciting a fierce competition for playing time that wasn’t always conducive to camaraderie, yet Wells “instantly became friends with everyone on the team,” Taylor recalled. Damion Miller, 21, at the time a junior cornerback who had the locker next to Wells, remembered the lanky freshman introducing himself on the first day of practice. “Every time you talk to Nolan you gon’ get a smile,” Miller recalled. He danced after touchdowns at practice and took jokes as easily as he gave them. If Miller had known Wells for longer, he said, “he’d be the best man at my wedding.”

The last time Hunter saw Wells was a few days before July 4. Hunter was working behind the counter at a Chipotle when Wells strolled in with a group of friends. Hunter’s face brightened. Back in town for the summer after his freshman year, Wells had a knack for turning the dullest of evenings into a good time.
“Go ’head and cook that chicken!” Wells hollered playfully.
“I ain’t cooking nothing!” Hunter shot back with a grin.

Wells was with a crew of laid-back white bros who wore flip-flops, drove pickups, lived in big houses along the bayou, and took out their parents’ boats on weekends. Hunter dubbed them the “preppy kids.” He was friendly with some of them, including Warren Hudson and Wyatt Pyron. “They were just cool,” Hunter said. “They’re not gonna try to play call you the N-word just because they think it’s funny.” As Wells headed out with the group, Hunter felt no inkling of anxiety, no sense of foreboding. It was just another summer night in Ocean Springs.

Wells-Wonsley spent the Fourth of July morning with her sister cooking up a big batch of pansit for a friend hosting a family reunion that day. After dropping off the food and returning home exhausted, she napped. Wonsley mowed the lawn. That evening, while preparing dinner, Wells-Wonsley wondered why Wells hadn’t checked in. She called and texted but got no response. Though she considers herself “an anxious person by nature,” she didn’t feel worried at the time, she said. Wells was a responsible 18-year-old out with his friends for his last weekend of summer revelry before returning to the grind of college-football practice. “Maybe he’s in a bad cell-service area or he doesn’t have his phone right there on him,” she said. “So I was just like, you know, Oh, he’ll call back later.” She tried calling again around 10:48 p.m. Still nothing. Twenty minutes later, she received a call from Hudson, who asked if she’d heard from Wells. “And I’m like, ‘What do you mean?’” she recounted. “‘He’s supposed to be with you.’”

Upon learning her son hadn’t ridden back from Horn Island with Hudson, she called authorities to file a missing-person report, then spread word on social media. Snapchat records show dozens of messages friends sent to Wells that night and through the next day asking where he was and if he was okay.
“ay fam i hope u get found soon bro i hope it’s not true they left u in horn island”
“Who tf left you on the island”

Hunter stayed hopeful through the first day as boats and helicopters scanned the water. Maybe Wells was sleeping off a hangover. Maybe he’d made new friends. Maybe he was with a girl. But Hunter woke up on July 6 with dread in his stomach. He was home on the phone with his girlfriend when he got the bad news. First, he felt only sorrow. At the funeral, he tried to keep it together, sitting in the pew with his lips trembling, looking at the casket, before crumpling into sobs. Then he felt anger.

What happened on the island? From the moment Wells went missing, the question cast a light on the friends who rode out with him. That his last known photo showed him as the sole Black teen with a trio of white friends launched the local tragedy into global scrutiny. In national television interviews, the attorney Crump and Wells’s parents shared the details that left them suspicious about some kind of cover-up. The night he went missing, Wells’s family tracked his phone to the house of one of his friends from the boat; when family friend Tashema Hands went with a group to pick it up, she said, his friends took 15 minutes to find it.

His friends from the boat told authorities Wells chose to stay longer on the island and was with a girl, later identified as Katie McCormack, when they last saw him, according to police and grand-jury reports. McCormack also spoke with authorities as well as with Wells’s parents. Her sister posted on social media that Wells had been with McCormack briefly but they parted ways on the island and he wasn’t on her boat back to the mainland. The trail went cold from there. But Wells had been drinking, and the waters around the island can get rough with a steep drop-off and swirling currents. Within 24 hours of authorities finding Wells’s body, Jackson County sheriff John Ledbetter declared no foul play was suspected in the death.

Wells’s family called for an independent investigation. The medical examiner they hired observed bruises on the back of Wells’s head from “blunt-force injury” but no conclusive evidence of foul play and nothing that ruled out an accidental drowning. There was no water in his stomach or airways, but that doesn’t mean much for a body found a day or two after death. Neither the county nor the independent examiner could definitively determine the cause and manner of death.

The mystery drew no shortage of amateur detectives who inspected records, photos, videos, and social-media posts for any detail that could help crack the case. Benign facts, stripped of context, spun into dubious clues suggesting conspiracy. When Roger Mitchell, the Washington, D.C.–based medical examiner, received Wells’s body, pieces of the neck were missing; though Mitchell reviewed them later on-site in Mississippi, his explanation that this was common practice in the autopsy process hardly quelled suspicions online. Crump drew attention to a viral video capturing an altercation on the island, but a different Black teen, Tracestin Shepherd, came forward to say it was his voice in the footage and Wells wasn’t involved.

Meanwhile, the names and faces of several boys on the boats rippled across the internet. They spoke out about receiving death threats. A lawyer for 21-year-old Bart Edmiston, a former high-school-football teammate on one of the boats, sent a cease-and-desist letter to an online influencer demanding she retract and correct social-media posts implicating him in the death. Hudson’s father offered a $50,000 reward for information leading to an arrest and conviction. Hudson, 19, and two others from the boats — Morgan Seymour, 19, and Jax Pitalo, 20 — hired local attorney J. Tyler Cox, who brought on Edward Andrew Paltzik, a defamation lawyer who has represented Donald Trump. The attorneys threatened lawsuits against Crump, Sharpton, and The View co-host Sunny Hostin. An online fundraiser for the boys’ legal fees has received more than $200,000.
Crump and his legal team are “grasping at straws,” Cox said. “It’s an undetermined death, but we just know that our three clients didn’t have anything to do with the death of Nolan.”

“It is undoubtedly a tragedy that Nolan Wells died,” Edmiston’s lawyer, Russ Latino, said. “It is also a different kind of tragedy that innocent young men are having their lives ruined by internet mobs that are inventing ‘facts’ out of thin air.”

Hunter knows those boys. He doesn’t want to believe they could have had anything to do with Wells’s death. But he does feel betrayal. These were supposed to be Wells’s friends, he said. He has heard them defend themselves, proclaiming their affection, cataloguing how often they hung out, seeking to clear their names through proof of their bond. But one thing is clear to Hunter: “Even if they didn’t do anything and just left him, that’s wrong. I feel like, as a friend group, they didn’t take care of the situation or they didn’t handle the situation the best they could, which resulted in the outcome we got.”
He hasn’t spoken to Hudson or Pyron since that night at Chipotle. “Since Nolan passed away,” he said, “they’ve been off the map.”

A few weeks after Wells’s death, four of his friends from the Horn Island trip told their side in a series of interviews with conservative commentator Brandon Tatum, a former cop and college-football player with more than 3 million subscribers to his YouTube channel. Tatum had been one of the boat boys’ earliest and loudest defenders, sharing videos and photos showing that Wells didn’t appear to be on Pyron’s boat as it departed the island. When the boys’ lawyers appeared on his show for a remote interview, local attorney Cox had on his desk, in the background just over his shoulder, a bottle of Tatum’s branded bourbon.

During his interview, Hudson told Tatum he appreciated “how you took our side, not based off someone’s agenda based off of race, because that’s a horrible thing.” He said Wells was like a brother to him. Shepherd, who rode out separately on his uncle’s boat and met up with Wells on the island, called him his best friend. Hudson recounted how Wells visited Seymour at college in Starkville and often caught a ride around Ocean Springs with Pitalo. “We didn’t make Nolan drive anywhere,” Hudson said. “That’s how much we loved him,” Pitalo added.

They said Wells joined them out on the water often. He had been with them on Horn Island the previous Fourth of July and for a birthday party earlier this summer. The night before this year’s Independence Day excursion, Wells and Hudson, among others, stayed at Pitalo’s house. Wells left his car in the driveway and his keys on top of the Xbox. In the morning, they joined a group of 30 people caravanning on three boats for the hourlong ride across Biloxi Bay. Pyron took Wells and seven others in his Triton. Hudson and his college friends piled into Edmiston’s Tideline. The last vessel hauled several more. They reached the island around 11:20 a.m., according to phone records. The shore was already lined with boats as far as the eye could see. “Every area of Horn Island was covered,” Hudson said.

The group’s boats anchored alongside one another. When Wells spotted a digital camera sitting on the console, he proposed that Pitalo, Seymour, and former teammate Erick Alcantara join him for a photo. Then they hopped into the waist-deep water and waded to shore. Everyone left their phones on the boat, scattered across the console. The party raged through the afternoon with hundreds drinking and grilling and bumping music across the beach, a blur of a good time. Shepherd remembered drunkenly telling Wells, “All right, buddy, I love you.” Phone records show Wells last unlocked his phone around 2:18 p.m.

The problems started shortly after three. Shepherd got into an argument with his girlfriend, and when a stranger criticized the way he talked to her, the guys started fighting before others broke it up. Shepherd’s uncle wrangled him back on their boat so they could go home. Then Pyron’s boat suffered mechanical issues. The splashing foot traffic on and off the boat all day had flooded the battery, Hudson said, and the bilge pump wasn’t draining the water. Hudson tried to help Pyron get the boat into working condition; Edmiston prepared to tow it into open water. Pyron called a boat-towing company, and a recording of that call captured a muddle of panicked voices. “We’re all freaking out, not focused on anything else other than the boat,” Hudson said later in the interview with Tatum.

By 4:30 p.m., word spread that the three boats were heading back. Hudson recalled last seeing Wells in the shallows with his arms around McCormack. “I looked at Nolan and Nolan was shaking his head, laughing,” Hudson said. Pyron urged Wells to “get the eff on the boat,” Hudson recalled. “Nolan said, ‘No, I’m staying out here. I’m gonna ride in with somebody else.’”

In their interviews, Hudson and Pitalo said that it was common for people to ride back on a different boat than the one they came in on and that Wells wasn’t the only person in their group who stayed on the still-bustling island that afternoon. “At Horn Island, you don’t even have to know somebody to ask for a ride back in,” Pitalo said. “If you ask anybody out there, 100 percent they’ll bring you back in.” Wells’s parents have questioned this version of events, asserting it would have been unlike him to split off from his friends.

At a house party that night, sometime before 11 p.m., Hudson asked Pyron and the others if they’d heard from Wells. Hudson texted Wells’s friend Jayvon Williams, who hadn’t heard from him either, then called Wells-Wonsley. Hudson called the Coast Guard next. The digital-camera photo showed what Wells was last seen wearing, so his family used that image in posts announcing his disappearance.

Pyron and Seymour were at Pitalo’s house later that night when Williams’s mother, Tashema Hands, showed up with a group of Wells’s friends seeking his phone. It was in Pyron’s truck along with other phones left on the boat. “We didn’t know who they belonged to,” Hudson said. Seymour described the encounter as “confrontational.”“They’re all up in our faces going crazy, asking where Nolan is,” Pitalo said. When the group demanded to inspect Pyron’s boat, Pyron gave his address, then called 911, Seymour recalled, telling the dispatcher, “These people are on the way to my house or already at my house. My mom and my dad are there alone, and they know nothing about this.” After looking through the boat and speaking with Pyron’s mother, the group returned to Pitalo’s house, “hanging out in my front yard,” he said, and “wouldn’t leave” until his brother called the cops. “They’re basically assuming we did something to our friend,” Pitalo said.
By the following afternoon, with Wells still missing, one group chat showed their dawning realization that many people on Facebook were blaming them.
“Our friend group is getting ass blasted on fb just don’t read that bs or be running yalls mouths bc ppl will make an inch turn into a mile”
“Turn off you locations they’ve been showing up to peoples houses too”
“No one say anything to anyone don’t talk out of our friendgroup”
“I love yall so much if anyone needs a place to go my house is always open if yall don’t want to be by yourselves”
“Deadass I don’t even wanna know what my fb looks like”

In his interview with Tatum, Hudson said he had received thousands of death threats and didn’t attend Wells’s funeral “for my own safety.” Seymour and Pitalo didn’t go either. “Imagine you were 19 years old and your best friend just died and now the whole internet is accusing you of killing him,” Hudson said. “We were Nolan’s closest friends … This was a brotherhood. This was my brother. For the internet to take away our privileges to go to his funeral because they think t

items.title: The Democratic Spam Trap
items.description: The Democratic Party is always losing ground, falling short of its goals, and running out of time. Candidates and PACs say this again and again, day after day, to loyal supporters, one-time donors, and what can feel like nearly every human being whose email ad
items.author: Alex Bronzini-Vender
paragraphs: The Democratic Party is always losing ground, falling short of its goals, and running out of time. Candidates and PACs say this again and again, day after day, to loyal supporters, one-time donors, and what can feel like nearly every human being whose email address or phone number they’ve gotten their hands on. A campaign’s cash has dried up. An opponent is gaining steam. A critical fundraising deadline has been missed. The midterms are approaching and Trump doesn’t want you to see this! Please help?

Sometimes their pleas are sheepish. Since the end of July, Sherrod Brown’s Senate campaign has warned supporters at least 17 times that “donations have taken a nosedive.” Ten of those emails included the same apology: “I’m sorry to be sending this, but I have no cards left to play.” (Luckily, he keeps finding more cards.) Other times candidates confess their nerves, hoping for sympathy. “I’m getting worried,” Roy Cooper wrote in October; “I am worried,” Gavin Newsom shared hours later; and “a very worried James Carville” emailed the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee’s list twice that month. At times, subject lines are only an attention-grabbing interjection: “Ugh …” from Yassamin Ansari, “Oof …” from John Hickenlooper, “Yikes” from Gina Hinojosa, “Uh oh ⏱️” from the Senate Majority PAC.

By now, we have gotten used to this register each campaign season. Most of these messages are so transparently ridiculous that they’re easy to ignore. Yet their sheer stupidity and volume raises an obvious question: If everyone you know immediately deletes these things, why on earth do they keep coming? The truth is they aren’t really for you. The unhinged dialect is the product of a modern and effective campaign apparatus built on half-lying to supporters and milking as much cash as possible from the shrinking pool of Americans who still find these panicked emails enlivening. Never mind the long-term cost to the party or to politics itself — it works.

Does it involve lying? Well, define lying. When House Majority PAC announced in August that it was matching donations 800 percent until a midnight deadline “for the FIRST time all year,” that may well have been true. But then it offered the same midnight-deadline match for the “FIRST time all year” in early September and again later that month. Was that lying? How about on September 24, when the PAC upped the ante, promising to match donations made before midnight by 900 percent, also “for the FIRST time all year” — a claim it proceeded to repeat, along with a midnight deadline, five more times in October? (House Majority PAC did not respond to a request for comment.)

And what should we call it when the party peddles essentially imaginary credentials to its supporters? From January 2025 through September 2026, the DSCC sent 122 separate emails urging recipients to activate their “Democratic Membership,” according to an archive maintained by the journalist Derek Willis. This year, the Democratic National Committee is peddling “2026 DNC Member Cards” for $7 apiece — official-sounding stuff, though not one of the 52 emails pitching them in Willis’s archive names a single benefit that “membership” actually confers.

Maybe it’s not so bad. You would never fall for these emails. “Most of us dismiss them as annoying spam,” Adam Bonica, a political scientist at Stanford, wrote in a Substack post in August. But not everyone does. “Federal election records reveal a hidden population,” Bonica concluded, “for whom these messages prove surprisingly effective.” Specifically, old people.

Ironically, Bonica stumbled onto the problem while trying to study young donors. As of 2020, he tells me, about 85 percent of donors who were millennials or younger were giving to Democrats. However, when he and the Berkeley political scientist Jake Grumbach updated their research on donor ages through the 2024 cycle, they noticed something strange. Instead of getting younger, the average Democratic donor had gotten older — way older. Much of that shift, they discovered, was being driven by a small group of elderly donors who were donating over and over again, hundreds and sometimes thousands of times.

And where is all the money from this small cluster of seniors — the ones who seem to really believe those urgent emails — ending up? Often not with candidates. When those panicked appeals come from actual campaigns or official party committees, the cash pays for door knockers and TV ads in swing states. But increasingly, candidates are competing for those donors against a vast ecosystem of PACs that raise millions through a barrage of breathless texts and emails, only to spend much of the haul on raising even more money.

Bonica calls these outfits “spam PACs,” and he counts 145 of them; he refers to their targets as “captive donors.” By his tally, some 138,000 people have donated to spam PACs at least 100 times each; their average age is 75. Though they make up less than one percent of all Democratic donors, this tiny cohort of givers has supplied nearly half of the $1.4 billion these PACs have hauled in since 2017. It is, Bonica feels, “tried-and-true, ridiculous but effective elder exploitation.” And the problem, he claims, is getting worse. Since the 2024 election, Bonica counts 58 brand-new Democratic committees that fit his definition of a spam PAC. In 2025 alone, he found, these groups raised more from individual donors than every Democratic Senate candidate combined.

Of course, both parties spam and mislead their donors. If anything, Republicans are worse. When CNN traced over $6 million that a group of vulnerable elderly donors gave between 2019 and 2024, nearly $4 million went to Republican candidates and groups. In January, Trump’s leadership PAC emailed supporters in the president’s name about an overdue “Citizens Only Survey.” “Don’t tell me,” it read, “YOU’RE AN ILLEGAL ALIEN?!?” This was the “FINAL MOMENT” to prove otherwise — if not, it warned, ICE would “track you down.” The survey led to a donation page.

With Republicans literally threatening to deport their would-be donors, why focus on Democrats? Bonica says it is because he’s trying to save the party from itself. Lately, the Republican Party’s small-dollar donation machine has begun sputtering. This cycle, roughly 1.5 million people have given to federal Republican candidates and committees through WinRed, down from 2.2 million at the same point in 2022, according to a Politico analysis of FEC filings. Bonica suspects that years of relentless spammy appeals to older donors have finally burnt out the GOP’s base. Now, he worries, Democrats are headed down the same path.

His research has drawn plenty of criticism, including from fellow Democrats (and, less surprisingly, from the lawyers for some of the groups he names). Still, even his critics concede he’s onto something. A Democratic consultant who has spent years analyzing donor data for nonprofits and is critical of Bonica’s work agrees that “scammy fundraising” is “definitely a thing,” as is “fundraising heavily from the elderly.” None of the operatives I spoke with deny that something has gone badly wrong. The party itself has acknowledged the problem. Over the past two years, the Harris campaign, ActBlue, and the DNC have all warned supporters about deceptive fundraising, blaming the problem on “bad actors.”

But the call is coming from inside the house. The Democratic Party’s flagship committees pioneered the high-volume, hair-on-fire email playbook. Their alumni peddled those tactics to an ever-growing ecosystem of outside firms and PACs. Today, even as candidates have backed away from the most notorious consultancies, the style they perfected has become the lingua franca of Democratic fundraising. “At any given time, the apocalypse happens maybe twice a day,” says a campaign staffer for a Democratic member of Congress. “Very, very few members of Congress,” he tells me, “don’t need to resort to things like this.”

This is the trap the Democratic Party has built for itself. Collectively, the spam machine is cannibalizing the party’s small-dollar base, funneling millions from competitive races into the pockets of fundraising consultants. Yet, individually, no campaign can afford to unilaterally disarm. Because donor lists are constantly exchanged, candidates are fighting for attention in the same inboxes as the most shameless spam PACs. And once voters have been conditioned to only respond to five-alarm fires, sending polite emails is a financial death sentence for almost any campaign.

Among megadonors, Republicans dominate, and the party’s flagship committees rely on small-dollar givers. For any single campaign on any given day, the annoying emails work. “It’s as simple as that,” says the Democratic campaign staffer. Even those who have spent years criticizing the tactics agree. “Is it scammy and treats people like shit and does real damage to the Democratic Party brand? Absolutely,” Amanda Litman, co-founder of the progressive group Run for Something, tells me. “But the job, for these people, is to raise money.”

Over the past two years, the party has ostensibly tried to kick the habit. Some operatives genuinely want to move on: They have read Bonica’s complaints and see the moral and strategic downsides of financially strip-mining MS NOW–watching grandparents. But if Democrats stop sending the psychotic texts and emails, they’ll struggle to compete. And with so many seats in play, and the stakes so high, few in the party are willing to risk falling behind by asking nicely. In a sense, the emails’ desperation — Susan, can’t you please spare a moment for democracy? — is real.

Before email fundraising became a vice, Democrats believed it was a force for good. The internet helped Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign rewrite the rules of political giving, shattering “every grassroots fundraising record that existed at the time,” says Josh Nelson, the CEO of the progressive ad platform Civic Shout. The new campaign workers thought they could use the techniques to build a better party. No longer would candidates and committees need to approach the rich hat in hand; they could go to everyone else.

By 2012, Democratic campaigns had turned the practice into a science. “We were running A/B tests and A/B/C/D tests all the time,” says Litman, then a junior staffer on the Obama email team. That year, most of Obama’s $690 million online haul came from email-based outreach. At one point, Litman says, the campaign wanted to know whether there was a limit to how many appeals it could send before supporters stopped giving. So she began blasting a random slice of the list with more emails than everyone else. More people did unsubscribe. But the people who remained gave more than usual — enough to make up for the defectors. Staffers began half-jokingly riffing on the Lindsay Lohan line in Mean Girls: When it comes to spamming donors, “the limit does not exist.”

Back then, the people sending those emails policed one another. Every December, Democratic digital staffers would convene at RootsCamp — a freewheeling, hippieish “unconference” in Washington, D.C. Notoriously, the conference had no preset program. On day one, RootsCampers would pitch and vote on session ideas. David Karpf, a George Washington University political scientist, attended nearly every year between 2008 and 2015. (He turned 30 at his first one.) Each RootsCamp, Karpf says, was a chance to argue about the field’s future. And from the outset, the most contentious question was volume. Some pro-spam staffers contended that while a high volume of emails would prompt some people to unsubscribe, the donations from those who remained would increase. Others disagreed, Karpf recalls. “You’re polluting the commons,” they’d say. “You’re ruining this tactic.”

In those days, it was a small world. Everyone had worked on campaigns together and would potentially do so again. “The perspective of your peers,” Karpf tells me, would exert “some real pressure.” Today’s most aggressive tactics “would not have flown back then,” he says. Whoever sent the most underhanded emails would show up at RootsCamp “and everyone would yell in their face.” Next campaign season, the culprit might not get hired.

After the Obama campaign, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee invested heavily in email, acquiring lists and building tools to help candidates swap donors. The group had seen Obama’s numbers, and it “essentially said, ‘We want in on that action,’” Nelson tells me. At the committee, every variable was up for testing, from subject lines and tone to “the level of urgency.” Along the way, Nelson says, the DCCC realized it could go much further than Obama; the committee began using fake donation matches and recurring life-or-death midnight deadlines. By 2011, Karpf noticed younger operatives routinely confronting staffers for “one of the major Democratic party organs,” charging them with “burning through their email lists and, in doing so, making all of this harder to do for everyone else.”

The problem? The DCCC’s strategy was a runaway success. Its online haul more than tripled in a single cycle, jumping from $14.6 million in 2010 to $49.3 million in 2012. By 2014, the committee’s emails read, per the Daily Beast, like “part fundraising pitch, part hostage note.” Steve Israel, the Long Island representative who chaired the committee at the time, was sorry but not that sorry. “I apologize all over the country for the volume of email people get,” he told reporters that year, “but it works.”

In 2014, the architects of the approach took their methods private and launched Mothership Strategies. They included Greg Berlin, who had served as the DCCC’s digital campaign director — helping more than two dozen House campaigns build their email programs — and Charles Starnes, the committee’s deputy digital director. In the early years, business was good.

Mothership ran email strategy for Jon Ossoff’s special-election campaign in Georgia in 2017, turning a sleepy off-year race into a nationwide liberal obsession that vacuumed up more than $30 million. Ossoff lost anyway. And in the aftermath, The New Republic concluded that the race had “only one winner: Mothership Strategies.” The firm became inescapable. Federal committees’ payments to the firm jumped from $7.1 million in the 2016 cycle to $96 million in 2020. Candidates from every faction of the Democratic Party wanted their turn at the money printer. That cycle, the firm took payments from Ossoff, Jaime Harrison, John Lewis, Ilhan Omar, and the eventual presidential nominee himself, Joe Biden.

Mothership made enemies too. In 2019, the Washington Post reported that, among Democratic insiders, Mothership was “derided as the ‘M-word’ because of its aggressive and sometimes misleading tactics.” Critics said the firm charged some clients a 15 percent commission, well above the industry-standard 7 to 10 percent. (Mothership told the Post that it had “retained less than half” of the $35 million committees had paid it over the previous two years, passing the rest on to vendors.) Even some of the firm’s clients were uncomfortable “with a lot of the tactics we used,” says a former Mothership digital strategist whose job included writing some of its now-infamous email copy.

“We would make our buttons larger so the area’s more clickable for old people to press donate,” the strategist tells me. Mothership borrowed techniques like optimizing user interfaces for macular degeneration from the sleaziest corners of e-commerce, she recalls. In many ways, she says, the company was “ahead of its field.” Now such tactics are normal.

Candidates tolerated the firm’s habit of “pushing the boundaries” throughout the late 2010s, Karpf says. In the 2020 cycle, they paid Mothership nearly $25 million. But the bad press kept coming. In 2021, the New York Times examined the major Democratic committees issuing the most refunds to givers in California — a telltale sign of regretted or accidental donations; the ten groups whose refunded donors skewed oldest were all Mothership clients. It was hard to chalk that up to coincidence. Payments from candidates plunged to $2 million in the 2022 cycle and about $70,000 in the 2024 cycle. This cycle, candidates have paid the firm just $1.4 million. (Even Ossoff, the firm’s golden boy, hasn’t paid the firm since 2021.)

Does that mean Mothership has withered away? Hardly. Independent PACs had long made up the bulk of the firm’s business, and as squeamish campaigns backed away, that side of the operation grew to fill the void. In 2024, PACs with no ties to a candidate or officeholder paid the firm about $70 million, more than in any previous cycle. Since Trump retook office, at least 46 committees have paid Mothership for the first time, many of them bearing generic names cobbled together from liberal buzzwords: Elect Diverse Democrats 2026, Dem Turnout 2026, Pro-Choice Majority 2026, and the No Kings PAC (which, its website helpfully notes in tiny print, is “not affiliated with NoKings.org”). Through mid-October, independent PACs and super-PACs had paid Mothership at least $47.9 million this cycle, 47 percent more than at the same point four years ago. In effect, by abandoning Mothership, candidates haven’t starved the spam machine. Instead, they’ve left it almost entirely in the hands of outside groups that aren’t accountable to voters and have no obligation to help actual campaigns. “Nothing grassroots was coming out of it,” the Mothership copywriter tells me.

“Our top priority is netting resources for candidates and advocacy groups, helping them raise money they otherwise wouldn’t have to invest in door-knocking, candidate donations, IEs, and other tactics to win elections for Democrats and advance progressive causes,” says Will Block, a partner at Mothership Strategies. “While we recognize that not everyone appreciates the urgency of these messages, publishing misleading allegations contributes to hand-wringing and hurts Democrats’ ability to raise resources needed to fight back against Republicans’ big- and small-dollar fundraising machines that continue operating without any scrutiny.” Mothership doesn’t “want anyone to be taken advantage of,” Block says, “and all of our clients have a no questions asked, full refund policy for unintended contributions.”

But what drives insiders crazy is not the spam. It’s that some of Mothership’s PAC clients take in millions and seem to spend it, as the campaign staffer puts it, on “just about fuck all.” Take Progressive Turnout Project, one of the firm’s biggest clients. This year, Bonica tallied the itemized expenses filed by PTP and seven other PACs overseen by the same treasurer, Harry Pascal. (Seven are current or past clients of Mothership.) From 2017 through 2025, he found, the network had relieved donors of more than $390 million. Only about $20 million of that — roughly five cents on the dollar — went to Democratic candidates or ads supporting them. By Bonica’s count, the network plowed most of the rest into raising more money. Some of these entities are open to the criticism. “We dislike the high cost of fundraising and hope to reduce that expense as the PAC grows,” the No Kings PAC told me when I asked about its budget. “While digital fundraising continues to face scrutiny — which we think is totally valid — there are costs to getting candidates elected, no matter how you do it.”

Progressive Turnout Project fiercely disputes Bonica’s math. He says that when the group’s lawyers reached out to him, they said it had spent $177 million on fundraising, not $249 million. “Progressive Turnout Project and our affiliated entities spend the majority of the funds we raise on programs that rally Democrats to vote,” the group tells me. Bonica attributes most of the gap between its estimate and his to about $48 million in Facebook ads that PTP labeled “digital organizing.” These ads function almost entirely as fundraising pitches, he argues. And even by the group’s accounting, he says, it spends over 40 cents of every dollar it raises on pulling in more money.

Insofar as the party has acknowledged the problem, it’s mostly cast the issue as the work of a few rogue outsiders, whom it insists it’s reined in. In summer 2024, as donations poured in behind Kamala Harris, her campaign warned that supporters were being “inundated” with texts “from bad actors trying to take advantage of the urgency Democrats are feeling.” A year later, in August 2025, ActBlue promised to “take faster action against bad actors” and “address the practices that frustrate and deceive donors.” The platform rewrote its rules to ban fake “membership programs” and “unverified matching claims.” Two months later, the DNC sent a cease-and-desist letter to a super-PAC called National Democrats, which had raised more than $500,000 largely through what the committee called “misleading text-message campaigns.”

But the party seems either unwilling or unable to shut down the racket. It can’t dictate what independent PACs send, operatives tell me. “This is the downside of nobody being really in charge of the Democratic Party,” Litman says. Nor can payment processors easily police the problem: It’s a game of whack-a-mole. When groups get booted off ActBlue for misleading donors, Litman says, “they’re just moving to different platforms.” Then there’s the awkward reality that the party’s own top committees, like the DCCC and DSCC, raise money pretty much the same way. Even if party leaders could do something, cracking down on Mothership’s methods would mean cracking down on their own. “If you say these tactics are unethical and should be illegal, it’s like, That’s how you’re raising money,” Litman says.

Democrats have plenty of plausible excuses. “Older Americans donate more to charity,” Block tells me. “They are more civically engaged, more financially stable, and more likely to have established patterns of philanthropic giving.” Bonica’s critics also say that the FEC filings he relies on don’t always tell the whole story, either: A line item that looks like a committee plowing money back into fundraising can sometimes mask real spending on voter outreach. And Republicans, of course, are often up to worse tactics. But does that excuse emails like the one the Progressive Turnout Project sent in January 2023? Styled as a forwarded message from a sender called “final attempt,” it informed the recipient that “Pro-Senior Groups” were “pushing for a fourth $1,400 stimulus payment for Social Security seniors.” And “if top supporters like you don’t respond,” the group warned, “then we won’t have any data.” An animated clock ticked down beneath the words “RESPONSES DUE IN: 60 MINUTES.”

Candidates who dropped Mothership are still competing on its terms. Donor lists get bought, rented, and swapped, Litman explains, so someone who gives to one candidate soon ends up on everyone’s list. Because people tend to respond to the most alarming and urgent-looking appeals they get, the worst actors set the bar. It’s a classic collective-action problem: As Litman puts it, the spammiest tactics will “pollute the well for everyone.” Today, a candidate who refuses to play along will generally need to be “willing to raise less money,” she says. Few are. “All of Mothership’s tactics,” Karpf says, are now “everybody else’s problem.”

In the upside-down moral universe of modern campaign finance, terrorizing retirees can be cast as a badge of progressive virtue. “You can’t win a war and keep your hands clean,” the campaign staffer tells me. When Democrats turn down money from AIPAC, big oil, crypto, sportsbooks, and AI, they “have to fundraise a lot more desperately.” Yes, the staffer concedes, the emails reach “people who are older and therefore more vulnerable to that type of messaging.” But if being “an end-of-the-world freak” keeps a candidate independent, so be it. It’s a noble trade-off: to keep a candidate pure of corporate corruption, Grandma simply has to take one for the team. “Tell me the sky is falling,” the staffer says. “I don’t give a shit.”

Arthur, 86, fits Bonica’s profile of a “captive donor” almost exactly. He lives in a gated community near Boca Raton, Florida. There’s a golf course a short walk away, but he hasn’t played since his back gave out. Mostly, he sits by the phone calling friends and family. A few hours later, he will call them all again with no memory of having done so earlier; he’s had Alzheimer’s disease for more than a decade. Between calls, he watches television. When it isn’t golf or football, “he’s got the MSNBC doom loop going,” his grandson, Eli, tells me. (At Eli’s request, both names are pseudonyms.)

Last year, after an operation on his back, Arthur spent six weeks in the hospital. Unable to reach his phone from bed, he relied on his family to monitor it for him. That’s how Eli discovered how relentlessly Democratic fundraisers were hitting up his grandfather for cash. Alongside the texts from worried friends and family, an inordinate number of buzzes came from Democratic campaigns or PACs asking for money. When Arthur went home and got back into his routine, his family could see the full scope of the problem. If the fundraisers asked, Arthur almost always said yes. Often, he seemed to have little recollection of the donations he’d made hours earlier. On a single Sunday that October, he donated at least ten times: four times to the DCCC; twice to a PAC called Democratic Movement; and once each to Nancy Pelosi, Colin Allred, Get Out the Vote PAC, and a PAC called Pro-Choice Democrats.

Arthur has probably never heard of Mothership Strategies. Still, nearly half of the 262 gifts he’s made since January 2025 have gone to committees that paid the firm this cycle, including six PACs that didn’t exist before Election Day 2024. Together, the 20 PACs on his list that employ Mothership have raised about $103 million this cycle, not counting money they shuffled among affiliated committees. They’ve paid nearly a third of it, $31.9 million, to Mothership.

Pro-Choice Democrats, Arthur’s most frequent beneficiary, registered with the FEC in August 2025. Five weeks later, Arthur made his first donation to the group, followed by three more that same day. He has paid it at least $15 a month since. By mid-October, the PAC had raised $2 million, mostly in small, unitemized gifts. It had not given a cent directly to a candidate. Instead, it paid more than $860,000 to Mothership — 42 cents of every dollar it raised — largely for “peer to peer texting” and “digital fundraising services.” It routed another $800,000 to Elect Democratic Women, a PAC that also employs the firm. Retired Dems 2026, another group near the top of Arthur’s list, is a super-PAC. Of the $2.42 million the group had spent through September, $1.37 million went to Mothership. In effect, over half of what the super-PAC spends appears to go to asking Arthur, and people like him, for more.

Across the country, families often discover that an aging parent has become a captive donor only after their funeral, when they finally go through their bank statements. Eli caught on sooner. But whom do you call? Block says that, if someone informs Mothership that “their loved one is unwell, these donors are immediately suppressed from future solicitations.” But Arthur gives to dozens of committees, only some of them Mothership clients. His family, like most, had never heard of the firm. His caretakers, all Democrats themselves, have tried to get him off the lists one-by-one instead. Eli says it hasn’t worked. “You might think you’ve gotten off,” Eli says, “and then just like that, you’re back on.” Every few days, another urgent plea slips through, and Arthur sends off another $15 or $25 to save the country he loves. He surely doesn’t realize how little of his money actually goes toward buying yard signs or TV ads — and how much of it will pay for the next ask.

items.title: Can Dems Actually Win the Senate? Here's a State-by-State Guide
items.description: The midterm elections are finally here, and all signs point to a successful showing from Democrats. The party has long been expected to take back control of the House of Representatives, but the Senate seemed like a pipe dream … that was until Donald Trump lau
items.author: Jack Crosbie; Nikki McCann Ramirez; Ryan Bort
paragraphs: The midterm elections are finally here, and all signs point to a successful showing from Democrats. The party has long been expected to take back control of the House of Representatives, but the Senate seemed like a pipe dream … that was until Donald Trump launched a war against Iran, driving costs up and causing his popularity to crater. Republican candidates have suffered as a result, and the GOP is suddenly in danger of losing Senate seats in red states they’ve held safely for years.

“Democrats are recognizing this opportunity and hoping that party leaders and the candidates that are able to finish the deal and win in these places where they have been extremely weak for decades,” Tatishe Nteta, provost of political science at UMass-Amherst, recently told Rolling Stone, noting that their polling has found “a clear enthusiasm gap between Democrats and Republicans about voting in the midterm election.”
“[Winning the Senate would] do untold damage to the Trump agenda for his last two years in office,” Nteta adds.

So how would Democrats have to perform on Tuesday to actually win the Senate, take total control of Congress, and put Trump and his administration on the defensive for the remainder of the president’s term?

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate. Vice President JD Vance represents a tie-breaking vote in an evenly split Senate, which means Democrats need to pick up a net of four seats to lock down the majority. There are 35 Senate seats up for election this year, 13 of which are particularly competitive. Nine of these seats are currently controlled by Republicans, which means whichever party wins the majority (seven or more) of these 13 seats will likely win control of the Senate. Democrats are in pretty good shape — according to the latest polls, anyway — including in red states like Texas and Ohio, but it’s going to be very, very close.
Here’s where each race stands:
Current status: Republican
Who’s running: Texas’ MAGA Attorney General Ken Paxton and Democratic State Rep. James Talarico. Paxton defeated current Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary earlier this year.
Election Day: Polls close as early as 7 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Texas may be the grand prize of the 2026 midterms. A Democrat has not won a statewide election in the Lone Star State in over three decades, but this year conditions might be just right for the party to achieve the elusive Texas flip. Trump’s popularity is so low that it’s dragging down the Republicans who are actually on the ballot, including Paxton. At the same time, the Texas constituencies that Trump managed to bring onboard in 2024 are being pummeled by his economic and immigration policies. To top it all off, Paxton is a notably weak candidate, with an extensive history of public corruption and little experience running a competitive campaign. While Republicans have settled on trying to paint Talarico as a “woke” warrior obsessed with trans kids and socialism, the former seminarian has run a highly disciplined campaign focused on economic issues, anti-corruption, and a common sense “love thy neighbor” ethos. He’s got a good shot but — like trying to kick the football Lucy is holding — Texas Democrats have ended up on their ass too many times to count, and the state won’t be a guarantee until it’s been won.

What are the polls saying: Polling shows a narrow race between Paxton and Talarico, with the Democrat consistently leading by a single-digit margin in most major polls. Trump and Republicans are pouring stupid amounts of money and time into the state to try to drag Paxton over the line, and gin up turnout. Whatever the outcome, it’s looking like it will be a nail-biter on election night.
Current status: Democratic
Who’s running: Epidemiologist and local public health official Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, and former Republican House Rep. Mike Rodgers. Democratic Sen. Gary Peters is retiring at the end of his term.
Election Day: Polls close as early as 7 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: This one’s been pretty ugly. Michigan, a state with a large Muslim population, has become the nexus of Democrats’ internal war over how the party — and the United States — should respond to the ongoing genocide in Gaza. Rogers sailed through the GOP primary, while the progressive El-Sayed fought a tooth-and-nail campaign against moderate Hayley Sevens — a pro-Israel Democrat backed by Senate leadership and tens of millions in outsider spending.

El-Sayed — an economic populist and advocate for universal healthcare — managed to pull off the win for the nomination over Stevens, who has since endorsed his candidacy, but the race has remained a mess of ideological and culture war proxy battles. Rogers and Republicans have attempted to malign El-Sayed’s Muslim faith by promoting false links to extremism and terrorist movements. They’re also doing all they can to highlight his association with socialist Twitch streamer Hasan Piker. All in all, both Republicans and Democrats are framing El-Sayed’s candidacy as symbolic of the progressive left’s ambitions toward higher office.
The race became even more chaotic days before the election, when Stevens endorsed Rogers after feeling jilted by the El-Sayed campaign. Will it matter?

What are the polls saying: That it’s too close for anyone’s comfort. El-Sayed has led in most major polls. Recent polling shows he may be building a lead as the campaign season enters its terminal phase, with a late September Maris poll giving him a seven-point advantage, and the final New York Times/Siena poll putting him up 11.
Current status: Republican
Who’s running: Republican incumbent Jon Husted and former Sen. Sherrod Brown
Election Day: Polls close at 7:30 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Ohio is bit of a strange case: Longtime Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who was ousted by Republican Bernie Moreno in the 2024 election, is looking to win back a seat in the Senate by knocking off incumbent Jon Husted in a special election to fill the seat vacated when J.D. Vance became vice president. Husted, a former lieutenant governor, was appointed to the seat by Gov. Mike DeWine in 2025, and hasn’t had long to establish himself as much of a political force. Brown has been a mainstay in the state for decades. Brown only narrowly lost his seat in 2024 with Trump at the top of the ticket — but now, with the president’s popularity in the dumpster, he has a good shot at winning back Ohio voters who see him as a safe, responsible, known quantity.

What are the polls saying: A Marist poll from late September has Brown up 51 to 43 over Husted. Ohio’s voters have overwhelmingly supported Trump each time he’s run, but the state’s strong ties to union labor and American industry mean that the brutal economic forecast has weakened their support for the overall Republican project. A recent Fox News poll showed that Ohio voters gave Trump a 42 percent approval rating, versus 57 percent disapproval. The final New York Times/Siena poll gave Brown a five-point edge.
Current status: Republican
Who’s running: Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper and former RNC Chair Michael Watley
Election Day: Polls close at 7:30 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: North Carolina is one of the most significant battlegrounds in the midterms, as retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis has decided to step down from his seat in a terrible climate for his party in the state. Roy Cooper, a Democrat and popular former governor of the state, has decided to step in — and thus far, he’s beating the pants off former RNC Chair Michael Watley. The gap is so big that the GOP’s top Super PAC has pulled ad funding from the state, figuring they’ll cut their losses and put the money into a more competitive race, like Kansas. Cooper is coming off two terms as the state’s governor, in which he presided over a popular and widespread Medicaid expansion.

What are the polls saying: The polls have Cooper up anywhere from +5 to +12. That could be overstating things, but considering Cooper was the first Democrat to beat a sitting Republican governor when he first ran in a statewide election in 2016 — with Trump on the ballot — it seems like about as safe of a bet as Democrats can get to flip a seat this cycle.
Current status: Republican
Who’s running: Longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, a former state senator
Election Day: Polls close at 8 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Woof. How long do you have? Democrats nominated Troy Jackson, an inoffensive, plainspoken former Maine state senator after getting off the absolute roller coaster of Graham Platner’s now-infamous candidacy. Platner’s journey from aw-shucks oyster farmer to poll-leading political juggernaut took the party by storm, and looked to put them in a commanding lead over Collins.
