That was until Platner’s past — which included a Nazi tattoo, repeated infidelity, and accusations of sexual assault — finally caught up with them. Jackson stepped in to fill the gap, and has been struggling to command the same kind of numbers while also navigating the delicate lane between straight talk and consultant-addled jargon. Collins, meanwhile, is currently weathering a shocking, blatant corruption scandal — although she’s proved almost impossible to unseat in the past, no matter the political headwinds.

What are the polls saying: It’s close. A New York Times poll from late September showed Collins up 49 to 46 over Jackson, but the same poll in early November has Jackson up five. An Emerson poll released just before the election had Collins up two.
Current status: Democratic
Who’s running: Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas is running against former Republican Sen. John Sununu. Current Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen is not seeking reelection.
Election Day: Polls close as early as 7 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: New Hampshire is a curious electoral case. In 2024, Vice President Kamala Harris barely managed to win the state. Its entire congressional delegation is Democratic, but the governorship and General Court (the fancy New Hampshire term for its state legislature) are Republican-controlled.

With name recognition, a monetary advantage, and persistent distaste among voters for Democrats, Sununu has managed to keep Democrats in the state on their toes, and may manage to squeeze out a much-needed victory for Republicans amid a potential blue wave election. Pappas on the other hand is riding the anti-incumbency wave beleaguering Republicans this cycle, and has flexed his credentials as a moderate Democrat to win over independents.
What are the polls saying: Recent polling has shown Pappas with a comfortable lead. The FiftyPlusOne polling average puts him at 51.8 percent to 43.0 for Sununu.
Current status: Democratic
Who’s running: Incumbent Democrat Jon Ossoff is facing off with Republican Rep. Mike Collins, a prominent Trump ally.
Election Day: Polls close at 7 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: In 2020, Ossoff helped deliver Democrats a 50-50 Senate majority under President Joe Biden. Now, in his first bid for reelection, Ossoff is reminding voters exactly how capable he is as a candidate, and even drawing speculation about a presidential run in 2028.

Collins, a close Trump ally and self-described “MAGA warrior” who supported Trump’s efforts to meddle with the GA election in 2020, is struggling to outrun his association with the president. Trump’s insistence that voters pretend he’s on the ballot seems to be dragging down the popularity of Republican candidates across the country, but Collins has continued to campaign alongside the president. Democrats will probably need to hold onto Ossoff’s seat in order to wrest the Senate majority from Republicans, and it seems like they have a good chance to do just that.
What are the polls saying: The race is rated as “likely Democratic” by the Cook Political Report, and Ossoff has built a solid lead in recent polls.
Current status: Republican
Who’s running: Democratic State Rep. Josh Turek is running against Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson. Current Sen. Joni Ernst is not seeking reelection.
Election Day: Polls close at 8 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Iowa wasn’t really even on the map for Democrats until pretty recently. But in August, the Cook Political Report moved the race from a “lean Republican” to a “toss-up.” Turek, a professional wheelchair basketball player and Paralympic athlete, managed to make significant inroads in the state won by Trump three elections in a row. He was also the first 2026 midterm candidate to secure an endorsement from (and cut an ad with) former President Barack Obama, giving a massive boost to his national profile.

Describing himself as a “prairie populist,” Turek has focused his platform on a message of affordability, access to healthcare, and anti-corruption policies. He has hit Hinson, who is endorsed by Trump, over the growth of her personal wealth while serving in Congress. Hinson in turn has been forced to distance herself from the president on certain critical policy issues given Trump’s floundering approval ratings. All in all, if Democrats manage to pull off a flip in the heartland of Trump country, it will be its own special kind of victory.
What are the polls saying: That it’s pretty much a dead heat. Recent polls flip-flop between giving Turek and Hinson a roughly two-point lead, well within the margin of error.
Current status: Republican
Who’s running: Democrat Mary Peltola is challenging incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan, who has two other Republicans to compete with, as well: Gerald Heikes and, confusingly, another Dan Sullivan.
Election Day: Polls close as early as 8 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Alaska’s election structure makes this a bit strange. For the second time, the state is using ranked choice voting to determine its senator. In some ways, it’s a traditional two-horse race: the Democrats have a viable challenger in Mary Peltola, and the Republicans have a longtime incumbent in Dan Sullivan who’s trying to hold his seat. But the RCV system makes things interesting in that there’s a second Dan Sullivan running, who has been accused of only entering in the race to siphon off votes from the incumbent Dan Sullivan. In the top-four election to decide the candidates, Peltola got over 49 percent of the vote, and Sullivan only got around 41 percent, with the other Dan Sullivan posting 2.5 percent and a couple other Republicans racking up a few percentage points here and there. Democrats think Peltola is their best shot to take a Senate seat in Alaska in years, but she’s not perfect. A recent New York Times report alleged that Peltola has a history of, in private, tossing slurs around and, shall we say, generally being an asshole to staff. It’s hardly a fatal scandal for her campaign, so we’ll have to see if it shifts the needle for voters in November.

What are the polls saying: Alaska is a conservative state in general, so most analysts have this one as a toss-up with a slight Republican lean — but still very much a battleground this fall. Pre-election polling has Peltola with a slight lead.
Current status: Republican
Who’s running: Lindsey Graham’s sister, Darline Graham, is running to keep his seat, which she was appointed to after her brother’s death. Her opponent is Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician.
Election Day: Polls close at 7 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Also a strange one! Darline Graham is, as far as we can tell, barely campaigning. She’s a political novice who only seems half-interested in the job beyond backing Trump. But she’s got the full support of the GOP — sort of. The party brass is behind her, but after she won a contested primary, elements of the conservative movement are also trying to mount a write-in effort for Congressman Ralph Norman, who narrowly lost to Graham in the primary. (Norman, for his part, has said he’ll support Graham.) Andrews, meanwhile, is battling the massive recognition of the Graham name, but has closed the gap considerably and is posting predictable leads with younger demographics.

What are the polls saying: It’s extremely close. South Carolina is a red state through and through, but Graham’s weak candidacy has opened the door and pre-election polling has the race in a dead heat.
Current status: Democratic
Who’s running: Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and Republican Michele Tafoya, a former sports anchor. Current Sen. Tina Smith is not seeking reelection.
Election Day: Polls close at 8 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Minnesota is a true purple state where the Democratic Farmer Labor Party (DFL) has managed to dominate Democratic success through a focus on working-class, economically progressive governance. Tafoya is a bit of a known entity in her own right. Her career as an Emmy-winning journalist and sideline reporter for NBC’s Sunday Night Football is a leg up in terms of sheer name recognition. While a Republican hasn’t held one of Minnesota’s Senate seats since 2009, a massive benefits fraud scandal uncovered under Flanagan and Gov. Tim Walz’s administration has given Tafoya a competitive boost. Tafoya is leaning hard into the fallout of the state fraud scandal, accusing her opponent of turning a blind eye to the abuse as Minnesotans were cheated out of millions in government funds.
What are the polls saying: It’s close, but Flanagan seems to have the polling edge heading into Election Day.
Current status: Republican
Who’s running: Republican incumbent Roger Marshall is facing Democrat Adam Hamilton, a pastor.
Election Day: Polls close as early as 7 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: Democrats think that they have an actual shot at Kansas for the first time in … 94 years. Hamilton is a relatively strong candidate: he’s a pastor who has made it explicitly clear that he does not want to be besmirched by the losing elements of the national party (“please, no,” he said when asked if he wanted Kamala Harris to come campaign with him). Kansas’ economy has been hit extremely hard by Trump’s trade policies and war in Iran, and Hamilton has even been endorsed by some Republicans, including one of Marshall’s primary opponents this year. Marshall, for his part, has been hit by a story alleging that he filed lawsuits against 700 of his patients when he was an OBGYN and has been struggling to paint the very normal, very moderate Hamilton as an “extremist.” The GOP has recognized this and is diverting resources away from their doomed effort in North Carolina to try to get Marshall across the finish line.
What are the polls saying: It was a dead head a month ago, but recent polls have shown Hamilton leading. Still, it’s been nearly a century since Democrats have won in the state.
Current status: Republican

Who’s running: Incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts is running against an independent candidate, Dan Osborn, who has inherited much of the Democratic Party’s support after Cindy Burbank, the Democratic primary winner, dropped out to make way for him.
Election Day: Polls close at 8 p.m. local time.

How’s the race been shaping up: This is also a strange race, notably because it is far closer than expected but does NOT feature two candidates from the two major parties. Osborn is an independent, blue-collar, union member who came within single digits of beating Nebraska’s other senator, Deb Fischer, in the 2024 election. The race is close enough that Trump was forced to head to Nebraska for emergency rallies in early October, where he called Osborn a “fake independent who will say anything to get elected.” We’ll see if that’s enough!

What are the polls saying: This one is close but not as tight as some of the others on this list. Polls from late October show Ricketts has a narrow lead, and Nebraska’s heavy GOP bias still in place. Still, Osborn has a fighting shot at the seat.

items.title: Wednesday and Mannequin Pussy Storm Nashville on the Rolling Stone Rock Tour
items.description: The members of Mannequin Pussy and Wednesday come together backstage for a Bitch Cabal group shot.
items.author: Rolling Stone
paragraphs: The members of Mannequin Pussy and Wednesday come together backstage for a Bitch Cabal group shot.
The Rolling Stone Rock Tour has featured must-see performances from Geese, Bleachers, Die Spitz, Wet Leg, and MJ Lenderman over the past couple of years.
Truth Club, an indie band that shares a home state of North Carolina with Wednesday, opened the show.
Shortly before taking the stage, Mannequin Pussy’s Marisa Dabice, Kaleen Reading, Colins Regisford, and Maxine Steen take a moment for a group huddle.

Marisa Dabice formed Mannequin Pussy with her friend Athanasios Paul back in 2010. The lineup has changed a bit over the years, and Paul departed in 2021, but they’ve grown exponentially more popular with each passing year. Their 2024 LP I Got Heaven was a huge critical favorite, even if their band name has made it hard for them to land TV bookings outside of Everybody’s Live with John Mulaney.
Guitarist Maxine Steen joined the band in 2021, and was a key architect of I Got Heaven. She’s playing here alongside touring member Carolyn Hayne.
Colins “Bear” Regisford has been Mannequin Pussy’s bassist since 2016, and he steps up to the mic every single night to belt out the protest song “Pigs is Pigs.”

Dabice faced enormous pressure to change the band’s name once they started to gain a following, but she refused. “I think we all expected that the world would become less puritanical,” she told Rolling Stone in 2023, “but in fact the opposite is true.”

Mannequin Pussy and Wednesday draw largely young fans to their shows. “We’re often playing to people that are 15 and just discovering rock music for the first time,” Dabice said in 2023. “I don’t think the barometer for rock is what’s on the cover of Rolling Stone or the top of the Spotify charts. It’s at these types of shows, where people are experiencing a collective catharsis.”

After two years of grueling road work in support of I Got Heaven, Mannequin Pussy entered the studio earlier this year to cut their fifth album. Over the past few months, they’ve been sprinkling in new songs like “Material Gains.”

Karly Hartzman formed Wednesday a little under a decade ago, and eventually brought drummer Alan Miller, pedal steel player Xandy Chelmis, bassist Ethan Baechtold, and guitarist MJ Lenderman into the fold. Lenderman has been focusing on his solo career over the past two years, and guitarist Jake “Spyder” Pugh has taken his spot in the touring band.
Wednesday played nine songs from their 2025 LP Bleeds at the Truth, and added in a cover of “Lonely Girls” by Lucinda Williams.
Mannequin Pussy bassist Colins “Bear” Regisford watches Wednesday’s set from the side of the stage.

Members of Wednesday rock out during the show. “Karly Hartzman is the kind of writer who can whisk you right into a stranger’s life with just a few words,” Rolling Stone‘s Rob Sheffield wrote earlier this year. “Her songs add up to a rootsy portrait of small-town heartache, as she evokes her cast of losers and dreamers, exploring the loneliest corners of American life. It’s like encountering Eudora Welty if she learned her licks playing in Southern hardcore bands.”

Karly Hartzman broke up with longtime partner MJ Lenderman shortly before cutting Bleeds, but they finished the record together and remain on good terms. “I was really at a breaking point exhaustion-wise,” she told Rolling Stone in 2025. “But I think I’m definitely more proud of it than any other thing we’ve ever made.”

items.title: The Great British Baking Show Recap: What I Like About Choux
items.description: I hate to come right out of the gate with the obvious baking pun, but didn’t Pastry Week fall a little flat? I feel like I had a bit more fun watching Léa Seydoux refuse to eat various croissants than watching this episode. The bakers have many triumphs, which
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: I hate to come right out of the gate with the obvious baking pun, but didn’t Pastry Week fall a little flat? I feel like I had a bit more fun watching Léa Seydoux refuse to eat various croissants than watching this episode. The bakers have many triumphs, which I think is usually a hallmark of a great episode, but from the on set, the editors are clearly telegraphing who is going home and who is going to be Star Baker yet again. Everyone is having fun and (nearly) everyone is triumphant, but the episode is lacking the suspense we usually get from a good reality-television program.

The first challenge is for the bakers to make eight handheld pies, which are ubiquitous in English bakeries. (I know Gail’s is basic, but its chicken, ham, and tarragon hand pie is basically delicious.) Many of the bakers are making a version of the pasty (with a short A so it rhymes with nasty, which they decidedly are not). Also known as the Cornish pasty, they come from Cornwall, the temperate and beachy region in England’s extreme southwest. They’re sort of like giant empanadas, but the crust is pinched together on one edge and crimped or braided into a thick closure that functions something like a handle. The idea was that farmers and miners — anyone who has watched Poldark knows Cornwall was famous for its mines — could hold the braid with their hands and eat their lunches without utensils since they were leagues underground trying not to die extracting undersea copper. Also, because their hands were filthy, they could throw the remainder of the crust to the crows. (While we’re on the subject of the Cornish, do not ask them about Cornish game hens. They are an American invention, and locals will laugh at you if you bring them up. Not that I know this from experience or anything.)

In the judging, we are close to two handshakes. Connie’s pasties, inspired by Jamaican patties and filled with jerk chicken, get praised by Paul, Nigella, and Alison, who seems to be angling to take over Paul’s job when he quits in a huff because people like Nigella more. Tom makes pasties inspired by banh mi, the delicious Vietnamese sandwich. Paul has never had a banh mi, and when he admits that, Tom says it’s a bit embarrassing, and he has never been more right about a single thing in his life. When Paul tries his first one, he says the spice is fantastic, and Nigella can’t get enough. Moyin’s Nigerian meat pie is so good that Alison also has to get a taste in, and you can almost see Paul swat her hand away with his eyes.

The one who struggles most is Clara, who makes venison pies that look like deer. As the judges explain to her how badly they could go, you know those antlers are going to be a failure. Because of their fiddly shape, they are about as full as a vegan at an all-you-can-eat barbecue buffet. Mo’s take on a samosa looks bright green, which is never a good idea for food unless it is a Jolly Rancher. (The thought of a Jolly Rancher handpie makes me think of that kombucha meme? Gross. But maybe! No.) Nigella tells him it’s too “gungy,” which is an English word for slime and also a uniquely British kink.

The judges don’t love Gabe’s bostin Brummie balti pie, and American viewers probably have no idea what any of those words are other than pie. “Bostin” is West Midlands slang for something that is great, like how people in Boston (no relation) say “wicked.” “Brummie” is what you call someone or something from Birmingham, England’s second-largest city, which is in the West Midlands and where Gabe lives and Alison is from. A “balti pie” is a Birmingham staple that takes a usual English meat pie and adds a filling typical of a curry, which is why Gabe’s are made with lamb, spices, mango chutney, and colonialism. I have never had one because they’re often served at football — sorry, soccer — games, and I do not go to those. Also, every person I’ve ever met from Birmingham says, “Don’t go, it’s terrible.” Not even for the bostin Brummie balti pies? (Don’t you feel smart now that you get that?)

The bakers all do similarly well at the technical challenge, which is solid but uninspired. Nigella tasks them with making a karpatka, a Polish dessert no one has ever heard of. But Nigella is right in her introduction. While it is unfamiliar, they should all be familiar with the components: two big slaps of choux pastry with vanilla custard in the middle. If these bakers haven’t made choux and custard, how did they get an invitation to the tente? While everyone seems confident in what they’re doing, Clara’s karpatka ends up not rising. Her choux is flat. (Oh, and you thought you would escape without one terrible shoe pun. Actually, that was two-thirds of a pun. P. U.)

After the technical, it’s clear Tom or Connie is going to be the winner and Clara or Mo is going home, unless something miraculous or disastrous occurs. I’m suitably impressed by Connie and Gary in this year’s competition. They both fulfill the archetype of an older baker who hews a little too closely to the classics and might not be as tidy as some of the other bakers. However, they’ve defied that, turning their knowledge bases and tidiness into strengths and lasting far longer in the competition than their archetype usually does.

The showstopper is to make a free-standing pie without using any pans, which is such a simple but, er, challenging challenge that I am impressed with the assignment for the third time in one episode. The result is seven amazing-looking P to the I to the E, pies! (It’s still stuck in my head.) Even Clara’s, which is cracked, looks great. Nigella says up close, it’s not that great, since she topped it with edible glitter, which settled into the cracks. Nigella, as relatable as ever, says that is what happens as you age and apply powder to your face. All the women (plus Tom and Gabe) nod in agreement. There is a groundswell of love and support even as Clara’s sun- and moon-shaped apple pie really dissatisfies the judges, and we all know the inevitable has come true: Clara, one of the front-runners, is going home.

The judges are also unimpressed with Moyin’s Nigerian mask–inspired apple pie, tanking what was otherwise a good week for him. Even still, all the pies look as beautiful as Nigella, powder in the cracks or no. Mo’s multicolored butterfly is like a stunning bit of stained glass, even though it was overbaked and underfilled. Gabe’s is shaped like his napping dog and looks spot on, but Paul says it’s too dry, even if Nigella disagrees. Connie’s sweet-potato-curry pie is inspired by a pet snake named Dave and looks like a delicious little cartoon. Gary makes a fish pie that looks like a fish because he is the most creative person in the tent. Still, it is prettier than Brad Pitt fishing in A River Runs Through It. Tom is similarly inspired making a Mexican chicken pie shaped like one of the chickens from the movie Chicken Run, even though he isn’t allowed to say the title, just like we’re not allowed to call it Bake Off.

It comes out of the oven like a little bit of ingenuity and looks exactly like the cartoon but also shockingly appetizing. He presents it to the judges, and they have their first bite. Nigella lavishes this chicken with praise, and Paul experiences the pressure. He feels the love she’s getting, the uneasy pang of people disagreeing with him, the camaraderie of talking about the difficulties of aging as a woman in society. He feels it all slipping away from him — the power, the control, the show — and he does the only thing he can: He approaches Tom, naturally Star Baker for the third time, with his hand extended, not in congratulations but to pull it all back toward him.

items.title: Dark Matter Season-Finale Recap: Into the Great Unknown
items.description: At the end of Dark Matter’s first season, the many Jasons of the Jason-pocalyse were still stuck somewhere between the anger and bargaining phase of the five stages of grief, having blown past denial yet still too engaged in reconnecting with Daniela and Charl
items.author: Scott Tobias
paragraphs: At the end of Dark Matter’s first season, the many Jasons of the Jason-pocalyse were still stuck somewhere between the anger and bargaining phase of the five stages of grief, having blown past denial yet still too engaged in reconnecting with Daniela and Charlie to move forward. The standalone fifth episode of this season, “Love and Be Loved,” marked a pivotal shift through depression and acceptance, as one such Jason contemplated suicide before opting to get a fresh start in a world where Jason Dessen had died as a child, and his mother was still alive to welcome his miraculous return. Even then, it took more than a few dark nights of the soul for this Jason to work his way through the fog, surrender his ties to the recent past, and build a new life with someone else. When he meets the Daniela of that world and is able to exchange pleasantries with her before heading home to his new partner, acceptance has been achieved.

And so now, in the final episode of the second season, one such Jason is able to have a conversation with Daniela as if they’ve gone through an amicable divorce years earlier and can reminisce about their history without falling into despair. This Jason is essentially escorting his wife through the box to find their son, but he’s resigned to the fact that there’s no getting either of them back. They laugh over a memory involving the twins when they were young, but Jason cuts the conversation short by opening the door to the world where he believes Charlie has landed. He rejects the idea of stepping through to see Charlie himself, because it’s not his role to play anymore. “It’s not fair to any of us, but we keep going,” he tells Daniela. “Thank you for a really great life.”

The tone of these sorts of interactions has changed over the course of this season, as different people from different worlds have collided and been able to get past the impossibility of it. When Charlie No. 1 proved to Max that he was a multidimensional traveler and not his twin brother coming home early from college, what choice did Max have but believe him? And when Daniela No. 1 goes looking for her son and gets caught in the house by this world’s Daniela, the show doesn’t pause long to register this shocking revelation before it turns into a metaphysical therapy session. Daniela gets to tell some version of herself how she feels about her marital problems and her lingering guilt over having to kill one of the Jasons to protect her family. Often in life you need to be able to forgive yourself, but Daniela gets the rare opportunity to make that idea as literal as possible. It’s the sci-fi version of Stuart Smalley looking into the mirror and doing his daily affirmations.

Though this season two finale is appropriately scaled up and exciting, with a lot of frantic action across multiple realities, the progression that Dark Matter has made to get to the acceptance phase of its premise raises an obvious question: Where could it go from here? There are some plot-related questions that will need to be answered next season — we’ll get to those in a bit — but there are signs in this last hour that Dark Matter has reached a potential dead end on an emotional and philosophical front. The impact of the two scenes with Daniela described above should be seismic given how much box-related upheaval she’s had to face since Jason No. 2 invaded her life. But this season, the show has reckoned so much with this type of emotional fallout that the scenes are feeling a little redundant and drippy. There’s no physical (or metaphysical) limit to where the series might go from here — the box does, after all, open up into infinite possible realities — but the door might have closed on a “Love and Be Loved”-type tearjerker again.

On the other hand, perhaps the dramatic realignment of the major characters in the finale will open up other avenues. Heading toward season’s end, there appeared to be two camps working at cross purposes: Jason No. 1, Amanda No. 2, Ryan No. 1, and Blair No. 2 have been fussing over the science and logistics of destroying the box, starting from the original sources in World No. 2, because the boxes everywhere else would just respawn. Meanwhile, Leighton No. 2 and Jason No. 2 have been looking to refine their project through the Pyramid and perhaps return to the idealistic vision of addressing big problems with multi-dimensional solutions. But in an abrupt turn of events, Leighton No. 2 and Jason No. 2 start to regret this monstrous invention they’ve unleashed on humanity. Leighton talks about a world where Mt. Rainier had blown, leading to massive crop death and starvation, but the ecological solution he offered wound up deepening the crisis, starting with developing countries before spreading to the rest of the world.

“We fucked up,” laments Leighton in a truly massive understatement. And in an even more surprising moment of self-awareness, he expresses regret over “letting millions of people die for money” and “walking around in awe of my own fucking greatness.” Jason No. 2 tries to ease the guilt that’s suddenly stabbing away at Leighton’s conscience by suggesting that the implications of the box were not knowable and “this thing has brought out the most terrifying aspects of who we are.” While it does seem a bit surprising that the Velocity braintrust didn’t think through the massive potential for disruption that the box would cause, it does track historically that scientists often think about what’s possible more than about where great advancements might lead humankind (see also: Oppenheimer). Still, it’s a startling gearshift for all parties to come around on the idea that the box (and the Pyramid) might be worth shutting down.

All parties, that is, except for Oluko, who has emerged as a late-breaking villain and ghost in the machine. Amanda No. 2 and Ryan No. 1 meet him at the Velocity building in Analog World with the intent of securing vaccines and medications to fight a plague in another dimension. But their true goal is to access the Analog World box in order to work back to the original box with the technology needed to “decohere” and destroy the entire system. Blair warns them that Oluko gave her “major creep vibes,” and indeed he sniffs out their intention and sends a security agent after them, leading to a splashy action sequence in which they’re being chased through multiple worlds, including one where Chicago has become a war zone. That sequence alone makes it seem like the show’s producers were saving the budgetary fireworks for the grand finale, just as last season ended with a rush of Jason-on-Jason violence.

But once the dust has settled, Dark Matter lands in a tricky spot for next season. As hard as it was to get back to the original box in World No. 2, it appears that Blair No. 2 and Jason No. 1 succeeded in their de-coherence plan, but as with all box-related issues, the result is messier than anticipated. Oluko winds up escaping to some unknown world, leaving him as a looming threat, and more crucially, time runs out before Daniela and Charlie can make it back to Analog World for a family reunion. They open a door into an unknown future, but it’s obvious that they’ll need these dimensional portals to be opened up once again. The second season of Dark Matter has been a significant improvement on the first, but if the show gets a third — news on a renewal has yet to be announced — it will need to open that portal door, too, and find new possibilities.

• Blair offers some wonderful sci-fi nonsense in explaining how her gizmo will kill the box: “Basically it’ll attack not just the local qubits but all programming for the adaptive shielding, slowly corrupting the error-correcting protocols.” Adaptive shielding, error-correcting protocols. Got it.

• Though the heart-tugging moments are not as potent in this episode as they were in earlier parts of the season, Daniela’s farewell to the grown-up version of Max she never knew is a killer. “It’s really nice to meet you” is a lovely bit of understatement.
• Good on Charlie for going record shopping in Max’s world. Nirvana’s Bleach is a solid choice.
• Oluko’s rise brings the first major character death in his doppelgänger, Leighton No. 2, whose murder ends up serving as a gruesome narrative sacrifice for his sins in exploiting the box.

items.title: Can Democrats Really Flip the Senate? Hollywood Holds Its Breath
items.description: Months of election drama will finally come to an end Tuesday as voters across America head to the polls. Like a Game of Thrones series finally working to the finale, hopefully with a less divisive resolution.
items.author: Steven Zeitchik
paragraphs: Months of election drama will finally come to an end Tuesday as voters across America head to the polls. Like a Game of Thrones series finally working to the finale, hopefully with a less divisive resolution.

The will-they-or-won’t-they saga has been more intense than pretty much anything else onscreen this season (well except for You Can See Everything, of course). Hollywood — at least judging from the fundraising efforts by major entertainment world figures for Democratic candidates in Texas, Georgia, Florida and elsewhere — has a vested interest in getting a Democratic flip in both chambers of Congress.

The House seems almost surely headed for a Democratic handover — the party needs to flip only three seats, and well over a dozen Republican seats are in polling trouble. A blue wave, or at least strong ripple, on that side. (High Democratic turnout in early voting is further encouraging for the party’s prospects.) But the Senate, where Democrats need to flip four of the 22 Republican seats up for reelection while holding all 13 of their own (or flip five if they lose one), seems a far murkier prospect.

Right now, Republicans are behind at the polls in at least eight races where they currently hold seats. Obvious flip, right? Not so fast. The Trump era has been defined by Republican undercounting in pre-election polling, which could make some of the Democratic leads illusory, though midterm polls tend to be more accurate. (MAGA supporters — those least likely to respond to polls — tend not to come out as much for midterm races, making their non-responses less impactful.)

That undercount makes very close races in Alaska, Maine and Iowa a lot more likely to break for Republicans. That’s especially true in Alaska, where recent backlash over Sullivan-gate — i.e., the alleged orchestration by the campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola to get a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot and potentially confuse supporters over the Republican nominee of the same name — could tip the election to the GOP. The Republican candidates in Maine and Iowa, meanwhile, have high likability ratings among voters.

Democrats do seem to have more sizable edges in Texas, Ohio and North Carolina, making those likely if not certain to turn blue. North Carolina’s Democratic Roy Cooper is firmly in control, Texas’ James Talarico has widened his advantage in recent days over Ken Paxton, and former Sen. Sherrod Brown has begun to open a clear if narrow advantage over Jon Husted, in the job only two years as JD Vance’s replacement.

That still means Democrats will have to pull off one more flip, and it’s unclear where that comes from. Kansas is perhaps the best bet, with the moderate Democratic pastor Rev. Adam Hamilton putting some daylight between himself and incumbent Roger Marshall. And Marshall is unpopular — but then Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since the Great Depression (or, in movie terms, the year Grand Hotel won best picture).

An X factor is South Carolina, which historically has been more red than Elmo but now faces some chaos with the candidacy of political newbie Darline Graham, sister of late Sen. Lindsey Graham, who has been seen as a nepotistic choice by voters in some polls. That could open the door to her pediatrician challenger, Annie Andrews, until a few months ago thought a lost cause.

If either Kansas or South Carolina go Dems’ way — and honestly had you raised that possibility six months ago, people would have thought you were Sarah Connor-level crazy — attention then turns to the Democrats trying to defend their contested seats. While that seems likely in previously in-play races in Minnesota, Georgia and New Hampshire, such a prospect is more uncertain in Michigan, where Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, facing a stunning Democratic mutiny from former primary challenger Haley Stevens, could see some moderates bleed to his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers. Should El-Sayed surprisingly not win the race — and, to be clear, with a five-point poll lead, the smart money is still with him — then Dems would need an additional flip beyond the targeted four.

Still, even if they don’t get it and the Senate ends up 50-50 (and decided by the vice president), it could hamper the GOP agenda, since such a count opens up the possibility of peeling any single Republican from the caucus to block a vote. (Democrats refer to this as Joe Manchin Syndrome.)

Democrats could take heart in one possible major blue-red reversal — but it’s not in the Senate. Florida hasn’t elected a Democratic governor in 32 years. But David Jolly is within a few points of the Trump-endorsed Byron Donalds, and the idea of a Democrat — even one who not that long ago was a Republican — replacing Ron DeSantis in the country’s third most-populous state would certainly add some thickener to the stew.

What’s at stake for Democrats and the many in Hollywood who support them? A bulwark against Donald Trump, for starters, but also a rare chance to control both chambers over the next term. The party has been able to do that only once in the past 16 years and only three times since 1994. Before then, it happened regularly — that 1994 election and its famous “Contract With America” Gingrichian revolution ended eight straight years of Democrats controlling both bodies.
Of course, who remembers that? You’d have to have been working in Hollywood when the first Lion King came out to harbor such a memory. A Senate majority rises and falls like the sun.
This is part of The Hollywood Reporter’s ongoing midterm coverage. You can check out all of the pieces here.

items.title: Jason Blum and James Wan Rename Their Company
items.description: Two years after the merger of Blumhouse and Atomic Monster, horror maestros Jason Blum are James Wan are renaming their company. Blumhouse Atomic Monster is no more. In its place is Blumhouse Atomic.
items.author: Aaron Couch
paragraphs: Two years after the merger of Blumhouse and Atomic Monster, horror maestros Jason Blum are James Wan are renaming their company. Blumhouse Atomic Monster is no more. In its place is Blumhouse Atomic.
Blumhouse and Atomic Monster will sit as separate labels underneath the larger company, with their respective teams developing movies and TV shows.

“When we merged our companies, we believed the whole would be greater than the sum of its parts, and that is exactly what has happened,” said Blum, who touted partner Wan for creating hit franchises The Conjuring, Insidious and Saw. “We have the output of a studio with the creative freedom and financial discipline of an independent company, and more opportunities than ever to take these stories beyond the theater and into television, games and live experiences.”

The rebranding comes after the combined company’s films have brought in $2.5 billion in box office receipts since the merger, against $330 million in production budgets. That haul has been led by the $525 million global tally for Obsession (which the company boarded after Focus Features acquired the indie production), The Conjuring: Last Rites (nearly $500 million globally) and Backrooms ($400.6 million globally).

“The future of horror comes from new voices, and Blumhouse Atomic gives us more ways to find them and support them for the long haul,” said Wan. “I got my start with a small film and people willing to take a chance on it, so creating those opportunities for others is personal to me. Working with filmmakers like Kane Parsons, Curry Barker, Josh Giuliano and Dylan Clark is a big part of that. We want to give them the freedom to make something distinctive and build relationships that last beyond one film.”

Indeed, Backrooms and Obsession sparked an arms race among studios for new filmmakers who could make an outsized impact on smaller budgets. Earlier this year, Blumhouse Atomic tapped Sam Zimmerman as as SVP, development and acquisitions, to oversee a genre slate of projects under $5 million. It also signed a first-look with horror producers Divide/Conquer to focus on high concept genre films that can be made for a price.

It also landed Barker’s first post-Obsession movie deal for an unknown project at Universal in a major coup, and has new versions Paranormal Activity, Blair Witch Project and Saw (with Wan producing after the company bought back into the Lionsgate franchise).
Coming up, the Blumhouse Atomic slate includes River, The Revenge of La Llorona, The Exorcist: Martyrs, Anything But Ghosts, Paranormal Activity, Molepeople, Blair Witch, Sleepover and Seasons.

items.title: In ‘Elsinore,’ Billie Piper Found “Beautiful Chaos” With Andrew Scott — And a New Career Chapter
items.description: At the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, just ahead of Halloween weekend, Billie Piper held a masterclass for college students. “It was basically me just rattling on about being an actor — I hope some of it was useful, not sure,” she says the next day from a quiet
items.author: David Canfield
paragraphs: At the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, just ahead of Halloween weekend, Billie Piper held a masterclass for college students. “It was basically me just rattling on about being an actor — I hope some of it was useful, not sure,” she says the next day from a quiet library in the Southern city’s downtown. “Their line of questioning was so insightful and kind of ahead of their years. They were all there with the little moleskin books taking notes. I just didn’t expect that.”

She’d have little reason to. Despite her decades in the business, despite the Olivier Award win and five BAFTA nominations, the English native hasn’t really traveled the film-festival circuit before. She came to town as an honoree for the Oscar contender Elsinore, receiving the Marquee Award for her vivacious turn as the imperious real-life casting director Patsy Pollock.
In spending time with the kids before the festivities kicked off, it dawned on her: “I actually thought: ‘God, I’ve done some really great jobs.’”

She arrives today with dark brown hair, a far cry from the striking blonde of Elsinore and her other most noted screen roles, and a tablet that she occasionally flashes open to reference movies she’s either seen recently or intends to soon watch. “It’s really fired me up about independent movies again,” she says of running around in support of Elsinore. (The film launched at Telluride, where star Andrew Scott emerged as an instant best-actor front-runner, and has since played all over the world.) “I felt like it was all dead, but it wasn’t dead. I just feel so jacked about all the movies I’m seeing.”

An intensely chameleonic actress unafraid to go big, Piper has never had the largest footprint in the feature space. “Often the films that I read weren’t that good for women,” she says. We may be at something of a turning point. Already, she’s received her first career British Independent Film Award nomination for Elsinore, competing in a supporting category alongside returning faces like Claire Foy and Tom Courtenay.

After breaking out as a teen pop star, the now-44-year-old has always followed the best work. She made her name onscreen by leading series like Doctor Who and Secret Diary of a Callgirl, then as a major stage actor in West End productions of The Effect and Yerma. For the latter revival of Federico García Lorca’s classic, she remains the only actor to have won every official Best Actress prize currently awarded for a single UK theater performance. She wowed again in HBO Max’s I Hate Suzie, a brilliant panic attack of a dark comedy about a moderately famous actress thrown into turmoil when nude photos on her phone leak online.

For one reason or another, these projects didn’t land with as much force in the US as back home. Indeed, Piper co-created I Hate Suzie with her Effect playwright Lucy Prebble, and the show aired right after other stellar series from British female multihyphenates, like Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s Fleabag and Michaela Coel’s I May Destroy You. Rest assured, Piper’s BAFTA-nominated performance is every bit as ferociously compelling — and revealing — as what her peers delivered in those Emmy-winning smashes.
For a good chunk of American audiences, at least, Suzie remains a hidden streaming gem waiting to be discovered. Piper seems comfortable in that zone.

Elsinore dramatizes the heartbreaking, inspiring final act of Ian Charleson, a gay actor not out publicly who was known for his starring role in Chariots of Fire. Charleson decided, shortly after being diagnosed with AIDS, to play Hamlet at the National Theatre while fighting for his life — and somehow pulled it off. Scott’s turn as the late great dominates the movie, but Piper becomes its sneaky heart. Patsy, Charleson’s best friend, emerges as his caretaker and as an anchor in their defiant chosen family.

“Their relationship was beautiful chaos,” Piper says. “They partied hard. He was a big figure in her daughter’s life. She was a single mother working in a male-dominated industry.” When it came to Charleson’s controversial choice to play Hamlet — his doctor, portrayed by Olivia Colman, was initially firmly against it — Patsy simply got it. So did Piper. “It makes complete sense to want to play one of, if not the most challenging parts at your most vulnerable point in your life as you approach your death,” Piper says. “Patsy understood that about him. I understand that about what he chose to do as well. I think a lot of actors get it, to be honest.”

Elsinore is a tearjerker, no doubt, but it’s stuffed with joy. Piper brings plenty of levity with her glamorous, haughty embodiment of an old showbusiness powerhouse. She is clearly having a ball. “I really miss people like Patsy in our industry — the larger-than-life characters — because everything’s so serious and there’s no money now,” Piper says. “It was fun to pull from the characters I knew in my early career. There were agents I had who were cut from a different cloth. It wasn’t all terribly kind, but it was unlike anybody I’d grown up with — the flamboyance, the drama, the quick shifts in tone and mood.”

Her chemistry with Scott is undeniable. The two veterans of the London theater scene previously worked together on Lena Dunham’s critically acclaimed Catherine Called Birdy, including a birthing scene for the ages. Like Piper, Scott is plenty decorated back home, but his frequent co-star finds him unusually playful to work with.

“With that skillset, you expect someone who’s a bit of a dick, but he’s not remotely a dick — he is warm, he is generous, he is informal. The work feels casual,” Piper says of Scott. “He takes it seriously, of course — he knows what he wants and knows what he likes — but it’s not the only thing that’s happening in his life, which I think is healthy.”

Piper can relate. She’s a mother of three and values the separation of the personal and professional. “I do my work, then I go home and am a parent — and so there’s no real processing of what I’ve done in the day, which is often really thrilling and rare and something I’d wanted to do since I was a child,” she says. Take, for instance, the job she’s just come back from: Wednesday season three. Piper grew up on Tim Burton and was now surrounded by his and his team’s singular designs. She got to act opposite the likes of Winona Ryder. And she was gone for nine months, a very long time. Too long, maybe.

“I haven’t worked on a nine-month shoot since Doctor Who, and I left that show for a reason,” she says. “The gratitude is there, but also it’s not without a cost.” Now, of course, she’s even further away, in the American south: “I’m doing a lot of being away. I feel terrible and also excited.”

Some viewers read into the whirring, control-obsessed anxiety of Piper’s I Hate Suzie tour-de-force as a thinly veiled commentary on her own struggles as an artist in the public eye. (Suzie’s career beginnings mirrored Piper’s to some degree.) The show was fiction, of course, but Piper’s guttural performance came from somewhere true.
“It’s really fun to play,” Piper says now, “but it’s just no way to live your life.”

The lesson took some learning. “I need things to be beyond good for me to take it seriously, to take myself seriously — it’s really got nothing to do with anyone else, but with insane levels of achievement,” Piper says. “It’s dysfunctional. I’ve been like that since I was a kid.” She believed the work should feel painful, that it should take everything out of her. She credits Yerma, which she performed in London and New York from 2016-2018 under the direction of Simon Stone — who so happens to be the director of Elsinore — with ushering in a new way forward in that regard.

“Simon completely changed my career for me — completely changed the way I looked at acting,” Piper says. “That’s a nice thing to have in a career that has been going on for a long time, to suddenly work with someone that completely rips up the rule book.”

Brick by brick, Piper is building a thrilling new chapter on that experience. Elsinore has proven a cozy fit. Not just as an awards-bound prestige movie offering her a meaty supporting role — also in the way it’s welcoming her into spaces she’s never even thought much of before. Her main goal this awards season? To hang out with Club Kid writer-director-star Jordan Firstman. “I’ve watched Rotting in the Sun about five times. It’s so funny and so free,” she says, referring to Sebastián Silva’s graphic meta comedy that starred Firstman as a vapid version of himself. “Now I just want to be his best mate.”

She’s written a film that she describes as “romantic horror,” which she’s planning to direct. (Her feature debut, Rare Beasts, premiered at Venice in 2019.) She knows it will be difficult to get off the ground. But she’s been feeling inspired by what she’s seeing. “It’s really useful going into a process of trying to get a film made that may never happen, may never see the light of day — it’s energized my passion,” she says.
Same goes for the students with whom she spent the previous afternoon.

“Even though we live in this difficult day and age, even though it might feel more compromised and frightening in terms of a career choice, they still want to pursue this,” Piper says. “There is still this appetite for the arts. I find it quite moving.”
Elsinore opens in limited North American theatrical release on November 20.

items.title: What Cut Editors Are Buying From the Sephora Savings Event
items.description: Your Sephora cart has been waiting for this moment, or at least that’s what I always tell myself this time of year. Early November doesn’t only mean it’s officially Mariah Carey season, but it also brings an early holiday treat for beauty lovers: the Sephora’s
items.author: Asia Milia Ware
paragraphs: Your Sephora cart has been waiting for this moment, or at least that’s what I always tell myself this time of year. Early November doesn’t only mean it’s officially Mariah Carey season, but it also brings an early holiday treat for beauty lovers: the Sephora’s annual savings event. It’s a great excuse to try the buzzy new launches you’ve been eyeing or restock on your favorite foundation (my cart hates to see the LYS foundation stick coming). The best thing about the savings event is that all of the holiday sets have already launched, too, so whether you’re shopping for family and friends or just selfishly want to buy a duo set of Charlotte Tilbury’s OG setting spray (same), there are plenty of reasons to fill your cart up.

The savings event goes live in three tiers. The more you shop throughout the year, the bigger your discount. Rouge members, who get 20 percent off, had first access to the sale starting on October 30; VIB members, who get 15 percent off, and insiders, who get 10 percent off, gain access on November 3. All Sephora Collection products are 30 percent off for everyone and the sale runs through November 9. Because we’ve been waiting for this over the past few months, our carts were already ready. Here’s a peek into what I’m buying, plus a few recommendations from my fellow Cut editors, if you’re wondering where to start.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Eadem’s softening lip balm has become a cult-classic product in just two years. I’ve gone through more tubes than I can count. It’s become my daily lip, so when I saw this kit with minis of my favorite shades I immediately added it to my cart because I know it’ll sell out fast. I’m going to grab some for my friends who love it, too.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Dyson launched a travel version of its Supersonic this year. It’s my favorite dryer for my 4B hair and my hairstylist loves it, too, so I’m surprising her with one for the holiday season. My No. 1 splurge rule to everyone during the savings event is: Buy the Dyson because you won’t regret it (and you probably won’t find it on sale anytime soon).
New! You can now save this product for later.
New! You can now save this product for later.

It’s rare I find a holiday bundle that’s actually worth it, but this has all of my Topicals favorites: the eye patches that suddenly make me look awake after a long flight, a hyperpigmentation go-to serum, and the body bar that I always turn to to remove body scars because it works so quickly. All three products in one kit feels like it’s too good to be true.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I’ve raved about this product for years. It’s the one peel that I do twice a month consistently for the smoothest and brightest skin. It’s a product I restock on during every savings event; that’s how much I use it.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Dior recently launched this tinted moisturizer and the formula is one of the most lightweight of any tinted moisturizer I’ve tried. It has light to medium coverage that seamlessly covers the skin’s imperfections with a dewy glow. It’s a complexion product you won’t want to put down.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I think people often forget that Sephora has some home products, too. Nest candles always help me create an alternate universe in my home. This one invites a spalike aroma with the eucalyptus notes. I can light it in one room and smell it throughout my entire place. I usually stock up on a few for myself and save the rest for last-minute gifts.
New! You can now save this product for later.

This candle is a great date-night go-to. Not only does it fill the space with a warm scent, but it also melts down into a jojoba oil so it doubles as a massage oil. When I first used it I definitely thought my skin would get burned, but it melts into a warm, relaxing oil that makes you wish you had hot stones to follow. A girl can dream.
New! You can now save this product for later.
On the days when I get out of the shower and body-care feels like a task, I pull out my Hanni for quick nourishment that feels weightless. It’s the lazy girl’s hack to hydrated and healthy skin.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Speaking of lazy-girl hacks, some people aren’t lazy but they just lack time. Enter: my mom friends. I’ve loved gifting them Kate McLeod body stones because they melt into the skin upon meeting the body’s natural heat. It’s an easy, fast way to have a self-care moment. This kit is the perfect gift because it comes with multiple scents for my friends to discover what’s right for them.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I have an 18-year-old niece who raids my beauty closet often and the first thing she reaches for are my makeup brushes, so I always use the sale to stock her up with some of her own. Sephora’s kit has a brush for everything and, because it’s a part of its collection, it has even more of a discount. I may even buy one for myself.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Fenty’s body milk is the type of lightweight lotion that instantly absorbs into the skin and doesn’t leave it a heavy or greasy feel. Rihanna knows a thing or two about smelling great and this scent range proves that. This is the first year she’s launched these trio pouches, and I know they’ll be perfect for my yearlong travels; I’m excited to add them to my cart and collection.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I wear lash extensions, but in between fills I like to wear strip lashes. I’m admittedly bad at applying lash glue so I stick to using Lilly Lashes self-adhesive band lashes. They’re easy to apply and this lash design is the perfect finishing touch to my makeup without being over the top for my eye shape. Because I use them so much, this is always the best time to restock.
New! You can now save this product for later.

My skin has been especially dry this fall, so my usual go-to setting sprays aren’t cutting it. I’m upgrading to this ceramide-infused mist that gives the skin a glowy finish. I love the Rhode Glazing Milk, so I have high hopes for this product. —Hanna Flanagan, senior shopping editor
New! You can now save this product for later.
My fellow editors are constantly raving about Cyklar body-care products, but I have yet to try out the brand for myself; the Sephora sale is the perfect time to see what all the hype is about. —H.F.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I really don’t need another cream bronzer, but as a fan of the cult-favorite LYS Beauty foundation stick, I’m very curious about this product so I’m going to snag it while it’s on sale. I’m hoping it’s as creamy, blendable, and buildable as the foundation stick. —H.F.
New! You can now save this product for later.

I hadn’t used an Urban Decay makeup product (or a tubing mascara) in years until this product arrived on my doorstep a few months ago — and now it’s my everyday mascara. I love the no-mascara trend, but I can’t really get away with it because my eyelashes are so blonde. This mascara, specifically the dark brown shade, is subtle and natural, so it gives me that no-mascara look while providing some much-needed definition. It adds length, gives the lashes a fluttery look, and never flakes off throughout the day. I’m stocking up during the Sephora sale. —H.F.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Dieux can do no wrong in my eyes (or skin). I’ve been using the retinal three times a week for the past two months, and my skin has never looked better. It’s extremely gentle on my sensitive skin, which is always what I’m looking for in a product. —Bianca Nieves, senior style partnerships editor
New! You can now save this product for later.

I don’t use concealer anymore; I just use this. I love how it matches my skin perfectly and goes on so smoothly. When I want to feel extra dewy, I pair it with the Charlotte Tilbury Flawless Filter. —B.N.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Winter hasn’t even arrived yet, but my skin is already going through it. This lotion is what’s keeping my dryness at bay. I love applying it right after I get out of the shower so I don’t have to wake up in the middle of the night to apply anything else. (Yes, my skin is that dry!) —B.N.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Hyperpigmentation hates to see this serum coming. I’ve been using this product for the past two years, and it really has evened out my skin. I used to have hormonal acne, and this is the product I credit for getting rid of the dark spots left by all the acne I picked and made ten times worse. —B.N.
New! You can now save this product for later.

Several estheticians have recommended I swap to a gel moisturizer for my dehydrated skin, so I’m opting for this lightweight option. It has peptides, glycerin, and hyaluronic acid, which are some of my favorite hydrating ingredients. —Chinea Rodriguez, shopping writer
New! You can now save this product for later.

Our beauty writer Carol Lee has a column called “K-Beauty Corner,” and it’s inspired me to dive into the newly launched Olive Young edit at Sephora. First on my list? This makeup-enhancing mist. —C.R.
New! You can now save this product for later.
New! You can now save this product for later.
For those who are still shopping (no judgement)
The Best Beauty-Device Deals

I always tell my friends that the savings event is the best time to buy beauty tools they’ve been eyeing throughout the year because they rarely go on sale. It’s also the perfect time to get a head start on your New Year’s beauty resolution of actually using game-changing devices consistently. Want to dedicate more time to your skin? Splurge on an LED mask (luckily for you, Shark Beauty just launched a new version of its CryoGlow mask that offers wider coverage) or depuffing tool. Want to try lymphatic drainage? Try a tool that will provide results at home first. Have fitness goals? Get a head start on recovery with an infrared sauna mat. Or, if you’re like me and want to make fewer trips to the hair salon, now’s the time to splurge on the best hair tools (I’ve tried them all and these are truly the best).

Whether you’re shopping the savings event for yourself or planning on gifting your purchases to friends and family this holiday season, fragrance is always one of my favorite categories to splurge on. There have been quite a few new fragrance additions since Sephora’s last savings event including Byredo, the luxury brand that Cut girls love, and Influxious, the new brand from fragrance creator Funmi Monet. Her debut collection features tropical, warm, and creamy scents that pay homage to her Nigerian culture. It sold out the same day it launched, but luckily it’s back in stock now (along with some other Cut favorites).
The Best Skin-Care and Body-Care Deals
Whether you’re finally indulging in Sephora’s K-beauty section, or restocking on shower favorites, like L’Occitaine’s bodywash, these are some of the best skin- and body-care deals.

If you need a restock on the OG Dior Lip Oil or if you’ve been wanting to try the Rhode cream bronzer (yes, it’s as good as everyone says it is), here’s your reminder that you have a few days to do so. It’s also a great time to try 2026 launches, like Hung Vanngo’s serum foundation, arguably one of the best complexion launches of the year.
If You Happen to Be Shopping for a Man

I know we just want to fill our carts for ourselves, but if you’re shopping for a dad or partner, Sephora has scents he’ll love. Thanks to my fiancé’s love of fragrance, I’ve been able to confirm that the options below actually smell good and last throughout the day.

items.title: So Should We Expect a Big Blue Wave on Tuesday Night?
items.description: All signs certainly seem to point to a big Democratic shake-up. Not that polls haven’t been completely and catastrophically wrong before, but ya know. Midterm elections do typically serve as a referendum on the current administration, and right now, President
items.author: Andrea González-Ramírez
paragraphs: All signs certainly seem to point to a big Democratic shake-up. Not that polls haven’t been completely and catastrophically wrong before, but ya know. Midterm elections do typically serve as a referendum on the current administration, and right now, President Donald Trump is the most unpopular he’s ever been. Voters are furious at rising prices, the war in Iran, the fascist excesses of ICE, and the administration’s general corruption and tomfoolery. Perhaps Trump saw this coming: In July 2025, he ordered Texas to redraw its congressional maps to give the GOP a leg up, which set off a nationwide redistricting war. And while, yes, gerrymandering efforts heavily favor Republicans, most polling projects that Democrats will still retake the House — and may pull stunning upsets elsewhere. So what should you be looking out for as results roll in? Below, a primer on the U.S. Congress, governor races, and ballot measures you need to know ahead of Election Night.

Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the U.S. Senate. To retake the chamber, Democrats must win 51 seats this election. (That way they’ll prevent a 50-50 scenario wherein Vice-President J.D. Vance can cast a tie-breaking vote.) To clinch the majority, Democrats must win four GOP-held seats and defend the 47 seats they currently have. It’s an uphill battle, especially since some of the seats that need to be flipped are in states Trump carried by double digits in the 2024 election. Here are the most competitive races that are considered toss-ups, according to the Cook Political Report’s most recent ratings.
Alaska: Democrat Mary Peltola versus Republican senator Dan Sullivan versus the other Dan Sullivan, an independent
Iowa: Democrat Josh Turek versus Republican Ashley Hinson
Kansas: Democrat Adam Hamilton versus Republican senator Roger Marshall
Maine: Democrat Troy Jackson versus Republican senator Susan Collins
Michigan: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed versus Republican Mike Rogers
Ohio: Democrat Sherrod Brown versus Republican senator Jon Husted
Texas: Democrat James Talarico versus Republican Ken Paxton

Honorable mentions: Former governor Roy Cooper seems likely to win North Carolina’s open Senate seat, and if he does, it’ll be the first time a Democrat has won a statewide federal election since President Obama’s 2008 victory. In Florida, progressive candidate Angie Nixon is giving Senator Ashley Moody a run for her money in a surprisingly tight election. Even South Carolina could be in play with recent polls showing Democratic candidate Annie Andrews tied at 48 percent with Senator Darline Graham, who succeeded her brother, Lindsey Graham, after his death in July.

Control of the House hinges on which party can win at least 218 seats. To flip the chamber, Democrats must win 14 out of the 18 races below, which Cook Political Report rates “lean Democratic.” To keep control of the House, Republicans must win four of the seats listed below in addition to the 18 races classified as toss-ups and the 17 contests rated “lean Republican.” (You can see all their ratings here.)
Arizona’s First District: Democrat Amish Shah versus Republican Jay Feely
Arizona’s 6th District: Democrat JoAnna Mendoza versus Republican representative Juan Ciscomani
California’s 48th District: Democrat Marni von Wilpert versus Republican Jim Desmond
Colorado’s Eighth District: Democrat Manny Rutinel versus Republican representative Gabe Evans
Florida’s 25th District: Democratic representative Jared Moskowitz versus Republican Scott Singer
Iowa’s First District: Democrat Christina Bohannan versus Republican representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks
Iowa’s Third District: Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott versus Republican representative Zach Nunn
North Carolina’s 11th District: Democrat Jamie Ager versus Republican Jennifer Balkcom
New Jersey’s Seventh District: Democrat Rebecca Bennett versus Republican representative Thomas Kean Jr.
New Mexico’s Second District: Democratic representative Gabe Vasquez versus Republican Gregory Cunningham
Ohio’s Ninth District: Democratic representative Marcy Kaptur versus Republican Derek Merrin
Pennsylvania’s Seventh District: Democrat Bob Brooks versus Republican representative Ryan Mackenzie
Pennsylvania’s Eighth District: Democrat Paige Cognetti versus Republican representative Rob Bresnahan Jr.
Pennsylvania’s Tenth District: Democrat Janelle Stelson versus Republican representative Scott Perry
Texas’s 34th District: Democratic representative Vicente Gonzalez versus Republican Eric Flores
Virginia’s Second District: Democrat Elaine Luria versus Republican representative Jen Kiggans
Washington’s Third District: Democratic representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez versus Republican John Braun
Wisconsin’s Third District: Democrat Rebecca Cooke versus Republican representative Derrick Van Orden

Honorable mentions: Two controversial Republicans whose contests are rated toss-ups are at risk of losing their seats. Representative Lauren Boebert, the right-wing flamethrower, is yet again in a closer-than-expected contest in Colorado’s Fourth District after a wave of personal scandals. In Ohio’s Seventh District, Representative Max Miller — a former Trump White House staffer — is fighting for his political life after his ex-wife accused him of domestic violence and child abuse.

This election, there are governor races in 36 states. Governors and state legislatures have either been the last line of defense against Trump’s policies or his closest allies promoting his agenda. These are the most competitive contests, according to the Cook Political Report.
Alaska: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins versus Republican Dave Bronson versus Republican Treg Taylor versus Republican Bernadette Wilson
Florida: Democrat David Jolly versus Republican Byron Donalds
Georgia: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms versus Republican Rick Jackson
Iowa: Democrat Rob Sand versus Republican Zach Lahn
Kansas: Democrat Cindy Holscher versus Republican Ty Masterson
Michigan: Democrat Jocelyn Benson versus Republican John James
Nebraska: Democrat Lynne Walz versus Republican governor Jim Pillen
Nevada: Democrat Aaron Ford versus Republican governor Joe Lombardo
Ohio: Democrat Amy Acton versus Republican Vivek Ramaswamy
Oregon: Democratic governor Tina Kotek versus Republican Christine Drazan
Texas: Democrat Gina Hinojosa versus Republican governor Greg Abbott
Wisconsin: Democrat David Crowley versus Republican Tom Tiffany

Idaho’s Prop 1: This citizen-led initiative seeks to enshrine the right to make reproductive health-care decisions without government interference. If it passes, it’d reverse Idaho’s near-total abortion ban, which is one of the strictest in the nation.

Missouri’s Amendment 3: In 2024, Missourians reversed the state’s near-total abortion ban when they passed Amendment 3, which codified the right to “reproductive freedom” in the state’s constitution. Now, two years later, Republican lawmakers have advanced a ballot measure also called Amendment 3, this time to overturn the right and make abortion care illegal once again. The measure would also ban gender-affirming care for minors.

Nevada’s Question 6: In 2024, Nevada voters voted to codify the right to abortion up until viability, or about 24 weeks of pregnancy, in the state constitution. The state requires an amendment to pass in two consecutive cycles before it can be added to the constitution, so the question will once again appear before voters.
Virginia’s Question 1: This ballot measure seeks to enshrine protections for reproductive care before, during, and after pregnancy in the state constitution.

Arizona’s Prop 318: This initiative seeks to ban trans youth from playing on sports teams that correspond with their gender identity. The measure would also prohibit them from using their preferred bathrooms and locker rooms at schools, athletic associations, and youth recreational groups.

Colorado’s Prop 134: This ballot measure would require trans athletes from kindergarten through college to play on school sports teams that match their biological sex rather than their gender identity.
Colorado’s Prop 135: This initiative would prohibit surgical gender-affirming care for transgender youth under the age of 18.
Nebraska’s Initiative Measure 442: This ballot measure would codify a sports ban in the state’s constitution prohibiting trans athletes from participating in girls’ or women’s sports.

Virginia’s Question 2: While the Supreme Court legalized same-sex marriages in 2015, Virginia’s constitution still includes language prohibiting them. This ballot measure would amend the constitution to say the state recognizes the marriage between two adults regardless of sex, gender, or race.
Washington’s IL26-001: This ballot measure would repeal recent pro-LGBTQ+ amendments to a state parental-rights law.

Washington’s IL26-638: This initiative seeks to ban trans athletes from joining girls’ or women’s sports teams from kindergarten through high school. It also requires that a health-care provider certify a player’s sex assigned at birth through genetic screening, a testosterone-level test, or an examination of their reproductive anatomy.
Colorado’s Amendment 81: This citizen-led initiative sponsored by a conservative group would amend the state constitution to require that local authorities collaborate with ICE.

items.title: The Products Our Beauty Writer Can’t Live Without
items.description: Not a week goes by without someone asking me, “What beauty products are you loving right now?” My mind immediately goes blank — not because I can’t think of any but because there are just too many. Do I discuss the hair dryer and towel that make drying my hair
items.author: Carol Lee
paragraphs: Not a week goes by without someone asking me, “What beauty products are you loving right now?” My mind immediately goes blank — not because I can’t think of any but because there are just too many. Do I discuss the hair dryer and towel that make drying my hair less of a chore? Should I dish about the bodywash that helps me relax at the end of the day? Or do I reveal my daily fragrance-layering routine? Sit me down, and I could talk beauty until the sun goes down.

I fell in love with beauty at an early age. I have pictures of me at 4 or 5 years old, looking blissful after my first makeover at a friend’s birthday party. As a teen, my true obsession with skin care and makeup began during my search to cure — and cover up — my severe acne, which led to reading countless blogs, watching hours of YouTube, and dragging my best friend to Sephora whenever we were at the mall. That love for this world never stopped. These days, nothing gets me going like a musky fragrance or the perfect ’90s-brown lip (inspired by pictures of my mom from the decade). Coming up with a list of my current top products was a dream, but it also made me want to pull my hair out because it was so difficult. I realized just how many incredible formulas I’ve tried — and how many I adore. There are quite a few that just barely didn’t make the cut, but below, you’ll find the ones that did.

Soon, you’ll see a few other Cut staffers’ favorite beauty products. For now, you can also check out our beauty editor Asia Milia Ware’s picks as well as the 100 Cut Beauty Closet selections we made as a team.

items.title: UFC Legend Conor McGregor Announces "Last Dance" MMA Return
items.description: Conor McGregor has announced plans for a "last dance" inside the Octagon for the final bout of his UFC contract
items.author: Joyce Li
paragraphs: Conor McGregor has announced plans for a "last dance" inside the Octagon for the final bout of his UFC contract
The former two-division champion took aim at Canelo Álvarez's recent fight metrics and vowed to break his own pay-per-view sales records
While McGregor is targeting a comeback in 2027 the UFC has yet to officially determine an opponent or confirm a bout date

Former two-division UFC champion Conor McGregor has announced plans for his “last dance” inside the Octagon for the final bout of his promotional contract. The Irish superstar took to social media to signal his return while weighing in on the commercial metrics of Saturday’s boxing match between Canelo Alvarez and Christian Mbilli in Saudi Arabia.

Coming off a 69-second defeat and torn meniscus against Max Holloway at UFC 329 in July—his third straight loss—McGregor dismissed the financial power of rival combat sports showcases. “How many views did the Canelo fight get? How many in attendance? Gate? Man, I outdo ALL of these people in sales. Majorly. EVERY SINGLE ONE. With ease. Maybe even combined. I don’t even be trying,” McGregor tweeted, asserting his continued dominance as a pay-per-view draw.

The former featherweight and lightweight champion emphasized that his impending return will conclude his storied MMA career on his own terms. “I was on the same time as the World Cup semi final and still done all them numbers in that last bulls*** that I’ve to sit with for another few months before I return,” McGregor added. “I’m going to actually try to sell the fight for my next one. My final fight. See what numbers I can generate. Keep outdoing my own records.” While McGregor is targeting an Octagon comeback in 2027, the UFC has yet to finalize an opponent or official date.
