items.title: The Wildest Details From the Haley Stevens Train Wreck
items.description: On Sunday morning, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens shocked her party by endorsing Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s hotly contested Senate race over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed — just hours after telling colleagues she would not do such a th
items.author: Bess Levin
paragraphs: On Sunday morning, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens shocked her party by endorsing Trump-backed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s hotly contested Senate race over Democrat Abdul El-Sayed — just hours after telling colleagues she would not do such a thing. Maryland representative Jaime Raskin, for one, said he was “dumbfounded” Sunday morning by the news after speaking with Stevens the previous night. Fellow Michigan representative Debbie Dingell said Stevens told her around midnight Saturday that rumors of switching sides were not true and had even texted her on Sunday morning: “Watching you on MS NOW, heart, heart.”

Unsurprisingly, the fallout has been swift. More than half of Stevens’s Congressional staff resigned, and words like “despicable betrayal,” “self-immolation over hurt feelings,” and “saddest sore loser in politics since Trump 2020” have been used to describe her about-face. But how, exactly did it all go down? Did she endorse Rogers on Sunday because El-Sayed disinvited her the day before to a church service? Did her fiancé, who bizarrely conducted his own series of interviews, pressure her into it? Does she think she still has a future in the Democratic Party?
Here’s what we’ve learned so far.
Stevens hasn’t come up with a great explanation for the 11th-hour Rogers endorsement

During an interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper that has been described as “one of the worst political interviews in modern history,” Stevens claimed she “absolutely” wants Democrats to win control of the Senate, despite publicly endorsing a Republican for the open seat in Michigan.

Asked what changed in the hours between Stevens telling various elected officials that she wouldn’t be endorsing Rogers and then going ahead and endorsing him, she replied, “This is a broader point about what’s going on in our own party.” Told “it’s actually not,” she then appeared to weirdly suggest maybe she’d vote for El-Sayed after all, saying, “I haven’t cast my vote yet.” But when asked by Cooper if she “might change her mind again,” Stevens told him, “Anderson, my mind is made up, I’m rock solid, I’m an independent woman, I’ve made my decision.”

When Cooper pointed out that in August, Stevens wrote on social media, “Mike Rogers will be another rubber stamp for Donald Trump’s dangerous agenda, we can’t afford to give MAGA another senate seat in November,” and asked the congresswoman, “Why is it okay now?” she dodged the question. “Why is it okay to have the Democratic Party and a top nominee injecting this type of anger and lack of kindness?” Stevens asked.

Stevens suggested in Sunday’s video announcement that El-Sayed was snubbing her drove her to endorse Rogers. “Our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away,” she said. “He’s right, and that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate.” She has mentioned other gripes with El-Sayed over the past day, including his ties to Twitch streamer and supporter Hasan Piker and a third-party ad that suggested higher grocery prices stemmed from U.S. aid to Israel — a spot that never aired in Michigan, which El-Sayed said he didn’t agree with, and which his campaign wasn’t affiliated with.

On Monday, conservative host Scott Jennings asked Stevens on his radio show why she made her decision, to which she responded: “Let’s go through the sequence of events, Scott. Immediately after the primary, I tried to do everything right. I did it right. I put party first. I endorsed him to which the response was — ignored. And cut off! I said, I get that, I’ll just go back to my regular life. Tuck this away. And then the ads came out, ads blaming Jews for everything!”
She’s saying things like how Mike Rogers could be the next John McCain

In an interview Sunday night with the Free Press — conducted on her fiancé’s couch while wearing “pink fuzzy slippers” and eating popcorn — Stevens said she endorsed Rogers because “I think he loves the country,” adding, “Maybe he can be a [John] McCain–type person or a Lisa Murkowski,” a reference to the moderate Republican senator from Alaska. She did not discuss the many, many substantive issues she disagrees with Rogers on — including abortion rights, health care, unions, and 2020-election denial — or that she has said Rogers is “just the latest MAGA grifter in politics for a paycheck.”
People close to Stevens think her fiancé may be to blame

In an interview with Gongwer News Service on Sunday, former Michigan governor James Blanchard said that during a dinner on Friday with Stevens; her fiancé, Jason Turkish; Blanchard’s wife; and another couple, Turkish criticized Stevens for endorsing El-Sayed. (Turkish, a Democratic attorney, publicly endorsed Rogers last week.)

“He was working her over,” Blanchard said of Turkish. “The way he was saying it was ‘Everyone is disappointed in you, they did everything they could to help you and then immediately after you lose the primary, you endorsed him.’” Blanchard told the outlet he pushed back in defense of Stevens, saying he told Turkish, “Yeah, because she’s a team player. You have to be gracious. Come on.” Turkish reportedly responded, “I know, but they’re really disappointed in her.” Blanchard, who was set to attend the church event with Stevens and El-Sayed on Sunday, believes “something snapped in her. And it snapped in 24 hours.” He added that Turkish has “terrible political judgment.”

On X, University of Michigan regent Jordan Acker wrote, “As Haley’s friend, I can’t be silent … I’ve known her fiancé, Jason Turkish, for years. I respect him as a brilliant lawyer and advocate for disabled Americans. But I have become deeply troubled by his behavior. I’ve heard serious concerns about his treatment of Haley’s staff, friends, and allies. My own experiences have only deepened those concerns. It is painful to watch someone you care about go through something like this.”

Acker also wrote on X that Turkish “took her phone away,” prompting a response from the fiancé: “Haley turned off her phone because of the amount of incoming calls. You are welcome to come over whenever you want. No need to make things up.”

On MS Now, Dingell said she’s “upset” and “very concerned” about what is going on with Stevens. Representative Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Michigan primary in July, said that if her husband “ever tried to speak for me the way” Turkish has for Stevens, she would divorce him.

Turkish attended an event for Rogers last week, where he called El-Sayed an antisemite. On Friday, he told TMZ of his fiancée, “I don’t think she’s going to be supporting Abdul El-Sayed very much longer.” As the New York Times notes, Turkish’s political commentary and public endorsement of Rogers seemingly came out of nowhere, and “though he is a veteran fund-raiser and an accomplished lawyer,” he “had not been a sought-after political surrogate.”
Stevens apparently found time Monday to send out save-the-date invitations:
Stevens still identifies as a Democrat
Asked if she will leave the party, the Congresswoman told Politico, “I am still very much a Democrat,” and said she will vote for Democrats for other races.
Stevens told the Free Press she is “at peace with this,” adding, “I’m not wrestling with this.”

items.title: Trump’s Closing Argument: Get a Load of the Reflecting Pool!
items.description: President Trump’s deep unpopularity is dragging down Republicans around the country. His personal intervention in Texas’s primary has made the GOP’s Senate majority significantly more difficult to defend. Some wonder if he even cares about Republicans winning
items.author: Benjamin Hart
paragraphs: President Trump’s deep unpopularity is dragging down Republicans around the country. His personal intervention in Texas’s primary has made the GOP’s Senate majority significantly more difficult to defend. Some wonder if he even cares about Republicans winning the midterm elections at all.

The president didn’t exactly allay those concerns on Monday, a day before polls close. As his X account rolled out pro forma endorsements of various Republicans, the real Trump was laser-focused on the one thing that really animates him right now: Washington renovations. During a roughly 20-minute address in front of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Trump took a rhetorical victory lap for restoring the beleaguered body of water, even though his administration first bungled the job in extremely high-profile fashion over the last few months. Holding up oversize posters and backed by visual aids, the president went into granular detail about the landmark, which is no longer glaringly empty.
He marveled at the new water’s hue:
He uttered the word “recaulked.”
And of course, he mulled adding his name to the finished product:
The New York Times’ Shawn McCreesh compiled a list of some of the topics Trump touched on:

Though deadlines prevent a full fact-check, it seems unlikely that any of these place highly on lists of Americans’ leading concerns at the moment. Nor do Trump’s other projects around town, like the gigantic White House ballroom or the club-ified Rose Garden. Still, Trump was intent on keeping the focus local. “We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation, but for that, you don’t have enough time,” Trump said, according to the Associated Press.

To be fair, Trump did touch on weightier topics like the Iran war he started (not actually a war, per Trump). But the star of his “weave” was the pool, which since the beginning of Trump’s second term has starred in a very Trumpian saga featuring cut-rate contractors and the unjust prosecution of a blameless ex-Olympian.

Oh, right, there’s an election coming up! Trump did get into all that, more than 20 minutes into his appearance. He went typically dark, remarking that “the Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history.” He called the election the “the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime.” But strangely, he also struck a tone of resignation.

The desultory nature of Trump’s comments was no surprise, and neither was his lack of enthusiasm for an election that polls project will be a drubbing. Trump has been holding rallies around the country, though at a lower rate than he has in the past. (He was scheduled for nine telerallies on Monday, but zero in-person events.) And while he has extolled the virtues of Republican lawmakers, and the ass of one in particular, he has mostly framed the proceedings around himself, urging Americans to vote as if he were on the ballot. Given his current poll numbers, Republicans would probably rather they not.
Still, the GOP can take comfort that by putting water back in the reflecting pool, Trump may have at least pleased some middle-schoolers on field trips, a key demographic for the midterms (of 2034).

items.title: RIO's New Era Proves Fashion Is Cyclical: And the Future Is Latino
items.description: There are moments in fashion that remind us why this industry matters beyond the clothes. The new era of RIO is one of those moments.
items.author: Ricardo Diaz
paragraphs: There are moments in fashion that remind us why this industry matters beyond the clothes. The new era of RIO is one of those moments.

What Rio Uribe has built over the years—from the groundbreaking days of Gypsy Sport to the evolution of his namesake label, RIO—has been nothing short of remarkable. At a time when conversations around inclusion, diversity, and representation often feel performative, Rio has consistently demonstrated what authentic community-building looks like. For many Latinos working in fashion, his journey has been proof that anything is possible.

I still remember attending the Gypsy Sport shows years ago. The energy was electric. Those presentations weren't simply runway shows; they were celebrations of creativity, individuality, and belonging. They were among the experiences that made me fall in love with fashion in the first place. Today, seeing Rio not only as a creative force but also as one of my closest friends has made witnessing this evolution even more meaningful.

Working alongside a Latino-led team that continues to push fashion forward has been an incredible experience. As Fashion Director, one of the most exciting parts of the process is hearing what Rio is dreaming up next—how we can engage with current trends while simultaneously developing our own visual language and creating statements that feel entirely original.
That spirit is captured perfectly in RIO's first campaign since the brand's transformation from Gypsy Sport in 2025.

Unveiled on June 15 in New York City, the campaign marks a defining new chapter for both the designer and the label. Photographed by Harry Eelman, the imagery captures a pivotal moment in RIO's ongoing evolution. Balancing rebellion with refinement, the campaign reflects a collection rooted in fearless self-expression while embracing a newfound creative maturity. You only need to take a look at the incredible hair and makeup to understand that the team truly understood the assignment and delivered. We are incredibly grateful to have the support of Oribe as a partner, as well as the exceptional work of Kien Hoang and David Velasquez. A quick visit to their Instagram accounts is enough to understand the caliber of artists we are talking about.

Of course, RIO's story didn't begin with this campaign. Long before the rebrand, Gypsy Sport was already creating defining moments that shifted the conversation around fashion and culture. Let's not forget the milestones: bringing a then-rising Cardi B to the runway before she became a global phenomenon, or having Rico Nasty close the Fall/Winter 2019 show with the kind of energy only Rio's universe could attract. These weren't simply celebrity cameos—they were cultural statements. They reflected a brand that has always had its finger on the pulse of what comes next.

The achievements and experiences built through Gypsy Sport have now evolved into something even greater with the arrival of this new campaign. At a moment when Latino culture is increasingly shaping every corner of the global creative landscape—just look at our model Kandrex’s appearance during Bad Bunny's Super Bowl halftime performance—RIO offers something refreshingly nuanced. The imagery feels like a breath of fresh air, presenting a different perspective on what it means to be Latine today.

Ten years later, a different generation has found its way to RIO. This audience is politically engaged, environmentally conscious, and deeply invested in conversations around sustainability, identity, and community. They care about the future of the planet just as much as they care about personal style. In Rio's world, those values aren't contradictory. The RIO generation understands that you can advocate for change, challenge the status quo, and still look incredibly hot while doing it.

The images feel both intimate and aspirational—grounded in authenticity while reaching toward something larger. They serve as a powerful introduction to RIO's next chapter, one that remains deeply connected to its roots while making subtle winks to iconic cultural moments many of us grew up with, from Jenny From the Block to the broader visual language of Latino pop culture. At the same time, the campaign confidently steps into a broader contemporary conversation.
More than a campaign, this moment establishes the foundation for the brand's future as RIO expands its design universe and builds momentum toward its highly anticipated September runway show.

Fashion has always been cyclical. Trends return, references are revisited, and aesthetics are constantly reinterpreted. But what makes RIO's current moment so significant isn't nostalgia—it's evolution. It's proof that a brand can grow without losing its identity, that representation can be both meaningful and aspirational, and that Latino voices continue to shape the future of fashion on a global scale.

items.title: Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross Scored 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth'
items.description: After rumors stirred last month, it’s official: Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross provided the score to The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, directed by David Fincher and written by Quentin Tarantino.
items.author: Jaeden Pinder
paragraphs: After rumors stirred last month, it’s official: Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross provided the score to The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, directed by David Fincher and written by Quentin Tarantino.
Reznor and Ross have scored six of Fincher’s movies, including The Social Network, Gone Girl, and Mank, the former receiving the Academy Award for Best Original Score in 2011.
The duo has also struck up a creative partnership with another director in recent years, scoring the last four movies directed by Luca Guadagnino, including Challengers and After the Hunt.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is a quasi-sequel to Quentin Tarantino’s 2019 film Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood and arrives in theaters on Nov. 25 before heading to Netflix on December 23. Tarantino will release a novelization of the Booth-centered film on Dec. 8, following the 2021 work Once Upon a Time in Hollywood: A Novel.

Brad Pitt reprises his role as the eponymous stuntman-turned-fixer and takes place in 1977, eight years after the events of Tarantino’s movie, which altered the events of the Tate-LaBianca murders committed by the Manson Family. Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Timothy Olyphant, and Yahya Abdul-Mateen II also appear in the spin-off.

As Nine Inch Nails, Reznor and Ross have kept busy. The pair released Nine Inch Noize, a collaborative record with Boys Noize, in April. Last September, they released the Tron: Ares soundtrack, which marked the first new Nine Inch Nails record in a half decade.

items.title: Trump Uses Final Pre-Midterm Speech to Ramble About Reflecting Pool
items.description: Donald Trump on Monday delivered his closing argument ahead of the midterm elections. He wasn’t in one of the critical swing states Republicans need no win in order to keep their majorities, or even one of the red states at risk of slipping into Democrats’ con
items.author: Nikki McCann Ramirez
paragraphs: Donald Trump on Monday delivered his closing argument ahead of the midterm elections. He wasn’t in one of the critical swing states Republicans need no win in order to keep their majorities, or even one of the red states at risk of slipping into Democrats’ control. He chose a location that embodied his own self of self-obsession, corruption, and federal mismanagement: the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. He might even rename it after himself.

“This is a massive piece of pool,” Trump said while delivering his closing message, one that focused on his vanity projects over the election. “It was treated with a lot of love. And then it was treated with a lot of hate, and we’ve got to stop the hate,” the president said. “I mean, they’ve had years here where you couldn’t see any water. It was just algae. And it had a bad aroma, to put it mildly. A lot of bad things happened.”

GOP candidates and lawmakers across the country are bracing for a schlacking that will very likely strip them of their majority in the House, and could cost them the Senate. Of top concern for voters is the cost of living strains that can be linked directly to Trump’s policies. High gas prices caused by the continued global disruption of Trump’s war against Iran. Economic downturns in border and industrial communities as a result of his tariff regime. Murders, beatings, and civil rights violations by ICE agents conducting mass arrests of migrants. Add to that the blatant self-enrichment of Trump, his family, and his allies.

The “renovations” the president has made to the White House and buildings in Washington, D.C., have become the physical representation of the corruption and narcissism of the administration. As Americans struggle to afford a home, groceries, and gas, the president is spending millions of taxpayer dollars building a ballroom for the White House, gilding everything he can get his hands on in gold leaf, and butchering the restorations and repairs of monuments like the Reflecting Pool and the Kennedy Center.

It’s no surprise that many Republican candidates have chosen to distance themselves from Trump this election cycle. Even so, the president has refused to get out of his own party’s way, insisting that voters frame the midterm elections as a direct referendum on his first two years back in office. Trump canceled planned rallies in Kansas in Iowa over the weekend, and instead retreated back to the capital, claiming he will do “tele-rallies” instead. On Monday, in the last best opportunity to address reluctant voters, the president spent almost 30 minutes rambling about the Reflecting Pool.

Trump reiterated his claims that his shoddy renovation of the Reflecting Pool — which was done without the competitive contractual bidding process required by Congress and instead given to Trump’s chosen pool guy — was botched due to vandalism. The $16.4 million polymer liner that was installed to stop leaks and water seepage from the pool peeled up almost immediately, and turned the landmark into a swampy, plasticy mess infested with overgrown algae. A federal review of the project and its aftermath concluded that the pool lining had not been damaged by vandals — as the president claimed — but was poorly installed by the contractor.

“I’m thrilled to announce the official opening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool that we are giving serious thought to changing the name to the Trump Reflecting Pool. We’ll announce that sometime tomorrow,” Trump said, before claiming he was just “kidding.”

The president went so far as to use a series of large poster boards on an easel as props for the event. These featured an aerial image of the pool with the caption: “Back, and more beautiful than ever!” At one point Trump demanded that an aid bring him a print out of “how it looked before.”
When he finally got around to talking about the midterms, the president seemed barely interested.

“As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections,” he finally said, in a sharp pivot away from an ode to the beauty of Corinthian columns. “The Democratic Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history.”

“There’s never been anything like what we’re seeing,” he claimed. “Jihadists and Muslim Brotherhood members and people that nobody can even believe what we’re looking at. And all committed to the same radical agenda: open borders, raising your taxes by trillions of dollars, taking away your guns, transgender mutilization of your children, abolishing oil and natural gas, sending energy caused skyrocketing and opening the floodgates to millions of migrants from all over the world — hoping to get them to be able to vote.”

Trump insisted that under his administration, Americans were living in the “golden age” of prosperity. “We’ve achieved more in less than two years than any administration in American history, and I’ve kept every single promise I made except far more. I’ve actually kept far more promises than I made. We’ve done much more than I promised,” he said.

It would be “foolish” to “let people that hate our country win an election,” Trump added. “Because if the people that voted for me and voted in the last election — where we had such a great victory — if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide.”

Before he ended the event, Trump made sure to take a moment to list off the other major monuments and projects he planned to build in the capitol in order to commemorate his glorious reign. An Arc de Triomphe-inspired arch next to the Lincoln Memorial, a brand new golf course on the East Potomac Park, a statue-filled “Garden of American Heroes.”

It was a speech to reflect the moment. As the nation screams for lower prices, less wars, and a return to the principles that allowed past generations to achieve the prosperity of the American Dream, the leader of the Republican Party is focused on his own self-aggrandizement.

items.title: The 76 Best Albums of 1976
items.description: The year was 1976. Everything was weird — but especially the music. Everyone walked around saying, “Dy-no-mite!” or “Up your nose with a rubber hose.” Jimmy Carter became the first president to hang out with the Allman Brothers. The Apple computer and VHS play
items.author: Jon Dolan; Angie Martoccio; Rob Sheffield
paragraphs: The year was 1976. Everything was weird — but especially the music. Everyone walked around saying, “Dy-no-mite!” or “Up your nose with a rubber hose.” Jimmy Carter became the first president to hang out with the Allman Brothers. The Apple computer and VHS player were invented. So was The Muppet Show. The Farrah Fawcett poster was everywhere. The radio was full of Stevie Wonder and Kiss. On Saturday Night Live, Lorne Michaels offered the Beatles $3,000 to reunite. A few months later, George Harrison showed up to collect. It was that kind of year.

You could go to the movies and see Sly Stallone in Rocky, Robert De Niro in Taxi Driver, and Sissy Spacek in Carrie. (Blood had a big year.) Or you could sit around the house, get high, and watch the tube for The Jeffersons, Charlie’s Angels, What’s Happening!!, Family Feud, Good Times, or Welcome Back, Kotter. It was a great baseball summer, thanks to The Bad News Bears and Rolling Stone cover star Mark “The Bird” Fidrych. Richard Pryor was dating Pam Grier. Everyone was workin’ on their night moves.

But nothing was weirder — or cooler — than the music. So let’s break it down, with our celebration of the 76 best albums of 1976. Wonder made everybody’s fave with Songs in the Key of Life. New sounds were rising up, from Jamaican dub to CBGB punk, from outlaw country to stoner rock. The Band played their farewell Last Waltz show on Thanksgiving. Frampton came alive. P-Funk met Dr. Funkenstein. It was the Bicentennial summer immortalized in Dazed and Confused. Rush traveled to 2112. The Eagles checked into the Hotel California, and last we heard, they’re still arguing with the front desk.

It was a glorious year for one-hit wonders on the radio — Number One hits included “Disco Duck” (feathers in the club), “Play That Funky Music” (“white booooy”), “A Fifth of Beethoven” (classical disco), “Convoy” (truckers on CB radio), or “Afternoon Delight” (don’t aaaask). But it’s the classic albums we’re toasting right now. Our list has disco, prog, soul, folk, metal, Chicago blues, Brazilian samba, New Orleans funk. We’ve got classic debuts from the Ramones, Boston, Blondie, and the Runaways. We’ve got singer-songwriter gems from Joni Mitchell, Jackson Browne, Bob Dylan, Al Green, and Warren Zevon.
But the one thing all these albums have in common? They still sound dy-no-mite 50 years after they came out. So here’s to the Spirit of ’76. Don’t fear the reaper, people, and have a nice day.

- Hall & Oates, ‘Bigger Than Both of Us’ Welcome to 1976, the kind of year where the hottest boy-boy duo in pop history could introduce themselves with the question “Do you believe in hot cars, leather bars, and movie stars?” Philly dogs Daryl Hall and John Oates hit the spotlight with their breakthrough album, Bigger Than Both of Us, and their first Number One smash, “Rich Girl.” It also has the awesome Me Decade pep talk “Do What You Want, Be What You Are,” where Daryl sings the wise words, “The strong give up and move on/While the weak give up and stay.” “John and I have never been lovers,” Daryl confided to Rolling Stone. “He’s not my type. Too dark and short.” But 50 years later, they’re still on top of … [touches earpiece] Wait, seriously? They broke up? Why? Get it together, you two! But Bigger is an archetypal 1976 pop classic — and the perfect place to start this party. —Rob Sheffield

- James Brown, ‘Get Up Offa That Thing’ In 1976, the Godfather of Soul was starting to key into the disco sounds of acts like Earth, Wind & Fire and the Ohio Players. But he wasn’t interested in their lavish productions, and his sound stayed as raw as ever. His second LP of three he’d released in 1976 opens with the in-the-red shriek that kicks off its title track, a nine-minute jam inspired by a audience members at a show in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, that stayed seated during Brown’s set. Their lameness is our lucky break — the song is one of his last true classics. Get Up Offa That Thing also has “I Refuse to Lose,” an empowerment anthem for the doldrums of the stagflation-plagued Seventies, and the good-footin’ workouts “Can’t Take It With You” and “This Feeling.” —Jon Dolan

- Al Stewart, ‘Year of the Cat’ Scottish singer-songwriter Al Stewart started out on the London folk scene of the mid-Sixties, briefly sharing a flat with another unknown guy on the scene named Paul Simon. By the mid-1970s, he was riding the soft-rock wave, with a yen for literary lyrics, meticulous arrangements, and lithe, airy guitar work. Stewart had his biggest success with his seventh album, Year of the Cat. “On the Border” floats an evocation of anti-colonial struggle in on a sea-breeze melody; on “Flying Sorcery,” planes in a fog are a metaphor for doomed lovers; “Broadway Hotel” is about a lonely woman having an affair with a hotel-room service attendant. It all flows into the hit title track, a Casablanca-inspired intrigue about a man on an exotic vacation who falls for a mysterious patchouli-scented woman and gets his travel itinerary upended and his life turned upside down. —J.D.

- Loretta Lynn, ‘When the Tingle Becomes a Chill’ By the time Loretta Lynn’s 27th solo album hit shelves, she’d already spent the past few years releasing songs that redefined how a woman in country music was able to sing about sexuality and desire (“The Pill,” “Rated X”). Made at producer Owen Bradley’s barn in Mount Juliet, Tennessee, When the Tingle Becomes a Chill boasted a title track, written by Lola Jean Dillon, that charted what happens when the spark leaves a relationship and the bedroom. (“The body performs, but the soul has no will.” Ouch.) Lynn also offered a gloriously glossy version of Glen Campbell’s hit “Rhinestone Cowboy,” the moody misdirection of “Red, White and Blue,” and “All I Want From You (Is Away),” which showcased her snappy sonic sense of humor. —Marissa R. Moss
- Kiss, ‘Rock and Roll Over’

Following the conceptual stretch of their other 1976 album, Destroyer (see Number 25), Kiss got back to straight-ahead hard rock on their fifth studio LP, hailed by some fans as their finest release. It was their first time in the studio with super-reliable producer Eddie Kramer, who’d mixed their breakthrough 1975 live album Alive!, and the sound is much punchier than their sometimes murky-sounding earlier records. “I Want You” starts off as sensitive acoustic schlock but quickly turns into irresistibly swaggering pop metal, and the solid songs keep on coming, from “Take Me” to “Calling Dr. Love” to “Hard Luck Women,” originally written for Rod Stewart and containing a spot-on Rod impression on vocals from drummer Peter Criss. —J.D.

- Burning Spear, ‘Garvey’s Ghost’ Garvey’s Ghost was the pioneering dub version of Burning Spear’s radical reggae statement, Marcus Garvey. Winston Rodney was on a tear in 1976 — he also released Man in the Hills. Garvey’s Ghost was mixed in London, but the goal was taking dub somewhere new sonically. “Now you get lots of artificial dub effects in Jamaica,” producer Jack Ruby explained in Sounds, “but I used none with this record, not to get in the way of the music.” The spectral grooves cast a spell by zoning in on individual instruments, especially Leroy “Horsemouth” Wallace’s drums, for an eerie sense of dread. “Jamaican surf music,” Greil Marcus called it. “Which is to say that slave ships are visible on the horizon.” —R.S.

- KC and the Sunshine Band, ‘Part 3’ A disco celebration, with a great big rainbow on the cover. On Part 3, KC and the Sunshine Band offer a tripartite plan for spiritual unity: (1) Shake shake shake, (2) Shake shake shake, (3) Shake your booty. Then start back at the top. The Miami funkateers, led by Harry Wayne Casey and Richard Finch, felt like strutting their stuff after their 1975 self-titled smash. So they upped the ante, refining disco bliss into pure tantric repetition: “Shake Shake Shake (Shake Your Booty),” “I’m Your Boogie Man,” “I Like to Do It,” and, best of all, “Keep It Coming Love.” KC and the Sunshine Band appeared on Dolly Parton’s variety show in December 1976: You haven’t lived till you’ve seen Dolly jam with them on “That’s the Way I Like It.” —R.S.

- Merle Haggard, ‘My Love Affair With Trains’ On Merle Haggard’s 20th album, My Love Affair With Trains, the slow death of the black iron horse is a metaphor for the loss of a way of life and a vision of America itself. On the Dolly Parton penned title track, Merle plays a settled down family man whose hobo blood boils every time he hears that lonesome whistle blow. “Here Comes the Freedom Train” chugs through our nation’s history with democratic progress pumping the engine and heroes from Washington to Lincoln to MLK as conductors. The heart of the album is in the nostalgia of “Where Have All the Hobos Gone” and “No More Trains to Ride,” songs that, in Hag’s words, “may make you a little bit sad when you realize what we’re leaving behind.” —J.D.

It was a golden age for funk upstarts, and Foxy were quintessential class-of-’76 disco weirdos. After KC and the Sunshine Band became stars, Foxy took over as the new house band at the crucial Miami indie-dance label T.K. Records, with Cuban-born bandleader Ish Ledesma. Their 1976 debut is an underground funk cult item, trashy and proud, with club hits like “Get Off Your Aahh and Dance,” an orgiastic conga groove where even the flutes sound like they’re panting lasciviously. Foxy went Top 40 with their 1978 hit “Get Off,” a perv-disco banger that spawned sequels like “RRRRRock.” (Take that, Charli XCX.) Ledesma moved on to a strange career writing and producing for one-hit wonders, like Oxo’s 1983 pop hit “Whirly Girl” and Company B’s 1987 freestyle classic “Fascinated.” —R.S.

- Genesis, ‘Wind & Wuthering’ Genesis kick-started 1976 by dropping their first post-Peter Gabriel LP, A Trick of the Tail (See Number 36), toured North America and Europe, and then headed right back into the studio to craft a follow-up, which they got into stores just a couple of weeks before 1977. Phil Collins was the face and voice of the band at this point, and still had his old job as drummer, but he hadn’t come into his own yet as a songwriter. This created space for guitarist-bassist Mike Rutherford to write the ballad “Your Own Special Way,” keyboardist Tony Banks to compose the 10-minute prog epic “One for the Vine,” and for everyone to come together on the soaring instrumental suite “Unquiet Slumbers for the Sleepers/In That Quiet Earth.” Guitarist Steve Hackett’s departure after this album solidified the three-man lineup that would go on to very big things in the Eighties. —Andy Greene

- George Harrison, ‘Thirty Three & 1/3’ The Beatles were riding a massive resurgence in 1976, years after they broke up — they shocked the industry with the blockbuster hit anthology Rock & Roll Music, while “Got to Get You Into My Life” became a Top 10 smash a decade after it was released. But George Harrison was coming out of a few hard years, with his voice, health, and career in rough shape. Fortunately, the Quiet One came back strong on Thirty Three & 1/3, revitalized by his new love Olivia Arias Harrison, with his tributes “Beautiful Girl” and “Learning How to Love You.” It also has one of his most soulful love songs ever: “Pure Smokey,” where he thanks the Lord for giving the world the genius of Smokey Robinson, always one of the Fabs’ biggest heroes. “Pure Smokey” was never a hit, but it’s Harrison at his most humane and lovable. —R.S.

- Bob Seger, ‘Live Bullet’ Much like it did with Cheap Trick, Kiss, and Peter Frampton, it took a live album to break Bob Seger. In his case, it followed a decade of grueling roadwork, and an astounding eight flop albums. But these lean years turned Seger & the Silver Bullet Band into a ferocious live band, and gave them a repertoire of songs like “Turn the Page,” “Travelin’ Man,” “Beautiful Loser,” “Heavy Music,” and “Katmandu” that crushed every time they went onstage. And once the public finally heard this live album taped across two nights at Detroit’s Cobo Hall in September 1976, Seger finally found the audience he long deserved. Many studio albums followed, and a handful of live ones, but none of them quite captured the magic of this one. It’s an artist right on the cusp of superstardom with a lot to prove. There’s simply no way to recreate that. —A.G.
- Rod Stewart, ‘A Night on the Town’

The cover of Rod Stewart’s seventh album, based on Pierre-Auguste Renoir’s painting Bal du moulin de la Galette, gives you a clue to its grand ambition. “Tonight’s the Night” pushed the envelope for suggestive radio ballads with the line “Spread your wings and let me come inside.” He closes Side One with the Dylanesque story song “The Killing of Georgie (Part I and II),” about a gay friend who gets killed by a street gang in New York. The album’s choice of covers is exquisite — a rollicking version of Hank Thompson’s honky-tonk classic “The Wild Side of Life,” a bar-band rip through Manfred Mann’s Sixties sunshine-pop tune “Pretty Flamingo,” and sensitive readings of Cat Stevens’ “The First Cut Is the Deepest” and “Trade Winds,” a politically minded ballad originally recorded by Roberta Flack for her landmark debut, First Take. —J.D.

- George Jones, ‘Alone Again’ A year after his divorce from Tammy Wynette, which she credited to “his nippin’,” the country icon opened Alone Again with “A Drunk Can’t Be a Man,” a devastating portrayal of alcoholic paralysis. The existential gut punches continue with “Ain’t Nobody Gonna Miss Me” and “Stand on My Own Two Knees.” Alone Again is one of the best albums Jones made during his historic run with producer Billy Sherrill, all heartbreaking ballads full of sad newly-single-guy angst and longing for anyone to take the pain away. The scorched-earth mood is interrupted by one upbeat novelty tune, “Her Name Is,” where Jones imagines the woman of his future with an electric clavinet chiming in every time he wants to say her name because he hasn’t found her yet and it doesn’t sound like she’s going to show up any time soon. —J.D.

- Bryan Ferry, ‘Let’s Stick Together’ Bryan Ferry, a man of wealth and taste, was also a man without a band on Let’s Stick Together. Roxy Music split up after their 1975 gem Siren and would take a few years to reunite, though almost everyone in Roxy played on Ferry’s next solo album. Let’s Stick Together is a strange but seductive collage, with the Divine Bryan embracing his new vocation as the ultimate art-rock lounge crooner. He interprets blues standards and pop ballads from the past, but also a batch of Roxy Music songs, giving them a jazzy new groove. Roxy played “Casanova” as a guitar screamer, but here it’s a smoldering torch song, as Ferry dismantles his own Don Juan image. The swinging title tune’s video stars a temptress in a tiger-stripe dress — played by Ferry’s paramour Jerry Hall. Bonus points for his brief fling with facial hair — nobody rocks a louche Seventies mustache like Bryan. —R.S.

- Lynyrd Skynyrd, ‘One More From the Road’ Lynyrd Skynyrd were one of the era’s great road bands, so thank the rock gods these Southern boys got to leave a definitive live testament, just a year before the fatal plane crash. One More From the Road is a blowout from the Fox Theatre in Hot’lanta. Ronnie Van Zandt sang barefoot — as he says in Cameron Crowe’s famous liner notes, “I love to feel that stage burn.” But the grease hits the skillet at the end of the night, when Ronnie asks the crowd one final question: “What song is it you wanna hear?” Shockingly, everyone in the 404 area code screams, “Freeee Birrrrrrd!” This album is why annoying people still yell “Free Bird,” a gag that started as soon as the album dropped. As Rolling Stone’s Greil Marcus noted in his review of the Band’s Last Waltz concert that Thanksgiving, “Damned if somebody didn’t yell for ‘Free Bird.’” —R.S.
- Queen, ‘A Day at the Races’

As its title suggests, A Day at the Races is a kind of sequel to Queen’s 1975 breakthrough, A Night at the Opera. Songs like “The Millionaire Waltz” and “Teo Torriatte (Let Us Cling Together)” reach for the Galileo grandeur of “Bohemian Rhapsody” without the same magnifico results, and there isn’t a standout pop hit like “Your My Best Friend.” Still, there are great moments here: “Tie Your Mother Down,” written by guitarist Brian May back in the band’s pre-Queen days, is pop-metal thunder. May sings lead on “Long Away,” a lovely light-touch moment of Beatles/Beach Boys prettiness. The peak is “Somebody to Love,” with one of Freddie Mercury’s toughest, realest heart-hungry vocals, an Olympian solo from May, and a mountainous build-up toward a grand finale — killer Queen indeed. —J.D.

- Son Seals, ‘Midnight Son’ A native of Osceola, Arkansas, where he grew up playing in his father’s juke joint, blues-guitar great Son Seals moved to Chicago and broke out with his excellent second album, Midnight Son, widely regarded as one of the 1970s best blues LPs. Unlike most upstart bluesman, he didn’t fill out his records with covers, giving Midnight Son a potent coherence. Backed by a sharp horn section, Seals’ playing on songs like “I Believe,” “Telephone Angel,” and the searing seven-minute closing track, “Going Back Home,” is explosive and precise, gritty and piercing, fitting the raw intensity of his singing, whether he’s lamenting the crummy Windy City job market or threatening to get his rod to settle a romantic situation. —J.D.

- Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers, ‘Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers’ Don’t let the leather jacket and bullets on the album cover fool you: Tom Petty and the Heartbreakers were not a punk band. “Call me a punk and I’ll cut you,” he kindly told the press. And while it was their debut, they were hardly a new band, having spent years on the road as Mudcrutch to little commercial success. The record showcased not just how seasoned they were as a band, but how much potential they had. Of the 10 tracks, two would become future hits: “Breakdown” and “American Girl,” the latter the best song of their career, fittingly recorded on the Fourth of July. How’s that for a little punk? —Angie Martoccio

- Wings, ’At the Speed of Sound’ Paul McCartney and Wings spent the summer at Number One with At the Speed of Sound, a concept album about filling the world with silly love songs. (And what’s wrong with that? We’d like to know.) The band at Number Two? The Beatles, with their surprise posthumous hit Rock & Roll Music. Speed of Sound has awesome lonely-yachts-club grooves like “She’s My Baby,” plus Linda McCartney’s first (and last) lead vocal, “Cook of the House.” Then there’s “Let ’Em In,” one of the most stoned-sounding Top 10 hits in history, about being too catatonically zonked in your bean-bag chair to get up and answer the damn door. That trombone solo alone was enough to get 1970s hippies reaching for the Visine. Speed of Sound remains influential — you can hear it all over Harry’s House, from Wings superfan Harry Styles. (The fact that Paul immediately added “Let ‘Em In” to his set list proved he’s a “Grapejuice” girlie.) —R.S.

- Dr. Buzzard’s Original Savannah Band, ‘Dr. Buzzard’s Original Savannah Band’ One of the most out-there and inventive products of the disco era, Dr. Buzzard’s Original Savannah Band was the vision of Stony Browder Jr. and his brother Thomas Browder (who adopted the stage name August Darnell), a band of Black and Latino musicians coming out of the Bronx who dressed like 1940s hepcats, sang in four languages, and reimagined the Big Band refinement of Cab Calloway for the anything-goes Seventies club scene. Highlighted by the hit “Cherchez La Femme” (a plush showcase for singer Cory Daye), the kids-choir urban pastoral “Sunflower,” and the swing banger “I’ll Play the Fool,” this joyously sophisticated album plays like the soundtrack to a night out in heaven. —J.D.

- The J. Geils Band, ‘Blow Your Face Out’ You were nobody in the 1970s rock hustle until you made a live album — but it was real boss behavior to crank out two of them. The J. Geils Band’s Blow Your Face Out was a frenzy of double-live gonzo, just three years after Live Full House, yet a whole different kind of fire-breathing blues-rock house party. The Geils gang raise hell onstage in Detroit and Boston, two quintessential live-album towns, with a gloriously scruffy desecration of the Motown classic “Where Did Our Love Go,” as Magic Dick honks his Hohner. But the peak is “Musta Got Lost,” with Peter Wolf’s epic intro monologue, a madman preacher testifying, “This is a song about L-O-V-E!” He riffs on fairy tales (“What’s the name of that chick with the long hair?” “Rapunzel!”) and proclaims himself the “Woofa Goofa with the green teeth.” —R.S.
- Bunny Wailer, ‘Blackheart Man’

Bunny Livingston co-founded the Wailers alongside Bob Marley and Peter Tosh, and contributed  spiritual stunners “Pass It On” and “Hellujuah Time” to 1974’s Burnin’, his last album with the group. His debut is a musically multifaceted statement of his Rastafarian ideals. Rather than sweeping Marley-size  anthems, he goes for the subtlety of his down-to-earth singing, sticky grooves and melodies, and ingenious musical flourishes, such as the Jew’s harp on the incredible title track, the laid-back sax on “Bide Up,” and the utopian synth on “Dream Land.” Bunny balances urgent political messages and playful escapism (see “Fig Tree,” about sitting in one), and he can sound equally deep whether he’s stoking revolution, prophesying armageddon, or simply advising “drink water children.” —J.D.
- Boz Scaggs, ‘Silk Degrees’

John Travolta said that when he was working on his moves for Saturday Night Fever he was “dancing to Stevie Wonder and Boz Scaggs.” Everybody in America was in 1976. Boz Scaggs’ multiplatinum hit Silk Degrees had the perfect mix of Southern rock, soul, and disco, sculpted with A-list L.A. session guys like keyboard player David Paich and drummer Jeff Porcaro. Ohio-born, Texas-raised Scaggs was a veteran with a long track record, and he lent a subtle old-soul warmth to the sublime slickness of “Lido Shuffle” and “Lowdown,” as well as the Mott the Hoople swagger of “Jump Street,” the reggae-tinged “Love Me Tomorrow,” and the New Orleans R&B bounce of “What Do You Want the Girl to Do.” —J.D.

- Blue Öyster Cult, ‘Agents of Fortune’ In the summer of 1976, Patti Smith spoke about why she thought Blue Öyster Cult’s new album was gaining traction. “After six years together, they finally decided to let each guy emerge personally,” she said. “They wanted to gamble, like the cover shot, to take risks, shoot for the stars.” Agents of Fortune did exactly that, making it the first — and only — Cult album to feature each member on lead vocals. Smith, who was dating guitarist-keyboardist Allen Lanier, also took the reins on the gloomy rocker “The Revenge of Vera Gemini.” And, oh yeah, the record also contains their biggest hit, “(Don’t Fear) the Reaper,” Buck Dharma’s haunting rock & roll odyssey about eternal love, the inevitability of death, and the importance of using the cowbell. “Reaper,” Laurie Strode’s toking song of choice, inspired Stephen King to write The Stand and one of the best SNL sketches in history. Shooting for the stars, indeed. —A.M.

- Marvin Gaye, ‘I Want You’ Three years after Let’s Get It On, Gaye linked up with co-writer and producer Leon Ware for his most sensual album yet, inspired by his second wife, Janis Hunter. “The time when we did I Want You had to be the most happy time in Marvin’s life,” Ware recalled. “Because he was freshly in love, and the album exhibits that atmosphere.” Come for the sugary funk of “Come Live With Me Angel,” stay for the sexy conga-filled “Soon I’ll Be Loving You Again” and various “I Want You” jams. “When I’m told by different people all over the world how many babies that album has made,” Ware said, “the record stands so high in my life.” —A.M.

- Led Zeppelin, ‘Presence’ For Robert Plant, Led Zeppelin’s seventh album was about pure survival. “There won’t be another album like it, put it like that,” he told us. “It was a cry from the depths, the only thing that we could do.” Led Zeppelin were hardly in a good place when they recorded Presence. Following their 1975 masterpiece Physical Graffiti, a frightening car crash on the Greek island of Rhodes left Plant unable to walk. Shows were canceled, and they headed into the studio to record new material. Besides the opening 10-minute epic “Achilles Last Stand,” several of the tracks remain underappreciated, like the jaunty “Hots on for Nowhere” and the searing “Tea for One,” both of which the band never performed live. “Presence was pure anxiety and emotion,” Jimmy Page said. “We didn’t know if we’d ever be able to play in the same way again. It might have been a very dramatic change, if the worst had happened to Robert. Presence is our best in terms of uninterrupted emotion.” —A.M.

- Max Romeo & the Upsetters, ‘War Ina Babylon’ The first salvo in Lee “Scratch” Perry’s “holy trinity” of dub records birthed at his mythical Black Ark studio, War ina Babylon found the producer merging Max Romeo’s commercially viable roots-reggae stylings with the dark, dense grooves of the Upsetters. Romeo, who previously sang one of reggae’s earliest international hits with 1968’s “Wet Dream,” instead focused on his burgeoning political consciousness at the time on the title track and opener, “One Step Forward.” War Ina Babylon also boasts what remains Romeo’s signature song, “Chase the Devil,” a track that Romeo himself tried to cut from the album before Perry intervened. —Daniel Kreps

- Michael Hurley, the Unholy Modal Rounders, Jeffrey Fredericks & the Clamtones, ‘Have Moicy!’ Few albums have aged as well as Have Moicy!, the ragtag folk-supergroup opus from a collection of musicians (Peter Stampfel, Michal Hurley, Jeffrey Frederick, and Paul Presti, to name just a few). The album, per the critic Robert Christgau, “renewe[ed] the concept of American folk music as a bizarre apotheosis of the post-hippie estate.” To say it’s become an influential cult classic is an understatement: The album has gone on to spin its tendrils into just about every corner of anything on the anti/freak-folk-outsider roots-indie-singer-songwriter spectrum in the 50 years since its release, resulting in covers by everyone from Yo La Tengo to Cass McCombs to JP Harris. —Jonathan Bernstein

- The Runaways, ‘The Runaways’ The Runaways were put together by sleazy L.A. rock mogul Kim Fowley as a teenage all-girl novelty band, but they broke through that cliché and immediately had their own identity and sound — “the Queens of Noise, the answer to your dreams.” The Runaways become pathfinding feminist heroes, playing hard rock with punk’s spirit and energy on fantastic songs like “American Nights,” “Thunder,” a hot-wired version of Lou Reed’s “Rock N Roll,” and the iconic album opener “Cherry Bomb,” later covered by 1990s riot grrrls Bratmobile. Along with putting out this killer debut, the Runaways were the launching pad for the legendary careers of guitarists Joan Jett and Lita Ford. —J.D.
- Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson, Jessi Colter, and Tompall Glaser, ‘Wanted! The Outlaws’

The first country-music album to ever be certified platinum was more of a compilation package meant to exploit the popularity of the outlaw-country trend than a proper album. Even so, the collection of songs, many of them previously released, by Willie Nelson, Waylon Jennings, Jessi Colter, and Tompall Glaser remains a touchstone within the genre. The Willie and Waylon entries — Jennings’ “Honky Tonk Heroes,” Nelson’s “Me and Paul,” and their duet “Good Hearted Woman” — are the most widely known, but some of Wanted!’s best and most lasting moments come from the voice of Colter, whom Jennings married in 1969. Her “I’m Looking for Blue Eyes,” one of the LP’s “new” songs, is a stunner. —Joseph Hudak

- Rose Royce, ‘Car Wash’ Rose Royce were R&B funk legends from L.A., led by the heavenly voice of Gwen Dickey. Car Wash was officially the soundtrack to the funky comedy flick, one of the best movies either Richard Pryor or George Carlin ever acted in. Director Michael Schultz had the soundtrack recorded before filming started, so the actors at the car wash would hear the same music as the audience. Motown legend Norman Whitfield produced and wrote, with the social-realist disco classic “Car Wash” (“This ain’t no place to be if you planned on being a star”) and the anti-capitalist funk chant “Put Your Money Where Your Mouth Is.” But Dickey’s voice makes the ballads irresistible — “I’m Going Down” and “I Wanna Get Next to You” have been classics ever since. —R.S.
- The Stills-Young Band, ‘Long May You Run’

“I don’t think there’s anybody who writes like Neil,” Emmylou Harris once said. “His songs are an odd combination of being straightforward and elusive at the same time.” It’s an astute description for a song like “Long May You Run,” the most romantic song anyone has ever written about a hearse. Nostalgic for their Buffalo Springfield days, Young linked up with Stephen Stills for a joint album down in Miami, yielding underrated Young gems like “Midnight on the Bay” and “Fontainebleau” (after the luxury hotel on Miami Beach). That unique combo of straightforwardness and elusiveness leaked outside of the music, as well. Graham Nash and David Crosby recorded backing vocals on the tracks, but Young ended up removing them. Then he briefly toured with Stills, only to abandon ship and leave a note. “Dear Stephen, funny how some things that start spontaneously end that way,” it read. “Eat a peach, Neil.” As Harris said, nobody writes quite like him. —A.M.
- Bob Marley, ‘Rastaman Vibration’
