items.title: Cupertino Recap: The Split
items.description: There’s one particular shot I love in this week’s Cupertino. The camera is fixed at a corner that connects two hallways in the labyrinthine San Mateo Hall of Justice. Michael and Olivia have been defending two tech bros, A.J. (Ben Cook) and Buddy (Taip Oskar Ć
items.author: Noel Murray
paragraphs: There’s one particular shot I love in this week’s Cupertino. The camera is fixed at a corner that connects two hallways in the labyrinthine San Mateo Hall of Justice. Michael and Olivia have been defending two tech bros, A.J. (Ben Cook) and Buddy (Taip Oskar Ćeman), who run a prediction-market website, WagerMode, that the state of California is trying to shut down. But because Michael has been talking to A.J. while Olivia handles Buddy — and because District Attorney Sally Clawson (Amanda Warren) has decided to offer a deal to whichever partner acts first — we get an amusing cut to Michael and Olivia flying down separate hallways, racing away from each other and off into the distance. It’s the whole theme of the episode in one snappy second: Partners zooming off in different directions.

“A.J. and Buddy” maintains that kind of energy — and visual flair — throughout most of its running time. It’s the closest Cupertino has come yet to doing a true stand-alone episode, with a story that pops up seemingly out of nowhere and then builds and builds for nearly a full 45 minutes. It’s a fantastic episode overall, harmed only by a few momentum-stalling digressions and an ending that feels a little abrupt. Not for the first time (and I’m sure not for the last), I found myself wondering how much better this show could be with another 10 to 15 minutes of running time.

The case-of-the-week begins with Christy (always a good starting point for any Cupertino). While clubbing, Christy fixates on a handsome, melancholy lad named A.J. and takes him back to her apartment without learning anything about him, which is understandable, given how many cocky Valley guys she probably encounters on a typical night out. So she’s mildly shocked the next morning when A.J. asks her to give him a ride to the airport, where a private jet is waiting. She’s even more surprised when she’s in the middle of touring the jet and it suddenly takes off for Saint Kitts.

From there, the story moves very quickly. A.J. explains that he needs Christy’s bosses to race to his house before the cops arrive to retrieve Buddy’s laptop. (They also find their retainer there, in wads of cash stashed among shelves full of shoe boxes and baking-powder cans.) When the police do arrive, what follows is a whirlwind of court appearances and client conferences, all while the DA and her officers try to move as quickly as possible to get what they need from the WagerMode boys — even if it risks violating due process.

All of this culminates in the kind of twist common to Michelle and Robert King’s legal dramas, where we often eventually discover that there are secret motivations behind what seem like simple cases. When it comes to WagerMode, Michael wants to prove that his client is a victim of selective prosecution, given that another site called PolyBetting runs an almost identical business and has a California gaming license. (It’s implied that PolyBetting does a lot of donating to politicians, including to the Trump family.) As much as DA Clawson tries to claim the moral high ground, noting that WagerMode takes bets on possible political assassinations, she eventually admits this case is really about election interference — and about the million-dollar bets from an anonymous customer: Go4Broke.

Similarly, this episode is, somewhat slyly, more about partnerships than prediction markets. It’s quite obviously about the title characters, A.J. and Buddy, who met in college and formed a symbiotic business relationship, with A.J. making bold plays while Buddy backs him up with programming genius. Yet A.J. is still a lonely little rich kid. At times he treats Christy like a playdate, offering her Pop-Tarts on a silver platter and asking her to “aisle surf” down his jet during takeoffs. And given the opportunity to betray his only real friend, the aptly named Buddy — who is actually Go4Broke — A.J. hesitates.

The other partnership examined in this episode is, of course, Michael and Olivia’s. When circumstances divide them, Olivia seizes the opportunity to show Michael that she can be more than just the sneakily sweet half of their dynamic. She defends Buddy fiercely, even getting a cut on her cheek while trying to physically prevent the police from unlocking Buddy’s computer. She also calls out Michael in front of the judge, accusing him of lying when he says he didn’t know A.J. was trying to flee the country. Michael rolls with his partner’s punches, seeing it as ordinary courtroom tussling. Olivia seems more uncertain about the parts they have to play in this case — although she’s quite good at being ruthless.

As I mentioned, this episode feels somewhat curtailed, with A.J. and Buddy’s case(s) stalling out after WagerMode starts posting odds on Clawson’s reelection. I feel like the issues this story raises — about partnerships and prediction markets — don’t get addressed as fully as they could have been. But hey, this is only episode 4 of a 20-episode season. Perhaps WagerMode will return to extract some more value from the million-dollar gold bar A.J. gave Christy as a retainer.

Part of me also wishes this episode had stuck with the WagerMode plot exclusively — although this is no knock against the scenes that keep interrupting the main story, which involve Natalia hanging around the empty PSA offices with a visiting Nichole. (A treat for Girls5Eva fans!) Some important news gets dropped during these interludes, namely that Nichole now represents Colt AI, which is suing PSA for “illegally accessing” Bo.

It’s also worth noting that as soon as Natalia wanders into the PSA backrooms, she sees the pillar where Michael and Olivia signed their partnership “contract” and adds her own name, with a new 33/33/33 split. Maybe that’s what it will take to keep Price and Siffre united: a third partner they can team up against.

Would Natalia’s power move hold up in court? Probably not. But as she herself points out, “Lawsuits are just the language of business.” In Silicon Valley, you don’t always go to court for justice. Sometimes you just want the people in your life to listen — really listen — to your complaints.
• It takes 15 minutes before the opening credits kick in this week. Good to see the Kings up to their old tricks.

• A big part of what makes this episode so fun is that for the first five minutes or so we’re just hanging out with Christy, who knows how to have a good time. We get to see the half-assed way she handles her wardrobe. (Sometimes she puts her dresses on hangers, but “then I get bored.”) And we get to see her fill her purse with all of the fancy soaps and lotions on A.J.’s PJ. (“I’m more of a Spirit Air kind of girl,” she tells him.)
• File this away for later: Olivia’s terrible sub-freeway apartment is also right above some guy running video-game servers, which make Olivia’s floor buzz all day.

• Robert King directed this episode, and one of the hallmarks of his directing style dating back to The Good Wife is his use of off-screen space and implied action, especially when it comes to the kind of technology we all use every day. Case in point: Olivia fights hard to keep the police from using Buddy’s finger to unlock his laptop, and right before the commercial break, as she falls to the floor, we hear the telltale chime of a Mac starting up.

• Another nice touch from King: the extreme close-ups on A.J. and Christy’s faces while they’re bantering and snacking on his jet. It’s unusually intimate and emphasizes how much A.J. needs close human contact.

• Another nice touch from the writers (including credited screenwriter Joey Hartstone): When the teetotaling Olivia joins her colleagues in drinking fancy Champagne to celebrate their sort-of win, her reaction to both the alcohol and the success is the same: “Bitter.”

items.title: Justin Timberlake to Release Four-Part ‘Tell-All’ Docuseries, Featuring Janet Jackson, on Apple (EXCLUSIVE)
items.description: Justin Timberlake is set to release a four-part docuseries on Apple TV in December, described as a “tell-all,” three sources confirm to Variety.
items.author: Jem Aswad; Matt Donnelly
paragraphs: Justin Timberlake is set to release a four-part docuseries on Apple TV in December, described as a “tell-all,” three sources confirm to Variety.

One source says the series will feature Janet Jackson discussing the infamous “wardrobe malfunction” that took place during the pair’s performance at the 2004 Super Bowl. Another source says that Timberlake discusses some of former girlfriend Britney Spears’ recent comments as well.

Further details on the series, which is directed by Fisher Stevens, were not available at the time of this article’s publication; reps for Timberlake, Jackson and Apple had no comment or did not respond to Variety‘s multiple requests for comment.
Timberlake has a relationship with the streamer dating back to 2021, when he starred in the Apple Original film “Palmer.”

The news comes during a comparatively low-profile period for Timberlake, who made a guest appearance during Jay-Z’s concert in Paris last month but otherwise has been off the radar since his “Forget Tomorrow” global tour in support of his most recent album, “Everything I Thought It Was,” which was released in March of 2024.

The singer announced in July 2025 that he has been diagnosed with Lyme disease, which affected some of his performances on the tour. Fans noticed that Timberlake appeared sluggish and low-energy during performances on the international leg of the trek, which he suggested was due to the nerve damage and fatigue he experienced from Lyme disease.

“I’ve been battling some health issues, and was diagnosed with Lyme Disease–which I don’t say so you feel bad for me – but to shed some light on what I’ve been up against behind the scenes,” he wrote. “If you’ve experienced this disease or know someone who has- then you’re aware: Living with this can be relentlessly debilitating, both mentally and physically.”

The tour, which wrapped in July of 2025, was further complicated by Timberlake’s DWI conviction, stemming from his arrest in Sag Harbor, New York, the previous year. He was pulled over by police in June 2024 after running a stop sign and veering out of his lane. The incident took place shortly before the tour’s launch, and Page Six reported that Timberlake said to officers, in a much-memed comment, “This is going to ruin the tour” — however, police bodycam footage released later showed that he did not say those words, rather something like “I’m on tour.”

items.title: ‘X-Men’: ‘Hunger Games’ Actor Ben Wang Circling Iceman Role in Marvel’s Reboot
items.description: After battling it out in the arena in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” and leading the latest “Karate Kid” installment, Ben Wang is circling another major franchise: Marvel Studios’ “X-Men” reboot.
items.author: Angelique Jackson
paragraphs: After battling it out in the arena in “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” and leading the latest “Karate Kid” installment, Ben Wang is circling another major franchise: Marvel Studios’ “X-Men” reboot.
Wang is in negotiations to play Bobby Drake, aka Iceman, who was one of the founding X-Men. Created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby, the character first appeared in “The X-Men #1” in September 1963.

If the deal closes, Wang would join a sprawling cast that features Sadie Sink (as Jean Grey), Kit Connor (as Cyclops), Samara Weaving (as Emma Frost), Inde Navarrette (as Rogue), Maya Boyd (as Storm), Asa Germann (as Angel), Christopher Abbott (as Professor Charles Xavier) and Adam Driver (as Mr. Sinister).

Marvel Studios chief Kevin Feige revealed the new “X-Men” cast at the D23 convention in August, after Sink’s Jean Grey debuted in the blockbuster “Spider-Man: Brand New Day.” The upcoming movie reboots the mutant team for the first time since the 2019 Fox film “X-Men: Dark Phoenix” and for their first outing under the Marvel Studios umbrella. Jake Schreier, who oversaw last year’s “Thunderbolts,” is directing the film from a script by Lee Sung Jin and Joanna Calo. “X-Men” is set for release on May 5, 2028.

In “Sunrise on the Reaping,” Wang plays Wyatt Callow, one of the tributes from District 12 alongside Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), who is the focus of the “Hunger Games” prequel movie. Wang has also starred in Lionsgate’s “The Long Walk,” Francis Lawrence’s adaptation of the Stephen King classic, as well as Will Ropp’s coming-of-age comedy “Brian,” David Wain’s comedy “Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass,” the 2024 “Mean Girls” reboot, and the Disney+ projects “American Born Chinese” and “Chang Can Dunk.” He is repped by Stewart Talent, Artists First and Schreck Rose Dapello.
Deadline first reported Wang’s potential involvement in the project. Marvel Studios could not be immediately reached for comment.

items.title: Apple Services Revenue Hits New Record of $31.6 Billion in September Quarter, but Growth Is Slowing Down
items.description: Apple continued to see sales in its flagship iPhone family balloon, while the tech giant’s services business hit a new all-time high, in the first earnings report under CEO John Ternus.
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: Apple continued to see sales in its flagship iPhone family balloon, while the tech giant’s services business hit a new all-time high, in the first earnings report under CEO John Ternus.

Apple’s Services segment revenue of $31.57 billion — a new record — was up 9.8%. But that’s slower growth than in the first two quarters of 2026 (which saw 16.3% and 12.4% year-over-year increases) and the September 2025 quarter (15% growth). In addition, Apple said services revenue is projected to rise 8%-9% in the year-end 2026 quarter, indicating further deceleration. The Services segment includes the App Store, Apple TV, Apple Music, Apple Pay, AppleCare, iCloud and advertising.

”Apple’s 12-quarter streak of double-digit Services growth ended in September, and growth will slow further in the December quarter,” LightShed Partners analysts Walter Piecyk and Joe Galone wrote in a research note Monday. Investors hoped that Siri AI would get customers to spend more on Services without Apple having to match its peers’ AI capex. Ternus suggested Apple could charge for expanded access to “server-side features of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence.” But while Apple’s massive installed base gives Siri “a good shot at being the first assistant people try” if they haven’t already settled on another AI, the analysts questioned why consumers would “pay for it let alone use it if the alternatives work better.”

For the September quarter, Apple posted total quarterly revenue of $114.5 billion, up 12% year over year. Overall gross margin was 47.9 percent, including a favorable impact of approximately one percentage point from tariff refunds, after the Supreme Court invalidated Trump’s tariffs. Diluted earnings per share came in at $2.10, up 14% year over year, and included a favorable impact of $0.05 from tariff refunds. The financial results were for Apple’s fiscal 2026 fourth quarter ended Sept. 26, 2026.

Sales of iPhone reached a September-quarter record and Services hit an all-time high, “capping off our best fiscal year ever,” Ternus said in a statement. Total iPhone revenue of $57.58 billion increased 17%.

Ternus was Apple’s head of hardware before taking over the CEO role from Tim Cook as of Sept. 1. He said the tech giant is “closing the year with our most ambitious lineup yet,” citing the foldable iPhone Duo, alongside iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. “We also just introduced a whole new generation of hardware for the home and brought Touch to Mac for the first time. Together with the all-new Siri AI, it’s an incredible lineup to carry us into the holiday season,” Ternus said.
Apple CFO Kevan Parekh said on the earnings call that it expects total revenue for the December 2026 quarter to increase 7%-10% on a year-over-year basis — lower than analyst forecasts.

items.title: Katey Sagal Returns to Fox in a Recurring Role on ‘Best Medicine’
items.description: Katey Sagal is returning to where it all really began for her: Fox. The actress, who helped launch the Fox network in primetime via “Married … With Children” and later was a key voice on Fox’s animated hit “Futurama” (now on Hulu), will return via a recurring
items.author: Michael Schneider
paragraphs: Katey Sagal is returning to where it all really began for her: Fox. The actress, who helped launch the Fox network in primetime via “Married … With Children” and later was a key voice on Fox’s animated hit “Futurama” (now on Hulu), will return via a recurring role in the network’s drama “Best Medicine.”

On the show, Sagal will recur as Kathleen Gavin, described as “Louisa’s (Abigail Spencer) estranged mother and the only person in the world who’s not welcome in Port Wenn. Combative, conniving, and always looking out for herself, Kathleen unexpectedly returns to town after a long absence, sending Louisa’s life into chaos. Martin (Josh Charles) quickly discovers there’s a reason why the people of Port Wenn refer to her as ‘Shady Katie.’”
Sagal will start her appearances on episodes set to air later this season.

Sagal’s recent credits include “One Piece,” “The Abandons,” “The Conners” and “Rebel.” She won a Golden Globe for “Sons of Anarchy” and earlier starred in the sitcoms “8 Simple Rules” and “Married … With Children.” Next up, Sagal will be seen in the Apple TV comedy “She’s Fine.”

Her film résumé includes “Trust,” “Bleed for This,” “Pitch Perfect 2” and “The Good Mother.” As a singer, she has released the albums “Well” and “Room.” And her book “Grace Notes: My Recollections” was published in 2017 by Simon and Schuster.
Sagal is represented by CAA and B&B Management.

items.title: Jon Stewart, Jimmy Kimmel, Seth Meyers Take Aim at Trump, Michigan’s Haley Stevens on Eve of Election Day
items.description: With less than 24 hours until Election Day, and a potential control flip of Congress, late-night hosts didn’t waste any time on Monday taking jabs at those making headlines heading into the midterms, namely Donald Trump and former Democratic Senate candidate H
items.author: Carly Thomas; Abid Rahman; Hilary Lewis
paragraphs: With less than 24 hours until Election Day, and a potential control flip of Congress, late-night hosts didn’t waste any time on Monday taking jabs at those making headlines heading into the midterms, namely Donald Trump and former Democratic Senate candidate Haley Stevens.

On The Daily Show, Jon Stewart seemed quite confused why Trump — who has been on the campaign trail for the past month, advocating for Republican candidates across the U.S. — used his final pre-election speech to talk about the controversial renovations he made to the newly reopened Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C.

“That was the president of the United States, on the day before the midterms, choosing to make a speech at the reflecting pool to talk about the reflecting pool. No symbolism, no metaphors, just straight-up pool maintenance. That was Donald Trump’s ‘I had it cleaned’ speech, if you will,” the host said, drawing laughter from his live audience.

After calling the president’s priorities “badly misplaced,” Stewart noted that “Democrats appear in position for a wave election” in the U.S. House and Senate “as long as the remaining couple of days before the election are bombshellless, drama-free, non-earthquakey.”

Welp… it looks like Michigan didn’t get that memo. Stevens caused quite the shakeup over the weekend with her shocking endorsement of GOP candidate Mike Rogers for Senate after breaking with Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

“We all knew there was drama in Michigan when Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Haley Stevens in a contentious primary for the Democratic nomination, but Stevens has always been very clear as to their shared goal of defeating Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers,” Stewart said, before clips played of Stevens repeatedly criticizing the GOP candidate.
“What the fuck happened? This is like the most diabolical episode of Fargo I’ve ever seen,” the host quipped.

On Jimmy Kimmel Live!, Kimmel kicked off his overtly political monologue with a reference to Trump and his continued legal woes, particularly in relation to the dead sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. “Remember that birthday card Trump didn’t draw for Jeffrey Epstein on his 50th birthday? This is why Donald Trump sued The Wall Street Journal for $10 billion for claiming he did draw that card,” said Kimmel. “He’s got a hefty bag full of frivolous lawsuits out there trying to protect himself against the blue wave, which seems to be headed his way tomorrow. Tomorrow is midterm election day.”

Kimmel then mocked Trump’s increasingly half-hearted rallies, focusing a recent event at the scandal-plagued reflecting pool in Washington D.C. “More than 57 million Americans have already cast their ballots. Trump made his closing arguments. He chose to do that in front of his ill-fated reflecting pool. What better way to reassure the public that they are in good hands than in front of a pool you’ve repeatedly botched to the tune of $16 million?” he joked. “Donald Trump, the man who famously promised to “drain the swamp,” made his last stand at the site of his own man-made swamp, standing victoriously in front of this hard-won pond like the soldiers who triumphed at Iwo Jima.”

He added, “Somehow, the ‘Energizer Dummy’ managed to blabber his way through 30 rallies over the past 32 days, and with the campaign for control of Congress at the 2-yard line, Trump is laser-focused on the issues that matter most.”

Over on Late Night With Seth Meyers, the host devoted his Monday night “Closer Look” segment to recent dramatic developments in the Alaska and Michigan Senate races. In Alaska, Meyers recapped that The New York Times reported that Democratic challenger Mary Peltola’s campaign was behind an effort to recruit independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan as a spoiler.
Meyers was shocked — and kind of impressed.
“This is very fucking funny. I mean, fuckin’ A, they finally did it: the Democrats finally did something as dirty as the Republicans,” Meyers said of the Times allegations.

“I mean it’s not systematically lobbying state election officials to send alternate slates of electors to Congress as part of an illegal scheme to undermine a presidential election and then storming the Capitol, shitting in the rotunda and threatening to kill Mike Pence dirty but it’s still pretty dirty,” he added.
Turning to Michigan, Meyers also addressed Stevens’ shocking Sunday endorsement of Rogers, or as Meyers described it: “All hell broke loose.”

In particular, Meyers highlighted Stevens’ awkward interview with Anderson Cooper on CNN Sunday night, in which she struggled to answer his questions. After one particularly long pause, Stevens asked if what Cooper had said was a question.
“No, I wanted to see if you wanted to fill in the silence but you don’t,” he responded.
Meyers seemed amazed by this as well.
“Damn that was a Game of Thrones-style burn,” Meyers said. “‘I merely hoped you would fill the silence but you did not so I will: Take him away.’”
He went on to call the interview “so brutal I watched it through my fingers like a horror movie.”
Meyers added, “I think I heard her audibly gulp more than I heard her say actual words.”

items.title: British Independent Film Awards: ‘Elsinore’ Leads Nominations With 12
items.description: Andrew Scott’s Elsinore leads the nominations for the 2026 British Independent Film Awards (BIFAs), which were unveiled on Tuesday.
items.author: Georg Szalai
paragraphs: Andrew Scott’s Elsinore leads the nominations for the 2026 British Independent Film Awards (BIFAs), which were unveiled on Tuesday.

BIFA-winning actors Jay Lycurgo and Posy Sterling revealed at One Hundred Shoreditch in London that the film received 12 nominations, followed by Clio Barnard’s I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning with eight, and Animol, the directorial feature debut of Adolescence star Ashley Walters, with seven.

In the best British independent film category, Simon Stone’s Elsinore and I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning are joined by Marc Evans’ Effi O Blaenau, Queen at Sea, directed by Lance Hammer, and Mike Leigh’s Tender Loving Care.
Stone and Barnard also scored best debut director nominations, along with Andrew Haigh for A Long Winter, Mark Jenkin for Rose of Nevada and Leigh for Tender Loving Care.
Best lead performance nominees include Scott for Elsinore, Juliette Binoche for her role in Queen at Sea,
Erin Doherty for Faith, Leisa Gwenllian for Effi o Blaenau, Jonathan Jules for Florid, and Tut Nyuot for Animol.

Claire Foy, Tom Courtenay, Sekou Diaby, Anna Calder-Marshall, Billie Piper and Bill Pullman were nominated as best supporting performers. And among the nominees in the best ensemble performance category are the likes of Bella Ramsey, Anthony Boyle, Joe Cole, Lycurgo, Daryl McCormack, Lola Petticrew, James Blunt, James Norton and Neil Patrick Harris.
Competing for the best international independent film are All of a Sudden, Club Kid, La Bola Negra, La Gradiva and Possible Love.
Meanwhile, nominated for the feature documentary award are All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea, Everybody to Kenmure Street, One in a Million, Something Familiar and We, the Hated.
And in a notable feat, the best music supervision award category features Connie Farr receiving two nominations.
The BIFAs 2026 ceremony takes place on Dec. 6 at the Camden Roundhouse in London. Check out the full list of nominees for the 2026 BIFAs below.

items.title: ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Disney Night Makes Magic (3 Perfect Scores!) as Group Dances Return, Another Celeb Departs: See the Scores, Who Went Home
items.description: [This story contains spoilers for episode nine of Dancing With the Stars season 35.]
items.author: McKinley Franklin
paragraphs: [This story contains spoilers for episode nine of Dancing With the Stars season 35.]
It’s time for Disney Night on Dancing With the Stars.

This year’s Disney-themed episode sported a new Broadway twist, with “performances inspired by beloved Disney stories and their iconic stage adaptations,” per ABC. Couples paid homage to classics from Mary Poppins, The Little Mermaid, Tangled, Beauty and the Beast and many more.

Tuesday night’s episode also saw the return of the team dances, as co-hosts Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough each joined one of the group performances. Cynthia Erivo was also in the ballroom, joining as the night’s guest judge.
Julia Stiles and Ezra Sosa were eliminated at the end of DWTS Disney Night. Earlier in the episode, they danced a paso doble to Hamilton‘s “Satisfied,” and were scored a 33/40.
Celebrities still competing on season 35 include Tatyana Ali, Jenna Dewan, Ezra Frech, Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins, Harry Shum Jr. and Connor Wood.

After the first dance of Disney Night, Hough announced that the couple who topped the leaderboard after the individual performances will receive immunity from next week’s dance-off. The couple who early on took that top spot was Harry and Jenna Johnson, who earned a perfect 40/40 for their jazz to “Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious” from Marry Poppins.
Harry and Jenna earned the first perfect score of DWTS season 35 last week, with Disney Night marking their second 40/40 in a row.
However, they weren’t left alone at the top of the Disney Night leaderboard for long, as Jenna and Val Chmerkovskiy also earned a 40/40 for their quickstep to Beauty and the Beast‘s “Be Our Guest.”

Because two couples tied at the top of the leaderboard, immunity for next week’s dance-off was given to the pair with the highest total of scores from across the season; Harry and Jenna toppled with a total of 236 (Jenna and Val had 235).
During last week’s Horror Movie Night, Jackson Olson and Tyler Cameron were kicked off the competition in a double elimination.

The couple with the lowest combined total of judges’ scores and viewer votes is eliminated at the end of each DWTS episode. Each viewer is allowed up to 10 votes per couple, per voting method (via ABC’s website and by text).

Live voting takes place during the East Coast airing of each show and ends shortly after the final performance; that means if you’re a West Coast viewer and want to vote, you must do so between 5 p.m. PT and roughly 6:45 p.m. PT, as voting ends after the final performance.

items.title: Versant Earnings Best Estimates in Quarter of Fandango, MS NOW Expansion
items.description: The cable TV-focused spinoff from NBCUniversal that owns CNBC, MS NOW, USA, Golf Channel and other assets beat Wall Street’s consensus third-quarter revenue estimate with $1.59 billion reported. $373 million (-5.3 percent) came from advertising and $245 millio
items.author: Tony Maglio
paragraphs: The cable TV-focused spinoff from NBCUniversal that owns CNBC, MS NOW, USA, Golf Channel and other assets beat Wall Street’s consensus third-quarter revenue estimate with $1.59 billion reported. $373 million (-5.3 percent) came from advertising and $245 million (+9.6 percent) from platforms ($935 million in linear distribution, $302 million in free cash flow.) Versant is pushing forward toward its goal of a 50/50 mix of advertising and platforms revenue. The company’s adjusted EBITDA dropped to $353 million (-7.4 percent); net income was $47 million, earnings per share was 34 cents.

Fandango had a strong quarter in ticket sales and launched its AVOD platform in the quarter. MS NOW’s direct-to-consumer product also debuted; CNBC’s will following next year. The company’s acquisition of Full Swing also closed this summer.

Versant says its networks are “reaching more than 120 million viewers monthly.” Anna Pigeon became cable’s most-watched new scripted series this year, though are not a whole bunch of those these days. Versant completed the major distribution deals it had on the table.

“Versant’s momentum continues, with audience growth and the completion of all planned Pay Television distribution renewals for the year, underscoring the value and enduring appeal of our brands,” said CEO Mark Lazarus. “In the third quarter, we advanced Fandango’s evolution into a comprehensive entertainment platform, integrated Full Swing into our golf ecosystem, and launched MS NOW Membership to connect directly with our audiences. We’re building deeper consumer relationships, expanding our reach and creating new opportunities for growth and monetization across our four core markets.”

“Our third quarter performance demonstrates the financial discipline and flexibility that underpins Versant’s strategy,” said CFO and chief operating officer Anand Kini. “We delivered strong Platforms revenue, continued operating efficiencies and significant cash flow. Looking ahead, we are reaffirming our full-year revenue and Adjusted EBITDA outlook, and we expect Free Cash Flow to exceed our prior $1.0 to $1.2 billion forecast. We believe that our ability to invest in growth, maintain a healthy balance sheet, and return capital to shareholders is a distinct advantage. With $457 million already returned to shareholders through today, this morning’s announcement of an additional planned $100 million ASR, along with the declaration of our quarterly dividend, underscores our commitment to delivering shareholder value.”

items.title: Peptides Are About to Flood the Market. And Bro Science Is Coming for Us All
items.description: This past February, Health and Human Services secretary and MAHA Final Boss Robert F. Kennedy Jr. made it known during an interview with Joe Rogan that he intended to direct the FDA to lessen restrictions on a handful of peptides that had previously been banne
items.author: Dean Stattmann
paragraphs: This past February, Health and Human Services secretary and MAHA Final Boss Robert F. Kennedy Jr. made it known during an interview with Joe Rogan that he intended to direct the FDA to lessen restrictions on a handful of peptides that had previously been banned under the Biden administration. The peptides in question, which included influencer favorites BPC-157 and TB-500 (collectively dubbed the “Wolverine stack” for their reported regenerative properties) had been placed on the FDA’s “do not compound” list, effectively barring pharmacies from providing them to patients, for reasons including serious safety concerns and a general lack of comprehensive human trials. No new research had emerged to prompt RFK Jr.’s announcement. Rather, the HHS head, a self-proclaimed “big fan” of peptides, believed the drugs should never have been banned in the first place—a decision that, in his view, was responsible for the subsequent explosion of a thriving black market for peptides online. So, for the past eight months, healthcare professionals have been waiting with baited breath for the other shoe to drop.
And then this past Wednesday hit with a thud.

In a seemingly unilateral decision—one that flies in the face of FDA scientists who warned earlier this year of the potential, largely unknown implications of effectively releasing scantily researched injectables into the wild—RFK announced that patients (or anyone with a prescription) would now have access to six of these previously outlawed peptides through a loophole-like policy called “enforcement discretion.”

To explain exactly what that means, I called up Edgar J. Asebey, a life sciences regulatory and transactional attorney and partner at the Frier Levitt law firm who leads the FDA Practice Group. “I always tell people I speak three languages: English, Spanish, and FDA,” he says. “Enforcement discretion means that the FDA will not enforce a certain regulation. And in this case, it's the prohibition against compounding these six peptides. That's what it boils down to.”

Enforcement discretion is typically considered a break-in-case-of-emergency avenue for freeing up availability of certain drugs when warranted, Asebey says. “For example, when the GLP-1s were in shortage, pharmacies could lawfully compound exact copies of Ozempic and Wegovy.” In other words, the six peptides in question—BPC-157, TB-500, MOTS-c, Semax, KPV, and Epitalon—are still categorically unapproved by the FDA for human use, but Kennedy is going to allow pharmacies to dispense them as if they were, until further notice.

While this may seem outrageous, not everybody is outraged. For one, obviously, peptides are big business. (Market research firm Grand View Research valued the global peptide industry at over 140 billion in 2025, with North America accounting for more than 60% of that revenue.) Aside from that, however, one of Kennedy’s stated motivations is to reduce people’s incentive to procure peptides from regulation-skirting med spas and the dark corners of the internet, where substances like BPC-157 can be ordered to your door with the same ease as buying paper towels on Amazon. Since July, the Alliance for Safe Online Pharmacies (ASOP Global) has tracked nearly 21,000 peptide listings across more than 300 websites, including upwards of 8,800 listings for BPC-157 alone. As you might imagine, quality and safety present serious concerns to anyone choosing to go that route—that is, beyond the potential risks of using these peptides even in their purest forms—hence the burgeoning cottage industry of peptide purity trackers and testing services.

“My view is simple,” says Meena Verma, MD, MPH, a board-certified internist and nephrologist, and founder of Blue Coast Longevity in Newport Beach, CA. “People are already using these peptides, and there is an urgent need for harm reduction. Allowing licensed pharmacies to compound them under physician guidance means patients can now have an accountable channel with assurance of safety.”

But how this policy change plays out may not be quite that simple. Whereas purveyors of these six peptides—whether operating online or in person—were previously identifiable as unlawful simply by virtue of offering the unapproved drugs, Kennedy's mandate to usher these peptides into the broader health marketplace muddies the waters, making it harder for consumers to tell which providers are legit. "The online market is already flush with illegal actors who now can more easily hide amongst the masses with limited risk of getting caught,” reads a statement that ASOP Global released within hours of Kennedy’s announcement on Wednesday. “Without enhanced and consistent new enforcement of the market, today’s policy will allow criminals to hide amongst the newly compliant.”

Kennedy’s plan notes that compounding pharmacies will be subject to specific safety criteria, like requiring that the peptides are manufactured in an FDA-registered facility, but as The New York Times has pointed out, “the step basically only requires a manufacturer to notify the agency of its address.”

When you consider the scale of the peptide market alongside the reality of what the FDA is actually capable of policing with its post-DOGE workforce—following the laying off of 3,500 workers—it begs the question of whether the criteria laid out in Kennedy’s plan will even matter at all.

"For one, if you're going to have guardrails, you're going to need to enforce them,” says Leigh Verbois, PhD, ASOP's global board chair and the former director of the FDA’s Office of Drug Security, Integrity, and Response. “There needs to be resources to actually take action, full stop. And two, the organizations that are intended to utilize those guardrails may not even look at them. There are too many [compounding pharmacies] to be able to enforce against."

But I’d argue there’s something far more dangerous, and more consequential, than the possibility that this latest decision might inadvertently feed the back-alley peptide market rather than curtail it. After all, not everyone is out there looking for peptides. (I know I’m certainly not.) But we all need to go to the doctor at some point—something that could now conceivably land you on the receiving end of a prescription for a drug that has never even been researched in a human being.

“To classify this as safe would just be irresponsible,” says Motisola Lewis, MD, an Internal Medicine physician and the founder of Lewis Medical NY. “If you have a cancer patient—say, a woman who just had breast cancer—and she wants to fix her knee that just got injured, and she ends up getting an injection of BPC-157. This is known to promote tissue growth. This is known to promote vascularization. We don't know what effect it has on a patient who has had cancer. Does it promote cancer growth? We don't know.”

The inescapable irony here is that not long ago it was the MAHA movement that was encouraging people to be skeptical of mainstream medical providers, to do your own research before just allowing your doctor to jab you with a COVID-19 vaccine. And now, by injecting these six potentially harmful peptides into mainstream medicine, where they will be readily available to physicians with varying degrees of familiarity with the substances themselves and the politics surrounding them, the administration has gone ahead and given the rest of us a very real reason to do our own research. Sure, this only applies to peptides at the moment, but a precedent has been set. And you can no longer afford not to pay attention. None of us can.

“When patients walk into their physician's office, or talk to a telehealth provider, they have an assumption that there will be a positive outcome—that the patient is seeking and that the physician is intending to meet,” says Dr. Verbois. “But without any of the quality, safety, or efficacy, it's completely the wild, wild west. If anyone in my family, in need of a drug for treatment, were to ask me if they should go down a path of utilizing a peptide of this sort, my response to them would be, ‘Never. Instead, seek out a treatment for that disease that's been shown to be safe and effective. These have not been, and you are putting yourself in harm's way.’”

items.title: Nobody Wants to Have a Baby Boy Anymore
items.description: It began, innocently enough, with a cake. In 2008, American blogger Jenna Karvunidis threw a party to announce the sex of her unborn baby. The reveal came when she cut a slice and found pink inside. She wrote about the experience online, the post went viral, a
items.author: Sam Parker; Karolina Burlikowska
paragraphs: It began, innocently enough, with a cake. In 2008, American blogger Jenna Karvunidis threw a party to announce the sex of her unborn baby. The reveal came when she cut a slice and found pink inside. She wrote about the experience online, the post went viral, and a new ritual was born.

Nearly 20 years later, we all know the drill. If it isn’t a cake, it’s a balloon or a cannon. Friends and family gather. Someone counts down; something explodes in blue or pink; the parents-to-be hug; a grandparent enters the frame looking thrilled and slightly confused. And, of course, there’s a camera rolling, meaning my daughter could have in theory earned her first “like” long before she drew her first breath.

For the first time in a century, nearly less than half of parents are circumcising their newborns. New dad Kevin Lincoln investigates how America’s favorite elective surgery became as debated as childhood vaccines—and considers his own decision.

The gender reveal has evolved from a modest party trick into a full-blown genre of internet spectacle, complete with its own newborn industrial complex. Private ultrasound companies now sell “gender-reveal experiences,” with rooms that glow pink or blue and teddy bears containing recordings of an unborn baby’s heartbeat. Online, the reveals have become more elaborate: smoke bombs, pyrotechnics (one of which started a wildfire in South California in 2020), choreographed dances, skydivers and, in one particularly memorable case, a Louisiana alligator called Sally biting through a blue jelly watermelon.

But the spectacle has moved on. A new kind of gender-reveal video is becoming a genre of its own, one in which a particular reaction is the main event. A recent compilation racked up 33 million views and three million likes on TikTok. Expecting couples do not scream with delight when the color appears. They scream in horror. They collapse and cry. The reason is nearly always the same: it’s blue. They’re having a boy.

What looks like internet absurdity may actually point to something much bigger. Last year, The Economist published data showing that in mostly higher-income countries, the centuries-old preference for sons is starting to reverse. And in some countries, the data shows that opinion has fully flipped: Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Portugal and the Czech Republic are showing evidence of a preference for girls.

In the US, the same trend appears among adoptive parents. According to the National Bureau of Economic Research, prospective parents were willing to pay an average $16,000 more for a girl than a boy. Among couples having IVF in the US—where, unlike the UK, sex selection is legal— leading clinics have reported that 75–80% of patients want a girl.

This is a big demographic plot twist. On one hand, it’s what progress looks like. For most of human history, boys have been the prize. They inherited the family name and property. They were expected to earn money and carry the family line into the future. Girls, in turn, were generally expected to marry out or care for relatives.

In the worst cases, the preference for sons has had lethal consequences. In China, where a one-child policy enforced by the government lasted 35 years, and in India, sex-selective abortion and the killing or abandonment of female babies has led to generations with far more boys than girls. Misogynist discrimination has been so pervasive that in 1990, the Nobel Prize–winning economist Amartya Sen estimated that more than 100 million women were “missing” from world history. (Researchers have since questioned the precise figure and methodology, but the point still stands.)

But there is another, stranger side to the reversal. You don’t have to spend long reading the 20,000-plus comments beneath a viral gender-reveal video to realize that some of this isn’t simply about girls finally being valued properly. There is a growing and increasingly open distaste for boys—a sense that they are inherently problematic, undesirable by default.
Having a son, in certain corners of modern parenthood, has become unfashionable. A curious society might ask itself why this is—and where it might lead.

Ruth Whippman is the mother of three boys. She grew up in England but now lives in America, in what she describes as a “progressive area of the country [with] very progressive school districts”. As she writes in her 2024 book, BoyMom, friends and neighbors kept saying versions of the same thing: “I hope for your sake this one is a girl.”

“We were a year into the [first] Trump presidency,” she tells me. “There were incels on the news. There was just this huge backlash against toxic masculinity. So it wasn’t even just a sense of, ‘Oh, boys, their clothes aren’t as nice; you don’t get to play Barbies.’ It was this sense that boys are actively toxic and harmful.”

When Whippman’s first son was due, she had the standard worries about raising a child of the opposite sex. Would they have enough in common? Would she know how to navigate experiences she hadn’t had? As a lifelong feminist, she tells me, the additional sense of cultural disapproval made everything worse. “It was really horrible, because nobody likes to be pitied,” she says. “Nobody likes to think that their children are second best. But I think it played into something in me as well, if I’m totally honest. I had my own fears and feelings about [having boys], and hearing everybody else’s reaction just made it much worse.”

Nearly a decade on from #MeToo, with Donald Trump back in the White House and male chauvinism metastasizing across the internet, it’s unusual to hear the word “masculinity” without the word “toxic” prefacing it. So parents can end up feeling—even if they’re guilty about it—that having a son is more complicated than it was for previous generations.

“When you hear about boys at the moment, at best, they’re this underachieving lunk who won’t go to college, is doing badly at school and will fail to launch,” says Whippman. “And at worst, he’s deep in the manosphere, commanding his AI girlfriend to let him choke her, or whatever. It gets to this wider consumerisation of parenthood. [The idea that] girls are better consumer products, in a way—which is a terrible, terrible way to talk about human beings.”

I’d be lying if I said it hadn’t crossed my mind, when I discovered I was having a daughter, that if I could raise her to be a confident, secure, kick-ass girl, I’d win the approval of the types of circle I move in. “Girl dads” who let daughters paint their nails are the subject of endless kind TikTok videos.

Parents of boys, not so much. Whippman, who has heard more and more fathers say they would prefer daughters, recognizes the problem. “Parenting a son is almost seen as a harm reduction project, rather than anything empowering,” she says. “That’s really at odds with our modern parenting culture, which is about encouraging [our kids] to reach for the stars and be happy and access all the world has to offer.”

And like everything else in 2026, the random, happy event of your unborn child’s sex can somehow thrust you into the us-versus-them culture war. “In the States and in the UK, there’s a sense that if you are on the progressive left, you are on the side of girls and women… any time you’re defending boys and men, it has this sniff of something right-wing, or being a bad actor,” says Whippman. “That’s a really hard thing to hold as a progressive, feminist parent of a son.”

There are other theories for why parents in Western countries, in particular, are increasingly downbeat about having boys. Millennials are having fewer children than any generation in history, and we’re doing it later in life. In other words, by the time it happens, we’re already exhausted. And boys are often perceived as more work, especially when they’re little: more physical, and harder to keep occupied and under control.

Lara Miller has been a midwife for more than 20 years. She uses social media to demystify pregnancy and childbirth. She thinks there is some truth to the idea that older parents may be wary of boys. “When you see older people having babies, they tend to be more controlling about everything to do with it,” she says. “I say this without judgment—I was an older mum myself—but you become used to doing things your own way and to your own routines.”

Of course, it would be silly to assume every girl will be content quietly coloring in while every boy spends his childhood trailing dog shit through the house. But according to Alex Trippier, a kids’ club leader who runs the social media account Be A Happier Parent, there can be real differences in behavior. “You get testosterone surges around age two, which I really see with the kids that I look after in my groups,” he says. “All of a sudden the boys come in and they’re going crazy. Parents who are on the quieter side can be overwhelmed by the sheer energy. Some people insist this is all nonsense, and [boys being more boisterous] is completely socialized. I think it’s a mixture of both. You’ve got that developmental layer going on, and you’ve got all the socialization on top of it.”

Trippier, who has two boys and a girl, thinks culture has shifted. Parents have always worried about teenage girls. But now, they have a whole new list of concerns for boys: porn, gaming addiction, exam results, algorithms. “There are all these fears we have for our sons, this kind of moral anxiety about the impossibility of raising good men,” he says.
In 2024, Zach Baron documented his long journey to fatherhood via IVF in GQ. Now, he reports on the mind-altering chaos (and occasional brilliance) of life with two walking, talking young boys.

Miller, who had similar feelings when she was pregnant but is now the happy mother of two sons, thinks there’s another factor: Schools aren’t always very good at accommodating boys. “We have changed as a society and we’re not as accepting of boys,” she says. “Boys don’t tend to fit the school model. You get worse reports. [Our school] gives the boys set days to be allowed to kick a football. Well, you don’t remember that at school, do you?”

She recalls being summoned by a headmaster after her son made a gun sign with his fingers. “The girls do better at school,” she says. “They’ve read 20 books; my boys have only read two. The teacher’s gone, ‘Well, if you buy a football magazine, do you think they’d read that?’ You’re like, ‘Oh, fuck off. Just fuck off.’”

There’s something else unusual about today’s parents, beyond grappling with the manosphere and Parkrun injuries. We’re the most psychologically literate generation to have ever lived. If we haven’t done therapy ourselves, we’re at least sufficiently fluent in the language of therapy to take a stab at self-reflection (or, as Boomer parents might call it, self-absorption). We know about childhood trauma. We know about attachment styles. We know that our parents’ behavior has consequences. We know that our childhoods don’t simply disappear when we become adults. It gives us an enormous number of things to worry about.

One of the most interesting conversations I’ve had on this subject is with a colleague who is expecting a son. He’s delighted now, but initially, the prospect of having a boy unnerved him—as it did me, before I knew the sex of my baby. We both agreed this probably came from remembering difficult experiences with our own fathers, and being afraid of repeating them. For me, it may have gone a step further. The idea of having a son scared me because I had a pretty broken relationship with myself.

Dr. Chrissy Jayarajah is a psychiatrist and the author of the world’s only academic paper on “gender disappointment.” She’s quick to point out that the term is not a clinical diagnosis, but what you might call a “known phenomenon” (particularly on TikTok, where thousands of videos are tagged with it).

“Something I always say is that becoming a parent will undoubtedly make you reflect on the way that you were parented,” she says. “Whether it was a good relationship, a bad relationship, an indifferent relationship or a non-existent relationship—they all play a part. An absent father is still very present in your mind. We are more psychologically minded and reflective compared with, maybe, the generation before. But I also think we don’t know what to do with that reflection.”

This can manifest in different ways, explains Jayarajah. “Working predominantly with mothers, I would say they fall into two camps,” she says. “They either want to emulate exactly how their mother was, from recreating those childhood memories, making those family favorite meals on a Sunday, and so on. Or they’re: ‘Oh my God, I’m turning into my mother.’”

That can produce powerful feelings about your baby’s sex. “We see that with women who have experienced abuse of some kind,” says Jayarajah. “Some absolutely do not want to have a girl, because they don’t want their daughter to experience what they went through. On the other hand, I have had women who say, ‘No, I definitely want a girl. I don’t want to have a son,’ because a son [would remind] them of the perpetrator.”

The sex of your baby, in other words, can become a vessel for all sorts of fears that existed long before the baby did. Then, there’s the demographic problem. There just aren’t enough babies. A rapid collapse in birth rates and fertility is playing out across the world. In 1990, global fertility was about 3.3 children per woman. Today it is around 2.2 to 2.3. More than half the countries in the world are already below “replacement level.”

The consequences will be huge. Labor shortages. Pressure on pensions. Rising social and healthcare costs. Less of the innovation and forward momentum traditionally associated with younger populations. In that context, favoring one sex over the other seems beyond counterproductive.

Maybe we are retreating into old, narrow assumptions. “We’ve never thought about gender more as a society than we do at this present day,” says Jayarajah. “Ideas about gender are in our face all day long. There was no such thing as a gender reveal party 20 years ago, let alone putting it online. What’s happening, in my opinion, is gender essentialism. This sexist idea of what it means to be a man, what it means to be a woman, is playing out in what we expect for our children.”

The following week, I saw this in action. I took my 19-month-old daughter to a soft-play morning, where she likes to roll around on the multicolored shapes and go down the slide on my lap. A few minutes after we arrived, I heard a scream. “Aaaargh!”

At one end of the ball pit, a little boy was staring at his own reflection in a mirror. “Aaaargh!” he went again, hammering his fists against the perspex and making the entire frame shake. A few feet away, my daughter watched him quietly. I made a mental note to keep them as far apart as possible.

The boy’s parents were nearby, deep in conversation. They seemed oblivious, or perhaps simply immune, to their son’s King Kong routine. A dozen judgmental thoughts zipped through my head. Why aren’t you keeping a closer eye on him? What kind of irresponsible shit are you pulling at home for him to do this? If he harms her, I swear to God…

I took a sip of my coffee, scrolled through my phone, then turned around, ready to rescue my sweet, innocent little girl. The boy who had been screaming a moment ago was now shyly handing her a dumper truck with a missing wheel. She closed her eyes, grinned, and took it with both hands.
A version of this story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of British GQ with the title “For Centuries, Everyone Wanted Boys. Now, Not So Much”
