items.author: Paresh Dave
paragraphs: Stanford researcher Chuyue Sun and her fellow computer scientists developed an AI tool that completed an engineering project in less than half a day for under $500, compared to the five months it took three highly skilled experts to do the same work manually. The dramatic reduction in time and cost, which Sun reported in a recent paper, is among the early results that are awakening an obscure field of coding and mathematics known as formal verification.

For decades, developers have envisioned using math to prove that their software is bug-free. This process is long and laborious, requiring engineers to write precise statements about the goals of their software and convert their code into formulas that can be validated. While companies already run sophisticated tests to identify as many flaws in their software as possible, they rarely shell out for formal verification, which can catch even more erratic behavior.

Now, a wave of startups is betting that generative AI will make formal software verification both practical and essential. Among them is &Truth, which Sun joined in August and which publicly launched on Thursday. Sun’s research demonstrated the technology’s potential by using AI to verify part of the code that encrypts conversations in the messaging app Signal.

“Bridges, buildings, they don’t collapse, because people did math before constructing them,” says Ilya Sergey, &Truth’s chief science officer. “Why don’t we do the same for code? The technology to mathematically reason was all there, just difficult to scale.”

&Truth has raised $70 million from investors and aims to eventually verify any programming language. Rival Harmonic, which was cofounded by Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev and has received $295 million in funding, announced this week that its math-focused AI agent Aristotle supports verifying software written in C and hardware designs in Verilog. It is evaluating the technology with potential users, including chipmakers Tensordyne and Nvidia, whose venture capital arm is one of the startup’s investors.

And just last week, Anthropic and the verification startup Theorem jointly announced they had used AI to assist in finding bugs in open source software that trillions of tests had failed to detect. They also introduced an add-on for Claude to help other developers with verification. Costs of the initial project were not disclosed.

The big promise is a future where software runs more reliably with fewer security headaches. But whether AI can bring formal verification beyond the most critical systems at organizations like NASA and Apple and into widespread use remains an open question.

The technology is still in the prototyping stage. Though demand is high, it’s unclear how much customers are willing to pay and how they prefer to adopt the technology. Formal verification relies on making assumptions about how computers and people interact with software, and some experts are skeptical about its ability to catch bugs stemming from user error and hardware breakdowns.

Will Wilson, who runs the bug-hunting AI software startup Antithesis, calls formal verification “a trap” for math nerds like himself. Antithesis spent millions of dollars to formally verify some of its cybersecurity defenses, a process Wilson describes as a “pain in the ass.” Yet the startup still uncovered additional errors using its own tool, and Antithesis has also found bugs in software that several of its customers had formally verified. “It can give you some assurance, but only robust exhaustive testing can prove your assurance is true,” Wilson says.

Or as Vitalik Buterin, the engineer known for creating the Ethereum cryptocurrency, put it in a blog post earlier this year, “formal verification is not a panacea.” But he and other proponents of the approach still believe it will be an important defense against AI systems launching cyberattacks and wreaking havoc.

Boeing planes, Amazon servers, and more than 2.5 billion active Apple devices contain at least some formally verified software, according to company disclosures. The code in question is typically security-related, and vulnerabilities in it could cause serious harm if exploited.

Byron Cook, a distinguished scientist and vice president at Amazon Web Services, says formal verification has eased customer concerns about cloud security and helped internal teams move faster by squashing big bugs early on.

But several midsized tech companies tell WIRED they have typically verified only one key feature of their products, if any at all. They cite a lack of verification engineers, costs that outweigh the potential risks, and, perhaps most importantly, concerns that waiting weeks for code to be formally verified could slow innovation.

Earlier this year, Apple’s security team said that some of the issues formal verification uncovered in its “corecrypto” library, which is used for encryption, could not have been found any other way. But the company added that it has to be “conservative” when adding new code to corecrypto to ensure it can keep pace with reviewing it.

Two cybersecurity executives at major companies that haven’t formally verified any code say they aren’t sure whether automation will make it worthwhile. But the executives, who weren’t authorized to speak publicly, say they could imagine paying major AI labs for “verified” AI-generated code.

Developers of open source software projects, which are the bedrock of many apps, are increasingly experimenting with AI-aided verification. The nonprofit Beneficial AI Foundation used a grant from Anthropic to validate the same encryption code this year as Sun did at Stanford. Michael Rosenberg, a maintainer of the library known as curve25519-dalek, hopes sustainable funding emerges for ongoing verification efforts. “I have no ideas as to how that’s going to happen, though, and we certainly shouldn’t rely on the goodwill of the AI companies,” he says.

Some of the startups eager to expand verification also aren’t sure whether to deploy their tools directly to customers or through intermediaries like Anthropic. Their general plan is to use AI to automate much of the work involved in defining how a program is supposed to behave. For example, specifications for a data table might require that it contain the same items before and after sorting, just in a different order. Further automation efforts, which may not involve AI, would translate that code into a format that math tools like Lean, Rocq, and Isabelle can use to check whether the code works as intended.

Another recent entrant to the formal verification field is Madan Musuvathi, who left Microsoft Research after more than 20 years to found the startup Truidic. After incidents like the OpenAI hack of Hugging Face, he felt there was an urgent need to commercialize his studies. “AI in the hands of attackers can be extremely powerful,” Musuvathi says, but verification can “make AI safe and secure for everyone, everywhere.”

Proofcraft, one of the few companies that has long offered traditional verification, says growing excitement about the process is translating into a flood of inquiries from potential customers. June Andronick, the company’s CEO, and Gerwin Klein, its chief scientist, say interest easily outpaces what they and their competition can provide.

But both worry that AI-generated specifications could inspire “unjustified trust” in the results. Verifiers are also eager to preserve the joy their work brings them. Klein calls it “pretty addictive, like a puzzle game.” If all goes well, he’ll be doing more solving than ever.

items.title: Roli Has Fallen Apart—and Left Customers Holding the Bag
items.description: Roli, the company behind expressive, touch-sensitive music devices like the Seaboard and Roli Blocks, has collapsed.
items.author: Boone Ashworth
paragraphs: Roli, the company behind expressive, touch-sensitive music devices like the Seaboard and Roli Blocks, has collapsed.

Although it hasn't been officially announced, Roli reportedly ousted its CEO and founder, Roland Lamb, earlier this year. Since then, Roli has all but dissolved. (In August, a new company called Instrumental Intelligence was registered with the UK government under Lamb's name, a potential move by the founder to acquire Roli's assets).

On Monday, Roli emailed users that two licensed insolvency practitioners were appointed joint administrators of Roli on October 20. The company went into administration, the UK process that manages corporate insolvency. This is the second time Roli has gone bankrupt.

That has left a small but bereft community of customers with no word on getting the products they paid for. The Roli community has expressed sadness, anger, or outright confusion. In Facebook groups, the r/Roli subreddit, and other forums, dismayed users have struggled to find recourse for Roli equipment purchases ranging from hundreds to thousands of dollars. The Roli subreddit has been awash with posts from customers who say they paid for orders months or years ago and have received no response or refund since then.

Existing owners also worry about the long-term impact. Roli instruments rely heavily on proprietary software launchers and companion apps to connect, map sounds, and configure settings. While the hardware still functions, users fear that lack of software support will eventually leave their gear bricked.

Roli has not publicly communicated about its future strategy with customers. The company did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment; Lamb did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Roli’s primary financial backers, investment firms TriplePoint Capital and Hoxton Ventures, also did not respond.
Roli has faced financial struggles before.

The company started in 2009 but really took off after musician Pharrell Williams invested in 2017 and Sony’s Innovation Fund in 2018. Musicians like Dream Theater keyboardist Jordan Rudess supported and touted Roli’s gadgets. Ryan Gosling’s character played a Seaboard Grand in the 2016 movie La La Land. In the late 2010s, the tech and the company were hailed as a hit.

That tune changed in 2020. The British government’s Future Fund—a taxpayer-funded relief package issued to help businesses during the pandemic—partially bailed out Roli from a Covid-19-induced financial crisis. Even then, Roli went into administration for the first time in 2021. It survived by relaunching as Luminary Roli and focusing on music-learning devices like the light-up Lumi keyboard and the Airwave, a digital theremin that doubled as an AI piano teacher.

Through all of that, customers have had issues with how the company communicates. Users who ordered the Lumi keyboard found orders unexpectedly delayed, with no indication from the company on what was happening.

“One of the problems they have had ever since I started with the Kickstarter is communication and explaining things—telling people what's going on,” Lluís Gerard, a YouTuber who has reviewed Roli products for years under the handle WasabiNoise, tells WIRED. “There's always been too much secrecy about things, or then you'd realize, oh, there are these delays.”

Former Roli employees—who spoke with WIRED but asked not to be named to avoid jeopardizing future employment opportunities—alleged a company culture that revolved around Lamb’s whims. Every person we spoke with who worked with Lamb compared him to a Steve Jobs-esque character. One person described the experience of being at Roli as being in a movie, where Lamb saw himself as the main character and everyone else as extras or set pieces.

“I love the company, love the culture, love the people—I didn’t love working for him,” the employee said. “Everyone has their story with him. You're buckled into his car—and he’s not going in the right direction.”

In 2021, another former Roli employee, who also asked not to be identified, uploaded files on GitHub that include various notes chronicling Roli as a hostile workplace. One 16-page PDF is titled “Keeping Roland Happy” and includes multiple sections about how to handle interacting with a pathological narcissist. Several former employees independently described what they viewed as Lamb’s narcissistic behavior, describing him as an arrogant visionary.

“Roland is the archetype of a pathological narcissist,” one employee told WIRED. “Unfortunately, that's what he became. Incredibly brittle when challenged, absolutely shameless, quite reckless, incapable of learning or growth, would rather gamble than take any lessons from the previous experience. It was very disheartening to see.”

“The tragedy here is that it was always fundamentally a great company,” another former employee says. “A lot of what made it great was the sort of all-powerful vision of the founder. But that was so obviously the critical flaw.”

Along with other touch-sensitive devices like the Linnstrument and the Sensel Morph, Roli was a key company in the rise of MIDI polyphonic expression (MPE) devices. MPE technology lets players control a note’s pitch and timbre through touch-based movement. Pressing or sliding fingers over the device’s surface produces varying MIDI notes that capture more expressive playing.

While inventive, Roli’s instruments were altogether very niche—a hard product category to build an Apple-sized audience around. Roli certainly tried, partnering with Apple to sell its Roli Blocks in Apple Stores. Alas, the pandemic caused dire supply chain issues, and the company couldn’t keep up with orders. After the pandemic, bankruptcy, and the rebrand, little remained to push the company forward except the founder's will.

“This was one of the leading lights of music technology in the world,” one former employee said. “It was truly an inventing company—the stuff it made had never been made before. So it's a real shame.”
The response to Roli’s collapse hasn’t been pure dismay. After months of delays and frustration, Reddit users have gathered to mourn the company—and to make sure its devices keep working.

Sam Hocking, a UK audio engineer who runs an audio tools company called Demix.me, also owns multiple Roli Seaboard Blocks. Even before Roli went into administration, Hocking had been building software that could keep the equipment working as a capable MIDI device. He shared his vibe-coded configuration tools in the Roli subreddit and on GitHub, so Roli’s Grand, Rise, Airwave, and Block devices can work without the Roli launcher.

Hocking says his Seaboards are nearly 10 years old and still working. Despite the company’s rocky history and poor communication, he still wants to keep his devices. They’re high quality, cost a good chunk of money, and feel somewhat irreplaceable.
He’s not alone. Other users on the subreddit have joined in, adding their own tweaks and fixes to the software that may keep at least a few of these devices alive.
“They're quite a unique product; there's not another keyboard type out there,” Hocking says. “Nobody likes to spend money and then not be able to use it.”

items.title: When You Should—and Shouldn’t—Use AI to Search the Web
items.description: If you've interacted with the likes of Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini, you've noticed that in addition to everything else they do, these AI chatbots can search the web for you. Depending on what you’re looking for, it can be easier to find more relevant results t
items.author: David Nield
paragraphs: If you've interacted with the likes of Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini, you've noticed that in addition to everything else they do, these AI chatbots can search the web for you. Depending on what you’re looking for, it can be easier to find more relevant results through a chatbot, which may explain why Google is so keen to push AI Mode for its own search engine.

When asked to search the web, the latest versions of these bots are combining elements of traditional web search (they're essentially just googling on your behalf) with knowledge they are able to pull out of their training data. Everything is then packaged and formatted in the now-familiar, polished generative AI style.
It's the added AI elements on top of the traditional googling where the differences come in, and that means AI-powered search may not always be the best option.
When to Use AI for Web Search

If you're looking up something simple and widely known—like the height of the Empire State Building—then AI search is a pretty safe bet. Not only is information like this easy to access online, the “autocorrect” probability patterns favored by large language models mean there's a near-certain chance that the results you see will include the right information.

If you just need a quick look-up, AI is OK. The more obscure the question, though, the closer you need to look at the answer. If you've asked something less well known, like the fifth-billed actor in an obscure television show, there might only be one or two references to it on the web, and an AI might choose the wrong one.

One of the takeaways from recent Stanford University research is that when AI finds an accurate source, it's very good at pulling the right information out of it. Where it tends to fall down is in not finding accurate sources (either because there aren't any or because the query has been misinterpreted) and presenting a confident answer anyway.

AI search is also helpful when you have a complex query that a standard Google search wouldn't be able to parse: "I need to know the best restaurants in San Francisco for a family of five who want to spend no more than $200." AI is able to query and collate multiple sources in response to a search like this, and then present a well-synthesized answer. A traditional web search would give you a list of blue links that most probably just rank San Francisco restaurants by more basic criteria.

Again though, sources are crucial. AI bots have never been to San Francisco or eaten there. They are relying on public accounts on the web, written by people who have. Where there are no exact page matches, they'll look for related words (like "affordable" or "family") and generate an answer.

For queries where there's lots of information online, like San Francisco restaurants, AI web search can feel incredibly useful. For less popular destinations and more specific requests ("dining tables shaped like stars"), you need to be more careful with the results, as the way that AI joins the dots then becomes less reliable.

So, with the caveat that you should always do some kind of double-check, AI web search works best for common queries that are likely to lead to a lot of accurate, up-to-date information online. In both the way they process search queries, and package together and synthesize answers, AI chatbots are a significant upgrade on googling.
When Not to Use AI for Web Search

The way generative AI bots and LLMs are put together means they work best when paraphrasing, synthesizing, and summarizing. But these processes can also introduce mistakes. If your search needs precise details (like a celebrity quotation, a report stat, or a device specification), a traditional Google search may work best.

Heading to Google and searching the old way is also likely to be better if you want full control over the sources used. Offloading web searches to AI is convenient, but you're relying on them to interpret your search correctly, find the right sources, and then extract accurate information from those sources. It saves time, but it's more opaque.

If you know the websites you trust most for technology news, for example, you can prioritize them in a traditional web search in a way that AI might not be able to. Researchers from UC San Diego have found that AI web searches will sometimes pick sources because they're more relevant to the query, rather than because they're ranked as more authoritative.

That means a personal blog might get chosen above a professional health care site if the AI deems it to be a closer match to what the user is actually searching for. This is a choice that you would be much less likely to make when scanning a traditional list of results, as you'd typically pick the one you trusted the most.

Other areas where traditional searching still wins out are for breaking news (there can sometimes be a lag in the timeliness of the data AI pulls up) and for high-stakes searches where you absolutely cannot make a mistake—searches related to health, the law, or your finances, for instance.

If you do feel like an AI approach is needed, be sure to double- and triple-check the sources the chatbot has used, which should be linked inside the answer. If you're in any doubt, you can ask the AI for clarification on where something was sourced from, to make sure it isn't an LLM invention.

Classic Google searches can still turn up false information on the web, of course, but you're in a much better position to discern what's true and accurate and what isn't without a chatbot in the middle. For queries where that's more important than convenience and speed, there's still a place for the old way of searching the web.

items.title: What’s the Sanest Approach to Teen Partying?
items.description: New York subscribers got exclusive early access to this story in our Brooding newsletter. Sign up here to get it in your inbox.
items.author: Kathryn Jezer-Morton
paragraphs: New York subscribers got exclusive early access to this story in our Brooding newsletter. Sign up here to get it in your inbox.

When my children were young, I never sought advice from friends and certainly not from experts, because I was one of those (probably very annoying) parents with blind faith in their instincts. My instincts seem to have served me pretty well up until now, but I find myself trusting them less than I used to. Maybe I moved through early parenthood in blissful ignorance, and I’ve finally clued into how little I really know.

Teen partying, for one thing: What’s the protocol here? Are we supposed to encourage all forms of social gathering since it’s better than them sitting at home on their phones? Is weed supposed to be decriminalized at home, too? Do kids still use fake IDs to get alcohol, even though IDs have embedded scannable features now? And at the risk of committing cringe kamikaze, what terms of art are currently being used by the youth to describe their substances of choice? Did I just overhear my 12-year-old dismissively refer to a vape as a “geek bar”?
In possession of no answers myself, I spoke to as many parents of teens and young adults as I could. I heard stories that both harrowed and comforted me. But I think we’re going to be okay.
No matter how much trust we build up with our teenagers, one inviolate truth is that the drugs are stronger than they used to be.

“We weren’t prepared for it,” a mom of an 18-year-old from a southern city told me. “There’s a park close to the river where a lot of high-school kids go to party. Our son called, after midnight, and he was like, ‘I’m sorry, we all ate a bunch of mushrooms, and I can’t put my buddy in an Uber.’ So we went down there, and this kid was just on another planet. It’s like someone had taken all the bones out of his body. He had missed dozens of calls from his dad, and we were trying to unlock his phone using facial recognition so we could call his dad back, but that wasn’t working.”

It took two people to get the friend loaded into her car, and she was able to find his address in his car’s glove box. “We had to drive across town, knock on this family’s door at 1 a.m., and be like, ‘Hi, we haven’t met. Your son’s in my car stoned on mushrooms.’”

A Brooklyn dad shared a similar story: His 16-year-old son called late at night from the home of his friend with the most permissive parents, who weren’t home, because someone was freaking out on mushrooms. In both cases, the parents were just relieved to have gotten a call and didn’t want to jeopardize that trust by cracking down in anger. “We just realized that we couldn’t scold or punish him. It no longer pertains, somehow. It’s a baffling place to find yourself,” said the dad.

Another source of bafflement is weed, which in the past couple of decades has become virtually undetectable as well as executioner-grade. (Shout-out to Josh, a dude I knew in high school whose bong was named the Executioner — simpler times.)

One mom I spoke to said that as her son was finishing high school and becoming more open with her, he admitted that he’d been high for months on end during his sophomore year of high school, and she hadn’t noticed. “Looking back, we were like, Wow, okay. He’s a low-key person, so it was really hard to tell.”

Another mom from the Southwest watched her 15-year-old daughter sink into a yearlong depression that, she later learned, involved heavy self-medication with cannabis — which she, too, was slow to detect, due to the absence of the telltale wafts. “I was not equipped for her ease of being able to buy stuff. Whether it’s through Snapchat — it’s just really available,” she said.

Alcohol may not be any easier to get ahold of than it was in previous decades, but parents’ attitudes about it may be shifting for the sake of ensuring that trust and lines of communication stay intact. Indeed, no parent I spoke to was comfortable playing the narc. One mother who had been a practicing attorney while her kids were in high school had a strict policy of not allowing underage drinking in her home — partly, she clarified, for reasons of professional propriety. “But what they did outside my house, I wasn’t too concerned about.”

Income and geography play a big part. In wealthier suburbs, it seemed to several moms I spoke to that it was somewhat de rigueur for parents to provide alcohol at their teens’ parties. “I think it’s a desire to seem cool, to seem permissive,” one mom from a Connecticut suburb told me.

“Around here, the parents enable drinking,” she continued. When her daughter was 14 and a high-school freshman, she was getting ready for a party at a friend’s house, and the friend’s mom called to check if it was okay if she gave the girls each a can of High Noon. “I remember saying to her, ‘I’m going to have to think about that and call you back.’ My husband and I talked and agreed that it felt really messed up. Fourteen? I called her back and was like, ‘Listen, you can do whatever you want with your daughter, but I don’t want my daughter to drink.’”

“A lot of senior parties have open bars,” a mom from the suburban Southwest told me. “I felt like that was bizarre. There’s a shift at some point where some parents want to share that with their kids. But I never would buy alcohol for kids. That’s just a hard line.”

That being said, this mom allows alcohol in her backyard, since “somehow they acquire it,” she said of the cans of Truly and Coors Lite that end up stuffed in her recycling bins. “I’m okay with it as long as I know that no one’s driving. And I don’t want to know how you got it.”

Naturally, phones have a role to play in all this. One dad in Montreal I spoke to was forwarded a screenshot of a Snapchat post of his 14-year-old son and his friends posing with a vape, a mickey of vodka, and what appeared to be a bottle of prescription pills. “My knees went a little weak when I saw it,” this dad recalled. “We had a long conversation after, and we told him he’s not allowed to ever take pills.”

After his son came home very late a few times, this dad began tracking his son’s location. “I’m not into all that. We didn’t used to track his location,” said the dad, but for the time being, it provides some peace of mind.

Location tracking, a handful of parents admitted, seems to create as many problems as it solves, with their teens lying and becoming more evasive when they’re tracked. But it’s a mixed bag, especially after midnight. One mom in a rural area was waiting for her daughter to return from a party in the woods at a spot known by the community at large. Beginning to worry, she checked her daughter’s location — it was at the local hospital, so she rushed over. “As much as I was upset that they hadn’t called us, her friends did a really good job of taking care of her.”

Her 15-year-old daughter had gotten very drunk, and her friends found something about her behavior worrying, so they brought her in. “If I’d have seen her, I would not have made that decision,” the mom said. “She’d just had too much to drink.” The mom took her home and put her to bed. But the rumor mill had begun to work, and her daughter woke up to exaggerated tales of how drunk she’d been, that she’d been “messy,” that she’d had seizures.

“It was a shitty experience, but it was also the kind of experience where you learn that things can get out of control very quickly. The friends did a lot of the right things. I would rather have those situations happen here, with people who have known her since she was young, than when she goes off to university.”

The greatest status marker among parents of this generation, it would seem, is to be considered a trusted adult. Perhaps this is why no one I spoke to took a hard-line approach to drugs and alcohol; they would rather be someone who hears the honest story and who can be available to help someone who needs it than one who is associated with consequences and disappointment. Being sober oneself can be a boon: You can always be counted on to drive.

A mom of four from the D.C. area got sober after her older children had already finished high school. “With my older two, it was common for me to be drinking four times a week or so,” she said. “But it got to the point where if they did need me to come pick them up, I wouldn’t really be able to. It was part of the motivation for me to be sober.”

One New Year’s Eve after she’d stopped drinking and her youngest daughter was in high school, she got a call from the younger sister of one of her daughter’s friends. “These girls, their mom had passed from cancer a few years earlier, and their dad was actively dating — he was out, it was New Year’s Eve. But the word had spread through the friend group that I was sober and you could call me. Here’s this freshman kid, and she’s drunk off her ass. She’s in over her head. And through friends, she knew to call me. It made me feel good.”

There’s one thing every parent I spoke with shared: a baseline assumption that they have some sense of what’s going on with their teen. In this regard, I think we belong to the proud tradition of people who don’t know what they don’t know. We are all defenseless against unknown unknowns. All we can really control is how we choose to react.
- Are We Raising a Generation of Heteropessimists?
- Why Can’t Parents Give Each Other Permission to Make Mistakes?
- The Fantasy of the Free-Roaming Child

items.title: Every ACOTAR Collaboration You Can Shop Right Now
items.description: It used to be that the easiest way to brag about the book you were reading was to read it in public. But now, signaling your status among the most devoted echelon of readers is about merch. These days, book merch is practically as ubiquitous as band merch — an
items.author: Chinea Rodriguez
paragraphs: It used to be that the easiest way to brag about the book you were reading was to read it in public. But now, signaling your status among the most devoted echelon of readers is about merch. These days, book merch is practically as ubiquitous as band merch — and the offerings expand well beyond the striped Hogwarts scarves you can buy at Universal Studios. Some of the biggest literary franchises, including Sarah J. Maas’s romantasy series, A Court of Thorn and Roses (ACOTAR), have put their stamp on the merch sphere with an increasing list of fashion-and-beauty collaborations.

Among these team-ups you’ll find the standard fare: graphic T-shirts, mugs, and the occasional tote. But Maas’s world of ACOTAR has also expanded into jewelry, intimates, and more elevated apparel. As fans celebrate the release of the latest entry in the author’s romantasy series, A Court of Splintered Harmony, brands have taken inspiration from the books to design satin slips and sequined dresses you wouldn’t mind wearing out on a date night. Below, you’ll find some of the best and biggest ACOTAR collabs to launch so far.

The brand’s recent Starfall collection lets you wear your love for the Maasverse on your sleeve, neck, and ears with jewelry ranging from $38 for a bracelet to $174 for a bracelet bundle. Die-hard fans already sold out the first collection, but some favorites have been restocked.

Your leakproof briefs are now ACOTAR themed. But if you want something fancier, like a slip dress, the intimates brand has that too. Separated into “courts” like those found in Maas’s fantasy world, Knix’s book-themed collection features socks, totes, lingerie, and underwear ranging from $25 to $165. You can even take a quiz to find out which court you belong to.

On the pricier side, For Love & Lemons’ ACOTAR collection offers subtle, elegant nods to the series, with details made for devoted fans. Readers can shop sequin-accented gowns, lacy lingerie, beaded dresses and mules, and bustier tops. For something a little more showy, you can join the wait list for a printed dress or sweatshirt.

Target knows what readers want: cozy essentials. The ACOTAR merch from the retailer leans more relaxing-night-at-home than gorgeous-fantasy-heroine. It offers a mix of bookmarks, totes, journals, and (of course) teas and color-changing mugs you can snuggle up with while reading the series.

While picking up a copy of the latest book in the series, you can also grab a few accessories. Similar to Target, Barnes & Noble’s selection of merch leans more toward cozier favorites like puzzles, bookmarks, and mugs. If you want a flashier nod to the series, it also has tote bags and enamel pins.

items.title: The ‘Sex Diaries’ That Brought Roommates Into the Mix
items.description: Since their very first entries in 2007, The Cut’s “Sex Diaries” have never only revealed what people do in bed. Over the seven days we spend with each anonymous diarist, we inevitably get broader context for the rest of their lives, including by meeting the ro
items.author: Alyssa Shelasky
paragraphs: Since their very first entries in 2007, The Cut’s “Sex Diaries” have never only revealed what people do in bed. Over the seven days we spend with each anonymous diarist, we inevitably get broader context for the rest of their lives, including by meeting the roommates on the other side of their bedroom door. (Though sometimes they’re also under the covers.)

Today, we’re looking back at the “Sex Diaries” that centrally included people’s roommates, whether they slept with them, fought with them, or begrudgingly overheard their cries of carnal ecstasy. Let these sordid tales of cohabitation serve as a reminder to us all: When you don’t live alone, it never hurts to be discreet — nor to exercise extreme caution before hooking up with someone splitting your rent. —Amy Rose Spiegel, senior editor, The Cut

This entry explores the pleasures and perils at hand when a new roommate wants to keep you company in a more intimate way than the occasional TV night. As her week goes on, she does her best to resist their charms to varying success. As to what happened after they moved in together, we can make an educated guess …

11 p.m. H. shows up to the bar in kitten heels and a denim tracksuit. We do poppers with an old lesbian couple, then make out outside after sharing a cig. But I make a point to take a separate Uber home — we can kiss, but I’m not messy enough to fuck my future roommate. Read the rest of the story here.

Ah, the ill-thought-out roommate hookup. As this diarist learns, there are strong reasons why people advise against mixing pleasure and sharing the electric bill … particularly when you have many, many months left on your lease should things go south.

3:47 a.m. Carson really wants to have sex. He’s practically begging. I explain that, due to the fact that we live together and what I know about his upbringing, I don’t want things to get too complicated too fast. He assures me he’s very casual when it comes to sex, and that it’s not as big of a deal as I’m making it out to be. I cave. Carson and I start to have sex, missionary … but he can’t get hard. As he profusely apologizes, I assure him it’s really no sweat. I tell him good night. His cheeks are red as he closes the door behind him. Read the rest of the story here.

Living with an ex often comes with blurry expectations around sex, as this diarist’s living situation illustrates. Fortunately for her, this sounds less like a tempest and more like she has access to orgasms when she feels like hopping into bed with her former boyfriend.

9 p.m. Finally head home. Shower and hang out with roommate/ex-boyfriend. Decide cuddling with him is better than sleeping alone. He asks if he can go down on me. I consent and sleep better than I have in ages. Read the rest of the story here.

This entry harks back to 2020, a uniquely bad year for people whose roommates were liberal about inviting sex randos over in the dog days of sheltering in place. Even worse for this diarist: One of her roommate’s unwelcome houseguests was a man the writer had a romantic history with.

7:30 a.m. Here’s where things get crazy. I wake up from almost 12 hours of sleep and see Trey in our kitchen trying to make coffee. He says “good morning” to me as if there’s nothing wrong with the situation. “What are you doing here?” I say, trying to put the pieces together in my mind. “Katy told me to come over,” he starts to say. “Oh, shit. You didn’t know. Okay, no drama …” I am not typically a drama queen, but I storm to my room and shut the door. There is so much wrong with this situation! Read the rest of the story here.
Anyone whose housemate has enjoyed constant PDA with their partner will feel for this diarist, whose week starts with a brief respite from nearby sex noises but continues in a different direction.

8:30 a.m. My roommate’s door is ajar, which means she must’ve slept at her girlfriend’s. On most nights I can hear them having sex and it wakes me up because our walls are half an inch thick and her room is technically my closet. It reminds me of how single and alone I’ve been in my bedroom. Read the rest of the story here.

This diary from a 24-year-old in Brooklyn is as much about her sexual exploits with a familiar face as it is a suddenly precarious housing situation, which unfolds when a friend’s homeowning parents change their minds about how generous they’re willing to be with their apartment.

2 p.m. My friend who is my third roommate (the three of us went to college together) texts that we have to rethink the rent situation. We rent our place from her family, so it’s cheap. But I wonder if that’s about to change. I start to feel a little bit sick. If she ups our rent, I might have to move home with my parents in New Jersey. The only reason I can live on my own is because of this rent situation. She asks if we can all meet up tonight to talk. I’m scared shitless. Read the rest of the story here.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: November 2, 2026
items.description: In the morning, the Leo moon aligns with Mars. You might get a confidence boost today, but that could come with an impulsive streak, too. Don’t be afraid to act boldly, but recognize that your judgment might not be quite as reliable as usual. So if your friend
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: In the morning, the Leo moon aligns with Mars. You might get a confidence boost today, but that could come with an impulsive streak, too. Don’t be afraid to act boldly, but recognize that your judgment might not be quite as reliable as usual. So if your friends are encouraging you to pump the brakes, listen to them. Then, in the evening, the Leo moon aligns with Jupiter, bringing luck and positivity your way. The best way to take advantage of this is to dream about what it would look like if things went right for you today. At the moment your optimism can make you more courageous, so lean into it.

You consider it smart, even strategic, to keep some of your feelings to yourself. That way, others can’t use your emotions against you! The problem is, you’re likely not going to be able to be secretive right now, even if you want to be. Your thoughts and feelings will be written all over your face. Today, you’re better off not trying to conceal what’s on your mind.

Anticipate some major emotional revelations today. Maybe you’ll suddenly understand why you acted the way you did in a stressful situation; maybe you’ll finally sort out how you feel about a dilemma you’ve been struggling with. You might want to tell everyone in your life about your newfound clarity, but for now, give yourself time to process it all privately. You’re probably still untangling some of the details, and you deserve to do that at your own pace. Once you feel more comfortable and assured, then you can get others involved.

You might feel certain that you’re right about something today. You’ve thought through your questions carefully and come to logical conclusions; you don’t see any reason to doubt yourself. But remember that other people might have considered the same questions with the same care and come to different conclusions. Consider the possibility that none of you are quite as objective as you think. Your emotions and personal experiences are all playing a role in your thinking. And together, you might come up with an even better answer than you would have on your own.

Most of the time, you try to be generous with your time and your resources. But today, make sure you’re not going so far in taking care of others that you end up neglecting yourself. You’re not selfish to want to prioritize your own basic needs — or even for wanting to enjoy yourself sometimes. The harder you’ve been working on behalf of everyone else lately, the more important it is to do something nice for yourself right now.

Today, you might be too focused on getting what you want to worry about what others need. As far as you’re concerned, that isn’t your job — if somebody needs something from you, they can ask for it. If you don’t hear from them, you’ll assume everything is fine. But remember that not everyone is as comfortable speaking up as you are. If you can put some extra effort into noticing other people’s feelings today, it’ll go a long way toward keeping your relationships healthy and strong.

Things are almost definitely not going to go according to plan today. Even if no major events arise, your routines will likely be interrupted in inconvenient ways, and you’ll be forced to adjust your expectations. The best way to deal with these disruptions is to roll with them. Resisting will only create bigger problems. If you can stay adaptable — and better yet, if you can muster up some optimism that these unexpected changes will work out for the best — you’ll avoid any serious trouble.

When people treat you poorly, you sometimes make excuses for them: You tell yourself they’re having a bad day, or that they didn’t really mean it, or that maybe you’re the problem. But when they treat someone else badly, you suddenly see their unkindness for what it is; you refuse to rationalize it away. Today, try to defend yourself the same way you’d protect someone you care about. You deserve kindness as much as they do.

Sometimes you underestimate your own ability to deal with difficulty. You feel it’s safer to avoid demanding situations altogether; you’d rather go around problems than through them. But today, you’ll save yourself time and energy by simply facing issues head-on. You’re smart and resourceful, and you don’t need to be so scared of failure. If you take things one step at a time, you’ll quickly make progress, and you’ll discover you have no reason to doubt yourself.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

When you’re bored with your life, you sometimes feel guilty about it. You tell yourself you should be grateful things aren’t worse; you should be happy with what you have. But today, stop brooding over what you “should” do or how you “should” feel. Instead, start dealing with reality. If you’re bored and restless, simply telling yourself to be more grateful won’t fix the problem. What you need is a new experience or two — so focus on finding something that’ll capture your attention and get you excited about the day ahead.

Seemingly mild disagreements could get surprisingly intense today. If you’re not careful, you might find yourself picking fights you don’t actually want — with people you don’t actually have a problem with. So before things get heated, take a step back and ask yourself whether you really need to start an argument right now. If there’s nothing meaningful at stake, consider letting it go. Find somewhere more worthwhile to direct your confrontational energy.

In general, you don’t mind being alone. You pride yourself on being independent. But today, you could feel surprisingly needy. You’ll want to be near the people you care about and to feel seen by them. But don’t expect your friends to magically intuit that you want to spend time together. You’ll have to make a point of seeking out their company. They might assume you’re happy doing things on your own; if that’s not the case right now, then say so.

When people are rude or careless, you try to be understanding. Maybe they’re stressed about personal problems you’re unaware of, or maybe you said something tactless without realizing it. But while your compassion is laudable, you don’t have to be endlessly accommodating. That’s especially true when people take advantage of your generosity. Today, continue being kind — but you’re allowed to hope for some kindness in return. If others refuse to give it, it might be time to reconsider your relationships.

items.title: Exclusive: The 'Hunger Games' Team Didn't Listen To Fan Casting For This Reason
items.description: The Hunger Games Team Didn’t Listen To Fan Casting For This Reason
items.author: Jake Viswanath
paragraphs: The Hunger Games Team Didn’t Listen To Fan Casting For This Reason
Sunrise on the Reaping director Francis Lawrence and producer Nina Jacobson reveal how they cast the new prequel.

When the cast of the new Hunger Games prequel Sunrise on the Reaping was announced one-by-one on social media, fans saw their dream casting come to life, from Mckenna Grace as District 12’s sassiest tribute, Maysilee Donner, to Elle Fanning stepping into Elizabeth Banks’ pastel wigs as Effie Trinket. Each reveal felt like Christmas came early, but despite how it looked, fans didn’t cast the movie.

In an exclusive interview with Bustle, Sunrise on the Reaping director Francis Lawrence and producer Nina Jacobson opened up about fan casting, admitting they love Suzanne Collins’ iconic book series as much as the fandom — but they didn’t intentionally listen to them.

“We don't go to fan casting feeds and make our lists based on that,” Lawrence said. “When Elle talks about the fans wanting her, she's 100% right, but she was at the top of our list of people to go to. She and I had worked together before, and she was who I wanted to play Effie. It just also is the fan choice.”

As Jacobson explained, she and Lawrence found out that Collins was writing Sunrise on the Reaping “way earlier” than any of her prior books, giving them extra time to adapt the novel into the film. “There was a long, long period where we could imagine our cast before people even knew the book was happening,” she says.

“We knew we wanted Jesse [Plemons] before the book was announced. We knew we wanted Elle before the book was announced,” Lawrence adds. “There are many, many, many people that we knew that we wanted to go for before anybody even knew there was a book.”

However, when the two realized their own hopes aligned with the fans, they knew they were on the right track. “It’s very easy for us to pay attention because we are the fans,” Jacobson says. “There’s very little distance ever between who they’re hoping for and who we envision because we’re kind of a hive mind in that regard.”

She went on to praise fans for trusting the creative team’s instincts and giving them the freedom other franchises usually don’t get. “I do think that we have the smartest, most thoughtful and expansive fans,” she says. “They’re not that kind of rigid haters whose things have to be exactly a certain way, or it’s not the way it’s supposed to be. There are a lot of franchises where the fans are like an albatross in a way. You need them, but you’re always worrying about them.”

items.title: Your November Horoscope Is Here — & Now Get Radically Honest About What You Want

items.author: Dossé-Via Trenou
paragraphs: Cosmic beings, November begins at a slower pace than we may be craving, but the second half of the month has some serious comeback energy written all over it. Scorpio Season continues through the first three weeks of November, encouraging us to dig deeper into our desires, confront our shadows, and get radically honest about what we want from life. With Mercury retrograde in Scorpio and Venus retrograde in Libra as the month begins, communication, relationships, money, and creativity are all still under review.

The energy starts shifting on November 9th, when the Scorpio New Moon strikes and invites us to set intentions around personal power, transformation, and emotional honesty. This lunation is especially potent because Scorpio’s traditional ruler, Mars, is in bold, passionate Leo, while its modern ruler, Pluto, is moving forward in innovative Aquarius. Both placements encourage us to take ownership of our futures, even if doing so requires us to confront some uncomfortable truths. Mercury and Venus  retrograde have spent weeks showing us what we needed to see, whether we liked it or not. Now the Scorpio New Moon asks a much more direct question: what are you going to do about it? The 10 days following this lunation are especially powerful for setting intentions that reflect who you are becoming, rather than who you’ve been conditioned to be.

Then on November 13th, both Mercury and Venus end their retrogrades, and the second half of the month can feel like a much-needed breath of fresh air. We’ll still be navigating the post-retrograde shadows for a few weeks, but forward momentum becomes easier to access. On November 22nd, Sagittarius Season begins, bringing fire, laughter, curiosity, and a renewed appetite for adventure after Scorpio Season took us through the emotional depths. The Gemini Full Moon on November 24th adds to that liberating energy, encouraging us to release the mental and emotional heaviness we’ve been carrying and remember that there’s a whole world beyond the situations we’ve been obsessing over.

And just when we’re ready to fly off into the sunset, Mars enters Virgo on November 25th and reminds us that the details still matter, babes. The end of November encourages us to get practical about the lives we’re creating: paying bills, organizing our environments, tending to our health, scheduling appointments, and simplifying routines that have become unnecessarily complicated. November ends with a beautiful reminder that the life we envision becomes more achievable when our everyday choices begin reflecting it.
Read your horoscopes for your Sun and Rising signs for the most in-depth forecast.

Aries, November begins with Scorpio Season pulling you into some of the deepest corners of your emotional world. Your intimacy, shared resources, and transformation zone is activated, and the Scorpio New Moon on November 9th could mark a powerful turning point in how you approach trust, vulnerability, and the things you share with others. With your ruling planet Mars in Leo, there’s a part of you that’s ready to reclaim your power and move forward. Just remember that transformation takes more than one  dramatic declaration. Give yourself room to shed the layers.

November 13th brings a double dose of relief as Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio and Venus ends hers in Libra. Mercury direct can help untangle misunderstandings involving intimacy, finances, or complicated emotional dynamics, while Venus direct in your partnership sector gives your closest relationships a chance to find their footing again. If the past few weeks have felt like an ongoing episode of What Are We Actually  Doing Here?, you may finally start getting some answers. Some Aries will feel ready to recommit, while others may realize they’ve been doing too much emotional heavy lifting. Either way, you’ll have a clearer sense of what reciprocity should look like.

Then Sag Season begins on November 22nd, activating your adventure, travel, and expansion sector and bringing back that spontaneous spark you’ve been missing. The Gemini Full Moon on November 24th lights up your communication realm, potentially bringing an important conversation, announcement, or writing project to a culmination. And when Mars enters Virgo on November 25th, your attention shifts toward your health, work, and daily routines. You may suddenly feel motivated to organize your schedule, clean up your habits, and get your life together before the year ends. Start with the little things, Aries. They’ll add up faster than you think.

Taurus, November begins with Scorpio Season shining a spotlight on your closest relationships, and you may be learning more about yourself through the people you love than you expected. With the sun moving through your partnership sector for the first three weeks of the month, questions around commitment, trust, intimacy, and reciprocity become harder to ignore. The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th could open a meaningful new chapter in a romantic or professional partnership, especially if you’ve been craving more emotional honesty. Just make sure you’re being honest with yourself about what you need, rather than agreeing to something simply because it feels familiar.

November 13th is a particularly significant date for you because your ruling planet, Venus, ends its retrograde in Libra, while Mercury simultaneously ends its retrograde in Scorpio. If your relationships have felt like one long game of emotional detective work lately, you may finally get to put the magnifying glass down. Mercury direct in your partnership sector makes it easier to communicate your feelings and understand where someone else is coming from, while Venus direct in your wellness and daily-routine sector helps you recognize which habits have been supporting your peace and which ones have been disrupting it. You may realize that certain relationship dynamics have been affecting your physical and emotional well-being more than you initially thought. Let that awareness guide your next steps.

Then Sag Season begins on November 22nd, shifting your focus toward intimacy, shared finances, and the deeper commitments you’re ready to make. The Gemini Full Moon on November 24th illuminates your money and self-worth sector, potentially bringing a financial milestone, an important purchase, or a realization about how much your time and energy are actually worth. And when Mars enters Virgo on November 25th, your creativity, romance, and pleasure sector gets a welcome boost. After  spending so much of November analyzing your relationships, you may be ready to flirt, create, laugh, and enjoy yourself again. Life is allowed to be delicious, Taurus.

Gemini, November begins with Scorpio Season asking you to take a closer look at how you’ve been treating yourself behind the scenes. Your health, work, and daily routines are under the cosmic microscope, and the Scorpio New Moon on November 9th could inspire you to make some long-overdue lifestyle changes. Scorpio energy wants you to get to the root of these patterns. With Mars in Leo energizing your communication zone, you may feel more motivated to speak up about what you need, set clearer boundaries, and stop treating exhaustion like a personality trait.

On November 13th, your ruling planet Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio, while Venus ends hers in Libra, and you may feel like someone finally turned the lights back on. If work has been chaotic, appointments have been rescheduled, or your usual routines have felt impossible to maintain, Mercury direct can help you regain a sense of order. Meanwhile, Venus direct brings fresh energy to your romance, creativity, and pleasure realm. As Venus moves forward, you’ll have a better understanding of what makes your heart feel genuinely excited and which connections deserve more of your attention.

Then Sag Season begins on November 22nd, illuminating your partnership zone and making relationships a major focus as the year winds down. But the real main-character moment arrives on November 24th with your annual Gemini Full Moon! This could be one of the most emotionally revealing lunations of your year, bringing a personal milestone, breakthrough, or realization about how much you’ve changed over the past six months. When Mars enters Virgo on November 25th, your attention shifts toward home, family, and creating a more supportive living environment.

Cancer, November begins with Scorpio Season bringing some much-needed passion,  playfulness, and creative inspiration into your world. As a fellow Water sign, Scorpio knows how to speak your emotional language, and with the sun illuminating your romance, pleasure, and inner-child realm for the first three weeks of November, you may feel more magnetic, expressive, and willing to follow your heart. The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th could mark a beautiful fresh start in your love life or inspire you to take a creative passion more seriously. With Mars in Leo activating your money and self-worth zone, you may also be realizing that your talents deserve to be valued, including financially. There’s something empowering about recognizing how much you have to offer without waiting for someone else to validate it first.

Then November 13th brings a welcome shift as Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio and Venus ends hers in Libra. If your romantic life has been giving mixed signals, or you’ve been second-guessing a creative decision, Mercury direct can help you understand what you actually want. Venus direct in your home and family realm may also bring relief after weeks of revisiting domestic tensions, family dynamics, or questions about where you truly belong. The second half of November gives you more room to make decisions from a place of emotional clarity rather than reacting to every little thing that comes up.

Sag Season begins on November 22nd, shifting your attention toward work, wellness, and getting your daily life into a rhythm that actually feels good. But before you start filling your calendar with a million responsibilities, the Gemini Full Moon on November 24th illuminates your spirituality and solitude zone, encouraging you to release emotional baggage you’ve been carrying for far too long. When Mars enters Virgo on November 25th, your communication and learning realm becomes energized, making the final weeks of the year ideal for writing, studying, having important conversations, and getting organized mentally. Your intuition has been speaking loudly all month, Cancer. Now it’s time to put some of those insights into words.

Leo, November begins with Scorpio Season drawing your attention toward home, family, and the emotional roots that have shaped who you are today. You may feel more nostalgic than usual, or find yourself questioning whether your current living environment truly reflects the person you’re becoming. The Scorpio New Moon on  November 9th could inspire a fresh start involving your home life, a family relationship, or even your definition of belonging. With Mars still moving through your sign, you’ve got plenty of fire and ambition to make things happen, but Scorpio Season may reveal that some of your biggest breakthroughs are happening behind closed doors.

November 13th brings some welcome clarity as Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio and Venus ends hers in Libra. If family conversations have been going in circles, household plans have been delayed, or you’ve been questioning a decision about where to live, Mercury direct can help you sort through the confusion. Meanwhile, Venus direct in your communication and immediate-environment zone may make it easier to reconnect with siblings, neighbors, or people you’ve had misunderstandings with lately. Give people a chance to show you they’ve grown, Leo, while remembering that you get to decide how much access they have to your life.

Then Sag Season begins on November 22nd, and as a fellow Fire sign, you may feel like someone finally turned the music back up! Your romance, creativity, and pleasure realm comes alive, encouraging you to flirt, celebrate, and make more room for whatever brings you joy. The Gemini Full Moon on November 24th illuminates your friendship and community zone, potentially bringing an exciting collaboration, or a realization about which friendships have evolved over the past six months. Some connections may naturally fade while others become stronger. And when Mars leaves your sign and enters Virgo on November 25th, your focus shifts toward money, self worth, and financial organization. You’ll have spent weeks rediscovering what matters emotionally, and now you’ll be ready to invest your time, energy, and resources  accordingly.

Virgo, November begins with Scorpio Season encouraging you to pay closer attention to the conversations you’re having, both with others and with yourself. Your communication, learning, and immediate environment are activated for the first three weeks of the month, and you may find yourself craving more meaningful exchanges rather than endless small talk. The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th could inspire you to begin a writing project, deepen your studies, or finally express something you’ve been keeping to yourself.

November 13th is especially significant because your ruling planet Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio, while Venus ends hers in Libra. If you’ve been dealing with misunderstandings, delayed responses, technology mishaps, or conversations that seem to go absolutely nowhere, Mercury direct can help you find your words again. Venus direct in your money and self-worth zone may also bring greater clarity around your finances, spending habits, and the value you place on your own skills. The second half of November gives you an opportunity to make more confident decisions about what deserves your time and resources.

Then Sag Season begins on November 22nd, shifting your attention toward home. You may feel inspired to make your living space more comfortable or reconnect with loved ones as the holidays approach. The Gemini Full Moon on November 24th illuminates your career and public-image realm, potentially bringing recognition, a professional milestone, or an important realization about where your ambitions are taking you. Something you’ve been building over the past six months could finally bear fruit. And on  November 25th, Mars enters your sign, Virgo, giving you a serious boost of motivation and personal drive. With Mars preparing for an extended stay in your sign, you’ll have plenty of opportunities to reinvent your routines, strengthen your confidence, and take the lead in shaping your next chapter.

Libra, November begins with Scorpio Season encouraging you to get serious about your money, self-worth, and the kind of security you want to create for yourself. After a birthday season that may have brought plenty of personal revelations, the sun’s journey through Scorpio asks you to examine how your financial choices reflect your evolving priorities. The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th could inspire you to rethink your income streams, negotiate better compensation, or finally confront a spending habit that’s been draining your resources. With Mars in Leo energizing your friendship and community realm, the people around you may play an important role in helping you recognize opportunities you hadn’t considered. Just be mindful of comparing your progress to someone else’s highlight reel.

November 13th is a major turning point for you, Libra, because your ruling planet Venus finally ends its retrograde in your sign, on the same day Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio. Whew! If the past several weeks have felt like an unsolicited personality audit, you may be more than ready to graduate from all that introspection. Venus direct can help you feel more comfortable in your skin again, especially if you’ve been questioning your appearance, relationships, or the direction your life is taking. Meanwhile, Mercury direct brings greater clarity to financial decisions that may have been delayed or complicated.

Then Sag Season begins on November 22nd, lighting up your communication, learning, and immediate-environment zone. Your social butterfly tendencies may return in full force, and you could feel inspired to reconnect with friends, explore your neighborhood, or share ideas you’ve been keeping to yourself. The Gemini Full Moon on November 24th activates your expansion realm, potentially bringing a breakthrough involving a trip, academic pursuit, publishing project, or long-term dream you’ve been nurturing for months. And when Mars enters Virgo on November 25th, your solitude and spirituality zone becomes activated, encouraging you to balance all that outward excitement with some much-needed rest.

Scorpio, happy birthday season! If there’s one sign that deserves to feel like they’re emerging from a chrysalis this November, it’s you. You’ve spent the past several weeks confronting old versions of yourself, questioning your desires, and shedding emotional layers you may have carried for years. And with the sun in your sign for the first three weeks of November, you’re finally getting a chance to celebrate the person you’re becoming.

The Scorpio New Moon on November 9th is especially powerful because it marks your annual cosmic rebirth, with Mars in Leo and Pluto in Aquarius encouraging you to reclaim your confidence and take your destiny into your own hands. Think back to who you were six months ago, or even at the beginning of the year. You’ve survived transformations that once felt impossible to navigate, and now you’re standing at the threshold of a new chapter. Let yourself get excited about it, Scorpio. You’ve earned this  moment.

November 13th brings another reason to celebrate as Mercury finally ends its retrograde in your sign, while Venus ends hers in Libra. Whew, enough character development already! Mercury direct helps you feel more confident expressing your thoughts, making decisions, and moving toward goals that may have been on pause. Meanwhile, Venus direct in your spirituality and solitude zone can bring emotional closure to situations you’ve been privately processing. You may notice that certain memories or relationships no longer have the same hold over you. That freedom is worth celebrating just as much as any external milestone.

Then Sag Season begins on November 22nd, shifting your focus toward money, self-worth, and building tangible security around this new version of yourself. The Gemini Full Moon on November 24th illuminates your intimacy realm, potentially bringing a breakthrough involving trust, financial commitments, or an emotional bond that’s been evolving over the past six months. You may finally feel ready to release something you’ve been holding onto out of loyalty or fear of the unknown. And when Mars enters Virgo on November 25th, your friendship, community, and future-goals zone gets energized, helping you connect with people who genuinely support your evolution. Your next chapter is calling, Scorpio, and you get to decide who has a front-row seat.

Sag, can you feel it? Your birthday season is right around the corner, but first, Scorpio  Season has a few final layers it wants you to shed. For the first three weeks of  November, the sun moves through your spirituality, solitude, and subconscious realm,  encouraging you to embrace a little hibernation before your annual comeback. The  Scorpio New Moon on November 9th is a powerful opportunity for shadow work,  emotional purging, and releasing the fears that have been keeping you attached to an outdated version of yourself. With Mars in Leo activating your adventure zone, part of you is already dreaming about your next big move. There’s something beautiful about clearing out your emotional closet before stepping into a brand-new solar chapter.

November 13th brings a welcome sense of relief as Mercury ends its retrograde in Scorpio and Venus ends hers in Libra. Mercury direct can help you make sense of the vivid dreams, resurfacing memories, and private revelations that have been occupying your mind lately. You may finally understand why a certain chapter needed to end or why you’ve been feeling unusually withdrawn. Meanwhile, Venus direct in your friendship and community realm helps you gain clarity about your social circle,  especially if old friends have resurfaced or certain group dynamics have felt off. As the retrograde fog begins to lift, your natural optimism may start returning, and you’ll feel increasingly ready to rejoin the world.

And then, on November 22nd, Sagittarius Season officially begins! Happy birthday, Sag! After weeks of emotional excavation, the sun enters your sign and brings a surge of confidence, charisma, curiosity, and main-character energy. You may feel like booking a trip, reinventing your look, saying yes to new experiences, or simply reminding everyone why you’re the life of the party. The Gemini Full Moon on November 24th illuminates your partnership realm, bringing an important relationship milestone or revelation about who deserves to accompany you into this next chapter. When Mars enters Virgo on November 25th, your career and public-image zone becomes energized, giving you the drive to turn your birthday-season inspiration into professional progress. The year may be winding down, but for you, a whole new adventure is just beginning.

Capricorn, November begins with Scorpio Season encouraging you to take a closer look at the people you’re surrounding yourself with and the future you’re working so hard to create.
